title: When moving the centre of gravity forward the stick force per g will:
optionA: increase.
optionB: not change.
optionC: decrease.
optionD: change but only at very high speeds.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The most direct appreciation of the maneuvering stability of an airplane is obtained from a plot of stick force versus load factor.

The airplane with positive maneuvering stability should demonstrate a steady increase in stick force with increase in load factor or “g”. The maneuvering stick force gradient - or stick force per “g” - must be positive but should be of the proper magnitude.

The stick force gradient must not be excessively high, or the airplane will be difficult and tiring to maneuver. Also, the stick force gradient must not be too low, or the airplane may be overstressed inadvertently when light control forces exist.

When the airplane has high static stability, the maneuvering stability will be high, and a high stick force gradient will result. A possibility exists that the forward CG limit could be set to prevent an excessively high maneuvering stick force gradient. As the CG moves forward, the stick force gradient increases with increasing maneuvering stability and the higher limit of stick force gradient may be reached.

title: An aircraft is on an approach with flaps in landing position. ATC instructs the pilot to perform a go around, at which point, he/she experiences an left engine failure. How will the aircraft behave when established in a nose up-attitude?
optionA: Bank towards the right, flaps decrease the roll.
optionB: Bank towards the right, flaps increase the roll.
optionC: Bank towards the left, flaps decrease the roll.
optionD: Bank towards the left, flaps increase the roll.
explanationTotal:
If a multi-engine aircraft suffers an engine failure when airborne, there are two immediate aerodynamic effects:
  • The initial effect is the yawing that occurs due to the asymmetry of the thrust line.
  • The second effect is roll. This occurs when the aircraft continues to yaw towards the failed engine resulting in a decrease in lift from the retreating wing and a yaw-induced roll towards the failed engine.
In this case, when experiencing a left engine failure, the aircraft will bank towards the left. This roll will be more marked if the flaps are extended, the right wing will create significantly greater lift.

title:
Refer to figure.
The diagram shows the parameter X against TAS. If horizontal flight is considered axis X represents:
optionA: the parasite drag.
optionB: the total drag.
optionC: the lift force.
optionD: the induced drag.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

The total drag is the resulting factor if you add induced drag and parasite drag together.

Parasite drag is caused if an airfoil is moving through the air. It is the result of form drag and skin friction drag.
Form drag arises from the shape of the object. The more streamlined the object, the less form drag is present.
Shape and size are most important in the amount of form drag resulting.
Form drag increases with increasing velocity, making it very important for high speed aircraft.
Skin friction drag is caused by the friction of the fluid (in case of aircraft this fluid is the atmosphere) against the skin of the object moving through it.
It is directly related to the surface area in contact with the fluid.
Skin friction increases with the square of the velocity.

Induced drag is caused when an object redirects the airflow. A wing produces lift by creating a pressure difference.
This pressure difference is caused by the shape of the airfoil, causing the airflow on top to accelerate, creating a low pressure on top of the wing and high pressure below the wing.
This pressure difference naturally wants to restore towards a uniform pressure, which creates vortices around the wingtip.
These vortices are deflected downwards, this phenomenon is also called downwash.
The induced drag decreases with airspeed and increases with angle of attack and increasing weight.

In the image we can see that the two vectors (induced and parasite drag) create a resulting vector, the total drag.
Where the induced and parasite drag vectors collide, we have the minimum drag speed (VMD); the speed where the total drag is the lowest.
This leads us to understand that during an acceleration from a total stand still, the total drag first decreases up until the minimum drag speed and then starts increasing again.

title: Which of the following statements about boundary layers is correct?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: The turbulent boundary layer will separate more easily than the laminar boundary layer.
optionB: The turbulent boundary layer has more kinetic energy than the laminar boundary layer.
optionC: The turbulent boundary layer is thinner than the laminar boundary layer.
optionD: The turbulent boundary layer gives a lower skin friction than the laminar boundary layer.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

The boundary layer is the layer of fluid (in our case this fluid is the atmosphere) in the immediate surface of a bounding surface (the airfoil) where the effects of viscosity are significant. There are two types of boundary layer; the laminar and the turbulent boundary layer.

In the laminar boundary layer, the flow moves parallel to the surface over which it flows. In the laminar boundary layer, the air flows very smoothly. The velocity increases with distance from the airfoil and there is no movement of air perpendicular to the surface of the airfoil. Laminar flow creates less friction drag than the turbulent flow, but is less stable.

At a distance from the leading edge of the airfoil, the air transitions from a laminar flow to a turbulent flow. This air does not flow smoothly, it contains swirls. There is flow in parallel and perpendicular direction. This air creates more drag than the laminar air flow, has more kinetic energy and breaks down less easily and is therefore more stable.

title: An aircraft climbs to FL210 with a CAS of 150 kt. Once reaching FL210 it accelerates to cruise speed whilst maintaining the same heading. What happens to the coefficient of lift?
optionA: Increases.
optionB: Decreases due to fuel burnt.
optionC: Decreases due to the pilot or autopilot reduce angle of attack.
optionD: Remains the same.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
In flight an aeroplane is subject to four types of four forces. The four forces are weight acting vertically downward, drag opposing the forward movement of the aeroplane acting parallel to the relative airflow, thrust acting in a forward direction and lift the upward force acting vertical to the relative airflow that enables the aeroplane to remain airborne. These forces must be in equilibrium during flight. Lift must balance weight and thrust must balance drag. These forces are depicted in figure 1.

Lift is defined by:

L = 1/2 x ρ x V2 x S x CL


For a given wing area (S), if the altitude (i.e. air density) and mass remain constant then the remaining factors in the formula, the coefficient of lift (CL) and the free air velocity (IAS), are variable but have a fixed relationship. CL and IAS must change in such a manner that the total lift formula remains balanced.

Lift coefficient increases with angle of attack up to a maximum (CLMAX), which corresponds to the “Critical” angle of attack. Continuing to increase the angle of attack beyond this point makes it impossible for the airflow to maintain its previous smooth flow over the contour of the upper surface, and lift will reduce. This is represented in figure 2.

At a constant mass and altitude, if the IAS is increased, the angle of attack must be decreased to maintain level flight otherwise the aeroplane will climb.

title: Which of the following tabs increases the effectiveness of the whole rudder?
optionA: Anti balance tab.
optionB: Balance tab.
optionC: Trim tab.
optionD: Spring tab.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
ANTI BALANCE TABS

Because the hinge moment on some airplanes is too small, often as the result of the CP being too close to the hinge-line of the control surface, it is too easy to deflect the control surface against the aerodynamic load. Consequently, there is little control column load and there is a lack of feel to the controls. This could lead to excessive deflection of the control surface and result in serious overstressing of the airframe.

To counteract these characteristics and assist the pilot to use the control surfaces correctly it is necessary to have anti-balance tabs fitted. These operate in the opposite sense to the balance tab by deflecting the anti-balance tab in the same direction as that of the primary control surface and increase the aerodynamic loading.

  • In small aircraft, it increases the control feel, and helps prevent you from over-controlling your aircraft's pitch.

title: From the buffet onset graph of a given jet transport aeroplane it is determined that at FL 310 at a given mass buffet free flight is possible between M = 0.74 and M = 0.88. In what way would these numbers change if the aeroplane is suddenly pulled up e.g. in a traffic avoidance manoeuvre?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Both Mach numbers increase.
optionB: Both Mach numbers decrease.
optionC: The lower Mach number decreases and the higher Mach number increases.
optionD: The lower Mach number increases and the higher Mach number decreases.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The buffet onset boundary chart has both high and low speed limits. The low speed buffet boundary marks the onset of the pre stall buffet with a 10% margin above stall speed. The high speed buffet boundary marks the onset of high speed buffeting. This speed is Mmo most of the time, sometimes it is slightly below.

These speeds come closer together as altitude increases. At a certain altitude the aircraft can encounter the so called “Coffin corner”. The speeds for high and low speed buffeting are very close together here, and thus it is easy to stall or hit Mmo. The coffin corner is a dangerous situation and is supposed to be avoided, as a slight amount of turbulence could cause the aircraft to stall.

The speeds for high and low speed buffeting are dependent on weight, altitude, load factor and CG position. On the buffet onset boundary chart we will find the variables for altitude, weight and load factor.
The margins between high and low speed buffeting can be decreased by:

  • Higher aircraft weight
  • Higher altitude
  • Higher load factor
  • More forward CG position

title: An aeroplane’s Lift/Drag (L/D) ratio is...
optionA: a measure of its efficiency.
optionB: maximum when drag is maximum.
optionC: obtained by multiplying CL with CD.
optionD: the inverse of the glide ratio.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

To determine the efficiency of an aircraft, consider the lift and drag curves together.

For maximum efficiency, the wings should produce maximum lift with the least possible drag.

The most important point on the lift/drag curve is the angle of attack that gives the best lift/drag ratio, in this case 3 or 4°. This is the most efficient (optimum) angle of attack, at which the airfoil gives its best all round performance (i.e. it produces the most lift for the least amount of drag). At any other angle of attack, the same lift will be obtained at a greater cost in drag.

title: A pallet of freight is added to an aircraft's forward hold mistakenly, instead of the rear hold. What effect will this have on the aircraft's handling characteristics?
optionA: It will make the aircraft more prone to a tailplane stall.
optionB: It will have an effect on the yaw of the aircraft.
optionC: It will make the aircraft more tail heavy, improving its climb gradient.
optionD: It will make the aircraft nose heavy, adversely affecting climb performance.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Note: This is more of a question that you would expect in performance, but it has been seen in PoF recently.

The pallet of freight being placed in the forward hold, instead of where it was supposed to be placed (the aft hold) means that the aircraft's CG is actually further forward than the pilots are aware of. The location of an aircraft's CG is an important factor for many things, both for stability and control as well as for the aircraft's performance.

When the CG of an aircraft is further forward, the aircraft will be more nose heavy, and to counteract this, the tailplane provides a downforce on the tail in order to keep the nose of the aircraft up. This downforce directly opposes what the main wing is doing, producing lift. Therefore, the greater the downforce, the greater the lift that the main wing needs to produce. For every bit of lift the wing produces though, there is some induced drag that occurs, which means that further forward CG locations cause higher drag, and therefore lower climb performance, shorter aircraft range, and generally worse efficiency.

It is possible that the forward CG would have an effect on yaw, due to the slightly longer moment arm of the fin and rudder, but the effect would be incredibly small, particularly when compared to the other effects it causes.

title: Parasite drag is made up of multiple different types of drag, which all...
optionA: act in two-dimensional airflow only.
optionB: do not act in two-dimensional airflow.
optionC: only act when the wings produce lift.
optionD: still act when the wings produce no lift.
explanationTotal:
Parasite drag is made up of all the forms of drag that act on any object that moves through a fluid. It is made up of

  • skin friction drag,
  • form drag,
  • interference drag.

Parasite drag is that which is produced even when lift is not produced, and induced drag is that which is caused when the airplane’s airfoils are producing lift.

Induced drag, on the other hand, is the section of lift that acts parallel to the relative airflow, due to the limited length of the wing, and the effect of three-dimensional aerodynamics.

title: Which of the following would cause a reduction in interference drag?
optionA: Increasing the wingspan and reducing the mean geometric chord length.
optionB: Reducing the number of external surfaces meeting at an angle.
optionC: Ensuring that all external surfaces meet at close to 90 degrees.
optionD: Tapering the fuselage to a point at the tail.
explanationTotal:
Interference drag is part of the profile drag and occurs when two (or more) bodies are connected (interact). Interference drag is caused mainly by the wing and fuselage connection and the most drag is observed when two surfaces meet at perpendicular angles.

Interference drag can be minimized by the appropriate use of fairings and fillets to ease the transition between components. Fairings and fillets use curved surfaces to soften the transition at the junction of two aircraft components.

title:
Regarding deep stall characteristics, identify whether the following statements are correct or incorrect:

I. The combination of a wing with sweepback and a T-tail make an aeroplane prone to deep stall.
II. A stick pusher system can be fitted to an aeroplane that exhibits abnormal stall characteristics.
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: I is correct, II is correct.
optionB: I is correct, II is incorrect.
optionC: I is incorrect, II is correct.
optionD: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
explanationTotal:
"I. The combination of a wing with sweepback and a T-tail make an aeroplane prone to deep stall." CORRECT.

A deep stall is a dangerous phenomenon that occurs when the turbulence created by the main wing encompasses the horizontal stabilizer of the aircraft, preventing the aircraft from recovering from the stall.

  • Aircraft with swept-back wings are prone to deep stall, regardless of horizontal stabilizer position (T-tail or low tail). T-tail will worsen recovery characteristics.
  • Swept-forward wings at very high angle of attack are prone to deep stall as well. However, if a low horizontal tail is fitted, some pitch down moment may be produced with the help of the horizontal stabilizer since it is out of the separated turbulent wake of the wing.

"II. A stick pusher system can be fitted to an aeroplane that exhibits abnormal stall characteristics." CORRECT.

A stick pusher is a system that will push the stick forward, lowering the nose and therefore decreasing the angle of attack to prevent a stall. Stick pushers are typically installed where the 'natural aerodynamic stall characteristics' of the aircraft are unacceptable and do not meet the regulatory requirements.

title: Why are Vortex generators mounted on the upper wing surface?
optionA: To increase the effectiveness of the spoiler due to increase in parasite drag
optionB: To decrease the stall speed by increasing spanwise flow over the wing
optionC: To combat the interference drag of the trailing edge flaps
optionD: To energise the boundary layer
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Flow separation occurs because the boundary layer loses kinetic energy as it flows against the adverse pressure gradient.
Increasing the kinetic energy of the boundary layer will reduce flow separation. Simple devices called vortex generators are used to re-energize the boundary layer.
Vortex generators are small plates, vanes, blades or wedges mounted in spanwise rows along the wing surface, as illustrated in figure 1.
Each vortex generator produces a vortex at its tip which will induce high energy air from the free stream flow to mix with the boundary layer, thus increasing its kinetic energy and with retarding separation.

title: Given an aeroplane in steady, straight and level flight at low speed and considering the effects of CG location and thrust, the highest value of wing lift occurs at:
optionA: forward CG and low thrust.
optionB: aft CG and low thrust.
optionC: forward CG and high thrust.
optionD: aft CG and high thrust.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
On the left side of the figure, we can see the effect of a forward moving c.g on the lift produced by the main wing. When moving forward, the c.g will cause either a reduced positive lift created by the horizontal stabilizer, or an increase in negative lift. This is dependant on whether the c.g is located in front or behind the centre of pressure.

Due to the decrease in positive lift or increase in negative lift of the tail, the main wing will have to compensate and produce more lift. Therefore a forward c.g will cause a higher value of wing lift.

Secondly, on the right side of the figure, we can see the effect of a decrease in thrust on the aircraft at high angle of attack (slow speed flight). At high AoA the thrust will have a strong vertical component, therefore a high thrust will help lift the aircraft up and reduce the lift required. This is opposite when the thrust is reduced at high AoA, then the wings will have to compensate and create more lift to remain in level flight.

title: A trim tab is an adjustable surface which can reduce the moment at the hinge line of the main control surface to zero. It can achieve this because its lift force...
optionA: is set far from the hinge line of the main control surface.
optionB: can be deflected through a larger angle compared to the main control surface.
optionC: is controlled from the cockpit just like the main control surface.
optionD: is set close to the hinge line of the main control surface.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Trim tabs are fitted to enable the pilot to set a required angle of deflection of the primary control surface and maintain that deflection. However, they are not suitable for jet airplanes because of their large range of operating speeds, preference, for this type of airplane, is given to the trimmable horizontal stabilizer. There are two types of trim tab in common use: the variable and the fixed.
The variable trim tabs may be manually or electrically controlled. If manually controlled, then trim wheels located on the center console are used.
For the elevator trim if the tab is deflected up the cockpit indication is nose-down and if the trim tab is deflected down the cockpit indication is nose-up. To remain in trim and maintain level flight following a deceleration the trimmer control is moved to give a nose-up movement that causes the trim tab to move down, which makes the elevator move up. This does not affect the static longitudinal stability.
The moment required to move the primary control surface to the required position (MM) is equal to the force (FM) multiplied by the length of the arm (Am) from the hinge of the elevator to the center of pressure of the elevator main control surface. The same moment can be applied to the elevators by a smaller force (FT) in the opposite direction generated by a trim tab multiplied by the longer arm distance (AT) from the center of pressure of the trim tab to the elevator hinge-line. In other words, (FM × AM) = (FT × AT). The trim tab thereby does the work required to maintain the elevator out of the neutral position and there is no need for any force from the pilot’s controls.

title: For a light aeroplane certified under CS23, the minimum positive G limit that it should be able to sustain is:
explanationTotal:
Limit load factors are specified by the EASA certification specifications for different aeroplane categories (EASA CS-23 for normal, utility, aerobatic, and commuter category aeroplanes and EASA CS-25 documents for large aeroplanes, in EASA questions often referred to transport aircraft). The maximum limit load factors for different classes of aeroplanes are typically:

CATEGORY FROM TO
Large / transport
aircraft (CS 25)		 -1.00 g +2.5 g (+2.0 g with flaps extended)
Normal (CS 23) -1.52 g +3.8 g
Utility (CS 23) -1.76 g +4.4 g
Aerobatic (CS 23) -3.00 g +6.0 g

title: What can be said about a T-tail configuration and a low stabiliser position?
optionA: A T-Tail is more stabilising because it is less affected by downwash from the wing.
optionB: A T-tail is more stabilising because it is more affected by downwash from the wing.
optionC: A T-tail is less stabilising because it is more affected by downwash from the wing.
optionD: A T-tail is less stabilising because it is less affected by downwash from the wing.
explanationTotal:
Wing downwash reduces the effectiveness of the tailplane in providing stability in pitch.

  • T-Tail. Since the horizontal stabilizer in this case is mounted at the top of the fin, it will be above the downwash of the wing. Consequently, it will be more effective
  • Low stabilizer. The relative airflow over the low stabilizer is influenced by changing levels of downwash.

title: The speed V<sub>B </sub>in gust diagram...
optionA: equals 50 ft/s.
optionB: equals 66 ft/s.
optionC: equals 55 ft/s.
optionD: equals 25 ft/s.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
It is a design requirement of CS25 (old JAR25) that an airframe structure must be strong enough to withstand gusts both positive and negative that would cause a change of angle of attack so increasing load factor at three specified design speeds.

  • Speed VB (max gust intensity speed): +/- 66 ft/sec
  • Speed VC (design cruise speed): +/- 50 ft/sec
  • Speed VD (design dive speed): +/- 25 ft/sec.

VB is quite a low airspeed so the aircraft would be flying at high alpha. It is a suggested speed for penetrating turbulent air when that turbulence is particularly severe.VB is the maximum speed at which a gust will not overly stress the aircraft.

title: What is the effect on landing speed when a trimmable horizontal stabiliser jams at high IAS?
optionA: No effect when landing on a high elevation runway.
optionB: In most cases, a higher than normal landing speed is required.
optionC: No effect with a forward CG.
optionD: In most cases, no effect.
explanationTotal: The ability to trim is lost when the stabiliser is jammed. The stabiliser jammed at high IAS, which means that it is stuck in a downward position (to compensate the pitch-up tendency of the aircraft due to high IAS). As the speed is now reduced for landing, the aircraft will have a large nose-down tendency which will be worse if the flaps are lowered. Therefore, the pilot should use less flaps than usual for landing. This, in turn, will result in a higher landing speed.

title: If the stall speed of an aeroplane is 60 kt, at what speed will the aeroplane stall if the load factor is 2?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionB: 66 kt.
optionC: 85 kt.
optionD: 72 kt.
explanationTotal:
The increase in load factor in a turn also increases stall speed. The stall speed in a manoeuvre increases as the square root of the load factor (LF):

  • VS = VS1g √ n
VS = 60 kts x √2
VS = 60 kts x 1.4142
VS = 85 kts

title: If a pilot initiates a level, co-ordinated turn from straight and level flight at the same altitude and does not change thrust, the speed will:
optionA: increase and the aeroplane will eventually stall.
optionB: increase.
optionC: decrease.
optionD: remain constant.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The basic four forces that act on an aircraft are thrust, drag, lift and weight.
If one of these forces changes, the opposite force shall have to change to have the same effect as before the change.

In this question we want to stay in level flight at the same altitude and thrust will not be changed.
We will go from a situation where the plane is going straight forward, to a situation where the plane is banked.

To understand this, we will have to understand the way lift works on the aircraft.
The lift vector goes directly vertical from the aircraft’s fuselage.

This means that if the aircraft flies straight, the lift vector points directly upwards.
If the aircraft banks to the right, the lift vector will move diagonally towards the right as well, creating a smaller upwards vector together with a vector towards the right, which creates the yaw moment resulting in the right turn.

If we look at the lift formula (CL * ½ * ρ * V^2 * S), we see that the lift coëfficiënt and speed are directly related.
In case of the banked aircraft, the upwards vector (vertical lift) decreased.

To remain at the same altitude, we must pitch up (increase in CL).
With a constant thrust position, speed will therefore decrease.

title: An aircraft wing has a CL of 0.38. The pilot deploys a stage of flaps, then decreases speed to maintain the same altitude. Which of the following is correct?
optionA: The new C<sub>L </sub>is greater than 0.38 because flaps always increase the C<sub>L</sub>.
optionB: The new C<sub>L</sub> must be greater than 0.38 to maintain the same altitude.
optionC: The new C<sub>L </sub>is less than 0.38.
optionD: The new C<sub>L </sub>is 0.38 because you're still at the same altitude.
explanationTotal:
Lift = 1/2 x ρ x V2 x CL x S

Where:
  • ρ is the air density
  • V is the TAS (True Airspeed)
  • CL is the Coefficient of lift
  • S is the wing area

Using the lift above, we can see that if an aircraft reduces in speed (V2 reduces), then the lift will decrease, unless one of the other components increases to cover the loss. In this case, the pilot has added a stage of flaps, which will increase the lift coefficient by increasing the camber of the wing.

The point of this question is not really to know that the flaps increase the camber, and therefore increase the available lift coefficient, but to know that the aircraft slowing down will require a higher coefficient of lift to maintain enough lift to overcome weight, therefore allowing it to maintain altitude. The same increase of CL could have been made by increasing the angle of attack, but this might have brought the aircraft close to or past the stalling angle of attack, so flaps might be the best choice.

Some may wonder why answer A, "The new CL is greater than 0.38 because flaps always increase the CL.", is not correct. It is because flaps do not always increase the CL. If we remain at the same AoA and add flaps, the CL will almost always increase, but this is rarely what we do. If we added flaps but remained at the same speed, and at the same altitude, the CL would stay the same, as none of the components in the Lift equation would have changed. We would then be flying at a lower angle of attack, though, and with higher drag.

title: During the Final Approach, the Pilot Flying is struggling to maintain the aircraft’s speed under control. At the correct altitude, the aircraft’s speed keeps increasing above the desired. From the options below, what would be the most likely causes?
optionA: The landing gear is extended too soon.
optionB: Excessive spoiler deflection.
optionC: The Flaps are extended too soon.
optionD: An inadequate flap setting.
explanationTotal:
Flap extension has a definite effect on the airplane’s pitch behavior. The increased camber from flap deflection produces lift primarily on the rear portion of the wing. This produces a nose-down pitching moment. Flaps produce greater lift and, consequently, greater drag, permitting a steep descent angle without airspeed increase.

In this case, if the airspeed continues to increase, a possible reason is incorrect flap setting is used.

title: Which of the following statements about a constant speed propeller is correct?
optionA: The blade angle increases with increasing aeroplane speed.
optionB: The selected RPM is kept constant by the manifold pressure.
optionC: The RPM decreases with increasing aeroplane speed.
optionD: The propeller system keeps the aeroplane speed constant.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The purpose of a variable-pitch propeller is to either manually or automatically maintain the optimum angle of attack to maximize the lift/drag ratio of the propeller as the airplane speed changes. This characteristic is the most significant advantage of the constant-speed (fixed RPM) propeller over the fixed-pitch propeller because it is able to maintain maximum efficiency over a range of airplane speeds.
This facility not only improves the propeller efficiency but also decreases the fuel consumption.
The pitch angle or blade angle of a constant-speed propeller (fixe RPM) increases (or coarsens) with increasing TAS.
Constant-speed propellers enable the pilot to select the RPM for maximum power or maximum efficiency and a propeller governor varies the propeller pitch angle as required to maintain the selected RPM. Propeller efficiency improves with increased TAS; however, it is limited to that blade angle beyond which the propeller will no longer produce any thrust.

title: For a given RPM, propeller efficiency is proportional to the ratio of:
optionA: Engine torque to propeller drag torque.
optionB: Drag to propeller drag torque.
optionC: Thrust to engine torque.
optionD: Lift to drag.
explanationTotal:
The ratio of the useful power of the propeller and the required power of the engine is the so called propeller efficiency.

Efficiency equals POWER OUT ÷ POWER In, where the “power out” equals the product of Thrust x TAS and the “power in” is the engine torque x RPM. For the propeller it translates into THRUST POWER ÷ SHAFT POWER.

title:
Which statement about an aeroplane entering ground effect is correct?

I. The downwash angle decreases.
II. The induced angle of attack decreases.
optionA: I is correct, II is correct.
optionB: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
optionC: I is incorrect, II is correct.
optionD: I is correct, II is incorrect.
explanationTotal:
Refer to the figure.
When taking-off or landing, the proximity to the ground prevents full development of the trailing vortices, making them much weaker than in normal flight. This leads to a decrease in downwash, therefore a higher effect angle of attack which also means a smaller induced angle of attack.

This question is asking what will happen when entering ground effect:

  • Downwash angle: When entering ground effect, the effect of the vortices is decreased therefore our downwash angle will decrease. Therefore statement 1 is correct!
  • Induced angle of attack: When entering ground effect, because of the decrease in downwash, the induced angle of attack will decrease leading to a decrease in induced drag. Therefore statement 2 is correct!

title:
Refer to figure Tromso chart 11-2 from Jeppesen GSPRM 2017.
During the missed approach for Tromso, Norway (ENTC) ILS Rwy 19, the initial turn for an approach category C aeroplane must be performed at a speed not exceeding 160 kt, as otherwise you might...
optionA: exceed the maximum speed for the final missed approach segment for the aircraft approach category.
optionB: NOT be able to complete the missed approach turn within 7.7 DME TR in tailwind conditions and thus fly close to terrain.
optionC: exceed the calculated radius of turn and thus fly outside the protected area of the procedure.
optionD: NOT be able to comply with the missed approach minimum climb gradient requirements.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
ICAO Doc 8168
1.3.8 The instrument approach chart (IAC) will specify the individual categories of aircraft for which the procedure is approved. Normally, procedures will be designed to provide protected airspace and obstacle clearance for aircraft up to and including Category D. However, where airspace requirements are critical, procedures may be restricted to lower speed categories.

1.3.9 Alternatively, the procedure may specify a maximum IAS for a particular segment without reference to aircraft category. In any case, it is essential that pilots comply with the procedures and information depicted on instrument flight charts and the appropriate flight parameters (...) if the aircraft is to remain in the areas developed for obstacle clearance purposes.

RADIUS OF TURN

Radius of turn is dependent on both airspeed and bank angle.

Turn Radius = V2 / g tan Ø

Where V = True Airspeed, g = acceleration of gravity constant of 9.81 m/s2, Ø = angle of bank

The radius of turn at any given bank angle is directly proportional to the square of the airspeed. Which means that doubling the airspeed results in a radius of turn that is four times greater

RATE OF TURN

Rate of turn is the rate of change of heading or angular velocity of the turn.

Rate of turn = g tan Ø / V

Increasing the speed results in a decrease of rate of turn. Whereas increasing bank angle, increases the rate of turn.

title: A light aircraft flying straight and level has a stall speed of 100 kts. It banks to an angle of 30°. Calculate the load factor and stall speed in this turn:
optionA: Load factor = 1.15; Stall speed = 107 kts.
optionB: Load factor = 1.07; Stall speed = 115 kts.
optionC: Load factor = 1.07; Stall speed = 107 kts.
optionD: Load factor = 1.15; Stall speed = 115 kts.
explanationTotal:
In a turn, the load factor (n) is equal to:

n = 1/cos(ø), where ø is the bank angle.

n = 1/cos(30º) = 1.15

The Stall Speed in the turn (VSNEW) is calculated by:

VSNEW = √n x VSOLD

VSOLD = 100kt

VSNEW = √1.15 x 100 = 107 kt

title: Consider a low subsonic flow through a stream tube. An increase in the temperature of the airflow will...
optionA: increase the mass flow.
optionB: increase the mass flow when the tube is divergent in the direction of the flow.
optionC: not affect the mass flow.
optionD: decrease the mass flow.
explanationTotal:
Be careful with this question!

Mass flow can be defined by:
Mass flow rate = density x velocity x cross section are

And we know that:

Mass flow rate = constant

Assuming constant velocity, we can say that an increase in temperature will decrease the air density and therefore decrease the mass flow. However this question does not specify that the velocity remains constant.

Now let’s create a situation that follows all the specified parameters of the question. Let’s say we have a tube with steady low subsonic flow. Halfway through this pipe we have a heating element that heats up the air, this will decrease the density of the airflow. So that means we have less mass flow right? Well no because mass flow will naturally always keep itself constant, therefore if the density of the air decreases without any change in cross section area, the velocity will increase. This is because the mass flow on the entry side of the tube will always be the same as the mass flow on the exit side of the tube, even if the air is warmer/colder.

Therefore, assuming no constant velocity is specified, any change in temperature will not affect the flow rate.

title: While flying slightly above the critical Mach number (MCRIT), a control surface is deflected down by a pilot input. What could happen?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: The control surface’s efficiency might be reduced due to shock-induced separation.
optionB: The shock wave will disappear due to the downwards deflection of the control surface.
optionC: The control surface’s efficiency might be increased due to the shock wave itself.
optionD: Low speed buffet could take place due to shock-induced separation.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
When shock waves form on the aircraft's wing, the shock induced separation behind them can lead to vibration and control surface ineffectiveness.

The disturbed airflow over the control surfaces may cause uncommanded erratic movements, although this will not directly affect the air ahead of the shock wave, because the resulting pressure disturbances are prevented from travelling forward. The pressure distribution over the front of the wing is, however, altered, which varies the position of the wing’s center of pressure and its overall pitching moment. This alters the wing’s angle of attack and results in rapid backward and forward movements of the shock waves.

A kind of instability is set up, and the rapid changes in the pressure distribution result in vibration of the whole aircraft. This is primarily due to the distributed airflow behind the shock wave hitting the tail plane. If shock waves form on the control surfaces, it will also affect the stick forces by altering their hinge moments.

title: The (subsonic) static pressure:
optionA: decreases in a flow in a tube when the diameter decreases.
optionB: is the total pressure plus the dynamic pressure.
optionC: increases in a flow in a tube when the diameter decreases.
optionD: is the pressure in a point at which the velocity has become zero.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
To understand the venturi effect, we must first introduce two conditions: The conservation of mass (Continuity Equation) and the Conservation of Energy (Bernoulli’s Theorem).

CONSERVATION OF MASS

The mass of air entering the pipe, in each unit of time, equals the mass of air leaving the pipe, in the same unit of time. - The mass flow through the pipe must remain constant.

The mass air flow 'm' is the product of the density, the area and the velocity:

m = ρ x Ax V

CONTINUITY EQUATION

m1 = m2= m3 = ρ1 x A1 x V1 = ρ2 x A2 x V2 = ρ3 x A3 x V3 = constant

The continuity equation explains the relationship between velocity and cross-sectional area: The speed is inversely proportional to the cross-sectional area.

CONSERVATION OF ENERGY - BERNOULLI'S THEOREM

The total energy of an airstream comes in two forms: potential energy (static pressure) and kinetic energy (dynamic pressure).

The total pressure of the airstream is the sum of the static pressure and the dynamic pressure and must remain constant, according to the law of conservation of energy.

Dynamic pressure (q) is expressed by:

q= 1/2 x ρ x V2

Assuming the total pressure to be constant, the static pressure and the dynamic pressure vary inversely: If one increases the other decreases and vice-versa.

As an airfoil (wing) moves through the air, varying changes in velocity occur on its surfaces. Air particles move around it in specific trajectories. These trajectories are called streamlines.

Diverging streamlines mean a decrease in airspeed.
Converging streamlines imply an increase in airspeed.

In Conclusion:

With a decrease in section area (from station 1 to station 2), flow speed increases, increasing dynamic pressure (streamlines converge). If dynamic pressure increases, static pressure decreases.

With a increase in section area (from station 2 to station 3), flow speed decreases, decreasing dynamic pressure (streamlines diverge). If dynamic pressure decreases, static pressure increases.

title: A twin engine aircraft is in the cruise when both of its engines fail simultaneously. The pilot deploys full flaps almost immediately. Was this the correct decision?
optionA: Yes, because the flaps increase lift, and therefore increase the glide range.
optionB: Yes, because the flaps will allow the aircraft to glide for a longer duration.
optionC: No, because the L/D ratio decreases and ROD increases.
optionD: No, because the flaps will interfere with any attempt to restart the engines.
explanationTotal:
Flaps are very useful on aircraft for decreasing the stall speed, allowing aircraft to safely land and take-off at much lower speeds than they would with a clean wing. This has numerous benefits, including the shortening of runways.

Flaps have very limited uses in flight, though, and there is a good reason why pilots are so hasty to get rid of them after take-off. Flaps increase the drag of a wing, reducing climb rates and increasing fuel burn.

The use of flaps in a glide descent increases the drag for no real increase in lift (flaps can increase lift, but the aircraft has not got any heavier, so does not need it), and therefore drastically reduce the L/D ratio (Lift to Drag ratio). The L/D ratio is what decides the glide angle, and flaps cause a steeper glide angle, leading to a greater rate of descent.

The pilot therefore made a very poor decision, and has drastically decreased their available glide distance and glide endurance. Usually, if gliding to a forced landing, the pilot will remain in a clean configuration as long as possible, until landing is assured, then can extend flaps as required to slow down sufficiently and make a slower landing.

title: Compared to a more forward CG, moving the CG aft will result in the following consequences on fuselage and directional stability:
optionA: Fuselage instability increases and directional stability decreases.
optionB: Fuselage stability increases and directional stability decreases.
optionC: Fuselage instability increases and directional stability increases.
optionD: Fuselage stability increases and directional stability increases.
explanationTotal:
Static directional stability is a measure of the aircraft's resistance to slipping. The main contributor to the static directional stability is the fin. Both the size and atm of the fin determine the directional stability of the aircraft. The further the vertical fin is behind the centre of gravity, the more static directional stability the aircraft will have.

If the centre of gravity moves aft, the destabilizing moment of the fuselage gets bigger, whereas the stabilizing moment of the vertical stabilizer reduces. Consequently, if CG moves aft, directional stability reduces.

title: An aeroplane flying at 100 kt in straight and level flight is subjected to a disturbance that suddenly increases the speed by 20 kt. Assuming the angle of attack remains constant, the load factor will initially...
optionA: increase to 1.10.
optionB: increase to 1.44.
optionC: increase to 1.20.
optionD: remain unchanged, since the Angle Of Attack does not change.
explanationTotal:
Load Factor is the ratio of the weight of an aircraft to the load imposed by lift: Load Factor = Lift / Weight
Lift is propotional to V2: L= CL × ½ rho × V2 × S

Therefore, n is proportional to V2 . An increase in "n" means lift has increased by a factor "n".

  • In this case, speed has increased by a factor of: 120/100 = 1.20

Consequently, lift has changed by a factor of: 1.202 = 1.44 ⇒ Load factor is now 1.44.

title: What is the definition and purpose of V<sub>C</sub>?
optionA: The "Design Cruise Speed", used to show compliance with gust intensity loading.
optionB: The "Design Dive Speed",  the highest speed planned to be achieved in testing.
optionC: The "Design Speed for Maximum Gust Intensity", used to show compliance with gust intensity loading.
optionD: Maximum landing gear extended speed, to prevent damage to aircraft with retractable undercarriage.
explanationTotal:
Design Cruising Speed VC

VC - is the design cruising speed. The minimum value of VC must exceed VB by a sufficient margin to allow for inadvertent speed increases that may be caused by severe turbulence.
This is a speed selected by the designer and used to assess the strength requirements in the cruise. Its value is determined by the requirements CS-25.335 and CS-23.335.

title:
An aerobatic aircraft has a VS0 (landing config) of 110 kt and a VS1 (clean) of 123 kt.
What is the VA for this aircraft?
optionA: 220 kt
optionB: 258 kt
optionC: 270 kt
optionD: 301 kt
explanationTotal:
Maneuvering Speed (VA) is the speed at which an airplane will stall before exceeding its maximum load limit. To calculate the VA we multiply the stall speed (VS1) by the square root of the load factor (n).
  • VA = VS1 x √n

CS 23.337 Limit manoeuvring load factors ED Decision 2003/14/RM

(a) The positive limit manoeuvring load factor n may not be less than –

  1. 2 ∙ 1 + 24000 𝑊+10000 for normal and commuter category aeroplanes (where W = design maximum take-off weight lb), except that n need not be more than 3•8;
  2. 4•4 for utility category aeroplanes; or
  3. 6•0 for aerobatic category aeroplanes.
VA = VS1 x √n
VA = 123 x √6
VA = 301 kt

title: The frontal area of a body, placed in a certain airstream is increased by a factor 3. If the shape does not alter, the form drag will increase by a factor of:
explanationTotal:
The drag equation states that drag (D) is equal to the drag coefficient (Cd) times the density (p) times half of the velocity (V) squared times the reference area (S).

  • Drag (D) = Cd 1/2 p V2 S
From the above equation, we can conclude that drag is proportional to the frontal area (S). Therefore, if frontal area increases by a factor of 3, drag will also increase by a factor of 3.

title: An inexperienced pilot inadvertently flies a light aircraft into a cloud, and due to lack of visual references allows the aircraft to enter a spiral dive. As the aircraft flies out of the cloud the pilot pulls hard on the control column to recover. The aircraft can still stall in this attitude due to the…
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: wing exceeding the critical angle of attack.
optionB: aircraft IAS being below the published stall speed.
optionC: aircraft being above manoeuvre speed.
optionD: wing exceeding best L/D angle of attack.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
When the lift developed by an aeroplane wing is no longer sufficient to sustain the mass of the aeroplane in flight, in the configuration being considered, the wing is stalled.

A stall is caused by airflow separation. Separation can occur when either the boundary layer has insufficient kinetic energy or the adverse pressure gradient becomes too great.

STALLING ANGLE OF ATTACK
At a constant mass and air density, the coefficient of lift (CL), and consequently the total amount of lift, is dependent on the angle of attack.

Graphically, lift increases almost linearly from an angle of attack of 0º to 4º, and then at an increasing rate to 15º. Lift cannot be obtained without incurring the penalty of drag.

At a specific angle of attack, depending on circumstances, the lift generated is insufficient to sustain the aircraft in level flight. The angle of attack at which this occurs is the stalling angle or critical angle and is the point at which CLMAX is attained. An aeroplane will not stall unless the critical angle is exceeded.

title: Mach buffet occurs:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: when the Mach number has increased to M<sub>CRIT</sub>.
optionB: when the stall angle of attack is exceeded.
optionC: following boundary layer separation due to shock wave formation.
optionD: directly after exceeding M<sub>CRIT</sub>.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
MACH BUFFET occurs as a result of supersonic airflow on the wing. Stall buffet occurs at angles of attack that produce airflow disturbances (burbling) over the upper surface of the wing which decreases lift. As density altitude increases, the AOA that is required to produce an airflow disturbance over the top of the wing is reduced until the density altitude is reached where Mach buffet and stall buffet converge (coffin corner).

Mach buffet => caused by shock stall (when the boundary layer separates behind the shock wave). Shock wave appears when exceeding MCRIT (the value of Mach Free Stream when at a given point on the aircraft, an airflow speed of Mach 1 is reached).

When Mcrit is exceeded => first shock waves form and they grow more powerful before they can produce enough separation for mach buffet to occur.

title: The Mach trim system will prevent:
optionA: tuck under.
optionB: buffeting.
optionC: Dutch roll.
optionD: shock stall.
explanationTotal:
As speed increases beyond the Critical Mach number (MCRIT), shock wave formation at the root of a swept-back wing will:

- reduce lift forward of the CG (CP moves rearward), and
- reduce downwash at the tail plane.

Together, these factors will generate a nose-down pitching moment.
At high Mach numbers, an aircraft will become unstable with respect to speed; instead of an increasing push force being required as speed increases, a pull force becomes necessary to prevent the aircraft accelerating further.
A small increase in Mach number will give a nose-down pitch which will further increase the Mach number. This in turn leads to a further increase in the nose-down pitching moment. This unfavorable high-speed characteristic, known as “Mach Tuck”, “High Speed Tuck” or “Tuck Under” would restrict the maximum operating speed of a modern high-speed jet transport aircraft.
To maintain the required stick force gradient at high Mach numbers, a Mach trim system must be fitted.

title: Which of these statements about stall speed is correct?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Increasing sweepback decreases stall speed.
optionB: Increasing wing anhedral decreases stall speed.
optionC: Increasing sweepback increases stall speed.
optionD: Decreasing wing anhedral decreases stall speed.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
When compared to a straight wing of the same section, a swept wing is less aerodynamically efficient:

  • At a given angle of attack CL is less.
  • CLMAX is less and occurs at a higher angle of attack.
  • The lift curve has a smaller gradient (change in CL per degree change in alpha is less).

The stall speed is defined by:

VS = √((2∗W) / (ρ∗S∗CLMAX))

From which we can conclude that the stall speed is inversely proportional to CLMAX.
Therefore, if sweepback reduces CLMAX, it increases the stall speed.

title:
A Flight Instructor is about to start a training flight with a student pilot on a multi-engine aeroplane, the lesson is on aeroplane control during engine failures. The training syllabus for this lesson includes practising engine failures during the cruise phase of flight.Which of the following possible conditions would be beneficial for this training flight and assist the student pilot with aircraft controllability?

Aircraft MTOW 6000 kg. An aeroplane mass of...
optionA: 2800 kg, for less yawing moment due to asymmetric thrust.
optionB: 5600 kg, for better rudder effectiveness.
optionC: 2800 kg, for better rudder effectiveness.
optionD: 5600 kg, for less yawing moment due to asymmetric thrust.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
When an engine fails on a multi-engine aircraft there will be a decrease in thrust and an increase in drag on the side with the failed engine:

  • airspeed will decay.
  • the nose will drop and.
  • most significantly, there will be an immediate yawing moment towards the failed engine.
The forces and moments acting on an aircraft following failure of the left engine are shown in figure 1. The aircraft has a yawing moment towards the dead engine. The pilot has applied rudder to stop the yaw. The vital action when an engine fails is to stop the yaw.
Any increase in weight ultimately reduces the aircraft’s overall performance, but in a banked condition, it induces greater side slip, making the rudder more effective for a given airspeed.
Thus, the greater the weight, the greater the induced side slip and the greater the rudder effectiveness. This benefit is insignificant compared to the penalties associated with any additional weight.

title:
Refer to figure.
A rotating propeller blade element produces an aerodynamic force F that may be resolved into two components:

a force T perpendicular to the plane of rotation (thrust).
a force R generating a torque absorbed by engine power.

Which diagram is correct during the cruise?
optionA: diagram 2.
optionB: diagram 1.
optionC: diagram 3.
optionD: diagram 4.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Propeller thrust is a component at right angles to the plane of rotation. The thrust force will vary along the length of each blade, reducing at the tip where the pressures equalize and towards the root where the rotational velocity is low. Thrust will cause a bending moment on each blade, tending to bend the tip forward.
Torque is the equal and opposite reaction to the propeller being rotated, which generates a turning moment about the aircraft longitudinal axis. Propeller torque also gives a bending moment to the blades, but in the opposite direction to the plane of rotation.

title: During a pull-up manoeuvre, the load factor...
optionA: Increase because the angle of attack increases.
optionB: Increase because weight acts as "apparent drag".
optionC: Decrease because weight acts as "apparent thrust".
optionD: Increase because a component of the thrust acts against the weight.
explanationTotal:
Note: This question was created from incomplete feedback. Please put any further exam feedback to the comments or email it to info@atplquestions.com, thank you.
Learning Objective 081.03.01.02.06: Explain why the load factor increases in a pull-up and decreases in a push-over manoeuvre.

A pull-up manoeuvre is simple and intuitive, we pull the control column, moving the elevator (trailing edge) upwards to create more downforce on the tail. This pitches the nose up, increasing the angle of attack of the wing, thereby increasing the wing's coefficient of lift, and increasing the lift force. As the lift has increased and the weight has remained the same, the load factor (Lift / Weight) increases.

This is why the pilot and passengers will feel an increased G-force pushing them down into their seats during a pull-up manoeuvre, the G-force felt is the same as the load factor on the wings.

title: When you have your flaps in clean configuration and lower the trailing edge flaps for take-off configuration what happens to the airplane?
optionA: Sink and pitch up
optionB: Sink and pitch down
optionC: Climb and pitch up
optionD: Climb and pitch down
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
An alternative to increasing the angle of attack to increase lift is to lower trailing-edge flaps provided the speed is at or below the maximum speed for lowering flap (VFO). This effectively increases the camber of the wing, the angle of attack and the coefficient of lift. However, the thrust may have to be increased to overcome the increased drag, even though when deployed they decrease the magnitude of the wing-tip vortices.
Not only does the extension of trailing-edge flaps decrease the critical angle of attack it also increases the CLMAX, increases the total lift generated, increases the total drag, unfavorably affects the lift/drag ratio and decreases the stalling speed no matter what the altitude or mass of the airplane.
Unlike slats, trailing-edge flaps increase lift at all angles of attack up to the stall. Thus, if the angle of attack remains constant during flap extension the airplane will begin to climb. All trailing-edge flaps when lowered, increase the acceleration of the airflow over the upper surface of the wing, which reduces the pressure above the wing and increases the upwash over the leading edge. Together these influences generate an increased nose-down pitching moment because of the altered pressure distribution around the flaps and the aft movement of the wing CP.

title: Assuming constant IAS, when an aeroplane enters ground effect:
optionA: the induced angle of attack increases.
optionB: downwash does not change.
optionC: the effective angle of attack decreases.
optionD: induced drag reduces.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
When an airplane flies at a height equal to or less than the length of its wingspan the efficiency of its wings is considerably improved. A low wing airplane, just before touchdown, experiences a 50% reduction of its total drag. This phenomenon is ground effect.
Ground effect occurs because the surface alters the airflow pattern around the wings. Primarily, the surface restricts the formation of the wingtip vortices.
When an aircraft enters ground effect during the landing phase of flight, the sudden increase in lift and reduction in drag cause it to experience a floating tendency. The aircraft also tends to pitch nose-down due to the reduction in download on the tail plane.
The magnitude of the wing tip vortices, and thus downwash, also determine the amount of induced drag produced by the wing. The closer the aircraft is to the surface, the greater the reduction in induced drag at any given angle of attack.

Aircraft entering ground effect:

  • Downwash decreases.
  • The effective angle of attack increases.
  • Increased lift during landing if the angle of attack remains constant.
  • The induced angle of attack decreases.
  • Induced drag decreases.
Aircraft leaving ground effect:
  • The effective angle of attack decreases.
  • Decreased lift during take-off if the angle of attack remains constant.
  • Induced drag increases.
  • Downwash increases.
  • The induced angle of attack increases.

title: An aircraft is flying in steady, straight and level flight with a Coefficient of Lift of 0.47. Calculate the final load factor if a vertical gust increases the angle of attack by 3°. Consider that a change in 1° of Angle of Attack produces a change in CL of 0.1.
optionA: 1.64
optionB: 1.77
optionC: 1.47
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
A gust is a localized sudden and rapid change to the speed of the air in the atmosphere that can be either horizontal or vertical. The horizontal gust is of little importance because it causes a change to an airplane’s dynamic pressure that results in an insignificant change to the load factor. The vertical gusts are far more important because they change the effective angle of attack, total lift, and the load factor.
The gust load is the extra load imparted to the airplane by vertical gusts or turbulence. Its magnitude is unaffected by increased altitude but is increased with increased aspect ratio and/or decreased mass.
The load factor for any given angle of attack can be derived from the basic load factor for the normal cruise angle of attack because it is increased by the same percentage as the increase of angle of attack.

It can be defined by:

load factor(n) = (Lift(L)) / (Weight(W))

In straight and level flight, Lift = Weight, thus n = 1.
In this exercise, the increment in CL from a gust will be of 0.1 for every degree of angle of attack impacted by the gust. We also know that the aircraft encounters a gust which increases its angle of attack by 3°.

In straight and level flight n = 1 or : n = 0.47 / 0.47
A 3° increase in angle of attack, 3 * 0.1 = 0.3
Will give an increment of 0.3 in the CL : 0.47+0.3 = 0.77
A gust which increases the angle of attack by 3° will increase the load factor to : n = 0.77 / 0.47 ≈ 1.64g

title:
Which of these statements are correct or incorrect regarding a sideslip, with the relative airflow coming from the right, on an aeroplane that exhibits both directional and lateral stability?

I. The initial tendency of the nose of the aeroplane is to move to the right.
II. The initial tendency of the left wing is to move down.
optionA: I is incorrect, II is correct.
optionB: I is correct, II is incorrect.
optionC: I is correct, II is correct.
optionD: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
Sideslip is the displacement angle of the airplane’s longitudinal axis in azimuth from the relative airflow. It is positive when the relative airflow is to the right of the longitudinal axis and negative when the relative airflow is left of the longitudinal axis.
An airplane has directional static stability if, when in a sideslip with the airflow coming from the right initially the nose tends to yaw right. Therefore, statement 1 is
correct.

The lateral static stability is a measure of the airplane’s tendency to return to the wings-level attitude after a disturbance has caused the airplane to be disturbed in the rolling plane.

Positive lateral static stability is the tendency of the airplane to roll to the left with a positive sideslip angle, nose to the left. Its ability to recover is dependent on the effect of sideslip. Therefore, statement 2 is correct.

title:
Refer to figure.
What is the angle represented in the attached figure?
optionA: Sideslip angle
optionB: Angle of attack
optionC: Bank angle
optionD: Helix angle
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
SIDESLIP ANGLE

The sideslip angle relates the displacement of the aeroplane centre line from the relative airflow.

Sideslip angle is provided the symbol β (beta) and is positive when the relative wind is displaced to the right of the aeroplane centre line

The sideslip angle, β, is essentially the “directional angle of attack” of the aeroplane and is the primary reference in directional stability as well as lateral stability considerations. Static directional stability of the aeroplane is appreciated by response to sideslip.

title: In straight and level flight at a speed of 1.4 V<sub>S</sub>, the lift coefficient, expressed as a percentage of its maximum C<sub>LMAX</sub>, would be:
explanationTotal:
To solve this question, we either need to know the relationship by heart, or know how to get to it. If remembering works better for you, skip the italic part, if you prefer understanding where the relationship comes from, see the italic part.

Knowing that:

L = CL ½ rho v2 S

If we re-organize to make the coefficient of lift (CL) the subject of the equation:

CL = L ÷ (½ rho v2 S)

Therefore, removing the constant from the equation, we can say that:

CL ∝ 1 ÷ v2

Now that we know the relationship, and knowing that v = 1.4 VS , we can solve the question:

CL = 1 ÷ 1.42

CL = 0.51

With that information we know that our coefficient of lift at 1.4 VS will be 0.51 (51%) of the coefficient at VS.

title: A jet transport aircraft flying in the cruise climbs from FL360 to FL380. The climb to the new level is performed with a constant Mach number. What is the effect of the change in level on the buffet margin?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: There will be NO effect on the buffet margin, and buffet will occur at the same load factor.
optionB: The buffet margin will be larger, and buffet will occur at a lower load factor.
optionC: The buffet margin will be smaller, and buffet will occur at a lower load factor.
optionD: The buffet margin will be larger, and buffet will occur at a higher load factor.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The ‘buffet-onset boundary chart’ (BOB) for the level cruise uses the low-speed and the high-speed buffet speeds as limitations to the manoeuvre envelope.
Any of the following factors reduces the margins between cruising speed and the high-speed and the low-speed buffets:
- increased altitude
- increased mass
- a forward CG position
- an increased bank angle

title: Maximum Operating Speed/Mach Number (VMO/MMO) is _____ the Design Dive Speed/Mach Number (VD/MD) or Flight Demonstrated Design Dive Speed/Mach Number (VDF/MDF).
optionA: sufficiently greater than
optionB: sufficiently less than
optionC: less than or equal to
optionD: greater than or equal to
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.

The question is very simple but includes some sections outside of the syllabus, which we can mostly ignore, as they don't affect the answer.

All aircraft have limitations to their speed and the loads that they can sustain at those speeds. In particular, we have to know about the load/speed diagram for CS-25 (large) aeroplanes. There is a diagram for the maximum load factors (positive and negative) that an aircraft can sustain, whether that limit was to do with a stall limit, or a structural load factor limit. There is also a limiting gust envelope diagram for the maximum gusts an aircraft must be able to handle at various speeds, see annex above.

This creates some set design speeds for the aircraft, such as VA, VB, VC and VD.

  • VA - Manoeuvring Speed, the speed where the aircraft will stall at exactly the limiting load factor (2.5 G for CS-25 aircraft).
  • VB - Design Speed for Maximum Gust Intensity, the speed where an aircraft must be able to manage a gust of up to 66 fps.
  • VC - Design Cruise Speed, the maximum speed an aircraft is able to cruise at, giving sufficient safety margin to VD, and means the aircraft will not exceed VD if a particular disturbance occurs when cruising at VC. It is also the point where gusts of up to 50 fps should be managed by the airframe. VC should not be more than 0.8 x VD.
  • VD - Design Dive Speed, the maximum speed that the aircraft can handle in a dive, often limited by vibrations, buffet or flutter. This is the absolute speed limit of the airframe, and the aircraft should be able to manage 25 fps gusts at this speed. There is also a flight demonstrated design dive speed (VDF) which is a demonstrated speed that the aircraft can handle without associated vibrations, buffet or flutter. It is different from VD but for the purposes of this question we do not need to know any more about it.

To keep the aircraft within safe operation, the VMO (maximum operating speed) must be kept below VC. This is still very fast, and should not be exceeded in normal operations. This means that it is always sufficiently less than from VD/MD and VDF/MDF.

CS 25.1505 Maximum operating limit speed
The maximum operating limit speed (VMO/MMO, airspeed or Mach number, whichever is critical at a particular altitude) is a speed that may not be deliberately exceeded in any regime of flight (climb, cruise, or descent), unless a higher speed is authorised for flight test or pilot training operations. VMO/MMO must be established so that it is not greater than the design cruising speed VC and so that it is sufficiently below VD/MD or VDF/MDF, to make it highly improbable that the latter speeds will be inadvertently exceeded in operations. The speed margin between VMO/MMO and VD/MD or VDF/MDF may not be less than that determined under CS 25.335(b) or found necessary during the flight tests conducted under CS 25.253.

title:
Given:

p = pressure
rho = density
T = absolute temperature

The relationship between pressure, density and absolute temperature of a given mass of air can be expressed as follows:
optionA: rho / ( T × p) = constant
optionB: p × rho / T = constant
optionC: p × T / rho = constant
optionD: p / (rho × T) = constant
explanationTotal:
An ideal gas is a gas in which the particles do not attract or repel one another and take up no space (have no volume). According to the Ideal Gas law:
P/rho = R x T

Where:

  • R is constant = 287.2 [J/kgK] (for air)
  • rho is density [kg/m3]
  • P is pressure [N/m2 = Pa]
  • T is temperature [T]
The above equation may also be written as follows:
P / rho T = R

title: Increasing air density will have the following effect on the drag of a body in an airstream (angle of attack and TAS are constant):
optionA: the drag decreases.
optionB: the drag is only affected by the ground speed.
optionC: this has no effect.
optionD: the drag increases.
explanationTotal:
The drag formula is as follows:

D = Cd * ½ * ρ * v² * A
D = Drag
Cd = Drag coefficient
ρ = Density
v = Velocity
A = Cross sectional area

Therefore, if density increases, drag will increase.

title: In a descending turn, the inner (down pointing) wing is travelling (1) _____ than the outer (up pointing) wing, so if the airspeed drops too low, a stall towards the (2) _____ is most likely.
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: (1) faster; (2) outside
optionB: (1) slower; (2) outside
optionC: (1) faster; (2) inside
optionD: (1) slower; (2) inside
explanationTotal:
In any turn, it is better to be coordinated, which means the airflow is hitting the aircraft exactly upon the nose, and the aircraft is not skidding or slipping into the turn. Whilst this will even out some of the common issues with different angles of attack, the inside wing of the turn will still be going slightly slower than the outside wing, and will have a higher angle of attack, especially when descending, so will be more prone to entering the stall if the airspeed drops too low.

This is a common problem on the turn from base to final in the circuit, and a killer of many pilots who didn't watch their airspeed. The slower inside wing will be quite likely to stall first. This is particularly bad as the aircraft is already banked in this direction, so will be quick to lose even more control and possibly even go inverted.

As a side note; slipping in the turn will make it more likely to stall the outside wing, which is slightly better. Skidding turns are especially bad, as they amplify the problems mentioned above, and make it very probable that the inner wing will stall first, which will quickly become a spin.

title: What are the hazards of excessive use of rudder to tighten a turn in a swept wing aircraft?
optionA: Excessive angles of bank can quickly develop.
optionB: The effect of the rudder is reversed, and the angle of bank will decrease.
optionC: The aircraft will tend to pitch up.
optionD: The hazards only exist at high levels.
explanationTotal:
If the rudder is moved to yaw the aeroplane about its normal axis the outside wing of the aeroplane travels slightly faster than the inner wing and therefore develops more lift. As a consequence, the outer wing will rise and the inner wing will fall.

WING DIHEDRAL AND RUDDER INPUT IN A TURN

Wing dihedral is very powerful in producing lateral stability. Dihedral effect is used to discribe the lateral stability contribution of other airplane components, such as rudder and sweptback wings.

Rudder input produces sideslip and contributes to the dihedral effect. The effect is proportional to the angle of sideslip - roll increases with sideslip angle and, therefore, roll increases with increasing rudder input.

The rudders on transport airplanes are sized to counter the yawing moment associated with an engine failure at very low takeoff speeds and to conduct crosswind takeoffs and landings, using up to maximum pedal input.

Any excessive rudder input can produce a large sideslip angle, which will generate a rolling moment that requires significant lateral control input to stop the airplane from rolling.

The rudder should not normally be used to induce roll through sideslip because it has the potential to induce rapid roll rates with significant time delays from the initial input. This overreaction can induce abrupt yawing moments and violent out-of-phase roll rates, which can lead to successive cyclic rudder deflections, known as rudder reversals as the pilot tries to control the resulting motions.

Large aggressive control reversals induce loads that can exceed structural design limits.

Except in crosswind takeoff and landing, keeping the sideslip as close to zero as possible will ensure that the maximum amount of lateral control is available for maneuvering.

Rudder should only be used in combination with ailerons/spoilers to eliminate sideslip, not create it.

title: Assuming constant speed induced drag is:
optionA: directly proportional to the airspeed.
optionB: proportional to the lift coefficient.
optionC: proportional to the square of the lift coefficient.
optionD: inversely proportional to the square of the lift coefficient.
explanationTotal:
The induced drag coefficient formula is as follows:

CDI = (CL2) / (pi * AR * e)
CDI = Induced drag coefficient
CL = Lift coefficient
Pi = 3.14
AR = aspect ratio
e = Efficiency factor

From this formula we can derive that induced drag is proportional to the square of the lift coefficient

title: Considering the airflow around a positively cambered aerofoil that is producing lift, the point of minimum static pressure is found...
optionA: at the point where the chord line originates from the leading edge.
optionB: slightly below the point at which the chord line originates from the leading edge.
optionC: at the point of maximum camber on the upper surface.
optionD: at the highest speed.
explanationTotal:
When considering the pressure, we know that the total pressure always remains constant in subsonic airflow. Next, knowing that the total pressure is equal to the dynamic pressure plus the static pressure, we know that if one increases, the other must decrease to maintain a constant total pressure.

Now what is the dynamic pressure and what is static pressure:

  • Dynamic pressure is equal to: q = ½ rho V2. Therefore we can say that the dynamic pressure is proportional to the velocity of the airflow.
  • Static pressure is the pressure that any object feels even when not moving. This pressure is caused by the force of gravity forcing particles closer together and pushing against each other and any objects around them.

Knowing that dynamic pressure is basically the velocity of the airflow, we can say that if the velocity increase, hence increasing the dynamic pressure, there has to be a reduction in static pressure.
This is known as Bernoulli’s principle!

Going back to the question, we can say that the point of minimum static pressure is the point of maximum dynamic pressure (airflow velocity). Therefore the point of minimum static pressure will be somewhere on the top of a positively cambered aerofoil.

title: Assuming ISA conditions and an aircraft which is travelling at the same IAS, what happens to the drag of the aircraft at 6 000 ft, compared to the drag at sea level?
optionA: It will increase by 10%.
optionB: It will increase by 21%.
optionC: It will decrease by 21%.
optionD: It will not change.
explanationTotal:
Indicated Airspeed (IAS) is obtained from Dynamic Pressure measurements and
  • Dynamic Pressure = 1/2 x p x V2
    So, IAS = 1/2 x p x V2
Drag formula: D = 1/2 x p x V2 x CD x S
Therefore, we can say that:
  • At MSL DMSL = 1/2 x pMSL x V2MSL x CD MSL x S
  • At 6000 D6000 = 1/2 x p6000 x V26000 x CD 6000 x S
Now, question states that IAS remains the same. Which means:
1/2 x pMSL x V2MSL = 1/2 x p6000 x V26000

From this we get:

(1/2 x pMSL x V2MSL x CD MSL x S) / (1/2 x p6000 x V26000 x CD 6000 x S) = 1
(CD MSL) / (CD 6000) = 1
Which equals:
CD MSL = CD 6000

title: An aeroplane flying with an airspeed of 250 kt and C<sub>L</sub> is equal to 0.3. The pilot is requested to reduce speed to 200 kt by the ATC. The new C<sub>L</sub> is…
explanationTotal:
The aerodynamic force of lift results from the pressure differential between the top and bottom surfaces of the wing.

This lift force can be defined by the following equation:

L = 1/2 x ρ x V2 x CL x S

The lift formula can be used to consider the relationship between speed and angle of attack at a constant altitude (air density). As speed is changed, angle of attack must be adjusted to keep lift constant:

- If speed is decreased, angle of attack must be increased, (if speed is halved, angle of attack must be increased to make CL four times its previous value).

To solve this exercise you can use the following formula:

New CL x (New Speed)2 = Old CL x (Old Speed)2

New CL x 2002 = 0.3 x 2502
New CL = (0.3 x 2502) / 2002

New CL = 0.47

title: Wing flutter may be prevented by:
optionA: Locating mass in front of the torsion axis of the wing.
optionB: Increasing the aspect ratio of the wing.
optionC: Mounting the engines on the fuselage.
optionD: Installing the fuel tanks in the fuselage.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Flutter is a periodic aeroelastic process. It is a self-induced oscillation, at which different oscillations are coupled via aerodynamic and inertial forces. Energy for the oscillation is provided by the airstream with velocity (v), the "channel" through which the energy is transmitted is lift (changes in lift) and used by the flexible system (having mass and elasticity).

If the CG is in the hinge, wing bending - controls surface flutter will not be started. Therefore, CG of the control is moved towards the hinge by the means of mass and balance by adding an extra weight in front of the torsion axis of the wing.

title: In order to provide an adequate "buffet boundary" at the commencement of the cruise a speed of 1.3 V<sub>S</sub> is used. At a mass of 120000 kg this is a CAS of 180 knots. If the mass of the aeroplane is increased to 135000 kg the value of 1.3 V<sub>S</sub> will be
optionA: increased to 191 knots, drag will decrease and air distance per kg of fuel will increase.
optionB: increased to 191 knots, drag will increase and air distance per kg of fuel will decrease.
optionC: unaffected as V<sub>S</sub> always occurs at the same angle of attack.
optionD: increased to 202 knots but, since the same angle of attack is used, drag and range will remain the same.
explanationTotal:
The formula to calculate the new speed is:

new VS = old VS x √new mass ÷ √old mass
new VS = 180 kts x √135 000 kg ÷ √120 000 kg
new VS = 191 kts

A higher mass implies that for a given airspeed, the angle of attack must be increased, thus increasing drag and decreasing range.

title: The location of the wing centre of pressure (CP) forward or aft of the CG, influences the:
optionA: Pitching moment, but it does NOT affect the magnitude of the stabiliser balancing force.
optionB: Pitching moment and consequently the direction of the stabiliser balancing force.
optionC: Tailplane arm and consequently the magnitude of the stabiliser balancing force.
optionD: Tailplane arm and consequently the direction of the stabiliser balancing force.
explanationTotal:
The centre of pressure is the point on the chord line of an aerofoil (a line through the aerofoil joining the leading edge and the trailing edge), where all the aerodynamic forces are concentrated. The centre of pressure (CP) will move during various phases of flight, but not because of mass shifting, but rather CP moves with changes in angle of attack.

The location of the wing centre of pressure forward or aft of the CG influences the pitching moment. A centre of gravity forward of the centre of pitch has a nosedown pitching moment. A centre of gravity aft of the center of pitch has a nose-up pitching moment.

To compensate for the pitching moments generated by the location of the CP, a balancing force must be created by the tailplane.

title: Consider the resultant force caused by pressure distribution around an aerofoil moving through the air, its originating point is the (1)_____ and its direction forms a(n) (2)_____ angle with the relative air flow.
optionA: (1) Aerodynamic Centre (AC); (2) 90 degrees
