optionB: (1) Aerodynamic Centre (AC); (2) acute (small)
optionC: (1) Centre of Pressure (CP); (2) 90 degree
optionD: (1) Centre of Pressure (CP); (2) acute (small)
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Centre of pressure

The center of pressure is represented as a single point acting on the wing chord line at a right angle to the relative airflow, through which the wing's lifting force is produced.

All the vectors can be represented by a single resultant acting at a particular point, called the centre of pressure, which is a theoretical point on the chord line through which the resultant of all forces (i.e. the total reaction) is said to act. So the sum of all moments there is zero.

title:
Fill in the blanks with the most suitable choice:

If the distance between Centre of Gravity (CG) and Centre of Pressure (CP) becomes (1) _____, a greater balancing force from the stabiliser will be needed, and that force will act (2) _____.

Assuming lift does not change, and CG is forward of CP.
optionA: (1) greater; (2) downward
optionB: (1) shorter; (2) downward
optionC: (1) shorter; (2) upward
optionD: (1) greater; (2) upward
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Centre of Pressure (CP) is considered as the point at which lift acts through, while Centre of Gravity (CG) is the point where weight of aircraft acts through.

Refer to the situation 1 in diagram: The moments have to be balanced for straight and level flight. Since the CG is forward of CP, lift (L) is producing an anticlockwise moment around the CG. To balance this anticlockwise moment from lift, we need a clockwise moment from the force of the stabiliser (F). To procedure a clockwise moment from the stabiliser, a downward force will be needed.
If we take moment at the point of CG, we can establish the formula Lx=F(x+y). With rearrangement we can see that F = Lx / ( x + y)

Refer to situation 2 in diagram: Now if the distance between CG and CP becomes larger than before, the new formula will become Wz + Lx = F'(x+y), if we take moment at the original GC position and F’ is the new force required from the stabiliser. With rearrangement, F’ = (Wz + Lx) / (x + y). If we compare F and F’, we can see that they share the same denominator while F’ has a larger numerator (Wz + Lx > Lx), with all parameters positive real numbers). Therefore, F’ is larger than F, which means as the distance between CG and CP becomes greater, the downward balancing force of the stabiliser becomes greater as well. (In this case)

Another way to visualise the situation is to plug in some convenient numbers. If lift, distance x and y are all 1, F will be 1/(1+1) = 0.5 originally (taking moment at the CG). Now, let’s say the x is increased to 2, with other parameters unchanged. Taking moment at the new CG, F’ will be 2/(2+1) = 0.67, which is larger than 0.5 previously.

Notes for further learning: This question assumes lift does not change when the distance between CG and CP increases. As the force from stabiliser becomes greater, the weight will have to be reduced in order to balance the upward and downward forces in this case.

title: Outboard ailerons are (1)_____ at (2)_____ speeds, to prevent (3)_____.
optionA: (1) unlocked; (2) high; (3) aeroelastic phenomena.
optionB: (1) locked; (2) low; (3) aeroelastic phenomena.
optionC: (1) unlocked; (2) low; (3) aileron reversal.
optionD: (1) locked; (2) high; (3) aileron reversal.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
OUTBOARD AND INBOARD AILERONS
Two sets of ailerons may be fitted, one at the wing tips (outboard ailerons) and one set inboard (inboard ailerons).

At low speeds, both the inboard and the outboard ailerons are controllable but once the aircraft gains speed (usually when the flaps are all the way up) only the inboard ailerons respond to control input. At high speeds, when the forces are greater and could cause greater structural distortion, outboard (low-speed) ailerons are "locked-out".

Due to wing elasticity, the effectiveness of outboard ailerons reduces or even aileron reversal can occur at higher speeds.

title:
An aircraft is flying through the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) at the planned cruising altitude when it experiences severe turbulence, which causes buffeting. Which action(s) should be taken?

1. Accurately maintain altitude,
2. Increase altitude,
3. Set turbulence speed,
4. Descend to a lower level.
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: 1 and 3
optionB: 3 and 4
optionC: 2 and 3
optionD: 2 only
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The ITCZ

The ITCZ in known for a trough that is centred on the thermal equator. High temperatures cause low pressure,

The main feature of the ITCZ is extensive Cu, Cb, and thunderstorms. The cloud tops are sometimes as low as 20,000 ft but more frequently 50,000 ft or more. Turbulence is usually severe, as is icing, which can be from 16,000 ft upwards.

Buffet Onset Chart

In the same way that separated airflow prior to a low speed stall can cause airframe buffet, shock induced separation (shock stall) at high speed can also cause buffeting.

Aerodynamic buffet is a valuable stall warning, but it can damage the aircraft structure. Because of the higher dynamic pressure when an aircraft is operating in the transonic speed region, any shock induced buffet will have a greater potential for severe airframe damage.

The ‘Buffet Onset’ chart is used by flight crews to ensure their aircraft is always operated with a specified minimum buffet margin.

Turbulence Penetration Speed

For flight in turbulence an airspeed must be chosen to give margin against stalling and overstressing the aircraft structure. This speed is VRA/MRA (the rough-air speed) or turbulence penetration speed. VRA/MRA will give adequate protection from over-stressing the aircraft with maximum protection from an inadvertent stall.

In conclusion, clear air turbulence (CAT) can be caused by jetstreams, Cb’s, mountain waves, etc. with the same consequences as the ITCZ or jetstreams.

Thunderstorms should be circumnavigated and preferably upwind. Extensive use of weather radar scanning is useful. A turbulence penetration speed should be selected to minimise the gust loads on the aircraft. When possible, descent to a lower altitude should be considered as it gives more performance and buffet margin to cope with gusts.

title: Which of the following are means to reduce induced drag?
optionA: Increasing the wing thickness, camber, and span.
optionB: Decreasing the taper ratio, increasing the root chord and sweep angle.
optionC: Increasing the aspect ratio and wing twist, adding winglets.
optionD: Decreasing the wingspan, increasing the approach speed and take-off weight.
explanationTotal:
Whenever a wing produces lift, concentrated vortices form at the wing tips. The vortices are strongest at the wing tips and become progressively weaker toward the centerline of the aircraft.

The vortices induce downwash to the airflow behind the wing, causing the lift vector to tilt rearward. The horizontal component of lift opposes the forward flight of the aircraft and is known as induced drag.

The larger the vortex, the greater the induced downwash, and the greater the induced drag.

It is advantageous to reduce induced drag to a minimum, and this is achieved using the following design features to minimize the formation of wing tip vortices:

Tapering the wing in planform toward the tip reduces the amount of air flowing from the lower surface to the upper surface, thereby reducing the size of the wing tip vortex.

Washout means constructing the wing with a small amount of twist from root to tip, so that the inboard wing section is at a higher angle of incidence, and hence a greater angle of attack, compared to the wing tip. This ensures that the inner part of the wing generates most of the lift, thus minimizing the leakage of airflow around the wing tips. This reduces the size of the wing tip vortex and reduces the total amount of induced drag.

Wing tip modifications reduce the leakage of airflow around the wing tip and limit the size of the vortex. Some of the more typical designs include winglets, wing tip fence and wing tip tank.

title:
Refer to figure.
Which of the following graphs illustrate the movement of the total drag curve when the undercarriage is extended?
optionA: Figure 3
optionB: Figure 1
optionC: Figure 4
optionD: Figure 2
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The Total drag is equal to the Parasite and the Induced drag. The lowest point of the total drag curve, which is the intersection point between the parasite and the induced drag, represents the VMD.

Parasite drag is the drag that comes from the airflow over the aircraft, i.e. the resistance to our efforts to push the airframe through the air at high speed, and has three elements: the Form drag, the Friction drag and the Interference drag. The undercarriage extension increases all the three elements, so parasite drag increases too.

Any change that increases parasite drag (dirty configuration such as extended undercarriage) will move the total drag curve up and to the left, crossing the induced drag at lower VMD. But, total drag will still be increased.

title: According to Bernoulli's theorem, which of the following is true?
optionA: The dynamic pressure depends on density only.
optionB: The dynamic pressure is zero when velocity is zero.
optionC: The dynamic pressure is always greater than the static pressure.
optionD: The dynamic pressure decreases as static pressure decreases.
explanationTotal:
Bernoulli's theorem expresses the conservation of energy for a flow of a fluid (without friction, for irrotational flow). The following equation is used as Bernoulli's theorem;

Ps + p/2 V2 (dynamic pressure) = constant
or
Ps + q = constant

Or - in other words - if in a flow velocity is increase, dynamic pressure increases and static pressure reduces.

Since "V" in the dynamic pressure is TAS, the equation may be written as follows:
  • PSTAT + ½rho × TAS2 = constant

title:
Which statement is correct regarding the gyroscopic effect of a clockwise rotating propeller on a single engine aeroplane?

I. Pitch down produces right yaw.
II. Left yaw produces pitch up.
optionA: I is correct, II is incorrect.
optionB: I is correct, II is correct.
optionC: I is incorrect, II is correct.
optionD: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
On take-off, rotation of a single-engine propeller causes an aircraft to swing to one side, particularly those fitted with a tail-dragger undercarriage. The main causes of this are:

  • Slipstream effect
  • Torque reaction
  • Gyroscopic effect
  • Asymmetric blade effect

Gyroscopic Effect

A rotating propeller has the properties of a gyroscope - rigidity in space and precession. The characteristic which produces “gyroscopic effect” is precession. Gyroscopic precession is the reaction that occurs when a force is applied to the rim of a rotating disc. When a force is applied to the rim of a propeller, the reaction occurs 90° ahead in the direction of rotation and in the same direction as the applied force. As the aircraft is pitched up or down or yawed left or right, a force is applied to the rim of the spinning propeller disc.

Note: Gyroscopic effect only occurs when the aircraft pitches and/or yaws.

For a clockwise rotating propeller:

Pitch up - forward force on the bottom, force emerges 90° clockwise, right yaw.
Right yaw - forward force on the left, force emerges 90° clockwise, pitch down.
Pitch down - forward force on the top, force emerges 90° clockwise, left yaw. Therefore, statement 1 is incorrect.
Left yaw - forward force on the right, force emerges 90° clockwise, pitch up. Therefore, statement 2 is correct.

title: What is the percentage of CLMAX at 2VS?
optionA: 26%
optionB: 25%
optionC: 52%
explanationTotal:
At CLMAX, 100% of the available lift is being created in level flight and the speed is 1 VS.

CL decreases in proportion to the square of the increase in speed, so:
New CL = Old CL x 1 / (change in speed)2
New CL = 100% x 1 / (2)2 = 25%

title: An aeroplane without icing protection ventures into atmospheric conditions where icing will occur. What effect will this have on the aeroplane?
optionA: Stall speed will remain unchanged, and the critical angle of attack and controllability will decrease.
optionB: Stall speed will increase, and both the critical angle of attack and controllability will decrease.
optionC: Stall speed, the critical angle of attack and controllability will all increase.
optionD: Stall speed will decrease, and both the critical angle of attack and controllability will increase.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Any deposit of ice, snow or frost on the external surfaces of an aeroplane, except as permitted in the flight manual, may drastically affect its performance due to reduced aerodynamic lift and increased drag resulting from the disturbed airflow.

An ice-contaminated wing will stall at a lower angle of attack (decreased critical AOA) or higher airspeed (increased stall speed) than a clean wing. Minute amounts of ice (equivalent to medium grit sandpaper) covering the leading edges or upper surfaces of wings can increase the stall speed up to 15 kt.

Ice will also increase the weight and, therefore the stall speed also increases, because a higher angle of attack is required to produce an increased lift. Stall happens when the maximum CL is reached, and that will be at a higher speed when the weight is increased.

title: Which of the following causes an increase in downwash behind a wing?
optionA: Increased dynamic pressure.
optionB: Stronger wingtip vortices.
optionC: The aeroplane entering ground effect.
optionD: Decreased lift.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
DOWNWASH

Downwash is the effect of a wing changing the local relative airflow. It is also the term for the air being forced downwards behind a wing. The terms are very closely linked, and often refer to the exact same thing, but there are subtle differences to how we view it in different contexts as part of the syllabus. Evaluating all possible meanings, the only correct answer is "stronger wingtip vortices".

INDUCED DRAG
Whenever a wing produces lift, some air tries to "cheat" the wing and travel around the wingtip, creating wingtip vortices that affect the lift of the rest of the wing. The vortices are strongest at the wing tips and become progressively weaker toward the centre-line of the aircraft. These vortices create upwash in front of the wing and downwash behind the wing, effectively changing the local relative airflow, and therefore changing the effective angle of attack of the wing. This produces inefficiencies and means the wing's lift is produced at an angle, and some of the lift turns into drag, called induced drag. The stronger the vortices, the greater the induced drag.

  • The stronger the wingtip vortices, the greater the downwash behind the wing.

As part of producing a lifting force on the aircraft, a wing must force air to go downwards, to satisfy Newton's 2nd law of motion (equal and opposite reactions). This is referred to as downwash also, and means that the air flowing away from a wing is pointing slightly downwards, but it arrived at the wing perfectly horizontal, for instance. The amount of "downwash" is directly proportional to the lift produced, and therefore:

  • Decreased lift produces less downwash.
  • Increased dynamic pressure means higher airspeed, but has no effect on the magnitude of lift, and therefore downwash, and will actually decrease the angle of the downwash, due to more air flowing over the wing for the same lift force. This is assuming the same lift force, which we see as much more realistic than assuming a constant angle of attack or lift coefficient, etc., for these questions.

Entering ground effect reduces the effect of wingtip vortices, making the wing more efficient, due to the reduced downwash (as the air cannot flow down as much due to the ground in the way).

title:
Which statement, about the effects on drag of fitting external tip tanks to the wings of an aeroplane, is correct?

I. Parasite drag increases.
II. Induced drag increases.
optionA: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
optionB: I is incorrect, II is correct.
optionC: I is correct, II is correct.
optionD: I is correct, II is incorrect.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Effect of fitting tips tanks:
  1. Parasite drag: Adding the tanks to the aircraft will add surface area in contact with the free flowing air. More surface area that will create friction which will increase parasite drag.
  2. Induced drag: the shape of the tip tanks help prevent the flow around the tip of the wing decreasing the vortices, and therefore decrease induced drag.
Effect of removing tip tanks:
  1. Parasite drag: Removing the extra module of the aircraft will decrease the overall surface area of the aircraft, therefore decreasing parasite drag.
  2. Induced drag: tips tanks help restrict the flow from the lower side of the wing to the upper side, therefore removing them will allow more flow and therefore create stronger vortices, hence increasing the induced drag.

title: At a constant airspeed, a reduction in an aerofoil’s angle of attack results in the speed of the flow over the upper surface to...
optionA: decrease and the lifting ability of the aerofoil to decrease.
optionB: increase and the lifting ability of the aerofoil to increase.
optionC: decrease and the lifting ability of the aerofoil to increase.
optionD: increase and the lifting ability of the aerofoil to decrease.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
The angle of attack (α) is the angle between the free stream relative airflow and the chord line of an airfoil section (figure1)
Changes in the angle of attack cause the velocity and pressure of the flow to vary as the air passes over the upper and lower surfaces. This in turn affects the pressure differential that exists and hence the amount of lift developed.
The angle of attack in conjunction with the actual shape of an airfoil section is therefore one of the factors that is instrumental to the production of lift.
Figure 2 represents the generation of lift in function of angle of attack.
The velocity of the airflow increases over the more curved surface, whilst the static pressure decreases. A pressure differential now exists, generating lift. With decreasing angle of attack, the flow speed decreases, decreasing the pressure differential which in turn decreases the overall lift production.

title: An aircraft with dirt on the airframe is subject to what type of drag?
optionA: Form Drag
optionB: Less Induced Drag
optionC: Decrease Parasite Drag
optionD: Friction Drag
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
SURFACE-FRICTION DRAG

Surface-friction drag is that portion of parasite drag caused by a boundary layer of almost static air that adheres to the skin of the aeroplane.

Air directly in contact with the surface of the aeroplane will be dragged along at a slightly lower speed than that of the aeroplane because of the inherent cohesion of the air. The air further away from the surface of the aeroplane will be pulled along but at a lower speed than the surface air. This dragging effect decreases with increasing depth of the layer of air until at a particular depth the movement of the aeroplane does not affect the air at all.

The depth of the layer of air from the aeroplane surface to the depth at which the air is unaffected is the boundary layer.

The value of surface-friction drag varies and is determined by:

- the total surface area of the aeroplane;
- the coefficient of the air viscosity;
- the rate of change of flow speed over the depth of the boundary layer.

FLOW TRANSITION
The nearer the transition point is to the leading edge of an aerofoil the greater is the amount of surface friction.

The location of the transition point from laminar flow to turbulent flow is dependent on four factors:

- surface condition;
- speed of flow;
- size of the object;
- adverse pressure gradient.

SURFACE CONDITION

The depth of the boundary layer, both laminar and turbulent, increase with distance from the leading edge of an aerofoil.

A rough, dirty, wet, or ice-covered surface will increase the depth of this layer causing greater interference with the airflow over the aerofoil. Polishing the aerofoil surface minimises the effect of this type of drag.

title: An aircraft suffers an engine failure on a light twin aircraft after take-off. Which of the following actions are appropriate?
optionA: Bank 7 to 10 degrees, and rudder towards the dead engine.
optionB: Bank 3 to 5 degrees, and rudder towards the live engine.
optionC: Bank 3 to 5 degrees, and rudder towards the dead engine.
optionD: Bank 7 to 10 degrees, and rudder towards the live engine.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
COUNTERACTING ASYMMETRIC THRUST

Rudder to Stop Yaw - Bank Towards Live Engine - This method produces minimum drag and gives the best ability to climb and is the preferred method of putting the aircraft in equilibrium following engine failure.

In the event of an engine failure in a non-centerline thrust twin or multi engine aircraft, the operative engine is going to create a strong yawing moment about the vertical axis of the aircraft in the direction of the dead engine. Uncorrected, this results in a forward slip toward the side of the good engine and, when combined with the fuselage blanking airflow over the wing on the dead engine side, a rolling moment also develops about the longitudinal axis in the direction of the dead engine.

  • The typical action is to apply rudder in the direction of the live engine to counteract this forward slip. However, while the nose will be aligned with the desired flight path doing this, the actual flight path is a side slip towards the dead engine side, which creates excess drag.
    The only available counter to this is to bank the airplane into the direction of the live engine to counteract the rudder force using the horizontal component of lift. The angle of bank must not exceed 5°, to prevent excessive loss of vertical lift component.

title: An aircraft has a V<sub>A</sub> speed of 100 kts, at 5.4 tonnes. Calculate the new V<sub>A</sub> speed at a mass of 4.7 tonnes...
explanationTotal:
Maneuvering Speed (VA) is the speed at which an airplane will stall before exceeding its maximum load limit. To calculate the VA we multiply the stall speed (VS1) by the square root of the load factor (n).

  • VA = VS1 x √n

VA is just a stalling speed. Thus, it varies with mass:

  • New VS = Old VS x √Change in mass factor

New VA = 100 x √ (4 700 / 5 400)

New VA = 100 x 0.93

New VA = approx. 93 kt

title:
Which of these statements about the strength of wing tip vortices are correct or incorrect?

I. Assuming no flow separation, the strength of wing tip vortices is not affected by angle of attack.
II. The strength of wing tip vortices increases as the aspect ratio increases.
optionA: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
optionB: I is correct, II is correct.
optionC: I is incorrect, II is correct.
optionD: I is correct, II is incorrect.
explanationTotal:
Wing tip vortices are a byproduct of lift. They are caused by the pressure differential between the top and bottom of the wing, which causes an updraft of high pressure air around the tip of the wing. This updraft turn into a downdraft behind the wing, creating a vortex. The higher the pressure difference between the top and bottom of the wing, the stronger the vortices.

This question is specifically asking for:

  • Angle of attack: The strength of the vortices (and therefore also induced drag) is proportional to the angle of attack. Therefore; the strength of the vortices increase as the angle of attack increases. And also; the strength of the vortices decrease as the angle of attack decreases. Therefore statement 1 is incorrect!
  • Aspect ratio: The strength of the vortices is inversely proportional with the aspect ratio. Meaning that the strength of the wing tip vortices increase as the aspect ratio decreases. And vice versa: the strength decreases as the aspect ratio increases. Therefore statement 2 is incorrect!

title: A forward CG shift:
optionA: has no influence on longitudinal manoeuvrability.
optionB: decreases static longitudinal stability.
optionC: increases longitudinal manoeuvrability.
optionD: increases static longitudinal stability.
explanationTotal:
The point where an aircraft’s total sum of a pressure field is acting upon the body is called the Center of Pressure (CP).
This is the point where the resultant vector of lift is said to be operating.
As the airfoil or Angle of attack changes (thus changing the lift coefficient), this pressure field will change and so will the center of pressure.

Aircraft longitudinal stability is directly related to Centre of Gravity (CG) position.
An aircraft with a more forward CG is more longitudinally stable than an aircraft with a more aft CG.
Placing the CG beyond the forward limit can cause an unacceptably high value of longitudinal stability, decreasing manoeuvrability by a significant amount.
Place the CG beyond the aft limit and the aircraft is too unstable, having excessive manoeuvrability.

If an aircraft is longitudinally stable, an increase in Angle of Attack (α) results in a negative pitching moment.
The nose will slightly fall down, decreasing the Angle of Attack.
If this aircraft has a decrease of Angle of Attack, the nose will come slightly upwards again, creating a positive pitching moment again by slightly raising the nose.

title:
Refer to figure.
Regarding the Buffet Onset Boundary Chart in the annex, which of these statements are correct or incorrect?

1. Flying at M = 0.8 provides the optimum margin with respect to buffet onset.
2. The maximum altitude that can be achieved with respect to buffet onset, according to Certification Specifications, is higher at M = 0.82 than at M = 0.75.
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: 1 is incorrect, 2 is correct.
optionB: 1 is correct, 2 is incorrect.
optionC: 1 is incorrect, 2 is incorrect.
optionD: 1 is correct, 2 is correct.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
In the same way that separated airflow prior to a low speed stall can cause airframe buffet, shock induced separation (shock stall) at high speed can also cause buffeting.

Aerodynamic buffet is a valuable stall warning, but it can damage the aircraft structure. Because of the higher dynamic pressure when an aircraft is operating in the transonic speed region, any shock induced buffet will have a greater potential for severe airframe damage.
High speed buffet must be completely avoided. The aircraft must therefore be operated in such a manner that a (safety) margin exists before aerodynamic buffet will occur.

If the variables which affect both high speed and low speed stall are considered it will be possible to identify the conditions under which buffeting will occur and a chart can be drawn to show all the factors involved.

This is called a ‘Buffet Onset’ chart which is used by flight crews to ensure their aircraft is always operated with a specified minimum buffet margin.

For any given combination of mass, center of gravity position and airspeed, the maximum operating altitude is that altitude at which a normal positive acceleration increment of 0.3g, without exceeding the buffet onset boundary, is possible.
It is, therefore, common practice to draw the ‘buffet-onset boundary chart’ for a range of cruise masses at 1.3 g. Any maneuver having a load factor exceeding 1.3 g will initiate the buffet onset.

In this exercise:

This chart is specific to an aircraft, and shows the relationship of altitude, load factor, cruise data, weight, Mach number, and IAS. The optimum speed can be found by intersecting the top of the altitude curve. In this case it is M0.80, therefore statement 1 is correct.

  • Start by drawing a vertical line from M0.82 and M0.75 to the FL410 curve (first altitude curve).
  • From here, draw a straight line from left to right that intersects the weight curves.
  • Finally, draw a vertical up from 1.3 g load factor that intersects the lines drawn in step 2.
As we can see, flying at M0.82 gives us the ability to carry a greater weight. We can then conclude that it also gives us a higher buffet onset margin, therefore statement 2 is correct.

title: A microburst encounter on the approach is a hazardous situation. When approaching the microburst the aeroplane will initially:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Tend to go below the glide path.
optionB: Have an increased rate of descent.
optionC: Encounter increasing headwind.
optionD: Encounter increasing tailwind.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Flying through a Microburst

1. Imagine you're approaching a microburst at 80 knots. As you enter the vortex ring, you experience turbulence and a rapid increase in IAS as you pick up a headwind. You start to climb as your performance increases.
2. As you enter the strongest part of the horizontal shaft, your airspeed peaks at 100 knots, an increase of 20 knots. You're still climbing as you enter the downdraft.
3. Inside the downdraft, your headwind starts to switch to a tailwind. You're caught in the downdraft, sinking quickly toward the ground. Your airspeed begins to decrease.
4. As you exit the downdraft, your tailwind increases rapidly. The shear drops your airspeed to 60 knots, which is 20 knots below your original speed. You're at a high angle-of-attack, and still descending.
5. You encounter more turbulence as you enter the final vortex. If you haven't already hit the ground, you may begin to climb again as you exit the vortex.

title: Just above the critical Mach number the first evidence of a shock wave will appear at the:
optionA: leading edge of the wing.
optionB: upper side of the wing.
optionC: lower side of the wing.
optionD: trailing edge of the wing.
explanationTotal: At Critical Mach number (M<sub>CRIT</sub>), somewhere on the profile, local sonic speed is reached. This is the point corresponding to maximum thickness at the upper side of the wing, as the flow is the fastest there. So the flow velocity reaches and slightly exceeds sonic speed, thus behind this point a normal shock wave occurs.

title: Approximately how long does it take to fly a complete circle during a horizontal steady co-ordinated turn with a bank angle of 15° and a TAS of 530 kt?
optionA: 95 s.
optionB: 650 s.
optionC: 125 s.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
In level flight, any turn will be coordinated or uncoordinated. A coordinated turn is one in which the only acceleration is along the normal axis of the airplane, towards the center of the turn, and the angle of bank is precisely correct for the aircraft speed and the radius of turn. If not all these factors are present, the turn will be uncoordinated and there will be a lateral acceleration either towards or away from the center of the turn. The total lift of a balanced turn provides the centripetal force and the force that opposes the mass of the airplane.
If there is acceleration towards the center of the turn the airplane is slipping and if it is away from the center of the turn the airplane is skidding. Either condition will be indicated on the turn and slip indicator. An overbanked airplane will slip into the turn and requires an increase of speed or a reduction in bank angle to correct this condition. An underbanked airplane will skid out of the turn, which requires a decreased speed or an increased bank angle to correct this condition. These are indicated on the turn and slip indicator by the needle one-way and the ball the other.
To maintain altitude and airspeed when executing a turn both the angle of attack and the thrust have to be increased above their level flight values.

In a turn, turn radius and rate of turn are defined as:

Turn radius=TAS 2/g tan Φ
Rate of Turn=g tan Φ/TAS

Therefore, turn radius is directly proportional to TAS squared and inversely proportional to bank angle and Rate of Turn is directly proportional to bank angle and inversely proportional to TAS.

In this exercise, TAS is equal to 530 knots and the bank angle is 15°:

First, convert 530kt to m/s:

530kt * 0.5144 = 272.63m/s

Then, calculate the turn radius

Turn radius = 272.63 2/10 ∗ tan 15
Turn radius ≈ 27739.66m

The circumference is given by:

c = 2 * π * r
c = 2 * π * 27739.66
c = 174293.45m
At 272.63 m/s, it would take approximately 640 seconds to complete the circumference.

title: Following a microburst encounter on approach, during the go around:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: It may be necessary to increase the pitch beyond the point at which a stall warning activates.
optionB: The pilot should delay applying maximum power until the aircraft is established in the climb.
optionC: A pitch angle may be required that is close to the point of the onset of a stall warning.
optionD: Speed control has greater priority than reaching an optimised pitch angle.
explanationTotal:
Wind shear are sudden changes in wind speed and/or wind direction. It may radically change the aerodynamic circumstances of the flight, particularly the critical phases of flight - during the final approach path and landing, take-off and initial climb-out flight paths. The aircraft may experience sudden increases and decreases in airspeed which increase the risk of stall or ground impact.

If the presence of windshear is confirmed, delay take-off or do not continue an approach. If windshear is suspected, be especially alert to any of the danger signals and be prepared for the possibility of an inadvertent encounter.

WINDSHEAR ESCAPE MANEUVER - Manual flight (Boeing 737)

  • Disengage autopilot
  • Push either TO/GA switch
  • Aggressively apply maximum thrust
  • Disengage autothrottle
  • Simultaneously roll wings level and rotate toward an initial pitch attitude of 15º
  • Retract speedbrakes
  • Follow flight director TO/GA guidance (if available)

Note: In all cases, the pitch attitude that results in intermittent stick shaker or initial buffet is the upper pitch attitude limit. Flight at intermittent stick shaker may be needed to obtain a positive terrain separation. Use smooth, steady controls to avoid a pitch attitude overshoot and stall.

title:
Which of these statements about propellers is correct or incorrect?

I. A cruise propeller has a smaller geometric pitch compared with a climb propeller.
II. A coarse pitch propeller is more efficient during take-off and in the climb, but is less efficient in the cruise, when compared with a fine pitch propeller.
optionA: I is incorrect, II is correct.
optionB: I is correct, II is incorrect.
optionC: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
optionD: I is correct, II is correct.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The blade angle of a fixed-pitch propeller is constant, but the helix angle and the angle of attack will vary according to its forward speed. To ensure its efficient operation the blade angle of attack of a fixed-pitch propeller must be close to the optimum and is that which produces the greatest excess of horizontal lift (thrust) over drag.
A large blade angle or coarse pitch is suitable for high-speed flight (cruise). The geometric pitch is the distance the propeller would travel forward in one complete revolution if it were moving through the air at the blade angle. The higher the blade angle the higher the geometric pitch. Therefore, statement 1 is incorrect.
In low forward speed flight, the angle of attack for is large. This produces a large amount of thrust but at the same time it creates a large amount of drag. To maintain a constant RPM, it is essential to overcome the drag and that requires a high propeller torque. The propeller efficiency in these circumstances is low.
By increasing the speed, the helix angle increases. Although the angle of attack of is smaller and less thrust is produced the amount of drag induced is significantly less, this makes the propeller efficiency proportionately greater. It is this speed that attains the greatest propeller efficiency. Therefore, statement 2 is incorrect.

title: What effect will shockwave induced separation have on a T-Tail horizontal stabiliser?
optionA: Increase downwash.
optionB: Decrease downwash.
optionC: Airflow separation will cause it to buffet.
optionD: No noticeable effect.
explanationTotal:
Note: the feedback is lacking for this question, so may not be exactly the same as the exam. Please send further feedback if you see this in the exam, either in the comments or by email to info@atplquestions.com, thank you.

The differences between conventional (low mounted) horizontal stabilisers and T-Tail (high mounted) horizontal stabilisers are many. Other than the increased efficiencies of the T-Tail, one of the primary differences is that it is not in the wake of the main wing during normal flight. They can be in the wake of the main wing at the stall though, causing a potentially unrecoverable deep stall.

At normal flying speeds, the pitch angle of the aircraft to maintain level flight is such that the T-Tail is far above the wake of the main wing, so when in the transonic speed range, the reducing downwash of the main wing will not really affect the tailplane, as it would do a conventional tailplane.

So for this question, we believe that the downwash will not change by a noticeable amount, and there will be little to no buffet on the horizontal stabiliser, due to its distance from the wake of the man wing.

We must remember that the main wing is the first place on the aircraft that forms a shockwave, so the separation will cause the main wing to have a turbulent wake. This is what we believe the examiner is asking about, not when the tailplane itself forms a shockwave.

title: Generally, ailerons are fitted towards the wing-tips. However, some aeroplanes are fitted with outboard and inboard ailerons. At high flight speeds only the inboard ailerons are used, this is done to...
optionA: reduce the rolling moments which might generate excessive bending forces at their wing root if the outboard ailerons were to be used.
optionB: ensure that the wing does NOT twist through aero elastic effects which would modify the local angle of attack and generate roll reversal.
optionC: reduce the effects of adverse yaw which are greater when using outboard ailerons.
optionD: increase flight control redundancy in the aeroplane’s roll control should the outboard aileron system fail.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
AILERONS

The primary effect of ailerons is to provide roll control about the longitudinal axis

A downward movement of the aileron causes an increase in the effective angle of attack and a corresponding increase in lift, whilst an upward movement of the aileron causes a reduction in the effective angle of attack and a decrease in lift.

The difference in lift between the two wings produces the necessary rolling moment.

INBOARD AILERONS

Ailerons are normally situated at the wing tips to give the greatest rolling moment for the force produced. However, this means they are also able to generate the maximum twisting loads on the wing.

For instance, a down-going aileron will twist the wing tip and decrease wing tip incidence. The wing is not a rigid structure and any twist will cause a decrease of aileron effectiveness.

As IAS increases, a down-going aileron will give more wing twist (decreased wing tip incidence). Eventually, an IAS will be reached at which the decrease in tip incidence will give a larger downforce than the upforce produced by the aileron.

This is called high speed “aileron reversal”; the wing will go down, rather than up as the pilot intended. To reduce this effect, the ailerons could be mounted further inboard. Unfortunately, this would reduce aileron effectiveness at low speed.

Alternatively, two sets of ailerons may be fitted: one set at the wing tips for use only at low speeds when the forces involved are low, and one set inboard for use at high speeds when the forces are greater and could cause greater structural distortion. Outboard (low speed) ailerons are “locked-out” as the flaps retract. At low speed both sets of ailerons work, but at high speed only the inboard ailerons respond to control input.

title: A swept-back wing, in comparison to a straight wing, has an increased tendency to...
optionA: mid-wing stall.
optionB: high-speed stall.
optionC: tip stall.
optionD: root stall.
explanationTotal:
The lift from a wing is generated by airflow over it from front to back.
If the span-wise flow increases, the boundary layer on the wing surface travels for longer.
This causes them to be thicker and more susceptible to transition to turbulence or flow separation.

The normal tip vortice on a swept wing joins up with a leading edge separation bubble, creating a larger vortex called the Ram’s horn vortex.
This vortex goes inboard along the wing’s leading edge.
The downward flow from the vortex induces pressure on the boundary layer at the wingtip, whereas on straight wings the exact opposite occurs.

With a swept wing, this creates a slow-moving layer of air at the wing tip.
This slow-moving air will separate into disturbed flow and will then stall the tip.

As the wingtips for a swept wing are positioned aft of the center of pressure (CP), the center of pressure upon a wing tip stall will move forward, creating a nose up moment.
This nose up moment will further increase the Angle of Attack if not corrected in time, increasing the layer of slow-moving air, worsening the situation.

The pitch up phenomenon is a dangerous characteristic of swept wing aircraft that move at high speed.
It could result in a quickly worsening stalling situation, making it very hard to recover.

title:
Complete the following statement:

Consider a wing with geometric positive dihedral in a sideslip. The dihedral (1) _____ contributes to static lateral stability, because the wing (2) _____ the wind is subject to an increase in angle of attack causing an increase in lift.
optionA: (1) positively; (2) away from
optionB: (1) negatively; (2) away from
optionC: (1) positively; (2) into
optionD: (1) negatively; (2) into
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
DIHEDRAL
If not corrected, an unstable aeroplane will side slip down when rolled to one side. This effect is not desirable, so how can we reduce it?

By tilting the wingtips upwards, the aeroplane becomes naturally more stable in the lateral plane. This is called dihedral.

Lift acts perpendicular to the relative airflow. If the aeroplane rolls to the side when disturbed by a gust of wind, the lift vector leans to the side with the aeroplane. This creates a resultant sideways facing force that makes the aeroplane side slip in the same direction. As a result of this side slip, the aeroplane is subjected to a sideways component of the relative airflow. Due to dihedral, the lower wing (into the wind) meets the upcoming airflow at a greater angle of attack than the upper wing. Consequently, the lower wing produces more lift and helps the aeroplane roll back to its original position. This is how dihedral improves lateral stability.

title: It is possible for the stabiliser to stall prematurely due to ice contamination. In this case...
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: the aeroplane will pitch down.
optionB: the aeroplane will pitch up.
optionC: longitudinal control of the aeroplane will NOT be affected.
optionD: lateral control of the aeroplane will be greatly affected.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
STABILIZER STALL DUE TO ICE

The tailplane is an aerofoil, and because it is thinner than the wing, it is likely to experience icing before the wing does. The effect will be the same as for the wing; the stall will occur at a lower angle of attack.

The tailplane is normally operating at a negative angle of attack, producing a down load, so if the tailplane stalls and the down load is lost, the nose of the aircraft will drop and longitudinal control will be lost.

Stalling of an ice contaminated tailplane could be precipitated by extension of the wing flaps. Lowering the flaps increases the downwash, and this increases the negative angle of attack of the tailplane. If the tailplane has ice contamination, this could be sufficient to cause it to stall. Recovery procedure in this situation would be to retract the flaps again, thus reducing the downwash.

Take care when increasing an aircraft's forward airspeed to compensate for ice on the wings, since every knot of airspeed added to prevent wing stall brings the aircraft a knot closer to tailplane stall. Consequently, it is vital that the tailplane, like the wing, is free from contamination. This type of stall does not usually occur, but if it does, recovery is normally impossible.

title: The likelihood of Dutch roll will increase...
optionA: With a strong directional stability.
optionB: With Anhedral wings.
optionC: Flying at high Mach.
optionD: Flying at low altitudes.
explanationTotal:
DUTCH ROLL

Basically speaking, Dutch roll is a series of out-of-phase turns, when the aircraft rolls in one direction and yaws in the other. When the yaw is introduced, the strong “dihedral effect” will roll the aircraft due to the lift increase on the wing into wind. The increased induced drag on the rising wing will yaw the aircraft in the opposite direction, reversing the coupled oscillations.

  • This occurs when a strong lateral stability is coupled with weak directional stability.
With increasing altitude (decreasing density) or increasing Mach number, the possibility of a Dutch roll increases.

title: The critical Mach number of an aeroplane is the Mach number:
optionA: at which there is subsonic flow over all parts of the aeroplane.
optionB: at which the aeroplane has zero buffet margin.
optionC: at which there is supersonic flow over a part of the aeroplane.
optionD: above which, locally, supersonic flow exists somewhere over the aeroplane.
explanationTotal:
Critical Mach number (MCRIT) is the free stream Mach number at which local speed of the airflow somewhere around the aircraft reaches local sonic speed (M = 1).

For all aircraft in flight, the speed of the airflow around the aircraft is not exactly the same as the airspeed of the aircraft due to the airflow speeding up and slowing down to travel around the aircraft structure. At the Critical Mach number, local airflow near some areas of the airframe reaches the speed of sound, even though the aircraft itself has an airspeed lower than Mach 1.0.

  • We can also say that MCRIT is the highest flight speed where there is no supersonic flow (M>1) over any portion of the airfoil.

title: Propeller blade twist is the:
optionA: varying of the blade angle from the root to the tip of a propeller blade.
optionB: varying of the helix angle from the root to the tip of a propeller blade.
optionC: angle between the blade angle and the direction of the flight of the aeroplane.
optionD: angle between the relative airflow and the propeller blade’s angle of attack.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Blade Twist

Sections near the tip of the propeller are at a greater distance from the propeller shaft and travel through a greater distance. Tip speed is therefore greater. The blade angle must be decreased towards the tip to give a constant geometric pitch along the length of the blade.

title: What is the impact of a change in Angle of Attack (AoA) on a normal shock wave at a constant Mach number?
optionA: The intensity of the shock wave decreases as AoA increases.
optionB: The location of the shock wave moves forwards on the wing.
optionC: The location of the shock wave moves rearwards on the wing.
optionD: The intensity of the shock wave increases as AoA increases.
explanationTotal:
The critical Mach number (MCRIT) is the lower limit of a speed band, known as the transonic range, in which the local Mach number may be either subsonic or supersonic. Its value varies with the angle of attack and is the free-stream Mach number at which sonic speed is reached over the upper surface of a wing. In other words, it is the speed at which the local Mach number is equal to the free-airstream Mach number. It is also the highest speed possible without supersonic flow over the wing.

The critical Mach number is inversely proportional to the angle of attack, i.e. MCRIT decreases with increasing angle of attack and vice versa. This is because, as the angle of attack increases the local peak velocity of the airflow over the wing also increases. It therefore reaches Mach 1 sooner than it would have done at a lower angle of attack; thus, the critical Mach number is less. A higher angle of attack decreases MCRIT and therefore, increases the shock wave intensity.

title: Consider an aircraft equipped with roll spoilers during a turn. Which spoilers are most likely to extend, and on which wing?
optionA: The outboard spoilers on the downgoing wing.
optionB: The inboard spoilers on the downgoing wing
optionC: The outboard spoilers on the upgoing wing
optionD: The inboard spoilers on the up-going wing
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
To function as a lateral control, the spoilers rise on the wing with the up-going aileron (down-going wing), proportional to the aileron input. On the wing with the down-going aileron, they remain retracted.

Unlike ailerons, spoilers cannot give an increase of lift, so a roll manoeuvre controlled by spoilers will give a net loss of lift. However, the spoiler has several advantages compared to the aileron:

- There is no adverse yaw.
- Wing twisting is reduced.
- At transonic speed, its effectiveness is not reduced by shock wave induced flow separation.
- They cannot develop flutter.
- Spoilers do not occupy the trailing edge, which can be utilised for more flaps.

An example is illustrated in the attached figure. Speed brakes have been selected, and then a turn to the left is initiated. The spoiler surfaces on the wing with the up-going aileron will stay deployed, or modulate upwards, depending on the speed brake selection and the roll input. The spoiler surfaces on the wing with the down-going aileron will modulate towards the stowed position. The spoiler surfaces on the wing with the down-going aileron may partially or fully stow, again depending on the speed brake selection and the roll input.

Note: Roll control spoilers are generally distributed throughout the wing, and the system depends on pilot input to modulate the degree of deflection and which spoilers to extend or retract. On this question, it seems that EASA considers the most likely to extend to be the outboard spoilers. If you see this question in your exam, we strongly recommend you appeal and report back to us any changes made to this question.

title: An aircraft is flying the intermediate approach phase of an arrival at a speed of 90 kt with the flaps in the approach position. The pilot extends the landing gear and lowers the nose to follow the glide path while initially aiming to maintain speed as the aircraft intercepts the 3° final approach path to the runway. The pilot notices that the aircraft can maintain a speed of 90 kt WITHOUT needing to adjust the thrust setting. This is due to...
optionA: thrust acts along the flight path in a more efficient manner during a descent when compared to a climb and therefore offsets the drag increase generated by landing gear extension.
optionB: the increase in parasite drag due to landing gear extension is offset by the reduction in induced drag due to the pilot pitching down when commencing the final descent.
optionC: the thrust vector from the engine does NOT coincide with the flight path of the aeroplane in a descent and therefore the effective thrust force is reduced.
optionD: gravity acts partially along the flight path when the aeroplane is descending and extending the landing gear increases drag sufficiently to prevent acceleration.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
A straight and steady power-on descent, with a certain power setting at which the engine creates a thrust vector, results in four forces acting on the airplane, i.e., weight, lift, thrust and drag.

The force of weight can be resolved into two components. One component acts perpendicular to the flight path and is balanced by lift, while the other acts forward along the flight path and adds to the thrust to balance drag.

If the nose of the aircraft is lowered with a constant thrust setting, the increased component of weight acting forward along the flight path will cause an increase in apparent thrust and IAS. The increased IAS will result in an increase in drag which will eventually balance the increased forward force of weight and equilibrium will be re-established.

title: If the RPM lever of a constant speed propeller is moved forward during a glide with idle power and whilst maintaining constant airspeed, the propeller pitch will:
optionA: increase and the rate of descent will increase.
optionB: increase and the rate of descent will decrease.
optionC: decrease and the rate of descent will increase.
optionD: decrease and the rate of descent will decrease.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

A single engine airplane fitted with a constant speed propeller may not have a “feathering” capability, as such. However, following engine failure, drag can be reduced to a minimum by “pulling” the RPM (prop) control to the fully coarse position.
In a steady glide with no shaft power from the engine (throttle closed), if the propeller pitch is decreased by pushing forward the prop’ lever, the aircraft Lift/Drag ratio will decrease. This will increase the rate of descent.
The opposite will be true if the propeller pitch is increased.

title: A large turbojet aeroplane is being flown at its optimum altitude and the crew try to achieve the most efficient flight performance. If the speed were to be increased slightly above the critical Mach number, the coefficient of lift would (1)_____, requiring (2) _____ in the angle of attack.
optionA: (1) increase; (2) decrease
optionB: (1) increase; (2) increase
optionC: (1) decrease; (2) decrease
optionD: (1) decrease; (2) increase
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Critical Mach number (MCRIT) is the free stream Mach number (MFS ) at which the airflow over the upper surface of the wing becomes sonic (M=1), after which shockwaves will form.

At speeds just above the Mcrit, only a tiny part of the wing is affected (wing root) and Coefficient of Lift (CL) continues to rise with EAS rise, until shock stall, as shown in figure.

Also, if a straight and level flight is desired, then the angle of attack must be reduced.

For best specific range (nautical miles per kg of fuel used) we need maximum TAS / Drag ratio. TAS can be maximised without a significant drag penalty, if we fly just above MCRIT. This is because, when Mcrit is first exceeded, the extra drag caused by the shock waves will be minimal, (especially on supercritical wings), provided that speed is kept below the drag divergence Mach number.

The TAS / Drag ratio also increases, if TAS can be increased without an increase in IAS. This can be achieved by increasing altitude.

So best specific range is achieved by cruising just above MCRIT, and by flying as high as other considerations permit.

title:
Refer to figure.
What do the numbers represent?
optionA: 2) Thrust (T); 8) Weight (W).
optionB: 4) Lift (L); 7) W cos a.
optionC: 2) Thrust (T); 4) Weight (W).
optionD: 7) Weight (W); 4) W cos a.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Forces During Climb
When an aircraft is in a steady climb, various forces come into play, including:

  • Lift (4): This force acts perpendicular or normal to the aircraft's flight path.

  • Weight (7): Weight acts along the local vertical and is parallel to the force of gravity.

  • Thrust (2): Thrust is directed parallel to the flight path. In some cases, the thrust vector may be slightly inclined upwards due to engine design and mounting, which helps balance the lift force against the weight force.

  • Drag (6): Drag operates parallel to the flight path.

In simple terms, all these forces are centered at the aircraft's center of gravity.

title: The positive manoeuvring limit load factor for a light aeroplane in the aerobatic category in the clean configuration may not be less than:
explanationTotal:
The maximum load factors which must be allowed for during maneuvers are shown in an envelope of load factor against speed (EAS).
The limit load factors will depend on the design category of the aircraft.

The EASA regulations state that:

  • For normal category aircraft, the positive limit load factor is 3.8.
  • The positive limit load factor for modern high-speed jet transport aircraft is 2.5.
  • For utility category aircraft the positive limit load factor is 4.4.
  • For aerobatic category aircraft the positive limit load factor is 6.0.
The negative limit load factor may not be less than:
  • -1.0 for normal category aircraft.
  • -1.76 for utility category aircraft.
  • -3.0 for aerobatic category aircraft.

title: V<sub>MCL</sub> is determined under the following aircraft flight configuration and trim setting:
optionA: Landing flap, trimmed for all engines operating.
optionB: Approach flap, trimmed for one engine operating.
optionC: Approach flap, trimmed for all engines operating.
optionD: Landing flap, trimmed for one engine inoperative.
explanationTotal:
CS 25.149 Minimum control speed

(f) VMCL, the minimum control speed during approach and landing with all engines operating, is the calibrated airspeed at which, when the critical engine is suddenly made inoperative, it is possible to maintain control of the aeroplane with that engine still inoperative, and maintain straight flight with an angle of bank of not more than 5º. VMCL must be established with –

(1) The aeroplane in the most critical configuration (or, at the option of the applicant, each configuration) for approach and landing with all engines operating;
(2) The most unfavourable centre of gravity;
(3) The aeroplane trimmed for approach with all engines operating;
(4) The most unfavourable weight, or, at the option of the applicant, as a function of weight;
(5) For propeller aeroplanes, the propeller of the inoperative engine in the position it achieves without pilot action, assuming the engine fails while at the power or thrust necessary to maintain a 3 degree approach path angle; and
(6) Go-around power or thrust setting on the operating engine(s).

title: An aeroplane that tends to return to its pre-disturbed equilibrium position after the disturbance has been removed is said to have:
optionA: positive dynamic stability.
optionB: neutral static stability.
optionC: positive static stability.
optionD: neutral dynamic stability.
explanationTotal:
An aircraft is in a state of equilibrium (trim) when the sum of all forces is zero and the sum of all moments is zero; there are no accelerations and the aircraft will continue in steady flight.

If equilibrium is disturbed by a gust, or deflection of the controls, the aircraft will experience accelerations due to an unbalance of moments or forces.

The type of static stability an aircraft possesses is defined by its initial tendency, following the removal of some disturbing force.

  • Positive static stability (or static stability) exists if an aircraft is disturbed from equilibrium and has the tendency to return to equilibrium.
  • Neutral static stability exists if an aircraft is subject to a disturbance and has neither the tendency to return nor the tendency to continue in the displacement direction.
  • Negative static stability (or static instability) exists if an aircraft tends to continue in the direction of disturbance.

title: Vortilons that are attached to the underside of a wing:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Create a vortex, at low angles of attack, to keep the boundary layer attached to the wing.
optionB: Re-energises the flow on the underside of the wing.
optionC: Improve low speed handling characteristics.
optionD: Minimises turbulent wake behind the wing.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Vortilons are fixed aerodynamic devices on aircraft wings used to improve handling at low speeds. They are situated on the underside of the wing leading edge. When the wing approaches stall, span-wise flow starts to flow across the vortilons which start to generate a vortex. The vortex energises the boundary layer over the wing. The turbulent flow in the boundary layer delays the flow separation resulting in increased controllability of the airplane in stall.

During high airspeeds (low angle of attack) vortilons have minimum drag as they are streamlined with the airflow and don’t generate any vortex.

Vortilons help to improve aileron performance at high angles of attack and thus improve the spin resistance of the airplane.

title:
Thunderstorms are reported in the vicinity of an aerodrome when a heavy jet transport is about to commence an approach. Which combination of these methods could be used by the crew to mitigate the risk of buffet or stall?

1. Delay the approach, and divert if necessary.
2. Plan a flapless approach and landing.
3. Maintain a speed at least 30 kts above normal approach speed.
4. Delay landing flap selection until 200 ft.
5. Expect and prepare for a windshear warning and a go-around.
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: 1 and 5
optionB: 1, 3 and 4
optionC: 2, 4 and 5
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.

ALL EFFORTS SHALL BE MADE TO AVOID THUNDERSTORM ACTIVITY AS IT POSES RISK TO FLIGHT SAFETY

Microbursts are associated with thunderstorms and are one of the most dangerous sources of windshear.

A windshear encounter is a very dynamic event which can strike suddenly and with devastating effect which has been beyond the recovery powers of experienced pilots flying modern and powerful aircraft. The first and most vital defence is avoidance.

AWARENESS AND AVOIDANCE

Awareness of the weather conditions that cause windshear will reduce the risk of an encounter.

If a windshear encounter is likely, the takeoff or landing should be delayed until the conditions improve, e.g. until a thunderstorm has moved away from the airport.

Windshear represents a severe threat to aviation safety, the best option is to avoid it whenever possible. Nevertheless, in the case of an actual encounter with windshear, it is essential to be to quickly recognize it and then recover from it.

PREVENTION

A key element of adverse weather avoidance strategies is the active monitoring of the overall meteorological situation by the crew, in addition to the optimum use of the weather radar and correct understanding of the information displayed.

The take-off, initial climb, final approach and landing phases of flight in the vicinity of thunderstorms may present the pilot with additional problems because of the airplane‘s proximity to the ground.

To maintain a safe flight path in these phases can be very difficult. Do not take off if a thunderstorm is overhead or approaching. At destination, hold if a thunderstorm is overhead or approaching or divert if necessary.

On the approach, if there is ever any doubt that you can regain a reasonable rate of descent, and land without abnormal manoeuvres, you should apply full power and go-around or make a missed approach.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

1. Delay the approach, and divert if necessary. CORRECT: As the explanation suggests, in case of thunderstorm activity, the first mitigating action should be to avoid and therefore delay take-off/landing or divert if necessary.

2. Plan a flapless approach and landing. INCORRECT: Flaps/slats should be used for every normal approach, including those with thunderstorms present as they lower the stall speed and in the case of slats increase the critical angle of attack.

3. Maintain a speed at least 30 kt above normal approach speed. INCORRECT: Choosing to fly at a speed slightly higher than normal approach speed is a good technique to aid with speed fluctuations characteristic of thunderstorm activity. However, this would be type specific, and there is no general rule for an approach to be flown 30 knots faster than normal.

4. Delay landing flap selection until 200 ft. INCORRECT: Delaying the configuration of the aircraft is not a recommended for this type of approach, specially to as low as 200 ft.

5. Expect and prepare for a windshear warning and a go-around. CORRECT: As stated above, the first mitigating action should be to avoid the thunderstorms. On the approach, if avoiding is not possible, the crew should be prepared to perform a go-around.

title: An aircraft which has a higher static longitudinal stability, the longitudinal manoeuvrability is (1) _____, because the necessary elevator deflections are (2) _____.
optionA: (1) reduced; (2) increased
optionB: (1) increased; (2) increased
optionC: (1) increased; (2) reduced
optionD: (1) reduced; (2) reduced
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Longitudinal stability is motion about the lateral axis.

Static Longitudinal stability is the aircraft's natural tendency when disturbed in pitch, to return to its former trimmed angle of attack without pilot input, and is desirable throughout the aircraft's complete speed range.

The control forces of the aeroplane should reflect the stability of the aeroplane and provide suitable reference to the pilot for precise control of the aeroplane.

When the CG position of the aeroplane is fixed, each elevator position corresponds to a particular trim lift coefficient. As the CG is moved aft, the slope of this line decreases, and the decrease in stability is evident by a given control displacement causing a greater change in trim lift coefficient.

This is evidence that decreasing stability causes increased controllability and, of course, increasing stability decreases controllability.

For the same value of CL, a more stable aircraft (forward CG) will require a higher elevator deflection.

If the CG is moved aft until the line of trim CL versus elevator deflection has zero slope, neutral static stability is obtained.

title: What will happen to the effective angle of attack when the aircraft enters ground effect?
optionA: Increases due to the decreased downwash
optionB: Decreases due to the increased downwash
optionC: Stays constant
optionD: Increases and then decreases
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
When taking-off or landing, the proximity to the ground prevents full development of the trailing edge vortices, making them much weaker than in normal flight. The runway serves as a physical barrier to downwash airflow, therefore downwash decreases. With less downwash, the effective angle of attack and lift increase.

All in all:

  • Entering ground effect: lift increases, induced drag reduces.
  • Leaving ground effect: lift reduces, induced drag increases.

title: A twin-engine aeroplane has its engines mounted on the wings. If after an engine failure thrust on the live engine is increased, the yawing moment will...
optionA: decrease.
optionB: remain the same provided proportional rudder to the thrust increase is applied.
optionC: remain the same.
optionD: increase.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
When an engine fails on a multi-engine aircraft there will be a decrease in thrust and an increase in drag on the side with the failed engine:

  • airspeed will decay.
  • the nose will drop and.
  • most significantly, there will be an immediate yawing moment towards the failed engine.
The forces and moments acting on an aircraft following failure of the left engine are shown in figure 1. The aircraft has a yawing moment towards the dead engine. The pilot has applied rudder to stop the yaw. The vital action when an engine fails is to stop the yaw.
The rolling and yawing moments and the power of the flight controls to balance them will determine the controllability of an aircraft with asymmetric thrust. Rolling and yawing moments with asymmetric thrust are affected by:
  • Thrust on the live engine
  • Altitude
  • Drag from the dead engine and propeller
  • Asymmetric blade effect (also known as ‘P’ Factor)
  • CG position
The fore and aft CG location has no effect on the yawing moment from a failed engine, but will influence the rudder arm, hence the rudder moment. CG on the aft limit will give the smallest rudder arm and the least ability to oppose the yawing moment from a failed engine.
  • Torque reaction
  • Difference in lift due to slipstream
  • Rolling moment due to sideslip
  • Weight
  • Airspeed

title: The aft CG limit can be determined by the:
optionA: minimum acceptable elevator deflection.
optionB: maximum elevator deflection available.
optionC: minimum acceptable static longitudinal stability.
optionD: maximum static longitudinal stability required.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
A variation of CG position can cause large changes in the static longitudinal stability. In the conventional airplane configuration, the large changes in stability with CG variation are primarily due to the large changes in the wing contribution.

As the CG is gradually moved aft, the airplane static stability decreases, then becomes neutral then unstable. The CG position which produces zero slope and neutral static stability is referred to as the “neutral point”.

The aft limit, which for safety reasons on a transport airplane is always forward of the neutral point, is confined by insufficient stick-force stability and/or excessive in-flight maneuverability (minimum acceptable stability). The minimum stick force per ‘g’ for the maximum permitted load factor, which is 2.5 for large transport airplanes, determines the aft limit of the CG envelope.

A CG position aft of this point would produce an unacceptably low value of maneuver stability and would make the airplane difficult to fly. For transport airplanes the aft limit is normally located at approximately 30% of the MAC.

title: Select the correct statement with reference to the relationship between V<sub>MCL</sub> and CG location for a common airplane (i.e. A320 or B737):
optionA: The CG has no influence on VMCL.
optionB: A forward CG decreases VMCL.
optionC: A forward CG increases VMCL.
optionD: It depends on the airplane type.
explanationTotal:
MINIMUM CONTROL SPEED

VMCL is the minimum control speed in the air for a multiengined aircraft in the approach and landing configuration, at and above which it is possible to maintain directional control of the aircraft around the normal/vertical axis by use of the rudder after failure of an off-center engine within defined limits while applying variations of power, i.e., idle to maximum thrust on the live engine(s).

As the center of gravity moves forward, the rudder arm increases, improving rudder effectiveness. Likewise, and aft CG shortens the arm to the centre of the rudder’s horizontal lift, which means a higher airspeed would be required to counteract the engine-out yaw. As a result a forward CG results in a lower VMCL. This is the reason the tests for VMCL is carried out at the rear most possible center of gravity

title:
VS = 120 kt
Bank angle = 25º
What is the load factor and stall speed in the turn?
optionA: V<sub>S</sub> = 136; Load factor = 1.4
optionB: V<sub>S</sub> = 136; Load factor = 1.2
optionC: V<sub>S</sub> = 126; Load factor = 1.1
optionD: V<sub>S</sub> = 132; Load factor = 1.1
explanationTotal:
In a turn, the load factor is equal to 1/cos(ø), where ø is the bank angle.

n = 1/cos(25º) = 1.1

VS is directly proportional to the square root of the load factor.

VS = √1.1 x 120 = 126 kt

title: In straight and level flight at a speed of 1.6 V<sub>S</sub>, the lift coefficient, expressed as a percentage of its maximum C<sub>LMAX</sub>, would be:
explanationTotal:
To solve this question, we either need to know the relationship by heart, or know how to get to it. If remembering works better for you, skip the italic part, if you prefer understanding where the relationship comes from, see the italic part.

Knowing that:

L = CL ½ rho v2 S

If we re-organize to make the coefficient of lift (CL) the subject of the equation:

CL = L ÷ (½ rho v2 S)

Therefore, removing the constant from the equation, we can say that:

CL ∝ 1 ÷ v2

Now that we know the relationship, and knowing that v = 1.6 VS , we can solve the question:

CL = 1 ÷ 1.62

CL = 0.39

With that information we know that our coefficient of lift at 1.6 VS will be 0.39 (39%) of the coefficient at VS.

title: Which of the following statements about buffet or stall is correct?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: With underslung engines, the use of the take-off/go-around power setting (TOGA) produces powerful nose-up pitching moments, increasing the risk of a stall.
optionB: Insufficient take-off flap increases the risk of encountering buffet but decreases the risk of a stall.
optionC: A higher rate of rotation on take-off or go-around decreases the risk of buffet or stall.
optionD: High bank angles decrease the risk of a stall.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
If the engine is located well below the CG (like most modern jets) adding maximum thrust (TOGA) produces a strong pitch-up moment. This pitch-up moment can be so pronounced, that from a trimmed approach condition, the aircraft pitches up until stall unless acted against by the pilot by pushing the control column.

title: Whilst maintaining straight and level flight with a lift coefficient C<sub>L </sub>= 1 what will be the new approximate value of C<sub>L</sub> after the speed is increased by 30%?
explanationTotal:
Lift can be calculated as follows:
L= CL × ½ rho × V2 × S

Where:

  • CL is lift coefficient (without dimension)
  • p is density
  • V is velocity [m/s] (velocity is TAS)
  • S is surface area [m2]
  • L is lift [N]
⇒ If the velocity increases by 30%, lift increases by 1.302 = 1.69 (69%). To maintain lift constant (straight and level flight), lift coefficient (CL) must be 0.60 of the old CL (x 0.60): 1 ÷ 1.69.

title: Aileron deflection causes a rotation around the longitudinal axis by:
optionA: causing sideslip, which generates a rolling moment.
optionB: aileron secondary effect.
optionC: changing the wing drag and the two wings therefore produce different lift values resulting in a moment about the longitudinal axis.
optionD: changing the wing camber and the two wings therefore produce different lift values resulting in a moment about the longitudinal axis.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

In an aircraft, spoilers can be installed to intentionally reduce lift for a specific wing by partially disrupting the airflow over the airfoil.
They can extend symmetrically or asymmetrically.
If spoilers on both sides are used, its primary purpose is to reduce the speed at which the aircraft is travelling.
Spoilers can also be used in a turn to assist the ailerons.
In this case, the spoiler mounted on the down-going wing will come up, reducing lift for that wing even more and therefore assisting the ailerons.
The spoiler on the up-moving wing will remain stowed.

For example, if the aircraft wants to enter a right turn, it will have to bank to the right.
The right wing will have to come down and the left wing will have to rise.
The aileron on the left will come down, producing more lift on the left wing by changing the wing camber and the aileron on the right will come up.
The spoiler mounted on the upper side of the right wing will also come up, reducing lift of the right wing even more.
This way the aircraft reaches its desired bank angle easier at low speeds.

title: A pilot is teaching a student the effects of individual control inputs. First, the pilot deflects the ailerons only, holding a constant deflection. Eventually, the aircraft enters a spiral dive. After recovering, the pilot then inputs a constant rudder deflection only. This also causes a spiral dive. Which of the following statements is correct regarding aircraft stability?
optionA: The ailerons are the main contributors to lateral stability and the rudder is the main contributor to directional stability.
optionB: The ailerons are secondary contributors to directional stability and the rudder is a secondary contributor to lateral stability.
optionC: Lateral and directional stabilities interact through sideslip, which is created when using either aileron or rudder alone.
optionD: Since the aeroplane enters an un-coordinated spiral dive, it is a result of both the lateral and directional stabilities being too weak.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
This is a very complex question, but the answer is the simplest one present. The examiner has put in a lot to try and confuse you. The answer to the question is right at the top, but keep reading if you want to know more and if you want to know why the other answers are incorrect.

Directional stability (stability in yaw) and lateral stability (stability in roll) are very well linked. The linkage between the two is via sideslip, the condition where the aircraft is not pointing in the same direction it is travelling through the air, so the relative airflow is arriving from one side of the nose, rather than straight on the nose. We can cause this by not flying the aircraft properly, and by flying uncoordinated, so using the ailerons without also using correct rudder, and vice-versa.

LATERAL/DIRECTIONAL STABILITY
Imagine that we have a left sideslip, so the aircraft is pointing forwards, but travelling to the left of that, and the relative airflow is hitting the left windshield first.

  • A directionally stable aircraft will naturally yaw into this (nose left moment), because of the positively stable effect of the fin (vertical stabiliser), any rear strakes or ventral fin, the differential drag of the wings, etc.
  • A laterally stable aircraft will roll away from this sideslip (right bank moment), due to the dihedral effect, sweepback, high wing effect, etc.

Both of these movements decreases the sideslip, just in different ways; the aircraft can either yaw into it, or roll away from it.

Most civilian aircraft are both laterally and directionally stable at once, in equal measure. If the stability becomes too high on one or the other, then it can cause either Dutch Roll or Spiral Instability.

DUTCH ROLL
Too much lateral stability and not enough directional stability can cause a periodic motion of sideslip and overcorrection which we call Dutch Roll. Imagine an aircraft with very long, dihedral wings, but a small tail fin.

SPIRAL INSTABILITY
The opposite of Dutch Roll, Spiral Instability is where we have too much directional stability but not enough lateral stability, which causes an increasing bank angle, with the aircraft constantly yawing further to keep the turn coordinated and ending up in a spiral dive. It is an aperiodic motion (it only happens once, not back and forth). Imagine a large tail fin and short, non-dihedral wings.

So in terms of this question, we have already seen the correct answer, "Lateral and directional stabilities interact through sideslip, which is created when using either aileron or rudder alone.". Whilst there are other ways to create sideslip, this is a very common one.

For two other options, we should mention that the rudder and ailerons are not contributors to stability. They are control surfaces, and the pilot has direct control over them.
