Stability has to be natural within the aircraft. If it takes a pilot to remove the sideslip, then the aircraft is not that stable. In a stable aircraft, we manipulate the ailerons and rudder against the natural stability of the aircraft design.

For the final option remaining, most aircraft would enter a spiral dive under the conditions mentioned in the question (depending on the extent of the deflection). However, with stronger lateral stability, the aircraft would be able to resist the spiral dive. Extra directional stability would just make a spiral dive easier to enter. So you could say that lateral stability is too weak, but not both lateral and directional stabilities.

title: An aeroplane is established on final approach descending through 1000 ft when the pilot realizes that the aeroplane is about to enter an area of heavy tropical rain. The pilot must consider that the stalling…
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: speed increase due to the C<sub>LMAX</sub> reduction because of water distorting the shape of the airfoil and the airflow pattern.
optionB: speed increase due to compressibility effects appearing earlier than normal because of the concentration of water on the wings.
optionC: angle of attack decrease due to the apparent decrease of the load factor from the heavy downpour of rain.
optionD: angle of attack decreases due to the associated gusts from the heavy downpour of rain.
explanationTotal:
The airframe may become contaminated by ice, frost or water either whilst it is in flight or when standing on the ground.

WATER CONTAMINATION

If the wings are contaminated with water due to heavy rain, the boundary layer may become turbulent further forward on the wing, particularly if the section is of the laminar flow type. This will cause increased drag and may disrupt the boundary layer resulting in a significantly higher stall speed.

EFFECT OF HEAVY RAIN ON STALL SPEED

- Weight
Heavy rain will form a film of water on an aircraft and increase its weight slightly, maybe as much as 1 - 2% this in itself will increase stall speed.

- Aerodynamic Effect
The film of water will distort the aerofoil, roughen the surface and alter the airflow pattern on the whole aircraft. CLMAX will decrease causing stall speed to increase.

- Drag
The film of water will increase interference drag, profile drag and form drag. In light rain, drag may increase by 5%, in moderate by 20% and in heavy rain by up to 30%.

- Impact
An additional consideration, while not affecting stall speed, is the effect of the impact of heavy rain on the aircraft. Momentum will be lost and airspeed will decrease, requiring increased thrust. At the same time, heavy rain will also be driving the aircraft downwards. The volume of rain in any given situation will vary, but an aircraft on final approach which suddenly enters a torrential downpour of heavy rain will be subject to a loss of momentum and a decrease in altitude, similar to the effect of microburst windshear.

title: What is correct about Clear Air Turbulence (CAT) at high level?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: It decreases when jet streams change direction.
optionB: It is only found close to thunderstorm activity.
optionC: It gives an increased risk of buffet or a stall.
optionD: It is only associated with jet streams.
explanationTotal:
Gusts, or in other word abrupt wind changes (or windshear), are known to occur close to or in thunderstorm cells, thus particularly in ITCZ, in clear air turbulence (jet streams) and in wake turbulence.

If an aerofoil encounters an upgust, it will experience an increase in angle of attack. For a given gust velocity, the increment in angle increases as the aircraft TAS decreases. If the angle of attack is already large (low speed), the increment due to the gust could cause the wing to stall.

title: How does the drag polar change with spoiler deployment?
optionA: The polar stays nearly the same.
optionB: The polar moves down and to the right.
optionC: The polar moves up and to the left.
optionD: The polar moves to the right.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Speed brakes affecting drag and lift are called spoilers as they spill or spoil part of the lift force. They are movable panels on the upper wing surface, hinged at their forward edge. They are operated hydraulically and controlled electrically. A raised spoiler will disturb the airflow over the wing, thus reducing lift and increasing drag.

On the drag polar, a decrease in lift and an increase in drag are represented by a curve shift down and to the right.

title:
Refer to figure.
Which of the three lift augmentation devices is/are represented by the graph in the annex?
optionA: 1 and 3
optionB: 3 only
optionC: 1 only
optionD: 1 and 2
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Aircraft are fitted with high lift devices to reduce the take-off and landing distances and improve slow flying characteristics.

The three leading edge devices shown in the annex are:

  1. Leading Edge Flaps - similar to trailing edge flaps, they increase the camber f the wing to increase CL and CLMAX
  2. Kreuger Flaps - part of the lower surface of the leading edge, which can be rotated about its forward edge to force more airflow over the top of the wing at high angles of attack.
  3. Slats - These are small "extra leading edges" that move forward in front of the leading edge of the wing, creating a small slot behind, where airflow is sped up and re-energised, delaying the stalling angle of attack without increasing the CL at normal angles of attack.

Kreuger Flaps and Slats are often used in conjunction, with Kreuger Flaps being used on the inboard section of an wing and slats being used outboard of the engine pylons, to promote root stall tendency due to the Kreuger Flaps being less effective.

Leading edge flaps, like trailing edge flaps, increase CL values for all angles of attack, also increasing drag, and not changing the stalling angle of attack very much (small increases or decreases are possible depending on the specifics).

Slats do not increase CL for normal values of AoA, instead, they just delay the stalling AoA, allowing for a higher CLMAX due to the higher critical AoA. This is what is being shown in the graph.

Kreuger flaps tend to sit somewhere in the middle of the two other devices on the graph, but are obviously very ineffective at low angles of attack.

title: If the propeller pitch of a windmilling propeller is decreased during a glide at constant IAS the propeller drag in the direction of flight will:
optionA: decrease and the rate of descent will decrease.
optionB: decrease and the rate of descent will increase.
optionC: increase and the rate of descent will decrease.
optionD: increase and the rate of descent will increase.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
In the event of an engine failure both the engine and the propeller will slow down. The CSU will attempt to maintain the selected RPM by driving the propeller blades to a fine position that will continue until reaching the fine pitch stop.
Despite the engine failing the airplane still has forward speed, for a single-engine airplane due to the glide descent the forward speed causes the propeller to have a negative angle of attack due to the direction of the relative airflow. This angle of attack generates sufficient torque to rotate the unpowered propeller in the normal direction of rotation.
The component of the force at right angles to the plane of rotation now acts rearwards and is no longer thrust but is now drag and presents a flat disc to the direction of travel.
Because the propeller is being driven only by the relative airflow it is said to be wind milling. As such, it causes a considerable amount of drag, reduces the IAS, reduces the Lift/Drag ratio and increases the rate of descent.

title: During a glide with idle power and constant IAS, if the RPM lever of a constant speed propeller is pulled back from its normal cruise position, the propeller pitch will:
optionA: decrease and the rate of descent will decrease.
optionB: increase and the rate of descent will decrease.
optionC: increase and the rate of descent will increase.
optionD: decrease and the rate of descent will increase.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
A single engine airplane fitted with a constant speed propeller may not have a “feathering” capability, as such. However, following engine failure, drag can be reduced to a minimum by “pulling” the RPM (prop) control to the fully coarse position.
In a steady glide with no shaft power from the engine (throttle closed), if the propeller pitch is increased by pulling back the prop’ lever, the aircraft Lift/Drag ratio will increase. This will decrease the rate of descent. The RPM would decrease because of the reduction in negative propeller torque.
The opposite will be true if the propeller pitch is decreased.

title: An aeroplane is flying in the transonic speed range in straight and level flight. If the Mach number decreases, what additional input or action will be required to maintain straight and level flight to compensate for the centre of pressure’s movement, whilst exiting the transonic region?
optionA: A pitch up input to the elevator or the stabiliser.
optionB: No pitch control input.
optionC: A pitch down input to the elevator or the stabiliser.
optionD: A lower IAS to compensate the nose up effect.
explanationTotal:
Transonic flow is said to be the airflow where air flows above, at, and below the speed of sound at the same time at different points on an object.

For example, the air on a wing flows faster, so that air could be supersonic while the air flowing over the body of an airplane could be subsonic.
The transonic speed range is found at Mach 0.8-1.2.

Severe instability can occur at transonic speeds.
Shock waves can cause large-scale separation downstream, increasing drag and adding asymmetry and unsteadiness to the flow around the aircraft.

When entering the transonic speed range, the Center of Pressure (CP) moves backward, causing a pitch down moment.
To counteract this, the aircraft should apply a pitch up moment to the elevator or stabilizer.

When exiting this range and returning to subsonic speed, the opposite should be done by applying a pitch down input to the elevator or stabilizer.

title: Assuming the CG always remains within limits, how does the CG position relate to the spin attitude of an aeroplane?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: The further forward the CG, the flatter the spin attitude.
optionB: The further aft the CG, the flatter the spin attitude.
optionC: CG position does not affect the spin attitude of the aeroplane.
optionD: The closer the CG to its limits (forward or aft), the flatter the spin attitude.
explanationTotal:
Flat spins are the worst and most dangerous type of spin. In a flat spin, the aircraft has no forward airspeed. It spins around its vertical axis as it sinks straight towards the ground.

Due to the high angle of attack of a flat spin, it is nearly impossible to recover, as the horizontal stabilizer is most likely in stall, too. The only possibility then is to move the CG forward. In small aircraft what you can do is to lean forward and hope for the best.

The type of spin a plane enters depends mainly on the CG Position (and thrust setting):

  • CG towards the forward limit makes an aircraft more stable, and control forces will be higher which makes it less likely that large, abrupt control movements will be made. When trimmed, the aeroplane will tend to return to level flight if the controls are released, but the stall speed will be higher.

  • CG towards the aft limit decreases longitudinal static stability and reduces pitch control forces, which tends to make the aeroplane easier to stall. Once a spin is entered, the further aft the CG, the flatter the spin attitude.

All in all, do not spin with an aircraft that is not designed for that or with too aft CG position.

Note: Watch the following video to understand the attitude of the aircraft during a flat spin https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=22eADnRqMwo&t=16s

title: Assuming that the RPM remains constant throughout, the angle of attack of a fixed pitch propeller will:
optionA: remain constant at a fixed value only if the airspeed decreases.
optionB: decrease with decreasing airspeed.
optionC: remain constant at a fixed value irrespective of any airspeed changes.
optionD: increase with decreasing airspeed.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
The blade angle of a fixed-pitch propeller is constant, but the helix angle and the angle of attack will vary according to its forward speed. To ensure its efficient operation the blade angle of attack of a fixed-pitch propeller must be close to the optimum and is that which produces the greatest excess of horizontal lift (thrust) over drag.
Figure 1 shows a “fixed pitch” propeller at constant RPM. Increasing TAS decreases the angle of attack of the propeller. Figure 2 shows a “fixed pitch” propeller at a constant TAS. Increasing RPM increases the angle of attack of the propeller.

title: Some wings are designed with a smaller angle of incidence towards the wing tip or a profile with a different camber towards the wing tip. The reason for this is to...
optionA: ensure that the entire wing stall occurs when the aeroplane is at a specific pitch angle, and to create an aeroplane with predictable stall characteristics.
optionB: delay the stall at the wing tip to reduce the likelihood of the aeroplane experiencing significant rolling moments when stalled.
optionC: reduce the stalling angle of attack at the wing tips to ensure the wing tips stall first so there is a more gradual loss of lift when stalling.
optionD: evenly spread the lift across the wing planform and increase its efficiency, resulting in minimum drag at the optimum angle of attack.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
In some wing designs, separation tends to occur first in the region of the tip, reducing lift in those areas. If an actual wing were allowed to stall in this way, stalling would give aileron buffet and perhaps violent wing drop.

To give favourable stall characteristics, a tapered wing must be modified using one or more of the following:

Geometric twist (washout), a decrease in incidence from root to tip. This decreases the angle of attack at the tip, and the root will tend to stall first.

The aerofoil section may be varied throughout the span such that sections with greater thickness and camber are located near the tip. The higher CLMAX of such sections delays stall so that the root will tend to stall first.

title: Outboard ailerons (if present) are normally used:
optionA: when the landing gear is up.
optionB: in low speed flight only.
optionC: in high speed flight only.
optionD: at transonic and supersonic speeds only.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
OUTBOARD AND INBOARD AILERONS
Two sets of ailerons may be fitted, one at the wing tips (outboard ailerons) and one set inboard (inboard ailerons). At low speeds, both the inboard and the outboard ailerons are controllable but once the aircraft gains speed (usually when the flaps are all the way up) only the inboard ailerons respond to control input. At high speeds, when the forces are greater and could cause greater structural distortion, outboard (low-speed) ailerons are "locked-out" as the flaps retract.

title: The air loads on the horizontal tailplane (tail load) of an aeroplane in straight and level cruise flight are generally directed:
optionA: upwards and will reduce in magnitude as the CG moves aft.
optionB: downwards and will increase in magnitude as the CG moves aft.
optionC: downwards and will reduce in magnitude as the CG moves aft.
optionD: upwards and will increase in magnitude as the CG moves aft.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
The point where an aircraft’s total sum of a pressure field is acting upon the body is called the Center of Pressure (CP).
This is the point where the resultant vector of lift is said to be operating. As the airfoil or Angle of attack changes (thus changing the lift coefficient),
this pressure field will change and so will the center of pressure.

Aircraft longitudinal stability is directly related to Centre of Gravity (CG) position.
An aircraft with a more forward CG is more longitudinally stable than an aircraft with a more aft CG. Placing the CG beyond the forward limit can cause an unacceptably high value of longitudinal stability, decreasing manoeuvrability by a significant amount.
Place the CG beyond the aft limit and the aircraft is too unstable, having excessive manoeuvrability.

If an aircraft is longitudinally stable, an increase in Angle of Attack (α) results in a negative pitching moment.
The nose will slightly fall down, decreasing the Angle of Attack. If this aircraft has a decrease of Angle of Attack, the nose will come slightly upwards again,
creating a positive pitching moment again by slightly raising the nose.

If an aircraft is very stable (forward CG), the elevator will have to produce a bigger moment to move the pitch and thus requires a larger deflection, as the forces on the tailplane often are deflected downwards.

title: The significance of V<sub>A</sub> for jet transport aeroplanes is reduced at high cruising altitudes because:
optionA: buffet onset limitations normally become limiting.
optionB: the engine has insufficient thrust to reach the limit load factor.
optionC: the elevator deflection is limited to prevent exceeding the limit load factor.
optionD: at high altitudes the bank angle is normally limited to 15° to prevent exceeding the limit load factor.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
VA is the highest speed at which sudden, full elevator deflection (nose-up) can be made without exceeding the design limit load factor.
When establishing VA, the airplane is assumed to be flying in steady level flight, and the pitch control is suddenly moved to obtain extreme positive pitch acceleration (nose-up). VA is slower than the speed at the intersection of the CLMAX line and the positive limit load factor line (figure 1, point A) to safeguard the tail structure because of the higher load on the tail plane during the pitch maneuver

At high altitude, the equivalent stalling speed increases with ‘g’ rather more rapidly than at sea level because of the Mach number effect on CLMAX. Above a certain altitude the buffet boundary may intersect the stall boundary at a value of ‘g’ lower than the structural limit, thus VA will become less limiting at high altitude.

title: From an initial condition of level flight the flaps are extended at a constant pitch attitude. The aeroplane will subsequently:
optionA: start to climb.
optionB: start to sink.
optionC: start to bank.
optionD: maintain level flight.
explanationTotal:
Knowing that the equation for lift is:

L = CL ½ rho V2 S

And knowing that extending flaps will increase our wing surface area (S) and the coefficient lift because of the change in profile (CL), our lift will subsequently also be increased and therefore cause the aircraft to climb. This is of course assuming that there is no change in speed, air density, which can be assumed, but also as the question states, no change in pitch and therefore no change in angle of attack.

title:
Comparing the differences between a horizontal trimmable stabiliser and an elevator trim tab, which statement is correct?

I. A trim tab is less suitable for jet transport aeroplanes because of their large speed range.
II. A trim tab is a more powerful means of trimming.
optionA: I is incorrect, II is correct.
optionB: I is correct, II is incorrect.
optionC: I is correct, II is correct.
optionD: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
explanationTotal: In a stabiliser trim system, the whole horizontal stabiliser is adjusted, rather than just the trim tab on the elevator. Clearly, adjusting this much bigger surface will produce much bigger forces which can compensate for large changes in pitching moments.  This is desirable on jet transport aircraft  because of their large speed range.

title: The drag of an aeroplane is 850 Newton. What is the new value of drag if wing surface area is increased by 10%?
explanationTotal:
The drag equation:
D = 1/2 p V2 S CD
  • Apart from change in wing surface area, no other changes are mentioned therefore we will assume they remain unchanged. 
  • As you can take from the above equation, drag is proportional to wing surface area (S) => which means that if surface area increases by 10%, drag will also increase by 10%:
    850 x 1.1 = 935 N

title: The load factor is greater than 1 (one):
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: in steady wings level horizontal flight.
optionB: when weight is greater than lift.
optionC: during a steady co-ordinated horizontal turn.
optionD: during a wings level stall before recovery.
explanationTotal:
The Load Factor is the ratio of lift compared to weight of the aircraft denoted by "n":

Load Factor (n) = Lift (L) / Weight (W)

The value of load factor in steady wings level horizontal flight is exactly 1(g). Load factors greater or less than one (or even negative) are the result of maneuvers or wind gusts. The value is less than one in a steady wings level climb, because a vertical component of thrust is balancing some of the weight. So the value of wing lift required is less.

  • Turning. In a horizontal coordinated turn, load factor is always higher than 1 (n = 1 / cos Ø).
  • Climb and Descent. In a climb or descent, n < 1 (L = W cos y)

title: In order to fly a steady co-ordinated horizontal rate one turn at a higher airspeed, the bank angle must be:
optionA: increased and the turn radius will decrease.
optionB: decreased and the turn radius will decrease.
optionC: increased and the turn radius will increase.
optionD: decreased and the turn radius will increase.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
In level flight, any turn will be coordinated or uncoordinated. A coordinated turn is one in which the only acceleration is along the normal axis of the airplane, towards the center of the turn, and the angle of bank is precisely correct for the aircraft speed and the radius of turn. If not all these factors are present, the turn will be uncoordinated and there will be a lateral acceleration either towards or away from the center of the turn. The total lift of a balanced turn provides the centripetal force and the force that opposes the mass of the airplane.
If there is acceleration towards the center of the turn the airplane is slipping and if it is away from the center of the turn the airplane is skidding. Either condition will be indicated on the turn and slip indicator. An overbanked airplane will slip into the turn and requires an increase of speed or a reduction in bank angle to correct this condition. An underbanked airplane will skid out of the turn, which requires a decreased speed or an increased bank angle to correct this condition. These are indicated on the turn and slip indicator by the needle one-way and the ball the other.
To maintain altitude and airspeed when executing a turn both the angle of attack and the thrust have to be increased above their level flight values.

In a turn, turn radius and rate of turn are defined as:

Turn radius = TAS 2/(g tan Φ)
Rate of Turn = g tan Φ/TAS

Therefore, turn radius is directly proportional to TAS squared and inversely proportional to bank angle and Rate of Turn is directly proportional to bank angle and inversely proportional to TAS.

title: A light airplane has an approach speed of 1.3 V<sub>S</sub> in landing configuration. At its Maximum Take-Off Mass of 1990 kg, the approach speed is 79 kt. What is the approach speed at a mass of 1590 kg?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: 99 kt.
optionB: 88 kt.
optionC: 71 kt.
optionD: 63 kt.
explanationTotal:
The stall speed is defined by:

VS = √((2 x W) / (ρ x S x CLMAX))

In this exercise there is a decrease in mass, therefore:

mNEW = 1590 kg
mOLD = 1990 kg
VAPP_OLD = 79kt

To calculate the new Approach speed, VAPP_NEW (1.3VS), in straight and level flight we use the above formula to get:

VAPP_NEW = √(mNEW /mOLD ) x VAPP_OLD

Replacing with the given data:

= √(1590 kg / 1990 kg) x 79 = 71 kt

With a decreased mass, the Approach Speed decreases to 71 kt.

title: The maximum glide range is achieved at _____ with an angle of attack of about 4°.
optionA: V<sub>MD</sub> (minimum drag speed)
optionB: V<sub>MO </sub>(maximum operating limit speed)
optionC: 1.30 x V<sub>MD</sub> (minimum drag speed)
optionD: V<sub>MP</sub> (minimum power speed)
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The most efficient manner in which to fly an aeroplane is with an angle of attack that creates the greatest amount of lift whilst causing the least amount of drag.

Therefore, the most efficient angle of attack is that which produces the highest lift/drag ratio.

This angle of attack is the same for all masses and altitudes and is usually 4°. The EAS at which this occurs is the most economical cruise EAS and varies in direct proportion to the gross mass of the aeroplane. In a glide descent from a specific altitude in still air the speed at the maximum lift/drag ratio will enable the aeroplane to attain the maximum glide distance.

title:
Refer to figure.
A pilot is flying an aeroplane that is in a level, coordinated turn while maintaining a constant airspeed is attempting to follow flight path number 3, but finds that the load factor is becoming increasingly uncomfortable in order to achieve the required rate of turn. What could the pilot do in an attempt to reduce the load factor?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: The pilot should follow flight path number 1, which will require less nose-up elevator and thrust to maintain altitude and speed.
optionB: The pilot should remain on flight path number 3 and apply more rudder as this enables a reduction in bank angle, which reduces the load factor.
optionC: Reduce speed as the load factor is a function of lift and proportional to the square of the airspeed in a level, coordinated turn.
optionD: The pilot should reduce both speed and the amount of nose-up elevator, while maintaining the required bank angle.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
Load Factor - The ratio of the weight of an aircraft to the load imposed by lift. The correct symbol for load factor is (n), but it is colloquially known as (g).

Load Factor = Lift / Weight

LOAD FACTOR IN A TURN

When an aircraft is in a banked turn, lift must be increased so as to maintain the vertical component of lift equal to weight. Load Factor (n) increases with bank angle at an increasing rate.

To maintain altitude and airspeed when executing a turn both the angle of attack and the thrust have to be increased above their level flight values.

This relationship may be expressed as:

Load Factor (n) = 1 / cos φ

Where φ = bank angle

In a turn, load factor is a function ONLY of bank angle.

RADIUS OF TURN

Radius of turn is dependent on both airspeed and bank angle.

Turn Radius = V2 / g tan Ø

Where V = True Airspeed, g = acceleration of gravity constant of 9.81 m/s2, Ø = angle of bank

The radius of turn at any given airspeed is inversly proportional to the bank angle. Which means that decreasing the bank angle results in a radius of turn that greater.

RATE OF TURN

Rate of turn is the rate of change of heading or angular velocity of the turn.

Rate of turn = g tan Ø / V

Increasing the speed results in a decrease of rate of turn. Whereas increasing bank angle, increases the rate of turn.

title: During a low-speed stall, how does a straight-wing airplane typically behave?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Reduced flight control authority, buffeting, and pitch down.
optionB: A descent along a steep, downward spiral path, yawing towards the low wing.
optionC: A descent along a steep, downward spiral path, yawing towards the high wing.
optionD: Reduced flight control authority, buffeting, and pitch up.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
On a straight wing, separation tends to begin at the root and spreads out towards the tip. The effective angle of attack is lower at the wing tip compared to the wing root due to the wingtip vortices at increased angles of attack.

The aircraft loses height with more or less level wings. Loss of lift is felt around the centre of gravity of the aircraft and the CP moves rearwards. The nose drops and angle of attack is reduced.

The separated and turbulent airflow from the root affects the empennage and aerodynamic buffet will provide a warning of the approaching stall to the pilot.

At low speeds, the dynamic pressure is low and greater control surface deflection will be required to achieve the same response. The flight controls will feel unresponsive or sloppy. It is important that the stall and recovery occurs without much wing drop.

title: What is the effect of ice accretion on a propeller?
optionA: Icing forms on the inner part of the propeller and reduces its efficiency by 20%.
optionB: Icing forms on the outer part of the propeller and reduces efficiency by 30%.
optionC: Icing does not form on a propeller and has no impact on its efficiency.
optionD: Icing forms on the outer part of the propeller and reduces efficiency by 25%.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
PROPELLER ICING.

Ice on an aerofoil changes its properties, reducing lift and increasing drag for a given angle of attack. Ice on a propeller blade reduces the efficiency of the propeller and reduces thrust. In addition, the weight of the ice increases the aircraft weight and therefore the lift required. If ice builds on an unprotected propeller, thrust reduces and you might not be able to climb out of the icing conditions or maintain the altitude.

  • The greatest quantity of ice normally collects on the spinner and inner radius of the propeller.
  • The estimated propeller efficiency loss is on the order of 15%-20%.

title: The critical Mach number of a conventional aerofoil section decreases if:
optionA: it is flown at lower angles of attack.
optionB: its thickness to chord ratio is reduced.
optionC: its leading edge radius is increased.
optionD: its camber is decreased.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
CRITICAL MACH

At the point where the first hint of supersonic air flow occurs above the wing, the aerofoil is said to be at its critical Mach number.

OBTAINING A HIGHER CRITICAL MACH NUMBER

  • In order to obtain a high critical Mach number from an airfoil at some low lift coefficient the section must have:
    1. Low thickness ratio. The point of maximum thickness should be aft to smooth the pressure distribution.
    2. Low camber. The mean camber line should be shaped to help minimize the local velocity peaks.
  • If supersonic flight is a possibility the thickness ratio and leading edge radius must be small to decrease wave drag.
SUMMARY:
In supersonic flight the streamline curvatures are small and the requirement is for slender, indeed sharp, leading edges for the inlet in order to reduce the pressure drag associated with bluntness-induced shock detachment.
MCRIT decreases when the airflow over the upper surface of the wing is given greater acceleration. Its speed will then reach M=1 at a lower speed. Increasing leading edge radius gives the aerofoil a thicker, more rounded leading edge, which gives greater airflow acceleration.

title: Why should excessive use of rudder be avoided when turning on a swept-wing aircraft?
optionA: “Rudder reversal” may occur. The aircraft will yaw the wrong way.
optionB: The aircraft will tend to roll in the wrong direction.
optionC: To avoid excessive structural loads on the fin.
optionD: The aircraft will tend to pitch-up.
explanationTotal: Incautious use of the rudder can generate excessively large aerodynamic loads on the fin. The fin is attached to the fuselage by bolts. If excessive aerodynamic force is created by large rudder deflections, the bolts can shear, resulting in the fin separating from the fuselage.

title: Longitudinal static stability is created by the fact that the:
optionA: centre of gravity is located in front of the neutral point of the aeroplane.
optionB: aeroplane possesses a large trim speed range.
optionC: wing surface is greater than the horizontal tail surface.
optionD: centre of gravity is located in front of the leading edge of the wing.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
A variation of CG position can cause large changes in the static longitudinal stability. In the conventional airplane configuration, the large changes in stability with CG variation are primarily due to the large changes in the wing contribution.

As the CG is gradually moved aft, the airplane static stability decreases, then becomes neutral then unstable. The CG position which produces zero slope and neutral static stability is referred to as the “neutral point”. The neutral point may be imagined as the effective aerodynamic center of the entire airplane configuration, i.e. with the CG at the neutral point, all changes in net lift effectively occur at that point and no change in pitching moment results. The neutral point defines the most aft CG position without static instability.

For an airplane to always have positive longitudinal static stability the CG must be ahead of the neutral point, so that the wing-pitching moment always exceeds the tail plane pitching moment. The further aft the neutral point is from the CG the greater is the static longitudinal stability.

title: If the elevator becomes jammed, then the:
optionA: Aeroplane can only be controlled by the use of a stabiliser trim.
optionB: Elevator trim tab’s effect will be reversed.
optionC: Elevator trim will become inoperative.
optionD: Static longitudinal stability is reduced.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Trim tabs are fitted to enable the pilot to set a required angle of deflection of the primary control surface and maintain that deflection. However, they are not suitable for jet airplanes because of their large range of operating speeds, preference, for this type of airplane, is given to the trimmable horizontal stabilizer. There are two types of trim tab in common use: the variable and the fixed.
The variable trim tabs may be manually or electrically controlled. If manually controlled, then trim wheels located on the center console are used.
For the elevator trim if the tab is deflected up the cockpit indication is nose-down and if the trim tab is deflected down the cockpit indication is nose-up. To remain in trim and maintain level flight following a deceleration the trimmer control is moved to give a nose-up movement that causes the trim tab to move down, which makes the elevator move up. This does not affect the static longitudinal stability.
If the elevator becomes jammed, the trim tab will work as a small elevator itself and so its effect will be reversed.

title: Spiral dive mode, also known as spiral divergence, is a movement which can be described as (1) _____, and the airplane will naturally yaw and roll in (2) _____.
optionA: (1) non-oscillatory; (2) the same direction.
optionB: (1) non-oscillatory; (2) the opposite direction.
optionC: (1) oscillatory; (2) the same direction.
optionD: (1) oscillatory; (2) the opposite direction.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Spiral divergence will exist when static directional stability is very large when compared to the dihedral effect. The character of spiral divergence is not violent. The aeroplane, when disturbed from the equilibrium of level flight, begins a slow spiral which gradually increases to a spiral dive.

When a small sideslip is introduced, the strong directional stability tends to restore the nose into the wind while the relatively weak dihedral effect lags in restoring the aeroplane laterally. The rate of divergence in the spiral motion is usually so gradual that the pilot can control the tendency without difficulty.

It is therefore considered non-oscillatory and both yaw and roll moments will occur to the same side.

title: How can a pilot recognise static stick force stability in an aeroplane during flight?
optionA: When speed increases the pull force increases.
optionB: To maintain a speed below the trim speed requires a pull force.
optionC: The elevator stick force remains constant with speed changes.
optionD: To maintain a speed below the trim speed requires a push force.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
There is an increment of force dependent on the trim tab setting which varies with the dynamic pressure or the square of equivalent airspeed. Figure 1 indicates the variation of stick force with airspeed and illustrates the effect of tab setting on stick force.

In order to trim the airplane at point (1) a certain amount of up elevator is required, and zero stick force is obtained with the use of the trim tab. To trim the airplane for higher speeds corresponding to points (2) and (3), less and less aircraft nose-up tab is required.

Note that when the airplane is properly trimmed, a push force is required to increase airspeed and a pull force is required to decrease airspeed. In this manner, the airplane would have positive stick force stability with a stable “feel” for airspeed.

title: Why would a pilot choose to glide for minimum rate of descent after complete engine failure?
optionA: To give the maximum time to complete emergency drills before a forced landing or ditching.
optionB: To give the best chance of reaching a suitable forced landing aerodrome.
optionC: To give maximum airflow through jet engines, to assist a restart.
optionD: To glide as far as possible in a headwind.
explanationTotal: If you’re more interested in staying in the air as long as possible to either fix the problem or to communicate your intentions and prepare for a forced landing, then minimum sink speed is what you’ll need.

title: During take-off, the right slat does not extend. What might happen on rotation?
optionA: Right wing will stall on rotation after the flaps have been retracted.
optionB: Left wing will stall on rotation after the flaps have been retracted.
optionC: Right wing will stall on rotation.
optionD: Left wing will stall on rotation.
explanationTotal:
Leading-edge slats increase the wing's chamber area and mean aerodynamic chord (MAC), thereby increasing its coefficient of lift (CL) maximum, which reduces the aircraft's stall speed. The mass flow over the upper surface is increased and so is its energy when air flows through the venturi-shaped slot.

These effects combine to delay the forward movement of the separation point as angle of attack increases. The stall is delayed until a higher angle of attack is reached.

The wind where the slats did not extend (right) will stall at a lower angle of attack than the left wing.

title:
Refer to figure.
The point in the annex showing zero lift is:
optionA: point D.
optionB: point C.
optionC: point A.
optionD: point B.
explanationTotal:
The graph directly indicates zero lift coefficient at point A, which also corresponds to zero lift. You can also have a look at the following formula, showing that a lift coefficient being zero results in a lift of zero.

Lift = lift coefficient x air density/2 x velocity2 x area

Note: do not get confused that point A is on the negative side (negative angle of attack). It's because this (cambered) profile already creates lift with an angle of attack of 0°.

title: What is correct about wingtip vortices? They are...
optionA: Stronger with a high aspect ratio.
optionB: Stronger in clean configuration.
optionC: Not related to aspect ratio.
optionD: Stronger at high speed.
explanationTotal:
WING-TIP VORTICES

Wing-tip vortices are created by span-wise airflow over the upper and lower surfaces of a wing/aerofoil that meet at the wing tips as turbulence and therefore induces drag.

Span-wise airflow is created because a wing producing lift has a lower static pressure on the upper surface than on the lower surface. At the wing tip, however, there can be no pressure difference, and the pressure is equalized by air flowing around the wing tip from the higher pressure on the lower surface to the lower pressure on the upper surface. There is therefore a span-wise pressure gradient, i.e., pressure changing along the wing span.

  • One of the primary factors which determine the magnitude of the vortices is the angle of attack. For a given speed, the wing lift, and thus the magnitude of the tip vortices, increases with the angle of attack. Slow, heavy, clean" are the three major conditions generating stronger wing vortices. Extending the flaps increases the coefficient of lift (CL), which means that for a given speed, a lower angle of attack will be required, which reduces the wing tip vortices strength.

“Stronger with a high aspect ratio” and “Not related to aspect ratio”. Incorrect. The magnitude of the wingtip vortices is inversely proportional to aspect ratio

title: Which statement concerning the local flow pattern around a wing is correct?
optionA: By fitting winglets to the wing tip, the strength of the wing tip vortices is reduced which in turn reduces induced drag.
optionB: Slat extension, at a constant angle of attack and normal extension speeds, will increase the lift coefficient, which will also increase the induced drag coefficient.
optionC: Sweepback reduces drag since, compared with a straight wing of equal area, the span increases.
optionD: Vortex generators on the wing partially block the spanwise flow over the wing leading to a reduction in induced drag.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
INDUCED DRAG
Whenever a wing produces lift, concentrated vortices form at the wing tips. The vortices are strongest at the wing tips and become progressively weaker toward the centre-line of the aircraft.

It is the production of lift itself which reduces the magnitude of the lift force being generated. To replace the lift lost by the increased downwash, the aircraft must be flown at a higher angle of attack. This increases drag. This extra drag is called induced drag.

The stronger the vortices, the greater the induced drag.

Wing tip modifications reduce the leakage of airflow around the wing tip and limit the size of the vortex.

WINGLETS

These are small vertical aerofoils which form part of the wing tip. Shaped and angled to the induced airflow, they generate a small forward force. Winglets partly block the air flowing from the bottom to the top surface of the wing, reducing the strength of the tip vortex.

title: For an aeroplane certified under CS-23, VNE is the maximum speed...
optionA: an aeroplane can be flown at with flaps extended.
optionB: at which the aeroplane may be flown in cruise.
optionC: at which the aeroplane may be flown.
optionD: which must not be exceeded in a dive.
explanationTotal:
VNE – The maximum IAS that must never be exceeded and is shown as a red line across the speed arc
on the ASI.

title: The load factor is less than 1 (one):
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: in steady wings level horizontal flight.
optionB: during a push-over manoeuvre.
optionC: during recovery after a wings level stall.
optionD: during a steady horizontal turn.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The balance of forces in steady climb show thrust is partly acting upwards and weight is partly adding to the drag.
Because the thrust is now assisting lift, there is less lift required than in level flight. For steady speed, the thrust and two effects of aerodynamic drag and weight must be equal.

T= Thrust
W= Weight
D= Drag
T= D + W sin(alfa)

This means that the climb angle (sin alfa) depends on excess thrust and weight.
In descent the formula will become T= D – W sin(alfa)
The load factor is the relationship between lift and weight. As the lift in a stall is decreased and the load factor in straight and level flight is 1, the load factor will now be less than 1. The steeper the climb-/descent angle, the lower the load factor.
A push-over manoeuvre is a manoeuvre where there is more weight than lift.
A negative G-force is therefore generated and the load factor is less than 1.

title: V<sub>FE</sub> means the:
optionA: Maximum speed with flaps extended.
optionB: Speed at which the critical engine is assumed to fail during take-off.
optionC: Design flap speed for procedure flight conditions.
optionD: Maximum flap extension or retraction speed.
explanationTotal:
CS 25.1511 Flap extended speed

The established flap extended speed VFE must be established so that it does not exceed the design flap speed VF chosen under CS 25.335 (e) and 25.345, for the corresponding wing-flap positions and engine powers.

Here are the different speeds with the associated visual indicators (colored arcs) of an airspeed indicator:

White arc:

  • Lower limit – VS0: stalling speed with flaps extended.
  • Upper limit – VFE: maximum speed with flaps extended.
Green Arc:
  • Lower limit – VS1: stalling speed in clean configuration.
  • Upper limit – VN0: maximum speed in normal operation.
Yellow arc:
  • Lower limit – VN0: maximum speed in normal operation.
  • Upper limit – VNE: Red Line - never exceed speed.

title: Which statement about minimum control speed is correct?
optionA: Crosswind is taken into account to determine V<sub>MCG</sub>.
optionB: V<sub>MCL</sub> is determined by maximum rudder only.
optionC: V<sub>MCA</sub> depends on the airport density altitude, and the location of the engine on the aeroplane (aft fuselage or wing).
optionD: The nose wheel steering control may be used to determine V<sub>MCG</sub>.
explanationTotal:
VMCA: Minimum Control Speed in Take-off Configuration
The speed at which the critical engine fails, and it is still possible to maintain straight flight (max. heading change 20º, no dangerous attitude occurs, no exceptional pilot skill required) with a maximum bank angle of 5º.

The major factor that affects VMC is the difference in engine thrust. VMC will therefore be lower at higher airport elevations and at a higher OAT, due to the associated lower thrust. Conversely, VMC will be higher at lower airport elevations and at a lower OAT.

If conditions are hot, high and humid the air is less dense. This reduces thrust and, consequently, when you lose the critical engine on take-off, there is less yawing effect from asymmetric thrust than there would be in denser air.

Furthermore, in case of engine failure, the yaw depends on the Moment Arm. The yaw is less on engines located on the aft fuselage.

title: An aeroplane’s flight path angle is defined as the angle between its:
optionA: lateral axis and the horizontal plane.
optionB: speed vector and its longitudinal axis.
optionC: longitudinal axis and the horizontal plane.
optionD: speed vector and the horizontal plane.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Angle of attack is the difference between pitch attitude and flight path angle.
It is defined as the angle between the chord of an airfoil and the relative wind.

Flight path angle is the angle between the horizon and the flight path (speed vector).
Also called climb or descent angle.

Pitch angle is the angle between the horizon and longitudinal axis of the aircraft, it is equal to Flight path angle + Angle of attack.

Bank angle is the angle between the lateral axis and the horizon.
Bank is rotated around the longitudinal axis, but during a bank at level flight, the angle between the longitudinal axis and the horizon does not change.
The angle between the lateral axis and horizon does.

title:
Which of the following statements is correct?

I. A higher limit load factor allows the manufacturer to design for a lower stick force per g.
II. The stick force per g is a limitation on aeroplane's operation, which the pilot can determine from the Aeroplane Flight Manual.
optionA: I. is correct, II. is incorrect.
optionB: I. is correct, II. is correct.
optionC: I. is incorrect, II. is incorrect.
optionD: I. is incorrect, II. is correct.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
MANOEUVRING STABILITY

Whenever an aircraft is manoeuvring, acceleration forces act on it (if, for example, the aircraft is pulling out of a dive, its flight path will be curved and the resultant pitching velocity provides aerodynamic damping in pitch due to the downward movement of the tailplane).

The tailplane provides the largest contribution toward damping in pitch, although other aircraft components such as the wings do assist. A graph of stick force versus load factor illustrates the manoeuvring stability of an aircraft.

The gradient of the graph should be positive (with increasing load factor the stick force must also increase). This gradient must not be excessively high or the aircraft would be difficult and tiring to manoeuvre. Conversely, it should not be too low or the stick forces would be too light and the aircraft could be over-stressed.

The maximum load factors which must be allowed for during maneuvers are shown in an envelope of load factor against speed (EAS).

  • If a higher limit load factor is set by the manufacturer, there's more margin for the aircraft to be controlled inside the envelope and therefore a lower stick force per g may be set. Statement I is correct.
  • The limit load factors will depend on the design category of the aircraft. For example, the limit load factor for modern high-speed jet transport aircraft is -1.0 g and 2.5 g. This value is stated in the Aircraft Flight Manual to be consulted by the pilot and should bever be exceeded. However, the stick force per g is not listed in the AFM. Statement II is incorrect.

title: What data may be obtained from the Buffet Onset Boundary chart?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: The values of the Mach number at which low speed and Mach buffet occur at different masses and altitudes.
optionB: The values of the Mach number at which low speed and shock stall occur at different masses and altitudes.
optionC: The values of M<sub>MO</sub> and V<sub>MO</sub> at different masses and altitudes.
optionD: The values of M<sub>CRIT</sub> at different masses and altitudes.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The buffet onset boundary chart has both high and low speed limits.
The low speed buffet boundary marks the onset of the pre stall buffet with a 10% margin above stall speed.
The high speed buffet boundary marks the onset of high speed buffeting.
This speed is Mmo most of the time, sometimes it is slightly below.

These speeds come closer together as altitude increases.
At a certain altitude the aircraft can encounter the so called “Coffin corner”.
The speeds for high and low speed buffeting are very close together here, and thus it is easy to stall or hit Mmo.
The coffin corner is a dangerous situation and is supposed to be avoided, as a slight amount of turbulence could cause the aircraft to stall.

The speeds for high and low speed buffeting are dependent on weight, altitude, load factor and CG position.
On the buffet onset boundary chart we will find the variables for altitude, weight and load factor.

The margins between high and low speed buffeting can be decreased by:

- Higher aircraft weight
- Higher altitude
- Higher load factor
- More forward CG position

title: Assuming no compressibility effects, induced drag at constant IAS is affected by:
optionA: engine thrust.
optionB: aeroplane mass.
optionC: outside air temperature.
optionD: altitude.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The total drag is the resulting factor if you add induced drag and parasite drag together. It acts in the direction of the relative wind. Lift is perpendicular to the relative wind.

Parasite drag is caused if an airfoil is moving through the air. It is the result of form drag and skin friction drag. Form drag arises from the shape of the object. The more streamlined the object, the less form drag is present. Shape and size are most important in the amount of form drag resulting. Form drag increases with increasing velocity, making it very important for high speed aircraft. Skin friction drag is caused by the friction of the fluid (in case of aircraft this fluid is the atmosphere) against the skin of the object moving through it. It is directly related to the surface area in contact with the fluid. Skin friction increases with the square of the velocity.

Induced drag is caused when an object redirects the airflow. A wing produces lift by creating a pressure difference. This pressure difference is caused by the shape of the airfoil, causing the airflow on top to accelerate, creating a low pressure on top of the wing and high pressure below the wing. This pressure difference naturally wants to restore towards a uniform pressure, which creates vortices around the wingtip. These vortices are deflected downwards, this phenomenon is also called downwash. The induced drag decreases with airspeed (with a rate of 1/V²) and increases with angle of attack and increasing weight.

In the image we can see that the two vectors (induced and parasite drag) create a resulting vector, the total drag. Where the induced and parasite drag vectors collide, we have the minimum drag speed (VMD); the speed where the total drag is the lowest.

This leads us to understand that during an acceleration from a total stand still, the total drag first decreases up until the minimum drag speed and then starts increasing again.

title: Considering the effect of wing downwash on the direction of the airflow approaching the tailplane, when flaps are extended the tailplane’s negative angle of attack...
optionA: increases, decreasing the tailplane’s effectiveness.
optionB: increases, increasing the tailplane’s effectiveness.
optionC: decreases, decreasing the tailplane’s effectiveness.
optionD: decreases, increasing the tailplane’s effectiveness.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

Tail plane effective angle of attack is determined by the downwash from the wing. If the flaps are lowered, the downwash will increase. This increased downwash will result in a higher angle of attack of the tailplane => increasing its effectiveness and producing a greater lift and causing a nose-up pitching moment.

title: An aeroplane has a stall speed of 100 kt. When the aeroplane is flying a level co-ordinated turn with a load factor of 1.5, the aeroplane will stall in this turn at:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionC: 82 kt.
explanationTotal:
Given that the equation to find the new stall speed is:

VS = VS1G √n

And given that VS1G = 100 kt and n = 1.5

VS = 100 √1.5
VS = 122 kt

title:
During training flights, it is normal to demonstrate accelerated stalls. These are carried out at speeds below 90kt and are induced by using excessive stick inputs to pull up during stall recovery. Spiral dives are also manoeuvres which are demonstrated during training flights. In this case, as the spiral dive develops, the speed is allowed to increase to 130kt. Considering the aeroplane limitations given below, which statement is correct?

VS: 45 kt
VA: 100 kt
VNO: 125 kt
VNE: 160 kt
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Careful application of the elevator must be used to recover from the spiral dive in order to avoid an excessive load factor.
optionB: The aeroplane may suffer an excessive load factor and damage during the stall recovery exercises.
optionC: If too much elevator is used to recover from the spiral dive, the aeroplane may stall and enter a spin.
optionD: The rudder must be used to roll the wings level from the spiral dive, as the ailerons may cause excessive wing bending.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
"The aeroplane may suffer an excessive load factor and damage during the stall recovery exercises." Incorrect.

  • The question's mention of "excessive" stick inputs, creates the impression that the aircraft might experience a high load factor and potential damage during recovery exercises. Nevertheless, the fact that they limit the speed increase to only 130 kt, well below VFE, minimizes the actual risk of structural damage.

"If too much elevator is used to recover from the spiral dive, the aeroplane may stall and enter a spin." Incorrect.

  • If excessive pulling occurs and surpasses the critical angle of attack, the aircraft will stall. However, what the examiner likely intends is that when initially employing ailerons to level the wings and recover from a spiral dive, there's no need for an "excessive" application of elevator. The essence of the statement is to emphasize not pulling too hard at the detection of a spiral dive but prioritizing leveling the wings first. It's crucial to recall that in a spiral dive, the wings are not yet stalled, making it imperative to first halt the rolling moment and then initiate a pull to recover lost altitude. In contrast, a spin involves a stall, necessitating a recovery process of pushing the control stick initially, followed by maintaining neutral ailerons and applying rudder in the opposite direction of the spin.

"The rudder must be used to roll the wings level from the spiral dive, as the ailerons may cause excessive wing bending." Incorrect.

  • In contrast to a spin, a recovery from a spiral dive involves initially leveling off to counteract the excessive static directional stability relative to lateral stability, thereby stopping the rolling moment. It's crucial to execute this maneuver cautiously to prevent any potential structural damage. If the rudder is applied before the ailerons in this situation, additional stress is imposed on the airframe because the aircraft is already in a nose-down attitude with a sideslip, further banking due to directional stability. This is why stall escape maneuvers or upset recovery procedures in commercial airliners explicitly avoid instructing the use of the rudder pedals.

title: During flight testing, the minimum control speeds are established. The V<sub>MCG</sub> must be established with (1) _____ CG position and (2) _____ the use of nose wheel steering.
optionA: (1) most unfavorable; (2) without
optionB: (1) most unfavorable; (2) with
optionC: (1) forward; (2) with
optionD: (1) forward; (2) without
explanationTotal:
VMCG, the minimum control speed on the ground, is the calibrated airspeed during the takeoff run, at which, when the critical engine is suddenly made inoperative, it is possible to maintain control of the aeroplane using the rudder control alone (without the use of nose wheel steering) to enable the take-off to be safely continued using normal piloting skill.

The rudder control forces may not exceed 150 pounds (68.1 kg) and, until the aeroplane becomes airborne, the lateral control may only be used to the extent of keeping the wings level. In the determination of VMCG, assuming that the path of the aeroplane accelerating with all engines operating is along the centre of the runway, its path from the point at which the critical engine is made inoperative to the point at which recovery to a direction parallel to the centre line is completed may not deviate more than 30 ft (9.144 m) laterally from the centre line at any point.

As with VMCA, this must be established with:

  • maximum available take-off power or thrust on the engines.
  • the aeroplane trimmed for take-off.
  • the most unfavourable CG position.
  • maximum sea level take-off weight.
Because the aircraft rotates around the CG, the position of the CG directly affects the length of the rudder arm and, thus, the power of the rudder and fin to maintain directional stability and control. The ‘worst case’ is with the CG at the aft limit. If the requirements can be met in this configuration, the ability to maintain directional control will be enhanced at any other CG location. A more forward CG decreases VMCG.

title: According to CS-23 and CS-25 an aeroplane must have controllable stall characteristics and be able to recover control at or slightly beyond the stalling angle of attack. Which of the statements that follow is a factor that, if certain design measures are not taken, might hinder the ability to meet the mentioned requirements?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Straight wings tend to stall at the root first, which creates a large nose-down pitching moment.
optionB: Tapered wings tend to stall at the tips first, making the aeroplane too stable in roll.
optionC: Highly cambered aerofoils tend to provide little or NO warning when approaching the stall.
optionD: Aft swept wings tend to stall at the tips first, which may create a nose-up pitching moment.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Wing sweep is a tendency for first stalling the wingtip and a pitch-up moment. Both are unwanted stall characteristics which can lead to a deep stall.

This tendency can be reduced by design modifications (wing fences, vortilons and saw tooth leading edges) which minimize the root-to-tip spanwise flow of the boundary layer. These devices delay tip stall. Vortex generators are also frequently used on a swept wing to delay tip stall and improve the stall characteristics.

The wing root can also be encouraged to stall first. This can be done by modifying the aerofoil section at the root, fitting stall strips and by fitting less efficient leading edge flaps (Kruger flaps) to the inboard section of the wing.

During the recovery ailerons can be used with smooth and coordinated application of rudder.

title: Static lateral stability will be increased by:
optionA: reducing the size of the vertical tail.
optionB: the use of a high, rather than low, wing mounting.
optionC: increasing wing anhedral.
optionD: reducing wing sweepback.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
The lateral static stability is a measure of the airplane’s tendency to return to the wings-level attitude after a disturbance has caused the airplane to be disturbed in the rolling plane.

Positive lateral static stability is the tendency of the airplane to roll to the left with a positive sideslip angle, nose to the left. Its ability to recover is dependent on the effect of sideslip.

A disturbance in the rolling plane causes the angle of attack of the upgoing wing to decrease and the angle of attack of the down going wing to increase. Provided the airplane is not flying close to the stalling speed, then the upgoing wing produces less lift than it did before the disturbance and the down going wing will produce more lift than it did. Together, these changes result in a rolling moment in opposition to the initial disturbance and have a ‘roll-damping’ effect. When the roll damping exactly matches the aileron torque the airplane has a steady rate of roll.

The airplane design features that increase the lateral static stability are:

  • dihedral.
  • sweepback.
  • high-wing mounting.
  • increased effective dihedral.
  • large, high vertical fin.
  • low CG.
The airplane design features that decrease the lateral static stability are:
  • anhedral.
  • forward-swept wings.
  • ventral fin.
  • low-wing mounting.
  • extending inboard flaps.

title: An aircraft is flying in the speed unstable region of the drag curve when a disturbance causes its airspeed to decrease. If the pilot maintains a constant thrust setting and altitude, the total drag will (1) _____ and the aircraft's IAS will (2) _____.
optionA: (1) increase; (2) increase.
optionB: (1) increase; (2) decrease.
optionC: (1) decrease; (2) increase.
optionD: (1) decrease; (2) decrease.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Learning Objective 081.01.05.07.05: Explain what happens to the IAS and drag in the non-stable region if speed suddenly decreases and why this could occur.

Looking at the figure above, we can see two distinct regions of the drag curve for speed stability. Below VMD the aircraft is speed unstable, whereas above VMD the aircraft is speed stable. Speed stability simply means a disturbance to the sped will return back to the equilibrium, whilst speed instability is the opposite.

As the aircraft is situated in the speed unstable region, a sudden decrease in speed will cause the total drag to increase, whilst the thrust remains the same. A thrust deficit will be created.

This thrust deficit, assuming no change in pitch is made to the aircraft, will result in a further decrease in airspeed until the aircraft cannot maintain altitude and stalls.

title: What is correct regarding the effect of displacement drag and impingement drag on take-off performance? There is a (1) _____ effect in case of a rejected take-off and a (2) _____ effect for continued take-off.
optionA: (1) positive; (2) positive
optionB: (1) negative; (2) positive
optionC: (1) positive; (2) negative
optionD: (1) negative; (2) negative
explanationTotal:
Fluid contaminants contribute to stopping force by:
  • Resisting forward movement of the wheels (i.e., causing displacement drag); and,
  • Creating spray that strikes the landing gear and airframe (i.e., causing impingement drag).

A slower acceleration due to an increase in drag as the aircraft tyres plow through the contaminant (displacement drag) and a spray of contamination is created which strikes the landing gear and airframe (impingement drag) can be expected => it has a negative effect on take-off distance and positive effect on rejected take-off distance.

Note: We assume that EASA refers to the rejected take-off distance only, rather than the ASDR (the runway required to accelerate to VR and bring the aircraft to a complete stop).

title: You are in the cruise, allowing the aircraft to accelerate with the autopilot engaged. The pilot observes the control trim moving continuously, and the aircraft is struggling to maintain level flight. What should the pilot do in this situation?
optionA: Leave the autopilot connected as any intervention from the pilot will worsen the situation.
optionB: Disconnect the autopilot and try to recover the situation.
optionC: Protect the movement of the CG so it doesn't exceed the limits.
optionD: Switch off the electrical master switch to remove power to the system.
explanationTotal:
Note: The feedback for this question was incomplete. Please send any further exam feedback to us in the comments or via email to info@atplquestions.com, so we can correct any differences and verify the answer, thank you!

There are two scenarios that this could be. Faulty autopilot or trim runaway. A faulty autopilot would be exactly as it sounds, the autopilot is inputting the incorrect command into the control system, and the feedback loop is not working correctly to fix it. The fix for this situation would be disconnecting the autopilot. Of course, the pilots must then be aware that the trim will be set massively different from normal, so the forces will be high upon autopilot disconnect.

The other situation is a trim runaway. It is difficult to tell from the question whether this is the situation or not. A trim runaway is where the electric trim system of an aircraft continues changing the trim angle, without command from the pilots. It could be due to the trims themselves, or the trims commanded by the autopilot. It is then up to the pilot to choose whether to disconnect the autopilot or not, as leaving the autopilot running reduces the forces the pilots have to bear, but disconnecting could fix the problem entirely.

We would say that as the aircraft is already struggling to maintain altitude, disconnecting the autopilot is the best bet, and the pilots can switch off the electric trim and use the manual one if the problem has not been fixed.

title: A windmilling propeller:
optionA: produces more thrust than drag.
optionB: produces neither thrust nor drag.
optionC: has a greater blade angle than a feathered propeller.
optionD: degrades the glide performance of an aeroplane.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

In the event of an engine failure both the engine and the propeller will slow down. The CSU will attempt to maintain the selected RPM by driving the propeller blades to a fine position that will continue until reaching the fine pitch stop.
Despite the engine failing the airplane still has forward speed, for a single-engine airplane due to the glide descent the forward speed causes the propeller to have a negative angle of attack due to the direction of the relative airflow. This angle of attack generates sufficient torque to rotate the unpowered propeller in the normal direction of rotation.
The component of the force at right angles to the plane of rotation now acts rearwards and is no longer thrust but is now drag and presents a flat disc to the direction of travel.
Because the propeller is being driven only by the relative airflow it is said to be wind milling. As such, it causes a considerable amount of drag, reduces the IAS, reduces the Lift/Drag ratio and increases the rate of descent.

title:
Given the following information, calculate the Thrust vector in a straight and steady power-on descent with an angle of 30°.

Weight: 11350 kg
Lift: 10320 kg
Drag: 11010 kg
optionA: 5335 kg
optionB: 1181 kg
optionC: 11010 kg
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The balance of forces in steady climb show thrust is partly acting upwards and weight is partly adding to the drag.
Because the thrust is now assisting lift, there is less lift required than in level flight.
For steady speed, the thrust and two effects of aerodynamic drag and weight must be equal.

T= Thrust
W= Weight
D= Drag
T= D + W sin(y)

This means that the climb angle (sin y) depends on excess thrust and weight.

In descent the formula will become T= D – W sin(y)

The load factor is the relationship between lift and weight.
As the lift is now decreased and the load factor in straight and level flight is 1, the load factor will now be less than 1.

Solving this excercise:

Thrust = drag- (W * sin(angle) )
Thrust = 11010- (11350 * sin (30) )
Thrust= 5335

title: Due to a mechanical failure, the flaps are only extended in one of the wings. What will happen?
optionA: The aircraft will roll to the side where the flaps are extended and yaw to the same direction of the roll.
optionB: The aircraft will roll to the side where the flaps are not extended and yaw to the direction of the wing with extended flaps.
optionC: The aircraft will roll and yaw to the side where the flaps are extended.
optionD: The aircraft will roll and yaw to the side where the flaps are not extended.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Since flaps significantly change the aerodynamic characteristics of the wing both by increased lift and increased drag, abnormal asymmetric operation of the augmentation device could seriously jeopardise flight safety by asymmetrically loading the wings.

If the situation is allowed to progress unchecked, it will result in a pronounced roll towards the wing with the lessor amount of flap extended. In this case, it is possible that the induced roll could exceed the amount of aileron authority available and could result in a spin or other loss of control situation.

In all cases of asymmetric flap, the wing with the greater amount of flap extended is producing a substantially higher amount of lift. At the same time, increased drag on the flaps-down side creates a pronounced adverse yaw situation, with the nose swinging toward the wing with most flaps deflected.

title: What is the SI unit of measurement for power?
optionA: Pa
optionB: J
optionC: N
optionD: W
explanationTotal:
Power
P = W ÷ Δt [J ÷ s = W]

Symbol W represents the unit watt.

title:
Refer to figure.
X, Y and Z in order of corresponds to:
optionA: Blade angle, helix angle, angle of attack.
optionB: Helix angle, blade angle, angle of attack.
optionC: Angle of attack, helix angle, blade angle.
optionD: Helix angle, angle of attack, blade angle.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The Blade Angle

Sometimes called the pitch angle, is the angle subtended between the plane of rotation and the chord line of the propeller blade, which may be fixed or variable. When the aeroplane is moving it comprises two parts, the angle of attack and the helix angle, but when it is stationary the blade angle is equal to the angle of attack.

The Helix Angle

The angle that the actual path of the propeller makes to the plane of rotation.

Angle of Attack

The path of the propeller through the air determines the direction of the relative airflow. The angle between the blade chord and the relative airflow is the angle of attack (α).
The angle of attack (α) is the result of propeller rotational velocity (RPM) and aircraft forward velocity (TAS

title: Immediately above M<sub>CRIT</sub> in the transonic speed regime, at a constant angle of attack, stall speed will...
optionA: decrease at high altitudes.
optionB: remain constant until reaching the lower end of the transonic speed regime.
optionC: remain constant until reaching the upper end of the transonic speed regime.
optionD: increase at high altitudes.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The stall speed is defined by:

VS=√((2∗W)/(ρ∗S∗CLMAX))

At the stalling angle CLMAX and S are constant, and the indicated airspeed is given by the dynamic pressure 1/2ρV2 . Therefore, for the same airplane mass and configuration in straight and level flight, if the slight difference between EAS and IAS caused by compressibility is ignored, an airplane will stall at the same IAS at all altitudes.

If, however, compressibility is not ignored then the stalling IAS value slowly increases with increased altitude, but the change only becomes significant at very high altitudes.

At a constant EAS, Mach number will increase as altitude increases.

Figure 1 shows the variation of stalling speed with altitude at constant load factor (n). Such a curve is called the stalling boundary for the given load factor, in which altitude is plotted against equivalent airspeed.

At this load factor (1g), the aircraft cannot fly at speeds to the left of this boundary. Over the lower range of altitude, stall speed does not vary with altitude. This is because at these low altitudes, the Mach number at VS is too low for compressibility effects to be present. Eventually (approximately 30000 ft), Mach number at VS has increased with altitude to such an extent that these effects are important, and the rise in stalling speed with altitude is apparent.
As altitude increases, stall speed is initially constant then increases, due to compressibility.

title: An aircraft with a 1 g stalling speed of 70 kt and limit load factor of 2.5 would have a VA of...
optionA: 111 kt.
optionB: 175 kt.
optionC: 44 kt.
explanationTotal:
VA - is the design maneuvering speed. This is the highest speed at which the airplane will stall before exceeding the maximum load factor and does not need to exceed VC. It is not less than the stalling speed with the flaps retracted multiplied by the square root of the limiting load factor at a speed of VC.
VA is not shown on the ASI, but it should be placarded close to the ASI. For a normal category light airplane having a maximum load factor of 3.8g then:

VA = VS1g ∗ √3.8 = 1.95VS1g

If only one value of VA is quoted, then it is the speed at which the airplane will stall at the maneuvering load factor at the MTOM.

In this exercise, the 1g stalling speed is 70kt and a limiting load factor of +2.5g is imposed:

VA = VS1g ∗ √n
VA = 70 ∗ √2.5
VA ≈ 111 kt

title: Ice contamination during flight will result in:
optionA: Increasing stall speed and increasing critical angle of attack, reduced CLMAX.
optionB: Increasing stall speed and decreasing critical angle of attack, increased CLMAX.
optionC: Increasing stall speed and decreasing critical angle of attack, reduced CLMAX.
optionD: Decreasing stall speed and decreasing critical angle of attack, increased CLMAX.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The formation of ice and frost on the airframe will:
- modify the profile of the aerofoil.
- increase the roughness of the aircraft surface.
- increase the weight of the aircraft.

The formation of ice along a wing's leading edge greatly alters its aerodynamic contour and leads to premature separation of the boundary layer. This reduces the wing's stalling angle of attack and also its maximum coefficient of lift by up to 50%.

Lift (CLMAX)

The larger the angle of attack, the larger the decrease of CL with a maximum decrease at CLMAX

Drag

More skin friction drag results in overall more drag and earlier boundary layer separation. In significant icing condition, ice build-up can also increase the form or pressure drag

Stall Speed

Due to decrease of CLMAX and increase of the aircraft weight, stall speed will increase.

Critical Angle of Attack

Increased surface friction results in quicker flow separation. This reduces the critical angle of attack and a stall will occur sooner.

Stability

The decreased CLMAX of the tailplane could cause a stal when the aircraft is flying at low speed and with an increased downwash due to flap extension. A tailplane stall will result in loss of longitudinal control. The changed CL of the main wing will create some small changes in the pitching moment.

title: An aircraft with a far aft CG location enters a spin, which becomes fully developed. Which of the following aircraft attitudes would be most likely in this scenario?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: A nose up pitch of more than 20 degrees.
optionB: Increasing nose down pitch with increasing speed.
optionC: Nose level.
optionD: The CG position does not affect the spin attitude of the aeroplane.
explanationTotal:
Flat spins are the worst and most dangerous type of spin. In a flat spin, the aircraft has no forward airspeed. It spins around its vertical axis as it sinks straight towards the ground.

Due to the high angle of attack of a flat spin, it is nearly impossible to recover, as the horizontal stabilizer is most likely in stall, too. The only possibility then is to move the CG forward. In small aircraft what you can do is to lean forward and hope for the best.

The type of spin a plane enters depends mainly on the CG Position (and thrust setting):

  • CG towards the forward limit makes an aircraft more stable, and control forces will be higher which makes it less likely that large, abrupt control movements will be made. When trimmed, the aeroplane will tend to return to level flight if the controls are released, but the stall speed will be higher.

  • CG towards the aft limit decreases longitudinal static stability and reduces pitch control forces, which tends to make the aeroplane easier to stall. Once a spin is entered, the further aft the CG, the flatter the spin attitude.

All in all, do not spin with an aircraft that is not designed for that or with too aft CG position.

Note: Watch the following video to understand the attitude of the aircraft during a flat spin https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=22eADnRqMwo&t=16s

title: From the following types of propeller, which is most efficient over a wide range of true airspeeds?
optionA: High-solidity propeller
optionB: Variable-pitch propeller
optionC: Left-rotating propeller only
optionD: Fixed-pitch propeller
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
The propeller blade is an aerofoil and the definitions for chord, camber, thickness/chord ratio and aspect ratio are the same as those given previously for the wing.

BLADE ANGLE OR PITCH

The angle between the blade chord and the plane of rotation. Blade angle decreases from the root to the tip of the blade (twist) because rotational velocity of the blade increases from root to tip.

CONSTANT SPEED PROPELLERS
