Modern aircraft have propellers which are controlled automatically to vary their pitch (blade angle) so as to maintain a selected RPM.

Veriable pitch propellers permit high efficiency to be obtained over a wider range of TAS, giving improved take-off and climb performance and cruising fuel consumption.

This type of propellers enable the pilot to select the RPM for maximum power or maximum efficiency and a propeller governor varies the propeller pitch angle as required to maintain the selected RPM.

title: An aeroplane in straight and level flight is subjected to a strong vertical gust. The point on the wing, where the instantaneous variation in wing lift effectively acts is known as the:
optionA: neutral point.
optionB: centre of thrust.
optionC: aerodynamic centre of the wing.
optionD: centre of gravity.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
THE AERODYNAMIC CENTRE

There is a point along the chordline at which the pitching moment, CM, remains the same no matter what the angle of attack. In other words, the pitching moment coefficient is constant at the zero lift value, CM0. This is the aerodynamic centre (AC) of the aerofoil.

Regardless of camber, aerofoil thickness or angle of attack the AC is located at a point approximately 25% of the chordline from the leading edge of the aerofoil for subsonic flight, rarely is it forward of 23% or aft of 27%. For supersonic flight it is at a point approximately 50% from the leading edge, which increases the static longitudinal stability. It is the point about which all lift changes effectively act.

title: An airfield is reporting low temperatures and high surface pressure. What is the effect that these conditions have on a propeller aircraft performing a go-around?
optionA: Yaw and roll will be less powerful. V<sub>MC</sub> will be unchanged.
optionB: Yaw and roll will be more powerful. V<sub>MC</sub> will be higher.
optionC: Yaw and roll will be less powerful. V<sub>MC</sub> will be higher.
optionD: Yaw will be more powerful. V<sub>MC</sub> will be lower.
explanationTotal:
VMC is defined as the minimum speed, whilst on the ground, that directional control can be maintained, using only aerodynamic controls, with one engine inoperative (critical engine on two engine airplanes) and take-off power applied on the other engine(s).

VMC is an indicated air speed, so theoretically it would not be affected by air density. However, if an engine failure occurs, the engine can produce more power in higher air density, which means that the yawing moment in higher air density will also be larger, and the force produced on the rudder is greater.

The angle of attack of the rudder is limited by its maximum deflection, therefore a higher speed (VMC) will be needed to create more counter-yawing force on the rudder and maintain the aircraft under control.

title: Assuming ISA conditions and a climb below the tropopause at constant Mach number and aeroplane mass, the:
optionA: lift coefficient decreases.
optionB: IAS decreases.
optionC: TAS remains constant.
optionD: lift coefficient remains constant.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The Mach number is defined as the ratio between the TAS and the LSS (Local speed of sound).
It is an indication of how fast an aircraft is travelling with relation to the sound waves that surround it.

The Mach number may be calculated as follows:

M=TAS/LSS=(TAS(kt))/(38.95∗√(T(K)))

The speed of propagation of small pressure waves depends upon the temperature of the air ONLY.

The Indicated Airspeed is defined by dynamic pressure:

IAS=1/2∗ρ∗TAS2

Effect on IAS of Climbing at a constant Mach number:

  • Temperature decreases with increasing altitude, so the speed of sound will decrease as altitude is increased.
  • If altitude is increased at a constant Mach number, the TAS decreases. Therefore, IAS also decreases.

title: Dutch roll is the result of a strong (a)_____ lateral stability and a weak (b)_____ stability.
optionA: (a) static; (b) static longitudinal
optionB: (a) static; (b) static directional
optionC: (a) static; (b) dynamic directional
optionD: (a) dynamic; (b) dynamic longitudinal
explanationTotal:
DUTCH ROLL

Basically speaking, Dutch roll is a series of out-of-phase turns, when the aircraft rolls in one direction and yaws in the other. When the yaw is introduced, the strong “dihedral effect” will roll the aircraft due to the lift increase on the wing into wind. The increased induced drag on the rising wing will yaw the aircraft in the opposite direction, reversing the coupled oscillations.

This might occur when the lateral stability is large compared to the directional stability.

To reduce the aircraft tendency to Dutch roll, either the lateral stability should be decreased or the directional stability increased => anhedral would decrease the lateral stability.

title: Which of these statements concerning propellers is correct?
optionA: The blade angle of a feathered propeller is approximately 180 degrees.
optionB: The blade angle of a feathered propeller is approximately 0 degrees.
optionC: A windmilling propeller causes less drag than a feathered propeller.
optionD: A feathered propeller causes less drag than a windmilling propeller.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
To prevent the propeller from ‘wind milling’ the propeller blade is rotated from the fine-pitch stop through the coarse-pitch stop to reach the angle of attack to the relative airflow that produces zero lift; and referred to as ‘feathering’ the propeller. It’s usually approximately 85°/90° because it is the best compromise for the whole blade length and accounts for the blade twist.
This blade position stops the propeller from rotating because there is no lift force to produce a torque reaction; it reduces the drag to a minimum level and prevents damage being caused to the engine.
For a single-engine airplane feathering the propeller blades improves the glide performance because it does not require such a steep glide angle to maintain the required airspeed. As such, feathering the propeller increases the gliding range and endurance. For a multi-engine airplane, the decreased drag reduces the amount of thrust required to counteract the asymmetric force of the propeller of the failed engine and there is sufficient rudder authority remaining to enable the pilot to safely control the airplane.

title: You are flying a crop duster in the utility category with a VSO of 45 kts and a VS1 of 54 kts. What is the VA speed?
optionA: 66 kt
optionB: 113 kt
optionC: 122 kt
optionD: 94 kt
explanationTotal:
VA = VS1 x √limiting load

EASA CS23, load limits for utility:

Maximum +4.4 g
Minimum -1.76 g

  • VA = 54 x √4.4
  • VA = 113 kt

title:
Which of the following items are needed to correctly complete the statement? The characteristics of wing sweep include:

1. a decreased tendency to tip stall
2. increased take-off and landing distances
3. a higher stall speed
4. an increased effectiveness of trailing edge control surfaces
5. a decreased effectiveness of high lift devices.
optionA: 2, 3, and 5
optionB: 4 and 5
optionC: 1, 2, and 3
explanationTotal:
Sweep Angle: The angle between the line of 25% chords and a perpendicular to the root chord.

Purpose of Sweepback: To increase MCRIT.

Sweepback factsheet:

A Swept Wing Increases the Critical Mach Number (MCRIT). All other effects from a swept wing are by-products, most of them disadvantages. However, the benefits from a higher MCRIT outweigh the associated disadvantages.
Increased tendency to stall at the tip first:

  • Tip stall can lead to pitch-up, a major disadvantage.
  • Pitch-up can give the tendency for a swept wing aircraft to Super Stall.
  • Aircraft that show a significant tendency to pitch-up at the stall must be fitted with a stall prevention device, a stick pusher.
When compared to a straight wing of the same section, a swept wing is less aerodynamically efficient.
  • At a given angle of attack CL is less, which increases the stall speed.
  • CLMAX is less and occurs at a higher angle of attack.
  • The lift curve has a smaller gradient (change in CL per degree change in alpha is less).
  • Swept wings must be fitted with complex high lift devices, both leading and trailing edge, to give a reasonable take-off and landing distance.
  • A swept wing must be flown at a higher angle of attack than a straight wing to give the required lift coefficient; this is most noticeable at low speeds.
A swept wing makes a small positive contribution to static directional stability.
A swept wing makes a significant positive contribution to static lateral stability.
At speeds higher than MCRIT a swept wing generates a nose-down pitching moment, a phenomenon known as Tuck Under.
The hinge line of trailing edge ‘flap’ type control surfaces is not at right angles to the airflow, which reduces the efficiency of the controls.

title:
Sweepback of a wing positively influences:

1. static longitudinal stability.
2. static lateral stability.
3. dynamic longitudinal stability.

The combination that regroups all of the correct statements is:
explanationTotal:
Sweep Angle: The angle between the line of 25% chords and a perpendicular to the root chord.

Purpose of Sweepback: To increase MCRIT.

Sweepback factsheet:

A Swept Wing Increases the Critical Mach Number (MCRIT). All other effects from a swept wing are by-products, most of them disadvantages. However, the benefits from a higher MCRIT outweigh the associated disadvantages.

Increased tendency to stall at the tip first:

  • Tip stall can lead to pitch-up, a major disadvantage.
  • Pitch-up can give the tendency for a swept wing aircraft to Super Stall.
  • Aircraft that show a significant tendency to pitch-up at the stall must be fitted with a stall prevention device, a stick pusher.
When compared to a straight wing of the same section, a swept wing is less aerodynamically efficient.
  • At a given angle of attack CL is less, which increases the stall speed.
  • CLMAX is less and occurs at a higher angle of attack.
  • The lift curve has a smaller gradient (change in CL per degree change in alpha is less).
  • Swept wings must be fitted with complex high lift devices, both leading and trailing edge, to give a reasonable take-off and landing distance.
  • A swept wing must be flown at a higher angle of attack than a straight wing to give the required lift coefficient; this is most noticeable at low speeds.

A swept wing makes a small positive contribution to static directional stability.

A swept wing makes a significant positive contribution to static lateral stability.

At speeds higher than MCRIT a swept wing generates a nose-down pitching moment, a phenomenon known as Tuck Under.

The hinge line of trailing edge ‘flap’ type control surfaces is not at right angles to the airflow, which reduces the efficiency of the controls.

title: Decreasing the aspect ratio of a wing:
optionA: increases induced drag.
optionB: decreases stall speed.
optionC: increases gust load.
optionD: decreases induced drag.
explanationTotal:
Wing tip vortices increase if we increase induced drag. This can be caused by for example increased speed, density or lift coefficient. If we increase Angle of Attack, lift will be increased, also increasing the strength of wing tip vortices.

Another factor increasing wing tip vortices is the aspect ratio (λ) of the wing.
This is the ratio of the wing span to its mean chord.
The aspect ratio of the wing is equal to the square of the wingspan divided by the wing surface area.
Therefore a short but wide wing has a low aspect ratio but a long, narrow wing has a high aspect ratio.
With a lower aspect ratio, the induced drag is higher, thus increasing wing tip vortices.
With a high aspect ratio, the induced drag is lower, reducing wing tip vortices.
We can therefore state that the relationship between wing tip vortices and aspect ratio is inversely proportional.

title:
Which of these statements about the strength of wing tip vortices are correct or incorrect?

I. Assuming no flow separation, the strength of wing tip vortices increases as the angle of attack increases.
II. The strength of wing tip vortices increases as the aspect ratio decreases.
optionA: I is correct, II is incorrect.
optionB: I is correct, II is correct.
optionC: I is incorrect, II is correct.
optionD: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
explanationTotal:
Wing tip vortices are a byproduct of lift. They are caused by the pressure differential between the top and bottom of the wing, which causes an updraft of high pressure air around the tip of the wing. This updraft turns into a downdraft behind the wing, creating a vortex. The higher the pressure difference between the top and bottom of the wing, the stronger the vortices.

This question is specifically asking for:

  • Angle of attack: The strength of the vortices (and therefore also induced drag) is proportional to the angle of attack. Therefore; the strength of the vortices increase as the angle of attack increases, hence statement 1 is correct!
  • Aspect ratio: The strength of the vortices is inversely proportional with the aspect ratio. Meaning that the strength of the wing tip vortices increase as the aspect ratio decreases, hence statement 2 is correct!

title: An aircraft is in a steady climb to high altitude at a constant thrust setting. The autopilot is set to maintain constant vertical speed. The danger associated with this autopilot selection is:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: The risk of a stall at high altitude.
optionB: The risk of exceeding M<sub>MO</sub>.
optionC: The risk of exceeding V<sub>MO</sub>.
optionD: The risk of exceeding V<sub>NE</sub>.
explanationTotal:
The autopilot's vertical speed mode allows you to perform constant-rate climbs and descents. In this mode, the vertical speed is prioritised over airspeed. When you engage the vertical speed mode, the FD/autopilot will attempt to maintain the specified vertical speed until you choose a different setting in autopilot, the aircraft reaches an assigned altitude set into the assigned altitude selector/alerter, or the autopilot is disconnected.

As altitude increases and the air gets thinner, the IAS will reduce for a given pitch setting. Consequently, the angle of attack also reduces. As a result, the vertical speed will reduce for a certain pitch attitude. The autopilot will therefore chase the selected vertical speed by pitching up. This results in further decreased IAS. Ultimately, this could lead to a stall.

title:
A light aircraft is flying straight and level at 110 kts and a CL of 0.42. Calculate the new CL, if the pilot immediately pulls into a climb with a load factor of 2.2.

CLMAX = 1.1
Aircraft mass = 1300 kg
optionD: Not able to calculate CL with the information provided
explanationTotal:
First off, if you are in level flight, load factor = 1.

Lift is directly proportional to CL and also load factor(LF).

It follows that New n = Original n x (New CL / Original CL), where original n = 1g
2.2 = 1 x (New CL / 0.42)
New CL = 0.92

title: Which statement best defines a periodic motion's dynamic stability when it doesn't increase over time?
optionA: Negative dynamic stability.
optionB: Positive dynamic stability.
optionC: Unstable motion.
optionD: Neutral dynamic stability.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Aircraft with neutral dynamic stability have oscillations that never dampen out. If a trimmed and neutrally dynamic stable aircraft is pitched up, it pitches nose low, then nose high again, and this oscillation continues, in theory, forever.

title:
Which of the following statements are correct with regard to a windmilling propeller on a twin-engine aeroplane?

1. Feathering the propeller may be delayed since windmilling produces more thrust than drag.
2. The aeroplane decelerates due to the propeller drag from the failed engine.
3. The yawing moment is intensified due to the propeller drag from the failed engine.
4. Low speed controllability of the aeroplane is increased due to increased stability.
5. Wing lift distribution varies due to airflow disturbance behind the propeller on the failed engine.
6. The glide performance of the aeroplane is improved due to the increased L/D ratio.
optionA: 2, 3, and 5
optionB: 1, 2, and 6
optionC: 3, 4, and 5
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
In the event of an engine failure both the engine and the propeller will slow down. The CSU will attempt to maintain the selected RPM by driving the propeller blades to a fine position that will continue until reaching the fine pitch stop.
Despite the engine failing the airplane still has forward speed, for a single-engine airplane due to the glide descent the forward speed causes the propeller to have a negative angle of attack due to the direction of the relative airflow. This angle of attack generates sufficient torque to rotate the unpowered propeller in the normal direction of rotation.
The component of the force at right angles to the plane of rotation now acts rearwards and is no longer thrust but is now drag and presents a flat disc to the direction of travel.
Because the propeller is being driven only by the relative airflow it is said to be wind milling. As such, it causes a considerable amount of drag, reduces the IAS, reduces the Lift/Drag ratio and increases the rate of descent.

title: If S is the frontal area of the propeller disc, propeller solidity is the ratio of:
optionA: S to the frontal area of one blade.
optionB: the total frontal area of all the blades to S.
optionC: the frontal area of one blade to S.
optionD: the mean chord of one blade to S.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
To increase power absorption, several characteristics of the propeller can be adjusted.
The usual method is to increase the ‘solidity’ of the propeller. Propeller solidity is the ratio of the total frontal area of the blades to the area of the propeller disc.

title: Compared with level flight prior to the stall, the lift (1) and drag (2) in the stall change as follows:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: (1) decreases (2) decreases.
optionB: (1) decreases (2) increases.
optionC: (1) increases (2) decreases.
optionD: (1) increases (2) increases.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The critical angle of attack is the angle of attack producing the maximum lift coefficient. If the aircraft increases angle of attack above this value, it will enter a stall. This value can be increased with the use of slats. Slats delay the separation of the boundary layer, by adding kinetic energy into it.

A clean wing has a lower value of CLMAX, causing the Angle of Attack for a clean wing to be lower than for a wing with slats extended. A wing with flaps extended has the lowest value of CLMAX.

In straight and level flight, prior to the stall, lift remains constant. Speed decreases and CL increases. In the stall (so after CLMAX has passed) the CL decreases again and speed is still low. Therefore lift decreases. The increased turbulent flow over the wing during the stall, the drag will be increased during the stall compared to the flight prior to the stall.

title: Regarding propeller efficiency and power absorption, increasing the chord of each propeller blade...
optionA: increases propeller efficiency and reduces power absorption.
optionB: reduces propeller efficiency and increases power absorption.
optionC: increases both propeller efficiency and power absorption.
optionD: does not affect propeller efficiency but increases power absorption.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The ability of a propeller to convert engine power into forward thrust is its power-absorption capability.

It is affected by:

  • the propeller-blade shape.
  • the number of propeller blades.
  • the propeller solidity.
Increasing the blade chord has the advantages that blade interference is reduced; the blade area is increased to transmit the power available within a set diameter and the power absorption is improved.
Its disadvantage is that it decreases the aspect ratio, consequently the lift, thrust and propeller efficiency.

title: A jet aeroplane is cruising at high altitude with a Mach number that provides a buffet margin of 0.3 g. In order to increase the buffet margin to 0.4 g the pilot must:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: fly at a larger angle of attack.
optionB: fly at a higher Mach number.
optionC: fly at a lower altitude and the same Mach number.
optionD: extend the flaps to the first selection.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Stall boundaries set a lower limit to the operating speed, according to the load factor. In the case of a high-speed aircraft, there is also an upper limit which is due to the approach of shock stall and the associated buffet which occurs if the aircraft enters the transonic speed range. The limits associated with these effects give the buffet boundaries.

The margin between the two types of stall narrows with increasing altitude. Notably the true airspeed of the low-speed stall increases with increasing altitude for a given indicated airspeed, whilst the true airspeed of the shock stall reduces up to the base of the tropopause, above which it remains constant.
The point at which the two stalls coincide is referred to as the 'coffin corner'. The altitude at which an aircraft can fly at one airspeed in a 1 g maneuver is called the aerodynamic ceiling. Since this condition has no safety margin, aircraft must be operated within a buffet margin of 0.3 g.
If this safety margin is to be increased, the aircraft must be flown at a lower altitude.

title: You are the pilot flying of a tailwheel aeroplane, with a single propeller turning clockwise from your point of view. During acceleration for take-off, you are forced to use considerable right rudder to keep the aircraft straight. This is because during the early part of the take-off run the propeller produces…
optionA: slipstream effect before the tail is lifted, and asymmetric blade effect after the tail is lifted.
optionB: gyroscopic precession before the tail is lifted, and slipstream effect after the tail is lifted.
optionC: asymmetric blade effect before the tail is lifted, and gyroscopic precession as the tail is lifted.
optionD: gyroscopic precession as the tail is lifted, and asymmetric blade effect only after the tail is lifted.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
On take-off, rotation of a single-engine propeller causes an aircraft to swing to one side, particularly those fitted with a tail-dragger undercarriage. The main causes of this are:

  • Slipstream effect
  • Torque reaction
  • Gyroscopic effect
  • Asymmetric blade effect

ASYMMETRIC BLADE EFFECT (figure 1)

This effect occurs when the axis of rotation of the propeller is inclined to the direction of flight. For example, when the tail wheel on a tail-dragger type aircraft is in contact with the ground, its longitudinal axis inclines above the horizontal.

This causes the down-going blade to have a greater effective angle of attack than the up-going blade, thus developing greater thrust .

The thrust asymmetry between the two blades causes the aircraft to yaw to the left.

GYROSCOPIC EFFECT (figure 2)
A rotating propeller has the properties of a gyroscope - rigidity in space and precession. The characteristic which produces “gyroscopic effect” is precession.

Gyroscopic precession is the reaction that occurs when a force is applied to the rim of a rotating disc. When a force is applied to the rim of a propeller, the reaction occurs 90° ahead in the direction of rotation and in the same direction as the applied force.

As the aircraft is pitched up or down or yawed left or right, a force is applied to the rim of the spinning propeller disc.

Note: Gyroscopic effect only occurs when the aircraft pitches and/or yaws.

For a clockwise rotating propeller:

Pitch down - forward force on the top, force emerges 90° clockwise, left yaw.
Left yaw - forward force on the right, force emerges 90° clockwise, pitch up.
Pitch up - forward force on the bottom, force emerges 90° clockwise, right yaw.
Right yaw - forward force on the left, force emerges 90° clockwise, pitch down.

title: How does the True Airspeed (TAS) vary during a descent above the troposphere with a constant Mach number?
optionA: TAS increases due to decreased air density.
optionB: TAS decreases due to decreased air density.
optionC: TAS remains the same.
optionD: TAS fluctuates unpredictably.
explanationTotal:
The Mach Number can be defined by the relation between True Airspeed (TAS) and Local Speed of Sound (LSS) as follows:

M = TAS ÷ LSS

If the Mach number is constant, it means that the above equation needs to be balanced. If one of the variables is changing (for example TAS), the other one (LSS) needs to change in the same way to equalize the relationship.

In the tropopause (above the troposohere), the Temperature is constant. Since the LSS is directly proportional to the temperature, it means the LSS is constant with decreasing altitude. Therefore, the TAS needs to be constant as well to balance the above equation and output a constant Mach number.

title: An large jet transport aeroplane has the following four flap positions: Up, Take-off, Approach and Landing and two slat positions: Retracted and Extended. Generally speaking, the selection that provides the highest positive contribution to C<sub>LMAX</sub> is:
optionA: slats from Retracted to Extended.
optionB: flaps from Take-off to Approach.
optionC: flaps from Up to Take-off.
optionD: flaps from Approach to Landing.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The sole effect that slats have is causing an increase in the maximum lift coefficient without increasing the overall coefficient of lift, see the diagram. Seeing as this is their only purpose it makes sense that they are more effective at this task than any notch of flaps. Therefore selecting slats from retracted to extended will create the highest positive contribution to CLMAX.

title: On a twin propeller aircraft, while performing a go-around, a yaw to the left would be more likely in an aircraft with (1) _____ propellers due to (2) _____.
optionA: (1) clockwise; (2) asymmetric blade effect
optionB: (1) clockwise; (2) gyroscopic effect
optionC: (1) counterclockwise; (2) asymmetric blade effect
optionD: (1) counterclockwise; (2) gyroscopic effect
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
At high propeller speeds and low forward speed (as in the take-offs, approaches to power-on stalls or go-around), the aircraft will have the tendecy to swing to one side, particularly those fitted with a tail-dragger undercarriage. The main causes of this are:

  • Slipstream effect
  • Torque reaction
  • Gyroscopic effect
  • Asymmetric blade effect

ASYMMETRIC BLADE EFFECT

This effect occurs when the axis of rotation of the propeller is inclined to the direction of flight. For example, when the tail wheel on a tail-dragger type aircraft is in contact with the ground, its longitudinal axis inclines above the horizontal.

This causes the down-going blade to have a greater effective angle of attack than the up-going blade, thus developing greater thrust .

On a clockwise rotating propeller, the thrust asymmetry between the two blades causes the aircraft to yaw to the left.

title: The Pilot of a light cargo aircraft has loaded a heavy piece of freight in the cargo bay. Due To the loading position, the centre of gravity is on the aft limit but moving the freight forward is difficult. Compared to a centre of gravity located in a more mid-position, the pilot will find that the stick- force stability is:
optionA: The same and positive
optionB: Higher and positive
optionC: Lower and positive
optionD: Neutral
explanationTotal:
The stick force gradient is the force required to change the load factor of the aircraft for a given amount. It has an upper and lower limit. This ensures acceptable control characteristics.

The stick force per g is dependent on:
  • Center of Gravity location; if the aircraft has more static longitudinal stability, the stick force per g will be higher. Therefore, a more forward CG means higher stick force per g.
  • Altitude; as altitude increases, aerodynamic damping decreases.

title: Consider a single engine aeroplane with a clockwise rotating propeller flying at a negative AoA. The P factor will move the thrust to the (1) _____ blade creating a (2) _____ yaw moment:
optionA: (1) downgoing; (2) right
optionB: (1) upgoing; (2) left
optionC: (1) upgoing; (2) right
optionD: (1) downgoing; (2) left
explanationTotal:
Asymmetric blade effect (also known as ‘P’ Factor)

Propeller blades are not flat, they are in fact shaped as small wings. As a consequence, as the angle of attack of the airplane increases, the air passing by hits the blades differently. It's way more common to study the effect of P factor from a perpective of a positive angle of attack (i.e. during take-off). However, in this case, we are confronted with a situation of negative angle of attack.

In such case (negative angle of attack), the up-going blade will have a larger angle of attack compared to the down-going blade, generating more thrust. This then means that the up-swinging (left) blade exerts a greater force than the down-going blade. This difference in thrust will give a yawing moment to the right with a clockwise rotating propeller in a nose-up attitude.

title: An aeroplane leaving the ground effect after take-off will experience...
optionA: an increase in induced drag.
optionB: a reduction in wing-tip vortices.
optionC: a nose-down pitching moment.
optionD: an increase in form drag.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
When an airplane flies at a height equal to or less than the length of its wingspan the efficiency of its wings is considerably improved. A low wing airplane, just before touchdown, experiences a 50% reduction of its total drag. This phenomenon is ground effect.
Ground effect occurs because the surface alters the airflow pattern around the wings. Primarily, the surface restricts the formation of the wingtip vortices.
When an aircraft enters ground effect during the landing phase of flight, the sudden increase in lift and reduction in drag cause it to experience a floating tendency. The aircraft also tends to pitch nose-down due to the reduction in download on the tail plane.
The magnitude of the wing tip vortices, and thus downwash, also determine the amount of induced drag produced by the wing. The closer the aircraft is to the surface, the greater the reduction in induced drag at any given angle of attack.

Aircraft entering ground effect:

  • Downwash decreases.
  • The effective angle of attack increases.
  • Increased lift during landing if the angle of attack remains constant.
  • The induced angle of attack decreases.
  • Induced drag decreases.
Aircraft leaving ground effect:
  • Downwash increases.
  • The effective angle of attack decreases.
  • Decreased lift during take-off if the angle of attack remains constant.
  • The induced angle of attack increases.
  • Induced drag increases.

title: You are climbing to your aerodynamic ceiling in a busy class bravo airspace and you experience windshear that increases the AOA, what will happen to your low speed mach buffet?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Increases
optionB: Decreases
optionC: Does not change
optionD: Decreases then increases
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
Windshear will cause an increased angle of attack, which in turn will increase lift and load factor. Increasing either gross weight or load factor (G factor) will increase the low speed buffet and decrease Mach buffet speeds.

title: Which of the following may occur when taking off in icing conditions?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: The aeroplane will develop a nose down moment and the effect is worse with flaps extended.
optionB: The aeroplane will develop a nose up moment and the effect is worse with flaps retracted.
optionC: The aeroplane will develop a nose up moment and the effect is worse with flaps extended.
optionD: The aeroplane will develop a nose down moment and the effect is worse with flaps retracted.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
Note: Our initial feedback said that this came from a Performance exam, but we think that may be incorrect, as there are no Performance LOs close to this topic, but in Principles of Flight, the LO 081.03.01.05.08 pertains to it exactly. Please let us know if you see it in your exam, and which exam that is, thank you!

TAILPLANE STALL
Whilst it is not immediately identifiable by the question, this is asking about tailplane stalls due to icing.

The tailplane (or horizontal stabiliser) is a second wing mounted at the rear of the aircraft to allow for stability, and for control (with the elevator), and in fact, is usually used to provide downwards lift to keep the aircraft's nose up, and counteract the weight/lift couple (which pushes the nose down).

The tailplane is often quite a lot thinner than the main wing, so it builds up ice quicker, and means that tailplane stall due to icing can occur when there is little to no main wing ice accretion.

A tailplane stall is made worse by the extension of flaps, as they increase the downwash from the main wing, which causes a larger negative angle of attack on the tailplane, which is more likely to stall the tailplane. Flaps also move the centre of pressure further back, which increases the Cg/Cp (Weight/Lift) couple, which means the elevator needs to create more downforce to keep the nose up.

As the downforce from the tail decreases due to tail stall, there is a strong nose-down moment created. This is made worse - as mentioned above - by the use of flaps. The worst speed/configuration for this type of stall is just under the maximum flap speed (VFE), with flaps extended.

title: Vortex generators (1)_____ boundary layer separation by (2)_____.
optionA: (1) delay; (2) adding energy to it.
optionB: (1) delay; (2) keeping the flow laminar.
optionC: (1) force; (2) making the flow turbulent.
optionD: (1) force; (2) adding drag to it.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Flow separation occurs because the boundary layer loses kinetic energy as it flows against the adverse pressure gradient.

Increasing the kinetic energy of the boundary layer will reduce flow separation. Simple devices called vortex generators are used to re-energize the boundary layer.

Vortex generators are small plates, vanes, blades or wedges mounted in spanwise rows along the wing surface.

Each vortex generator produces a vortex at its tip which will induce high energy air from the free stream flow to mix with the boundary layer, thus increasing its kinetic energy and with retarding separation.

title: For an aircraft with a wingspan of 20 m, at which of the following heights above a runway would the highest induced drag be felt?
optionA: 60 ft
optionB: 30 ft
optionC: 10 ft
optionD: 120 ft
explanationTotal:
When an aircraft flies close to the ground, the downwash of air causing induced drag has nowhere to go, it is stopped by the fixed ground beneath. Therefore, being close to the ground decreases downwash and decreases induced drag. This is called ground effect.

Ground effect increases as an aircraft flies closer to the ground, so the lowest height would give the lowest induced drag. Obviously then, the highest induced drag would occur when at the greatest height above the ground.

Ground effect is usually cited as taking effect at approximately half the wingspan of height (which would be 30 ft here), as that is when it becomes significant and noticeable, but as with everything in aerodynamics, it is not a binary effect (on or off), it is a gradual change, so the correct answer here is simply the greatest height.

title: A tapered wing will have a taper ratio of...
optionA: less than 1.
optionB: more than 1.
optionC: equal to 1.
optionD: less than 0.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
A tapered wing means that the wing chord line gets shorter going from root to tip. The chord of the wing is long at the root but shorter at the tip. Tapered wings are structurally very strong, as the wing root is a lot bigger, allowing for a stronger connection to the fuselage, and the wing gradually gets thinner towards the wingtip where less reinforcement is required.

There are some aerodynamic benefits to tapered wings as well, which includes a small reduction in induced drag, due to the majority of the lift coming from the wing closer to the root.

One of the problems with a tapered wing is the stall handling. On a rectangular wing, the stall begins at the back near the root, whereas on a tapered wing, the stall will begin near the tip instead, which leads to the aileron area becoming stalled, and losing aileron (roll) control (see first annex above).

The taper of a wing is measured by the taper ratio, which is simply

Taper ratio = tip chord / root chord

So if the taper ratio is 0.5, the wingtip is half as wide as the root. Any number less than 1 indicates that the wing is tapered. 1 means the chord stays the same along the whole wingspan, more than 1 would be a wing that gets wider.

title: Which type of aeroplane and situation will experience a larger decrease in induced drag at heights between ground level and a wingspan?
optionA: High wing on take-off
optionB: Low wing on take-off
optionC: High wing on landing
optionD: Low wing on landing
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
Short explanation:
During landing, a low wing aircraft experiences a reduced amount of lift reduction compared to a high wing aircraft because of its wing's proximity to the ground. This proximity generates a ground effect, which increases lift and reduces drag, resulting in a more stable and controlled landing. In comparison, during takeoff, a high wing aircraft has the advantage of a clearer view of the runway, while a low wing aircraft may have a portion of its wing blocked by the runway surface, reducing lift.

Ground effect occurs because the surface alters the airflow pattern around the wings. Primarily, the surface restricts the formation of the wingtip vortices. This results in a reduction in the amount of induced downwash behind the wing and increases the wing’s effective angle of attack.

THE INFLUENCE OF GROUND EFFECT ON LANDING

  • When an aircraft enters ground effect during the landing phase of flight, the sudden increase in lift and reduction in drag cause it to experience a floating tendency. The aircraft also tends to pitch nose-down due to the reduction in download on the tailplane.

THE INFLUENCE OF GROUND EFFECT ON TAKE-OFF

  • During the take-off phase of flight, as the aircraft leaves ground effect the wing tip vortices rapidly grow in magnitude producing an increase in downwash behind the wing. This causes a reduction in the lift produced at a given angle of attack and the associated rapid increase in induced drag may prevent a successful take-off. The increased downwash acting on the tailplane increases the download, resulting in a nose-up pitching moment.

Based on the above, we can say that the answer must be one that includes "Landing".

Ground effect has greater effect on low wing aircrafts than high wing aircrafts due to being closer to the ground.

title: A tricycle-shaped aircraft with a propeller turning in a clockwise direction frequently demonstrates a tendency to veer to the left during takeoff. What fundamental aerodynamic phenomenon is behind this behaviour?
optionA: Torque effect generated by the clockwise propeller rotation
optionB: P-Factor causing increased thrust on the left side
optionC: Weight imbalance on the left landing gear
optionD: Spiralling slipstream created by the clockwise-rotating propeller
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The high-speed rotation of an aircraft propeller gives a corkscrew or spiraling rotation to the slipstream. At high propeller speeds and low forward speed (as in the take-offs and approaches to power-on stalls), this spiraling rotation is very compact and exerts a strong sideward force on the aircraft’s vertical tail surface.

When this spiralling slipstream strikes the vertical fin, it causes a yawing moment about the aircraft’s vertical axis.The more compact the spiral, the more prominent this force is. On clockwise-rotating propellers, the spiralling slipstream causes a yawing moment to the left.

As the forward speed increases, however, the spiral elongates and becomes less effective. The corkscrew flow of the slipstream also causes a rolling moment around the longitudinal axis.

title:
A large jet aircraft is designed to be operated with a positive longitudinal stability and is equipped with a Fly-By-Wire (FBW) system. Prior to each flight, the pilots input the aircraft mass and CG location into the Flight Management System (FMS). The aircraft's FMS then informs the FBW system of this data, allowing for the correct control forces and limitations to be used, giving flight envelope protection and ensuring stability is maintained.

Consider what will happen to the aircraft's high altitude handling characteristics if the pilot inputs the INCORRECT CG position into the FMS, located forward of the actual CG position. Which of the following statements is correct?
optionA: Due to the design criteria applied, the longitudinal stability of the aircraft is always ensured, irrespective of the location of the CG.
optionB: The actual longitudinal stability is lower than calculated by the FBW system, and the system may allow for control surface deflections that result in instability.
optionC: The aircraft consumes more fuel than expected during the cruise phase of the flight, as the FBW system deflects the horizontal stabiliser more to counteract the error of the pilot.
optionD: The pitch rates commanded by the FBW system are lower at higher altitudes compared to the pitch rates required to ensure that the longitudinal stability remains positive.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
An aircraft's stability, and in particular its longitudinal stability (stability in pitch) is massively dependent on the location of the aircraft's Centre of Gravity (CG). As long as the CG is in front of the "neutral point", the aircraft will be longitudinally stable. The "neutral point" is a sort of average Centre of Pressure (CP) for the whole aircraft, and it goes towards where there are more aerodynamic surfaces. Think of a throwing dart, the front had a weight and the back has a set of fins, therefore a very far forward CG and a far back "neutral point". This is a very stable system.

A far forward CG therefore is a more stable condition. This also means a less manoeuvrable condition. Less manoeuvrability means that the pilot will have to push and pull harder on the controls to achieve the same result, as the control surfaces need to move further to achieve the same angular change. The controls feel "heavier" with a further forward CG, but the aircraft is more stable.

This can be counteracted by the Fly-By-Wire system, which uses the knowledge of the aircraft's weight and CG position to estimate the required control surface deflection, and make the controls feel the same as for any other CG position, so the pilot has the same control of the aircraft, no matter the weight or CG position. If the CG is further forwards, the FBW system will amplify the pilot's inputs more than normal in the pitch axis, to make the aircraft control as it would do "normally".

This means that, in this scenario, the pilot has entered an artificially far forward CG, so the FBW system will amplify the pilot's actions in pitch, but without any need to do so, as the CG is not actually that far forward. This could lead to overcontrolling of the aircraft by the fly-by-wire system, as the aircraft is not as stable as the FMS/FBW believes. The overcontrolling could potentially reduce the stability of the aircraft, or even cause instability.

As this question is easy to misread or misunderstand, we will quickly go through each option:

  • "Due to the design criteria applied, the longitudinal stability of the aircraft is always ensured, irrespective of the location of the CG."
    • Whilst this looks plausible, the longitudinal stability is not ensured (and will be reduced or removed) when the CG goes out of the aft limit.
  • "The actual longitudinal stability is lower than calculated by the FBW system, and the system may allow for control surface deflections that result in instability."
    • As mentioned above, this is correct, due to the incorrectly entered CG position, which may allow the FBW to overcontrol the aircraft. The aircraft is less stable than the FBW system believes.
  • "The aircraft consumes more fuel than expected during the cruise phase of the flight, as the FBW system deflects the horizontal stabiliser more to counteract the error of the pilot."
    • The aircraft will actually consume less fuel than expected, but because the aircraft expects a forward CG in the cruise, which causes the tailplane to produce more downforce, and requires more lift from the wing, causing higher drag. However, the aircraft actually has a further aft CG, so will burn less fuel than expected. This is also not connected to the FBW system creating larger deflections, that is an effect which would occur in this case, but has negligible effect on fuel consumption.
  • "The pitch rates commanded by the FBW system are lower at higher altitudes compared to the pitch rates required to ensure that the longitudinal stability remains positive."
    • This has nothing to do with the scenario mentioned in the question (incorrectly inputted CG location).

title:
Which of the following affect the setting of the stabiliser trim for take-off?

1. Flap setting
2. CG position
3. Actual take-off mass
4. Outside air temperature
optionA: 1 and 4 only
optionB: 1, 2, and 3
optionC: 2 and 3 only
explanationTotal:
The position of the CG directly affects the amount of trim necessary for the angle of attack required. A forward CG adds to the inherent longitudinal stability of the airplane; the pilot may run out of elevator up movement and be unable to maintain the required attitude. An aft CG decreases the longitudinal stability and makes the airplane more difficult or impossible to control in pitch.

The CG must always remain within the CG safe envelope to ensure that the airplane remains controllable in all phases of flight. The elevator trim or stabilizer trim setting must be preset to a value for take-off and initial climb that will ensure a minimum stick force during this critical stage of flight.
Usually, there is a graph in the airplane performance manual from which the setting appropriate to the total mass and CG position for take-off can be determined.

Factors that affect the stabilizer trim position for take-off are:

  • CG position
  • Take-off mass
  • Flap setting
In comparison with a correctly balanced airplane during take-off, the position of the stabilizer for a nose-heavy airplane requires nose-up trim from a decreased stabilizer angle of incidence.

title: The pilot's control input in a Fly-By-Wire system is:
optionA: linked by mechanical cables directly to the flight control surface.
optionB: converted into an electrical signal and linked via a computer to the flight control surface.
optionC: linked mechanically to a computer and then to the flight control surface.
optionD: linked by electrical wires directly to the flight control surface.
explanationTotal:
Fly by wire systems
A fly by wire control system is a powered system (irreversible) that uses electronic inputs to a solenoid servo valve instead of mechanical inputs from conventional powered controls. The pilot operates the controls, these can be a sidestick and rudder pedals or a conventional yoke with rudder pedals. These controls are fitted with transducers which convert the mechanical movement into an electrical output which is then amplified and processed by several computers. These computers provide the input for the servo valves which controls the movement of the hydraulic actuators attached to the flight control surfaces.

Advantages of fly by wire

  • Weight reduction, as there is no need for the long and heavy control cables this is a big reduction in the weight of the aircraft.
  • Pilot work load is reduced because the pilot is supported by the computers with automated features like auto trim and turn coordination.
  • Flight envelope protection, which can prevent the pilot from pitching up too much beyond the stalling angle of attack. It can limit the controls in such a way that the airframe will not endure Gforces out of the limits.
Disadvantages
  • Reliability, as conventional systems might give some indication of an upcoming failure, a fly by wire system can lose a computer would could result in loss of control. This means there is need for redundancy in the form of additional computers and hydraulic systems.

title: Which of the following conditions could result in the absence of a stall warning on a jet aeroplane?
optionA: Ice on the fuselage increasing the aeroplane's mass and leading to a stall at a higher speed.
optionB: Ice on the wings causing a stall at a lower angle of attack than the normal critical angle of attack.
optionC: Icing of the pitot tubes causing erroneous speed indications and leading to a stall at a higher indicated speed.
optionD: Ice on the tailplane causing premature boundary layer separation on the stabiliser.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The CL of an aerofoil increases with angle of attack up to a maximum (CLMAX). Any further increase above this stalling angle, or critical angle of attack, will make it impossible for the airflow to smoothly follow the upper wing contour, and the flow will separate from the surface, causing CL to decrease and drag to increase rapidly.

A stall is caused by airflow separation. Separation can occur when either the boundary layer has insufficient kinetic energy or the adverse pressure gradient becomes too great.

The formation of ice along a wing's leading edge greatly alters its aerodynamic contour and leads to premature separation of the boundary layer. This reduces the wing's stalling angle of attack and also its maximum coefficient of lift by up to 50%

The increase in stall speed due to ice formation is not easy to quantify, as the accumulation and shape of the ice formation is impossible to predict. Ice or frost must never be allowed to remain on any aerodynamic surfaces in flight, nor must ice, frost, snow or other contamination be allowed to remain on the aircraft immediately before flight.

title: Based on the two dimensional drag formula, drag is:
optionA: Proportional to the square root of the speed.
optionB: Proportional to the square of the speed.
optionC: Inversely proportional to the airspeed.
optionD: Proportional to speed.
explanationTotal:
The drag equation:
D = 1/2 p V2 S CD
  • From the formula, we can conclude that drag is proportional to the square of the speed.

title: In straight flight, as speed is increased, whilst trimming to keep the stick force zero:
optionA: the elevator and trim tab do not move.
optionB: the elevator is deflected further upwards and the trim tab further downwards.
optionC: both elevator and trim tab are deflected further downwards.
optionD: the elevator is deflected further downwards and the trim tab further upwards.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

There is an increment of force dependent on the trim tab setting which varies with the dynamic pressure or the square of equivalent airspeed. Figure 1 indicates the variation of stick force with airspeed and illustrates the effect of tab setting on stick force.

To trim the airplane at point (1) a certain amount of up elevator is required, and zero stick force is obtained with the use of the trim tab. To trim the airplane for higher speeds corresponding to points (2) and (3), less and less aircraft nose-up tab is required.

Note that when the airplane is properly trimmed, a push force is required to increase airspeed and a pull force is required to decrease airspeed. In this manner, the airplane would have positive stick force stability with a stable “feel” for airspeed.

title:
When speed is increased in straight and level flight on a positively cambered aerofoil, what happens to the:

1. centre of pressure and
2. the magnitude of the total lift force?
optionA: 1 moves forward and 2 decreases.
optionB: 1 moves aft and 2 remains constant.
optionC: 1 moves aft and 2 increases.
optionD: 1 moves forward and 2 remains constant.
explanationTotal:
As we want to remain in straight and level flight, we know for sure that the lift required will remains constant.

Now that we know that lift remains constant, looking at the lift formula:

L = CL ½ rho v2 S

We can tell that to remain equal, as the speed is increasing we need to either decrease S or CL. Now assuming we don’t change any flaps settings, its clear we need to reduce the coefficient of lift. Reducing the coefficient of lift means applying a smaller angle of attack (AoA). And we know that reducing the AoA leads to a aft movement of the Centre of pressure, therefore the correct answer is: 1 moves aft and 2 remains constant.

title: The angle of attack of a propeller blade element is the angle between the blade element chord line and the:
optionA: propeller plane.
optionB: TAS vector.
optionC: propeller axis.
optionD: resultant airflow vector.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The path of the propeller through the air determines the direction of the relative airflow. The angle between the blade chord and the relative airflow is the angle of attack (α).
The angle of attack (α) is the result of propeller rotational velocity (RPM) and aircraft forward velocity (TAS).

title: What happens to the strength, the length, and the location of a normal shock wave when the Mach number (M) is increasing at positive lift? The strength of the shock wave...
optionA: decreases, its length decreases, and the shock wave moves downstream.
optionB: increases, its length increases, and the shock wave moves upstream.
optionC: decreases, its length decreases, and the shock wave moves upstream.
optionD: increases, its length increases, and the shock wave moves downstream.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
An airplane does not have to be flying at the local speed of sound for the airflow over the wings to be supersonic. A normal shockwave can develop at any time the airplane is in the transonic speed range. The function of the wing is to accelerate the air passing over its upper surface. The airflow may be subsonic at the leading edge of the wing but can be accelerated to become supersonic by the trailing edge of the wing, despite the fact that the airplane is flying at a speed of less than Mach 1.0. This is transonic flight, which usually occurs between Mach 0.75 and Mach 1.2.

At speeds less than Mach 0.75 all the airflow over the wing is subsonic and as the airplane accelerates the first shockwave will form on the upper surface at the wing root.
When the air over the upper surface of the wing becomes sonic, a shockwave forms because the pressure waves over the rear of wing at the wing root are attempting to move forward and meet the air moving aft from the leading edge at exactly the same speed but in the opposite direction. The meeting point is usually just aft of the point of maximum camber because this is where the air over the upper surface of the wing is accelerating at the greatest rate.

The meeting point of the two air-pressure waves is the shockwave and is where the airflow changes from being sonic or supersonic to become subsonic. Air passing through the shockwave experiences an increase of pressure, temperature, and density. If the airplane speed continues to increase the area of supersonic air on top of the wing spreads backward towards the trailing edge, resulting in the shockwave moving aft.

title:
Which statement is correct?

I. Stall speeds are determined with the CG at the aft limit.
II. Minimum control speeds are determined with the CG at the aft limit.
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: I is correct, II is correct.
optionB: I is correct, II is incorrect.
optionC: I is incorrect, II is correct.
optionD: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

  1. Stall speeds are determined with the least favourible CG position. For an aircraft, this is the most forward point because then the main wing will be producing the most lift. With the CG furthest ahead of the centre of pressure, the horizontal stabilizer will be producing a downwards force, which the main wings will have to compensate for by producing more lift. The main wings will therefore have to be at a higher angle of attack and therefore be closer to the stall.

Hence the stall will occur at higher speeds with a forward cg then with a rearward cg.

  1. Minimum control speeds are also determined with the least favourible conditions. When considering an engine failure, we know that the aircraft will rotate around its CG, but the distance of the moment doesn’t change when it moves fore or aft, the engines moment would only change when we move it along the lateral axis of the aircraft. However, the position of the CG will influence the rudder arm, and hence the rudder moment. A CG on the af limit will provide a small arm and therefore the least ability to oppose the yawing moment of the engine failure.

title: Consider a large transport jet aircraft with a conventional tail design in straight and level flight. The horizontal stabiliser (tailplane) will be producing a force (1) _____, which will (2) _____ as the indicated airspeed increases.
optionA: (1) upwards; (2) increase
optionB: (1) downwards; (2) increase
optionC: (1) upwards; (2) decrease
optionD: (1) downwards; (2) decrease
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
Note: this question is much too vague to be able to correctly work out in its current format. There are so many clarifying questions that need to be asked in order to work out the second part of the question correctly. Therefore, we will explain to you the basics here, then you can let us know if you see it in the exam, and what the correct answer was (or if the question/options were different at all), thank you!

This comes back to stability, and longitudinal stability in particular (stability in pitch). Think of a stable aircraft like a throwing dart, weight at the front, fins at the back, and it is incredibly stable flying through the air, always landing facing into the dartboard. This is the same for an aircraft, and we have to make our "weight" (Centre of Gravity, CG) in front of our "wings", which are dictated by the Centre of Pressure (CP)/Centre of lift (CL) of our wings and other aerodynamic features. The "neutral point" is the average location of the pressure effects from all our wings, fuselage, engine cowlings and other aerodynamic features, sort of the balanced centre of pressure of the whole aircraft.

As long as our CG is in front of our neutral point, then the aircraft will be longitudinally stable. Also, the weight, acting through the CG, is not in line with all the lift, acting through the CP. This means that the further forward weight will cause a nose-down moment. We obviously have to counteract this moment, and this is why the tailplane is tasked with providing a downwards force on the aircraft tail, causing a balancing nose-up moment.

Of course, the movement of the CG and CP can change how much downforce the tail needs to produce. If the CG moves further forwards, the tailplane has to produce higher downforce to counteract the larger nose down moment, and vice-versa.

The way that the tailplane produces downforce is two-fold. It usually has a low/negative angle of incidence, to provide a negative angle of attack, and the downwash from the wings causes an even larger negative angle of attack, particularly at high aircraft AoA (low speed), when the wing downwash angle is greater. This is why tailplanes have elevators, to change their angle of attack for control, and for trimming at different speeds.

This does not unfortunately help us get a solid answer for this question. Of course, the increased speed means a higher airflow over the tailplane, but also leads to decreased downwash angle from the main wing (due to lower angle of attack), but now with a more negative angle of attack without accounting for downwash due to the lower pitch angle of the aeroplane. These are opposing effects, and without knowing the aircraft and speed range, it is really very difficult to say whether the force increases or decreases. Our tendency is to say that the downwash angle and pitch angle mostly cancel each other out, and that the increased airflow increases the down-force of the tailplane.

We can also justify this by saying that when an aircraft gets faster, we have to trim down, which is us artificially decreasing the downforce of our tailplane via the elevator, this means the downforce must have been too large after the speed increase, therefore the force increased. We do not like having to use this as an justification, as there are other forces at play, but it works quite well for everyone to understand.

title: The calibrated airspeed in a twin-engine aircraft at which it is possible to maintain control of the aeroplane when the critical engine is suddenly made inoperative, and maintain straight flight with an angle of bank of not more than 5°, is called...
optionA: VMCG.
optionB: VMCL-2.
optionC: VMU.
optionD: V<sub>MC</sub>.
explanationTotal:
The minimum control speed (VMC) is the calibrated airspeed of an aircraft below which directional or lateral control of the aircraft can no longer be maintained after the failure of one or more engines.
At least one engine must still be operative for the VMC to apply. It depends on the stage of the flight.
At VMC the aircraft is still able to maintain straight flight with a bank angle of not more than 5 degrees.

title: Two identical aeroplanes A and B, with the same mass, are flying steady level co-ordinated 20 degree bank turns. If the TAS of A is 130 kt and the TAS of B is 200 kt:
optionA: the turn radius of A is less than that of B.
optionB: the lift coefficient of A is less than that of B.
optionC: the rate of turn of A is less than that of B.
optionD: the load factor of A is greater than that of B.
explanationTotal:
The formula for turning radius is as follows:

r = v2 / ( g * tan(bank angle) )
r = radius
v = velocity
g = gravitational constant (9.81, however in some questions stated to be 10)

From this formula we can derive that the radius of turn decreases with decreasing airspeed.

title:
Refer to figure.
Which line represents the total drag line of an aeroplane?
optionA: Line D.
optionB: Line C.
optionC: Line B.
optionD: Line A.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Plotting graphs of profile or parasite drag and induced drag on the same axes shows the relationship between them.

Adding these two drag values together at any given velocity produces a total drag curve. It is essential to remember that this curve only applies to an aircraft of constant weight and configuration in level flight at any given altitude.

Total drag is at its minimum when the profile or parasite drag, and induced drag are equal.

For an airplane at constant mass, acceleration from VS to VNE causes the total drag to decrease until VMD (Minimum
Drag Speed) is attained and then increase as shown in figure 1.

The value of parasite drag varies in proportion to the square of the IAS, whereas the value of the induced drag is
inversely proportional to the square of the speed.

title:
Which of these statements about the gust load factor on an aeroplane are correct or incorrect?

I. When the slope of the lift versus angle of attack curve increases, the gust load factor decreases.
II. When the wing loading increases, the gust load factor increases.
optionA: I is correct, II is incorrect.
optionB: I is correct, II is correct.
optionC: I is incorrect, II is correct.
optionD: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
A gust is a localized sudden and rapid change to the speed of the air in the atmosphere that can be either horizontal or vertical. The horizontal gust is of little importance because it causes a change to an airplane’s dynamic pressure that results in an insignificant change to the load factor. The vertical gusts are far more important because they change the effective angle of attack, total lift, and the load factor.
The gust load is the extra load imparted to the airplane by vertical gusts or turbulence. Its magnitude is unaffected by increased altitude but is increased with increased aspect ratio and/or decreased mass.
The load factor for any given angle of attack can be derived from the basic load factor for the normal cruise angle of attack because it is increased by the same percentage as the increase of angle of attack.
The load factor deriving from a gust is determined by the magnitude of the vertical velocity of the gust and the forward speed of the airplane.
Vertical gusts will affect the load factor (n) by changing the angle of attack of the wing.
For a given gust speed and aircraft TAS, the increment in the load factor depends on the increase in CL per change in angle of attack due to the gust (the slope of the lift curve). If the lift curve has a steep slope, the ‘g’ increment will be greater. Factors which affect the lift curve are aspect ratio and wing sweep.
Wings having a low aspect ratio, or sweep, will have a lower lift curve slope, and so will give a smaller increase in ‘g’ when meeting a given gust at a given TAS. Therefore, statement 1 is incorrect.
High wing loading reduces the ‘g’ increment in a gust. This is because the lift increment produced is a smaller proportion of the original lift force for the more heavily loaded aircraft.
For a given TAS and gust speed, the increase of lift will be proportional to the wing area. Therefore, the increase in load factor is inversely proportional to the wing loading.

Wing Loading = Weight/(Wing Area)

Therefore, statement 2 is incorrect.

title: During a steady glide, increasing descent angle will:
optionA: Both lift and weight will increase
optionB: Increase difference between lift and weight
optionC: Lift and weight will remain the same for the new angle of descent
optionD: Decrease difference between lift and weight
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Lift = W x cos y
(y equals the descent angle)

Increasing the descent angle does not change the weight (W), however "cos y" decreases. So lift decreases, and the difference between lift and weight increases.

title: How will the Centre of Gravity (CG) affect asymmetric yaw?
optionA: CG FWD will result in an increased yaw.
optionB: CG FWD will result in a reduced yaw.
optionC: CG AFT will result in a reduced yaw.
optionD: It is independent on CG.
explanationTotal:
Basically speaking, Asymmetric yaw is a result of the moment generated by the drag of the dead engine and the moment generated by the thrust of the live engine. The CG moves along the longitudinal axis which will not alter its distance to both engines => the Asymmetric moment is independent of the CG. However, the damping moment created by the vertical stabilizer depends on the CG position. 
  • If the CG moves forward, the damping moment increases. Consequently, Asymmetric yaw decreases.
If the airplane has an aft CG at the time of engine failure, the effective moment arm of the rudder is reduced, since all yawing movements take place about the CG. The greater the permissible limits in the travel of the CG, the larger the difference between the effect of engine failure at the two CG limits.

title: When an aeroplane wing’s angle of attack is increased, downwash causes the horizontal tailplane to experience...
optionA: a lower increase in angle of attack.
optionB: an initial lower angle of attack which then increases.
optionC: the same increase in angle of attack.
optionD: a higher increase in angle of attack.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The downwash of the airstream over the upper surface of the mainplane directly influences the effectiveness of the elevators of a fuselage-mounted tail plane. A change of downwash alters the effective angle of attack of the tail plane and the lift that it generates. This changes the pitching moment of the tail plane and requires a deflection of the elevators to maintain a given attitude.

For example, if a pitch-up attitude causes the angle of the downwash to increase then the effective angle of attack of the tail plane is decreased. Consequently, the restoring moment of the tail plane is decreased, and the longitudinal static stability is diminished. If such were the case the aircraft designer would have to move the CG forward to regain the longitudinal static stability of the airplane.

Note: In the figure, the "low speed" as a similar effect to a higher angle of attack.

title: An aerodynamic balancing device, which makes it possible for a large surface to be deflected by a relatively small control force, is called...
optionA: a servo tab.
optionB: a balance tab.
optionC: an anti-balance tab.
optionD: a horn balance.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The force required to operate the primary control surfaces, even using balance tabs, is often too great to be acceptable. To relieve the pilot of the need to apply so much force to operate the controls servo-tabs are fitted to carry out this function.
The servo-tab is a small tab hinged on the trailing edge of the primary control surface and linked directly to the control column. There is no direct link between the control column and the primary control surface.
The function and operation of the servo-tab is the same as the balance tab and moves the trim tab in the opposite direction to the movement of the primary control surface. However, at low IAS the servo-tab makes the main control surface less effective. The position of a servo-controlled primary control surface cannot be determined until a positive pressure is applied to the servo-tab by the airflow.

title: Determine the glide distance for an airplane with a L/D of 12 at an altitude of 10 km?
optionA: 10 km
optionB: 100 km
optionC: 120 km
optionD: 240 km
explanationTotal:
Glide Distance = Height Loss x Lift / Drag

A L/D ratio of 12 means that an aircraft will glide a distance of 12 km for each km of altitude lost (in still air).

The gliging range:

  • 10 x 12 = approx. 120 km

title: When is the airplane longitudinal stable?
optionA: When the CG is behind the CP/Neutral point
optionB: When the CG is at the CP/Neutral point
optionC: When the CG is in front of the CP/Neutral point
optionD: It is independent of the CG location
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
A variation of CG position can cause large changes in the static longitudinal stability. In the conventional airplane configuration, the large changes in stability with CG variation are primarily due to the large changes in the wing contribution.

  • As the CG is gradually moved aft, the airplane static stability decreases, then becomes neutral then unstable. The CG position which produces zero slope and neutral static stability is referred to as the “neutral point”.
  • For an airplane to always have positive longitudinal static stability the CG must be ahead of the neutral point, so that the wing-pitching moment always exceeds the tail plane pitching moment. The further aft the neutral point is from the CG the greater is the static longitudinal stability.

title: When descending with a constant TAS, what happens?
optionA: Mach speed decreses then increases.
optionB: IAS decreases.
optionC: IAS increases and then decreases.
optionD: Mach speed decreases.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Mach number = True Air Speed (TAS) / Local Speed of Sound (LSS)
LSS = 38.96 √ Absolute Temperature (K)

  • Below the tropopause, temperature decreases with increasing altitude. Local Speed of sound being only dependant on temperature, will increase during descent.
    Since TAS remains constant, as LSS increases => Mach Number decreases

title: The movement of the aerodynamic centre of the wing when an aeroplane accelerates through the transonic range causes:
optionA: an increase in static longitudinal stability.
optionB: a decrease in static directional stability.
optionC: a decrease in static longitudinal stability.
optionD: an increase in static directional stability.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The airplane should have sufficient longitudinal control power to attain the maximum usable lift coefficient or the limit load factor during maneuvers.
As shown in figure 1, forward movement of the CG increases the longitudinal stability of an airplane and requires larger control deflections to produce changes in trim lift coefficient.

For the example shown, the maximum effective deflection of the elevator is not capable of trimming the airplane at CLMAX for CG positions ahead of 18 percent MAC.
This control requirement can be most critical for an airplane in supersonic flight. Supersonic flight is usually accompanied by large increases in static longitudinal stability (due to aft CP movement) and a reduction in the effectiveness of control surfaces.

To cope with these trends, powerful all-moving surfaces must be used to attain limit load factor or maximum usable CL in supersonic flight.
This requirement is so important that once satisfied, the supersonic configuration usually has sufficient longitudinal control power for all other conditions of flight.

Note: When supersonic flight is being discussed, both the aerodynamic center (AC) and the center of pressure (CP) of a wing tend to shift towards the midpoint of the wing, which is typically around 50% of the chord.

title: The boundary layer will separate from the aerofoil immediately...
optionA: behind the shock wave on the lower wing surface.
optionB: in front of the shock wave on the lower wing surface.
optionC: behind the shock wave on the upper wing surface.
optionD: in front of the shock wave on the upper wing surface.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Critical Mach Number: (MCRIT) The critical Mach number is the Mach number of the aircraft when the speed of the airflow over some part of the aircraft first reaches the speed of sound.

At low subsonic speeds, the lift coefficient CL is assumed to be constant at a given angle of attack. With increasing Mach number, however, it will vary as shown in figure 1.
At high altitude, a large high-speed jet transport aircraft will be cruising at a speed marginally above its critical Mach number, and it will have a small shock wave on the wing.

If such an aircraft overspeeds, the shock wave will rapidly grow larger, causing the static pressure to increase sharply in the immediate vicinity of the shock wave. The locally increased adverse pressure gradient will cause the boundary layer to separate immediately behind the shock wave. This is called a ‘shock stall’ because it results from a separated boundary layer just as the low speed stall does.
Shock stall occurs when the lift coefficient, as a function of Mach number, reaches its maximum value (for a given angle of attack).

title: Slat or flap asymmetry occurring after either extension or retraction, may have an effect on controllability since:
optionA: slat asymmetry causes a yawing moment, whereas flap asymmetry causes a large rolling moment.
optionB: slat and flap asymmetry both cause a large rolling moment.
optionC: slat asymmetry causes a large rolling moment, whereas flap asymmetry causes a large yawing moment.
optionD: slat and flap asymmetry both cause a large yawing moment.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

Slats are aerodynamic surfaces that extend from the leading edge of the wing during slow flight. Their main purpose us to increase the leading edge camber, which delays separation and in so increases the stall angle and corresponding CLMAX.
Their main contribution is to increase the maximum lift coefficient, but not increase the lift coefficient at a certein AoA. The negative influence of extending slats is a slight increase in drag. Therefore we can say that at a certain AoA, slats will not increase lift, but they will increase drag slightly, therefore the only resultant moment will be a yaw.

Flaps are aerodynamic surfaces that extended from the trailing edge of the wing. Their main purpose is to increase the camber of the wing to increase the coefficient of lift for a certain AoA. This can be seen on the figure. Their main contribution to the wing is extra lift. Whilst drag is also a side effect, lift it more significant.

Therefore the correct answer is: “slat asymmetry causes a yawing moment, whereas flap asymmetry causes a large rolling moment.”

title: The angle between the direction of the undisturbed airflow (relative wind) and the chord line of an aerofoil is the:
optionA: climb path angle.
optionB: same as the angle between chord line and fuselage axis.
optionC: angle of attack.
optionD: glide path angle.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Angle of attack is the difference between pitch attitude and flight path angle. It is defined as the angle between the chord of an airfoil and the relative wind.

Flight path angle is the angle between the horizon and the flight path (speed vector). Also called climb or descent angle.

Pitch angle is the angle between the horizon and longitudinal axis of the aircraft, it is equal to Flight path angle + Angle of attack.

Bank angle is the angle between the lateral axis and the horizon. Bank is rotated around the longitudinal axis, but during a bank at level flight, the angle between the longitudinal axis and the horizon does not change. The angle between the lateral axis and horizon does.

title: Which parameters are at least required for the determination of Mach number to show on a display?
optionA: Outside air temperature and static pressure.
optionB: Dynamic pressure and static pressure.
optionC: Outside air temperature and dynamic pressure.
optionD: Density altitude and dynamic pressure.
explanationTotal:
Note: This question belongs in the Instrumentation bank, not PoF, and there is a very similar question there (222051), but recent feedback has indicated that this may have been seen in principles of flight. Please let us know in the comments if you see this question in PoF, thank you!

MACHMETER

The Machmeter measures the airspeed relative to the speed of sound. In essence, the Mach meter is a combined airspeed indicator (ASI) and altimeter that comprises the following:

1. A capsule feed with pitot pressure inside an ambient static pressure feed case that acts as an ASI and measures dynamic pressure against static pressure as the airspeed.
2. A sealed capsule containing international standard atmosphere (ISA) mean sea level (MSL) conditions inside the ambient static pressure feed case, which acts as an altimeter by measuring the static pressure only, which it relates to an altitude.

(Pitot - static) / static = Mach number

In simpler terms, the Mach number can be determined using dynamic pressure and static pressure alone.

Even though our usual method for calculating Mach No. uses the LSS (Local Speed of Sound) which is calculated using temperature, this is not the only way, nor is it the easiest way for an analog instrument to determine/display it.

title: Which of the following statements is correct?
optionA: As the angle of attack increases, the stagnation point on the aerofoil's profile moves downwards on the profiles leading edge.
