optionB: The centre of pressure is the point on the aerofoil leading edge where the airflow splits up.
optionC: The stagnation point is another name for centre of pressure.
optionD: The stagnation point is always situated on the chord line, the centre of pressure is not.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

STAGNATION POINT

In aerodynamics, the stagnation point is the point in a flow field where the local velocity of the fluid (in our case the atmosphere) is zero. This point is located on the leading edge of the wing. Air above the stagnation point will move upwards and air below it will move downwards if looked at from the side.

  • If we increase the angle of attack, the stagnation point will move down, causing more air to move upwards over the upper side of the wing and moving the point of lowest static pressure forwards.
At a certain angle of attack, this air will move the stall warning upwards, letting off an audible warning horn in the cockpit.

title: Interference drag is the result of:
optionA: the addition of induced and parasite drag.
optionB: separation of the induced vortex.
optionC: downwash behind the wing.
optionD: aerodynamic interaction between aeroplane parts (e.g. wing/fuselage).
explanationTotal:
Interference Drag is drag that is generated by the mixing of airflow streamlines between airframe components like the wing and fuselage.

It is generated when the airflows of both components are forced to mix, creating a turbulent layer of air, adding drag on top of the individual drag of the two components.

Interference drag can be minimized by smoothing the transition between components, for example by using fairings.

title: Positive static lateral stability is the tendency of an aeroplane to:
optionA: roll to the left in a right turn.
optionB: roll to the right in a right turn.
optionC: roll to the left in the case of a sideslip angle (with the aeroplane nose pointing to the right of the incoming flow).
optionD: roll to the left in the case of a sideslip (with the aeroplane nose pointing to the left of the incoming flow).
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
The lateral static stability is a measure of the airplane’s tendency to return to the wings-level attitude after a disturbance has caused the airplane to be disturbed in the rolling plane.

Positive lateral static stability is the tendency of the airplane to roll to the left with a positive sideslip angle, nose to the left. Its ability to recover is dependent on the effect of sideslip.

A disturbance in the rolling plane causes the angle of attack of the upgoing wing to decrease and the angle of attack of the down going wing to increase. Provided the airplane is not flying close to the stalling speed, then the upgoing wing produces less lift than it did before the disturbance and the down going wing will produce more lift than it did. Together, these changes result in a rolling moment in opposition to the initial disturbance and have a ‘roll-damping’ effect. When the roll damping exactly matches the aileron torque the airplane has a steady rate of roll.

The airplane design features that increase the lateral static stability are:

  • dihedral.
  • sweepback.
  • high-wing mounting.
  • increased effective dihedral.
  • large, high vertical fin.
  • low CG.
The airplane design features that decrease the lateral static stability are:
  • anhedral.
  • forward-swept wings.
  • ventral fin.
  • low-wing mounting.
  • extending inboard flaps.

title: The lift coefficient (CL) of an aeroplane in steady horizontal flight is 0.42. An increase in angle of attack of 1 degree increases CL by 0.1. A vertical up gust instantly changes the angle of attack by 3 degrees. The load factor will be:
explanationTotal:
In steady horizontal flight, the load factor is 1.
For every degree of angle of attack, CL increases by 0.1, leading to a total increade of 0.1 * 3 = 0.3
New CL / Old CL = Load factor
(0.42 + 0.3) / 0.42 = 1.71

title: Why would an aircraft in a coordinated turn during an approach suddenly stall?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: An aircraft always stalls at the critical angle of attack.
optionB: In a turn, the stall speed increases.
optionC: In a coordinated turn, the angle of attack decreases.
optionD: In a coordinated turn, the aircraft experiences a decrease in weight.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Load factor is the ratio of the weight of an aircraft to the lift.

In a 45° level turn, weight always acts vertically downwards and lift acts perpendicular on the main wing. For the aircraft to maintain altitude, the vertical force components must be balanced. Lift is inclined from the vertical by the bank angle φ of 45° and must be increased in order to balance the weight and produce a force to perform the turn. More lift compared to the same weight increases the load factor n.

Influence of the Load Factor (n) on Stall Speed

VS = VS1G x √ n

Because the load factor (n) increases in a turn, stall speed will increase accordingly.

An accelerated stall is caused by abrupt or excessive control movements inducing an increased load factor. An accelerated stall can occur during a sudden change in the flight path, during manoeuvres such as steep turns or a recovery from a descent. It is called an accelerated stall because it occurs at a load factor greater than 1g. The stall is more violent than a 1g stall and is often unexpected because of the relatively high airspeed.

title: What happens to induced drag when airspeed increases?
optionA: Induced drag increases.
optionB: Induced drag decreases.
optionC: Induced drag remains the same.
optionD: Induced drag is not affected by airspeed.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
INDUCED DRAG

Whenever a wing produces lift, concentrated vortices form at the wing tips. The vortices are strongest at the wing tips and become progressively weaker toward the centre-line of the aircraft.

It is the production of lift itself which reduces the magnitude of the lift force being generated. To replace the lift lost by the increased downwash, the aircraft must be flown at a higher angle of attack. This increases drag. This extra drag is called induced drag.

The stronger the vortices, the greater the induced drag.

INDUCED DRAG vs. AIRSPEED

The Effect of Airspeed relates to the changes in induced drag with the variation of airspeed.

Induced drag is most significant at low airspeeds and high angles of attack (i.e. during take-off and landing, when it can account for approximately three-quarters of the total drag).

To maintain steady level flight, as the airspeed decreases and the angle of attack increases, the slower passage of air rearward over the wing increases the spanwise flow of air around the wing tip. This results in larger wing tip vortices and greater induced drag.

title: If the sum of all the moments in flight is not zero, the aeroplane will rotate about the:
optionA: neutral point of the aeroplane.
optionB: centre of gravity.
optionC: centre of pressure of the wing.
optionD: aerodynamic centre of the wing.
explanationTotal: All moments are referenced to the Centre of Gravity (CG) and if they are not 0, angular acceleration (motion) will happen unless it is neutralised by another equal and opposite moment. In flight, any aircraft will rotate about its centre of gravity, a point which is the average location of the mass of the aircraft.

title: The altitude where the speed is too low and too high at the same time is denominated:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: High speed buffet.
optionB: Supersonic flight.
optionC: Coffin corner.
optionD: M<sub>CRIT</sub>.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

COFFIN CORNER

At a jet's operating ceiling, its Maximum Mach Number (MMO) is often extremely close to its stall speed. And that region of flight is called the "Coffin Corner"

Coffin Corner is defined as the altitude at which, at a given gross weight and G force loading, a fast fixed-wing aircraft’s stall speed is equal to the critical Mach number. At such altitude, it becomes nearly impossible to maintain stable flight.
  • The region is deadly. Get too slow, and you'll stall the jet at high altitude (not something you want to do). Get too fast, and you'll exceed your critical mach number. The air over your wings will go supersonic, you'll pitch down, the aircraft will accelerate, and your wings will fall off. Also bad.
Note: Coffin corner is an altitude, not a speed. Please, let us know if this question is still coming up with this same wording.

title: A body is placed in a certain airstream. If the airstream velocity increases by a factor of 4, the parasite drag will increase by a factor of:
explanationTotal:
The drag equation states that drag (D) is equal to the drag coefficient (CD) times the density (p) times half of the velocity (V) squared times the reference area (S).

  • Drag (D) = CD 1/2 p V2 S
From the above equation, we can conclude that drag is proportional to velocity squared (V2). Therefore, if the velocity increases by a factor of 4, drag will increase by a factor of 42 = 16.

title: An example of a combined lateral and directional periodic motion is a...
optionA: phugoid.
optionB: spiral dive.
optionC: short period oscillation.
optionD: Dutch roll.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

DUTCH ROLL. This is an oscillation involving roll, yaw and sideslip. Because of these characteristics of the Dutch roll oscillation, lateral dynamic stability has always been more of a problem than longitudinal dynamic stability.

With a dominant lateral stability this will, when a yaw is introduced, roll the aircraft due to the lift increase on the wing into the wind. The increased induced drag on the rising wing will yaw the aircraft in the opposite direction, reversing the coupled oscillations. This is called Dutch roll. Dutch roll might occur when the lateral stability is large compared to the directional stability. Therefore, the moments involved are roll and yaw.

title: What is a possible cause for the auto-recovery of an aeroplane after the stall?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: The Angle of incidence of the wing is smaller than the angle of incidence of the horizontal stabiliser.
optionB: The angle of attack of the stabiliser is bigger than the angle of attack of the wing.
optionC: The wing surface is bigger than the surface of the horizontal stabiliser.
optionD: The angle of incidence of the wing is larger than the angle of incidence of the horizontal stabiliser.
explanationTotal:
With the angle of incidence of the wing higher than that of the tail, the wing will stall first, while the tail is still 'flying.'

This is desirable because it means that while the wing isn't producing lift anymore, the tail still is, so the tail will tend to rise, and thus the nose drop - and nose down is what you need to recover.

You see this when you actually practise stalling, often it will become impossible even with full back stick to prevent the nose dropping.

The fact the tail is still flying also means means the elevator still has control authority so you can actually use it to lower the nose further and break the stall completely.

title: An aeroplane is on final approach at a CAS within the non-stable region of the CAS/drag graph. The aeroplane experiences a change in the wind direction to be less of a headwind with little change in wind speed. This condition will cause...
optionA: a reduction in air speed, which will cause an increase in total drag.
optionB: a reduction in air speed, which will cause a decrease in total drag.
optionC: an increase in air speed, which will cause an increase in total drag.
optionD: an increase in air speed, which will cause a decrease in total drag.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
During flight, an aircraft will experience two types of drag:

- Parasite Drag (proportional to IAS2, increases with increasing “Parasite Area”: flaps, undercarriage or speed brakes)

- Induced Drag (inversely proportional to IAS2, increases with increasing weight).

The sum of Parasite Drag and Induced Drag is the Total Drag.

The Total Drag will be minimum at the IAS where Parasite Drag = Induced Drag. This speed is called Minimum Drag Speed (VMD). Flying at a slower or faster speed than VMD will generate more drag.

Flying at a slower speed than VMD (back side), the aircraft will be in the unstable speed region. Any loss of speed will result in an increase in drag and further speed loss (which must be corrected by an increase in thrust). The sudden change to a tailwind (or a decrease in headwind) will cause a loss of airspeed.

title: Considering the airflow around a positively cambered aerofoil that is producing lift, the point of minimum static pressure is found...
optionA: at the point where the chord line originates from the leading edge.
optionB: where the streamlines are closest together.
optionC: slightly below the point at which the chord line originates from the leading edge.
optionD: at the point of maximum camber on the upper surface.
explanationTotal:
When considering the pressure, we know that the total pressure always remains constant in subsonic airflow. Next, knowing that the total pressure is equal to the dynamic pressure plus the static pressure, we know that if one increases, the other must decrease to maintain a constant total pressure.

Now what is the dynamic pressure and what is static pressure:

  • Dynamic pressure is equal to: q = ½ rho V2. Therefore we can say that the dynamic pressure is proportional to the velocity of the airflow.
  • Static pressure is the pressure that any object feels even when not moving. This pressure is caused by the force of gravity forcing particles closer together and pushing against each other and any objects around them.

Knowing that dynamic pressure is basically the velocity of the airflow, we can say that if the velocity increase, hence increasing the dynamic pressure, there has to be a reduction in static pressure.
This is known as Bernoulli’s principle!

Therefore, going back to the question, we can say that the point of minimum static pressure is the point of maximum dynamic pressure (airflow velocity). Therefore the point of minimum static pressure will be somewhere on the top of a positively cambered aerofoil. This would most commonly be at the point of maximum camber, but not always! Changes in angle of attack will move the point of maximum velocity forwards and backwards, therefore the most correct answer is where streamlines are closest together.

title: Assuming ISA conditions and a descent above the tropopause at constant Mach number and aeroplane mass, the:
optionA: lift coefficient increases.
optionB: IAS decreases.
optionC: TAS remains constant.
optionD: lift coefficient remains constant.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The Mach number is defined as the ratio between the TAS and the LSS (Local speed of sound).

It is an indication of how fast an aircraft is travelling with relation to the sound waves that surround it.

The Mach number may be calculated as follows:

M=TAS/LSS=(TAS(kt))/(38.95∗√(T(K)))

The speed of propagation of small pressure waves depends upon the temperature of the air ONLY.

Effect on TAS of descending at a constant Mach Number (above tropopause):

  • Above the tropopause the temperature is constant, so the speed of sound will remain the same.
  • If altitude is decreased at a constant Mach Number, the TAS is also constant. This is because, above the tropopause, LSS is constant.

title: What can happen to the aeroplane structure flying at a speed just exceeding V<sub>A</sub>?
optionA: It will collapse if a turn is made.
optionB: It may suffer permanent deformation if the elevator is fully deflected upwards.
optionC: It may suffer permanent deformation because the flight is performed at too large dynamic pressure.
optionD: It may break if the elevator is fully deflected upwards.
explanationTotal:
VA = Maximum Design Manoeuvring Speed

VA is the maximum speed where an aircraft stalls at a sudden full elevator deflection (nose-up) but does not exceed the design limit load factor.

Obviously, it means that at or below this speed, a full elevator deflection will not cause damage on the airframe, however, it will lead to accelerated stall. Above this speed, full elevator deflection can cause structural damage as load factor will reach its maximum limit value.

title: In order to decrease the Dutch roll at high altitude, the speed should be (1) _____ than the current (2) _____.
optionA: (1) higher; (2) Mach number
optionB: (1) higher; (2) IAS
optionC: (1) lower; (2) IAS
optionD: (1) lower; (2) Mach number
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Dutch roll is a coupled lateral and directional oscillation which is objectionable because of the oscillatory nature. Dutch roll will occur when the dihedral effect is large when compared to static directional stability.

Assymetric Nature of Shockwaves

Generally, flight at high altitude will be flown at high Mach numbers by aircraft with sweepback wings. Drag increase encountered at these higher speeds is called wave drag. At and above MCRIT, the drag of the airplane wing increases rapidly and there is a large reduction of lift. If the shockwave develops earlier on wing than the other (assymetrically), the wing drops and tends to yaw creating the conditions for a coupled lateral and directional oscillation or Dutch roll.

With increasing altitude (decreasing density) or increasing Mach number, the possibility of a Dutch roll increases. This means that the correct course of action following a Dutch roll is to reduce the Mach number and to descend.

title: Regarding the transonic speed range:
optionA: it starts at M<sub>CRIT</sub> and extends to Mach number equal to 1.
optionB: both subsonic and supersonic speeds exist in the flow around the aeroplane.
optionC: it starts at a Mach number just above 1.
optionD: it starts at a Mach number equal to 1.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Figure 1 shows the flow speed ranges with their approximate Mach number values, where: MFS (Free Stream Mach number) is the Mach number of the flow sufficiently remote from an aircraft to be unaffected by it. (In effect, the Mach number of the aircraft through the air). This is the Mach number shown on the aircraft Mach meter.

ML (Local Mach number) is the actual speed of the flow over a surface. When an aircraft flies at a certain MFS the flow over it is accelerated in some places and slowed down in others.

The transonic speed region is located between MCRIT and MDET (Detachment Mach number). In this region, ML is both subsonic and supersonic.

title: Behind a normal shock wave, the downwash is greatly reduced. As a consequence, this causes...
optionA: an increase in C<sub>L</sub>.
optionB: a reduction in C<sub>D</sub>.
optionC: an increase in critical AoA.
optionD: tuck under.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
In transonic flight it is the nature of the airflow behind a shock wave that determines the stability characteristics of the aircraft.

Longitudinal stability is the most commonly affected form of stability. It is determined by movement of the centre of pressure, coupled with changes in the coefficient of lift and the amount of downwash acting on the tailplane.

The nose-down pitching moment produced by the wing is counteracted by placing a small download on the tailplane. If the shock stall occurs, any lift aft of the shock wave is destroyed and the tailplane becomes covered in disturbed airflow.

The downwash acting on the tailplane is consequently eliminated causing a smooth and radical change in its angle of attack. The angle of attack becomes more positive and the download acting on the tailplane becomes an upload which, in conjunction with the wing pitching moment, causes a violent nose-down pitching moment, known as tuck-under.

The exact nature and strength of the changes in trim and stability depend on the design of the aircraft.

title: An object has a drag of 785 N at sea level. Assuming ISA conditions and that the object is travelling at the same speed, calculate the drag of the object at 6 000 ft.
explanationTotal:
Drag force= 1/2.ρ.v2.CD.S
Every variable except ρ (density) is constant in equation.
Air density at sea level is 1.225 kg/m3

We need to find what is the density of air at 6000 ft. No need to know exact values. We can guess it based on pressure. At 6 000 ft pressure is around 850 hPa. Therefore

850/1013 x ρ = 0.84 ρ is approximate density at 6000 ft.

As a result, drag will be 84% of the drag at MSL: 785 N x 0.84 = 659 N (Closest option available is 656 N)

title: What happens at the “deterrent buffet”?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: The pilot cannot prevent pitch down movement.
optionB: The pilot cannot prevent pitch up movement.
optionC: The pilot feels the need to leave those conditions.
optionD: The pilot is unable to recover.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

  • At buffet initiation, the pilot starts to feel airfl ow separation on wings upper surface.
  • The buffet onset corresponds by defi nition to 1.3 g (corresponding to 40° of bank angle in level fl ight).
  • The “deterrent buffet” is so strong that any pilot will feel he/she needs to leave these buffet conditions. It corresponds to one of the definitions of stall and is considered to be the stall limit on a jet transport aircraft.

Deterrent Buffet - the airplane exhibits sufficient buffet that the flight crew will be deterred from commanding even higher AOA.

title:
Refer to figure.
Two points are marked on the wing: V1 and V2. Given an air velocity of V, select the correct option.
optionA:
V1 = 0
V2 > V
optionB:
V1 > V
V2 = 0
optionC:
V1 = 0
V2 < V
optionD:
V1 < V
V2 = 0
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The Stagnation Point is that point where the airflow goes from freestream speed to a standstill (velocity reduced to zero). Any airstream above will flow over the wing, and any airflow below will pass under the wing.

  • The flow over the top of the section accelerates rapidly around the nose and over the leading portion of the surface - inducing a substantial decrease in static pressure in those areas. A wing is shaped and tilted so the air moving over it moves faster than the air moving under it. As air speeds up, its pressure goes down. So the faster-moving air above exerts less pressure on the wing than the slower-moving air below. The result is an upward push on the wing—lift.
=> V1 is the stagnation point - therefore, V1 = 0
=> Air accelerates over the upper surface - therefore, V2 > V

title: How does icing affect a propeller?
optionA: Decrease thrust.
optionB: Decrease thrust due to increase AoA.
optionC: Increases thrust.
optionD: Due to the high speed of the propeller the ice will melt away and don’t affect the thrust.
explanationTotal:
Ice on an aerofoil changes its properties, reducing lift and increasing drag for a given angle of attack. Ice on a propeller blade reduces the efficiency of the propeller and reduces thrust.

As the drag of an ice contaminated airplane increases, the resisting force on the propeller increases for a given RPM and blade angle. Since ice on the propeller blades reduces the available thrust, extra power may be required from the engine to overcome the increased drag, decreasing propeller efficiency.

Note: Propeller icing can be expected to reduce propeller efficiency by up to 10% normally, but could up to 20% in very severe icing.

Propeller icing occurs on the leading edge, but is least at the tip of the blade, where the high rotational speed tends to shed the ice more easily.

title: The maximum angle of bank which can be achieved with a 0.13 g buffet margin is:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
explanationTotal:
In a turn: Load factor (n) = 1 / cos (bank º)
cos (bank º) = 1 / n
cos (bank º) = 1 / 1.13
bank º = cos -1(1 / 1.13)
bank º = approx. 28º

Note: a 0.13 g buffet margin means that the aeroplane experiences buffeting at 1.13 g load factor.

title: An aeroplane has static directional stability if, when in a sideslip with the relative airflow coming from the right, initially the:
optionA: nose of the aeroplane tends to yaw right.
optionB: right wing tends to go down.
optionC: nose of the aeroplane tends to yaw left.
optionD: nose of the aeroplane does not move.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The rotation of an aircraft about its normal, or vertical, axis is a yaw. If this movement is the result of an undesirable disturbance, then the ability of the airplane to return to its original heading without the assistance of any control-surface movement is a measure of its directional static stability. It is a measure of the aircraft’s ability to realign itself with the relative airflow.

Sideslip is the displacement angle of the airplane’s longitudinal axis in azimuth from the relative airflow. It is positive when the relative airflow is to the right of the longitudinal axis and negative when the relative airflow is left of the longitudinal axis.

An airplane has directional static stability if, when in a sideslip with the airflow coming from the right initially the nose tends to yaw right. An airplane that has excessive directional static stability compared to its lateral static stability is more prone to spiral dive.

title: Which one of the following statements about the lift-to-drag ratio in straight and level flight is correct?
optionA: The highest value of the lift/drag ratio is reached when the lift is equal to the aeroplane weight.
optionB: The lift/drag ratio always increases as the lift decreases.
optionC: The highest value of the lift/drag ratio is reached when the lift is zero.
optionD: At the highest value of the lift/drag ratio the total drag is lowest.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
LIFT/DRAG RATIO

An appreciation of the efficiency of lift production is gained from studying the ratio between lift and drag, a high L/D ratio being more efficient.

For maximum efficiency, the wings should produce maximum lift with the least possible drag.

The L/D ratio increases with angle of attack up to a maximum at about 4° - this is called the “optimum” angle of attack.

If an aircraft is operated at the (L/D)MAX angle of attack, drag will be a minimum while generating the required lift force.

title: Which tab used in aerodynamic balancing moves in the same direction as the control surface and also increases control effectiveness?
optionA: Servo tab
optionB: Trim tab
optionC: Anti-balance tab
optionD: Balance tab
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Because the hinge moment on some airplanes is too small, often as the result of the CP being too close to the hinge-line of the control surface, it is too easy to deflect the control surface against the aerodynamic load. Consequently, there is little control column load and there is a lack of feel to the controls. This could lead to excessive deflection of the control surface and result in serious overstressing of the airframe.
To counteract these characteristics and assist the pilot to use the control surfaces correctly it is necessary to have anti-balance tabs fitted. These operate in the opposite sense to the balance tab by deflecting the anti-balance tab in the same direction as that of the primary control surface and increase the aerodynamic loading.

title:
Refer to figure.
What does line 3 represent?
optionA: Induced drag
optionB: Parasite drag
optionC: Total drag
optionD: Profile drag
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
In level flight, at a specific weight and configuration, the change in total drag with indicated airspeed (IAS) for an aircraft is composed of both induced and parasite drag. The combined effect of these two types of drag is referred to as total drag.

At low speeds, induced drag tends to dominate, while parasite drag becomes more significant at higher speeds. Due to the distinct characteristics of how parasite and induced drag change with speed, there exists a particular speed at which total drag is minimized. This speed is known as the Velocity Minimum Drag (VMD) and occurs when the magnitudes of induced and parasite drag are equal.

In this figure:

  • Line 1: Total Drag
  • Line 2: Parasite Drag
  • Line 3: Induced Drag

title: An aeroplane is entering the transonic range whilst maintaining straight and level flight. If the Mach number increases, what additional input or action will be required to maintain straight and level flight to compensate for the centre of pressure’s movement, when the transonic region has been entered?
optionA: No pitch control input.
optionB: A pitch up input of the elevator or the stabiliser.
optionC: A higher IAS to compensate the nose down effect.
optionD: A pitch down input of the elevator or the stabiliser.
explanationTotal:
As speed increases beyond the Critical Mach number (MCRIT), shock wave formation at the root of a swept-back wing will:
  • reduce lift forward of the CG (CP moves rearward), and
  • reduce downwash at the tail plane.

Together, these factors will generate a nose-down pitching moment.

At high Mach numbers, an aircraft will become unstable with respect to speed; instead of an increasing push force being required as speed increases, a pull force becomes necessary to prevent the aircraft accelerating further.

A small increase in Mach number will give a nose-down pitch which will further increase the Mach number. This in turn leads to a further increase in the nose-down pitching moment. This unfavorable high-speed characteristic, known as “Mach Tuck”, “High Speed Tuck” or “Tuck Under” would restrict the maximum operating speed of a modern high-speed jet transport aircraft.

To maintain the required stick force gradient at high Mach numbers, a Mach trim system must be fitted.

title: An aircraft with a mass of 60 tons is performing a co-ordinated level turn with 60º angle of bank. What is the magnitude of the Centripetal Force?
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
During a steady, co-ordinated turn, at a constant altitude, a force must continually act toward the centre of the turn (centripetal force). If it is not present, the aircraft will be unable to maintain a curved path, but instead will fly off at a tangent.

When the aircraft banks, the total lift force tilts; the horizontal component of lift provides the centripetal force and the vertical component of lift supports the weight of the aircraft.

There are a few ways to calculate the centripetal force.

You can use the formula -- Centripetal force = Lift x sin(bank angle) -- but this would require some extra steps in this question, as the lift is not equal to weight, during the banked turn. You can certainly work out the lift from the formula -- Lift = Weight / cos(bank angle) -- if you like, and this will work fine, followed by the formula above to work out the centripetal force.

Instead, using basic trigonometry, we can work out that the weight and the centripetal force are linked by the tan function, and the following formula exists (There is a formula derivation in the explanation of question 819095 if you are interested but you do not need to know it for the exams, just remember the formula).

Centripetal force = Weight x tan(bank angle)

Before we can make the calculation, we must first calculate the weight from the mass, using the formula -- Weight = Mass x acceleration due to gravity (g)

The acceleration due to gravity is a value of 9.81 m/s2 on the Earth's surface (sometimes questions will ask you to use 10 m/s2 for this).

Weight = 60 000 x 9.81 = 588 600 N

Using the above formula, Centripetal force = 588 600 x tan(60) = 1 019 485 N

title: The chord line of an aerofoil section is:
optionA: the line, relative to the upstream airflow.
optionB: the line, drawn from the leading edge to the trailing edge.
optionC: the tangent at the leading edge of the camber line.
optionD: the line from the leading to the trailing edge equidistant from the upper and lower surfaces.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Chordline: The straight line joining the leading-edge and the trailing edge of an aerofoil.

title: During a co-ordinated climbing turn to the right the:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: angle of attack of the left wing is larger than the angle of attack of the right wing.
optionB: angle of attack of both wings is the same.
optionC: stall angle of attack of the left wing will be larger than the corresponding angle for the right wing.
optionD: angle of attack of the left wing is smaller than the angle of attack of the right wing.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
CLIMBING TURNS

During a steady, level banked turn an aircraft has a tendency to overbank because the faster moving outer wing produces greater lift. During climbing and descending turns the aircraft is subject to additional rolling moments resulting from the variation in each wing’s angle of attack.

Although the whole aircraft covers the same altitude during a complete turn, the wings follow differing spiral paths due to the variation in turn radius.

During climbing turns, an aircraft describes an upward spiral path. Thus, the relative airflow comes downward to meet the wings, thereby reducing their angles of attack and hence their coefficients of lift.

The faster moving outer wing is subject to a smaller reduction in angle of attack. This makes the net coefficient of lift higher than on the inner wing, thereby producing greater lift. Its increased velocity further enhances the lifting capability of the outer wing.

An aircraft in a climbing turn therefore tends to overbank more than in a steady level turn. If necessary, utilise the ailerons to maintain the desired angle of bank.

title: A commercial jet aeroplane is performing a straight descent at a constant Mach number with constant mass. The operational speed limit that may be exceeded is:
optionA: V<sub>NE</sub>.
optionB: V<sub>D</sub>.
optionC: M<sub>MO</sub>.
optionD: V<sub>MO</sub>.
explanationTotal:
The Mach number is defined as the ratio between the TAS and the LSS (Local speed of sound).
It is an indication of how fast an aircraft is travelling with relation to the sound waves that surround it.

The Mach number may be calculated as follows:
M= TAS/LSS = (TAS(kt)) / (38.95∗√(T(K)))

The speed of propagation of small pressure waves depends upon the temperature of the air ONLY.

Effect on Mach Number of Climbing at a Constant IAS:

- Temperature decreases with increasing altitude, so the speed of sound will decrease as altitude is increased.
- If altitude is increased at a constant IAS, the TAS increases.
- Therefore, the Mach number will increase if altitude is increased at a constant IAS. This is because TAS gets bigger and LSS gets smaller.

As the climb continues, an altitude will be reached at which the flight crew must stop flying at a constant IAS and fly at a constant Mach number, to avoid accidentally exceeding MMO.

Effect on TAS of descending at a constant Mach Number:

- Temperature increases with decreasing altitude, so the speed of sound will increase as altitude is decreased.
- If altitude is decreased at a constant Mach Number, the TAS increases. This is because LSS gets bigger.

As the descent continues, an altitude will be reached at which the flight crew must stop flying at a constant Mach Number and fly at a constant IAS, to avoid accidentally exceeding VMO.

title: After an engine failure on a twin-engine aircraft, banking towards the live engine is limited to 5 degrees. What is correct if greater angles of bank are used?
optionA: Lift required increases, but drag decreases.
optionB: The risk of fin stall decreases.
optionC: Lift required increases.
optionD: Drag decreases.
explanationTotal:
COUNTERACTING ASYMMETRIC THRUST

Up to 5 degrees bank into the live engine

During engine-out flight, keeping the ball centered and the wings level will actually cause a side-slip situation because of the one failed engine and the resulting drag and loss of lift. A sideslip would make stall characteristics worse, would decrease climb and acceleration capability, and would increase VMC. Turning up to 5 degrees towards the good (operating) engine will prevent the airplane from being in a sideslip condition, will improve climb capabilities, improve stall capabilities, improve performance and will decrease VMC

  • The angle of bank must not exceed 5°. Using more than 5º of bank may create enough sideslip towards the lower wing to give a risk of fin stall. When using bank angles greater than 5 degrees, the lift required increases and so does the drag.

title: Preparing to make a flight in a B737, you notice that the yaw damper is INOP, and after consulting the Minimum Equipment List (MEL), you see that flight without the yaw damper is restricted to not above FL170. Why does this restriction exist?
optionA: Aerodynamic damping decreases with altitude, so the aircraft could experience a series of unwanted rolling and yawing motions.
optionB: This exists as the yaw damper is a requirement for RVSM airspace which exists above FL170.
optionC: The aircraft may get control reversal at the high speeds encountered above FL170, without the yaw damper operative.
optionD: The yaw damper is required to balance any manually flown turns above FL170.
explanationTotal:
Note: We only know the correct option here, and the incorrect options were reported as being easy to identify as incorrect, so we have made up some suitably wrong options until we get further feedback about this question. Please send us any further feedback in the comments or by email to info@atplquestions.com, thank you!

The yaw damper's main purpose is to prevent Dutch roll.

Basically speaking, Dutch roll is a series of out-of-phase turns, when the aircraft rolls in one direction and yaws in the other due to a high amount of lateral stability but not quite enough directional stability. When the yaw is introduced, the strong “dihedral effect” will roll the aircraft due to the lift increase on the wing into wind. The increased induced drag on the rising wing will yaw the aircraft in the opposite direction, reversing the coupled oscillations.

Since the possibility of a Dutch roll increases with increasing altitude due to the lower aerodynamic damping at high altitude, aircraft can sometimes be restricted to fly at lower altitudes only when the yaw damper is unserviceable.

title: A light aircraft with mechanical flight controls occasionally experiences uncomfortable pitch oscillations after encountering normal turbulence. The pilot does not note any such oscillations when cruising in smooth air at normal cruising speed, but does notice some excessive slack or play in the elevator linkages after the flight. What potential hazards could this situation cause if not addressed by maintenance?
optionA: This phugoid-type oscillation is likely to increase in magnitude and the aeroplane may enter a stall or encounter an overspeed situation if the oscillation worsens.
optionB: A poorly balanced control surface is creating excessive restoring forces and this short-period motion may cause excessive stress on the airframe.
optionC: The flutter may gradually worsen, and the elevator may vibrate so vigorously that it comes off the hinges and separates from the aeroplane in flight.
optionD: Compared to a phugoid, the short period motion leads to a change in pitch and speed, which, if NOT corrected, may lead to a stall or overspeed situation.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
NOTE: We have had conflicting feedback about this question. The current answer is the one we believe to be most correct, but we are seeing some possible different answers with different authorities. We are in need of more feedback about this one, so please send us anything you can remember from the exam via the comments, the feedback section of the website, or by email to info@atplquestions.com, thank you!

FLUTTER
Flutter occurs because a wing (or other aerodynamic surface) is not perfectly stiff, and will bend and twist under high aerodynamic loads. The control surfaces can cause a cyclic movement where the wing moves but the control surface "lags behind", creating an even larger force on the wing. The wing will then do the same thing in the opposite direction, and at certain frequencies can build up to a large, short term oscillation that can cause significant damage ton the aircraft. The risk of experiencing flutter increases with IAS.

A control surface oscillation can also be intensified or created by any slack (free play) in the control lines, where the control surface can move freely without pilot input. This means that small disturbances such as turbulence could cause un-commanded control surface movements, which then begin a period of flutter, as eluded to in the question.

To go through the options:

  • "This phugoid-type oscillation is likely to increase in magnitude and the aeroplane may enter a stall or encounter an overspeed situation if the oscillation worsens."
    • It is not a phugoid type oscillation being described, as a phugoid has a greater time period than this short interval flutter.
  • "A poorly balanced control surface is creating excessive restoring forces and this short-period motion may cause excessive stress on the airframe."
    • The control surface is not necessarily poorly balanced; the cause of the flutter is the free play in the control lines, so we would say this is not correct. However, the rest of the option is correct, so it's not far off.
  • "The flutter may gradually worsen, and the elevator may vibrate so vigorously that it comes off the hinges and separates from the aeroplane in flight."
    • We believe this is fully correct. The free play in the control lines can cause this kind of response.
  • "Compared to a phugoid, the short period motion leads to a change in pitch and speed, which, if NOT corrected, may lead to a stall or overspeed situation."
    • For a while, the Polish ULC considered this to be correct (we believe), but recent feedback indicates they no longer do. The short period motion doesn't really cause large speed changes (that would be a phugoid) and therefore it is not very likely to cause a stall or overspeed situation.

title: Upon first contact with their destination aerodrome, the crew of a jet aeroplane is informed to expect a few holds due to high traffic. What can the crew do to increase their aircraft's maximum endurance?
optionA: Cruise with V<sub>MAX RANGE</sub> in order to increase the fuel mileage.
optionB: Climb to the optimum altitude in order to increase specific range.
optionC: Cruise with V<sub>MD</sub> in order to minimise fuel used per unit of time.
optionD: Request a continuous descent in order to reduce the thrust setting.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The pilot of an aircraft in this scenario knows that they are going to have to wait some time before landing, which usually means entering a holding pattern. In order to maximise the amount of fuel they have left at this point, the crew should slow down and fly the rest of the way at the best endurance speed. As they are only going to end up holding anyway, they might as well save some fuel in the cruise, and have to do less holding patterns later on.

This is assuming that they have already "joined the queue" at their destination airport, which is implied in the question.

The best endurance speed in a jet aircraft is the speed at which the engines need to produce the least thrust, as thrust is directly proportional to fuel flow, and we want to make our fuel flow the lowest it can be. The speed of minimum thrust required is the speed of least drag (as thrust directly opposed drag). We called this VMD, for minimum drag speed, and it is the speed that aircraft fly in the holding pattern, and when it is time in the air that is most desirable, rather than distance gone.

It occurs at the bottom of the "total drag" curve as shown in the annex above, where the combination of induced and parasite drag equals the lowest value.

There is no point climbing up to the optimum altitude at this stage, as it is not an efficient use of fuel to climb just before descent. Also, that option is not correct because we do not care about maximum range now, only maximum endurance.

title:
Refer to Alicante chart 11-2 from Jeppesen GSPRM 2017.
An aircraft is flying outbond on radial 298 from ALT VOR and exceeds the MAX speed for the base turn. From the following, what could be the possible result?
optionA: The turn radius will increase and aircraft will fly close to terrain west of the airport.
optionB: A risk of overshooting the baseturn, ending up too high before final approach fix.
optionC: A risk of undershooting the baseturn, ending up too high before final approach fix.
optionD: The turn radius will decrease and aircraft will fly closer to the airport.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
ICAO Doc 8168
1.3.8 The instrument approach chart (IAC) will specify the individual categories of aircraft for which the procedure is approved. Normally, procedures will be designed to provide protected airspace and obstacle clearance for aircraft up to and including Category D. However, where airspace requirements are critical, procedures may be restricted to lower speed categories.

1.3.9 Alternatively, the procedure may specify a maximum IAS for a particular segment without reference to aircraft category. In any case, it is essential that pilots comply with the procedures and information depicted on instrument flight charts and the appropriate flight parameters (...) if the aircraft is to remain in the areas developed for obstacle clearance purposes.

RADIUS OF TURN

Radius of turn is dependent on both airspeed and bank angle.

Turn Radius = V2 / g tan Ø

Where V = True Airspeed, g = acceleration of gravity constant of 9.81 m/s2, Ø = angle of bank

The radius of turn at any given bank angle is directly proportional to the square of the airspeed. Which means that doubling the airspeed results in a radius of turn that is four times greater

RATE OF TURN

Rate of turn is the rate of change of heading or angular velocity of the turn.

Rate of turn = g tan Ø / V

Increasing the speed results in a decrease of rate of turn. Whereas increasing bank angle, increases the rate of turn.

title: If the centre of gravity moves forward, the stick force (1) _____ and the elevator authority (2) _____.
optionA: (1) increases; (2) increases
optionB: (1) decreases; (2) increases
optionC: (1) increases; (2) decreases
optionD: (1) decreases; (2) decreases
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
Static Longitudinal stability is the aircraft's natural tendency when disturbed in pitch, to return to its former trimmed angle of attack without pilot input, and is desirable throughout the aircraft's complete speed range.

The position of the CG directly affects the magnitude of the longitudinal static stability, the tailplane downforce and the stalling speed because its position determines the length of the arm of any restoring moment.

A forward movement of the CG increases the positive longitudinal static stability of an aircraft but decreases the manoeuvrability and control response because the moment arm is increased in length and increases the nose-down pitching moment. Thus, the elevators have less nose-up authority.

MANOEUVRING STABILITY

The most direct appreciation of the manoeuvring stability of an aeroplane is obtained from a plot of stick force versus load factor.

The aeroplane with positive manoeuvring stability should demonstrate a steady increase in stick force with increase in load factor or “g”.

When the aeroplane has high static stability, the manoeuvring stability will be high and a high stick force gradient will result. As the CG moves aft, the stick force gradient decreases with decreasing manoeuvring stability.

title: During a short period oscillation, the altitude:
optionA: varies significantly, as it does during a phugoid.
optionB: varies significantly, whereas during a phugoid it remains approximately constant.
optionC: remains approximately constant, whereas during a phugoid it varies significantly.
optionD: remains approximately constant, as it does during a phugoid.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
In trimmed level flight a disturbance in pitch usually oscillates about its original state causing fluctuations in the values of speed, height and indicated load factor. When an airplane has positive longitudinal dynamic stability the amplitude of the oscillations gradually diminish as the aircraft returns to its original trimmed flight state.

The oscillatory motion of the airplane in pitch after a disturbance to its trimmed state can be shown as two separate oscillations. One is a short-period oscillation and the other is a long-period oscillation called a phugoid. The phugoid is usually poorly damped; it has large variations of speed and height and has an almost uniform load factor (n). It has a constant energy motion in which the potential energy and the kinetic energy are continuously interchanging.

The motion that causes short-period oscillation is normally heavily damped. It not only involves small changes of speed and height but also large changes of load factor. The speed and height of the airplane remain approximately constant.

title: Select the option which correctly completes the following sentence: A constant-speed propeller…
optionA: has a more simple construction than a fixed-pitch propeller.
optionB: operates at a constant RPM from take-off to landing.
optionC: maintains high efficiency across a range of speeds.
optionD: can achieve high efficiency in climb performance, but the cruise performance will be less efficient.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
The propeller blade is an aerofoil and the definitions for chord, camber, thickness/chord ratio and aspect ratio are the same as those given previously for the wing.

BLADE ANGLE OR PITCH

The angle between the blade chord and the plane of rotation. Blade angle decreases from the root to the tip of the blade (twist) because rotational velocity of the blade increases from root to tip.

CONSTANT SPEED PROPELLERS

Modern aircraft have propellers which are controlled automatically to vary their pitch (blade angle) so as to maintain a selected RPM.

Veriable pitch propellers permit high efficiency to be obtained over a wider range of TAS, giving improved take-off and climb performance and cruising fuel consumption.

This type of propellers enable the pilot to select the RPM for maximum power or maximum efficiency and a propeller governor varies the propeller pitch angle as required to maintain the selected RPM.

title:
What sort of characteristics should a pilot expect from a swept-back wing when it begins to stall, and why?

The aeroplane will:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Pitch up, due to forward movement of the centre of pressure, caused by the wing tips stalling first.
optionB: Pitch down, due to aft movement of the centre of pressure, caused by the wing root stalling first.
optionC: Pitch up, due to reduced downwash at the tailplane, caused by the wing root stalling first.
optionD: Pitch down, due to increased downwash at the tailplane, caused by the wing tips stalling first.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
A simple swept-wing will stall at the wing tip first if not induced/controlled to stall at another wing section first by the designer. This is so because the outer wing section experiences a higher aerodynamic loading due to the wing taper, which causes a greater angle of incidence to be experienced to a degree where the airflow stalls at the wing tips. The boundary layer span-wise airflow, also a result of sweep, further contributes to the airflow stalling at the wing tips.

A stall at the wing tip causes a loss of lift outboard and therefore aft (due to the wing sweep), which moves the center of pressure inboard and therefore forward; this produces a pitch-up tendency that continues as the wing stalls progressively further inboard.

title: An aeroplane flying with an airspeed of 200 kt and C<sub>L</sub> is equal to 0.6. The pilot is requested to increase speed to 250 kt by the ATC. The new C<sub>L</sub> is…
explanationTotal:
The aerodynamic force of lift results from the pressure differential between the top and bottom surfaces of the wing.

This lift force can be defined by the following equation:

L = 1/2 x ρ x V2 x CL x S

The lift formula can be used to consider the relationship between speed and angle of attack at a constant altitude (air density). As speed is changed, angle of attack must be adjusted to keep lift constant:

- If speed is increased, angle of attack must be decreased, (if speed is doubled, angle of attack must be decreased to make CL four times its previous value).

To solve this exercise you can use the following formula:

New CL x (New Speed)2 = Old CL x (Old Speed)2

New CL x 2502 = 0.6 x 2002
New CL = (0.6 x 2002) / 2502

New CL = 0.384

title: A pilot is on approach and is momentarily distracted by an alternator failure. On turning final, the controls feel light, the control surfaces are unresponsive and the pilot struggles to maintain bank angle. This is due to:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: A strong gust
optionB: Loss of thrust
optionC: Approaching stall
optionD: Loose control cables
explanationTotal:
Stall characteristics vary with different types of aircraft. However, for modern aircraft during most normal manoeuvres, the onset of stall is gradual. The first indications of a stall may be provided by any or all of the following:

- unresponsive flight controls,
- a stall warning or stall prevention device, or
- aerodynamic buffet.

title:
Refer to figure.
Where on the curve in the diagram does the aeroplane exhibit static longitudinal instability?
optionA: Point 2.
optionB: The whole curve.
optionC: Part 3.
optionD: Part 1.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
Static longitudinal stability depends upon the relationship of angle of attack and pitching moment (CM).

A variation of CG position can cause large changes in the static longitudinal stability. In the conventional airplane configuration, the large changes in stability with CG variation are primarily due to the large changes in the wing contribution. If the incidence of all surfaces remains fixed, the effect of CG position on static longitudinal stability is typified by the chart in figure 1:

As the CG is gradually moved aft, the airplane static stability decreases, then becomes neutral then unstable. The CG position which produces zero slope and neutral static stability is referred to as the “neutral point”. The neutral point defines the most aft CG position without static instability.

Moving the CG forward, will increase static longitudinal stability and this is represented by a (steeper) negative slope.

Noticeable changes in static stability can occur at high lift coefficients (low speed). This condition is illustrated in figure 2.

The curve of CM versus CL of this illustration shows a good stable slope at low values of CL (high speed). Increasing CL gives a slight decrease in the negative slope hence a decrease in stability occurs. With continued increase in CL, the slope becomes zero and neutral stability exists. Eventually, the slope becomes positive and the airplane becomes unstable.

title: The Mach-trim function is installed on most commercial jets in order to minimise the adverse effects of:
optionA: increased drag due to shock wave formation.
optionB: changes in the position of centre of pressure.
optionC: uncontrolled changes in stabiliser setting.
optionD: compressibility effects on the stabiliser.
explanationTotal:
As speed increases beyond the Critical Mach number (MCRIT), shock wave formation at the root of a swept-back wing will:
  •   reduce lift forward of the CG (CP moves rearward), and
  •   reduce downwash at the tail plane.
Together, these factors will generate a nose-down pitching moment.
At high Mach numbers, an aircraft will become unstable with respect to speed; instead of an increasing push force being required as speed increases, a pull force becomes necessary to prevent the aircraft accelerating further.
A small increase in Mach number will give a nose-down pitch which will further increase the Mach number. This in turn leads to a further increase in the nose-down pitching moment. This unfavorable high-speed characteristic, known as “Mach Tuck”, “High Speed Tuck” or “Tuck Under” would restrict the maximum operating speed of a modern high-speed jet transport aircraft.
To maintain the required stick force gradient at high Mach numbers, a Mach trim system must be fitted.

title: A last minute change to the weight and balance of an aircraft adds more weight in a forward area. The aircraft remains within limits after the weight addition; what will happen to the stabiliser trim for take-off?
optionA: Set trim nose-down, leading edge up.
optionB: Set trim nose-up, leading edge down.
optionC: Set trim nose-up, leading edge up.
optionD: Set trim nose-down, leading edge down.
explanationTotal:
Learning Objective 081.05.08.03.03: Explain the relationship between CG position, take-off trim setting, and stabiliser trim position.

Weight and CG location massively affect the handling characteristics of an aircraft. This is why most large jet aircraft calculate different pitch trim settings to use for take-off, depending on the position of the CG and the take-off mass of the aircraft. This is so the pilot can always feel roughly the same force when rotating the aircraft, and in the first phase of flight.

If the aircraft has a far forward CG location, the nose will feel heavy to the pilot, so during the setup, the pilots will set a much more nose-up trim setting, so that at rotation, the feeling will be roughly the same.

This is exactly what the question is referring to. Extra weight at the front of the aircraft will make the aircraft nose heavy, requiring nose-up stabiliser trim to feel the same. A nose up stabiliser trim is caused by providing extra downforce (or less lift force) on the tail. That is created by setting the horizontal stabiliser at a lower angle, with its leading edge pointing more downwards.

title:
Refer to figure.
Assuming no pilot input the motion of the aeroplane in the diagram shows:
optionA: static longitudinal stability and dynamic longitudinal instability.
optionB: static and dynamic longitudinal stability.
optionC: neutral dynamic longitudinal stability.
optionD: static longitudinal instability.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Dynamic Stability is the subsequent long-term response of an airplane to a disturbance to its equilibrium. It is the change to the stability of an airplane with the passage of time. Any disturbance causes changes to the aerodynamic forces and moments acting on the airplane that are complex, particularly if the displacement is to its directional stability because it affects the airplane in both the yawing and rolling planes.

An airplane that is statically stable is not necessarily dynamically stable. However, for an airplane to be dynamically stable it must be statically stable. In other words, it
cannot have long-term stability without first having short-term stability. An airplane that has positive static stability may be dynamically neutral, stable, or unstable; but an airplane that is statically unstable can never attain dynamic stability. The dynamic stability of an airplane is dependent on the airplane design, its speed, and the altitude at which it is flying.

There are five states of dynamic stability and for each of them the airplane must have positive static stability.

Negative dynamic stability – the amplitude of the oscillation increases with the passage of time.

Neutral dynamic stability – the amplitude of the oscillation remains constant with the passage of time.

Positive dynamic stability – the amplitude of the oscillation decreases with the passage of time.

‘Dead beat’ positive dynamic stability – the oscillations cease immediately because they are heavily damped.

‘Divergent’ negative dynamic stability – the oscillations cease because the motion completely diverges from the original motion.

title: Its a cold day, the pilot did not do de-ice nor anti-ice the aircraft. How will ice accretion affect the aircraft performance?
optionA: The drag will increase due to contamination, but the aircraft will take off normally.
optionB: The drag will increase, it is fine as long the aircraft can become airborne.
optionC: The drag will increase due to contamination and C<sub>LMAX</sub> will reduce.
optionD: Stall speed increases, the drag decreases.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

Any deposit of ice, snow or frost on the external surfaces of an aeroplane, except as permitted in the flight manual, may drastically affect its performance due to reduced aerodynamic lift and increased drag resulting from the disturbed airflow.

An ice-contaminated wing will stall at a lower angle of attack (decreased critical AOA) or higher airspeed (increased stall speed) than a clean wing. Minute amounts of ice (equivalent to medium grit sandpaper) covering the leading edges or upper surfaces of wings can increase the stall speed up to 15 kt.

Ice will also increase the weight and, therefore the stall speed also increases, because a higher angle of attack is required to produce an increased lift. Stall happens when the maximum CL is reached, and that will be at a higher speed when the weight is increased. The profile shape is distorted, which causes the CLMAX to decrease.

title: Propeller efficiency is defined as the ratio between:
optionA: the usable (power available) power and the maximum power.
optionB: usable (power available) power of the propeller and shaft power.
optionC: the thrust and the maximum thrust.
optionD: the thermal power of fuel-flow and shaft power.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The efficiency of any system is determined by the ratio of the output power to the input power. The force developed by the engine and delivered to the propeller via the shaft is the rotational force of the propeller, the propeller torque.
The power delivered to the propeller is the product of the torque and the angular velocity of the propeller shaft (Torque × Rotational Speed).
The thrust developed by the propeller is the product of the mass of air moved and the acceleration given to it by the propeller. The power developed by the propeller is the product of the thrust and the TAS (Thrust × Axial Speed).
Propeller efficiency is the ratio of the propeller power developed to the engine power delivered. A well-designed propeller is typically 80% efficient when operating at its optimum blade angle of attack.

Propeller Efficiency = ((Thrust × Axial Speed)) / ((Torque × Rotational Speed))

title: Static stability means that:
optionA: following a disturbance from the equilibrium condition, a force and/or moment is generated that tends to increase the effects of that disturbance.
optionB: following a disturbance from the equilibrium condition, a force and/or moment is generated that tends to counter the effects of that disturbance.
optionC: the amplitude of the oscillatory motion of an aeroplane tends to increase over time.
optionD: the amplitude of the oscillatory motion of an aeroplane tends to decrease over time.
explanationTotal:
Dynamic stability is said to be present if, after a disturbance upon the aircraft that disrupted its intended flight path, the aircraft damps these oscillations.

Static stability is said to be present if the aircraft, after a disturbance upon the aircraft that disrupted its intended flight path, it counteracts this effect.
For example, if a gust causes the airplane to have a nose up momentum, the airplane automatically reduces the angle of attack and goes nose down.

title: Consider only the wing and tail moments of an aircraft. How will the following changes affect the relationship between C<sub>M</sub> and Alpha?
optionA: Moving the tailplane aft and increasing the surface will increase the negative CM for a given AoA.
optionB: Moving the wing forward will have the same effect as moving the tailplane aft.
optionC: Moving the tailplane forward and decreasing the surface will increase the positive C<sub>M</sub> for a given AoA.
optionD: Increasing the wing area will decrease the C<sub>M</sub> variation with AoA.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
Static longitudinal stability depends upon the relationship between angle of attack (α) and pitching moment coefficient (CM). Consideration must be given to the pitching moment contribution of each aircraft component. The pitching moment coefficients contributed by all the various components of the aircraft are summed and plotted versus lift coefficient (angle of attack).

Figure 1, shows the variation of pitching moment coefficient (CM) with lift coefficient (CL) for an aircraft with positive static longitudinal stability. Static stability is shown by a return to equilibrium, or trim, upon displacement. The aeroplane described by graph A is in trim or equilibrium when CM = 0. If the aeroplane is disturbed to some different CL, the pitching moment change tends to return the aircraft to the point of trim.

  • If the aeroplane were disturbed to some higher CL (point y), a negative or nose-down pitching moment is produced which tends to decrease angle of attack back to the trim point.
  • If the aeroplane were disturbed to some lower CL (point x), a positive or nose-up pitching moment is developed which tends to increase the angle of attack back to the trim point.

Positive static longitudinal stability is indicated by a negative slope of CM versus CL. The degree of static longitudinal stability is indicated by the slope of the curve.

Effect of Wing and Tail Position (figure 2)

When the aerodynamic stability of a configuration is looked at, power effects are ignored and the stability is considered by a build-up of the contributing components. If the CG is set at 30 ̊ percent MAC, the contribution of the wing alone is destabilising, as indicated by the positive slope of CM versus CL. The combination of the wing and fuselage increases the instability. The contribution of the tail alone is highly stabilising from the large negative slope of the curve.

By moving the tail aft (increasing the distance to the CG) and increasing its area both contribute to the stabilising moment, which means that the slope will be steeper, making this the correct answer.

title: The negative manoeuvring limit load factor for a light aeroplane in the normal category in the clean configuration may not be less than:
explanationTotal:
EASA regulations for flight manoeuvring envelope
The load factor and speed limits for a given aircraft are strictly regulated by EASA. The requirements are described in CS-25 (Certification Specification 25) for transport aircraft MTOW > 5 700 kg and in CS-23 for smaller aircraft MTOW < 5 700 kg.

Note: This is not the full description of classification of CS-23 and CS-25 aircraft but it is enough for us to know.

For the CS-25 category, the maximum positive and minimum negative limitation of load factor is:
nMAX = 2.5; nMIN = -1 in clean configuration (high lift devices not extended)

The CS-23 category includes three subparts:

Normal [N] nMAX = 3.8 nMIN = -1.52
Utility [U] nMAX = 4.4 nMIN = -1.76
Aerobatic [A] nMAX ≥ 6

nMIN ≤ 3

If flaps are deployed nMAX = 2; nMIN = 0 are the required limits for both categories.

title: While cruising at constant Mach number and with autothrottle operative, an aircraft experiences wind shear. Due to autothrottle delay, the aircraft's speed momentarily increased beyond M<sub>MO</sub>. Apart from the aural warning, what can happen given these conditions?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: The pilot has to abruptly recover the pitch down tendency.
optionB: Shock stall.
optionC: Buffet.
optionD: Increase in noise.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
In the same way that separated airflow prior to a low speed stall can cause airframe buffet, shock induced separation (shock stall) at high speed can also cause buffeting.

Aerodynamic buffet is a valuable stall warning, but it can damage the aircraft structure. Aircraft must therefore be operated with a (safety) margin to aerodynamic buffet.

Because of the higher dynamic pressure when an aircraft is operating in the transonic speed region, any shock induced buffet will have a greater potential for severe airframe damage. High speed buffet must be completely avoided.

If the variables which affect both high speed and low speed stall are considered it will be possible to identify the conditions under which buffeting will occur and a chart can be drawn to show all the factors involved:

- Load factor.
- Mach number.
- Angle of attack.
- Pressure altitude.
- Weight.
- CG position.

Stall boundaries set a lower limit to the operating speed, according to the load factor. In the case of a high-speed aircraft, there is also an upper limit which is due to the approach of shock stall and the associated buffet which occurs if the aircraft enters the transonic speed range. The limits associated with these effects give the buffet boundaries.

title: Many aeroplanes are equipped with speed brakes. Speed brakes are usually made up of one or several panels:
optionA: Which extend from the wings upper surface into the airstream to disrupt the laminar flow, reducing lift and increasing induced drag.
optionB: Somewhere on the fuselage or wing which extends into the airstream to create a turbulent airflow and increase parasite drag.
optionC: That form part of the primary flight controls and deflect to generate more downash which in turn increases induced drag.
optionD: Which extend into the airstream to create vortices that re-energise the boundary layer resulting in an increase in parasite drag.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Speedbrakes (flight spoilers) are secondary flight control surfaces that can be deployed manually by the pilot. Dependant upon the aircraft type, the speed brake(s) may consist of a single panel or symetrically mounted pairs of panels.

In most cases, speedbrakes are fuselage mounted panels (most frequently on the upper surface of the wing) which, when selected by the pilot, extend into the airstream to produce drag. Their operating principle is simple. Cross-sectional area increases, boundary layer becomes turbulent, which increases parasite drag and reduces lift. Since drag increases and lift reduces, lift to drag ratio reduces significantly.

title: After losing all engines and starting a glide descent, the pilot lowers the flaps in an attempt to increase the glide range. The pilot acted...
optionA: Correctly, because lowering the flaps can help improve the glide range and potentially reach a farther landing site.
optionB: Correctly, as lowering the flaps can help the pilot achieve a more efficient glide and extend the range for landing options.
optionC: Incorrectly, because lowering the flaps decreases glide range and increases glide angle.
optionD: Incorrectly, because lowering the flaps decreases glide range and decreases glide angle.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
In a power-off descent or glide there are only three forces acting on the aeroplane (i.e., lift, weight and drag).

For relatively small descent angles, up to about 20°, lift can be considered as equal to the weight. The cos γ is close to 1, so the sin γ can be interpreted as the vertical change if the horizontal 1 unit is changed. Expressed as a percentage, it is called the descent or glide gradient.

Starting from D = W x sin γ, which is derived from the attached figure, we can rearrange to:

sin γ = D ÷ W

and assuming L = W, finally we get

sin γ = D ÷ L

Glide angle is only function of the L/D ratio. The descent (glide) angle will be minimum when the L/D ratio is maximum at the optimum angle of attack. Maximum distance in a glide can be achieved when the aircraft is flown at L/DMAX (VMD).

The maximum L/D ratio of an aircraft will be obtained in the clean configuration. Extension of flaps, spoilers, speed brakes or landing gear etc. will reduce L/DMAX and give a steeper glide angle thus reducing glide range. A lower L/D Ratio due to an increase of drag, will increase the ROD and reduce the glide duration at any speed.

title:
Refer to figure.
Consider the following airfoil sections. Which one produces the least amount of drag?
optionA: Figure 1
optionB: Figure 2
optionC: Figure 3
optionD: Figure 4
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
Trim Tabs (figure 1)

A trim tab is a small adjustable surface set into the trailing edge of a main control surface. Its deflection is controlled by a trim wheel or electrical switch in the cockpit, arranged to operate in an instinctive sense.

To maintain the primary control surface in its required position, the tab is moved in the opposite direction to the control surface until the tab moment balances the control surface hinge moment.

Stabiliser Trim (figure 2)

This system of trimming may be used on manually operated and power operated controls. To trim, the tailplane incidence is adjusted by the trim wheel until the tailplane load is equal to the previous elevator balancing load required. Stick force is now zero. The main advantages of a variable incidence (trimming) tailplane are:

- The drag is less in the trimmed state as the aerofoil is more streamlined.
- Trimming does not reduce the effective range of pitch control as the elevator remains approximately neutral when the aircraft is trimmed.
- It is very powerful and gives an increased ability to trim for larger CG and speed range.

The disadvantage of a variable incidence (trimming) tailplane is that it is more complex and is heavier than a conventional trim tab system.

In this exercise, Figures 1 and 3 refer to trim tabs, and Figures 2 and 4 refer to stabiliser Trim. The least amount of drag would be produced by a stabiliser trim where the position of the elevator is neutral, which, in this case, is Figure 4.

title: For an engine failure on a multi-engined propeller driven aircraft:
optionA: Use of flap is advised to counteract the loss of propeller slipstream over the wing, but this must be limited to take-off settings only.
optionB: The loss of propeller slipstream over the wing will cause a rolling moment towards the failed engine.
optionC: Flaps can be used to counteract the loss of propeller slipstream over the wing with the failed engine.
optionD: There will be no tendency to descend as long as the use of rudder has stopped any movement in yaw.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Following an in-flight engine failure on a twin-engine turboprop, there are two immediate effects:

  • The initial effect is the yawing towards the dead engine that occurs due to the asymmetry of the thrust line.
  • The second effect is roll, which occurs when the airplane continues to yaw towards the failed engine, resulting in a decrease in lift from the ‘retreating’ wing and a yaw-induced roll towards the failed engine. This roll is reinforced by the offset of the wings and the loss of the slipstream lift in airplanes with the propeller in front of the engine.
The use of high-lift devices is not recommended. High lift devices will increase lift on both wings. The difference in lift between the two wings will increase which will result in an even larger rolling moment. Drag will also be increases which may result in a serious lack of performance.

title: An aeroplane's angle of attack can be defined as the angle between its:
optionA: speed vector and longitudinal axis.
optionB: lateral axis and the horizontal plane.
optionC: speed vector and the horizontal plane.
optionD: longitudinal axis and the horizontal plane.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
Terminology definition angle of attack: angle between the chord line and the relative (undisturbed) air flow. Local airflow = downwash at the trailing edge of the airfoil for example.

Angle of attack (AOA, α - Greek letter alpha) is a term used in aerodynamics to describe the angle between the chord line of an airfoil and the vector representing the relative motion between the airfoil and the air through which it is moving. For a two-dimensional airfoil, angle of attack is the angle between the chord line and the direction of arrival of the incoming air.

In aviation, angle of attack is used to describe the angle between the chord line of the (three dimensional) wing of a fixed-wing aircraft and the vector representing the relative motion between the aircraft and the atmosphere. Since a wing can have twist, a chord line of the whole wing may not be definable, so an alternate reference line is simply defined. Often, the chord line of the root of the wing is chosen as the reference line.

The angle of attack is often confused with the pitch angle of an aircraft and the angle of incidence. Pitch angle and angle of incidence are measured from the same reference line as angle of attack (conceptually the chord line), but pitch refers to the horizon and angle of incidence to the longitudinal axis of the aeroplane. Whereas, the angle of attack is measured from the (same) reference line to the direction of the arrival of the air to the wing (caused by the relative motion between the wing and the atmosphere).

Note: Some tricky questions ask about the angle of attack of the aeroplane (not the wing) => angle between speed vector and longitudinal axis.

title:
In level flight, an aircraft has a CL value of 0.35 at a speed of 1.6 VS.
Determine the value of CL if speed is reduced to 1.1 VS:
explanationTotal:
LIFT = ½ ρ V2 S CL

Since other variables are kept constant, exercise can be solved applying the following formula derived from the lift formula:

  • New CL x (New Speed)2 = Old CL x (Old Speed)2
New CL x 1.12 = 0.35 x 1.62
New CL = (0.35 x 1.62) / 1.12
New CL = 0.74

title:
Consider two elevator control systems:

1. is fitted with a trim tab.
2. is fitted with fully powered hydraulic controls and an adjustable horizontal stabiliser.

For both cases and starting from a trimmed condition, how will the neutral position of the control column change, after trimming for a speed decrease?
optionA: 1 does not change, 2 moves aft.
optionB: 1 moves forward, 2 moves forward.
optionC: 1 moves aft, 2 does not change.
optionD: 1 does not change, 2 does not change.
explanationTotal:
When speed is decreased, angle of attack must be increased, therefore the aircraft must be trimmed nose up otherwise the pilot will have to keep applying backpressure on the control column in order to keep level flight. When a trim tab is installed, in this case, it will move down in order to maintain the new elevator deflection. The control column is then held in a more aft position. Remember that the trim tab is deflected in the opposite direction than the elevator.

For a trimmable horizontal stabiliser, the whole stabiliser's incidence angle can be changes as trimming. The pilot can control the stabiliser by using the trim wheel. If the linkage is mechanic or power-assisted, the neutral point of the control column changes with trim setting. However, in a fully powered flight control system, neutral point will not change since there is no actual trim, only a feel unit (if you are trimmed, the elevator deflection is 0).

title: Which statement is true regarding positive limit load factor on CS25 and CS23?
optionA: CS23 has a higher value
optionB: CS25 has a higher value
optionC: CS23 and CS25 have the same value
