They are caused by the pressure differential between the top and bottom of the wing, which causes an updraft of high pressure air around the tip of the wing. This updraft turn into a downdraft behind the wing, creating a vortex. The higher the pressure difference between the top and bottom of the wing, the stronger the vortices.

This question is specifically asking for:

  • Angle of attack: The strength of the vortices (and therefore also induced drag) is proportional to the angle of attack. Therefore; the strength of the vortices increase as the angle of attack increases. And also; the strength of the vortices decrease as the angle of attack decreases. Therefore statement 1 is incorrect!
  • Aspect ratio: The strength of the vortices is inversely proportional with the aspect ratio. Meaning that the strength of the wing tip vortices increase as the aspect ratio decreases. And vice versa: the strength decreases as the aspect ratio increases. Therefore statement 2 is correct!

title:
Which statement about induced drag is correct?

I. Induced drag increases as angle of attack increases.
II. At constant load factor, induced drag decreases with increasing aeroplane mass.
optionA: I is incorrect, II is correct.
optionB: I is correct, II is incorrect.
optionC: I is correct, II is correct.
optionD: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The total drag is the resulting factor if you add induced drag and parasite drag together.

Parasite drag is caused if an airfoil is moving through the air. It is the result of form drag and skin friction drag.
Form drag arises from the shape of the object. The more streamlined the object, the less form drag is present.
Shape and size are most important in the amount of form drag resulting. Form drag increases with increasing velocity, making it very important for high speed aircraft.
Skin friction drag is caused by the friction of the fluid (in case of aircraft this fluid is the atmosphere) against the skin of the object moving through it.
It is directly related to the surface area in contact with the fluid. Skin friction increases with the square of the velocity.

Induced drag is caused when an object redirects the airflow. A wing produces lift by creating a pressure difference.
This pressure difference is caused by the shape of the airfoil, causing the airflow on top to accelerate, creating a low pressure on top of the wing and high pressure below the wing.
This pressure difference naturally wants to restore towards a uniform pressure, which creates vortices around the wingtip.
These vortices are deflected downwards, this phenomenon is also called downwash.
The induced drag decreases with airspeed and increases with angle of attack and increasing weight.

In the image we can see that the two vectors (induced and parasite drag) create a resulting vector, the total drag.
Where the induced and parasite drag vectors collide, we have the minimum drag speed (VMD); the speed where the total drag is the lowest.
This leads us to understand that during an acceleration from a total stand still, the total drag first decreases up until the minimum drag speed and then starts increasing again.

title: A pilot is performing a flight in an aeroplane with mechanical flight controls. The aeroplane makes one flight at its MTOM of 1900 kg with a CG near the aft limit. On the following flight, the pilot is the only occupant on board; the aeroplane is approximately 400 kg lighter and the CG has moved forward. How will this change the feel of the aircraft as experienced by the pilot?
optionA: There is NO change to the feel since the CG remains within its limitation and mass has NO effect on the stick force per g.
optionB: There is NO change to the feel since the increased stick force per g, caused by the lighter mass, is offset by the forward CG.
optionC: The stick force per g is reduced since the aeroplane is lighter, but the forward CG makes this reduction less noticeable to the pilot.
optionD: The stick force per g is increased since the lighter aeroplane and forward CG both reduce the manoeuvrability of the aeroplane.
explanationTotal:
Important Note: This question ventures outside of the learning objectives and therefore should be appealed if seen in the exam. We have had various different pieces of feedback come through for this question and similar questions, and they don't really make sense. We do not know whether this question is currently being asked, and we very much hope that it has been removed. Please send us any further questions or exam feedback in the comments, or by email to info@atplquestions.com, thank you!

The feel of an aeroplane is how much force is required to make a particular manoeuvre, often referred to in the units of "stick force per G" for longitudinal stability (pitch changes). Stability and manoeuvrability are intrinsically linked, in that the more manoeuvrable an aircraft is, the less stable it is, and vice-versa. Stick force per G simply measures how much force the pilot needs to exert on the controls to cause a 1G change in load factor, the higher this value, the more stable (less controllable) an aircraft is.

The movement (forward/aft) of the CG is incredibly important to longitudinal stability, as having a forward CG means that the CG is further in front of the neutral point. This means greater stability, and therefore lower manoeuvrability.

A change in mass (without a change in CG) is much more complicated. It appears that mass change has an effect on the manoeuvrability that cannot be simply stated for the average aircraft, as mass and wing loading (a function of mass) appear to have opposing effects, but with different values, and the effect of different speeds for higher masses is not accounted for anywhere in the question. As you can probably tell, this is already much too complex for the ATPL exams. This is likely why the effect of mass on manoeuvring stability/stick force per G is not on the learning objectives. It is intuitive to think that a lighter aircraft is more manoeuvrable, but that is not something that can be absolutely stated without further information, and not even something the learning objectives mention.

We think that the examiner has written a question to test knowledge of CG movements, assuming that their intuition on the change in weight is correct, but has ended up making a question much more complicated, which ventures outside the learning objectives.

Therefore, our new recommendation here would be to answer the question assuming that the weight reduction decreases the stick force per G, even though that is not an absolute statement.

This leaves us with the answer "The stick force per g is reduced since the aeroplane is lighter, but the forward CG makes this reduction less noticeable to the pilot."

title:
Refer to figure.
Choose the correct statement:
optionA: Aerofoil 4 corresponds to line 3.
optionB: Aerofoil 3 corresponds to line 2.
optionC: Aerofoil 1 corresponds to line 4.
optionD: Aerofoil 3 corresponds to line 1.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
A completely symmetrical airfoil will intersect the vertical axis of the graph at the origin (0).
A positively cambered airfoil will generate more lift at the same speed (and therefore has a higher CL) than a symmetrical airfoil and therefore intersects the vertical axis above the origin (and generates 0 lift at a negative angle of attack).
A negatively cambered airfoil will generate less lift at the same speed (which translates into a lower CL at a certain speed) and therefore intersects the vertical axis below the origin.

An increased camber generates a higher value of CL at the same Angle of Attack.

Therefore, we have the following combinations:

  • Aerofoil 1 corresponds to line 3.
  • Aerofoil 2 corresponds to line 4.
  • Aerofoil 3 corresponds to line 1.
  • Aerofoil 4 corresponds to line 2.

title: Whilst setting up for landing, the crew are distracted by an external event on the radio. In doing so, they forget to set the final stage of flaps. The aircraft system automatically adjusts the approach speed for the reduced flap setting, but does not notify the pilots, so they land with a lower flap setting (less flaps) than planned and computed. The landing distance will (1) _____ due to (2) _____ and (3)_____ being generated by the lower flap setting, and therefore a (4) _____ touchdown speed.
optionA: (1) increase; (2) less drag; (3) less lift; (4) higher
optionB: (1) increase; (2) less drag; (3) more lift; (4) lower
optionC: (1) decrease; (2) less drag; (3) less lift; (4) lower
optionD: (1) increase; (2) more drag; (3) more lift; (4) higher
explanationTotal:
Note: This is similar to question 812314, but includes more/less drag as an option. This has been seen as a drop-down menu question in the UK CAA exams.

Learning Objective 081.01.09.01.09: Explain the effects of flap-setting errors, such as mis-selection and premature/late extension or retraction of flaps, on: take-off and landing distance and speeds; climb and descent performance; stall buffet margins.

This scenario is effectively asking what happens if we land with less flaps. Well of course, with less flaps, our stall speed will be higher, as flaps increase the camber (and sometimes area) of the wing, allowing an aircraft to fly slower with the same amount of lift.

With a higher stall speed, the approach speed VREF will be higher, the aircraft will touch down with more groundspeed, causing a longer landing distance than if a higher flap setting were to be used.

So that is (1) and (4) answered, and we must remember that with a lower flap setting we have less lift available for the same IAS. This is the component that influences our landing distance, as the lack of lift means we have to fly at a higher speed, and land at a higher speed.

As for the drag, lower flap settings produce less drag. This is not the main factor behind the increased landing distance though, as most of the braking action during landing comes from the brakes (and reverse thrust, if available), and the flaps actually reduce the weight of the aircraft on the wheels, so reduce braking ability slightly.

title: An aeroplane has static longitudinal stability when the:
optionA: Aerodynamic centre is in front of the neutral point.
optionB: Centre of pressure is in front of the aerodynamic centre.
optionC: Centre of gravity is in front of the neutral point.
optionD: Centre of pressure is in front of the neutral point.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
A variation of CG position can cause large changes in the static longitudinal stability. In the conventional airplane configuration, the large changes in stability with CG variation are primarily due to the large changes in the wing contribution.

As the CG is gradually moved aft, the airplane static stability decreases, then becomes neutral then unstable. The CG position which produces zero slope and neutral static stability is referred to as the “neutral point”. The neutral point may be imagined as the effective aerodynamic center of the entire airplane configuration, i.e. with the CG at the neutral point, all changes in net lift effectively occur at that point and no change in pitching moment results. The neutral point defines the most aft CG position without static instability.

For an airplane to always have positive longitudinal static stability the CG must be ahead of the neutral point, so that the wing-pitching moment always exceeds the tail plane pitching moment. The further aft the neutral point is from the CG the greater is the static longitudinal stability.

title: Which statement is correct about a normal shock wave?
optionA: The airflow changes direction.
optionB: The airflow changes from subsonic to supersonic.
optionC: The airflow expands when passing the aerofoil.
optionD: The airflow changes from supersonic to subsonic.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

(Normal meaning perpendicular to the upstream flow).

Whenever supersonic airflow is slowed to subsonic speed without a change in direction, a ‘normal’ shock wave will form as a boundary between the supersonic and subsonic region. This means that some compressibility effects will occur before the aircraft reaches Mach 1.0.

title: An aeroplane, with a CG location behind the centre of pressure of the wing can only maintain a straight and level flight when the horizontal tail loading is:
optionA: zero.
optionB: upwards or downwards depending on elevator deflection.
optionC: downwards.
optionD: upwards.
explanationTotal:
If the Center of Gravity (CG) is located behind the Center of Pressure (CP), it means that the lift acts in front of the CG.
This causes a nose up movement.
To keep an aircraft level, the two moments from the wing and tailplane will have to cancel each other out.
The CP always points upwards.
This means that if the CP is in front of the CG, the nose wants to move upwards.

To cancel this movement, the tailplane generates an upwards moment to keep the nose straight. In this case, the CP is located ahead of the CG.
To have the nose not move upwards, an upwards moment has to be created by the tailplane, so the tail comes up again and the nose goes down to a 0 angle.

title: What is the advantage of a swept back wing when compared to a rectangular wing of the same wing area and wing loading?
optionA: It has greater strength.
optionB: It has a lower stalling speed.
optionC: The longitudinal stability is increased for a swept wing.
optionD: Higher critical Mach number.
explanationTotal:
For a swept wing, the free stream velocity is broken down to two components: a component which is perpendicular to the leading edge and a component parallel to the leading edge.
The magnitude of the pressure distribution (and MCRIT) is determined by the perpendicular component which, for a swept wing, is less than the free stream velocity. Consequently, In transonic flight, a swept wing allows a higher Critical Mach Number (MCRIT) than a straight wing of similar chord and camber. This results in the principal advantage of wing sweep which is to delay the onset of wave drag.

title: Which of these statements about a trimmable horizontal stabiliser is correct?
optionA: A trimmed aeroplane with an aft CG requires the stabiliser leading edge to be lower than in the case of a forward CG in the same condition.
optionB: Because take-off speeds do not vary with CG position, the need for stabiliser adjustment is dependent on flap position only.
optionC: At the aft CG limit, stabiliser trim is adjusted fully nose up to obtain maximum elevator authority at rotation during take-off.
optionD: A trimmed aeroplane with an aft CG requires the stabiliser leading edge to be higher than in the case of a forward CG in the same condition.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
A nose-heavy airplane (forward CG position) requires the stabiliser to produce downforce to prevent the nose from dopping. To counteract this, a larger negative angle of attack must be achieved, therefore the stabiliser leading edge must be lower than the trailling edge.

A tail-heavy airplane (aft CG position) would require the stabilizer to produce less downforce. Thus, the stabiliser leading edge is higher than the trailing edge.

title:
(For this question use annex 081-013 issue date November 2005).
The blade angle of a rotating propeller blade element shown in the annex is:
optionA: angle 3.
optionB: angle 2.
optionC: not correctly indicated in the diagram.
optionD: angle 1.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The Blade Angle

Sometimes called the pitch angle, is the angle subtended between the plane of rotation and the chord line of the propeller blade, which may be fixed or variable. When the airplane is moving it comprises two parts, the angle of attack and the helix angle, but when it is stationary the blade angle is equal to the angle of attack.

The Helix Angle

The angle that the actual path of the propeller makes to the plane of rotation.

Angle of Attack

The path of the propeller through the air determines the direction of the relative airflow. The angle between the blade chord and the relative airflow is the angle of attack (α).
The angle of attack (α) is the result of propeller rotational velocity (RPM) and aircraft forward velocity (TAS).

title: Extension of trailing-edge flaps (1) _____ downwash. In case of ice contamination, the risk of premature stabiliser stall (2) _____.
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: (1) increases; (2) increases
optionB: (1) increases; (2) decreases
optionC: (1) decreases; (1) increases
optionD: (1) decreases; (2) decreases
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
STABILIZER STALL DUE TO ICE

The tailplane is an aerofoil, and because it is thinner than the wing, it is likely to experience icing before the wing does. The effect will be the same as for the wing; the stall will occur at a lower angle of attack.

The tailplane is normally operating at a negative angle of attack, producing a down load, so if the tailplane stalls and the down load is lost, the nose of the aircraft will drop and longitudinal control will be lost.

Stalling of an ice contaminated tailplane could be precipitated by extension of the wing flaps.

Lowering the flaps increases the downwash, and this increases the negative angle of attack of the tailplane. If the tailplane has ice contamination, this could be sufficient to cause it to stall.

Recovery procedure in this situation would be to retract the flaps again, thus reducing the downwash.

Take care when increasing an aircraft's forward airspeed to compensate for ice on the wings, since every knot of airspeed added to prevent wing stall brings the aircraft a knot closer to tailplane stall. Consequently, it is vital that the tailplane, like the wing, is free from contamination. This type of stall does not usually occur, but if it does, recovery is normally impossible.

title: After reaching its cruising altitude, an aircraft accelerates to a speed where compressibility in the airflow becomes aerodynamically significant. The term “compressibility” means that there are changes in the _____ of the free stream airflow.
optionA: dynamic pressure
optionB: temperature
optionC: density
optionD: static pressure
explanationTotal:
The terms compressibility and incompressibility describe the ability of molecules in a fluid to be compacted or compressed (made more dense) and their ability to bounce back to their original density, in other words, their "springiness."

An incompressible fluid cannot be compressed and has relatively constant density throughout. Liquid is an incompressible fluid. A gaseous fluid such as air, on the other hand, can be either compressible or incompressible.

Generally, for theoretical and experimental purposes, gases are assumed to be incompressible when they are moving at low speeds (under approximately M0.4). The motion of the object traveling through the air at such speed does not affect the density of the air. This assumption has been useful in aerodynamics when studying the behavior of air in relation to airfoils and other objects moving through the air at slower speeds.

However, when aircraft began traveling faster than M0.4, assumptions regarding the air through which they flew that were true at slower speeds were no longer valid. At high speeds some of the energy of the quickly moving aircraft goes into compressing the fluid (the air) and changing its density.

The air at higher altitudes where these aircraft fly also has lower density than air nearer to the Earth's surface. The airflow is now compressible, and aerodynamic theories have had to reflect this.

title: An aeroplane on final approach is flying at a CAS lower than V<sub>MD</sub>, which means it is speed unstable. If the speed suddenly decreases, what effect do parasite and induced drag have on total drag?
optionA: Parasite drag increases, induced drag reduces by the same amount, so total drag stays the same.
optionB: Parasite drag reduces, induced drag increases by a larger amount, so total drag increases.
optionC: Parasite drag reduces, induced drag increases by a smaller amount, so total drag reduces.
optionD: Parasite drag increases, induced drag reduces by a smaller amount, so total drag increases.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
During flight, an aircraft will experience two types of drag:

- Parasite Drag (proportional to IAS2, increases with increasing “Parasite Area”: flaps, undercarriage or speed brakes)

- Induced Drag (inversely proportional to IAS2, increases with increasing weight).

The sum of Parasite Drag and Induced Drag is the Total Drag.

The Total Drag will be minimum at the IAS where Parasite Drag = Induced Drag. This speed is called Minimum Drag Speed (VMD). Flying at a slower or faster speed than VMD will generate more drag.

Flying at a slower speed than VMD (back side), the aircraft will be in the unstable speed region. Any loss of speed will result in an increase in drag and further speed loss (which must be corrected by an increase in thrust). The sudden change to a tailwind (or a decrease in headwind) will cause a loss of airspeed.

title: Which of these statements concerning propellers is correct?
optionA: An unfeathered propeller causes less drag than a feathered propeller.
optionB: The blade angle of a feathered propeller is approximately 0 degrees.
optionC: A windmilling propeller causes less drag than a feathered propeller.
optionD: The blade angle of a feathered propeller is approximately 90 degrees.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

To prevent the propeller from ‘wind milling’ the propeller blade is rotated from the fine-pitch stop through the coarse-pitch stop to reach the angle of attack to the relative airflow that produces zero lift; and referred to as ‘feathering’ the propeller. It’s usually approximately 85°/90° because it is the best compromise for the whole blade length and accounts for the blade twist.
This blade position stops the propeller from rotating because there is no lift force to produce a torque reaction; it reduces the drag to a minimum level and prevents damage being caused to the engine.
For a single-engine airplane feathering the propeller blades improves the glide performance because it does not require such a steep glide angle to maintain the required airspeed. As such, feathering the propeller increases the gliding range and endurance. For a multi-engine airplane, the decreased drag reduces the amount of thrust required to counteract the asymmetric force of the propeller of the failed engine and there is sufficient rudder authority remaining to enable the pilot to safely control the airplane.

title:
Which statement about an aeroplane entering ground effect is correct?

I. The downwash angle decreases.
II. The induced angle of attack remains constant.
optionA: I is incorrect, II is correct.
optionB: I is correct, II is correct.
optionC: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
optionD: I is correct, II is incorrect.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
When taking-off or landing, the proximity to the ground prevents full development of the trailing vortices, making them much weaker than in normal flight. This leads to a decrease in downwash, therefore a higher effect angle of attack which also means a smaller induced angle of attack.

This question is asking what will happen when entering ground effect:

  • Downwash angle: When entering ground effect, the effect of the vortices is decreased therefore our downwash angle will decrease. Therefore statement 1 is correct!
  • Induced angle of attack: When entering ground effect, because of the decrease in downwash, the induced angle of attack will decrease leading to a decrease in induced drag. Therefore statement 2 is incorrect!

title:
Which of these statements are correct or incorrect regarding a sideslip, with the relative airflow coming from the right, on an aeroplane that exhibits both directional and lateral stability?

I. The initial tendency of the nose of the aeroplane is to move to the right.
II. The initial tendency of the right wing is to move down.
optionA: I is correct, II is correct.
optionB: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
optionC: I is correct, II is incorrect.
optionD: I is incorrect, II is correct.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
Sideslip is the displacement angle of the airplane’s longitudinal axis in azimuth from the relative airflow. It is positive when the relative airflow is to the right of the longitudinal axis and negative when the relative airflow is left of the longitudinal axis.

An airplane has directional static stability if, when in a sideslip with the airflow coming from the right initially the nose tends to yaw right. Therefore, statement 1 is correct.

The lateral static stability is a measure of the airplane’s tendency to return to the wings-level attitude after a disturbance has caused the airplane to be disturbed in the rolling plane.

Positive lateral static stability is the tendency of the airplane to roll to the left with a positive sideslip angle, nose to the left. Its ability to recover is dependent on the effect of sideslip. Therefore, statement 2 is incorrect.

title: An engine failure can result in a windmilling (1) propeller and a feathered (2) propeller. Which statement about propeller drag is correct?
optionA: (2) is larger than (1).
optionB: (1) is equal to (2).
optionC: impossible to say which one is largest.
optionD: (1) is larger than (2).
explanationTotal:
Blade pitch refers to the process of turning the propeller blades’ angle of attack into or out of the wind, depending on the best performance at that point.Propeller pitch is often referred to as ‘coarse’ for a greater horizontal blade angle and ‘fine’ for a more vertical angle.

The thrust from a propeller depends on its speed and angle of attack.As the tip of the propeller has a higher speed than the hub, propellers ate often twisted along the blade to remain uniform thrust along the blade.

In case of an engine failure, a propeller that is not generating thrust is only generating drag, which is not beneficial for flying.Thus, we want to reduce the drag from this propeller.

A propeller that is catching a lot of air and therefore generating a lot of drag is called a windmilling propeller.
We can use a technique called feathering to adjust the angle of attack of the propeller so that it meets the least amount of air, thus generating less drag.

title: Which of these statements about boundary layers is correct?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Compared with a turbulent boundary layer, a laminar boundary layer is better able to resist a positive pressure gradient before it separates.
optionB: A turbulent boundary layer turns into a laminar one at the transition point.
optionC: A laminar boundary layer is thicker than a turbulent one.
optionD: A turbulent boundary layer produces more friction drag than a laminar one.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
There is a layer of air that clings to the surface of an object and resists movement. This characteristic of the air is its viscosity, which although very small, is enough for the molecules of the air in contact with a surface to stick to the surface. It is static and therefore causes the laminar streamline flow adjacent to this layer to slow down, which in turn produces turbulence.

The speed of the airflow changes from zero at the surface of the airfoil to the full speed of the free flow airstream a few millimeters away from the surface.

This thin layer of sluggish air that clings to the surface of the object and in which the speed change of the airflow takes place is the boundary layer.
In aerodynamics the boundary layer is important when considering wing stall, skin friction drag and heat transfer in high-speed flight.

Boundary layers may be laminar (layered) or turbulent (disordered).
The boundary layer increases in thickness as it moves rearward over an aircraft wing, with the turbulent boundary layer being proportionally thicker than the laminar boundary layer under the same free stream velocity conditions.
The turbulent boundary layer has much higher local velocities immediately adjacent to the surface. The airflow in this region therefore possesses much higher kinetic energy than the laminar boundary layer at the same distance above the surface.

The rapid velocity change associated with the turbulent boundary layer is evidence of high skin friction drag.
The turbulent boundary has less tendency to separate from the airfoil surface over which it is flowing than the laminar boundary layer because it is better able to withstand the positive pressure gradient.

title: Stick force per g:
optionA: has a maximum value related to acceptable controllability, the minimum value is of no concern.
optionB: is dependent on CG location.
optionC: does not change with increasing altitude.
optionD: is selected by the pilot by electronic means before each flight.
explanationTotal:
The stick force gradient is the force required to change the load factor of the aircraft for a given amount.

The stick force per g is dependent on:

- Center of Gravity location; if the aircraft has more static longitudinal stability, the stick force per g will be higher.Therefore, a more forward CG means higher stick force per g.

- Altitude; as altitude decreases, aerodynamic damping increases, increasing stick force per g.

title: Consider an aerofoil section. The relative thickness is the ratio of...
optionA: maximum thickness to chord length.
optionB: maximum thickness to maximum camber.
optionC: average thickness to medium camber-line length.
optionD: average thickness to chord length.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
THICKNESS/CHORD RATION

The ratio of the maximum thickness of an aerofoil to the chord length expressed as a percentage is the thickness/chord ratio. This is usually between 10% and 12%.

title: Assuming no flow separation and no compressibility effects, the location of the aerodynamic centre of an aerofoil section:
optionA: moves backward when the angle of attack increases.
optionB: is at approximately 25% chord irrespective of angle of attack.
optionC: moves backward when the angle of attack decreases.
optionD: is at approximately 50% chord irrespective of angle of attack.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
AERODYNAMIC CENTRE

The Aerodynamic center is a fixed point on the chord line where all changes in the magnitude of the lift force effectively take place. Assuming no flow separation and no compressibility effects, the location of the aerodynamic centre of an aerofoil section is independent of angle of attack.
  • When considering subsonic airflows the AC is located at the 25% chord point for any aerofoil regardless of camber, thickness and angle of attack. In the trans. and supersonic speed region, the AC will move to about mid chord (50%). Resulting in an increase in static longitudinal stability.

title: While flying an aircraft fitted with a constant speed propeller, during a glide with idle power and whilst maintaining constant airspeed, pushing the propeller lever forward will...
optionA: increase pitch angle and increase RPM.
optionB: increase pitch angle and decrease RPM.
optionC: decrease pitch angle and decrease RPM.
optionD: decrease pitch angle and increase RPM.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
The propeller blade is an aerofoil and the definitions for chord, camber, thickness/chord ratio and aspect ratio are the same as those given previously for the wing.

Blade Angle or Pitch
The angle between the blade chord and the plane of rotation. Blade angle decreases from the root to the tip of the blade (twist) because rotational velocity of the blade increases from root to tip.

Constant speed propellers
Modern aircraft have propellers which are controlled automatically to vary their pitch (blade angle) so as to maintain a selected RPM.

A variable pitch propeller permits high efficiency to be obtained over a wider range of TAS, giving improved take-off and climb performance and cruising fuel consumption.

Figure 1
Illustrates a ‘typical’ set of engine and propeller controls for a small piston engine aircraft with a variable pitch propeller:

“Pulling back” on the prop’ control will decrease RPM.
“Pushing forward” on the prop’ control will increase RPM.

Figure 2
Shows the conditions at high forward speed in level flight. As the TAS increased, the CSU continually increased the blade angle (coarsened the pitch) to maintain a constant blade angle of attack.

In a steady glide with no shaft power from the engine (throttle closed), if the propeller pitch is decreased by pushing forward the prop’ lever, the aircraft Lift/Drag ratio will decrease. This will increase the rate of descent.
The opposite will be true if the propeller pitch is increased.

title: CS-23 and CS-25 require that an aeroplane must be statically stable and specify the acceptable range of stability and manoeuvrability. An aircraft's stability is affected by the CG location and the gross weight of the aircraft, amongst other factors. For a given aeroplane, the manoeuvrability...
optionA: cannot be affected by the pilot or operator as it is determined by the aircraft design.
optionB: is determined by the size of the control surfaces only, not the CG position or the weight.
optionC: is significantly higher when the centre of gravity is at the forward limit, and/or when the aeroplane is heavy.
optionD: tends to be reduced when the aeroplane is heavy or has a forward centre of gravity location.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

This question is unnecessarily long and wordy, but does give some hints which help to remove incorrect options quickly.

Static stability pertains to how a system reacts immediately when disturbed. In a statically stable system, it initially moves back toward its equilibrium state. An aircraft's type of static stability is defined by its initial reaction after some external force is removed. We use the term "static" because we're only concerned with the initial tendency to return to equilibrium, without considering subsequent motion.

Manoeuvrability, on the other hand, is the aircraft's ability to change its position or attitude in response to pilot inputs, allowing it to perform various manoeuvres.

Stability and manoeuvrability are effectively opposite, and the greater an aircraft's stability, the lower the manoeuvrability, and vice-versa. An aircraft with a further forward CG has greater stability (but lower manoeuvrability) and aircraft with aft CG locations have lower stability, but higher manoeuvrability. Higher weight also tends to reduce manoeuvrability, but this rule isn't always as simple as the CG locations.

The question tells us that stability is affected by the CG location and the gross weight of the aircraft, and, knowing that manoeuvrability and stability are closely (and inversely) linked, that hints to us that those factors also affect the manoeuvrability, which they do. That removes the following options:

  • "cannot be affected by the pilot or operator as it is determined by the aircraft design.", as the CG location and weight can be affected by the operator/pilot, so therefore, the manoeuvrability can be too; and
  • "is determined by the size of the control surfaces only, not the CG position or the weight.", as the manoeuvrability is changed by the CG location and weight.

The other options can be chosen between based on the CG location and weight, and the effects of those mentioned above.

title: When the elevator is deflected upwards, it creates a moment around the centre of (1) _____ which will result in the aeroplane pitching (2) _____.
optionA: (1) gravity; (2) up
optionB: (1) pressure; (2) up
optionC: (1) pressure; (2) down
optionD: (1) gravity; (2) down
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The elevator is located on the horizontal stabilizer. It can be deflected up or down to produce a change in the downforce produced by the horizontal tail. The angle of deflection is considered positive when the trailing edge of the elevator is deflected upward. Such a deflection increases the downforce produced by the horizontal tail causing the nose to pitch upward.

The change in lift created by deflecting the elevator will cause the airplane to rotate about its centre of gravity (CG).

title: Two identical aeroplanes A and B, with the same mass, are flying steady level co-ordinated 20 degree bank turns. If the TAS of A is 130 kt and the TAS of B is 200 kt:
optionA: the turn radius of A is greater than that of B.
optionB: the lift coefficient of A is greater than that of B.
optionC: the rate of turn of A is less than that of B.
optionD: the load factor of A is greater than that of B.
explanationTotal:
We have two aircraft at different speeds, same mass and bank angle.

⇒ Radius of Turn is greater, the faster the aircraft is [Radius = TAS2 ÷ (g x tan ɸ)]
⇒ Rate of Turn is greater, the slower the aircraft is [Rate of Turn = 1/TAS]
⇒ Lift coefficient is greater, the slower the aircraft is. According to the lift formula (L = 1/2 p V2 CL), in order to fly steady level (same lift), if V reduces CL must increase.

title: Compared with straight and level flight in order to maintain constant speed during a level, co-ordinated turn, the pilot must:
optionA: increase thrust and angle of attack.
optionB: increase thrust and keep angle of attack unchanged.
optionC: increase angle of attack and keep thrust unchanged.
optionD: increase thrust and decrease angle of attack.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
In level flight, any turn will be coordinated or uncoordinated. A coordinated turn is one in which the only acceleration is along the normal axis of the airplane, towards the center of the turn, and the angle of bank is precisely correct for the aircraft speed and the radius of turn. If not all these factors are present, the turn will be uncoordinated and there will be a lateral acceleration either towards or away from the center of the turn. The total lift of a balanced turn provides the centripetal force and the force that opposes the mass of the airplane.

If there is acceleration towards the center of the turn the airplane is slipping and if it is away from the center of the turn the airplane is skidding. Either condition will be indicated on the turn and slip indicator. An overbanked airplane will slip into the turn and requires an increase of speed or a reduction in bank angle to correct this condition. An underbanked airplane will skid out of the turn, which requires a decreased speed or an increased bank angle to correct this condition. These are indicated on the turn and slip indicator by the needle one-way and the ball the other.

To maintain altitude and airspeed when executing a turn both the angle of attack and the thrust have to be increased above their level flight values.

title: An aeroplane is maintaining straight and level flight at the stalling speed. If the pilot now reduces the angle of attack and accelerates, the total drag will initially:
optionA: Exceed the thrust.
optionB: Remain constant.
optionC: Increase.
optionD: Decrease.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

For this question, its vital to understand whether the aircraft is flying in the speed stable region or the speed unstable region; as this will determine whether our drag increases or decreases with changes in speed. Seeing as the questions specifies that we are initially flying at the stall speed, we know that we are in the speed unstable region.

In the speed unstable region, any decrease in speed will be met with an increase in drag, which will cause an even higher decrease in speed. Hence ‘speed unstable’.
On the other hand, in the speed stable region, a decrease in speed will cause a decrease in total drag (see graph)

Therefore the correct answer is that initially the total drag decreases when the pilot accelerates from the stall speed.

title: What is the time for a heading change of 3 degrees in a steady co-ordinated horizontal rate one turn?
optionA: 15 seconds.
optionB: 20 seconds.
optionC: 2 minutes.
optionD: 1 second.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
If the turn is unbalanced, an aircraft either slips into, or skids out of the turn, thereby reducing the aerodynamic efficiency of the aircraft. To help correct for these unwanted conditions, the aircraft is flown using the balance part of the turn and balance indicator

During a balanced turn the ball remains in the centre of the balance indicator and the pilot remains upright in the seat relative to the aircraft, with no tendency to lean.

Rate of turn is the measurement of how long it takes for an aircraft to turn, measured in degrees per second. This is particularly important during instrument flying where rate-1 turns are usually carried out at a rate of 3° per second. This means that the aircraft turns through 180° in 1 minute, or 360° in 2 minutes. A steeper angle of bank is required to carry out a rate-1 turn at higher airspeeds.

title: Which design characteristic is typical for a supercritical aerofoil when compared to a conventional positive-cambered aerofoil?
optionA: A flatter upper surface.
optionB: A smaller leading edge radius.
optionC: A smaller thickness.
optionD: A thinner trailing edge.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
A supercritical wing is one that has been designed with specific streamwise segments to delay the onset of the adverse effects of the shockwave, i.e. wave drag and its severity and decreased lateral stability, when the airplane is flying in the transonic speed range or just above MCRIT. It increases the cruise Mach number, the range, and the endurance of the airplane. The main features of a supercritical wing are:

The upper surface is flattened but the lower surface is reflex cambered towards the trailing edge. Thus, the airflow over the upper surface is not accelerated as much as conventional airfoils, which delays the formation of the shockwave to a higher speed.

Compared with a conventional airfoil section it has a larger leading-edge radius, a flatter upper surface and both positive and negative camber and enables a relatively thick wing to be used for approximately the same cruise Mach number.

The curved lower surface increases the lift generated by the aft end of the airfoil and replaces some of the lift lost from the flat upper surface. Because of the rear-loaded lift generation it is often called an aft-loaded wing.
The leading edge of the supercritical wing has a greater radius than traditional airfoils that suffer from excessive wave drag and the loss of longitudinal stability (tuck under).

By ensuring that its profile is carefully designed any expansion waves will be reflected from the subsonic boundary back to the shockwave, thereby weakening its intensity.

title: An aircraft is flying straight and level at 100 kts with a C<sub>L</sub> of 0.35. Its C<sub>LMAX</sub> is 1.22. Determine the maximum achievable load factor:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionD: Insufficient information to make the calculation
explanationTotal:
The load factor (n) can be defined as the ratio of the actual lift of an aircraft to its weight (n = Lift / Weight). In straight and level flight, load factor equals 1.

The Lift (L) can be calculated using the following formula:

L = CL x Q x S
Where CL stands for coefficient of lift, Q is dynamic pressure and S represents wing area.

The question states that CL can be increased from 0.35 (present value) to 1.22 (CLMAX). Therefore, the maximum increase in lift is represented by a factor of: 1.22 / 0.35 = 3.49

  • Maximum achievable load factor = 1 x 3.49 = 3.49

title: An aircraft climbs below the tropopause at constant Indicated Airspeed. What would be the most likely cause for aircraft buffet?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: High Angle of Attack due to the increase in TAS.
optionB: High Angle of Attack due to the decrease in TAS.
optionC: High Mach Number due to the increase in TAS.
optionD: High Mach Number due to the increase in LSS.
explanationTotal:
M = TAS ÷ LSS

During a climb, air density is decreasing. Therefore, the TAS needs to constantly increase to maintain a constant IAS/CAS.
The OAT decreases with increasing altitude, so the LSS will decrease since LSS = 38.95 x √ (°K) (directly proportional to temperature).

According to the above equation, if the TAS increases and the LSS decreases, the Mach number will increase. The Mach number will steadily increase, potentially beyond MMO to a point at which high speed buffet develops.

title: What is the effect of increasing wing aspect ratio on induced drag?
optionA: It reduces because the effect of wing-tip vortices is reduced.
optionB: It increases because increasing aspect ratio produces greater downwash.
optionC: It increases because increasing aspect ratio increases frontal area.
optionD: It is unaffected because there is no relation between aspect ratio and induced drag.
explanationTotal:
Wing tip vortices increase if we increase induced drag. This can be caused by for example increased speed, density or lift coefficient. If we increase Angle of Attack, lift will be increased, also increasing the strength of wing tip vortices.

Another factor increasing wing tip vortices is the aspect ratio (λ) of the wing. This is the ratio of the wing span to its mean chord. The aspect ratio of the wing is equal to the square of the wingspan divided by the wing surface area. Therefore a short but wide wing has a low aspect ratio but a long, narrow wing has a high aspect ratio. With a lower aspect ratio, the induced drag is higher, thus increasing wing tip vortices. With a high aspect ratio, the induced drag is lower, reducing wing tip vortices. We can therefore state that the relationship between wing tip vortices and aspect ratio is inversely proportional.

A wing with a higher aspect ratio has a lower value for CLmax and will have a higher value of CL for a certain angle of attack.

title: In order to prevent flight control surface flutter, the centre of mass of the flight control should be…
optionA: in the middle of the flight control surface.
optionB: in front of the hinge line.
optionC: at the hinge line.
optionD: behind the hinge line.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Flutter is an oscillation of the control surface which can occur due to the bending and twisting of the structure under load.

If the control surface CG is behind the hinge line, inertia will cause the surface to oscillate about its hinge line. The oscillations can be divergent and cause structural failure.

Flutter involves:
- aerodynamic forces.
- inertia forces.
- the elastic properties of a surface.

An aircraft is subject to many aerodynamic excitations (gusts, control inputs, etc.) and the aerodynamic forces at various speeds have characteristic properties for rate of change of force and moment.

The interaction of the aerofoil mass and the aerodynamic load imposed on the aerofoil causes distortion by bending and torsion of the structure that can result in a violent vibration in the resonance frequency, which if excessive can cause structural failure. This is ‘flutter’ and the aeroelastic coupling will affect its characteristics. The risk of experiencing flutter increases with IAS.

CONTROL SURFACE FLUTTER
Control surface flutter can develop as a result of an oscillation of the control surface coupled with an oscillation in bending or twisting of the wing, tailplane or fin.

A control surface oscillation can result from backlash (free play) in the control system or from a disturbance (gust).

MASS BALANCE
Flutter may be prevented by adding weight to the control surface in front of the hinge line.

This brings the centre of gravity of the control forward to a position on, or slightly in front of the hinge, but always to the point required by the designers. This reduces the inertia moments about the hinge and prevents flutter developing.

title: The load factor is less than 1 (one):
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: in steady wings level horizontal flight.
optionB: when weight is greater than lift.
optionC: during recovery after a wings level stall.
optionD: during a steady horizontal turn.
explanationTotal:
Load Factor - The ratio of the weight of an aircraft to the load imposed by lift. The correct symbol for load factor is (n), but it is colloquially known as (g).

Load Factor = Lift / Weight

Certain maneuvers require the aircraft weight to be greater than the lift force. For example, weight is greater than lift in a steady climb or descent. In this case, Load Factor is less than 1.

title: The speed for minimum sink rate, (I)_____ , is (II)_____ than the speed for minimum descent angle.
optionA: (I) V<sub>MP</sub>, (II) higher
optionB: (I) V<sub>MP</sub>, (II) lower
optionC: (I) V<sub>MD</sub>, (II) lower
optionD: (I) V<sub>MD</sub>, (II) higher
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Minimum Sink Rate is achieved by flying at VMP => the Minimum Power Speed.
Minimum Descent Angle is achieved by flying at the faster speed VMD => Minimum Drag Speed.

The polar curve of an airfoil is the graphical relationship of the coefficients of lift and drag plotted against each other, the resulting graph is as shown in the attached graph - where the speed decreases from a maximum at point A to a minimum at point D:

  • Point A: is between VMD and the maximum speed and has the minimum drag coefficient. It therefore approximates VY for a jet airplane.
  • Point B: is the point at which a tangent from the origin touches the polar curve, which is at the point at which the total drag is minimum, the lift/drag ratio is maximum and the IAS in level flight is VMD. This is also the speed at which the longest glide distance will be achieved and Minimum descent angle.
  • Point C: falls between VMD and VS and is approximately VMP, which approximates to the speed of VY for a piston/propeller airplane and indicates the value at which the minimum sink rate will occur. It is the speed that will attain the maximum endurance during a descent.
  • Point D: is where CL and CD are both maximum and the point at which the minimum speed in level flight, the stalling speed, VS is attained.

title:
Refer to figure.
Which type of flap is shown in the picture 1?
optionA: Slotted flap
optionB: Fowler flap
optionC: Plain flap
optionD: Split flap
explanationTotal:
1. Plain flap
2. Slotted flap
3. Fowler flap
4. Slipt flap

A plain flap simply lowers the trailing edge of the wing, increasing camber.

A Fowler flap not only extends rearwards but also moves downward, resulting in an increased wing surface area and an amplified camber.

A split flap solely lowers the underside of the wing while keeping the upper surface unaltered.

title: Regarding the speeds V<sub>NO</sub>, V<sub>MO</sub> and V<sub>NE</sub>, which of the following answers is correct?
optionA: V<sub>NO</sub> is the maximum normal operating airspeed for an aeroplane certified under CS-25. It can only be exceeded in smooth air.
optionB: V<sub>MO</sub> is the maximum operating speed permitted in normal conditions for an aeroplane certified under CS-25. It may be exceeded by a maximum of 10% in an emergency descent.
optionC: For an aeroplane certified under CS-25, V<sub>MO</sub> is the maximum speed that must not be deliberately exceeded in any regime, unless a higher speed has been authorised for a particular flight.
optionD: For an aeroplane certified under CS-23, V<sub>NE</sub> is the maximum speed to be flown with the flaps extended.
explanationTotal:
According to CS 25.1505, VMO/MMO is the maximum operating IAS (or Mach number, whichever is critical at a particular altitude), which must not be deliberately exceeded in any flight condition, is referred to as VMO/MMO. VMO is the maximum operating IAS and MMO is the maximum operating Mach number.
This speed is that which, allowing for moderate upsets ensures the aircraft will remain free from buffet or other undesirable flying qualities associated with compressibility. It must not exceed VC. When climbing at VMO, the TAS and the Mach number are increasing, so care must be taken to ensure that MMO is not exceeded. Conversely, when descending at MMO, the TAS and IAS increase, and care must be taken not to exceed VMO.

title: The maximum speed that flaps can be extended is:
optionA: V<sub>FE</sub>
optionB: V<sub>LE</sub>
optionC: V<sub>NO</sub>
optionD: V<sub>Y</sub>
explanationTotal:
CS 25.1511 Flap extended speed

The established flap extended speed VFE must be established so that it does not exceed the design flap speed VF chosen under CS 25.335 (e) and 25.345, for the corresponding wing-flap positions and engine powers.

Here are the different speeds with the associated visual indicators (colored arcs) of an airspeed indicator:

White arc:

  • Lower limit – VS0: stalling speed with flaps extended.
  • Upper limit – VFE: maximum speed with flaps extended.
Green Arc:
  • Lower limit – VS1: stalling speed in clean configuration.
  • Upper limit – VN0: maximum speed in normal operation.
Yellow arc:
  • Lower limit – VN0: maximum speed in normal operation.
  • Upper limit – VNE: Red Line - never exceed speed.

title: For a twin-engine aeroplane, a reason for limiting a propeller’s diameter is to...
optionA: avoid excessive propeller-tip velocities at high RPMs.
optionB: increase ground clearance.
optionC: reduce the aeroplane’s minimum control speed.
optionD: avoid a reduction in power absorption.
explanationTotal:
The ability of a propeller to convert engine power into forward thrust is its power-absorption capability.

It is affected by:

  • the propeller-blade shape.
  • the number of propeller blades.
  • the propeller solidity.
There is a finite aerodynamic limit to the maximum length of a propeller blade because of its tip speed. For any given RPM, the speed reached by the blade tip is most often sonic, even at low RPM.
Propeller efficiency is adversely affected by the compressibility created at sonic tip speeds reducing the thrust generated and increasing the torque required (the blade drag).
Apart from the aerodynamic limitation the noise produced by the propeller at supersonic tip speeds is unacceptably high and could cause structural fatigue as well as environmental damage.

title: Which of the following flight phenomena can only occur at Mach numbers above the critical Mach number?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Elevator stall.
optionB: Speed instability.
optionC: Mach buffet.
optionD: Dutch roll.
explanationTotal:
Critical Mach Number: (MCRIT) The critical Mach number is the Mach number of the aircraft when the speed of the airflow over some part of the aircraft first reaches the speed of sound.

At high altitude, a large high-speed jet transport aircraft will be cruising at a speed marginally above its critical Mach number, and it will have a small shock wave on the wing. If such an aircraft overspeeds, the shock wave will rapidly grow larger, causing the static pressure to increase sharply in the immediate vicinity of the shock wave. The locally increased adverse pressure gradient will cause the boundary layer to separate immediately behind the shock wave. This is called a ‘shock stall’.
Shock induced separation (shock stall) at high speed can also cause buffeting. Aerodynamic buffet is a valuable stall warning, but it can damage the aircraft structure.
As the shock wave moves aft over the surface of the wing, the CP also moves aft. This aft movement combined with the reduced downwash at the tail plane due to the presence of the shockwave will lead to Tuck Under.

As we can see, from all the options, only one of them occurs when operating above MCRIT (transonic speed regime) and that’s ‘Mach buffet’.

title: The pilot of a modern, large turbojet aeroplane sets the vertical speed mode of the autopilot to carry out a climb. What must he/she be particularly careful of?
optionA: The autopilot may select a rate of climb outside the maximum permissible limit of the aeroplane.
optionB: The engines may overspeed as the autothrottle attempts to maintain airspeed.
optionC: The aeroplane may overspeed in an attempt to maintain the rate of climb.
optionD: If the climb is prolonged, there is a risk that the airspeed may reduce towards the stall.
explanationTotal:
Vertical Speed is an autopilot flight guidance vertical mode. In this mode, the Flight Management and Guidance Computer (FMCG) pitch mode guides the aircraft to the target V/S. The corresponding thrust mode is SPEED or MACH.

The V/S guidance has priority over the speed guidance. If the selected target V/S is too high (relative to the current thrust condition and speed), the FMGC will steer the aircraft to the target V/S, but the aircraft will also accelerate or decelerate.

As altitude increases and the air gets thinner, the IAS will reduce for a given pitch setting. Consequently, the angle of attack also reduces. As a result, the vertical speed will reduce for a certain pitch attitude. The autopilot will therefore chase the selected vertical speed by pitching up. This results in further decreased IAS. Ultimately, this could lead to a stall.

title:
A crew calculate speeds for a take-off using 15⁰ of flap but, due to distraction, perform the take off with flaps fully retracted.
Choose the correct statement:
optionA: With better acceleration, the risk of a tail strike or stall is reduced.
optionB: With better acceleration, runway used on take-off will be less.
optionC: The aircraft may remain on the ground after rotation.
optionD: Once safely airborne, climb performance is reduced.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
EFFECT OF FLAPS ON LANDING/TAKE-OFF RUN AND CLIMB GRADIENT

The use of high life devices (Flaps) will have an impact on the take-off and Landing roll and climb gradient.

For a given runway length and airplane weight, selecting a greater flap setting will increase the wing’s effective camber and the lift coefficient, which reduces the stalling speed.

  • As a consequence, the take-off speeds are reduced (the same lift will be created at smaller air speed due to greater lift coefficient). This will reduce the take-off run.

The down side of the use of flaps is that it generates more parasite drag: The parasite drag from the extended flap results in a degraded climb angle and climb gradient.

In this case, for a take-off using 15º of flaps compared to a clean take-off (flaps retracted), the take-off speeds will be reduced, which results in a reduced take-off run. For fully retracted flaps, the take-off speeds will increase, meaning that the aircraft may remain on the ground after rotation.

title: When a strongly swept-back wing stalls and the wake of the wing contacts the horizontal tail, the effect on the stall behaviour can be a(n):
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: nose up tendency and/or lack of elevator response.
optionB: tendency to increase speed after initial stall.
optionC: nose down tendency.
optionD: increase in sensitivity of elevator inputs.
explanationTotal:
The lift from a wing is generated by airflow over it from front to back. If the span-wise flow increases, the boundary layer on the wing surface travels for longer.
This causes them to be thicker and more susceptible to transition to turbulence or flow separation.
The normal tip vortice on a swept wing joins up with a leading edge separation bubble, creating a larger vortex called the Ram’s horn vortex.
This vortex goes inboard along the wing’s leading edge.
The downward flow from the vortex induces pressure on the boundary layer at the wingtip, whereas on straight wings the exact opposite occurs. With a swept wing, this creates a slow-moving layer of air at the wing tip.
This slow-moving air will separate into disturbed flow and will then stall the tip.

As the wingtips for a swept wing are positioned aft of the center of pressure (CP), the center of pressure upon a wing tip stall will move forward, creating a nose up moment.
This nose up moment will further increase the Angle of Attack if not corrected in time, increasing the layer of slow-moving air, worsening the situation.
Due to the decreased downwash on the elevator, the elevator could be less responsive, creating a so called deep stall. Unswept wings do not have this problem.

The pitch up phenomenon is a dangerous characteristic of swept wing aircraft (with a T-tail) that move at high speed.
It could result in a quickly worsening stalling situation, making it very hard to recover.

title: During an normal spin recovery:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: the control stick is moved side ways, against the angle of bank.
optionB: the ailerons are held in the neutral position.
optionC: the control stick is moved side ways, in the direction of the angle of bank.
optionD: the control stick is pulled to the most aft position.
explanationTotal: During a spin, the aircraft should be recovered by holding ailerons neutral and rudder in the opposite direction to the spin direction. When the aircraft has stopped spinning, angle of attack is to be increased (if sufficient airspeed is present) for minimum descent rate, level flight or climb (if possible).

title: One of the disadvantages of excessive increasing of the number of propeller blades (beyond a certain number) is:
optionA: Less power can be absorbed by the propeller.
optionB: Decreased propeller efficiency.
optionC: Increased noise.
optionD: Higher tip-speed.
explanationTotal:
Power absorption capability of the propeller mainly depends on propeller solidity. Propeller solidity is defined as frontal area of all the blades compared to the propeller disk area. Increasing the number of blades or increasing chord length increases propeller solidity. If propeller solidity is high, power absorption capability of the propeller increases.

Increasing the number of blades is beneficial only up to a certain number. Beyond this number, overall efficiency will decrease - The vortices from a close preceding blade will upset the airflow around the blade and thereby reduce its efficiency.

title: A wing is often designed having a different profile shape and/or a different angle of incidence along its span, creating a washout effect. Why is that?
optionA: To ensure that the wing tip stalls after the wing root to increase the stability in roll and reduce the likelihood of a wing-drop.
optionB: This increases the lift towards the wing tip, thereby ensuring a more even distribution of lift along the spanwise direction, Increasing efficiency.
optionC: This reduces the drag produced by the wing as the entire wing can operate at its optimum angle of attack along the spanwise direction.
optionD: To reduce the effect of wing-tip vortices and therefore ensure a more even distribution of lift along the chordwise direction.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Normally, the incidence angle of the wing tip is smaller than the root (wing twist/washout). Consequently, lift will be even smaller at the wing tip, resulting in smaller induced drag, which prevents wing tip stall.

Ailerons are generally located in the outer wing sections. As consequence of washout, the wing tips (aileron section) will be the last to exceed MCRIT which allows roll control to be maintained.

  • In simple words: The purpose for washout is to control the stall characteristics of the wing. It ensures the root will stall before the tips to maintain aileron authority for as long as possible.

title: An aircraft has a C<sub>L</sub> value of 1.22 at a speed of 1.1 V<sub>S</sub>. Determine the C<sub>L</sub> at a speed of 1.8 V<sub>S</sub>:
explanationTotal:
This exercise can be solved applying the following formula:
  • New CL x (New Speed)2 = Old CL x (Old Speed)2
New CL x 1.82 = 1.22 x 1.12
New CL = (1.22 x 1.12) / 1.82
New CL = 0.456

title: What is the name of two propellers rotating in opposite directions on the same engine shaft?
optionA: Double-bank propeller
optionB: Counter-rotating propellers
optionC: Contra-rotating propellers
optionD: Variable pitch propellers
explanationTotal: Contra-rotating propellers are mounted on the same shaft and are driven in opposite directions, usually by the same engine.

title: Just after take-off, a pilot inadvertently retracts the flaps instead of the landing gear. What are the consequences?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: The take-off may be continued normally as the aeroplane has already lifted-off.
optionB: None, because in accordance with the certification requirements, an interlock prevents retracting the flaps if the gear is down.
optionC: The aeroplane will stall if the speed is lower than the stall speed in clean configuration.
optionD: The rate of climb will be increased as drag will be less than with take-off flaps.
explanationTotal:
Let's just start by stating that Flaps allow you to fly slower, but they generate a lot of extra drag. You are paying the price of slower speeds by using more power to fly, and also by having a reduced climb performance. This alone means that the pilot usually wants to retract the flaps to a clean configuration as-soon-as-possible. How soon that is, is a bit more complicated to answer.

For starters, you need a specific (safe) speed for each notch of flaps to be retracted. Stall speed will increase every time you retract a notch of flaps so you want to be well above that speed before putting your hand on the flaps lever.

So, in theory, the second the wheels are off the ground, you can just level off, keep flying a few feet above ground and keep accelerating until a safe speed is reached then retract flaps all the way to a clean configuration.

In this case, the flaps are retracted right after take-off, when a positive rate of climb is observed (the pilot retracts the flaps when he/she should have retracted the landing gear). At this point, the speed is likely to be slower than the stall speed for a clean configuration - the aircraft may stall.

title: The most important problem of ice accretion on a transport aeroplane during flight is:
optionA: increase in weight.
optionB: increase in drag.
optionC: blocking of control surfaces.
optionD: reduction in C<sub>LMAX</sub>.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The formation of ice and frost on the airframe will:
- modify the profile of the aerofoil.
- increase the roughness of the aircraft surface.
- increase the weight of the aircraft.

Ice will normally form on and around the leading edges of wings and tailplane and can result in severe distortion of the leading edge profile. This will give a large increase in drag and a substantial decrease in CLMAX. The skin friction drag will increase and the boundary layer will have an earlier separation, giving a reduced critical angle of attack, thereby a higher stall speed.

title: During a go around, the crew forgets to retract the trailing edge flaps. What could be a consequence?
optionA: Degraded climb performance and possible V<sub>FE</sub> exceedance.
optionB: Increase of climb performance and decrease angle of climb.
optionC: Increases rate of climb and decreases angle of climb.
optionD: Decreases rate of climb and increases angle of climb.
explanationTotal:
Flaps reduce climb rate. Flaps add drag which is a good thing for landing, but not good for the climb performance. Some aircraft have such limited performance that they simply will not climb with full flaps, even at typical elevations and in typical weather.

Retracting the flaps allows for acceleration to climb speed and above without the risk of overspeed damage to the flaps. It is very possible, in some aircraft, to overspeed the flaps after the go-around if they are not retracted soon enough.

Each type of aircraft has a speed limit for how fast the aircraft is allowed to go with flaps extended (VFE). This is for structural considerations so that the flaps and wings are not damaged by excessive speed.

title: Determine the value of thrust when the climb angle equals 9º, drag is 300 000 N and weight is 5 750 000 N:
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
T = D + W sin y
T = 300 000 + 5 750 000 sin 9º
T = 1 199 498 N

Further information:

CLIMB

There are four forces that act on an aircraft in a steady unaccelerated climb: Lift, Weight, Thrust and Drag. Lift, Drag and Thrust are aerodynamic forces which are defined relative to the flight path. Where Lift is perpendicular to the flight path, whereas Drag and Thrust act along it. The Weight of an aircraft is directed towards the centre of the Earth and is, therefore, along the vertical axis.
Weight will be resolved into two different components, as you can see on the attached figure: a force which is opposite to the lift (W cos y) and another force which acts in the same direction as drag (W sin y).

  • In order for the aircraft to be in equilibrium in a steady climb, Thrust will be equal to Drag + backwards component of weight; and Lift must be equal to the opposing component of weight. Lift will be less than Weight because Lift only has to oppose a portion of Weight.

title:
Refer to figure.
Which of the figures shows the change in the total drag graph when density altitude is increased?
optionA: Figure 1.
optionB: Figure 2.
optionC: Figure 3.
optionD: Figure 4.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
When density altitude increases, the air gets "thinner", meaning that there are less air particles per cubic metre, and therefore less air particles will hit our aircraft and flow over its wings per mile flown. This would decrease lift and drag if we were trying to maintain the same TAS. However, to counteract this effect, we fly our aircraft at a constant IAS/CAS (Indicated Airspeed/Calibrated Airspeed), which is a simple measure of dynamic pressure. This value measures the amount of air particles hitting the aircraft, and their speed.

If we fly at a constant IAS, but climb higher in the atmosphere, the lower air density means that we have to fly faster to get the same amount of dynamic pressure, meaning the same amount of air particles over the wing, etc. This is an increase in TAS (True Airspeed) for a constant IAS.

IAS directly controls our drag and our lift, as they vary proportionally to dynamic pressure, see the lift or drag equation for the mathematical proof here, it is very easy to spot.

D = (1/2 x ρ x V2)x CD x S

As dynamic pressure is 1/2 x ρ x V2, which is measured by the IAS, then drag is directly proportional to IAS, coefficient of drag, and surface area.

If the graph was for total drag against IAS, then the curve would remain in exactly the same position with increased altitude (ignoring compressibility at very high altitudes).

As the X-axis on the graphs is TAS, not IAS, then with an increase in altitude, the drag curve will look the same, but will be shifted to the right, due to the increased TAS for the same IAS at higher altitudes, but as the same forces of drag exist at each point on the curve, the curve will not move up or down. The answer is therefore figure 3, moving to the right.

title:
Which of these statements about the equilibrium of forces and moments at VMCA are correct or incorrect?

I. Equilibrium of moments about the normal axis is provided by rudder deflection.
II. Equilibrium of forces along the lateral axis requires either bank angle or side slip or a combination of both.
optionA: I is correct, II is correct.
optionB: I is correct, II is incorrect.
optionC: I is incorrect, II is correct.
optionD: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
explanationTotal:
If an engine fails during the take-off of a multi-engine aircraft a significant yawing moment will be experienced due to asymmetric thrust. In order to maintain directional control and keeping the aircraft in equilibrium around the yaw axis, the pilot must apply corrective action. Above a certain speed this will be possible using aerodynamic controls only. If the aircraft is still on the ground this means the use of the rudder, if the aircraft is airborne, the pilot can also apply bank by using the ailerons. The greater the thrust of this operating engine(s), the greater the yawing moment will be and the greater the aerodynamic forces to counteract this yawing moment would be required.

VMCA = Minimum control speed in the take-off configuration with gear up – the minimum calibrated airspeed at which, when the critical engine is suddenly made inoperative, it is possible to maintain control and maintain straight flight using no more than 5° of bank without required exceptional piloting skill or the aeroplane adopting a dangerous attitude or changing heading by more than 20°. An increased bank angle beyond 5°, while keeping the rudder centered, may lead to a fin stall, due to an extreme sideslip angle, but when decreasing the bank angle below 5° to 0°, rudder deflection has to be increased and therefore VMCA will increase, too.

  • Equilibrium of moments about the normal axis (also called yaw or vertical axis) is provided by rudder deflection (yaw)
  • Equilibrium of moments about the lateral axis is provided by elevator deflection (pitch)
  • Equilibrium of moments about the longitudinal axis is provided by aileron deflection (roll)
Note: Forces along the lateral axis is not the same like moments around the lateral axis. Forces along the lateral axis act around the longitudinal axis. Therefore an equilibrium along the lateral axis always requires bank or sideslip.

title: During a descent at a constant Mach number (assume zero thrust and standard atmospheric conditions):
optionA: the pitch angle will increase.
optionB: the TAS will decrease.
optionC: the descent angle will decrease.
optionD: the angle of attack will decrease.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The Mach number is defined as the ratio between the TAS and the LSS (Local speed of sound). The Mach number may be calculated as follows:

M = TAS / LSS

Lift is defined by:

L=1/2 ρ TAS2 S CL

Effect on IAS when descending at a constant Mach number:

  • Temperature increases with decreasing altitude. Consequently, the speed of sound will increase as altitude is decreased. If the bottom of the equation (LSS) increases, the TAS must be gradually increased to compensate for the increasing LSS due to higher temperatures.
  • Considering the lift formula, if TAS increases, to maintain Lift constant, CL must decrease. This is achieved by decreasing the angle of attack.

title: The descent angle of a given aeroplane in a steady wings level glide has a fixed value for a certain combination of: (ignore compressibility effects and assume zero thrust)
optionA: configuration and mass.
optionB: configuration and angle of attack.
optionC: mass and altitude.
optionD: altitude and configuration.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
The above diagram shows that the forces in the steady glide are simplified because of the absence of thrust. Because forces in opposite directions must be equal, it should be clear that:

- The component of the weight in the direction of the glide path must equal drag; and

- The component of the weight normal to the glide path must equal lift.

To glide at the shallowest glide angle, giving maximum still-air range:

- The L/D ratio must be maximum
- The aircraft must fly at VMD
- The aircraft must fly at 4º angle of attack
  • Fundamentally, your angle of glide/descent is a function of lift/drag ratio. All you have to do is fly at VMD for your aircraft, which means flying at the correct angle of attack => If the angle of attack is away from the optimum then the aircraft will descend steeper due to the increase in drag.
  • Extending flap or airbrake (configuration) will also have an effect on your gliding angle => For instance, if you take a look at the drag polar (CL against CD diagram, you may notive that flaps reduce the lift/drag ration, which will steepne the glide path. Flaps increase the angle of descent and reduce the range.
Note: Glide angle is independent of mass. For example: A heavier aircraft will have a higher VMD and descend faster but with the same glide angle.

title: When a jet transport aeroplane takes off with the CG at the forward limit and the trimmable horizontal stabiliser (THS) is positioned at the maximum allowable nose up position for take-off:
optionA: early nose wheel raising will take place.
optionB: rotation will be normal using the normal rotation technique.
optionC: rotation will require a higher than normal stick force.
optionD: there will be a tendency to over-rotate.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
A forward CG position (nose-heavy airplane) results in the greatest nose-down tendency and the aircraft rotates slowly on take-off. The position of the stabiliser for a nose-heavy aeroplane requires nose-up trim.

title: Propellers on light twin engined aircrafts are length limited:
optionA: To increase solidity.
optionB: To prevent loss of power absorption.
optionC: To provide ground clearance.
optionD: To prevent excessive tip speed at high speed flight.
explanationTotal:
The amount of thrust that is produced by a propeller is proportional to the blade area => Longer blades will approach transonic tip speed at a lower RPM than shorter ones.
  • Larger the propeller blades, the faster the propeller tip speeds will be.

Excessive tip speed results in increased drag and reduced lift of the propeller.

Note: Technically all the options available are correct, we believe this is another one of those questions where you have to choose the most correct option.

title: When an aeroplane enters ground effect:
optionA: drag and lift are reduced.
optionB: the lift is increased and the drag is decreased.
optionC: the induced angle of attack is increased.
optionD: the effective angle of attack is decreased.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
When taking-off or landing, the proximity to the ground prevents full development of the trailing edge vortices, making them much weaker than in normal flight. The runway serves as a physical barrier to downwash airflow, therefore downwash decreases. With less downwash, the effective angle of attack and lift increase.

All in all:

  • Entering ground effect: lift increases, induced drag reduces.
  • Leaving ground effect: lift reduces, induced drag increases.

title: In straight and level flight at a speed of 1.3 V<sub>S</sub>, the lift coefficient, expressed as a percentage of its maximum C<sub>LMAX</sub>, would be:
explanationTotal:
Knowing that:

L = CL ½ rho v2 S

If we re-organize to make the coefficient of lift (CL) the subject of the equation:

CL = L ÷ (½ rho v2 S)

Therefore, removing the constant from the equation, we can establish that the Lift Coefficient (CL) is directly proportional to the inverse of Speed squared:

CL ∝ 1 ÷ V2

Now that the relationship is established, and knowing that v = 1.3 VS , we can solve the question:

CL = 1 ÷ 1.32

CL = 0.59

We can conclude that our Lift Coefficient (CL) at 1.3 VS will be 0.59 (59%) of the coefficient at VS.

title: An aeroplane in straight and level flight at 200 kt is subjected to a sudden disturbance in speed. Assuming the angle of attack remains constant initially and the load factor reaches a value of 1.69:
optionA: the speed will have decreased by 30 kt.
optionB: the speed will have decreased by 60 kt.
optionC: the speed will have increased by 60 kt.
optionD: the speed will have increased by 30 kt.
explanationTotal:
Let’s start by identifying the equations used to answer the question.

Load factor is defined as:

n = L/W

Now we replace the lift with the full equation:

L = CL ½ rho V2 S

n = (CL ½ rho V2 S) / W

By removing all the constants, we can say that:

n = (CL ½ rho V2 S) / W

n ∝ V2
