To find the change in load factor (nΔ), we have to divide nNEW by nOLD:

nΔ = nNEW / nOLD

nΔ = VNEW2 / VOLD2

For those who prefer remembering equations, remember the above

This question wants us to find the VNEW so let’s rearrange the formula to make it the subject of the equation:

VNEW = √(nΔ x VOLD2)

VNEW = √(1.69 x 2002)

VNEW = 260 kt

Knowing now that the new speed is 260 and the old speed was 200, we know that there was an increase in airspeed of 60 kt.

title:
Refer to figure.
Which type of flap is shown in the picture 2?
optionA: Slotted flap
optionB: Fowler flap
optionC: Plain flap
optionD: Split flap
explanationTotal:
1. Plain flap
2. Slotted flap
3. Fowler flap
4. Split flap

A plain flap simply lowers the trailing edge of the wing, increasing camber.

A Fowler flap not only extends rearwards but also moves downward, resulting in an increased wing surface area and an amplified camber.

A split flap solely lowers the underside of the wing while keeping the upper surface unaltered.

title: What is a pitching motion?
optionA: It is about the longitudinal axis, related to longitudinal stability.
optionB: It is about the lateral axis, related to longitudinal stability.
optionC: It is about the longitudinal axis, related to lateral stability.
optionD: It is about the lateral axis, related to lateral stability.
explanationTotal: A pitch motion is an up or down movement of the nose of the aircraft about the lateral axis. The pitching motion is being caused by the deflection of the elevator of this aircraft. The longitudinal axis is stabilised by pitching moments.

title: For most jet transport aeroplanes, the maximum operating limit speed, V<sub>MO</sub>:
optionA: is expressed as a true air speed.
optionB: is replaced by M<sub>MO</sub> at higher altitudes.
optionC: is equal to V<sub>D</sub>.
optionD: is lower than V<sub>NE</sub>.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The maximum operating limit speed (airspeed or Mach number, whichever is critical at a particular altitude is a speed that may not be deliberately exceeded in any phase of flight. As VMO is IAS, as altitude increases, the Mach number corresponding to VMO will increase. During climb VMO will be superseded by MMO (Maximum operating Mach number) approximately between 24 000 and 29 000 ft, depending on atmospheric conditions.

As an example, the diagram shows the flight envelope for the 757-200. Notice that below approximately FL270, the airplane is VMO restricted to 350 KIAS. Above approximately FL270, the airplane is MMO restricted to 0.86 Mach. Therefore, 350 KIAS/0.86M defines VMO/MMO for this airplane respectively.

  • VMO – is expressed in CAS, which is usually associated with operations at lower altitudes and deals with structural loads and flutter;
  • MMO – is expressed in Mach number, is associated with operations at higher altitudes and is usually more concerned with compressibility effects and flutter.

title:
Which statement is correct regarding the gyroscopic effect of a clockwise rotating propeller on a single engine aeroplane?

I. Pitch down produces left yaw.
II. Left yaw produces pitch down.
optionA: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
optionB: I is incorrect, II is correct.
optionC: I is correct, II is correct.
optionD: I is correct, II is incorrect.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
On take-off, rotation of a single-engine propeller causes an aircraft to swing to one side, particularly those fitted with a tail-dragger undercarriage. The main causes of this are:

  • Slipstream effect
  • Torque reaction
  • Gyroscopic effect
  • Asymmetric blade effect

Gyroscopic Effect

A rotating propeller has the properties of a gyroscope - rigidity in space and precession. The characteristic which produces “gyroscopic effect” is precession. Gyroscopic precession is the reaction that occurs when a force is applied to the rim of a rotating disc. When a force is applied to the rim of a propeller, the reaction occurs 90° ahead in the direction of rotation and in the same direction as the applied force. As the aircraft is pitched up or down or yawed left or right, a force is applied to the rim of the spinning propeller disc.

Note: Gyroscopic effect only occurs when the aircraft pitches and/or yaws.

For a clockwise rotating propeller:

Pitch up - forward force on the bottom, force emerges 90° clockwise, right yaw.
Right yaw - forward force on the left, force emerges 90° clockwise, pitch down.
Pitch down - forward force on the top, force emerges 90° clockwise, left yaw. Therefore, statement 1 is correct.
Left yaw - forward force on the right, force emerges 90° clockwise, pitch up. Therefore, statement 2 is incorrect.

title:
Refer to figure.
Name the CL augmentation devices represented in the annex:
optionA: 1. Krueger Flaps; 2. Variable Camber Flaps; 3. Slats.
optionB: 1. Krueger Flaps; 2. Slats; 3. Variable Camber Flaps.
optionC: 1. Slats; 2. Krueger Flaps; 3. Variable Camber Flaps.
optionD: 1. Variable Camber Flaps; 2. Krueger Flaps; 3. Slats.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
1. Variable Camber Flaps => For a variable camber leading edge device, the whole leading edge is deflected and positioned into the airstream. The working principle upon which the moveable leading edge is based, is that by increasing the camber, the CL -a graph shifts upwards as a consequence.

2. Krueger Flaps => A Krueger flap is one where the underside of the leading edge folds out forwards to create an air dam which sends more air mass flow over the upper surface. When it deploys, no slot is created.

3. Slats => A slat is a high lifting device which, on deployment, the leading edge is moved forward and down. A venturi-shaped slot is created allowing air to flow from underneath the wing to the upper surface.

title: Select the correct statement in regard to a symmetrical aerofoil section.
optionA: A nose up pitching moment exists when the Lift Coefficient equals zero.
optionB: A nose down pitching moment exists when the Lift Coefficient equals zero.
optionC: The Angle Of Attack has a positive value when the lift coefficient equals zero.
optionD: The Angle Of Attack is zero when the Lift Coefficient equals zero.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
If a symmetrical airfoil section is in a steady airstream at zero degrees Angle of Attack, a stagnation point forms on the leading edge.
The airflow velocity above and below the airfoil increases by an equal amount and the static pressures reduce by an equal amount. Consequently, no pressure differential exists, and no net lift is created.

title:
Refer to figure.
The wings can be seen out of the aircraft windows as depicted in the annex above. What is happening, and what will be the effect?
optionA: Flap asymmetry; the aircraft will roll to the left.
optionB: Flap asymmetry; the aircraft will yaw to the left.
optionC: Slat asymmetry; the aircraft will roll to the left.
optionD: Slat asymmetry; the aircraft will yaw to the left.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
In the image, the right wing has its trailing edge flaps set down, but the left wing is clean (no flaps). This will cause the two wings to act in very different ways. The extension of flaps causes a very large increase in the coefficient of lift, as well as a significant increase in drag.

If this happens for just one wing, but not the other, it can lead to very difficult handling characteristics for the pilot to try and control. This is called flap asymmetry.

The right wing has its flap down, but the left wing does not. That means the lift from the right wing will be higher than the left wing, so a strong roll to the left will occur. This will be accompanied by a yaw to the right, due to the increased drag on the right wing, but with flap asymmetry, the roll is the dominant effect by far.

title: What is the approximate radius of a steady, level, co-ordinated turn with a bank angle of 30 degrees and a TAS of 500 kt?
optionA: 12 km.
optionB: 24 km.
optionC: 10 km.
optionD: 7 km.
explanationTotal:
The formula for turning radius is written as follows:

R = V2 / (g tan α)

Where:

  • R = radius
  • V = velocity
  • g = gravitational constant (9.81, however in some questions stated to be 10)
  • α = bank angle

R = (500 x 0.5144 m/s/kt)2 / (9.81 tan (30º))
R = (257.2 m/s)2 / (9.81 x 0.57735 m/s2)
R = 11 679.76 m ≈ 12 km

title:
Considering the data below, calculate the value of the Coefficient of Lift for an aircraft flying at stall speed.

Mass: 1400 kg
G: 9.8 m/s2
VS: 70 kt
Density: 1.225 kg/m3
Wing area:13.5 m2
optionC: There is insufficient information to answer the question
explanationTotal:
The aerodynamic force of lift results from the pressure differential between the top and bottom surfaces of the wing.

This exercise can be solved by using the following equation:

L = ½ x ρ x V2 x CL x S

We will consider straight and level flight so that L = W = m x g. In this case, mass (m) is 1400 kg and the acceleration of gravity (g) is 9.8 m/s2:

W = 1400 x 9.8 = 13720 N

Another factor we need to consider is that the unit for speed in this formula is m/s and not knots. We must, therefore, convert 70 kt to m/s. Knowing that 1 kt = 0,5144 m/s:

70 kt x 0,5144 m/s = 36,008 m/s

All we have left to do is reorganise the Lift formula in order to obtain the value of CL.

CL = (2 x W) ÷ (V2 x ρ x S)
CL = (2 x 13720) ÷ (36.0082 x 1.225 x 13.5)
CL = 1.28

title: Consider a conventional aircraft with positive stability in its roll, pitch and yaw axes. During flight the Centre of Gravity (CG) moves aft. Due to this CG shift, the longitudinal stability (1)_____ and the directional stability (2)_____.
optionA: (1) increases; (2) decreases
optionB: (1) decreases; (2) increases
optionC: (1) increases; (2) increases
optionD: (1) decreases; (2) decreases
explanationTotal:
A variation of CG position can cause large changes in the static longitudinal stability. In the conventional airplane configuration, the large changes in stability with CG variation are primarily due to the large changes in the wing contribution. As the CG is gradually moved aft, the airplane static stability decreases.

The position of the CG will affect the balance between the fin and the AC. So an aft CG will have a destabilizing effect on directional stability.

title: On an aircraft leaving ground effect after lift-off, wing tip vortices (1) _____ and the induced angle of attack will (2) _____.
optionA: (1) decrease; (2) decrease
optionB: (1) decrease; (2) increase
optionC: (1) increase; (2) increase
optionD: (1) increase; (2) decrease
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
GROUND EFFECT

Ground effect occurs because the surface alters the airflow pattern around the wings. Primarily, the surface restricts the formation of the wingtip vortices.

This results in a reduction in the amount of induced downwash behind the wing and increases the wing’s effective angle of attack.

It also alters the pressure distribution around the wing and the amount of lift developed. This occurs because the change in effective angle of attack increases the wing’s coefficient of lift (CL) and thus its lifting capability at any given angle of attack.

THE INFLUENCE OF GROUND EFFECT ON TAKE-OFF

The magnitude of the wing tip vortices, and thus downwash, determine the amount of induced drag produced by the wing. The closer the aircraft is to the surface, the greater the reduction in induced drag at any given angle of attack.

During the take-off phase of flight, as the aircraft leaves ground effect the wing tip vortices rapidly grow in magnitude producing an increase in downwash behind the wing. This causes a reduction in the lift produced at a given angle of attack and the associated rapid increase in induced drag may prevent a successful take-off. The increased downwash acting on the tailplane increases the download, resulting in a nose-up pitching moment.

Downwash angle: Increasing the effect of the vortices will increase downwash angle.

Induced angle of attack: The increase in downwash will cause the induced angle of attack to increase leading to a increase in induced drag.

title: When flying with a 1.3 g buffet onset, at what bank angle will buffet be encountered in a level turn?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
explanationTotal:
In other words, this question is asking what bank angle results in a Load Factor (n) of 1.3 g.

n = 1 / cos a

(a = bank angle)

  • 1.3 = 1 / cos a
  • a = cos-1(1/1.3)
  • a = 39.72º

title: When landing an aircraft at an airfield during a hot day, the increased temperature of the runway will:
optionA: Subtrcact from the consequences of entering ground effect.
optionB: Add to the consequences of leaving ground effect.
optionC: Add to the consequences of entering ground effect.
optionD: Have no effect on the consequences of ground effect.
explanationTotal:
Ground Effect is the name given to the positive influence on the lifting characteristics of the horizontal surfaces of an aircraft wing when it is close to the ground. It is important to note that temperature has no effect on ground effect itself. However, it adds to the ground effect.

But how will an increased temperature add to the ground effect? It's simple, convective currents from a warm runway will add to the upward forces caused by the ground effect, increasing the tendency of the aircraft to float beyond the touchdown point.

title: Consider a multi-engine aeroplane with counter-rotating propellers turning inward. If the left engine fails, to counteract the yaw moment, you would need to apply a smaller force if compared to an aircraft equipped with two clockwise rotating propellers, because...
optionA: at slow speed the thrust vector is closer towards the aircraft’s longitudinal axis.
optionB: the rolling moment is in the same direction as the yawing moment.
optionC: the slipstream effect acts on the rudder in the opposite way.
optionD: when pitching up, gyroscopic effects make the aircraft pitch up.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.

ENGINE FAILURE

If one engine on a conventional twin-engine aircraft fails in flight, it adversely affects its performance and controllability.

If one engine fails in flight, the remaining thrust forces are asymmetrically displaced and the aircraft yaws in the direction of the failed engine.

YAWING MOMENT

The yawing moment is the product of thrust from the operating engine multiplied by the distance between the thrust line and the CG (thrust arm), plus the drag from the failed engine multiplied by the distance between the engine centre line and the CG.

The strength of the yawing moment will depend on:
- how much thrust the operating engine is developing (throttle setting and density altitude).
- the distance between the thrust line and the CG (thrust arm).
- how much drag is being produced by the failed engine.

ASYMMETRIC BLADE EFFECT

If both engines rotate clockwise (figure 2), the right engine has a longer thrust arm. Failure of the left engine will give a larger yawing moment.

This effect will be absent on an aircraft with counter-rotating propellers, contra-rotating propellers or jet engines.

RUDDER MOMENT

The rudder moment, which balances the yawing moment, is the result of the rudder force multiplied by the distance between the fin CP and the CG (rudder arm)

The ability of the pilot to counteract the yawing moment due to asymmetric thrust will depend on:
- rudder displacement (affecting rudder force).
- CG position (affecting rudder arm).
- the IAS (affecting rudder force).

title: What is the effect on induced drag of an increase in aspect ratio?
optionA: Induced drag decreases, because the effect of tip vortices decreases.
optionB: Induced drag decreases, because a larger aspect ratio causes more downwash.
optionC: Induced drag increases, because the effect of tip vortices increases.
optionD: Induced drag increases, because a larger aspect ratio increases the frontal area.
explanationTotal: The induced drag coefficient is inversely proportional to the aspect ratio of an aircraft. This is because the tip vortices of a high aspect ratio wing affect a smaller proportion of the wingspan. This leads to a a decrease in downwash and therefore a smaller rearward vector of the lift force.

title: You are above the tropopause and descending to FL 340 at a constant Mach speed, which statement is true?
optionA: Coefficient of lift increases
optionB: IAS decreases
optionC: Coefficient of lift remains the same
optionD: TAS constant
explanationTotal:
The Mach Number can be defined by the relation between True Airspeed (TAS) and Local Speed of Sound (LSS) as follows:

M = TAS ÷ LSS

The Local Speed of Sound (LSS) varies proportionately with the air temperature.

Air temperature decreases with increased height above the surface until the tropopause is reached above which the temperature remains constant through the stratosphere.

Considering the above, with constant Mach Number and constant LSS, for the formula to remain balanced: TAS also has to be constant.

title: Assuming ISA conditions and a descent below the tropopause at constant Mach number and aeroplane mass, the:
optionA: TAS remains constant.
optionB: IAS decreases.
optionC: lift coefficient increases.
optionD: lift coefficient decreases.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The Mach number is defined as the ratio between the TAS and the LSS (Local speed of sound). The Mach number may be calculated as follows:

M = TAS / LSS

Lift is defined by:

L=1/2 ρ TAS2 S CL

Effect on IAS when descending at a constant Mach number:

  • Temperature increases with decreasing altitude. Consequently, the speed of sound will increase as altitude is decreased. If the bottom of the equation (LSS) increases, the TAS must be gradually increased to compensate for the increasing LSS due to higher temperatures.
  • Considering the lift formula, if TAS increases, to maintain Lift constant, CL must decrease.

title: A shock wave that is perpendicular to the direction of the flow is...
optionA: a normal shock wave.
optionB: an oblique shock wave.
optionC: a bow wave.
optionD: an expansion wave.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
(Normal meaning perpendicular to the upstream flow).

Whenever supersonic airflow is slowed to subsonic speed without a change in direction, a ‘normal’ shock wave will form as a boundary between the supersonic and subsonic region. This means that some compressibility effects will occur before the aircraft reaches Mach 1.0.

title: In the event of an engine failure on a twin engine aeroplane, the most aerodynamically efficient way of counteracting the yawing moment from the asymmetric thrust is by using...
optionA: trimmers only.
optionB: The rudder and flaps/slats.
optionC: the rudder and ailerons.
optionD: ailerons and spoilers.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

When an engine fails on a twin-engined aircraft, it creates asymmetric thrust, and a significant yawing moment towards the failed engine. This can very quickly result in a strong rolling moment also, and can cause a full loss of directional control. The pilot must counteract this initial yawing moment with opposite rudder input (rudder input towards the live engine). This rudder input creates a sideslip condition, which is controllable, but given the fact the engine has just lost half of its available thrust, is slightly undesirable due to the higher drag it causes.

This is why a small bank towards the live engine may be desirable. Often called "five to the live", a bank angle of up to 5º towards the operating engine uses the lifting of the wings to keep the aircraft flying in the same direction it is pointing, and therefore reduces the amount of sideslip required, and also slightly reduces the required rudder input. Both of these act to reduce drag, and therefore increase the possible rate of climb, or reduce the fuel flow to the engines, etc.

The question asks for the most aerodynamically efficient method of counteracting the yaw moment, which we would consider to be "the method producing the least drag", which is certainly by using the rudder and ailerons.

The other options are mostly possible to regain control after an engine failure, but are either very high drag, very slow to use, or just incredibly inefficient (in terms of drag) for counteracting yaw.

title:
Calculate the Mach number, given the following:

CAS: 293 kt
TAS: 385 kt
Temperature: -48°C
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The Mach number is defined as the ratio between the TAS and the LSS (Local speed of sound).
It is an indication of how fast an aircraft is travelling with relation to the sound waves that surround it.

The Mach number may be calculated as follows:

M=TAS/LSS=(TAS(kt))/(38.95∗√(T(K)))

The Local Speed of Sound is defined by:

LSS=38.95∗√(T(K))

The speed of propagation of small pressure waves depends upon the temperature of the air ONLY.

In this exercise:

T(°C)=−48°C
T(K)= -48+273.15=225.15 K
M=385/(38.95∗√225.15)⇔M=0.658
The Mach number is equal to M 0.658.

title: According to the pilot operating handbook, an aerobatic aeroplane has a flaps-down stall speed (VS0) at its maximum certified operating mass of 48 kt. Its flaps-up stall speed (VS1) is 57 kt. What is the value of VA?
optionA: 140 kt
optionB: 101 kt
optionC: 118 kt
optionD: 120 kt
explanationTotal:
VS1 is the stalling speed of an aircraft in 1g level flight, with flaps retracted.

VSO is the stalling speed in the landing configuration, and therefore not relevant.

VA is the design manoeuvring speed at which the aircraft will stall when achieving its maximum load factor, i.e. it is the stalling speed of an aircraft at its Limit Load Factor ("g" limit) with flaps retracted.

On an aircraft, where only one VA is published, maximum mass is assumed. In practice, like any stalling speed, VA will change during flight, decreasing as fuel is burnt and mass reduces.

The significance of VA is that below this speed, the pilot can apply full elevator deflection and the aircraft will stall before reaching its "g" limit. But above VA, it becomes possible to exceed the "g" limit and there is risk of overstressing and deforming the airframe.

For an aerobatic aircraft, the "g" limit is 6g.

For this question, VA is given by the stall speed formula with flaps retracted: VA = VS1 x √(Limit Load Factor) = 57 x √6 = 140 kt.

NOTE: Do not confuse the "Limit Load Factor" with the "Ultimate Load Limit".

title: You are in the transonic speed range and compressibility comes into effect. Which of the following factors is affected?
optionA: Dynamic pressure.
optionB: Static pressure.
optionC: Temperature.
optionD: Density.
explanationTotal:
LOs reference 081.02.01.04.01: State that compressibility means that density can change along a streamline, and that this occurs in the high subsonic (from Mach 0.4), transonic, and supersonic flow.

In low-speed aerodynamics, compressibility is so small that it can be neglected. However, airliners fly very close to their critical Mach number, consequently compressibility cannot be neglected anymore.

In fluid mechanics, compressibility is the change of density of a fluid in response to a change in pressure (or mean stress).

At supersonic speeds, streamlines do not avoid the body in front of it, as the speed of the profile is higher than the speed of the disturbance. Compressibility can also be considered as density change along a streamline

title: An aeroplane which has low static lateral stability is more prone to have controllability problems in:
optionA: roll and pitch
optionB: roll only
optionC: roll and yaw
optionD: yaw only
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
SPIRAL INSTABILITY

Spiral instability occurs when the directional stability of an aeroplane is strong and the lateral stability is weak. When a wing drops, due to a disturbance, the tendency of the aeroplane to correct this departure from the balanced condition in level flight is dependent on the lateral stability of the aeroplane. Additionally, when a wing drops, it causes other secondary motions to be initiated. The fin and rudder tend to yaw the aeroplane into the airflow in the direction of the dropped wing.

Because of the yaw, the higher wing on the outside of the turn is travelling faster than the lower wing and develops a greater amount of lift. This generates a rolling moment in the opposite direction to the correcting moment of the dihedral and if the rolling moment is greater it will tend to increase the angle of bank.

If the rolling moment is of sufficient magnitude to overcome the correcting force, produced by the dihedral and the damping yaw effect, the bank angle will increase and the aeroplane will enter a steadily steepening spiral dive. This is spiral instability that can be described as a combined lateral and directional aperiodic motion.

title:
Regarding deep stall characteristics, identify whether the following statements are correct or incorrect:

I. The combination of a wing with sweepback and a T-tail make an aeroplane prone to deep stall.
II. A stick shaker system is fitted to an aeroplane to resolve deep stall problems.
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: I is correct, II is correct.
optionB: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
optionC: I is incorrect, II is correct.
optionD: I is correct, II is incorrect.
explanationTotal:
"I. The combination of a wing with sweepback and a T-tail make an aeroplane prone to deep stall." CORRECT.

A deep stall is a dangerous phenomenon that occurs when the turbulence created by the main wing encompasses the horizontal stabilizer of the aircraft, preventing the aircraft from recovering from the stall.

  • Aircraft with swept-back wings are prone to deep stall, regardless of horizontal stabilizer position (T-tail or low tail). T-tail will worsen recovery characteristics.
  • Swept-forward wings at very high angle of attack are prone to deep stall as well. However, if a low horizontal tail is fitted, some pitch down moment may be produced with the help of the horizontal stabilizer since it is out of the separated turbulent wake of the wing.

"II. A stick shaker system is fitted to an aeroplane to resolve deep stall problems." INCORRECT

A stick shaker, as the name suggests shakes the control colum warning the pilot of an impeding stall. It does not apply any corrective measures.

title:
Which of these statements about induced drag are correct or incorrect?

I. Induced drag increases as angle of attack increases.
II. At constant load factor, induced drag increases with increasing aeroplane mass.
optionA: I is correct, II is incorrect.
optionB: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
optionC: I is correct, II is correct.
optionD: I is incorrect, II is correct.
explanationTotal:
Induced drag is created as a byproduct of lift. The pressure differential between the top and bottom of the wing creates a upwash around the tip of the wing that turns into a downwash behind the wing. This is known as a vortex, which creates a rearward force known as induced drag.

This question is asking for the effect of:

  • Angle of attack: The induced drag is proportional to the angle of attack. Therefore, induced drag increases as the angle of attack increases, and, induced drag decreases and the angle of attack decreases.
This is because, to maintain lift constant, as the velocity decreases, the coefficient of lift will have to be increased. This is achieve by increasing the angle of attack. At higher coefficients of lift, the pressure differential between the top and bottom of the wing will be greater and therefore produce stronger vortices = stronger induced drag. (and vice versa)
  • Changing mass: Induced drag is proportional to the mass. Therefore, induced drag increases with increasing aeroplane mass, and, induced drag decreases with decreasing aeroplane mass.

This is because, as the aircraft get heavier, the lift that the wings will have to produce increases. To achieve that, the coefficient of lift will have to increase, meaning a higher AoA, which creates stronger vortices. (and vice versa)

Summary:

  • Higher AR = Lower induced drag
  • Higher AoA = higher induced drag
  • Higher weight = higher AoA = higher induced drag
  • Higher speed = lower AoA = lower induced drag
  • Winglets = lower induced drag.

title: An aircraft with an AFT CG enters a spin. What attitude can be expected?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Pitch up to about 28º.
optionB: Nose level.
optionC: It is not possible to know what the attitude will be as it depends on other factors such as wind component and TOM.
optionD: A nose down attitude as the aircraft seeks to regain speed.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
Spinning is a condition of stalled flight in which an aircraft describes a downward spiral path, and is normally the by-product of wing drop when operating near the stall.

THE INCIPIENT SPIN (figures 1 and 2)
If the wing drops at the stall, the resulting rolling action alters the direction of the relative airflow on to the wing. It increases the angle of attack of the down-going wing and reduces the angle of attack of the up-going wing.

The down-going wing becomes more stalled, leading to a reduction in the coefficient of lift and an increase in the coefficient of drag.

Conversely, the up-going wing becomes less stalled, leading to an increase in the coefficient of lift and a reduction in the coefficient of drag.

The difference in lift between the wings produces a rolling moment and the aircraft rolls in the direction of the down-going wing. The yawing moment resulting from the large difference in drag between the down-going and up-going wings further aids this.

These moments lead to autorotation: the aircraft continues to roll, a side-slip develops, and the nose drops. Without corrective action, the rate of rotation steadily increases, resulting in a fully developed spin.

FULLY DEVELOPED SPIN
It is usual for the aircraft to rotate several times around a spin axis before settling into a steady state spin, with the final pitch attitude depending mainly on the position of the centre of gravity.

The spin can be either flat or steep. This condition is reached when the rate of rotation and sink stabilise at constant values.

When this occurs, the forces and moments acting are considered to be in equilibrium and the relative airflow comes vertically upward to meet the aircraft.

FORWARD CG
This results in a steeper spin and a faster rate of sink. This makes the recovery easier because the spin is less stable.

AFT CG
This results in a flatter spin and a lower rate of sink. This makes the recovery more difficult, because the spin is more stable.

If the centre of gravity is aft of its permitted limits, it significantly reduces the likelihood of recovery from a settled spin condition.

When an aircraft is in a steep spin rotation it is primarily in roll, whereas in a flat spin it is primarily in yaw.​​​​​​​ (figure 3)

title:
The most aft CG location may be limited by:

1. insufficient stick force stability.
2. insufficient flare capability.
3. excessive in-flight manoeuvrability.
4. insufficient in-flight manoeuvrability

The combination that regroups all of the correct statements is:
explanationTotal:
The point where an aircraft’s total sum of a pressure field is acting upon the body is called the Center of Pressure (CP).
This is the point where the resultant vector of lift is said to be operating.
As the airfoil or Angle of attack changes (thus changing the lift coefficient),
this pressure field will change and so will the center of pressure.

Aircraft longitudinal stability is directly related to Centre of Gravity (CG) position.
An aircraft with a more forward CG is more longitudinally stable than an aircraft with a more aft CG.
Placing the CG beyond the forward limit can cause an unacceptably high value of longitudinal stability, decreasing manoeuvrability by a significant amount.
Place the CG beyond the aft limit and the aircraft is too unstable, having excessive manoeuvrability.

If an aircraft is longitudinally stable, an increase in Angle of Attack (α) results in a negative pitching moment.
The nose will slightly fall down, decreasing the Angle of Attack.
If this aircraft has a decrease of Angle of Attack, the nose will come slightly upwards again, creating a positive pitching moment again by slightly raising the nose.

title:
Which of the following are the first indications of a stall?

1. uncommanded yaw
2. light buffering before the stall
3. less control effectiveness
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionD: 3 only.
explanationTotal:
STALL

A stall is an aerodynamic condition which occurs when smooth airflow over the airplane’s wings is disrupted, resulting in loss of lift. Specifically, a stall occurs when the AOA—the angle between the chord line of the wing and the relative wind—exceeds the wing’s critical AOA. It is possible to exceed the critical AOA at any airspeed, at any attitude, and at any power setting.

Stall warnings can be either natural (aerodynamic) and/or synthetic (non-aerodynamic, artificial) indications:

1. Aerodynamic stall warnings may include one or more of the following indications:

  • Buffet of the elevator
  • Higher than normal attitude
  • Light and less effective controls
  • Uncommanded pitch down
  • Uncommanded roll
  • Inability to maintain altitude or arrest a rate of descent.
2. Νon-aerodynamic stall warnings, in comparison with the aerodynamic ones, may include one or more of the following indications:
  • Audible stall warning sounds
  • Stick shaker activation
  • Stick pusher

title: What happens to the flow velocity over the wing when angle of attack decreases?
optionA: It increases, and lift capability decreases.
optionB: It increases, and lift capability increases.
optionC: It decreases, and lift capability decreases.
optionD: It decreases, and lift capability increases.
explanationTotal:
L = CL x p/2 x V2 x S

Where:

  • CL is lift coefficient
  • P is density
  • V is velocity
  • S is surface area

Angle of attack is important and is represented in CL. As you can see from the above formula, lift is proportional to CL. Therefore, it will also be proportional to angle of attack. Lift is greater if angle of attack is higher.

A reduction in angle of attack decreases the acceleration given to the flow over the wing. Thus, the speed of the flow is decreased. If speed decreases, static pressure increases. Since the reduction in pressure over the wing is less, less lift will be generated.

title: A stick pusher:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: pushes the elevator control forward when a specified value of angle of attack is exceeded.
optionB: vibrates the elevator control.
optionC: pushes the elevator control forward prior to stick shaker activation.
optionD: pushes the elevator control to avoid a stall at a negative load factor.
explanationTotal:
A stick shaker, as the name suggests shakes the control colum warning the pilot of an impeding stall. It does not apply any corrective measures.

A stick pusher is a system that will push the stick forward, lowering the nose and therefore decreasing the angle of attack to prevent a stall. The stick pushers will automatically disengage when the angle of attack reaches below a suitable value. Stick pushers are mandatory for aircraft that are prone to deep stalls.

For an aircraft mounted with both the stick shaker system and stick pusher system, the sequence of events is as follows:

  1. First as a warning of impeding stall, the stick shaker will activate and a corrective action by the pilot is expected.

  2. As the angle of attack keeps increasing and reaches a pre set dangerous value that might be unrecoverable, the stick pusher will activate and force the nose down. The stick shaker will stay active during the entire duration of the stick pusher, but not vice versa.

title: During which of the following phases of flight is a fixed pitch propeller’s angle of attack lowest?
optionA: Take-off run.
optionB: Low-speed glide.
optionC: Climb.
optionD: High-speed glide.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
For a fixed-pitch-propeller airplane during a glide descent, maintaining a constant IAS with idle thrust, the propeller pitch and lift/drag ratio will decrease but the rate of descent will increase because the TAS gradually increases during the descent.
In the case of a high-speed glide, it is possible that the TAS increases so much that the blade angle of attack becomes negative.

title: The drag coefficient at constant angle of attack:
optionA: starts to decrease rapidly above the drag divergence Mach number.
optionB: starts to increase rapidly above the drag divergence Mach number.
optionC: starts to increase rapidly above M<sub>CRIT</sub>.
optionD: increases only when M<sub>CRIT</sub> is above unity.
explanationTotal:
The critical Mach number, or Mcrit, is the lowest Mach number at which the airflow over some point of the aircraft reaches the speed of sound (Mach 1),
but does not exceed it. At the lower critical Mach number, the airflow around the entire aircraft is subsonic.
At the higher critical Mach number, the airflow around the whole aircraft is supersonic.

Because of the critical Mach number, it is possible that shockwaves can occur at speeds even below Mach 1.
As the aircraft speeds up beyond this critical Mach number, drag increases dramatically.
If the aircraft is not designed for transonic or supersonic flight, this could lead to controllability problems.
The critical Mach number increases with increasing wing sweepback. Thinner airfoils also increase the value of Mcrit.

The drag divergence Mach number is the Mach number at which the aerodynamic drag on an airfoil begins to increase rapidly as the Mach number increases.
The drag coefficient can multiply to 10 times its size compared to its low speed value.
The drag divergence Mach number is a number bigger than Mcrit and smaller than Mach 1.
The drag divergence Mach number can be increased by increasing wing sweepback.

title: With regard to asymmetric thrust conditions and an increase in density altitude, the minimum control speeds...
optionA: decrease, due to the loss of effectiveness of flight controls for a given angle of deflection, and the need for a lower CAS to maintain control.
optionB: increase, due to the loss of effectiveness of flight controls for a given angle of deflection, and the need for a higher CAS to maintain control.
optionC: increase, due to less thrust being developed by the engines, and the need for a higher CAS to maintain control.
optionD: decrease, due to less thrust being developed by the engines, and therefore control being able to be maintained at a lower CAS.
explanationTotal:
The minimum control speed (VMC) is the calibrated airspeed of an aircraft below which directional or lateral control of the aircraft can no longer be maintained after the failure of one or more engines.
At least one engine must still be operative for the VMC to apply. It depends on the stage of the flight.
At VMC the aircraft is still able to maintain straight flight with a bank angle of not more than 5 degrees.

At higher density altitude, with one engine inoperative, the operating engine(s) will produce less thrust.
This decreases the thrust asymmetry, which decreases VMC.

title:
(For this question use annex 081-001 issue date July 2009).
Regarding the Buffet Onset Boundary Chart in the annex which of these statements are correct or incorrect?

1. Flying at M = 0.84 provides the optimum margin with respect to buffet onset.
2. The maximum altitude that can be achieved with respect to buffet onset according to Certification Specifications is lower at M = 0.82 than at M = 0.75.
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: 1 is incorrect, 2 is incorrect.
optionB: 1 is correct, 2 is incorrect.
optionC: 1 is correct, 2 is correct.
optionD: 1 is incorrect, 2 is correct.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
In the same way that separated airflow prior to a low speed stall can cause airframe buffet, shock induced separation (shock stall) at high speed can also cause buffeting.

Aerodynamic buffet is a valuable stall warning, but it can damage the aircraft structure. Because of the higher dynamic pressure when an aircraft is operating in the transonic speed region, any shock induced buffet will have a greater potential for severe airframe damage.
High speed buffet must be completely avoided. The aircraft must therefore be operated in such a manner that a (safety) margin exists before aerodynamic buffet will occur.

If the variables which affect both high speed and low speed stall are considered it will be possible to identify the conditions under which buffeting will occur and a chart can be drawn to show all the factors involved.

This is called a ‘Buffet Onset’ chart which is used by flight crews to ensure their aircraft is always operated with a specified minimum buffet margin.

For any given combination of mass, center of gravity position and airspeed, the maximum operating altitude is that altitude at which a normal positive acceleration increment of 0.3 g, without exceeding the buffet onset boundary, is possible.

It is, therefore, common practice to draw the ‘buffet-onset boundary chart’ for a range of cruise masses at 1.3 g. Any maneuver having a load factor exceeding 1.3 g will initiate the buffet onset.

In this exercise:

This chart is specific to an aircraft, and shows the relationship of altitude, load factor, cruise data, weight, Mach number, and IAS. The optimum speed can be found by intersecting the top of the altitude curve. In this case it is M0.80, therefore statement 1 is incorrect.

  • Start by drawing a vertical line from M0.82 and M0.75 to the FL410 curve (first altitude curve).
  • From here, draw a straight line from left to right that intersects the weight curves.
  • Finally, draw a vertical up from 1.3 g load factor that intersects the lines drawn in step 2.
As we can see, flying at M0.82 gives us the ability to carry a greater weight. We can then conclude that it also gives us a higher buffet onset margin, therefore statement 2 is incorrect.

title:
Which of these statements about the strength of wing tip vortices are correct or incorrect?

I. Assuming no flow separation, the strength of wing tip vortices decreases as the angle of attack increases.
II. The strength of wing tip vortices increases as the aspect ratio increases.
optionA: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
optionB: I is correct, II is incorrect.
optionC: I is incorrect, II is correct.
optionD: I is correct, II is correct.
explanationTotal:
Wing tip vortices are a byproduct of lift. They are caused by the pressure differential between the top and bottom of the wing, which causes an updraft of high pressure air around the tip of the wing. This updraft turns into a downdraft behind the wing, creating a vortex. The higher the pressure difference between the top and bottom of the wing, the stronger the vortices.

This question is specifically asking for:

  • Angle of attack: The strength of the vortices (and therefore also induced drag) is proportional to the angle of attack. Therefore; the strength of the vortices increase as the angle of attack increases, hence statement 1 is incorrect!
  • Aspect ratio: The strength of the vortices is inversely proportional with the aspect ratio. Meaning that the strength of the wing tip vortices decreases as the aspect ratio increases, hence statement 2 is incorrect!

title: Incipient spin is the term assigned to the phase of a spin:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: After the initial couple of rotations and the aerodynamic forces present are in balance.
optionB: After the initial couple of rotations but the aerodynamic forces present are not yet fully balanced.
optionC: When the initial rotation starts and the aerodynamic forces present are in balance.
optionD: When the initial rotation starts but the aerodynamic forces present are not yet fully balanced.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
SPIN. A stall must occur before a spin can take place. A spin occurs when one wing stalls more than the other.

There are three phases of spin:

  1. INCIPIENT phase - exists from the time the aeroplane stalls and rotation starts until the spin is fully developed. This may not occur until 2 to 4 rotations have been completed - however, according to EASA, incipient spin starts already whenever, in the post stall regime, there is an uncommanded roll in excess of 45 degrees which is the result of yaw assymetry during a stall. During this phrase, the aerodynamic forces are not balanced and the aircraft is more or less tumbling.
  2. DEVELOPED phase - begins when the aerodynamic forces are in balance (the angular rotation rates, airspeed and vertical descent rate are stabilized from one turn to the next). The spin, although chaotic looking from inside the cockpit, has been established and recovery procedures are now necessary to break the spin.
  3. RECOVERY phase - controls are applied to stop spin, recover from the unusual attitude and maintain straight and level.

title: The main purpose of a boundary-layer fence on a swept wing is to...
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Improve the high speed handling characteristics.
optionB: Increase the critical Mach number.
optionC: Improve the lift coefficient of the trailing edge flaps.
optionD: Prevent spanwise flow to prevent the wingtips from stalling first.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The main purpose of a boundary-layer fence on a swept wing is to prevent spanwise flow and promote a more uniform flow distribution over the wing. This helps to delay the onset of flow separation and stall, particularly at the wingtips, which are prone to stalling first on swept wings. By preventing spanwise flow and promoting a more uniform flow distribution, the boundary-layer fence helps to increase the effective span of the wing and improve its overall performance.

title: Which CG position contributes to flat spin?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Within the range of CG (both for and aft limit).
optionB: The CG position does not matter.
optionC: Forward CG.
optionD: Aft CG.
explanationTotal:
Flat spins are the worst and most dangerous type of spin. In a flat spin, the aircraft has no forward airspeed. It spins around its vertical axis as it sinks straight towards the ground.

Due to the high angle of attack of a flat spin, it is nearly impossible to recover, as the horizontal stabilizer is most likely in stall, too. The only possibility then is to move the CG forward. In small aircraft what you can do is to lean forward and hope for the best.

The type of spin a plane enters depends mainly on the CG Position (and thrust setting):

  • CG towards the forward limit makes an aircraft more stable, and control forces will be higher which makes it less likely that large, abrupt control movements will be made. When trimmed, the aeroplane will tend to return to level flight if the controls are released, but the stall speed will be higher.

  • CG towards the aft limit decreases longitudinal static stability and reduces pitch control forces, which tends to make the aeroplane easier to stall. Once a spin is entered, the further aft the CG, the flatter the spin attitude.

All in all, do not spin with an aircraft that is not designed for that or with too aft CG position.

Note: Watch the following video to understand the attitude of the aircraft during a flat spin
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=22eADnRqMwo&t=16s

title: Static directional stability is the...
optionA: tendency of an aeroplane to raise the low wing in a sideslip.
optionB: natural ability of an aeroplane to recover from a disturbance about the longitudinal axis.
optionC: tendency of an aeroplane to recover from a disturbance about the lateral axis.
optionD: tendency of an aeroplane to recover from a skid without control input from the pilot.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The rotation of an aircraft about its normal, or vertical, axis is a yaw. If this movement is the result of an undesirable disturbance, then the ability of the airplane to return to its original heading without the assistance of any control-surface movement is a measure of its directional static stability. It is a measure of the aircraft’s ability to realign itself with the relative airflow.

Sideslip is the displacement angle of the airplane’s longitudinal axis in azimuth from the relative airflow. It is positive when the relative airflow is to the right of the longitudinal axis and negative when the relative airflow is left of the longitudinal axis.

An airplane has directional static stability if, when in a sideslip with the airflow coming from the left initially the nose tends to yaw left. An airplane that has excessive directional static stability compared to its lateral static stability is more prone to spiral dive.

title: An aeroplane flying at 200 kt in straight and level flight is subjected to a disturbance that suddenly increases the speed by 100 kt. Assuming the angle of attack remains constant, the load factor will initially:
optionA: remain unchanged, since the angle of attack does not change.
optionB: increase to 2.
optionC: increase to 2.25.
optionD: increase to 1.5.
explanationTotal:
Initial speed Vi = 200
Speed after disturbance Vii = 300

Load factor= Lift/Weight, Weight is constant here.

Assuming the angle of attack is constant initially CL is constant.
Lift=1/2.CL.S.V2.d (d=density and S=wing area which are constant as well)

Therefore the only variable is speed. Lift changes with the square of speed. (Lift=1/2.CL.S.V2.d)
Vi/Vii=300/200=1.5
(1.5)2=2.25 is the load factor after disturbance.

title: Which considerations have to be taken into account by the pilot when flying a multi-engine aircraft with a failed left engine, causing a sideslip, and the nose pointed to the right?
optionA: The pilot should apply full rudder input to the left to counteract the sideslip and nose deviation to the right caused by the left engine failure.
optionB: Throttle should be reduced on the operating engine to correct the sideslip.
optionC: The angle of attack AoA of the fin increases when there is an increase in rudder input to the operating engine side of the aircraft.
optionD: The pilot should apply full power on the operating engine to counteract the left engine failure, without any additional consequences.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
ENGINE FAILURE

If one engine on a conventional twin-engine aircraft fails in flight, it adversely affects its performance and controllability.

If one engine fails in flight, the remaining thrust forces are asymmetrically displaced and the aircraft yaws in the direction of the failed engine.

YAWING MOMENT

The yawing moment is the product of thrust from the operating engine multiplied by the distance between the thrust line and the CG (thrust arm), plus the drag from the failed engine multiplied by the distance between the engine centre line and the CG.

The strength of the yawing moment will depend on:
- how much thrust the operating engine is developing (throttle setting and density altitude).
- the distance between the thrust line and the CG (thrust arm).
- how much drag is being produced by the failed engine.

RUDDER MOMENT

The rudder moment, which balances the yawing moment, is the result of the rudder force multiplied by the distance between the fin CP and the CG (rudder arm)

The ability of the pilot to counteract the yawing moment due to asymmetric thrust will depend on:
- rudder displacement (affecting rudder force).
- CG position (affecting rudder arm).
- the IAS (affecting rudder force).

Note: In this exercise, the left engine failed, which means that initially the yawing moment would be to the left, causing the nose to point to the left. If after the nose is to the right, it means that the pilot might have made a too big rudder input and the nose is now to the right, creating a sideslip. This is why it is important to know what factors influence the rudder moment, one of which is that an increase in rudder input increases its angle of attack, which increases the overall force that the rudder produces.

title:
Refer to figure.
Which of the augmentation(s) in the annex will increase the wings CL?
optionA: Only 1
optionB: Only 2
optionC: 2 and 3
optionD: Only 3
explanationTotal:
The annex in the question gives us 3 changes, which all include the extension or retraction of high lift devices.

  • 1 - Leading edge flaps - The leading edge of the wing droops slightly to increase the camber of the wing, thereby increasing the CL and CLMAX, much similar to trailing edge flaps. They do increase drag also.
  • 2 - Kreuger flaps - The underside of the leading edge unfolds, to split the airflow much further down than the usual stagnation point, thereby forcing more air over the upper surface wing, generating higher lift and a faster boundary layer, delaying the stall. There is some drag penalty for using Kreuger flaps.
  • 3 - Slats - The most effective high lift devices; very little increase in drag, but a much delayed stall, so the wing can have a much higher CLMAX. They achieve this by squeezing some high speed air through that slot from beneath to above the wing.

The annex here is not perfectly descriptive, but we will assume that the old position is outlined only, and the new position is filled in with colour. This means that item 1 is being extended, whereas items 2 and 3 are being retracted. This means that only item 1 is increasing the CL (and in fact, even extending item 3 (slats) does not actually increase the CL really, it only increases CLMAX by delaying the stall).

Note: If you get an annex just like this in the exam, it would be worth commenting or appealing based on the annex, as it is very difficult to work out which whether each is retracting or extending without any indication of what position comes first and what comes last.

title:
Calculate the turn radius for an aircraft with a TAS of 120 kt and a 60° bank angle.
(Assume g = 10 m/s2)
explanationTotal:
The formula to work out radius of turn is;
Radius = (TAS)2 / (g x tan(bank angle))

Where g = the acceleration due to gravity, usually 9.81 m/s2, but assumed to be 10 m/s2 in some questions, like this one.
All units are in metric. Radius (m), TAS (m/s), g (m/s2).

First lets convert 120 kt into metres per second. 120 kt is 120 nautical miles per 1 hour, so multiple by the amount of metres in a nautical mile [1852] (now you have metres per hour). Then divide by the amount of seconds in an hour [3600]. Now you have metres per second.

TAS = 120 kt x 1852 / 3600 = 61.73 m/s

Substituting the known figures into the radius formula above, we get;

Radius (m) = (61.73)2 / (10 x tan(60º)) = 220 m

title: Whilst maintaining straight and level flight with a lift coefficient C<sub>L</sub>=1, what will be the new value of C<sub>L</sub> after the speed has doubled?
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Firstly lets identify the equation that we will use to solve this question:
L = CL ½ rho V2 S

Now the question asks us what our new lift coefficient will be after the speed has doubled.

There are several assumptions we need to make:

  • Since we are remaining is straight and level flight, we know that our lift will remain constant.
  • “½” is a constant that will not change with increasing speed
  • The air density “rho” will also remain constant
  • The wing surface area will also remain constant

Therefore we can say that:
L ∝ CL V2

After our speed has doubled, to maintain a constant lift, our coefficient of will have to be divided by four to compensate for the quadratic factor of the velocity increase. Therefore dividing 1 by 4 gives us a lift coefficient of 0.25; the coefficint of lift after doubling the airspeed.

title: What could happen if there is ice accumulation on the elevator or stabiliser and the flaps are lowered?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Increased downwash.
optionB: Decreased drag, leading to better fuel efficiency.
optionC: Increased lift due to improved aerodynamics.
optionD: Improved stall characteristics, making stalls less likely.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
STABILIZER STALL DUE TO ICE

The tailplane is an aerofoil, and because it is thinner than the wing, it is likely to experience icing before the wing does. The effect will be the same as for the wing; the stall will occur at a lower angle of attack.

The tailplane is normally operating at a negative angle of attack, producing a down load, so if the tailplane stalls and the down load is lost, the nose of the aircraft will drop and longitudinal control will be lost.

Stalling of an ice contaminated tailplane could be precipitated by extension of the wing flaps.

Lowering the flaps increases the downwash, and this increases the negative angle of attack of the tailplane. If the tailplane has ice contamination, this could be sufficient to cause it to stall.

Recovery procedure in this situation would be to retract the flaps again, thus reducing the downwash.

Take care when increasing an aircraft's forward airspeed to compensate for ice on the wings, since every knot of airspeed added to prevent wing stall brings the aircraft a knot closer to tailplane stall. Consequently, it is vital that the tailplane, like the wing, is free from contamination. This type of stall does not usually occur, but if it does, recovery is normally impossible.

title:
In the cruise, the pilot of a large commercial jet aircraft notices the trim wheels turning in one direction whilst the aircraft yoke moves in the opposite direction. What should the pilot do?

(1) Disengage the autopilot because the autopilot may be defective.
(2) Disengage the electric trim switches, as the autopilot masks the trim runaway and a problem with controlling the aircraft may arise.
optionA: (1) Correct; (2) Incorrect
optionB: (1) Correct; (2) Correct
optionC: (1) Incorrect; (2) Correct
optionD: (1) Incorrect; (2) Incorrect
explanationTotal:
There are two scenarios that this could be; a faulty autopilot or trim runaway. A faulty autopilot would be exactly as it sounds, the autopilot is inputting the incorrect command into the control system, and the feedback loop is not working correctly to fix it. The fix for this situation would be disconnecting the autopilot. Of course, the pilots must then be aware that the trim will be set massively different from normal, so the forces will be high upon autopilot disconnect.

The other situation is a trim runaway. It is impossible to tell from the question whether this is the situation or not. A trim runaway is where the electric trim system of an aircraft continues changing the trim angle, without command from the pilots. It could be due to the trims themselves, or the trims commanded by the autopilot. It is then up to the pilot to choose whether to disconnect the autopilot or not, as leaving the autopilot running reduces the forces the pilots have to bear, but disconnecting could fix the problem entirely.

Therefore, first, the pilot must disconnect the autopilot to stop any autopilot fault from making the situation worse. They should then attempt to control the aircraft manually, and if the trim runaway continues, switch off the electric trim and trim manually.

On balance, we would say that both of the actions in the question are correct, and with pretty much correct reasoning, although there will be an order in which to do these actions, set out by the manufacturer. We haven't had this answer confirmed though, so please let us know if you see this in the real exam, and anything you can remember about it, thank you!

title: As the CG of an aircraft moves forward from the neutral point, the amount of elevator deflection required to control the aircraft...
optionA: decreases and then increases.
optionB: remains the same.
optionC: increases.
optionD: decreases.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.

The point where an aircraft’s total sum of a pressure field is acting upon the body is called the Center of Pressure (CP).
This is the point where the resultant vector of lift is said to be operating.
As the airfoil or Angle of attack changes (thus changing the lift coefficient), this pressure field will change and so will the center of pressure.
Aircraft longitudinal stability is directly related to Centre of Gravity (CG) position.
An aircraft with a more forward CG is more longitudinally stable than an aircraft with a more aft CG.
Placing the CG beyond the forward limit can cause an unacceptably high value of longitudinal stability, decreasing manoeuvrability by a significant amount.
Place the CG beyond the aft limit and the aircraft is too unstable, having excessive manoeuvrability.

If an aircraft is longitudinally stable, an increase in Angle of Attack (α) results in a negative pitching moment.
The nose will slightly fall down, decreasing the Angle of Attack.
If this aircraft has a decrease of Angle of Attack, the nose will come slightly upwards again, creating a positive pitching moment again by slightly raising the nose.
In this case, if an aircraft is very stable (forward CG), the elevator will have to produce a bigger moment to move the pitch and thus requires a larger deflection

title: A jet transport aeroplane is in a straight climb at a constant IAS and constant weight. The operational limit that may be exceeded is:
optionA: M<sub>MO</sub>.
optionB: V<sub>A</sub>.
optionC: M<sub>D</sub>.
optionD: V<sub>MO</sub>.
explanationTotal: VMO and MMO are fix values independent of altitude. As VMO is IAS, when climbing at a constant IAS, the margin to VMO will remain the same. However, with increasing altitude, TAS increases and the local speed of sound decreases (as temperature decreases). Mach Number being TAS divided by LSS will increase. As the Mach number corresponding to VMO will increase, MMO could be exceeded.

title: In preparation for departure, the pilot sets the aircraft's CG position at 12% of the MAC not knowing that the actual aircraft CG is at 21% of MAC What is the possible outcome for this aircraft setting?
optionA: Higher stick force than expected.
optionB: Poor climb performance.
optionC: Longer take-off run.
optionD: Tail-strike may occur.
explanationTotal:
The chord line that passes through the geometric centre of the plan area of an aerofoil is the Mean Aerodynamic Chord (MAC) and for any planform is equal to the chord of a rectangular wing having the same wing span and the same pitching moment and lift. The MAC is often used to reference the location of the centre of gravity.

Tail strike – the rotation is started before it is possible to lift-off, consequently angle of attack might be increased up to tail strike.

In this case, a 12% CG position will tend to hold the nose down (nose-heavy). To counter this, the pilots need to set a nose up trim in order to create a nose-up pitching moment at rotation.

The actual CG position is however more aft which will naturally help lifting the aircraft nose. This natural tendency, combined with a nose-up trim, will result in a tendency of the nose lifting of earlier than intended and faster, increasing the risk of a tail strike.

title: The angle of attack of a fixed pitch propeller blade decreases when:
optionA: forward velocity and RPM decrease.
optionB: forward velocity and RPM increase.
optionC: forward velocity decreases and RPM increases.
optionD: forward velocity increases and RPM decreases.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
The blade angle of a fixed-pitch propeller is constant, but the helix angle and the angle of attack will vary according to its forward speed. To ensure its efficient operation the blade angle of attack of a fixed-pitch propeller must be close to the optimum and is that which produces the greatest excess of horizontal lift (thrust) over drag.
Figure 1 shows a “fixed pitch” propeller at constant RPM. Increasing TAS decreases the angle of attack of the propeller. Figure 2 shows a “fixed pitch” propeller at a constant TAS. Increasing RPM increases the angle of attack of the propeller.

title: Vortex generators on the upper side of the wing surface will:
optionA: increase the magnitude of the shock wave.
optionB: decrease the span wise flow at high Mach numbers.
optionC: increase the critical Mach number.
optionD: decrease shock wave induced flow separation.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The unfavorable characteristics associated with compressibility are due to boundary layer separation behind the shock wave (shock stall).
Flow separation occurs because the boundary layer loses kinetic energy as it flows against the adverse pressure gradient. Shock wave formation increases the adverse pressure gradient so the loss of kinetic energy in the boundary layer will be greater.

Increasing the kinetic energy of the boundary layer will reduce flow separation. Simple devices called vortex generators are used to re-energize the boundary layer.
Vortex generators are small plates, vanes, blades, or wedges mounted in spanwise rows along the wing surface.

Each vortex generator produces a vortex at its tip which will induce high energy air from the free stream flow to mix with the boundary layer, thus increasing its kinetic energy and helping it flow through the shock wave with much less separation.

Vortex generators are usually located on the upper wing surface, particularly ahead of control surfaces, but may be used anywhere where separation is causing high drag or reduced control effectiveness.

It should be noted that vortex generators may also be used on subsonic aircraft to prevent separation caused by high adverse pressure gradients due to the contours of the surface.

title: Which component of drag increases most when an aileron is deflected upwards?
optionA: Interference drag.
optionB: Wave drag.
optionC: Induced drag.
optionD: Form drag.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
When an aileron is deflected upwards, lift is decreased. Thus, induced drag decreases. However, Form Drag, also known as Pressure Drag or Profile Drag, is the drag caused by the separation of the boundary layer from a surface and the wake created by that separation and it is primarily dependent upon the shape of the object. An upward defected aileron will change the wing profile and cause eddies, increasing form drag.

title: You are flying with the autopilot climbing in vertical speed mode, what may happen?
optionA: Airspeed will decrease as the autopilot pitches up to keep the vertical speed.
optionB: Airspeed will decrease until the autopilot pitches down on approaching V<sub>S</sub> to prevent stall.
optionC: The autopilot disconnects before stall onset.
optionD: It is not possible to climb at a constant vertical speed.
explanationTotal:
The autopilot's vertical speed mode allows you to perform constant-rate climbs and descents. In this mode, the vertical speed is prioritised over airspeed. When you engage the vertical speed mode, the FD/autopilot will attempt to maintain the specified vertical speed until you choose a different setting in autopilot, the aircraft reaches an assigned altitude set into the assigned altitude selector/alerter, or the autopilot is disconnected.

As the power of aircraft is limited at a certain altitude it may not be able to achieve targeted vertical speed. If you command it to climb at a greater FPM rate than your aircraft can perform at that altitude airspeed decays, the autopilot will continually pitch the aircraft up in an attempt to maintain the vertical speed selected. This could happen all the way to the point of stalling.

title: A light aeroplane is in steady, straight and level fight at a low subsonic speed, with no flaps. On reaching a turning point the pilot at a constant speed, uses a load factor of 1.15 to maintain level flight. Due to the turn, the coefficient of lift:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Increases by 32%.
optionB: Remains constant.
optionC: Increases by 15%.
optionD: Increases by 7%.
explanationTotal:
The load factor (n) can be defined as the ratio of the actual lift of an aircraft to its weight (n = Lift / Weight).

In level flight, lift equals weight. However, if the aircraft maneuvers (i.e. turn), load factor n will be higher than 1. To have a general formula, lift has to be equal to weight, multiplied by the load factor.

L = W n
CL p/2 V2 S = W n
CL = (2W n) / (p V2 S)

  • W, p, V and S remain constant.
CL is proportional to n, therefore coefficient of lift increases by 15%.

title: How does the Local Speed of Sound (LSS) change with increasing altitude?
optionA: LSS will increase in the lower stratosphere
optionB: LSS will decrease in the lower stratosphere
optionC: LSS will decrease in the troposphere
optionD: LSS will remain constant below the troposphere
explanationTotal:
The Earth's atmosphere is an extremely thin sheet of air extending from the surface of the Earth to the edge of space, about 60 miles above the surface of the Earth. The first two zones are the troposphere and the stratosphere.
The troposphere runs from the surface of the Earth to 36,152 feet. In the troposphere, the temperature decreases linearly with altitude at a constant rate of -1,98°C/1000 ft.
The lower portion of the stratosphere is an isothermal layer where the temperature remains constant (approximately -57°C) with increasing height, and then in its upper layers the temperature increases to around 0° C at the stratopause.

For the study of high speed flight we are interested in the speed at which the infinitesimally small pressure disturbances (waves) travel through the atmosphere. Pressure waves ‘propagate’ from their source, that is, each air molecule is rapidly vibrated in turn and passes on the disturbance to its neighbour. The speed of propagation of small pressure waves depends upon the temperature of the air ONLY. The higher the temperature, the higher the speed of propagation.

Therefore only possible answer can be LSS will decrease in the troposphere. Since temperature decreases with increasing altitude in the troposphere LSS would decrease with temperature as well.

title: Aileron reversal can occur at...
optionA: low speeds when wing with the up-going aileron exceeds that wing’s critical Angle Of Attack.
optionB: low speeds when the wing with the down-going aileron twists, increasing that wing’s camber.
optionC: high speeds when the wing with the down-going aileron twists, reducing that wing’s Lift Coefficient.
optionD: high speeds when the wing with the up-going aileron causes sufficient drag, leading to adverse yaw.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Aileron reversal can occur at high speed when the wing twists as a result of the loads caused by operating the ailerons. In figure 1 the aileron has been deflected downwards to increase lift and raise the wing. Aerodynamic forces act upwards on the aileron, and as this is behind the flexural axis of the wing, it will cause a nose-down twisting moment on the wing structure. This will reduce the angle of attack of the wing which will reduce its lift. If the twisting is sufficient, the loss of lift due to decreased angle of attack will exceed the gain of lift due to increased camber, and the wing will drop instead of lifting.

title: Often, the tip of a wing will have a lower angle of incidence than the wing section near the root. Why?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: To encourage the wingtip to stall first, keeping the aircraft controllable at high angles of attack.
optionB: To prevent tip stall.
optionC: To extend the boundary layer towards the wingtip.
optionD: To reduce induced drag, aiding with supersonic flight characteristics.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
In some wing designs, separation tends to occur first in the region of the tip, reducing lift in those areas. If an actual wing were allowed to stall in this way, stalling would give aileron buffet and perhaps violent wing drop. The ailerons would become uncontrollable, so designers make modifications to stop this.

To give favourable stall characteristics, many wing types must be modified using one or more of the following:

Geometric twist (washout), a decrease in incidence from root to tip. This decreases the angle of attack at the tip, and the root will tend to stall first, which is desirable.

The aerofoil section may be varied throughout the span such that sections with greater thickness and camber are located near the tip. The higher CLMAX of such sections delays stall earlier, so that the root will tend to stall first.

title: An aeroplane's bank angle is defined as the angle between its...
optionA: lateral axis and the horizon.
optionB: longitudinal axis and the horizon.
optionC: lateral axis and the relative airflow.
optionD: longitudinal axis and the relative airflow.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Angle of attack is the difference between pitch attitude and flight path angle.
It is defined as the angle between the chord of an airfoil and the relative wind.

Flight path angle is the angle between the horizon and the flight path.
Also called climb or descent angle.

Pitch angle is the angle between the horizon and longitudinal axis of the aircraft, it is equal to Flight path angle + Angle of attack.

Bank angle is the angle between the lateral axis and the horizon.
Bank is rotated around the longitudinal axis, but during a bank at level flight, the angle between the longitudinal axis and the horizon does not change.
The angle between the lateral axis and horizon does.

title: With regards to the effect of an aerofoil's thickness on high speed flight, M<sub>CRIT</sub> is (2) _____ by a thicker aerofoil and (2) _____ by a thinner aerofoil.
optionA: (1) increased; (2) increased
optionB: (1) decreased; (2) increased
optionC: (1) increased; (2) decreased
optionD: (1) decreased; (2) decreased
explanationTotal:
When air travels over an aerofoil in normal operation, the air above the aerofoil, near the leading edge, increases in velocity, due to the "squashing" of the streamlines together, causing a venturi effect, creating the low pressure zone that is required as part of creating lift. This means that air is usually going faster over the top of the wing than anywhere else on the airframe.

As an aircraft approaches the speed of sound, Mach 1, the air above the wing will get there first, as it is faster than the freestream airflow (TAS). In particular, it is usually the air just above the wing root, where the wing is thickest, and the streamlines get "squashed" the most, that is the first bit of air to reach the sound barrier. The TAS at which the first particle of air becomes sonic (exactly Mach 1) is called MCRIT, and is the beginning of the transonic speed regime. Above this speed, shockwaves will begin to form on various parts of the airframe.

MCRIT is variable, and in particular depends on the airspeed increase over the wing. If the speed increase equates to M0.2, for instance, then the aircraft will have an MCRIT of M0.8, a higher MCRIT than if the speed increase due to the wing was M0.25, giving an MCRIT of M0.75. A higher MCRIT is better, as the drag increases rapidly just above the MCRIT, at MDD, the drag divergence speed, and we would like to fly as fast as possible with the lowest drag.

A large factor of the MCRIT is the thickness of the aerofoil, as thicker aerofoils "squash" the air above the wing more, thereby speeding it up more. Therefore, thinner aerofoils are more suited to high speed flight, as they have a higher MCRIT, and also handle the transonic speed regime better in general.

For this question, then, thicker aerofoils decrease the MCRIT (which is bad), and thinner aerofoils increase MCRIT (good).

title: A pilot of a single-engined aircraft has calculated their glide range in the event of an engine failure. In still air, from 4 000 ft, the aircraft will glide for a lateral distance of 9.8 NM. What distance will the aircraft manage to reach if it is gliding into a headwind of 15 kt? The best glide speed gives a TAS of 100 kt in both cases.
optionA: 9.8 NM
optionC: 8.4 NM
optionD: 9.3 NM
explanationTotal:
This question may look like it requires a few calculations, but actually it is really simple. The aircraft does not know what the wind component is, it will glide exactly the same, wind or no wind. The only difference will be where it ends up. Therefore the rate of descent in the glide will be exactly the same, and the time to descend will be exactly the same. So if that is the case, then it is only the Groundspeed which influences how far the aircraft can glide, and it is a directly proportional relationship.

The "long" way of calculating this is to calculate the time to descend by dividing the distance by the groundspeed/60 for the still air case. Still air means groundspeed = TAS = 100 kt.

Time (minutes) = 9.8 / (100/60) = 5.88 minutes.

Then multiply that time by the new groundspeed, 100 kt TAS - 15 kt Headwind Component = 85 kt Groundspeed.

Distance (NM) = 5.88 x (85/60) = 8.33 NM, closest answer 8.4 NM

Or, even more simply, now you know that there is a directly proportional relationship, next time just do distance x (new GS/old GS):

9.8 x (85/100) = 8.33 NM

title: Static directional stability is mainly provided by:
optionA: the elevator.
optionB: wing anhedral.
optionC: the fin.
optionD: wing dihedral.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The rotation of an aircraft about its normal, or vertical, axis is a yaw. If this movement is the result of an undesirable disturbance, then the ability of the airplane to return to its original heading without the assistance of any control-surface movement is a measure of its directional static stability. It is a measure of the aircraft’s ability to realign itself with the relative airflow.

Sideslip is the displacement angle of the airplane’s longitudinal axis in azimuth from the relative airflow. It is positive when the relative airflow is to the right of the longitudinal axis and negative when the relative airflow is left of the longitudinal axis.

An airplane has directional static stability if, when in a sideslip with the airflow coming from the right initially the nose tends to yaw right. An airplane that has excessive directional static stability compared to its lateral static stability is more prone to spiral dive.

The fin (vertical stabilizer) is the major source of directional stability for the airplane. As shown in figure 1, in a sideslip the fin will experience a change in angle of attack. The change in lift (side force) on the fin creates a yawing moment about the center of gravity which tends to yaw the airplane into the relative airflow.
The magnitude of the fin contribution to static directional stability depends on both the change in fin lift and the fin moment arm.

title:
The VA speed of a light aircraft is 147 kt. Determine the aircraft's limit load factor, given the following information from the airspeed indicator.

Green arc: 73 kt - 165 kt
White arc: 55 kt - 85 kt
VNE: 185 kt
optionA: The limit load factor cannot be calculated from this information
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
IMPORTANT NOTE: This is created from quite old feedback, and the figures are not known/confirmed. We have had to choose some figures to fit an answer, which are unlikely to be the same in the exam! Please send us any further exam feedback you can remember if you get this in your exam, so we can make it more exact, thank you!
