An aircraft has a limit load factor, that signifies the maximum G-force that the aircraft can handle, before potential damage may occur to the airframe.

VA is an aircraft's manoeuvring speed, and exists where the aircraft can handle exactly its limit load factor before stalling. If the aircraft is flying slower than VA, then it will stall before reaching the limit load factor, and if it flying above VA, the limit load factor can be exceeded before stalling.

We can therefore use VA in calculations, as it is the stall speed of an aircraft at it's limit load factor. Stall speed calculations are based on the lift force required by the wings, and that varies with weight and load factor (G-force). The higher the weight, or the higher the load factor, the higher airspeed that is required (more airflow makes the wing able to produce greater forces before stalling).

For load factor, the formula is:

  • New VS = VS(1G) x sqrt(load factor)
Where VS(1G) is the stall speed at 1G (straight level flight)

So for the manoeuvring speed

  • VA = VS(1G) x sqrt(limit load factor)

We can then re-arrange this to find the limit load factor if we know the VA and the VS(1G) (which we do in this question). The VS(1G) is given in the question as the bottom of the green arc.

  • (VA / VS(1G))2 = limit load factor
  • Limit load factor = (147/73)2 = 4.06 G

title:
Which of these statements about the strength of wing tip vortices are correct or incorrect

I. Assuming no flow separation, the strength of wing tip vortices is not affected by angle of attack.
II. The strength of wing tip vortices is not affected by aspect ratio.
optionA: I is correct, II is incorrect.
optionB: I is correct, II is correct.
optionC: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
optionD: I is incorrect, II is correct.
explanationTotal:
Wing tip vortices are a byproduct of lift. They are caused by the pressure differential between the top and bottom of the wing, which causes an updraft of high pressure air around the tip of the wing. This updraft turn into a downdraft behind the wing, creating a vortex. The higher the pressure difference between the top and bottom of the wing, the stronger the vortices.

This question is specifically asking for:

  • Angle of attack: The strength of the vortices (and therefore also induced drag) is proportional to the angle of attack. Therefore; the strength of the vortices increase as the angle of attack increases. And also; the strength of the vortices decrease as the angle of attack decreases. Therefore statement 1 is incorrect!
  • Aspect ratio: The strength of the vortices is inversely proportional with the aspect ratio. Meaning that the strength of the wing tip vortices increase as the aspect ratio decreases. And vice versa: the strength decreases as the aspect ratio increases. Therefore statement 2 is incorrect!

title: What happens when the trailing edge flaps are lowered to the fully extended position?
optionA: The wing CP moves forward and the L/D ratio increases.
optionB: The stalling angle reduces and the L/D ratio increases.
optionC: The stalling angle increases and the L/D ratio reduces.
optionD: The wing CP moves aft and the L/D ratio decreases.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Trailing edge devices, also known as flaps, are designed to increase the wing camber which will increase the downwash and the circulation relative the aerofoil. It will also move the CP rearwards creating a nose-down moment.

The lift/drag ratio can be changed very effectively by means of the flaps. Small flap deflections increases the margin to stall with only a moderate increase in drag, whiles greater flap setting is set to increase the drag

With any flap extension, the increase in drag is always greater than the increase in lift. The greater the extension the worse L/D ratio you get. This full deflection of flaps is therefore normally used from final approach down to landing to allow a rather steep descent while maintaining low speed.

title: Increasing dynamic pressure will have the following effect on the total drag of an aeroplane:
optionA: total drag increases across the whole speed range.
optionB: at speeds above the minimum drag speed, total drag increases.
optionC: at speeds below the minimum drag speed, total drag increases.
optionD: total drag decreases across the whole speed range.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The total drag is the resulting factor if you add induced drag and parasite drag together. It acts in the direction of the relative wind. Lift is perpendicular to the relative wind.

Parasite drag is caused if an airfoil is moving through the air. It is the result of form drag and skin friction drag. Form drag arises from the shape of the object. The more streamlined the object, the less form drag is present. Shape and size are most important in the amount of form drag resulting. Form drag increases with increasing velocity, making it very important for high speed aircraft. Skin friction drag is caused by the friction of the fluid (in case of aircraft this fluid is the atmosphere) against the skin of the object moving through it. It is directly related to the surface area in contact with the fluid. Skin friction increases with the square of the velocity.

Induced drag is caused when an object redirects the airflow. A wing produces lift by creating a pressure difference. This pressure difference is caused by the shape of the airfoil, causing the airflow on top to accelerate, creating a low pressure on top of the wing and high pressure below the wing. This pressure difference naturally wants to restore towards a uniform pressure, which creates vortices around the wingtip. These vortices are deflected downwards, this phenomenon is also called downwash. The induced drag decreases with airspeed (with a rate of 1/V²) and increases with angle of attack and increasing weight.

In the image we can see that the two vectors (induced and parasite drag) create a resulting vector, the total drag. Where the induced and parasite drag vectors collide, we have the minimum drag speed (VMD); the speed where the total drag is the lowest.

This leads us to understand that during an acceleration from a total stand still, the total drag first decreases up until the minimum drag speed and then starts increasing again.
If we add flaps to the clean configuration, CL will increase, but so will the drag. This degrades glide performance. The rate of descent will increase and glide range will decrease.

title: Artificial feel systems are installed in aircraft with (1) _____, which prevent reaching the (2) _____.
optionA: (1) Reversable controls, (2) Stall
optionB: (1) Reversable controls, (2) aerodynamic limit
optionC: (1) Fully Powered controls, (2) Stall
optionD: (1) Fully Powered controls, (2) aerodynamic limit
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
With a fully powered flying control the pilot is unaware of the aerodynamic force on the controls, so it is necessary to incorporate “artificial feel" to prevent the aircraft from being overstressed.

As shown schematically in the diagram, a device sensitive to dynamic pressure (1⁄2 ρ V2). Pitot pressure is fed to one side of a chamber and static pressure to the other, which moves a diaphragm under the influence of changing dynamic pressure with airspeed. This causes “regulated” hydraulic pressure to provide a resistance or ‘feel’ on the pilot’s input controls proportional to IAS2, just as in a manual control. In addition, stick force should increase as stick displacement increases.

An advantage of artificial feel is that it can be configured to provide envelope protection, which prevents the pilot over stressing the aircraft. The Boeing777 fly- by-wire system employs envelope protection. This feature of the artificial-feel system provides increasingly greater force when the aircraft is pushed to its limits.

title: A forward CG...
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Increase VMCA
optionB: Increases VS
optionC: Increase V2
optionD: Decreases V<sub>S</sub>
explanationTotal:
The stick force required to maintain level flight with a forward CG is considerably more than it is with a neutral CG, because the aeroplane is nose-heavy; effectively it is the same as a mass increase. Because forward CG means that we have a longer arm between CG and CP where lift acts. However, the distance between CG and the tail is not increased by the same proportion. Therefore tailplane needs to produce more downforce to balance. This force adds up to weight.

The stall speed is defined by:

VS = √((2∗W) / (ρ∗S∗CLMAX))

The stall speed is directly proportional to the square root of the aircraft weight. A forward CG will give an ‘apparent increase in weight’, thus the stall speed will increase.

title: A vintage single-engine aeroplane with a left-hand rotating propeller (ANTI-CLOCKWISE from the pilot's perspective) performs a go-around, applying full thrust and a large pitch up. Which of the following effects would occur?
optionA: Gyroscopic precession causing a yaw to the right.
optionB: Asymmetric blade effect causing a yaw to the right.
optionC: Slipstream effect causing a yaw to the left.
optionD: Torque effect causing a yaw to the right.
explanationTotal:
Note: This is a very similar question to Q813311, but only one answer is correct instead of multiple statements. Please be aware that we do not yet have the full feedback for either of these questions, and you should know the effects well to ensure you get the correct answer in the exam (questions appear to differ slightly betwen authorities. Please send any further feedback about this question to us via the comments, the feedback area on the dashboard, or by email to info@atplquestions.com, thank you!

Propellers generate 4 main secondary effects on an aircraft:

  • Torque effect
  • Gyroscopic precession
  • Slipstream
  • Asymmetric blade effect
For this question, we can go through each statement and check whether the effect is correct or not for the scenario.

TORQUE EFFECT - Option D
The anti-clockwise rotating propeller gains more anti-clockwise rotational momentum when the pilot adds thrust (higher RPM), so the aircraft experiences the opposite (clockwise) rotation, and is rolled to the right (this can be corrected using left aileron). Option D is therefore incorrect.

GYROSCOPIC PRECESSION - Option A
The propeller is a mass, spinning at high speed, and therefore acts as a gyroscope. That means that any rotation of the aircraft in pitch or yaw will gain a different force from the propeller due to gyroscopic precession. The force from the propeller will be rotated by 90º in the direction of rotation. In this case, the pitch-up will cause an forward force on the bottom of the propeller disc, which is rotated by precession to a forwards force on the right of the propeller disc. This creates a yaw to the left. Option A is therefore incorrect.

SLIPSTREAM EFFECT - Option C
The spinning of the propeller affects the air that it pushes backwards, and imparts a spiral onto that air, in this case spiralling anti-clockwise around the aircraft, hitting the tail fin on the right hand side, causing a tail-left, nose-right moment. The slipstream increases with an increase in thrust, causing a yaw to the right. Option C is therefore incorrect.

ASYMMETRIC BLADE EFFECT - Option B
The asymmetric blade effect comes from the aircraft being at an angle of attack to the air, so the air does not flow perpendicular to the propeller disc. The down-going propeller blades always produce more thrust than the up-going blades, so the thrust line of this anti-clockwise propeller is to the left of centre. An increase in thrust will therefore cause a larger force through this location (left of centre), which yaws the aircraft to the right. Option B is correct.

title: The units of wing loading (I) W / S and (II) dynamic pressure q are:
optionA: (I) N / m2, (II) N / m2.
optionB: (I) N / m3, (II) kg / m2.
optionC: (I) N / m, (II) kg.
optionD: (I) kg / m, (II) N / m2.
explanationTotal:
WING LOADING

The total aircraft weight supported per unit area of the wing; measured in Newtons per square metre (N/m2).

Wing Loading can be described by the following formula:

Wing Loading = Aircraft Weight / wing area

PRESSURE

The force per unit area acting on a surface; This is measured in Newtons per square metre (N/m2).

Dynamic Pressure: Occurs when moving air is brought to rest on the surface of a body (i.e. when relative movement exists between the surface and the airflow)

Dynamic Pressure is expressed as:

Q = 0.5 x ρ x V2

title: An aeroplane is executing a missed approach after entering a microburst on the approach. The aeroplane may be very close to the stall due to the:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Initial reduction in the rate of descent.
optionB: Increasing airspeed.
optionC: Increasing tailwind.
optionD: Energy gain.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
A microburst during takeoff or landing is particularly dangerous if the pilot has reduced power and lowered the nose in response to the headwind. This leaves the aircraft in a low-power, nose-low configuration, making it difficult to recover when the wind switches to a tailwind. Due to the potential of a 30-90 knot loss in headwind, the airplane could stall or land short of the runway.

Flying through a Microburst

1. Imagine you're approaching a microburst at 80 knots. As you enter the vortex ring, you experience turbulence and a rapid increase in IAS as you pick up a headwind. You start to climb as your performance increases.
2. As you enter the strongest part of the horizontal shaft, your airspeed peaks at 100 knots, an increase of 20 knots. You're still climbing as you enter the downdraft.
3. Inside the downdraft, your headwind starts to switch to a tailwind. You're caught in the downdraft, sinking quickly toward the ground. Your airspeed begins to decrease.
4. As you exit the downdraft, your tailwind increases rapidly. The shear drops your airspeed to 60 knots, which is 20 knots below your original speed. You're at a high angle-of-attack, and still descending.
5. You encounter more turbulence as you enter the final vortex. If you haven't already hit the ground, you may begin to climb again as you exit the vortex.

title: During an emergency descent, the pilot of an aeroplane inadvertently exceeds V<sub>NE</sub> . In these conditions, what type of hazard should the pilot be aware of?
optionA: Structural damage if unexpected turbulence is encountered.
optionB: Mach tuck.
optionC: Uncontrollable yaw moment towards the failed engine in case of an engine failure.
optionD: Structural damage.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
Each type of aircraft has its own specific flight envelope, within which it can be safely operated in accordance with the EASA Certification Specifications. This is represented on a velocity against load factor, or V-n diagram.

The high-speed limit is the never exceed speed (VNE) and is a design reference point for the aircraft beyond which structural damage or failure may occur. Conversely, the stall governs the low speed limit and this limit increases with increasing load factor.

VNE will be shown by a radial red line on the airspeed indicator at the high speed end of the yellow arc.

title: The negative manoeuvring limit load factor for a transport aeroplane in the clean configuration at V<sub>D</sub> may not be less than:
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
For large aircraft a limit load factor of -1 must be considered up to VC. From VC to VD the negative load factor varies linearly from -1 to 0.

  • As you can see in the graph, at VD the minimum load factor is 0.

title: The intensity or strength of the wing-tip vortices is...
optionA: smallest in the clean configuration.
optionB: inversely proportional to the speed of the aeroplane.
optionC: greater the faster the aeroplane flies.
optionD: directly proportional to the wingspan of the aeroplane.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

Whenever a wing produces lift, concentrated vortices form at the wing tips. The vortices are strongest at the wing tips and become progressively weaker toward the centerline of the aircraft.
The vortices induce downwash to the airflow behind the wing, causing the lift vector to tilt rearward. The horizontal component of lift opposes the forward flight of the aircraft and is known as induced drag.
The larger the vortex, the greater the induced downwash, and the greater the induced drag.

The induced drag can be defined by:

CDI= CL2 / π * AR
Where,
CDI– Induced Drag Coefficient
CL2 – Lift Coefficient squared
AR – Aspect Ratio

Decreasing the speed of an aircraft maintaining straight and level flight will increase its angle of attack and therefore increase the CL. It is true that CL is inversely proportional to speed.
From the formula we can deduct that Induced drag is directly proportional to CL squared. Therefore, Induced drag is inversely proportional to speed.

title: Which of the following actions can be taken to reduce the chance of a tail strike during take-off?
optionA: Increase the rotation rate.
optionB: Add a small margin onto the rotation speed.
optionC: Reduce the take-of speed.
optionD: Maintain a steep take-off angle after rotation.
explanationTotal:
The two major threats for tail strikes to occur are during the landing flare/touchdown and during rotation on take-off. As many large jet transport aircraft are extended in length for larger passenger numbers, the long tail leaves very little tail margin during rotation, and factors such as crosswinds, gusty head/tailwinds and different weight and CG locations can lead to the potential for reduced tail clearance or tail strike.

To mitigate this risk, pilots can choose to rotate at a slightly higher speed, if, for instance, they feel a gust just before rotation that might reduce their airspeed significantly. A higher airspeed means more airflow over the wings and therefore the aircraft will lift-off at a lower pitch angle, and the tail will therefore be further clear of the ground before reaching the tail strike angle.

The pilot could also reduce the rate of rotation to further reduce the chance of tail strikes occurring (as might be done in an engine failure after V1 scenario), but this is not usually recommended in normal operation, and remember that both of these measures are not accounted for in the take-off performance calculation, so be careful not to run out of runway.

title: A light-weight fillet is installed at the wing root of an airplane, combining the wing shape into the fuselage with a gentle curve. This fillet's primary aerodynamic effect is to:
optionA: reduce interference drag.
optionB: reduce induced drag.
optionC: increase lift.
optionD: reduce wave drag.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
When considering a complete aircraft, parasite drag will be greater than the sum of the individual parts. Additional drag results from boundary layer interference at the junction of different parts as wing/fuselage, wing/engine nacelle, etc.

Fairings and filleting will be used to minimise interference drag. They soften the transition between two components of the aircraft.

title: An aeroplane has a stall speed of 100 kt at a mass of 1000 kg. If the mass is increased to 2000 kg, the new value of the stall speed will be:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
explanationTotal: The stall speed at increased weight is VS NEW = VS OLD × √(New W ÷ Old W) = 100 kts × √(2 000 kg ÷ 1 000 kg) = 100 × √2 = 141.42 kts ~ 141 kts.

title:
Refer to figure.
Choose the correct statement:
optionA: Aerofoil 4 corresponds to line 3.
optionB: Aerofoil 2 corresponds to line 4.
optionC: Aerofoil 1 corresponds to line 1.
optionD: Aerofoil 3 corresponds to line 2.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
A completely symmetrical airfoil will intersect the vertical axis of the graph at the origin (0).
A positively cambered airfoil will generate more lift at the same speed (and therefore has a higher CL) than a symmetrical airfoil and therefore intersects the vertical axis above the origin (and generates 0 lift at a negative angle of attack).
A negatively cambered airfoil will generate less lift at the same speed (which translates into a lower CL at a certain speed) and therefore intersects the vertical axis below the origin.

An increased camber generates a higher value of CL at the same Angle of Attack.

Therefore, we have the following combinations:

  • Aerofoil 1 corresponds to line 3.
  • Aerofoil 2 corresponds to line 4.
  • Aerofoil 3 corresponds to line 1.
  • Aerofoil 4 corresponds to line 2.

title: During a short period oscillation altitude (1)_____, but during a phugoid it (2)_____.
optionA: (1) varies; (2) remains constant.
optionB: (1) remains constant; (2) remains constant.
optionC: (1) remains constant; (2) varies.
optionD: (1) varies; (2) varies.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
In trimmed level flight a disturbance in pitch usually oscillates about its original state causing fluctuations in the values of speed, height and indicated load factor. When an airplane has positive longitudinal dynamic stability the amplitude of the oscillations gradually diminish as the aircraft returns to its original trimmed flight state.

The oscillatory motion of the airplane in pitch after a disturbance to its trimmed state can be shown as two separate oscillations. One is a short-period oscillation and the other is a long-period oscillation called a phugoid.

  • The phugoid is usually poorly damped; it has large variations of speed and height and has an almost uniform load factor (n). It has a constant energy motion in which the potential energy and the kinetic energy are continuously interchanging.
  • The motion that causes short-period oscillation is normally heavily damped. It not only involves small changes of speed and height but also large changes of load factor. The speed and height of the airplane remain approximately constant.

title: During flight, IAS is adjusted. In order to generate a constant lift force, this action must be met with an adjustment in:
optionA: The load factor.
optionB: The bank angle.
optionC: The angle of attack.
optionD: The flap setting.
explanationTotal:
Lift Formula:
L = 1/2 p V2 S CL

The lift remains constant if the variables in the above equation also remain the same. If one of the variables is changed, another variable must be changed in the opposite direction in order to balance it out and keep a constant lift.

  • In the equation "V" equals IAS. Consequently, if V is changed (i.e reduced), another variable must be changed in the opposite direction (i.e. increased) to balance it out. The only variable we can increase is the Coefficient of Lift (CL) => by increasing the angle of attack.

title: An aeroplane in straight and level flight at 100 kt is subjected to a sudden disturbance in speed. Assuming the angle of attack remains constant initially and the load factor reaches a value of 1.44:
optionA: the speed will have decreased by 20 kt.
optionB: the speed will have decreased by 10 kt.
optionC: the speed will have increased by 10 kt.
optionD: the speed will have increased by 20 kt.
explanationTotal:
Load Factor is the ratio of the weight of an aircraft to the load imposed by lift: Load Factor = Lift / Weight
Lift is propotional to V2: L= CL × ½ rho × V2 × S

Therefore, n is proportional to V2 . An increase in "n" to 1.44 means lift has increased by a factor of 1.44. Consequently, "V" must change by a factor of √1.44 = 1.2.

The speed has increased to: 100 x 1.2 = 120 kt (= an increase of 20 kt)

title: As altitude increases, the stall speed (IAS):
optionA: remains constant until the tropopause but at higher altitudes increases.
optionB: initially remains constant but at higher altitudes increases.
optionC: remains constant regardless of altitude.
optionD: initially remains constant but at higher altitudes decreases.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The stall speed is defined by:

VS=√((2∗W)/(ρ∗S∗CLMAX))

At the stalling angle CLMAX and S are constant, and the indicated airspeed is given by the dynamic pressure 1/2 ρV2. Therefore, for the same airplane mass and configuration in straight and level flight, if the slight difference between EAS and IAS caused by compressibility is ignored, an airplane will stall at the same IAS at all altitudes.

If, however, compressibility is not ignored then the stalling IAS value slowly increases with increased altitude, but the change only becomes significant at very high altitudes.
At a constant EAS, Mach number will increase as altitude increases.

Figure 1 shows the variation of stalling speed with altitude at constant load factor (n). Such a curve is called the stalling boundary for the given load factor, in which altitude is plotted against equivalent airspeed.

At this load factor (1g), the aircraft cannot fly at speeds to the left of this boundary. Over the lower range of altitude, stall speed does not vary with altitude. This is because at these low altitudes, the Mach number at VS is too low for compressibility effects to be present. Eventually (approximately 30000 ft), Mach number at VS has increased with altitude to such an extent that these effects are important, and the rise in stalling speed with altitude is apparent.

As altitude increases, stall speed is initially constant then increases, due to compressibility.

title: A pilot gets an engine failure and forgets to feather the propeller, what will happen?
optionA: Climb gradient will increase
optionB: Decrease the rate of descent and decrease the climb gradient
optionC: Climb gradient will decrease
optionD: Increase the rate of descent and Climb gradient will increase
explanationTotal:
Feathering the propeller is usually required for multi-engine aircraft, as windmilling (unfeathered) propellers create higher drag than non-rotating propellers. When the propeller is feathered, only parasite drag of the propeller exists which is much smaller than induces and parasite drag + energy absorbed to rotate the engine if the propeller is windmilling.
  • As stated above, compared to a feathered propeller, an unfeathered propeller produces greater drag, which reduces the climb gradient.

title: The following is a correct design gust value factor applied in certification under EASA CS-25:
optionA: 25 ft/sec at V<sub>B</sub>.
optionB: 50 ft/sec at V<sub>C</sub>.
optionC: 55 ft/sec at V<sub>C</sub>.
optionD: 66 ft/sec at V<sub>D</sub>.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
It is a design requiremnt of CS25 (old JAR25) that an airframe structure must be strong enough to withstand gusts both positive and negative that would cause a change of angle of attack so increasing load factor at three specified design speeds.

  • Speed VB (max gust intensity speed): +/- 66 ft/sec
  • Speed VC (design cruise speed): +/- 50 ft/sec
  • Speed VD (design dive speed): +/- 25 ft/sec.

VB is quite a low airspeed so the aircraft would be flying at high alpha and it would take some time for an aircraft to slow from VC (the design cruising speed) to VB if it flew into turbulence. Therefore, another design strength requirement is for the aircraft also to be strong enough to withstand a vertical gust of 50 ft/ sec at VC.

title: In comparison to a conventional aerofoil section, typical shape characteristics of a supercritical aerofoil section are:
optionA: a larger nose radius, flatter lower surface and negative as well as positive camber.
optionB: a larger nose radius, flatter upper surface and negative as well as positive camber.
optionC: a sharper pointed nose, negative camber and a flatter upper surface.
optionD: a sharper pointed nose, flatter lower surface and positive camber at the rear of the aerofoil section.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
A supercritical wing is one that has been designed with specific streamwise segments to delay the onset of the adverse effects of the shockwave, i.e. wave drag and its severity and decreased lateral stability, when the airplane is flying in the transonic speed range or just above MCRIT. It increases the cruise Mach number, the range, and the endurance of the airplane. The main features of a supercritical wing are:

The upper surface is flattened but the lower surface is reflex cambered towards the trailing edge. Thus, the airflow over the upper surface is not accelerated as much as conventional airfoils, which delays the formation of the shockwave to a higher speed.

Compared with a conventional airfoil section it has a larger leading-edge radius, a flatter upper surface and both positive and negative camber and enables a relatively thick wing to be used for approximately the same cruise Mach number.

The curved lower surface increases the lift generated by the aft end of the airfoil and replaces some of the lift lost from the flat upper surface. Because of the rear-loaded lift generation it is often called an aft-loaded wing.

The leading edge of the supercritical wing has a greater radius than traditional airfoils that suffer from excessive wave drag and the loss of longitudinal stability (tuck under). By ensuring that its profile is carefully designed any expansion waves will be reflected from the subsonic boundary back to the shockwave, thereby weakening its intensity.

title: Which statement is true regarding a reduction in induced drag?
optionA: Decrease upwash and decrease induced angle of attack.
optionB: Decrease downwash and increase induced angle of attack.
optionC: Increase upwash and decrease induced angle of attack.
optionD: Increase downwash and decrease the induced angle of attack.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
INDUCED DRAG
Whenever a wing produces lift, concentrated vortices form at the wing tips. The vortices are strongest at the wing tipsand become progressively weaker toward the centre-line of the aircraft.

It is the production of lift itself which reduces the magnitude of the lift force being generated. To replace the lift lost by the increased downwash, the aircraft must be flown at a higher angle of attack. This increases drag. This extra drag is called induced drag.

The stronger the vortices, the greater the induced drag.

Downwash angle: Decreasing the effect of the vortices will decrease downwash angle.

Induced angle of attack: The decrease in downwash will cause the induced angle of attack to decrease leading to a decrease in induced drag.

Note: An increase/decrease in downwash is preceded by a respective increase/decrease in upwash.

title: The CG of an aeroplane is in a fixed position forward of the neutral point. Which of these statements about the stick force stability is correct?
optionA: Stick force stability is not affected by trim.
optionB: Maintaining a steady speed below the trim speed requires a push force.
optionC: Aeroplane nose down trim increases the stick force stability.
optionD: An increase of 10 kt from the trimmed position at high speed has less effect on the stick force than an increase of 10 kt from the trimmed position at low speed.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

Figure 1 indicates the variation of stick force with airspeed and illustrates the effect of tab setting on stick force.

You can see from the graph, that dependent on EAS (Equivalent Air Speed) and trim tab setting, the stick force to hold a 1 kt change in airspeed from the trimmed speed DECREASES as the trimmed speed increases. There are a few factors at play that cause this, including the change to elevator displacement, effect of the trim tab, dynamic pressure change, etc.

This means that holding the aircraft 10 kts from its trimmed speed requires less stick force at a high trimmed speed than if it were trimmed at low speed.

Stick position stability exists when the aircraft responds "correctly" to a push or pull. For example, pushing the stick causes a pitch down and an airspeed increase (this is binary, an aircraft either has stick position stability or it doesn't).

Stick force stability is a further continuation of that, and in an aircraft has stick force stability, a greater push force produces a greater increase in airspeed. The level of stick force stability is proportional to the slope of the curve of stick force vs. speed (annex above). The steeper the curve, the higher the stick force stability (a 1 kt change to airspeed requires more force).

title:
A “stall warning” can be produced synthetically by electronic means, by a system that may malfunction. What are the natural stall warnings confirming an approaching stall?

(1) Aerodynamic buffeting
(2) Increased aileron effectiveness
(3) Inability to arrest a rate of descent
(4) Stick pusher activation
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: 1 and 3.
optionB: 1 and 4.
optionC: 2 and 4.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
STALL

A stall is an aerodynamic condition which occurs when smooth airflow over the airplane’s wings is disrupted, resulting in loss of lift. Specifically, a stall occurs when the AOA—the angle between the chord line of the wing and the relative wind—exceeds the wing’s critical AOA. It is possible to exceed the critical AOA at any airspeed, at any attitude, and at any power setting.

  • Impending Stall—an impending stall occurs when the AOA causes a stall warning, but has not yet reached the critical AOA. Indications of an impending stall can include buffeting, stick shaker, or aural warning.

  • Full Stall—a full stall occurs when the critical AOA is exceeded. Indications of a full stall are typically that an uncommanded nose-down pitch cannot be readily arrested, and this may be accompanied by an uncommanded rolling motion. The flying controls will feel unresponsive or “mushy”. For airplanes equipped with stick pushers, its activation is also a full stall indication.

Note: The question asks for natural stall warnings.

title: The subsonic speed range:
optionA: implies both subsonic and supersonic speeds exist in the flow around the aeroplane.
optionB: ends at M = 1.
optionC: ends at a Mach number just above M = 1.
optionD: ends at M<sub>CRIT</sub>.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

Figure 1 shows the flow speed ranges with their approximate Mach number values, where: MFS (Free Stream Mach number) is the Mach number of the flow sufficiently remote from an aircraft to be unaffected by it. (In effect, the Mach number of the aircraft through the air). This is the Mach number shown on the aircraft Mach meter.

ML (Local Mach number) is the actual speed of the flow over a surface. When an aircraft flies at a certain MFS the flow over it is accelerated in some places and slowed down in others.

The subsonic speed region is located between zero and MCRIT. In this region, ML is only subsonic.

title: Which statement about negative tail stall is correct?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: When negative tail stall occurs, the aeroplane will show an uncontrollable pitch-up moment.
optionB: When negative tail stall occurs, the aeroplane will show an uncontrollable pitch-down moment.
optionC: Negative tail stall is a stall of the fin with a negative sideslip angle (nose pointing to the right of the relative airflow).
optionD: Negative tail stall is a stall of the tailplane when the aerodynamic force is in upward direction.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The tailplane is a smaller lifting surface found aft of the main wing, on the tail of many fixed wing aircraft. Like the main wing, a tailplane is designed to operate with smooth airflow along its surface. When the airflow separates from the tailplane, this is referred to as a tailplane stall. The tailplane is designed to produce a downward force (resulting in "negative" lift). When the tailplane stalls, this downforce will no longer exist, resulting in a sudden uncommanded nose down pitching moment.

title: Induced drag is created by the:
optionA: separation of the boundary layer over the wing.
optionB: spanwise flow pattern resulting in the tip vortices.
optionC: propeller wash blowing across the wing.
optionD: interference of the air stream between wing and fuselage.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The total drag is the resulting factor if you add induced drag and parasite drag together. It acts in the direction of the relative wind. Lift is perpendicular to the relative wind.

Parasite drag is caused if an airfoil is moving through the air. It is the result of form drag and skin friction drag. Form drag arises from the shape of the object. The more streamlined the object, the less form drag is present. Shape and size are most important in the amount of form drag resulting. Form drag increases with increasing velocity, making it very important for high speed aircraft. Skin friction drag is caused by the friction of the fluid (in case of aircraft this fluid is the atmosphere) against the skin of the object moving through it. It is directly related to the surface area in contact with the fluid. Skin friction increases with the square of the velocity.

Induced drag is caused when an object redirects the airflow. A wing produces lift by creating a pressure difference. This pressure difference is caused by the shape of the airfoil, causing the airflow on top to accelerate, creating a low pressure on top of the wing and high pressure below the wing. This pressure difference naturally wants to restore towards a uniform pressure, which creates vortices around the wingtip. These vortices are deflected downwards, this phenomenon is also called downwash. The induced drag decreases with airspeed (with a rate of 1/V²) and increases with angle of attack and increasing weight.

In the image we can see that the two vectors (induced and parasite drag) create a resulting vector, the total drag. Where the induced and parasite drag vectors collide, we have the minimum drag speed (VMD); the speed where the total drag is the lowest.

This leads us to understand that during an acceleration from a total stand still, the total drag first decreases up until the minimum drag speed and then starts increasing again.

explanationTotal:

Divide the new speed by the old speed

CL is inversely proportional to V2 therefore:

1 / 1.712 = 0.34

title: Lift is generated when:
optionA: a certain mass of air is accelerated in its flow direction.
optionB: a symmetrical aerofoil is placed in a high velocity air stream at zero angle of attack.
optionC: the flow direction of a certain mass of air is changed.
optionD: a certain mass of air is retarded.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Lift is created by the flow of air over an airfoil. Air moving over the curved upper surface of the wing will travel faster and thus produce less pressure than the slower air moving across the flatter underside of the wing. This difference in pressure creates lift which is a force of flight that is caused by the imbalance of high and low pressures.

title: Above M<sub>CRIT</sub> in the transonic speed regime, at a constant angle of attack, C<sub>L</sub> will...
optionA: remain constant throughout this regime.
optionB: always increase as the Mach number increases.
optionC: always decrease as the Mach number increases.
optionD: vary depending on the Mach number.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
At low subsonic speeds, the lift coefficient CL is assumed to be constant at a given angle of attack. With increasing Mach number, however, it will vary as shown in figure 1.
At high subsonic speed CL increases. This is the result of the changing pattern of streamlines.
At low speeds, the streamlines begin to diverge well ahead of the airfoil. At high subsonic speeds they do not begin to deflect until closer to the leading edge, causing greater acceleration and pressure drop around the leading edge. This phenomenon causes the stall speed to increase at high altitudes.

title:
Consider the following statements about VMCG:

1. VMCG is determined with the gear down.
2. VMCG is determined with the flaps in the landing position.
3. VMCG is determined by using rudder and nosewheel steering.
4. During VMCG determination the aeroplane may not deviate from the straight-line path by more than 30 ft.

The combination that regroups all of the correct statements is:
explanationTotal:
VMCG, the minimum control speed on the ground, is the calibrated airspeed during the takeoff run, at which, when the critical engine is suddenly made inoperative, it is possible to maintain control of the airplane using the rudder control alone (without the use of nose wheel steering) to enable the take-off to be safely continued using normal piloting skill.
The rudder control forces may not exceed 150 pounds (68.1 kg) and, until the airplane becomes airborne, the lateral control may only be used to the extent of keeping the wings level. In the determination of VMCG, assuming that the path of the airplane accelerating with all engines operating is along the center of the runway, its path from the point at which the critical engine is made inoperative to the point at which recovery to a direction parallel to the center line is completed may not deviate more than 30 ft (9.144 m) laterally from the center line at any point. As with VMCA, this must be established with:
  • maximum available take-off power or thrust on the engines.
  • the airplane trimmed for take-off.
  • the most unfavorable CG position.
  • maximum sea level take-off weight.
Because the aircraft rotates around the CG, the position of the CG directly affects the length of the rudder arm and, thus, the power of the rudder and fin to maintain directional stability and control. The ‘worst case’ is with the CG at the aft limit. If the requirements can be met in this configuration, the ability to maintain directional control will be enhanced at any other CG location. A more forward CG decreases VMCG.

title: When an aircraft with stabiliser trim is trimmed "nose up", what is the position of the stabiliser and elevator compared to the horizontal axis of the aircraft? Consider the stabiliser movement to be that occurring at its trailing edge.The stabiliser will be...
optionA: parallel to the horizontal axis, with the elevator in line with it.
optionB: defected up with the elevator down.
optionC: deflected up with the elevator in line with it.
optionD: deflected down with the elevator in line with it.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Instead of using elevators to change the angle of attack and camber of the tail plane, the whole of the tail plane lifting surface is constructed in such a manner that it has a mutable incidence or changeable angle of attack. This is known as the trimmable horizontal stabilizer (THS).

One of the advantages of a trimmable stabilizer is that the elevator will be in line with the stabilizer when the aircraft is in trim. This reduces drag, and maintains full control authority, i.e., full elevator deflection can still be applied in either direction, if required.

As seen in the attached figure, an airplane trimmed for nose up would require the stabilizer to be deflected down. When the variable incidence tail plane is trimmed, it has no elevator deflection.

The question asks to consider the reference as the TRAILING EDGE. In that case we can conclude that for an airplane trimmed for nose up it would require the stabilizer’s trailing edge to be deflected up.

Match the various wing types with their corresponding slopes:
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The lift coefficient of an airfoil is affected by various factors, including its thickness. The lift coefficient (CL) is a dimensionless coefficient that represents the lift generated by an airfoil at a given angle of attack.

An increase in thickness will result in an increase of CL and CLmax. Thicker airfoils tend to produce more lift compared to thinner airfoils at the same angle of attack. This is because a thicker airfoil typically has a larger camber, which allows it to generate more lift.

Based on the above, we can conclude that thicker airfoils will have steeper slope:

  • C - 3

title: Which of the following statements is correct for an aircraft flying at a speed above V<sub>A</sub>?
optionA: The aircraft is unable to stall.
optionB: During a turn, the airframe may collapse.
optionC: A high speed warning will be activated.
optionD: A full elevator deflection could cause a structural damage.
explanationTotal:
In aviation, VA, maneuvering speed of an aircraft is an airspeed limitation selected by the designer of the aircraft. At speeds close to, and faster than, the maneuvering speed, full deflection of any flight control surface should not be attempted because of the risk of damage to the aircraft structure - at such speeds, it is possible to exceed the limit load factor (structural damage) without stalling first.

Further info on VA:

CS 25.335 Design airspeeds
(c) Design manoeuvring speed, VA. For VA, the following apply:

(1) VA may not be less than VS1 n where –
(i) n is the limit positive manoeuvring load factor at VC; and

(ii) VS1 is the stalling speed with wing-flaps retracted.

(2) VA and VS must be evaluated at the design weight and altitude under consideration.

(3) VA need not be more than VC or the speed at which the positive CNMAX curve intersects the positive manoeuvre load factor line, whichever is less.

title:
Which of these statements about the strength of wing tip vortices are correct or incorrect?

I. Assuming no flow separation, the strength of wing tip vortices increases as the angle of attack decreases.
II. The strength of wing tip vortices decreases as the aspect ratio decreases.
optionA: I is incorrect, II is correct.
optionB: I is correct, II is incorrect.
optionC: I is correct, II is correct.
optionD: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
explanationTotal:
Wing tip vortices increase if we increase induced drag.This can be caused by for example increased speed, density or lift coefficient.

If we decrease Angle of Attack, lift will be decreased, also decreasing the strength of wing tip vortices.
This shows that statement I is incorrect.

Another factor increasing wing tip vortices is the aspect ratio (λ) of the wing.This is the ratio of the wing span to its mean chord.

The aspect ratio of the wing is equal to the square od the wingspan divided by the wing surface area.
Therefore a short but wide wing has a low aspect ratio but a long, narrow wing has a high aspect ratio.
With a lower aspect ratio, the induced drag is higher, thus increasing wing tip vortices.

With a high aspect ratio, the induced drag is lower, reducing wing tip vortices.
We can therefore state that the relationship between wing tip vortices and aspect ratio is inversely proportional.
Statement number II is incorrect, as the correct answer would be “The strength of wing tip vortices increases as the aspect ratio decreases.

title:
Which of the following are reasons for trimming an aircraft in pitch?

1. Changes of speed
2. Changes of power
3. Varying CG positions
4. Lateral displacement of CG
optionA: 1 and 2 only
optionB: 1, 2, and 3
optionC: 2, 3, and 4
optionD: 1 and 4 only
explanationTotal:
An airplane is trimmed when it will maintain its attitude and speed without the pilot having to apply any load to the cockpit controls. If it is necessary for a control surface to be deflected to maintain balance of the aircraft, the pilot will need to apply a force to the cockpit control to hold the surface in its deflected position. This force may be reduced to zero by operation of the trim controls.

The aircraft may need to be trimmed in pitch as a result of:

  • changes of speed.
  • changes of power.
  • varying CG positions.
  • changes of configuration.
Trimming in yaw will be needed:
  • on a multi-engine aircraft if there is asymmetric power.
  • as a result of changes in propeller torque.
Trimming in roll is less likely to be needed but could be required if the configuration is asymmetric, or if there is a lateral displacement of the CG.

title: One advantage of a supercritical wing aerofoil over a conventional one is:
optionA: that there is no need for spoilers.
optionB: improved Dutch roll damping at cruise altitude.
optionC: it allows a wing of increased relative thickness to be used for approximately the same cruise Mach number.
optionD: a lower value of M<sub>CRIT</sub> at the same relative thickness.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
A supercritical wing is one that has been designed with specific streamwise segments to delay the onset of the adverse effects of the shockwave, i.e. wave drag and its severity and decreased lateral stability, when the airplane is flying in the transonic speed range or just above MCRIT. It increases the cruise Mach number, the range, and the endurance of the airplane. The main features of a supercritical wing are:

The upper surface is flattened but the lower surface is reflex cambered towards the trailing edge. Thus, the airflow over the upper surface is not accelerated as much as conventional airfoils, which delays the formation of the shockwave to a higher speed.

Compared with a conventional airfoil section it has a larger leading-edge radius, a flatter upper surface and both positive and negative camber and enables a relatively thick wing to be used for approximately the same cruise Mach number.

The curved lower surface increases the lift generated by the aft end of the airfoil and replaces some of the lift lost from the flat upper surface. Because of the rear-loaded lift generation it is often called an aft-loaded wing.

The leading edge of the supercritical wing has a greater radius than traditional airfoils that suffer from excessive wave drag and the loss of longitudinal stability (tuck under). By ensuring that its profile is carefully designed any expansion waves will be reflected from the subsonic boundary back to the shockwave, thereby weakening its intensity.

title: An increase in wing loading will:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: increase C<sub>LMAX</sub>.
optionB: increase the stall speed.
optionC: increase sensitivity to turbulence.
optionD: decrease the minimum glide angle.
explanationTotal:
Wing loading is directly proportional to weight, and as we have seen above, an increase in weight, increases stall speed since the wings need to fly at a higher angle of attack to generate enough lift for a given airspeed.

  • Wing Loading = Weight / Wing Area

Any airplane, within the limits of its structure and the strength of the pilot, can be stalled at any airspeed.

VS = √(2W ÷ p S CLMAX)

The equation above well defines the factors affecting the stall speed, in summary; aircraft weight, air density, maximum lift coefficient, and the load factor.

AIRCRAFT WEIGHT.

Stall speed is proportional with the aircraft weight. Stall speed increases, as the weight increases; and decreases as the weight decreases.

AIR DENSITY.

Aircraft stall speeds are usually given in terms of CAS or IAS as an aircraft limitations. However, as seen in the equation above, it is actually a true airspeed which is inversely proportional with the density. Therefore, although it is constant in terms of CAS/IAS, it increases with the altitude because of the density variation.

MAXIMUM LIFT COEFFICIENT.

Maximum lift coefficient may be varied by high lift devices such as flaps and slats. Higher maximum lift coefficients will result in slower stall speeds. Lowest maximum lift coefficient is obtained when flaps are retracted (airplane in clean configuration), thus highest stall speed occurs in clean configuration.

LOAD FACTOR.

Stall speed is proportional with the load factor. It increases as the load factor increases. If VSS is the stall speed of an aircraft in steady level flight, then stall speed during maneuvers will be:
VSN =√n VSS

Or during a turn maneuver:
VSN = VSS ÷ √ cos a

title:
For the given data, calculate the value of the manoeuvring speed VA for a large transport jet aircraft with a maximum takeoff mass of 344 tonnes.

VS0 = 140 kt
VS1 = 208 kt
optionB: 294 kt
optionD: 328 kt
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Maneuvering Speed (VA) is the speed at which an airplane will stall before exceeding its maximum load limit. To calculate the VA we multiply the stall speed (VS1) by the square root of the limiting load factor (n).

VA = VS1 x √n

The question considers a large transport jet aircraft, which has a limiting load factor of 2.5 g. By replacing this value with the value of VS1 in the above formula:

VA = 208 x √2.5

VA = 328 kt

title: The result of propeller tip speeds exceeding sonic speeds is:
optionA: Propeller efficiency is unchanged.
optionB: Increased propeller efficiency.
optionC: Decreased noise.
optionD: Increased noise.
explanationTotal: If the tips of the propeller blades are moving near the speed of sound a shock wave can form which will increase noise. There will be a loss of lift and an increase in drag associated with the shock wave, resulting in a reduced propeller efficiency.

title: Which of these statements concerning flight in turbulence is correct?
optionA: The load factor in turbulence may fluctuate above and below 1 and can even become negative.
optionB: In severe turbulence, speed should be reduced to approximately 1.2 V<sub>S</sub>.
optionC: When encountering turbulence during flight, the speed should be adjusted to the design speed for maximum gust intensity V<sub>B</sub>.
optionD: Above V<sub>B</sub> the aeroplane can never be overstressed by a gust.
explanationTotal:
Unlike a gust that has only a short duration, turbulence is a disturbance in the atmosphere caused by frictional influences of the air resulting in the same changes of air velocity but over a longer period.

Turbulence is categorized as slight, moderate, or severe. Throughout its duration an airplane may experience sudden changes from positive ‘g’ to negative ‘g’ and the ‘bumps’ or jolts will vary in severity and will cause stress to the airframe.

title:
Calculate the new value of drag force, given: An airplane flying at 100 kt at an angle (alpha 1) of 4º, has a drag coefficient (CD1) of 0.028. Total drag force is 900 N.
The airplane decelerates to 55 kt, flying at an angle of attack (alpha 2) of 15º, when drag coefficient (CD2) is 0.148.
explanationTotal:
(1) Find the speed change ration:

V2 / V1 = Speed change ratio
55 / 100 = 0.55
=> Speed decreased from 100 kt to 55 kt: Speed decrease by x 0.55.

(2) Find the Coefficient of Drag change ration:

CD2 / CD1 = Drag Coefficient change ratio
0.148 / 0.028 = 5.29

=> CD1 has increased by x 5.29.

(3) Drag Equation: D = 1/2 p V2 S CD

The question does not mention any other changes apart from speed and CD, therefore we can assume that wing area (S) and density (p) remain unchanged. 1/2 is also a constant.

D = V2 CD
New Drag ratio of increase = (0.55)2 x 5.29 = 1.6
  • New Drag (D2) is 1.6 times greater than previous Drag (D1): 900 x 1.6 = 1440 N
Closest option: 1420 N

title:
Which of these statements about the strength of wing tip vortices are correct or incorrect?

I. Assuming no flow separation, the strength of wing tip vortices decreases as the angle of attack increases.
II. The strength of wing tip vortices is not affected by aspect ratio.
optionA: I is correct, II is correct.
optionB: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
optionC: I is correct, II is incorrect.
optionD: I is incorrect, II is correct.
explanationTotal:
Wing tip vortices are a by-product of lift. They are caused by the pressure differential between the top and bottom of the wing, which causes an updraft of high pressure air around the tip of the wing. This updraft turn into a downdraft behind the wing, creating a vortex. The higher the pressure difference between the top and bottom of the wing, the stronger the vortices.

This question is specifically asking for:

  • Angle of attack: The strength of the vortices (and therefore also induced drag) is proportional to the angle of attack. Therefore; the strength of the vortices increase as the angle of attack increases. And also; the strength of the vortices decrease as the angle of attack decreases. Therefore statement 1 is incorrect!

  • Aspect ratio: The strength of the vortices is inversely proportional with the aspect ratio. Meaning that the strength of the wing tip vortices increase as the aspect ratio decreases. And vice versa: the strength decreases as the aspect ratio increases. Therefore statement 2 is incorrect!

title:
Given the following information,calculate the climb angle...

Thrust: 200 000 N
Mass: 50 000 kg
Drag: 50 000 N
(assume g = 10 m/s2)
explanationTotal:
The formula for climb angle is as follows:

Sin(γ) = (T – D) / W
γ = climb angle (gamma)

However, all the units of measurement must be the same for this calculation, and we have been given mass, not weight.

Weight = mass x acceleration due to gravity (g)
W = m x g
W = 50 000 x 10 = 500 000 N

Now that is sorted, we can input them into the climb angle formula.

Sin(γ) = (200 000 – 50 000) / 500 000
Sin(γ) = 0.3
γ = sin-1(0.3) = 17.458°
Correct answer 17.5°
