Refer to figure.
The critical angle of attack is the angle of attack producing the maximum lift coefficient.If the aircraft increases angle of attack above this value, it will enter a stall.This value can be increased with the use of slats.

Slats delay the separation of the boundary layer, by adding kinetic energy into it.

A clean wing has a lower value of CLMAX, causing the Angle of Attack for a clean wing to be lower than for a wing with slats extended.A wing with flaps extended has the lowest value of CLMAX.

title:
Refer to figure.
Which statement is correct regarding the pitching moment coefficient CM versus angle of attack diagram?
optionA: Line 4 shows an aeroplane with reducing static longitudinal stability at very high angles of attack.
optionB: Line 3 shows an aeroplane with greater static longitudinal stability at low angles of attack than that shown in line 4.
optionC: Line 3 shows an aeroplane with increasing static longitudinal stability at high angles of attack.
optionD: Line 1 shows an aeroplane with increasing static longitudinal instability at very high angles of attack.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Static longitudinal stability depends upon the relationship of angle of attack and pitching moment (CM).

A variation of CG position can cause large changes in the static longitudinal stability. In the conventional airplane configuration, the large changes in stability with CG variation are primarily due to the large changes in the wing contribution. If the incidence of all surfaces remains fixed, the effect of CG position on static longitudinal stability is typified by the chart in figure 1:

As the CG is gradually moved aft, the airplane static stability decreases, then becomes neutral then unstable. The CG position which produces zero slope and neutral static stability is referred to as the “neutral point”. The neutral point defines the most aft CG position without static instability.

Positive static stability is indicated by the curve with negative slope. Moving the CG forward, will increase static longitudinal stability and this is represented by a (steeper) negative slope.

Neutral static stability would be the result if the curve had zero slope. If neutral stability existed, the airplane could be disturbed to some higher or lower lift coefficient without change in pitching moment coefficient.

An airplane which demonstrates a positive slope of the CM versus CL curve would be unstable.

title: A flight instructor is teaching a student of a multi-engine piston airplane the practice of an engine failure. What is the most favourable configuration during the first engine failure exercise?
optionA: An airplane mass of 4 400 lbs so that the resultant yaw from the engine failure is minimized.
optionB: An airplane mass of 3 800 lbs so that the resultant yaw from the engine failure is minimized.
optionC: An airplane mass of 4 400 lbs so that the rudder has greater effectiveness.
optionD: An airplane mass of 3 800 lbs so that the rudder has greater effectiveness.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
When an engine fails on a multi-engine aircraft there will be a decrease in thrust and an increase in drag on the side with the failed engine:

  • airspeed will decay.
  • the nose will drop and.
  • most significantly, there will be an immediate yawing moment towards the failed engine.
The forces and moments acting on an aircraft following failure of the left engine are shown in figure 1. The aircraft has a yawing moment towards the dead engine. The pilot has applied rudder to stop the yaw. The vital action when an engine fails is to stop the yaw.
Any increase in weight ultimately reduces the aircraft’s overall performance, but in a banked condition, it induces greater side slip, making the rudder more effective for a given airspeed.
Thus, the greater the weight, the greater the induced side slip and the greater the rudder effectiveness. This benefit is insignificant compared to the penalties associated with any additional weight.

title: An aircraft accelerates towards the transonic speed region. What happens to C<sub>LMAX</sub> and stall speed?
optionA: C<sub>LMAX</sub> will decrease and the stalling speed will increase.
optionB: C<sub>LMAX</sub> will decrease and the stalling speed will decrease.
optionC: C<sub>LMAX</sub> will increase and the stalling speed will decrease.
optionD: C<sub>LMAX</sub> will increase and the stalling speed will increase.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
LOW SPEED VS. HIGH SPEED STREAMLINE (figure 1)
As an aircraft flies faster, the streamline pattern around the wing changes. Faster than about four tenths the speed of sound (M 0.4) these changes start to become significant. This phenomenon is known as compressibility.

At low speed, the streamline pattern is affected far ahead of the wing and the air has a certain distance in which to upwash. As speed increases, the wing gets closer to its leading pressure wave, and the streamline pattern is affected a shorter distance ahead so must approach the wing at a steeper angle.

EFFECT OF MACH NUMBER ON CLMAX (figure2)

This change in the streamline pattern accentuates the adverse pressure gradient near the leading edge and flow separation occurs at a reduced angle of attack. Above M0.4 CLMAX decreases.

The stall speed is defined by:

VS=√((2 x W)/(ρ x S x CLMAX))

At the stalling angle CLMAX and S are constant, and the indicated airspeed is given by the dynamic pressure 1/2ρV2. Therefore, for the same airplane mass and configuration in straight and level flight, if the slight difference between EAS and IAS caused by compressibility is ignored, an airplane will stall at the same IAS at all altitudes.

If, however, compressibility is not ignored then the stalling IAS value slowly increases with increased altitude, but the change only becomes significant at very high altitudes.

STALLING SPEED vs. ALTITUDE (figure 3)

At a constant EAS, Mach number increases as altitude increases.

The variation of stalling speed with altitude at constant load factor (n). Such a curve is called the stalling boundary for the given load factor, in which altitude is plotted against equivalent airspeed.

At this load factor (1g), the aircraft cannot fly at speeds to the left of this boundary. Over the lower range of altitude, stall speed does not vary with altitude. This is because at these low altitudes, the Mach number at VS is too low for compressibility effects to be present.

Eventually (approximately 30000 ft), Mach number at VS has increased with altitude to such an extent that these effects are important, and the rise in stalling speed with altitude is apparent.

As altitude increases, stall speed is initially constant then increases, due to compressibility.

title: Assuming no flow separation and no compressibility effects the location of the centre of pressure of a symmetrical aerofoil section:
optionA: moves forward when the angle of attack decreases.
optionB: is independent of angle of attack.
optionC: is at approximately 50% of the chord irrespective of angle of attack.
optionD: moves backward when the angle of attack decreases.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The centre of pressure is the theoretical point through which we assume all the lift to act.

For cambered aerofoils, we know that the centre of pressure moves forwards as angle of attack increases, and moved backwards as the angle of attack decreases.
For symmetrical aerofoils, the centre of pressure is at a fixed and does not move with changes in angle of attack.

title: If an aeroplane performs a steady co-ordinated horizontal turn at a TAS of 200 kt and a turn radius of 2000 m, the load factor (n) will be approximately:
explanationTotal:
Load factor in a Turn: n = 1 / cos ø (always higher than 1)
Turn Radius = TAS2 ÷ (g x tan ɸ)
Where, ø = bank angle

Let's start by determining the bank angle:

tan ɸ = (200 kt x 0.5144 m/s/kt)2 ÷ (9.81 m/s2 x 2 000 m)
tan ɸ = (102.88 m/s)2 ÷ 19 629 m/s2
tan ɸ = 0.53946
ɸ = tan-1(0.53946) = 28.35º

Now that we know the bank angle, we can determine the load factor:
n = 1 / cos (28.35º)
n = 1.136

title: The contribution of swept-back wings to static directional stability:
optionA: is negative.
optionB: is positive.
optionC: decreases as the sweepback increases.
optionD: is nil.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

The rotation of an aircraft about its normal, or vertical, axis is a yaw. If this movement is the result of an undesirable disturbance, then the ability of the airplane to return to its original heading without the assistance of any control-surface movement is a measure of its directional static stability. It is a measure of the aircraft’s ability to realign itself with the relative airflow.

An airplane has directional static stability if, when in a sideslip with the airflow coming from the right initially the nose tends to yaw right.
The drag of a swept wing is less than that of an unswept wing. The advantage of this type of wing at high speeds is gained at the expense of its poor performance at low speed. The drag experienced with a swept wing is the component of the relative airflow at 90◦ to the line joining the aerodynamic center of the wing, which if the wing has parallel leading and trailing edges will be the normal to the leading edge of the wing.

In figure 1 the normal component of the relative airflow is greater on the port wing than the normal component on the starboard wing.

The drag on the leading wing, the port wing, in figure 1 is of greater magnitude than that of the trailing starboard wing because of its decreased effective sweep angle. It is therefore a stabilizing influence. Positive sweepback has a stabilizing effect on directional stability because the CP is further aft, and the stalling angle is increased. The significance and magnitude of this effect on directional static stability is directly proportional to the angle of sweepback.

title: Consider a constant speed propeller. Which of the following forces or moments tend to decrease the pitch angle of the propeller blades (move them towards fine pitch)?
optionA: The blade pitch angle cannot be changed by any forces or moments.
optionB: The centrifugal twisting (turning) moment.
optionC: The aerodynamic twisting moment.
optionD: The thrust bending force.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
This is not too often mentioned in the ATPL exams, and can get quite complicated very quickly if you dig too far, but we will keep it simple.

Naturally, there are a few different forces acting on a propeller blade:

  • Torque force - acting against the direction of rotation (against the engine torque)
  • Thrust force - acting in the direction of flight (perpendicular to the plane of rotation). (this can be a negative force when windmilling or providing reverse thrust).
There are also a few different moments (bending/twisting forces on the propeller blades)
  • Torque bending force - causing the tips to lag behind the blade hubs due to the torque force.
  • Thrust bending force - bending the edges of the propeller disc in the direction of flight due to the thrust force.
  • Centrifugal twisting moment (CTM) - twisting the propeller to the "fine" direction due to the centrifugal pulling force on the blade (trying to flatten the blade onto the plane of rotation).
  • Aerodynamic twisting moment (ATM) - twisting the propeller to the "coarse" direction (unless windmilling) due to the location of the centre of pressure ahead of the point of rotation.

The torque bending moment and thrust bending force are not usually asked in the exams, but the CTM and ATMs are a larger part of the syllabus (though still very rare).

Between the CTM and the ATM, they work in opposite directions and CTM is stronger (except when the propeller is windmilling when they work in the same direction (both to "fine")).

In this case, the CTM (Centrifugal Twisting Moment) is the correct answer as it tries to decrease the blade pitch angle (make the blade more fine).

title: Induced drag is the result of:
optionA: boundary layer separation on the aft portion of the wing.
optionB: downwash generated by tip vortices.
optionC: propeller slipstream over the wing.
optionD: aerodynamic interaction between aeroplane parts.
explanationTotal:
To explain, lets compare all the answers and see why each is correct or incorrect.

1) Boundary layer separation on the aft portion of the wing. – Incorrect
Boudary layer separation is a normal phenomenon that occurs during flight. This has nothing to do with induced drag.

2) Propeller slipstream over the wing. – Incorrect
The slipstream from a propeller will cause a couple effects, such as yaw, and torque, but it will have no effect on induced drag.

3) Aerodynamic interaction between aeroplane parts. – Incorrect
The drag because of aerodynamic interaction between aeroplane parts is known as interfrerence drag, and has nothing to do with induced drag.

4) Downwash generated by tip vortices. – Correct
Firstly, one could simply deduce the correct answer through cancelling out the incorrect answer.

Secondly, we know that induced drag is a secondary effect of lift. Wing tip vortices are a result of the upwash and downwash effect near the tip of the wings, which produces a rearward component of lift knows as induced drag. Therefore this is the correct answer.

title: An aerospace company needs to attach a testing device to the outside of their aircraft. How can the least amount of drag be achieved?
optionA: Aerodynamic fairing.
optionB: Lightening the testing device's weight.
optionC: Placing it on the leading edge of the wing to prevent shock wave formation.
optionD: Placing it underneath the tail section.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Fairing - A secondary structure added to any part to reduce its drag.

Drag is the force which resists the forward motion of the aircraft. Drag acts parallel to and in the same direction as the relative airflow (in the opposite direction to the flight path).

Total Drag is sub-divided into two main types:

INDUCED DRAG - the result of lift generation.
PARASITE DRAG - independent of lift generation.

Parasite drag is further sub-divided into:

- Skin Friction Drag
- Form (Pressure) Drag
- Interference Drag

INTERFERENCE DRAG
The total drag experienced by an aircraft is greater than the sum of the drag caused by individual parts of the aeroplane.

This additional drag is caused by flow interference at the junction of the various parts of the aeroplane such as the wing/fuselage and wing/nacelle junctions.

Interference drag is caused by the mixing of the boundary layers at the junction of adjoining aerofoil surfaces

Adding fairings at the junctions, e.g. trailing-edge wing roots and blended winglets, can reduce its effect.

title:
Refer to figure.
The attached graph represents a wing in two configurations: the black line in clean configuration and the blue line with a lift augmentation device extended. What type of profile does the basic wing have and what type of lift augmentation device is used?
optionA: Symmetrical wing with flaps extended.
optionB: Symmetrical wing with leading edge device extended.
optionC: Asymmetrical wing with flaps extended.
optionD: Asymmetrical wing with leading edge device extended.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
SYMMETRICAL AEROFOIL

The distribution of pressure is important in aerodynamics, since it determines:
- The amount of lift generated
- Any pitching moments
- The form drag of an aerofoil section

The lift and drag forces of a wing cross-section are dependent on the pressure distribution around the wing. The pressure distribution around an aerofoil is the resultant of the angle of the aerofoil chordline to the oncoming airflow, the angle of attack.

If a symmetrical aerofoil section is in a steady airstream at zero degrees Angle of Attack, a stagnation point forms on the leading edge.

The airflow velocity above and below the aerofoil increases by an equal amount and the static pressures reduce by an equal amount. Consequently, no pressure differential exists, and no net lift is created.

CLMAX AUGMENTATION

One of the main factors which determine the CLMAX of an aerofoil section is the camber. Increasing the camber of an aerofoil section increases the CL at a given angle of attack and increases CLMAX.

TRAILING EDGE FLAPS

Aircraft are fitted with high lift devices to reduce the take-off and landing distances and when low airspeeds are beneficial. This permits operation at greater weights from given runway lengths and enables greater payloads to be carried.

Returning the flaps to their neutral position when no longer required, returns the wing to its former aerodynamic characteristics.

The increase in lift comes mainly from the variation in effective camber that occurs when the flaps are deflected.This alters the lift curve and also produces a higher maximum coefficient of lift.

In some instances, the trailing edge flaps may also increase the wing's surface area. Extending the trailing edgeflaps alters the pressure distribution around the wing.

LEADING EDGE DEVICES

Leading edge devices increase maximum value of CL and critical angle of attack. But for the constant angle of attack CL is the same or less. (Curve extends to the right and up).

title: The point of minimum static pressure on a positively cambered aerofoil flying at a low subsonic speeds at a positive angle of attack is…
optionA: on the upper surface, where the speed is highest.
optionB: on the upper surface, where the speed is lowest.
optionC: on the lower surface, where the dynamic pressure is lowest.
optionD: on the lower surface, where the dynamic pressure is highest.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Bernoulli’s theorem when applied to the airflow past an aerofoil at less than Mach 0.4 shows that the total pressure is equal to the sum of the dynamic pressure (the pressure caused by the movement of the air) and the static pressure (the pressure of the air not associated with its movement) and can be expressed as the following equation:

Total Pressure (pt) = Dynamic Pressure (q) + Static Pressure (ps)

The total pressure is constant along a streamline flow. Therefore, if dynamic pressure increases then static pressure decreases and vice versa.

The flow over the top of the section accelerates rapidly around the nose and over the leading portion of the surface - inducing a substantial decrease in static pressure in those areas.

The pressure reduces continuously from the stagnation value through the free stream value to a position on the top surface where a peak negative value is reached. From there onwards the flow continuously slows down again and the pressure increases back to the free stream value in the region of the trailing edge.

title: Which of the following are most effective at reducing induced drag?
optionA: Higher Aspect Ratio and removal of winglets.
optionB: Lower Aspect Ratio and flaps.
optionC: Lower Aspect Ratio and wing fences.
optionD: Higher Aspect Ratio and winglets.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
INDUCED DRAG. is an inevitable consequence of lift and is produced by the passage of an aerofoil (e.g. wing or tailplane) through the air. It is created by the vortices at the tip of an aircraft's wing. The magnitude of induced drag depends on the amount of lift being generated by the wing and on the shape and size of the wing.

Induced drag can be reduced by:

  • Using a high aspect ratio wing planform => Wings with high aspect ratio have lower induced drag than wings with low aspect ratio for the same wing area. So wings with a long span and a short chord have lower induced drag than wings with a short span and a long chord.
  • Using a tapered wing planform with wing twist and/or spanwise camber variation, or incorporation of wing end plates, tip tanks, winglets or various wing tip shapes.
Note: Winglets are small vertical aerofoils which form part of the wing tip; they reduce tip vortex intensity, thus reduce induced drag - this is their only function.

title: Following a disturbance, an aeroplane oscillates about the lateral axis at constant amplitude. The aeroplane is:
optionA: statically stable – dynamically neutral.
optionB: statically stable – dynamically unstable.
optionC: statically unstable – dynamically stable.
optionD: statically unstable – dynamically neutral.
explanationTotal:
Dynamic stability is said to be present if, after a disturbance upon the aircraft that disrupted its intended flight path, the aircraft damps these oscillations.

Static stability is said to be present if the aircraft, after a disturbance upon the aircraft that disrupted its intended flight path,
it counteracts this effect. For example, if a gust causes the airplane to have a nose up momentum, the airplane automatically reduces the angle of attack and goes nose down.

The aircraft oscillates around the lateral axis at a constant amplitude, meaning that it pitches up and down the same amount every time.
The aircraft is statically stable, as the nose comes down after it has been up for a while.
The aircraft is dynamically neutral, as it is not damping the oscillations, but not making them worse either.

title: Consider an aircraft flying in unaccelerated level flight in the speed stable region. What would be the result on the drag following a sudden increase in aircraft speed with no change in thrust available?
optionA: The total drag increases.
optionB: The total drag decreases.
optionC: The induced drag increases.
optionD: The parasite drag Increases until It equals the Induced drag.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
During flight, an aircraft will experience two types of drag:

- Parasite Drag (proportional to IAS2, increases with increasing “Parasite Area”: flaps, undercarriage or speedbrakes)

- Induced Drag (inversely proportional to IAS2, increases with increasing weight).

The sum of Parasite Drag and Induced Drag is the Total Drag.

The Total Drag will be minimum at the IAS where Parasite Drag = Induced Drag. This speed is called Minimum Drag Speed (VMD). Flying at a slower or faster speed than VMD will generate more drag.

Flying at a slower speed than VMD (back side), the aircraft will be in the unstable speed region. Any gain of speed will result in an decrease in drag and further speed increase. The sudden change to a headwind (or a decrease in tailwind) can cause a gain of airspeed.

Flying at a faster speed than VMD (front side), the aircraft will be in the stable speed region. Any increase of speed will result in an increase in drag. This increase in drag will cause the speed to decrease again (unless the thrust has changed). Therefore, a sudden increase in headwind (or a decrease in tailwind) can cause a momentary increase of airspeed, which eventually settles back to the original airspeed.

title:
Considering subsonic incompressible airflow through a Venturi, which statement is correct?

I. The dynamic pressure in the throat is the same as in the undisturbed airflow.
II. The total pressure in the throat is higher than in the undisturbed airflow.
optionA: I is correct, II is incorrect.
optionB: I is incorrect, II is correct.
optionC: I is correct, II is correct.
optionD: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
To understand the venturi effect, we must first introduce two conditions: The conservation of mass (Continuity Equation) and the Conservation of Energy (Bernoulli’s Theorem).

Conservation of Mass (Continuity Equation)

The mass of air entering the pipe, in each unit of time, equals the mass of air leaving the pipe, in the same unit of time. The mass flow through the pipe must remain constant.

The mass air flow 'm' is the product of the density, the area and the velocity:

m = ρ * A * V

Continuity equation:

m1 = m2 = m3 = ρ1 * A1 * V1 = ρ2 * A2 * V2 = ρ3 * A3 * V3 = constant

The continuity equation explains the relationship between velocity and cross-sectional area: The speed is inversely proportional to the cross-sectional area.

Conservation of Energy (Bernoulli’s Theorem)

The total energy of an airstream comes in two forms: potential energy (static pressure) and kinetic energy (dynamic pressure).
The total pressure of the airstream is the sum of the static pressure and the dynamic pressure and must remain constant, according to the law of conservation of energy.
Thus, an increase in one form of pressure, must result in a decrease in the other.

Dynamic pressure (q) is expressed by:

q = 1 / 2 * ρ * V2

Assuming the total pressure to be constant, the static pressure and the dynamic pressure vary inversely: If one increases the other decreases and vice-versa.

In Conclusion:

With a decrease in section area (from station 1 to station 2), flow speed increases, increasing dynamic pressure. Statement 1 is therefore incorrect.
The total pressure of the airstream is the sum of the static pressure and the dynamic pressure and must remain constant, according to the law of conservation of energy. Statement 2 is therefore incorrect.

title: What is correct about aircraft stall?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: A stalled condition can occur at any airspeed, attitude or altitude.
optionB: When aircraft attitude exceeds about 15°.
optionC: Only when speed is below 2V<sub>S</sub>.
optionD: Never below critical alpha.
explanationTotal:
Stalls can happen at any airspeed, but only one angle of attack, the critical angle of attack.

Because a stall is dependent only upon angle of attack, an airplane can stall at any airspeed, attitude, configuration, power setting, or weight. However, an airplane's stall speed is affected by many factors, including weight, center-of-gravity location, load factor, and power setting. Since a stall is dependent upon the wing's angle of attack, and the elevator is the primary control for angle of attack, it could be said that the elevator stalls or "unstalls" the airplane.

title: An aircraft with swept wings is better suited to cruising at higher Mach numbers due to reduced speed in the direction (1) _____ to the wing span, compared to the (2) _____. This speed varies with the (3) _____ of the sweep angle.
optionA: (1) perpendicular; (2) free stream flow; (3) sine
optionB: (1) perpendicular; (2) free stream flow; (3) cosine
optionC: (1) parallel; (2) free stream flow; (3) sine
optionD: (1) parallel; (2) free stream flow; (3) tangent
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Note: We do not have complete feedback for this question, and have created the best possible question from what we have. This exact question has not yet been verified, and there may be important wording differences that we do not know about. This may well be a drop-down question in the UK CAA. Please put any further exam feedback in the comments or email it to info@atplquestions.com, thank you.

One of the most used methods of increasing MCRIT is to sweep the wing back.

As shown in figure 1, it can be considered that compared to a straight wing, a swept-back wing of the same airfoil section has a smaller effective thickness chord ratio. Sweeping the wing back increases the effective aerodynamic chord for the same dimensional thickness, so the wing acts the same as a thinner wing.

The other way to consider this relationship, is that the velocity of air flowing perpendicular to the wing span will be lower than the velocity of the free stream air. In this way, the MCRIT of an aeroplane with a swept wing will be higher and the transonic drag rise will be delayed.

The air velocity perpendicular to the wing span corresponds to the free stream velocity multiplied by the cosine of the sweepback angle.

The sweepback angle is the angle between a straight wing (the aeroplane's lateral axis) and the 25% chord line of the swept wing. The red line on the diagram above is the free stream flow, and the blue line is the component of that which flows perpendicular to the wing span.

title: A single engine aeroplane flying at 3 000 ft suffers an engine failure. With a lift to drag ratio of 16:1, a TAS of 90 kt and a 10 kt headwind, how far can the aircraft glide?
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Glide angle (and glide range) assumes no thrust, and therefore is determined directly by the lift over drag (L/D) ratio. The best L/D ratio occurs at VMD, the speed for minimum drag.

Glide angle = CD / CL

GLIDING DISTANCE
Wind speed is an important practical influence on gliding distance over the surface.

  • With a tailwind, the glide distance achieved will be increased as a result of the increased groundspeed.
  • Whereas with a headwind, it will be reduced because of the consequently slower groundspeed.

There are two ways to calculate this question.

METHOD 1

With a L/D ratio of 16:1, this means the glide ratio is 16:1 (horizontal distance : vertical distance). Therefore, at a TAS of 90 kt, the vertical speed is 90/16 = 5.625 kt

5.625 kt = 5.625nm per hour. Multiply by 6080 to get feet per hour, then divide by 60 to get feet per minute, giving 570 fpm rate of descent.

The aircraft will take a time of 3 000 / 570 = 5.263 minutes to descend 3 000 ft. 5.263 minutes (divide by 60) is 0.0877 hours. Multiply this by the groundspeed this time (90 - 10 = 80 kt) to get the distance travelled over the ground in that time.

0.0877 x 80 = 7.016 nm, closest answer 7.02 nm

METHOD 2

3 000 ft to descend at glide ratio of 16:1 means that the horizontal distance travelled is 3 000 x 16 = 48 000 ft. Divide this by 6080 ft/nm to get a still air ground distance of 7.895 nm. With a headwind, this distance is reduced slightly (already the correct answer can likely be guessed).

The reduction is the headwind as a proportion of the TAS, so the distance is reduced by 10kt/90kt = 0.111..., or in other words, the new distance is 88.9% of the still air distance. 7.89 x 0.889 = 7.018 nm, closest answer 7.02 nm.

This second way is faster if you are comfortable with visualising it like this, especially as the correct answer can be identified quite early on with gross error checking, but if in doubt, use METHOD 1.

title: In a steady, level, co-ordinated turn the load factor n and the stall speed V<sub>S</sub> will be:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: n smaller than 1, V<sub>S</sub> lower than in straight and level flight.
optionB: n greater than 1, V<sub>S</sub> higher than in straight and level flight.
optionC: n greater than 1, V<sub>S</sub> lower than in straight and level flight.
optionD: n smaller than 1, V<sub>S</sub> higher than in straight and level flight.
explanationTotal:
The Load Factor is the ratio of lift compared to weight of the aircraft denoted by "n":

Load Factor (n) = Lift (L) / Weight (W)

The value of load factor in steady wings level horizontal flight is exactly 1(g). Load factors greater or less than one (or even negative) are the result of maneuvers or wind gusts. The value is less than one in a steady wings level climb, because a vertical component of thrust is balancing some of the weight. So the value of wing lift required is less.

  • Turning. In a horizontal coordinated turn, load factor is always higher than 1 (n = 1 / cos Ø).
  • Climb and Descent. In a climb or descent, n < 1 (L = W cos y)

Stall speed is proportional with the load factor. It increases as the load factor increases. If VSS is the stall speed of an aircraft in steady level flight, then stall speed during maneuvers will be:
VSN = √n VSS

Or during a turn maneuver:
VSN = VSS ÷ √ cos a

title: The pilot of an aeroplane with a single engine and right-turning propeller (clockwise from the pilot’s viewpoint) decides to go around. The pilot raises the nose too much as the power increases and stalls the aircraft. Most probably, the aircraft will…
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: enter an incipient spin to the left due to roll and yaw caused by the propeller.
optionB: enter an incipient spin to the right due to roll and yaw caused by the propeller.
optionC: maintain lateral stability because symmetrical thrust will NOT cause control problems.
optionD: enter a spiral descent to the right due to the effects of the propeller.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
A stall must occur before a spin can take place. A spin occurs when one wing stalls more than the other. The wing that is more stalled will drop and the nose of the aircraft will yaw in the direction of the lower wing.

An accidental power-on stall, during take-off or go-around, when a pilot’s attention is diverted, could easily turn into a spin.

Power-on stall and recovery in a single-engine propeller aircraft has additional complications. At the high nose attitude and low airspeed associated with a power-on stall, there will be considerable “turning effects” from the propeller. E.g. for an aircraft with a clockwise rotating propeller the effect is to roll and yaw to the left.

title: While flying under icing conditions, the largest ice build-up will occur, principally, on:
optionA: the frontal areas of the aeroplane.
optionB: the pitot and static probes only.
optionC: the upper and lower rudder surfaces.
optionD: the upper and lower surfaces on the rear of the wing.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The formation of ice and frost on the airframe will:
- modify the profile of the aerofoil.
- increase the roughness of the aircraft surface.
- increase the weight of the aircraft.

Ice will normally form on and around the leading edges of wings and tailplane and can result in severe distortion of the leading edge profile. This will give a large increase in drag and a substantial decrease in CLMAX. The skin friction drag will increase and the boundary layer will have an earlier separation, giving a reduced critical angle of attack, thereby a higher stall speed.

Ice builds up on an aircraft when the super-cooled water droplets (SCWDs) hit the cold airframe and freeze onto the surface. This will happen most in particular sections of the aircraft, such as the leading edges of the wings, the nose, propeller spinners, the tail leading edges, and any protrusions such as the windshield, pitot tubes, AoA vanes, etc.

This effect is much more pronounced when the items are sharp, instead of curved. Take a wing for example: when it is a very curved wing, useful for low speed flight, it will have a leading edge with a large radius, and the pressure waves that propagate from the front of the wing during flight are effectively giving the air advanced warming that the wing is coming, so it can move out of the way. This means that the SCWDs also move out of the way, so do not hit the wing as much.

This means that sharp wings (with a smaller radius - used for higher speed flight) give less of a "warning" to the air, and the SCWDs will not move out of the way as much, thereby causing more ice accretion. This is the same for sharp protrusions such as the AoA vanes and pitot tubes.

title: Which of the following combinations will result in a larger decrease in C<sub>DI</sub>?
optionA: Low wing Take-off
optionB: Low wing Landing
optionC: High wing Take-off
optionD: High wing Landing
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
Ground effect occurs because the surface alters the airflow pattern around the wings. Primarily, the surface restricts the formation of the wingtip vortices.

This results in a reduction in the amount of induced downwash behind the wing and increases the wing’s effective angle of attack.

It also alters the pressure distribution around the wing and the amount of lift developed. This occurs because the change in effective angle of attack increases the wing’s coefficient of lift (CL) and thus its lifting capability at any given angle of attack.

THE INFLUENCE OF GROUND EFFECT ON LANDING
When an aircraft enters ground effect during the landing phase of flight, the sudden increase in lift and reduction in drag cause it to experience a floating tendency. The aircraft also tends to pitch nose-down due to the reduction in download on the tailplane.

THE INFLUENCE OF GROUND EFFECT ON TAKE-OFF
During the take-off phase of flight, as the aircraft leaves ground effect the wing tip vortices rapidly grow in magnitude producing an increase in downwash behind the wing. This causes a reduction in the lift produced at a given angle of attack and the associated rapid increase in induced drag may prevent a successful take-off. The increased downwash acting on the tailplane increases the download, resulting in a nose-up pitching moment.

The magnitude of the wing tip vortices, and thus downwash, determine the amount of induced drag produced by the wing. The closer the aircraft is to the surface, the greater the reduction in induced drag at any given angle of attack. Thus, a low wing aircraft on landing will produce the least amount of Induced Drag. (figure 2)

title: The induced drag coefficient, C<sub>DI</sub> is proportional to:
optionA: C<sub>L</sub>.
optionB: square root (C<sub>L</sub>).

optionD: CL².
explanationTotal:

CDI = CL2 ÷ (π AR e)

CDI∝ CL2

Knowing that ∝ means proportional, we know that the coefficient of induced drag is proportional to the coefficient of lift squared.
