title:
Given a constant load factor, which of these statements about the variation of induced drag with changes of speed and mass are correct or incorrect?

1. When speed decreases, induced drag increases.
2. When mass decreases, induced drag decreases.
optionA: 1 is correct, 2 is incorrect.
optionB: 1 is incorrect, 2 is correct.
optionC: 1 is incorrect, 2 is incorrect.
optionD: 1 is correct, 2 is correct.
explanationTotal:
Induced drag is created as a byproduct of lift. The pressure differential between the top and bottom of the wing creates a upwash around the tip of the wing that turns into a downwash behind the wing. This is known as a vortex, which creates a rearward force known as induced drag.

This question is asking for the effect of:

  • Speed: The induced drag is inversely proportional to the speed. Therefore, induced drag increases as the speed decreases, and, induced drag decreases and the speed increases.
This is because, to maintain lift constant, as the velocity decreases, the coefficient of lift will have to be increased. At higher coefficients of lift, the pressure differential between the top and bottom of the wing will be greater and therefore produce stronger vortices = stronger induced drag. (and vice versa)
  • Changing mass: Induced drag is proportional to the mass. Therefore, induced drag increases with increasing aeroplane mass, and, induced drag decreases with decreasing aeroplane mass.

This is because, as the aircraft get heavier, the lift that the wings will have to produce increases. To achieve that, the coefficient of lift will have to increase, meaning a higher AoA, which creates stronger vortices. (and vice versa)

Summary:

  • Higher AR = Lower induced drag
  • Higher AoA = higher induced drag
  • Higher weight = higher AoA = higher induced drag
  • Higher speed = lower AoA = lower induced drag
  • Winglets = lower induced drag.

title: Considering a rectangular unswept wing, which statement is correct?
optionA: The flow on the upper surface of the wing has a component acting in the direction of the wing root.
optionB: Tip vortices can be diminished by vortex generators.
optionC: Tip vortices and induced drag decrease with increasing Angle Of Attack.
optionD: The flows on the upper and lower surfaces of the wing are both in the direction of the wing tip.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Whenever a wing produces lift, concentrated vortices form at the wing tips. The vortices are strongest at the wing tips and become progressively weaker toward the centerline of the aircraft.

The third dimensional flow is the movement of air laterally as it moves to the aft edge of the airfoil. This is called spanwise flow. As shown in figure 1 the resulting air-pressure distribution around an airfoil, caused by its movement through the air, is that for all positive angles of attack in level flight there is an excess area of low pressure above the upper surface of the airfoil. Thus, air will flow from the relatively high pressure under the lower surface around the wing tip to the lower pressure over the upper surface.

Consequently, the flow of air moves outward from the wing root towards the wing tip on the lower surface and from the tip inwards towards the wing root on the upper surface.

This is spanwise flow and is a slightly diagonal movement of the rearward airflow. Thus, the airflow over the two surfaces is moving in different directions when they meet at the trailing edge of the airfoil causing vortices to form along its entire length.

title: In the fly-by-wire flight envelope protection system, the protections which can be overridden are:
optionA: Hard protections.
optionB: Soft protections.
optionC: Both hard and soft protections.
optionD: Neither hard nor soft protections.
explanationTotal:
There are two main approaches to fly-by-wire systems, namely:
  • Soft protection: Fly-by-wire is used to transmit signals to the hydraulic actuators. The system does not alter the pilot signals or if the signal is modified it can be overrided by the pilot. (Common with Boeing aircraft)
  • Hard protection: Fly-by-wire is used to transmit and transform signals by the flight computers. The pilot does not have full authority (pilot cannot override it) and certain flight envelope protections are installed. (Common with Airbus aircraft)

title:
Refer to figure.
Given:
Aircraft mass: 100 t
Bank angle / load factor: 30°

What is the minimum Mach number to avoid low speed buffet?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

This is called a ‘Buffet Onset’ chart which is used by flight crews to ensure their aircraft is always operated with a specified minimum buffet margin.

In this exercise:

  • Start by drawing a line from the 30° bank that intersects the 100-ton curve.
  • From here, draw a straight line from right to left that intersects the FL410 and the FL380 curves.
  • The goal is to have 2 intersection points, which correspond to the lowest and highest limits of the buffet boundaries. In this case, the low speed boundary at FL410 is M0.70 and at FL380 is M 0.64.

Therefore:
=> For a flight at or below FL410, the Mach number to avoid low speed buffet is ≤M0.71; and
=> For a flight at or above FL380, the Mach number to avoid low speed buffet is ≥ M0.65.

title: Consider a symmetrical wing with a control surface in the trailing edge. When the control surface is deflected downwards, it (1) _____ the camber, producing a force in the (2) _____ direction of the deflection.
optionA: (1) increases; (2) same
optionB: (1) increases; (2) opposite
optionC: (1) decreases; (2) opposite
optionD: (1) decreases; (2) same
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
In flight, an aircraft can rotate about any one, or any combination of, its three axes. These axes are at right angles to each other and all pass through the aircraft’s centre of gravity.

The moment around an axis is produced by changing the aerodynamic force on the appropriate aerofoil. The magnitude of the force is a product of the dynamic pressure (IAS) and the angular displacement of the control surface.

Aerodynamic force can be changed by:

- adjusting the camber of the aerofoil.
- changing the incidence of the aerofoil.
- decreasing lift and increasing drag by “spoiling” the airflow.

Changing the camber of any aerofoil (wing, tailplane or fin) will change its lift. Deflecting a control surface effectively changes its camber.

AILERONS

The primary effect of ailerons is to provide roll control about the longitudinal axis

A downward movement of the aileron causes an increase in the effective angle of attack and a corresponding increase in lift, whilst an upward movement of the aileron causes a reduction in the effective angle of attack and a decrease in lift.

The difference in lift between the two wings produces the necessary rolling moment.

title: Approximately how long does it take to fly a complete circle during a horizontal steady co-ordinated turn with a bank angle of 45° and a TAS of 200 kt?
optionA: 95 s.
optionB: 650 s.
optionC: 65 s.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
In level flight, any turn will be coordinated or uncoordinated. A coordinated turn is one in which the only acceleration is along the normal axis of the airplane, towards the center of the turn, and the angle of bank is precisely correct for the aircraft speed and the radius of turn. If not all these factors are present, the turn will be uncoordinated and there will be a lateral acceleration either towards or away from the center of the turn. The total lift of a balanced turn provides the centripetal force and the force that opposes the mass of the airplane.
If there is acceleration towards the center of the turn the airplane is slipping and if it is away from the center of the turn the airplane is skidding. Either condition will be indicated on the turn and slip indicator. An overbanked airplane will slip into the turn and requires an increase of speed or a reduction in bank angle to correct this condition. An underbanked airplane will skid out of the turn, which requires a decreased speed or an increased bank angle to correct this condition. These are indicated on the turn and slip indicator by the needle one-way and the ball the other.
To maintain altitude and airspeed when executing a turn both the angle of attack and the thrust have to be increased above their level flight values.

In a turn, turn radius and rate of turn are defined as:

Turn radius = TAS 2/g tan Φ
Rate of Turn = g tan Φ/TAS

Therefore, turn radius is directly proportional to TAS squared and inversely proportional to bank angle and Rate of Turn is directly proportional to bank angle and inversely proportional to TAS.

In this exercise, TAS is equal to 200 knots and the bank angle is 45°:

First, convert 200kt to m/s:

200kt x 0.5144 = 102.88m/s
Then, calculate the turn radius
Turn radius = 102.88 2/10 x tan 45
Turn radius ≈ 1058.43m

The circumference is given by:

c = 2 * π * r
c = 2 * π * 1058.43
c = 6650.31 m
At 102.88 m/s, it would take approximately 65 seconds to complete the circumference.

title: Which of the following is a characteristic of a turbulent boundary layer?
optionA: Greater laminar flow transition tendency.
optionB: Reduced ability to follow a profile.
optionC: Lower drag due to reduced mixing.
optionD: Better ability to follow a profile.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

In contrast to a laminar layer, a turbulent boundary layer exhibits greater thickness and higher skin friction. With increased energy, it displays a reduced tendency to separate from the surface. This higher level of kinetic energy, results in the ability of a turbulent layer to follow a shape better than a laminar flow.

The thin laminar layer is highly responsive to surface irregularities. Any roughness on the leading portion of an aircraft's skin triggers a transition to turbulence at that point. This results in the thickening of the turbulent boundary layer, which fans out downstream and leads to a significant rise in skin friction drag.

title: Which of these statements about the transonic speed range is correct ?
optionA: The transonic speed range starts at M = 0.5 and ends at M<sub>CRIT</sub>.
optionB: The airflow everywhere around the aeroplane is subsonic.
optionC: The airflow everywhere around the aeroplane is supersonic.
optionD: The transonic speed range starts at M<sub>CRIT</sub> and extends to Mach numbers above M = 1.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

Figure 1 shows the flow speed ranges with their approximate Mach number values, where: MFS (Free Stream Mach number) is the Mach number of the flow sufficiently remote from an aircraft to be unaffected by it. (In effect, the Mach number of the aircraft through the air). This is the Mach number shown on the aircraft Mach meter.

ML (Local Mach number) is the actual speed of the flow over a surface. When an aircraft flies at a certain MFS the flow over it is accelerated in some places and slowed
down in others.

The transonic speed region is located between MCRIT and MDET (Detachment Mach number). In this region, ML is both subsonic and supersonic.

title: When the speed over an aerofoil section increases from subsonic to supersonic, its aerodynamic centre:
optionA: does not move.
optionB: moves aft by approximately 10% of the chord.
optionC: moves from approximately 25% to about 50% of the chord.
optionD: moves slightly forward.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
AERODYNAMIC CENTRE

The Aerodynamic center is a fixed point on the chord line where all changes in the magnitude of the lift force effectively take place. Assuming no flow separation and no compressibility effects, the location of the aerodynamic centre of an aerofoil section is independent of angle of attack.
  • When considering subsonic airflows the AC is located at the 25% chord point for any aerofoil regardless of camber, thickness and angle of attack. In the trans. and supersonic speed region, the AC will move to about mid chord (50%). Resulting in an increase in static longitudinal stability.

title: In a stationary subsonic streamline flow pattern, if the streamlines converge, in this part of the pattern, the static pressure will (1) _____ and the velocity will (2) _____.
optionA: (1) decrease; (2) decrease
optionB: (1) increase; (2) decrease
optionC: (1) decrease; (2) increase
optionD: (1) increase; (2) increase
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
A streamline is the path traced by a particle of air in a steady airflow, and streamlines cannot cross. Converging streamlines illustrate an accelerating airflow, with resultant decreasing pressure.

title: An aircraft is trimmed so that after a disturbance in pitch, it starts an oscillatory motion that does not decrease over time. In this case, the aircraft has (1)_____ static stability and (2)_____ dynamic stability.
optionA: (1) positive; (2) positive
optionB: (1) positive; (2) neutral
optionC: (1) neutral; (2) neutral
optionD: (1) neutral; (2) positive
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
While static stability is concerned with the initial tendency of an aircraft to return to equilibrium, dynamic stability is defined by the resulting motion with time. If an aircraft is disturbed from equilibrium, the time history of the resulting motion indicates its dynamic stability.

Aircraft with neutral dynamic stability have oscillations that never dampen out. If a trimmed and neutrally dynamic stable aircraft is pitched up, it pitches nose low, then nose high again, and this oscillation continues, in theory, forever.

title: Wing spoilers are deflected symmetrically in flight in order to:
optionA: assist the ailerons in obtaining a higher roll rate.
optionB: decelerate the aeroplane and/or increase its rate of descent.
optionC: improve glide performance (increase lift /drag ratio).
optionD: prevent aeroplane yaw.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

SPOILERS
Spoilers are flap type control surfaces, normally located on the upper surface of the wing, just in front of the trailing edge flaps.

These surfaces individually hinge at their leading edges and are actuated by hydraulic power supplied by dedicated power control units. The main purpose of the surfaces is to disturb the smooth airflow over the top of the wing, thereby reducing the wings lifting capability. When fully extended, they considerably increase aircraft drag.

Roll Spoilers operate asymmetrically in flight whenever the control wheel rotates, assisting the ailerons in providing roll control, particularly at high airspeeds.

Flight Spoilers (speed brakes) operate symmetrically about the aircraft’s longitudinal axis to increase drag, when it is required to decelerate quickly or to descend rapidly. Their deflection angle is determined from the flight deck in response to movements of a speed brake lever, typically located on the centre pedestal on transport category aircraft.

title: Given an aeroplane in steady, straight and level flight at low speed and considering the effects of CG location and thrust, the lowest value of wing lift occurs at:
optionA: aft CG and high thrust.
optionB: aft CG and low thrust.
optionC: forward CG and low thrust.
optionD: forward CG and high thrust.
explanationTotal:
Refer to the figure.
  • CG location: As you can see in the diagram, rearward cg location requires less lift than a forward one because the horizontal stabilizer can contribute to the total lift instead of it working against (downwards) the total lift in the case of a forward cg. Therefore, a rearward cg requires least wing lift.
  • Thrust: Assuming a pitch up attitude (otherwise thrust would be irrelevant), thrust helps to lift up the aircraft and can reduce the lift required by the wing. This is because at high pitch angle, thrust will produce a vertical component, as can be seen in the right hand side of the figure. Therefore, a high thrust requires the least wing lift.

title: How does the Mach number change during a climb at constant IAS from sea level to 40000 ft?
optionA: Initially remains constant until approximately 25000 ft and then decreases with increasing altitude.
optionB: Initially remains constant until approximately 25000 ft and then increases with increasing altitude.
optionC: Decreases with increasing altitude.
optionD: Increases with increasing altitude.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The Mach number is defined as the ratio between the TAS and the LSS (Local speed of sound).

It is an indication of how fast an aircraft is travelling with relation to the sound waves that surround it.

The Mach number may be calculated as follows:
M=TAS/LSS=(TAS(kt))/(38.95∗√(T(K)))

The speed of propagation of small pressure waves depends upon the temperature of the air ONLY.

Effect on Mach Number of Climbing at a Constant IAS:

  • Temperature decreases with increasing altitude, so the speed of sound will decrease as altitude is increased.
  • If altitude is increased at a constant IAS, the TAS increases.
  • Therefore, the Mach number will increase if altitude is increased at a constant IAS. This is because TAS gets bigger and LSS gets smaller.

title: Calculate the VA for an aerobatic aeroplane with a VS0 of 43 kt and a VS1 of 58 kt.
optionA: 103 kt
optionB: 117 kt
optionC: 142 kt
optionD: 120 kt
explanationTotal:
To calculate the VA we multiply the stall speed (VS1) by the square root of the load factor.

CS 23.337 Limit manoeuvring load factors ED Decision 2003/14/RM

(a) The positive limit manoeuvring load factor n may not be less than –

  1. 2 ∙ 1 + 24000 𝑊+10000 for normal and commuter category aeroplanes (where W = design maximum take-off weight lb), except that n need not be more than 3•8;
  2. 4•4 for utility category aeroplanes; or
  3. 6•0 for aerobatic category aeroplanes.

(b) The negative limit manoeuvring load factor may not be less than –

  1. 0•4 times the positive load factor for the normal, utility and commuter categories; or
  2. 0•5 times the positive load factor for the aerobatic category.

(c) Manoeuvring load factors lower than those specified in this paragraph may be used if the aeroplane has design features that make it impossible to exceed these values in flight.

From this article we can derive that the manoeuvring load factor for an aerobatic aircraft is 6
The calculation will therefore be as follows: 58 * sqrt(6) = 142 kt

title: You are in cruise flight and maintaining a constant pressure altitude (flight level) and IAS, which keeps you flying close to M<sub>CRIT</sub>. You suddenly encounter a cold air mass. What is most probable to happen?
optionA: Mach speed stays constant.
optionB: Mach speed increases or decreases, depending on the exact temperature of the cold air mass.
optionC: Mach speed decreases, and you could stall if you do not intervene.
optionD: Mach speed increases
explanationTotal:
The Indicated Airspeed is defined by dynamic pressure:

IAS = 1/2 ρ TAS2

As temperature decreases, density rises. Consequently, when density increases while maintaining a constant IAS, the TAS must be reduced.

The Mach number is defined as the ratio between the TAS and the LSS (Local speed of sound).
It is an indication of how fast an aircraft is travelling with relation to the sound waves that surround it.

The Mach number may be calculated as follows:

M = TAS / LSS

LSS is determined by the formula LSS = 38.95 √ T in Kelvin. Hence, when temperature decreases, LSS also declines. With both TAS and LSS experiencing reduction, the Mach Number remains constant.

Note: In terms of its impact on True Airspeed (TAS), density (ρ) holds a greater significance compared to temperature. When flying at a constant altitude through a cold air mass, only temperature influences TAS, leading to a decrease. This response aligns with the principles of general gas laws.

title: What is correct about crossing the intertropical convergence zone (ITCZ) in the high level cruise?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Wind shear and icing associated with ITCZ thunderstorms give an increased risk of buffet or stall.
optionB: There is no risk of buffet or stall if the aircraft remains outside the cloud.
optionC: The aircraft should fly as close as possible to the Aerodynamic Ceiling.
optionD: Modern jet transports can cruise above the thunderstorm hazards.
explanationTotal:
The Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) appears as a band of clouds (extensive Cu, Cb and thunderstorms). These areas should be avoided as they impose great risks to flight safety, namely moderate to severe icing and turbulence.

Gusts, or in other word abrupt wind changes (or windshear), are known to occur close to or in thunderstorm cells, thus particularly in ITCZ, in clear air turbulence (jet streams) and in wake turbulence.

If an aerofoil encounters an upgust, it will experience an increase in angle of attack. For a given gust velocity, the increment in angle increases as the aircraft TAS decreases. If the angle of attack is already large (low speed), the increment due to the gust could cause the wing to stall.

Furthermore, ice on the wings can raise the stall speed in various ways. The weight of ice adds to the aeroplane’s total weight, increasing the stall speed. Ice can change the shape of the aerofoil, either by reducing the coefficient of lift or the stalling angle of attack. Even a thin coating of ice can trigger separation by disrupting the smooth flow of air.

title: Which of the following answers is correct regarding the formation of ice on a propeller?
optionA: To counter icing conditions in a light aeroplane without de-icing, the pilot should reduce propeller RPM as far as possible.
optionB: Considering the whole aeroplane, the most critical effect of icing conditions is through ice formation on the propeller blades.
optionC: The presence of ice on propeller blades causes propeller efficiency to be reduced by up to 20%.
optionD: On a propeller blade, ice tends to form first towards the tip, due to the sharp leading edge.
explanationTotal:
Ice contamination on the propeller has the same effect as ice on the wings, in that both reduce the efficiency of the airfoils. Leading edge ice on the propeller reduces the generated thrust in the same way the lift of the wing is reduced; by creating turbulent air flow.

In the same way, as the drag of an ice contaminated airplane increases, the resisting force on the propeller increases for a given rpm and blade angle. Ice separating from the propeller blades, as well as vibration due to propeller imbalance, may cause damage to the airplane structure. Since ice on the propeller blades reduces the available thrust, extra power may be required from the engine to overcome the increased drag, decreasing propeller efficiency.

title: The lift force, acting on an aerofoil: (no flow separation)
optionA: is mainly caused by reduced pressure on the upper surface.
optionB: is mainly caused by overpressure at the underside of the aerofoil.
optionC: increases, proportional to the angle of attack until 40 degrees.
optionD: is maximum at an angle of attack of 2 degrees.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
A plane can remain in the air by the wings generating lift. If this lift is equal to the weight (and the aircraft is in the air), the aircraft will remain in level flight. A wing operates through the principle of pressure differential and equal and opposite reactions.

An aerofoil segment can generate lift by either having an angle of attack to the relative airflow, or but being cambered (bulging more in one direction), or both.

Both these things mean that, to create lift upwards, the air flowing over the top of the wing must travel faster than the air underneath the wing, in order to provide a low pressure area above the wing due to the venturi effect. The way this occurs can be thought of through many different approaches, but it is easiest for our purposes just to say that the streamlines of air going over the wing get squashed together more than those under the wing (there is a little more to it, but we don't want to make it any more complex).

The venturi effect creates a low pressure area above the wing, and the relatively higher pressure beneath the wing means that there is a net force upwards on the wing (from high to low), which is our lift. The air behind the wing is also given some downwash by this effect, and that satisfies the "equal and opposite forces" of Newton's 3rd law, in that the air going downwards forces the aircraft to go upwards.

It is important to know that the low pressure air is the main contributor to the lifting effect, and not the "high" pressure beneath the wing, as that is only high relative to the low, not relative to ambient pressure.

title: Modern jet aeroplanes usually fly at speeds faster than M<sub>CRIT</sub>, since the increase in speed is more significant than the increase in drag. How is this achieved?
optionA: The aeroplanes are capable of flying at a higher altitude where the air is less dense and therefore the effects of the shock waves are less severe and create less wave drag.
optionB: The aeroplanes are flown at lower altitudes where the TAS is higher for a given Mach number and therefore experience a delay in the onset of shock waves and wave drag.
optionC: By using a supercritical aerofoil to reduce the severity of shock waves and the amount of wave drag at a given Mach number, when compared to a conventional aerofoil.
optionD: By using an advanced wing technology with a greater curvature underneath to balance the acceleration over the top and therefore reduce the severity of the shock waves.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
A wing accelerates air over its upper surface, which, at high subsonic speeds, has the effect of causing that air to become supersonic (above Mach 1). The speed at which this first happens is known as MCRIT, above which speed, a shockwave will form on the upper section of the wing, usually near the wing root.

In aircraft which are not designed for these high speeds, that can be dangerous, as the shockwave can cause airflow separation and loss of lift behind it.

However, modern high speed jet aircraft are designed with this in mind, with swept back, supercritical wings, etc. These allow the aircraft to operate just above MCRIT, with a small penalty of increased drag, in return for extra speed.

To reduce the severity of the shock stall and allow aircraft to travel faster, some modern jet transport category aircraft have supercritical wings.

title: An aeroplane has a stall speed of 78 kt at its mass of 6850 kg. What is the stall speed when the mass is 5000 kg?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: 57 kt.
optionB: 78 kt.
optionC: 67 kt.
optionD: 91 kt.
explanationTotal:
The stall speed at increased weight can be determined applying the following formula:

VS NEW = VS OLD × √(New W ÷ Old W)
VS NEW = 78 kt × √(5 000 kg ÷ 6 850 kg)
VS NEW = 67 kt

title: Planning an IFR flight, the pilot must comply with the published speeds at arrival. What may happen if the aircraft is faster than the published speed?
optionA: Outside limit of safe zone/roll rate.
optionB: Outside limits of safe zone/radius.
optionC: Rate of turn/stall speed limited.
optionD: Bank angle/stall speed limited.
explanationTotal:
LOs reference 081.08.01.05.12: Explain situations in which turn radius is relevant for safety, such as maximum speed limits on departure or arrival plates, or outbound speed categories on approach plates, and the implications/hazards of exceeding given speeds.

Turn radius is dependent on airspeed and bank angle only. However, during normal airline operations, bank angle is limited to ensure a coordinated turn with the average piloting skills. As bank angle is maximized, turn radius is a function of speed only. Therefore, should any arrival or approach area be limited by, for example, airspace structure or terrain, speed must also be limited.

title:
Refer to figure.
An aeroplane is flying straight and level, and moving from position 2 to position 4 on the polar diagram. Which of the following is happening?
optionA: The airspeed is decreasing.
optionB: The airspeed is increasing.
optionC: The aeroplane has stalled.
optionD: The airspeed is not changing.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The polar curve of an airfoil is the graphical relationship of the coefficients of lift and drag plotted against each other, the resulting graph is as shown in the figure above. It is important to understand that the graph is not originally based on speed. The graph simply shows a relationship between CL and CD for different angles of attack of the wing (which is the only possible variable here), turned into a continuous curve. We do know that angle of attack decreases as speed increases though in straight and level flight, so we can read off relative changes in speed from the graph.

Firstly, we can note a few points from the graph.

Position 1 has no CL, therefore no lift is produced and this is an impossible scenario for straight and level flight. It also shows that the CD is lowest at this point, as no induced drag is produced, so the only drag remaining is parasite drag. We would have to fly impossibly fast to fly straight and level at position 1, it shows the high speed boundary of the curve.

Position 2 has the highest CL for the lowest CD on this graph, this is the point of best Lift/Drag ratio. A very useful point to know; in terms of speed, it is the minimum drag speed VMD.

Position 4 is the next easiest to note, it is the point of highest CL, but quite high CD also. This is the critical angle of attack, and in speed terms, is VS. To the right of this point, the lift reduces and drag continues to increase, and is the stalled region.

Position 3 is between the stall speed and VMD, and is assumed to be VMP (minimum power required speed). There is no defining feature of VMP on this type of diagram, such as a tangent or highest/lowest point.

From these positions, we can see that the speed of the aircraft increases going from 4 to 1, the speed trend is marked on the figure above. Therefore, going from position 2 to position 4 in straight and level flight means that the aircraft's airspeed is decreasing.

title: Which of these statements about weight or mass is correct?
optionA: The weight of a body can be determined by dividing its mass by the acceleration due to gravity.
optionB: The weight of a body can be determined by dividing the acceleration due to gravity by its mass.
optionC: The mass of a body can be determined by multiplying its weight by the acceleration due to gravity.
optionD: The mass of a body can be determined by dividing its weight by the acceleration due to gravity.
explanationTotal:
Mass is constant regardless of gravity, but weight is not. Weight it the force exerted on a body by gravity:

W = m x g [N] ⇔ m = W ÷ g

Where g is gravitational acceleration.

g ≈ 9.81 m/s2 on Earth
W ≈ m x 9.81

title: Compared with the clean configuration, the angle of attack at C<sub>LMAX</sub> with trailing edge flaps extended is:
optionA: smaller.
optionB: unchanged.
optionC: smaller or larger depending on the degree of flap extension.
optionD: larger.
explanationTotal: Trailing edge flap increases camber which increases the coefficient of lift, and reduces stalling speeds. Increased camber decreases the angle of attack at which the wing stalls, which is the angle of attack at C<sub>LMAX</sub>

title:
An aircraft with a mass of 60 tons is performing a co-ordinated level turn with 30 degrees of bank. In these conditions what is the magnitude of the lift force?
Assume g = 10 m/s2
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
In a steady horizontal turn, the total lift is greater than the weight (as some of the lift force is used as centripetal force in the turning direction). The conditions of equilibrium can be expressed in the form:

L cos φ = W
L = W / cos φ
Where (L) is the wing lift in newtons, (W) is the weight of the aircraft in newtons and φ the angle of bank.

To get the weight of the aircraft in newtons, just multiply the weight in kg by the value of g (acceleration due to gravity, usually 9.81 if not otherwise told) which is given as 10 in this question.

W = 60 000 kg x 10 = 600 000 N

  • Therefore, we have:
    L = 600 000 / cos (30)
    L = 692 820 N

Tip: remember that in a turn, lift will be greater than the weight to remain at the same altitude. Now, the cosine of any angle is always between -1 and 1, so for L to be greater than W, the equation must be L cos φ = W (any bank angle requires a larger lift to balance the same weight).

If you get stuck with whether to divide or multiply by cos φ, sometimes you can just try it and see if the answer goes the correct way (i.e. gets larger or gets smaller), which is a very useful gross error check.

title: What happens to the lift to drag ratio in the transonic regime?
optionA: Decreases slowly then increases
optionB: Increases
optionC: Decreases
optionD: Stays the same
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Although the curve of CL / CD is unique at low speeds, at transonic speeds when compressibility becomes significant, the curve will change.

Figure 1 shows the variation of CL / CD with Mach number. The point at which the tangent from the origin touches the curve corresponds to the maximum CL / CD.
In the transonic region, the CL / CD ratio is reduced.

title: The aspect ratio of a wing is the ratio between the:
optionA: wing span and the mean geometric chord.
optionB: tip chord and the wing span.
optionC: wing span and the root chord.
optionD: chord and root chord.
explanationTotal:
Wing tip vortices increase if we increase induced drag. This can be caused by for example increased speed, density or lift coefficient. If we increase Angle of Attack, lift will be increased, also increasing the strength of wing tip vortices.

Another factor increasing wing tip vortices is the aspect ratio (λ) of the wing. This is the ratio of the wing span to its mean chord. The aspect ratio of the wing is equal to the square of the wingspan divided by the wing surface area. Therefore a short but wide wing has a low aspect ratio but a long, narrow wing has a high aspect ratio. With a lower aspect ratio, the induced drag is higher, thus increasing wing tip vortices. With a high aspect ratio, the induced drag is lower, reducing wing tip vortices. We can therefore state that the relationship between wing tip vortices and aspect ratio is inversely proportional.

A wing with a higher aspect ratio has a lower value for CLMAX and will have a higher value of CL for a certain angle of attack.

title: What would warn of an imminent stall when flying close to V<sub>S</sub>?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Difficulty in maintaining altitude, loss of elevator effectiveness and/or low speed buffet.
optionB: Sharp, uncommanded pitch-down.
optionC: Loss of all control effectiveness.
optionD: Loss of engine power.
explanationTotal:
An imminent stall is one in which the airplane is approaching a stall but is not allowed to completely stall. Indications of an imminent stall can include buffeting, stick shaker, or aural warning.
Other sensory cues for the pilot include: The pilot will feel control pressures change as speed is reduced. With progressively less resistance on the control surfaces, the pilot must use larger control movements to get the desired airplane response. The pilot will experience difficulty in maintaining altitude.

A full stall occurs when the critical AOA is exceeded. Indications of a full stall are typically that an uncommanded nose-down pitch cannot be readily arrested, and this may be accompanied by an uncommanded rolling motion. For airplanes equipped with stick pushers, its activation is also a full stall indication.

title: For an aeroplane equipped with a two-position variable pitch propeller it is advisable to select a:
optionA: coarse pitch for take-off and climb.
optionB: fine pitch for cruise.
optionC: fine pitch for cruise and coarse pitch for landing.
optionD: fine pitch for take-off and climb.
explanationTotal:
The purpose of a variable-pitch propeller is to either manually or automatically maintain the optimum angle of attack to maximize the lift/drag ratio of the propeller as the airplane speed changes. This characteristic is the most significant advantage of the constant-speed (fixed RPM) propeller over the fixed-pitch propeller because it is able to maintain maximum efficiency over a range of airplane speeds.
Originally there were only two pitch settings, fine for take-off and climb and coarse for cruise and high-speed flight. Subsequently, the fully variable pitch constant-speed propeller was introduced so that the optimum blade angle of attack could be maintained over the whole range of operating speeds for that airplane.
This facility not only improves the propeller efficiency but also decreases the fuel consumption.
The pitch angle or blade angle of a constant-speed propeller (fixe RPM) increases (or coarsens) with increasing TAS.
Constant-speed propellers enable the pilot to select the RPM for maximum power or maximum efficiency and a propeller governor varies the propeller pitch angle as required to maintain the selected RPM. Propeller efficiency improves with increased TAS; however, it is limited to that blade angle beyond which the propeller will no longer produce any thrust.

title:
Given a constant load factor, which of these statements about the variation of induced drag with changes of speed and mass are correct or incorrect?

1. When speed decreases, induced drag increases.
2. When mass decreases, induced drag increases.
optionA: 1 is correct, 2 is incorrect.
optionB: 1 is incorrect, 2 is correct.
optionC: 1 is incorrect, 2 is incorrect.
optionD: 1 is correct, 2 is correct.
explanationTotal:
Induced drag is created as a byproduct of lift. The pressure differential between the top and bottom of the wing creates a upwash around the tip of the wing that turns into a downwash behind the wing. This is known as a vortex, which creates a rearward force known as induced drag.

This question is asking for the effect of:

  • Speed: The induced drag is inversely proportional to the speed. Therefore, induced drag increases as the speed decreases, and, induced drag decreases and the speed increases.
This is because, to maintain lift constant, as the velocity decreases, the coefficient of lift will have to be increased. At higher coefficients of lift, the pressure differential between the top and bottom of the wing will be greater and therefore produce stronger vortices = stronger induced drag. (and vice versa)
  • Changing mass: Induced drag is proportional to the mass. Therefore, induced drag increases with increasing aeroplane mass, and, induced drag decreases with decreasing aeroplane mass.

This is because, as the aircraft get heavier, the lift that the wings will have to produce increases. To achieve that, the coefficient of lift will have to increase, meaning a higher AoA, which creates stronger vortices. (and vice versa)

Summary:

  • Higher AR = Lower induced drag
  • Higher AoA = higher induced drag
  • Higher weight = higher AoA = higher induced drag
  • Higher speed = lower AoA = lower induced drag
  • Winglets = lower induced drag.

title: How can the designer of an aeroplane with straight wings increase the static lateral stability?
optionA: By fitting a ventral fin (a fin at the under side of the aeroplane).
optionB: By applying wing twist.
optionC: By increasing the aspect ratio of the vertical stabiliser, whilst maintaining a constant area.
optionD: By increasing anhedral.
explanationTotal:
"By increasing anhedral." Incorrect.Wing dihedral increases lateral stability, while anhedral reduces it.

"By fitting a ventral fin (a fin at the under side of the aeroplane)." Incorrect. A ventral fin is placed on the underside of the aircraft’s fuselage. Any fin placed on the underside of the fuselage is called a ventral fin, it improves static directional stability and reduces lateral stability.

"By applying wing twist." Incorrect. Wing twist has no effect on lateral stability.

"By increasing the aspect ratio of the vertical stabiliser, whilst maintaining a constant area." Correct. The vertical stabiliser will produce a larger correcting force in case of a sideslip when its aspect ratio is increased, thereby increasing the static lateral stability.

title: When a student becomes distracted during a flight and enters a spin, which instrument can be used to determine the direction of the turn?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Turn coordinator.
optionB: Attitude indicator.
optionC: Turn indicator.
optionD: Ball of skid turn.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The spin is a complex flight manoeuvre. It may be defined as an aggravated stall resulting in a rotation. The rotation is stable and will continue due to remaining aerodynamic forces. During the spin, the wings remain unequally stalled.

Recovery from a normal stall is achieved by reducing the angle of attack which restores the airflow over the wing. Spin recovery additionally involves stopping the rotation. The more complex aerodynamics of a spin require different recovery procedures depending on the aeroplane design.

Spin direction is most reliably determined from the turn coordinator or by looking outside. Do not use the ball in the slip indicator as its indication is not reliable and may be affected by its location within the flight deck.

title: A jet engine aeroplane is cruising close to its maximum altitude when it suffers an engine failure. While concentrating on completing the appropriate checklist, the pilots fail to notice the aeroplane’s speed decreasing. The aeroplane develops buffeting, which eventually becomes strong enough to be considered a deterrent. This means that the aircraft is…
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: stalled.
optionB: speed unstable.
optionC: becoming over-stressed.
optionD: below VMC.
explanationTotal:
The aeroplane is considered stalled when the behaviour of the aeroplane gives the pilot a clear and distinctive indication of an acceptable nature that the aeroplane is stalled.
Acceptable indications of a stall, occurring either individually or in combination, are:
- A nose-down pitch that cannot be readily arrested;
- Buffeting, of a magnitude and severity that is a strong and effective deterrent to further speed reduction; or
- The pitch control reaches the aft stop and no further increase in pitch attitude occurs when the control is held full aft for a short time before recovery is initiated.

title:
Which of these statements about drag divergence Mach number are correct or incorrect?

1. The drag divergence Mach number is equal to MCRIT.
2. Below the drag divergence Mach number and for a given angle of attack the drag coefficient CD is practically constant as the Mach number changes.
optionA: 1 is incorrect, 2 is incorrect.
optionB: 1 is incorrect, 2 is correct.
optionC: 1 is correct, 2 is incorrect.
optionD: 1 is correct, 2 is correct.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The Mach number at which the aerodynamic drag begins to increase rapidly is called the drag divergence Mach number. The Drag Divergence Mach Number is usually close to, and always greater than, the Critical Mach Number. Therefore, statement 1 is incorrect.

As speed increases above MCRIT shock waves begin to form and drag increases more rapidly than it would have done without the shock waves. The additional drag is called wave drag and is due to energy drag and boundary layer separation.

The change in drag characteristics is shown by the CD curve for a basic section at a constant angle of attack in figure 1. The ‘hump’ in the curve from M 0.89 to M 1.2 is caused by:

  • The drag directly associated with the trailing edge shock waves (energy loss).
  • Separation of the boundary layer.
  • The formation of the bow shock wave above M 1.0.
The drag divergence Mach number is the Mach number at which the aerodynamic drag begins to increase rapidly. As seen in figure 1, below the drag divergence Mach number, drag is practically constant. Therefore, statement 2 is correct.

title:
Refer to figure.
Which figure best illustrates how the CL/alpha curve changes as the aspect ratio increases?
optionA: Figure 1
optionB: Figure 3
optionC: Figure 4
optionD: Figure 2
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Aspect ratio (AR) is the proportion of the span and the average chord.

The aspect ratio of the wing determines the aerodynamic characteristics and structural weight. Typical aspect ratios vary from 35 for a high-performance sailplane to 3 for a jet fighter. The aspect ratio of a modern high-speed jet transport is about 12.

The effect of increasing aspect ratio on the lift curve is to decrease the overall wing angle of attack necessary to produce a given lift coefficient. Higher aspect ratio wings are more sensitive to changes in angle of attack but require a smaller angle of attack for maximum lift generation CLMAX.

title: Consider that the angle of attack of a swept-back fin in a sideslip is increased. What happens to the static directional stability?
optionA: The fin will stall earlier due to the sweep angle but will also reduce the directional stability.
optionB: The fin will stall later due to the sweep angle but will increase the directional stability.
optionC: The fin will stall later due to the sweep angle but will also reduce the directional stability.
optionD: The fin will stall earlier due to the sweep angle but will increase the directional stability.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
The fin (vertical stabilizer) is the major source of directional stability for the aeroplane. In a sideslip the fin experiences a change in angle of attack.

The change in lift (side force) on the fin creates a yawing moment about the centre of gravity which tends to yaw the aeroplane into the relative airflow.

The magnitude of the fin contribution to static directional stability depends on both the change in fin lift and the fin moment arm.

The lift curve slope of the fin determines how sensitive the surface is to change in angle of attack. While it is desirable to have a high lift curve slope for the fin, a high aspect ratio surface is not necessarily practical or desirable due to:

- Bending
- Lower stalling angle
- Hangar roof clearance

The stall angle of the surface must be large enough to prevent stall and subsequent loss of effectiveness at expected sideslip angles. Sweepback or low aspect ratio increases the stalling angle of attack of the fin and reduces the lift curve slope, therefore reducing static directional stability.

title: Which of the following statements about tailplanes is correct?A T-tail is...
optionA: more stabilising than a low tailplane because it is less affected by downwash behind the wings.
optionB: less stabilising than a low tailplane because it is less affected by downwash behind the wings.
optionC: less stabilising than a low tailplane because it is more affected by downwash behind the wings.
optionD: more stabilising than a low tailplane because it is more affected by downwash behind the wings.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Tail plane effective angle of attack is determined by the downwash from the wing. If the flaps are lowered, the downwash will increase and the tail plane angle of attack will increase, increasing its effectiveness and causing a nose-up pitching moment.

A low mounted tail plane will have its effective angle of attack modified by the changing downwash angle behind the wing. A high mounted tail plane may be outside the influence of the changing downwash angle and not suffer the same disadvantages.

title: A modern jet transport aeroplane is cruising at 35000 ft in an area of mountain waves. The cruising speed is at M 0.79 with M<sub>MO</sub> at M 0.81 when the aeroplane suddenly experiences a positive wind shear. The autothrust is slow at reacting and the aeroplane reaches a speed of M 0.82 before starting to decelerate again. Apart from an overspeed warning, are there any other indications of the overspeed that may be apparent to the pilots?
optionA: with their feet resting on the floor, a slight vibration is felt through the fuselage structure, otherwise the aeroplane observes normal behaviour.
optionB: the aeroplane is buffeting and a significant pitch-down moment suddenly develops, requiring an immediate corrective action to avoid entering a dive.
optionC: strong shock waves will be forming, creating separation of the boundary layer, causing a significant buffet as the aeroplane enters a high-speed shock stall.
optionD: unusually high levels of ambient wind noise followed by severe buffeting requiring a pitch-up input to ensure a rapid deceleration to a speed below M<sub>MO</sub>.
explanationTotal:
The buffet boundary has both low and high speed limits:

  • The low speed buffet boundary (left hand limit of the graph), which marks the onset of the pre-stall buffet at a 10% margin above VS.
  • The high speed limit (right hand limit of the graph), which is the maximum Mach number at high altitudes, MMO, and marks the onset of the Mach related buffer, but sometimes slightly below that.

In this case, the aircraft has exceeded the MMO by 0.01 Mach, which is just over 1% of the MMO of M0.81.

The correct use of the buffet boundary graphs will provide a safe margin for such minor events, like a positive wind shear during the cruise phase of flight.

The likelihood is that the pilots would feel very little at this stage and probably a slight vibration through the fuselage structure, with their feet resting on the floor.

However, when faced with this situation, the pilot would be wise to descend in order to increase the buffet margin so that the aircraft remained within limits.

title: Which of the following statements regarding wake turbulence is correct?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Wake turbulence can be avoided by flying just below the flightpath of the aircraft ahead.
optionB: On final approach, wake turbulence is a bigger hazard in light crosswinds.
optionC: Wake turbulence is a bigger hazard at high level.
optionD: Wake turbulence is not an issue on take-off.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

WAKE TURBULENCE

Whenever an airplane generates lift, air spills over the wing tips from the high pressure areas below the wings to the low pressure areas above them. This flow causes rapidly rotating whirlpools of air called wingtip vortices. An aircraft generates vortices from the moment it rotates on take-off to touchdown.

The intensity depends on aircraft weight, speed and configuration. The greatest wake turbulence danger is produced by large, heavy airplanes operating at low speeds, high angles of attack and in a clean configuration.

Although wake turbulence settles, it persists in the air for several minutes, depending on wind conditions. In light winds of 3 to 7 knots, the vortices can stay in the touchdown area, sink into your take-off or landing path, or drift over a parallel runway

=> Light crosswinds may cause the vortices to drift. A 3 to 5 knot crosswind will tend to keep the upwind vortex in the runway area and may cause the downwind vortex to drift toward another runway.

title:
Which of these statements about drag divergence Mach number are correct or incorrect?

1. MCRIT is lower than the drag divergence Mach number.
2. Assuming a given angle of attack and for M < 1 the drag coefficient CD decreases above the drag divergence Mach number.
optionA: 1 is incorrect, 2 is correct.
optionB: 1 is correct, 2 is incorrect.
optionC: 1 is correct, 2 is correct.
optionD: 1 is incorrect, 2 is incorrect.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The Mach number at which the aerodynamic drag begins to increase rapidly is called the drag divergence Mach number. The Drag Divergence Mach Number is usually close to, and always greater than, the Critical Mach Number. Therefore, statement 1 is correct.

As speed increases above MCRIT shock waves begin to form and drag increases more rapidly than it would have done without the shock waves. The additional drag is called wave drag and is due to energy drag and boundary layer separation.

The change in drag characteristics is shown by the CD curve for a basic section at a constant angle of attack in figure 1. The ‘hump’ in the curve from M 0.89 to M 1.2 is caused by:

  • The drag directly associated with the trailing edge shock waves (energy loss).
  • Separation of the boundary layer.
  • The formation of the bow shock wave above M 1.0.
The drag divergence Mach number is the Mach number at which the aerodynamic drag begins to increase rapidly. This increase in drag can be seen in figure 1. Therefore, statement 2 is incorrect.

title: A twin engine jet transport aeroplane is taking off from runway 27 with a wind of 210°/15 kt and an outside Air Temperature (OAT) of 20 °C. The failure of which engine would require the largest control inputs to maintain runway centreline?
optionA: It makes no difference.
optionB: Failure of the left engine.
optionC: It depends on the direction of rotation of the engines.
optionD: Failure of the right engine.
explanationTotal:
During a crosswind take-off, an airplane tends to weathercock into wind (yaw into the wind), due to the wind acting on the fin which produces a yaw moment.

In this case, the aircraft is taking-off from RW27 with a wind of 210/15 kt (from the left), the aircraft will tend to yaw left.
  • If a right engine fails, the left side will produce much more thrust than the right side, resulting in a right-yaw. This will oppose the yaw-left moment.
  • If a left engine fails, the right side will produce more thrust than the left side, resulting in a left-yaw. This will add to the left-yaw moments.

Therefore, the failure of the engine on the windward side of the airplane is the most difficult to counteract.

title:
Which of these statements about the strength of wing tip vortices are correct or incorrect?

I. Assuming no flow separation, the strength of wing tip vortices decreases as the angle of attack increases.
II. The strength of wing tip vortices decreases as the aspect ratio increases.
optionA: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
optionB: I is correct, II is correct.
optionC: I is correct, II is incorrect.
optionD: I is incorrect, II is correct.
explanationTotal:
Wing tip vortices are a byproduct of lift. They are caused by the pressure differential between the top and bottom of the wing, which causes an updraft of high pressure air around the tip of the wing. This updraft turn into a downdraft behind the wing, creating a vortex. The higher the pressure difference between the top and bottom of the wing, the stronger the vortices.

This question is specifically asking for:

  • Angle of attack: The strength of the vortices (and therefore also induced drag) is proportional to the angle of attack. Therefore; the strength of the vortices increase as the angle of attack increases. And also; the strength of the vortices decrease as the angle of attack decreases. Therefore statement 1 is incorrect!
  • Aspect ratio: The strength of the vortices is inversely proportional with the aspect ratio. Meaning that the strength of the wing tip vortices increase as the aspect ratio decreases. And vice versa: the strength decreases as the aspect ratio increases. Therefore statement 2 is correct!

title: When an aeroplane performs a straight steady climb with a 20% climb gradient, the load factor is equal to:
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Consider an aircraft in a straight steady climb along a straight flight path inclined at an angle (γ) to the horizontal. γ (gamma) is the symbol used for climb angle. The forces on the aircraft consist of Lift, normal to the flight path; Thrust and Drag, parallel to it; and Weight, parallel to the force of gravity.
Weight is resolved into two components: one opposite Lift (W cos γ) and the other acting in the same direction as Drag (W sin γ), backwards along the flight path. The requirements for equilibrium are: Thrust must equal the sum of Drag plus the backwards component of Weight; and Lift must equal its opposing component of Weight. For equilibrium at a greater angle of climb, the Lift required will be less, and the backwards component of Weight will be greater.

L = W cos γ
T = D + W sin γ

In a straight steady climb, Lift is less than Weight because Lift only has to support a proportion of the weight, this proportion decreasing as the climb angle increases. The remaining proportion of Weight is supported by engine Thrust.
It can be seen that for a straight steady climb the Thrust required is greater than Drag. This is to balance the backward component of Weight acting along the flight path.

The climb gradient can be described as:

sin γ = (T−D)/W

For very shallow flight path angles (γ), we can assume that lift is approximately equal to Weight, therefore the climb gradient can be described as:

sin γ = (T/W)−(D/L)

From the exercise, the climb gradient is 20%:

sin γ = 0.2

We can find the climb angle by applying:

γ= sin-1 0.2 ≈11.54°

Knowing that:

L = Wcos γ ⇒ L/W = cos γ = n

The load factor is:

n = cos11.54° ≈ 0.98

title: The stall speed line in the manoeuvring load diagram runs through a point where the:
optionA: speed = V<sub>A</sub>, load factor = +1.
optionB: speed = V<sub>S</sub>, load factor = +1.
optionC: speed = V<sub>B</sub>, load factor = +1.
optionD: speed = 0, load factor = +1.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The flight load factor, generally referred to as the load factor, is defined as the ratio of aerodynamic force component acting at right angles to the longitudinal axis of the airplane, (i.e. the lift), to the airplane mass in the same units of measurement. It is therefore a nondimensional number and is positive in an upward direction.

The operating limitations of an airplane in terms of speed and load factor can be shown graphically and is used to specify the design requirements for new airplanes or to illustrate the performance of an airplane type for comparison purposes. The load factor is plotted against the vertical axis and the speed as an EAS is plotted against the horizontal axis. This is the maneuver envelope.

From the options offered stall speed line intersects load factor +1 at VS.

title: In general, control forces are reduced by:
optionA: a horn balance, servo tab and spring tab.
optionB: a balance tab, forward shift of the CG and a servo tab.
optionC: a servo tab, spring tab and mass balancing.
optionD: mass balancing, a trim tab and spring tab.
explanationTotal:
The primary function of any aerodynamic control surface balancing method is to reduce the force required to operate the control. The most common methods employed to achieve this aim and reduce the maneuver stick force are:
  • the hinge balance.
  • the horn balance.
  • the internal balance (sealed chamber).
  • the balance tab.
  • the spring tab.
  • the servo-tab.
Note: "mass balance" is incorrect as it is used to reduce flutter and not stick forces.

title:
When supersonic airflow passes through a normal shock wave, how do the following conditions change?

I. static pressure,
II. density,
III. local speed of sound.
optionA: I. increases, II. increases, III. increases
optionB: I. decreases, II. decreases, III. decreases
optionC: I. increases, II. increases, III. decreases
optionD: I. remains constant, II. decreases, III. increases
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
During high-speed flight, significant changes occur in the flow and pressure distributions around the aircraft, which result in a loss of lift and an increase in drag. This is caused by the formation of shock waves, which adversely affect the stability and control characteristics of the aircraft.

The speed of sound is defined as the rate at which small pressure disturbances are propagated through the air, which is solely a function of air temperature.

THE DEVELOPMENT OF SHOCK WAVES
When aircraft fly through the air, every part of them sets up tiny pressure disturbances, which radiate outward at the speed of sound in all directions.

As Mach number increases, the flow over the wing continues to accelerate and eventually reaches a sonic value at a particular point on the wing, normally the point of maximum thickness.

With increasing Mach number, this point grows into an area of supersonic flow, so the air moving over the upper surface will be moving rearward faster than the pressure disturbances can move forward. These disturbances consequently pile up on each other and form a shock wave.

The shock wave acts perpendicular, or normal, to the surface, and is more commonly referred to as a normal shock wave. Notably, this occurs where the flow changes from supersonic back to subsonic.

The overall direction of the airflow remains the same, but as it passes through the shock wave, the following changes take place:
- The flow is rapidly decelerated to a subsonic Mach number.
- Static pressure increases.
- Temperature increases.
- Density increases.
- The energy of the airstream (total pressure) is greatly reduced.

As stated above, the Local Speed of Sound (LSS) is solely dependent on the Air Temperature. After the shockwave, the temperature increases and, therefore, the LSS also increases.

title:
Which of these statements about the strength of wing tip vortices are correct or incorrect?

I. Assuming no flow separation, the strength of wing tip vortices increases as the angle of attack increases.
II. The strength of wing tip vortices decreases as the aspect ratio increases.
optionA: I is correct, II is incorrect.
optionB: I is incorrect, II is correct.
optionC: I is correct, II is correct.
optionD: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
explanationTotal:
Wing tip vortices are a byproduct of lift. They are caused by the pressure differential between the top and bottom of the wing, which causes an updraft of high pressure air around the tip of the wing. This updraft turn into a downdraft behind the wing, creating a vortex. The higher the pressure difference between the top and bottom of the wing, the stronger the vortices.

This question is specifically asking for:

  • Angle of attack: The strength of the vortices (and therefore also induced drag) is proportional to the angle of attack. Therefore; the strength of the vortices increase as the angle of attack increases. And also; the strength of the vortices decrease as the angle of attack decreases. Therefore statement 1 is correct!
  • Aspect ratio: The strength of the vortices is inversely proportional with the aspect ratio. Meaning that the strength of the wing tip vortices increase as the aspect ratio decreases. And vice versa: the strength decreases as the aspect ratio increases. Therefore statement 2 is correct!

title: The manouveuring speed (VA) of a Cessna Skyhawk at 1 550 lb is 102 kt. What is the VA at mass of 2 500 lb?
explanationTotal:
The following formula may be used:

VNEW = VOLD x √ New weight ÷ Old weight
VNEW = 102 x √(2 500 ÷ 1 550)
VNEW = 129.5 kt

title:
Refer to figure.
Identify the significant points on the polar curve:
optionA: 1) Stall speed; 2) V<sub>MP</sub>; 3) V<sub>MD</sub>; 4) 1.32 V<sub>MD</sub>.
optionB: 1) Stall speed; 2) V<sub>MD</sub>; 3) V<sub>MP</sub>; 4) 1.32 V<sub>MD</sub>.
optionC: 1) 1.32 V<sub>MD</sub>; 2) V<sub>MP</sub>; 3) V<sub>MD</sub>; 4) Stall speed.
optionD: 1) 1.32 V<sub>MD</sub>; 2) V<sub>MD</sub>; 3) V<sub>MP</sub>; 4) Stall speed.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Some characteristic points can be identified on the polar curve or CL-CD Graph:

  • Point 1 – CLMAX (stalling speed): This is the point where CL and CD are both maximum and the point at which the minimum speed in level flight, the stalling speed, VS is attained.
  • Point 2 – Minimum power (VMP) (min vertical speed in descent): This point falls between VMD and VS and is approximately VMP, which approximates to the speed of VY for a piston/propeller airplane and indicates the value at which the minimum sink rate will occur. It is the speed that will attain the maximum endurance during a descent.
  • Point 3 – Maximum lift to drag ratio (VMD) (best glide): The point at which a tangent from the origin touches the polar curve, which is at the point at which the total drag is minimum, the lift/drag ratio is maximum and the IAS in level flight is VMD. This is also the speed at which the longest glide distance will be achieved.

  • Point 4 – 1.32 VMD: This point is between VMD and the maximum speed and has the minimum drag coefficient. It therefore approximates VY for a jet airplane.

title: V<sub>SR</sub> is:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: the stall speed in a specified configuration.
optionB: the stall speed in the landing configuration.
optionC: the reference stall speed.
optionD: the minimum speed at which the aeroplane can develop a lift force (normal to the flight path) equal to its weight.
explanationTotal:
VSR is the reference stalling speed, which is a calibrated airspeed selected by the manufacturer and is
used as the basis for the calculation of other speeds.

title: The Lift Coefficient versus Angle Of Attack curve of a symmetrical aerofoil section intersects the vertical axis of the graph..
optionA: above the origin.
optionB: below the origin.
optionC: to the right of the origin.
optionD: at the origin.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Camber is the asymmetry between two acting surfaces on an airfoil.
For an aircraft, this is the top and the bottom of the wing.
Positive camber means that a wing is thicker on the top end of the wing, than on the bottom if looked at from the chord.
In case of positive camber, a wing will generate lift with airspeed, as the air on top of the airfoil will get accelerated more than on the bottom, creating a low pressure on the top and high pressure at the bottom.
This is “pushing” the wing up into the air as the pressure difference wants to restore itself to 0 difference.
In case of negative camber, the exact opposite happens and the lift coefficient for a certain speed is lower than for a positively cambered wing.

A completely symmetrical airfoil will intersect the vertical axis of the graph at the origin (0).
A positively cambered airfoil will generate more lift at the same speed (and therefore has a higher CL) than a symmetrical airfoil and therefore intersects the vertical axis above the origin.
A negatively cambered airfoil will generate less lift at the same speed (which translates into a lower CL at a certain speed) and therefore intersects the vertical axis below the origin.

title: When the Mach number is slowly increased in straight and level flight the first shock waves will occur:
optionA: On the upper wing, close to the leading edge.
optionB: On the lower surface of the wing.
optionC: On the upper wing, where it is thickest.
optionD: Somewhere on the horizontal tail.
explanationTotal: At Critical Mach number (M<sub>CRIT</sub>), somewhere on the profile, local sonic speed is reached. This is the point corresponding to maximum thickness at the upper side of the wing, as the flow is the fastest there. So the flow velocity reaches and slightly exceeds sonic speed, thus behind this point a normal shock wave occurs.

optionA: the minimum speed at which the aeroplane can develop a lift force equal to its mass.
optionB: the maximum speed at which the aeroplane can develop a lift force (normal to the flight path) equal to its weight.
optionC: the minimum speed at which the aeroplane can develop a lift force (normal to the flight path) equal to its weight.
optionD: the maximum speed at which the aeroplane can develop a lift force equal to its mass.

VS: Stall speed [m/s]

VSW: Stall warning speed [m/s]

title: An aircraft with a TAS of 300 kts is turning with 15 degrees angle of bank. Determine its radius of turn, expressed in km:
explanationTotal:
Turn radius (R) = (TAS2 ÷ (g × tan Φ))
Where Φ is the bank angle.

Since this expression is independent on aircraft weight, the same speed and bank angle gives the same radius.

Turn radius (m) = (300 x 0.514)2 ÷ (9.81 x tan 15º)
Turn radius (m) = 9 045.8 m

title: Pilot is trimming the aircraft during climb-out. At some point the trim gets stuck. Speed and power remain constant. What happens to stick force with increasing altitude?
optionA: Increases
optionB: Decreases
optionC: Stays the same
optionD: Increases and then decreases
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The most direct appreciation of the manoeuvring stability of an aeroplane is obtained from a plot of stick force versus load factor. The aeroplane with positive manoeuvring stability should demonstrate a steady increase in stick force with increase in load factor or “g”.

The pitch damping of the aeroplane is related to air density. At high altitudes the pitch damping reduces. Thus, a decrease in stick force can be expected with increased altitude.

title: Which of these statements about boundary layers is correct?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Compared with a turbulent boundary layer, a laminar boundary layer is better able to resist a positive pressure gradient before it separates.
optionB: A laminar boundary layer is thicker than a turbulent one.
optionC: A turbulent boundary layer produces less friction drag than a laminar one.
optionD: A laminar boundary layer turns into a turbulent one at the transition point.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

Let’s look at each statement:

  • “Compared with a turbulent boundary layer, a laminar boundary layer is better able to resist a positive pressure gradient before it separates.”
This statement is incorrect, because a turbulent boundary layer is better at resisting a positive pressure gradient than a laminar layer.
  • “A laminar boundary layer is thicker than a turbulent one.”
This statement is incorrect, because as you can see in the figure, the turbulent boundary layer is thicker than the laminar one.
  • “A turbulent boundary layer produces less friction drag than a laminar one.”
This statement is incorrect, the turbulent boundary layer produces more friction than the laminar boundary, this is because turbulent flow has a higher rate of change in velocity which increases skin friction.
  • “A laminar boundary layer turns into a turbulent one at the transition point.”
This statement is correct, laminar turns into turbulent at the transition point. This process cannot occur in the reverse sense. Laminar turns into turbulent because of any roughness on the skin at the leading portion of the wing.

title:
An aircraft is flying near the ITCZ and begins to suffer from considerable turbulence. Which of the following actions could be done by the pilot to ease the turbulence?

1. Climb to a higher cruising altitude.
2. Descend to a lower cruising altitude.
3. Fly at the turbulence penetration speed.
4. Fly at VMO/MMO to clear the turbulent area fastest.
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: 1 and 4
optionB: 1 and 3
optionC: 2 and 3
optionD: 2 and 4
explanationTotal:
Note: this is based on incomplete feedback on questions 819856 and 815947, please put any further exam feedback in the comments or email it to us at info@atplquestions.com so we can verify the question, thanks!

The ITCZ (Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone) is an area of very large uplift and often violent thunderstorms due to converging air at the surface. It is also a region where the tropopause will be incredibly high, sometimes in the region of 55-60,000 ft. This makes it often impossible to climb away from the turbulence experienced in that region.

The turbulence can cause lots of passenger distress and potential for airframe fatigue and damage when it gets severe enough. It can also change our airspeed enough to put us into either the high- or low-speed buffeting region, so we should instead descend to a lower altitude, out of the potential “coffin corner” and fly at turbulence penetration speed (this usually means slowing down from cruise speed) to get the best safety margin for turbulence.

title: An aircraft manufacturer changed one of their aircraft designs in order to obtain better OEI handling. To do this, they increased the size of both the tail and the rudder. What could be a possible consequence?
optionA: Rudder authority decreases as it is harder to move
optionB: Lateral stability increases
optionC: Directional stability decreases
optionD: Pitch up due to increased drag from the larger tail
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

The fin can provide a small dihedral effect contribution. If the fin is large, the side force produced by sideslip may produce a rolling moment as well as the important yawing moment contribution. The fin contribution to purely lateral static stability is usually very small.

title: Shock stall:
optionA: occurs as soon as M<sub>CRIT</sub> is exceeded.
optionB: occurs when the lift coefficient, as a function of Mach number, reaches its maximum value.
optionC: results from flow separation behind the bow wave.
optionD: results from flow separation at the underside of the aerofoil.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Critical Mach Number: (MCRIT) The critical Mach number is the Mach number of the aircraft when the speed of the airflow over some part of the aircraft first reaches the speed of sound.

At high altitude, a large high-speed jet transport aircraft will be cruising at a speed marginally above its critical Mach number, and it will have a small shock wave on the wing. If such an aircraft overspeeds, the shock wave will rapidly grow larger, causing the static pressure to increase sharply in the immediate vicinity of the shock wave. The locally increased adverse pressure gradient will cause the boundary layer to separate immediately behind the shock wave. This is called a ‘shock stall’ because it results from a separated boundary layer just as the low speed stall does.
Shock stall occurs when the lift coefficient, as a function of Mach number, reaches its maximum value (for a given angle of attack).

title: During a flight, the stall warning goes off and the pilot does not notice it. What happens in a full stall?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: The aircraft nose rises even though the elevator is deflected fully downwards.
optionB: The aircraft nose will remain the same if the elevator is neutral.
optionC: Nose drops even though the elevator is deflected fully upwards.
optionD: The aircraft nose drops and then will rise independently of the elevator position.
explanationTotal:
STALL. A stall is an aerodynamic condition which occurs when smooth airflow over the airplane’s wings is disrupted, resulting in loss of lift. 
  • Impending Stall—an impending stall occurs when the AOA causes a stall warning, but has not yet reached the critical AOA. Indications of an impending stall can include buffeting, stick shaker, or aural warning.
  • Full Stall—a full stall occurs when the critical AOA is exceeded. Indications of a full stall are typically that an uncommanded nose-down pitch cannot be readily arrested, and this may be accompanied by an uncommanded rolling motion. For airplanes equipped with stick pushers, its activation is also a full stall indication.
The longer it takes for the pilot to recognize an impending stall, the more likely it is that a full stall will result. 

A stalled wing may be accompanied by one or more of the following:

  • Buffet
  • Poor pitch authority poor roll control (unresponsive flight controls).
  • An inability to arrest descent.

title: When an aircraft's Centre of Gravity (CG) is at the forward limit, the longitudinal static stability is (1) _____ and the pitch control forces are (2) _____ than when the CG is at the aft limit.
optionA: (1) highest; (2) higher
optionB: (1) lowest; (2) higher
optionC: (1) highest; (2) lower
optionD: (1) lowest; (2) lower
explanationTotal:
Aircraft longitudinal stability is directly related to the Centre of Gravity (CG) position. An aircraft with a more forward CG is more longitudinally stable than an aircraft with a more aft CG.

Placing the CG beyond the forward limit can cause an unacceptably high value of longitudinal stability, decreasing manoeuvrability by a significant amount. Placing the CG beyond the aft limit and the aircraft is too unstable, having excessive manoeuvrability.

If stability increases (CG moves forward) higher control forces are needed.

SUMMARY:
  • CG towards the forward limit makes an aircraft more stable, and control forces will be higher.
  • CG towards the aft limit decreases longitudinal static stability and reduces pitch control forces.

title: An aeroplane, when flying at its design speed for maximum gust intensity (VB) shall be able to withstand vertical gusts of up to...
optionA: 50 ft/sec
optionB: 25 ft/sec
optionC: 66 ft/sec
optionD: 100 ft/sec
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
It is a design requirement of CS25 that an airframe structure must be strong enough to withstand gusts both positive and negative that would cause a change of angle of attack so increasing load factor at three specified design speeds.

  • Speed VB (max. gust intensity speed): +/- 66 ft/sec
  • Speed VC (design cruise speed): +/- 50 ft/sec
  • Speed VD (design dive speed): +/- 25 ft/sec.

VB is quite a low airspeed so the aircraft would be flying at high alpha and it would take some time for an aircraft to slow from VC (the design cruising speed) to VB if it flew into turbulence. Therefore, another design strength requirement is for the aircraft also to be strong enough to withstand a vertical gust of 50 ft/ sec at VC.

title: During a take-off roll with a strong crosswind from the right, a four-engine jet aeroplane with wing-mounted engines experiences an engine failure. The failure of which engine will cause the greatest control problem?
optionA: The right outboard engine.
optionB: The left inboard engine.
optionC: The left outboard engine.
optionD: The right inboard engine.
explanationTotal:
During a crosswind take-off, an airplane tends to weathercock into wind (yaw into the wind), due to the wind acting on the fin which produces a yaw moment.

In this case, with a crosswind from the right, the aircraft will tend to yaw right.
  • If a left engine fails, the right side will produce much more thrust than the left side, resulting in a left-yaw. This will oppose the yaw-right moment.
  • If a right engine fails, the left side will produce more thrust than the right side, resulting in a right-yaw. This will add to the right-yaw moment.

The engine's distance to the CG is greatest for outboard engines, which means that they have the largest moment arms. The loss of an outboard engine will result in the strongest yaw tendency.

Therefore, the failure of the outboard engine on the windward side of the airplane is the most difficult to counteract.

title: An aircraft departs with MTOW and with the CG on the aft limit. On the return flight, due to no payload being carried the CG shifts to the forward limit. How will the static stability have changed on the second leg?
optionA: Increased.
optionB: Decreased.
optionC: Same.
optionD: CG position does not affect stability.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Longitudinal stability is motion about the lateral axis.

Static Longitudinal stability is the aircraft's natural tendency when disturbed in pitch, to return to its former trimmed angle of attack without pilot input, and is desirable throughout the aircraft's complete speed range.
