For the study of stability, we consider the changes in magnitude of lift force due to changes in angle of attack, acting through a stationary point, the aerodynamic centre (AC).

There are two moments to consider: the wing moment and the tail moment. The wing moment is a function of the change in wing lift multiplied by arm ‘x’. The tail moment is a function of the change in tailplane lift multiplied by arm ‘y’. The length of both arms is dependent upon CG position. If the CG is considered in a more forward position, the tail arm is larger and the wing arm is smaller. A more forward CG position increases static longitudinal stability.

If the nose-down (negative) tail moment is greater than the nose-up (positive) wing moment, the aircraft will have static longitudinal stability.

title: Consider two aircraft, the only difference between the two is that one has larger winglets than the other. In the aircraft with the larger winglets, ground effect is expected to:
optionA: decrease because the winglets reduce overall wing tip vortices.
optionB: increase because the winglets reduce overall wing tip vortices.
optionC: decrease because winglets increase overall Drag.
optionD: increase because winglets increase overall Drag.
explanationTotal:
Ground effect is caused by rising warm air off the ground, by a reduction in the amount of downwash behind the wings, and by the tendency of the aircraft not to slow (decreased drag) resulting from the reduction of wing-tip vortices.

Winglets are aerodynamically eficient surfaces located at the wing tips. They are designed to reduce induced drag. They dispense the span-wise airflow from the upper and lower surfaces at different points, thus preventing the intermixing of these airflows that otherwise would create induced-drag vortices.

Winglets reduce the size of the vortices and so ground effect will decrease. Larger winglets are more effective at reducing the size of the vortices.

title:
Which of these statements about VMCG determination are correct or incorrect?

I. VMCG may be determined using both lateral and directional control.
II. During VMCG determination, the lateral deviation from the runway centreline may be not more than 30 ft.
optionA: I is correct, II is correct.
optionB: I is correct, II is incorrect.
optionC: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
optionD: I is incorrect, II is correct.
explanationTotal:
According to CS 25.149 and CS 23.149 - Minimum Control Speed:

Minimum Control Speed on the ground (VMCG) is defined as the calibrated airspeed during the take-off run at which, when the critical engine is suddenly made inoperative, it is possible to maintain control of the aeroplane using the primary aerodynamic control (rudder control) alone (without the use of nosewheel steering), as limited by 667 N of force (150 lbf), and the lateral control to the extent of keeping the wings level to enable the take-off to be safely continued using normal piloting skill.

In the determination of VMCG, assuming that the path of the aeroplane accelerating with all engines operating is along the centreline of the runway, its path from the point at which the critical engine is made inoperative to the point at which recovery to a direction parallel to the centreline is completed, may not deviate more than 9.1 m (30 ft) laterally from the centreline at any point.

title: An aeroplane has a stall speed of 100 kt at a load factor n = 1. In a turn with a load factor of n = 2, the stall speed is:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionD: 70 kt.
explanationTotal:
The increase in load factor in a turn also increases stall speed. The stall speed in a manoeuvre increases as the square root of the load factor (LF):

  • VS = VS1g √ n
VS = 100 kts x √2
VS = 100 kts x 1.4142
VS = 141 kts

title: When flaps are deployed at constant angle of attack the lift coefficient will:
optionA: remain the same.
optionB: increase.
optionC: decrease.
optionD: vary as the square of IAS.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Slats and flaps increase lift. This can help the aircraft take off with a shortened ground roll, as the aircraft generates more lift at a lower speed with flaps and slats extended. However, flaps and slats shorten the ground roll, but also decrease climb performance as they generate drag. Therefore, after takeoff these two devices are retracted. Flaps and slats both decrease stall speed, but flaps generate much more drag. The flaps are therefore retracted first and slats afterwards.

Flaps increase CL for a specific angle of attack, giving a wing with flaps extended a higher CL and therefore higher lift than a wing without. Flaps also increase CLMAX and the CD for a wing, they decrease critical AoA. Slats do not necessarily increase CL for a specific AoA, but they increase the value for CLMAX, meaning that the aircraft stalls at a much higher AoA than normal. They also increase the drag a little on the wing where they are extended.

title: A pilot makes a turn with a speed higher than V<sub>S</sub>. What could be the cause of a stall?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Increased load factor and stall speed in the turn without adding power.
optionB: Decreased load factor and stall speed in the turn.
optionC: A coordinated turn.
optionD: Pitch down.
explanationTotal:
An aircraft will stall at a constant angle of attack (known as the critical angle of attack). Because most aircraft do not have angle of attack indicators (except "eyebrows" on some electronic flight instrument system displays), the pilot has to rely on airspeed indications. However, the speed at which the aircraft will stall is variable depending on the effects of the following properties.

For instance, load factor (i.e. in a turn) can increase the stall speed. Remember that stall speed is proportional to "√n", where “n” equals the load factor.

In a steady coordinated turn, the load factor (n) will increase according to the following equation:
  • n = 1 / cos a
  • where “a” is the bank angle.

To compensate for the increased load factor and, consequently, greater stall speed and avoid a stall/spin, the pilot must add power

title: Which type of force tends to decrease the angle of attack on a propeller (fixed or variable pitch)?
optionA: Aerodynamic force.
optionB: Centrifugal force.
optionC: No forces reduce the blade angle of attack.
optionD: Centripetal force.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
The centrifugal force to which a rotating propeller is subject creates tensile stress at the blade root and a torque across the chord of the blade, about the pitch-change axis. The centrifugal force (CF) acting along a radial from the propeller hub is divided into components parallel to the pitch-change axis and at right angles to that axis.

Because in normal flight the propeller blade has a positive angle of attack the blade leading edge is above the blade trailing edge, which creates a twisting moment about the pitch-change axis (the blade’s longitudinal axis) attempting to bring the blade mass in line with the plane of rotation.

The Centrifugal Twisting Moment tends to decrease the blade angle of attack, thereby ‘fining’ the pitch. Therefore, the fitted pitch-change mechanism requires little energy to reduce the blade angle but needs a lot more effort to increase the blade angle, i.e. coarsen the propeller pitch.

title:
The correct drag formula is:
(note: RHO = density)
optionA: DRAG = CD × ½ (1 / RHO) × V<sup>2</sup> × S
optionB: DRAG = CD × ½ RHO × V × S
optionC: DRAG = CD × 2 × RHO × V<sup>2</sup> × S
optionD: DRAG = CD × ½ RHO × V<sup>2</sup> × S
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The force directly opposing the forward movement of the aeroplane through the air is referred to as drag. It is the resistance to forward motion and is assumed to act along a line parallel to the longitudinal axis.

Total Drag is sub-divided into two main types:

INDUCED DRAG - the result of lift generation.
PARASITE DRAG - independent of lift generation.

The sum of parasite drag and induced drag is the total drag, which can be calculated from the formula:

Total Drag = CD x 1/2 x ρ x V2 x S

Where V = the free airspeed

title: An aircraft is flying straight and level when it experiences moderate turbulence. The pilot observes a rapid reduction in IAS towards zero, while all other instrument indications are unchanged. What should the pilot do?
optionA: Ensure that the existing aircraft attitude and thrust settings remain unchanged.
optionB: Immediately apply full power to restore IAS.
optionC: Immediately pitch the aircraft down to avoid a stall.
optionD: Switch off anti-icing equipment, which may have malfunctioned.
explanationTotal:
UNRELIABLE AIRSPEED

A failure to promptly recognise and respond to erroneous flight instrument indications can result in loss of control.

The most probable reason for erroneous airspeed and/or altitude information is an obstruction of the pitot and/or static probes.

It is highly unlikely that the aircraft probes will be obstructed at the same time, to the same degree and in the same way.

Abnormally large Mach number or IAS fluctuations, and differences between the indications at each pilot position, or between target and actual speed, may suggest an unreliable airspeed condition.

Abnormal correlation between the basic flight parameters (pitch, thrust, airspeed, altitude, and vertical speed indications) allow the flight crew to suspect an erroneous speed/altitude indication:

- The altitude does not increase, whereas there is an important nose-up pitch and high thrust
- The IAS increases, whereas there is an important nose-up pitch
- The IAS decreases, whereas there is an important nose-down pitch
- The IAS decreases, whereas there is a nose-down pitch and the aircraft is descending.

In the event of unreliable airspeed indications, a crew should fly the approximate pitch and thrust normally expected at that stage of flight until it is discovered which (if any) system is indicating correctly or the problem is resolved.

Aircraft manufacturers issue appropriate guidance for specific aircraft types including pitch and thrust settings to fly at different stages of flight if airspeed information is not available.

The pilots should use sources independent from the pitot static systems, capable of providing reliable information for situational awareness:

- RPM (N1) for engine thrust indication
- Attitude indicator
- Stall warning
- Ground speed and position information from Navigation systems.

title: How does the Drag vs. TAS graph change as altitude increases?
optionA: The graph shows a rightward shift, indicating an increase in TAS for the same level of drag.
optionB: The graph remains unchanged, indicating a consistent level of drag across varying TAS.
optionC: The graph shows a fluctuating pattern, with no consistent trend in drag with increasing TAS.
optionD: The graph shows a leftward shift, indicating an increase in TAS for the same level of drag.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
If density decreases, TAS will have to increase to keep the dynamic pressure constant. The values of drag will remain the same, but occur at a higher TAS.

The effect of a higher-pressure altitude or a lower density is a shift of the total drag graph to the right (higher TAS for a certain drag). If density decreases, VDMIN (TAS) will increase and minimum drag will remain the same.

title:
An airplane's sideslip angle is defined as the angle between:

1. lift vector
2. speed vector
3. x-z plane of symmetry
4. normal axis
5. horizontal plane
optionA: 1 and 3
optionB: 2 and 5
optionC: 2 and 3
optionD: 2 and 4
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The rotation of an aircraft about its normal, or vertical, axis is a yaw. If this movement is the result of an undesirable disturbance, then the ability of the airplane to return to its original heading without the assistance of any control-surface movement is a measure of its directional static stability. It is a measure of the aircraft’s ability to realign itself with the relative airflow.

Sideslip is the displacement angle of the airplane’s longitudinal axis (plane of symmetry) in azimuth from the relative airflow (speed vector).

It is positive when the relative airflow is to the right of the longitudinal axis and negative when the relative airflow is left of the longitudinal axis.

title: A pilot is performing flight tests on two airplanes: Airplane 1 and Airplane 2, which has double the mass of Airplane 1. While flying Airplane 1, the pilot performs a steady level turn with 18° angle of bank and notes the radius of turn using external visual cues and/or references. If the pilot performs the same steady level turn at the same TAS with Airplane 2, the required angle bank to maintain the same radius of turn would…
optionA: be greater than 18°, because the centripetal force to maintain the same radius of turn will quadruple.
optionB: be greater than 18°, because the centripetal force to maintain the same radius of the turn will increase by the same proportion.
optionC: be less than 18°, because the centripetal force to maintain the same radius of turn will decrease by the same proportion.
optionD: still be 18°, because the centripetal force to maintain the same radius of the turn will increase by the same proportion.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
TURNING

For an aircraft to change direction, a force is required to deflect it towards the centre of the turn. This is called the centripetal force.

Banking the aircraft inclines the lift - it is the horizontal component of lift which causes the aircraft to turn. If the aircraft is banked and the angle of attack kept constant, the vertical component of lift will be too small to balance the weight and the aircraft will start to descend.

As the angle of bank increases, the angle of attack must be increased to bring about a greater total lift. The vertical component must be large enough to maintain level flight, while the horizontal component is large enough to produce the required centripetal force.

EFFECT OF WEIGHT ON TURNING

In a steady level turn, if thrust is ignored, lift provides a force to balance weight and centripetal force to turn the aircraft. If the same TAS and angle of bank can be obtained, the radius of turn is basically independent of weight or the aircraft type.

Not all aircraft can reach the same angle of bank at the same TAS. If weight increases, the vertical component of lift required increases, but the centripetal force to maintain the same radius of turn also increases in the same proportion. The lift required, although it is greater, has the same inclination to the vertical as before and the bank angle is the same.

title: What is the position of the elevator in relation to the trimmable horizontal stabiliser of a power assisted aeroplane that is in trim?
optionA: The elevator is always deflected slightly downwards in order to have sufficient remaining flare capability.
optionB: The elevator deflection (compared with the stabiliser position) is always zero.
optionC: At a forward CG the elevator is deflected upward and at an aft CG the elevator is deflected downward.
optionD: The position depends on speed, the position of slats and flaps and the position of the centre of gravity.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Instead of using elevators to change the angle of attack and camber of the tail plane, the whole of the tail plane lifting surface is constructed in such a manner that it has a mutable incidence or changeable angle of attack. This is known as the trimmable horizontal stabilizer (THS).

The advantages of this tail plane over a conventional fixed tail plane, with an elevator and trim tab, is that the trim is more powerful, it creates less drag, retains full elevator movement at extreme trim angles and is able to cope with a larger range of CG positions than traditional elevator trim tabs.

The angle of incidence of an adjustable stabilizer is controlled by the airplane’s trim system, which alters the jack datum setting. The position of a properly trimmed variable-incidence tail plane depends, most importantly on, the CG position, the airspeed, the thrust setting and on the flap/slat position.

When correctly trimmed the elevator angle relative to the horizontal stabilizer is neutral and the stabilized speed is referred to as the ‘trim speed.’ Thus, the trim may be used to set the desired speed without having to hold the elevator out of its trimmed position.

A tail-heavy airplane would require the elevator to be deflected downward, which when the variable incidence tail plane is trimmed has no elevator deflection; it is in the neutral position and the leading edge of the adjustable stabilizer is up.

If it becomes jammed in the cruise position, when approaching to land select a higher landing speed and/or use a lower flap setting. When trimmed for a forward CG position (nose heavy) the stabilizer leading edge is lower than the trailing edge.

title: Why would smooth fairings and fillets be used on an aircraft's fuselage?
optionA: To increase the structural strength of the fillet area.
optionB: To enhance the aircraft's visual appearance.
optionC: To increase the lift generated by the fillet.
optionD: To reduce interference drag.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
When considering a complete aircraft, parasite drag will be greater than the sum of the individual parts. Additional drag results from boundary layer interference at the junction of different parts as wing/fuselage, wing/engine nacelle, etc.

Fairings and filleting will be used to minimise interference drag. They soften the transition between two components of the aircraft.

title:
Refer to figure.
Which of the three lift augmentation devices is/are represented by the graph in the annex?
optionA: 1 and 3
optionB: 3 only
optionC: 1 only
optionD: 1 and 2
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Aircraft are fitted with high lift devices to reduce the take-off and landing distances and improve slow flying characteristics.

The three leading edge devices shown in the annex are:

  1. Leading Edge Flaps - similar to trailing edge flaps, they increase the camber of the wing to increase CL and CLMAX
  2. Kreuger Flaps - part of the lower surface of the leading edge, which can be rotated about its forward edge to force more airflow over the top of the wing at high angles of attack.
  3. Slats - These are small "extra leading edges" that move forward in front of the leading edge of the wing, creating a small slot behind, where airflow is sped up and re-energised, delaying the stalling angle of attack without increasing the CL at normal angles of attack.

Kreuger Flaps and Slats are often used in conjunction, with Kreuger Flaps being used on the inboard section of an wing and slats being used outboard of the engine pylons, to promote root stall tendency due to the Kreuger Flaps being less effective.

Leading edge flaps, like trailing edge flaps, increase CL values for all angles of attack, also increasing drag, with only a small increase in the critical angle of attack (but that varies depending on the specifics of the wing). They are less common to use on large commercial aircraft than the other leading edge devices, but are used on a few different fighter jets, amongst other aircraft types.

Slats do not increase CL for normal values of AoA, instead, they just delay the stalling AoA, allowing for a higher CLMAX due to the higher critical AoA.

Note: The feedback for this question has not confirmed the correct answer, and we have had to make a few educated guesses whilst creating the annex from limited feedback. Please let us know if you see this in the exam, and any differences you can remember, as well as if you got it correct/what the correct answer is, thank you!

title:
Which of these statements about flutter are correct or incorrect?

I. Aero-elastic coupling does not affect flutter characteristics.
II. The risk of flutter increases as IAS increases.
optionA: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
optionB: I is incorrect, II is correct.
optionC: I is correct, II is correct.
optionD: I is correct, II is incorrect.
explanationTotal:
Incorrect balancing or slack control runs may cause a control surface to vibrate in the airflow this is not a torsional vibration or flexural vibration. The wing is subject to the interaction of the airfoil mass and the aerodynamic load imposed on the airfoil causing distortion by bending and torsion of the structure that can result in a violent vibration in the resonance frequency, which if excessive can cause structural failure.
This is ‘flutter’ and the aeroelastic coupling will affect its characteristics. Therefore, statement 1 is incorrect.
The risk of experiencing flutter increases with IAS. Therefore, statement 2 is correct.

title: An aeroplane has the following flap settings: 0°, 15°, 30° and 45°. Slats can also be selected. Which of the following selections will most adversely affect the C<sub>L</sub>/C<sub>D</sub> ratio?
optionA: Flaps from 30° to 45°.
optionB: The slats.
optionC: Flaps from 0° to 15°.
optionD: Flaps from 15° to 30°.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
Figure 1 and figure 2 show the variation of the lift increment with flap angle and the variation of drag increment with flap angle. The increment in lift is decreasing and the increment in drag is increasing as flaps are deployed. It is important to note that any amount of flap increases drag.

As in the case of the lift increments, the drag increments with increasing flap angle are not constant: the increments in drag get larger as the flap angle increases.

As flap angle increases, the value a drag becomes progressively larger than the value of lift. This means that the ratio
CL / CD will become progressively smaller as flaps are deployed. Therefore, the CL / CD ratio will be more adversely affected with higher settings of flaps.

title: An aircraft flying straight and level is displaced from equilibrium and enters in a spiral dive. After recovering from the spiral dive, the pilot applies again opposite rudder. How does this affect the aircraft?
optionA: The aircraft may enter a secondary spiral dive.
optionB: The aircraft will recover faster from the spiral dive.
optionC: The aircraft will recover from the spiral dive with some delay.
optionD: The aircraft will stall.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
SPIRAL DIVERGENCE/INSTABILITY

Spiral divergence will exist when static directional stability is very large when compared to the lateral stability. The character of spiral divergence is not violent.

When a small sideslip is introduced, the strong directional stability tends to restore the nose into the wind while the relatively weak “dihedral effect” lags in restoring the aeroplane laterally. The rate of divergence in the spiral motion is usually so gradual that the pilot can control the tendency without difficulty.

Spiral instability is normally considered less objectionable than oscillatory instability, so most aircraft are designed to be spirally unstable.

With this characteristic, when the aircraft is yawed, either by the prolonged application of rudder or asymmetric power, a rolling moment in the direction of yaw occurs and the aircraft quickly enters a spiral dive.

This can occur when flying at low airspeeds under asymmetric power conditions, when excessive yaw due to too much power is coupled with insufficient rudder control to balance it, and may quickly place an aircraft in a dangerous attitude.

title: Following an engine failure, rudder is used to counteract yaw and aileron to bank towards the live engine. For a given airspeed, aeroplane controllability will be better at a...
optionA: low aeroplane mass, due to greater rudder effectiveness because of less sideslip.
optionB: low aeroplane mass, due to greater rudder effectiveness because of greater sideslip.
optionC: high aeroplane mass, due to greater rudder effectiveness because of greater sideslip.
optionD: high aeroplane mass, due to greater rudder effectiveness because of less sideslip
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
When an engine fails on a multi-engine aircraft there will be a decrease in thrust and an increase in drag on the side with the failed engine:

  • airspeed will decay.
  • the nose will drop and.
  • most significantly, there will be an immediate yawing moment towards the failed engine.
The forces and moments acting on an aircraft following failure of the left engine are shown in figure 1. The aircraft has a yawing moment towards the dead engine. The pilot has applied rudder to stop the yaw. The vital action when an engine fails is to stop the yaw.
Any increase in weight ultimately reduces the aircraft’s overall performance, but in a banked condition, it induces greater side slip, making the rudder more effective for a given airspeed.
Thus, the greater the weight, the greater the induced side slip and the greater the rudder effectiveness. This benefit is insignificant compared to the penalties associated with any additional weight.

title:
Refer to figure.
Choose the correct statement:
optionA: Aerofoil A corresponds to line 3.
optionB: Aerofoil A corresponds to line 4.
optionC: Aerofoil D corresponds to line 1.
optionD: Aerofoil C corresponds to line 2.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
A completely symmetrical airfoil will intersect the vertical axis of the graph at the origin (0).
A positively cambered airfoil will generate more lift at the same speed (and therefore has a higher CL) than a symmetrical airfoil and therefore intersects the vertical axis above the origin (and generates 0 lift at a negative angle of attack).
A negatively cambered airfoil will generate less lift at the same speed (which translates into a lower CL at a certain speed) and therefore intersects the vertical axis below the origin.

An increased camber generates a higher value of CL at the same Angle of Attack.

Therefore, we have the following combinations:

  • Aerofoil A corresponds to line 3.
  • Aerofoil B corresponds to line 4.
  • Aerofoil C corresponds to line 1.
  • Aerofoil D corresponds to line 2.

title: The induced angle of attack is the result of:
optionA: a large local angle of attack in a two-dimensional flow.
optionB: downwash due to tip vortices.
optionC: change in direction of flow due to the effective angle of attack.
optionD: downwash due to flow separation.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
We know that induced drag is a side effect of the creation of lift. The pressure differential between the top and bottom of the wing creates a vortex at the tip of the wing. This is because of the upwash of high pressure air that flows around the tip and then becomes a downwash behind the upper side of the airfoil. This downwash reduces the effective angle of attack and therefore reduces the lift created, and also causes and additional drag.

title: Which combination produces the least amount of induced drag?
optionA: Low wing at landing.
optionB: High wing at landing.
optionC: Low wing at take-off.
optionD: High wing at take-off.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
Ground effect occurs because the surface alters the airflow pattern around the wings. Primarily, the surface restricts the formation of the wingtip vortices.

This results in a reduction in the amount of induced downwash behind the wing and increases the wing’s effective angle of attack.

It also alters the pressure distribution around the wing and the amount of lift developed. This occurs because the change in effective angle of attack increases the wing’s coefficient of lift (CL) and thus its lifting capability at any given angle of attack.

THE INFLUENCE OF GROUND EFFECT ON LANDING
When an aircraft enters ground effect during the landing phase of flight, the sudden increase in lift and reduction in drag cause it to experience a floating tendency. The aircraft also tends to pitch nose-down due to the reduction in download on the tailplane.

THE INFLUENCE OF GROUND EFFECT ON TAKE-OFF
During the take-off phase of flight, as the aircraft leaves ground effect the wing tip vortices rapidly grow in magnitude producing an increase in downwash behind the wing. This causes a reduction in the lift produced at a given angle of attack and the associated rapid increase in induced drag may prevent a successful take-off. The increased downwash acting on the tailplane increases the download, resulting in a nose-up pitching moment.

The magnitude of the wing tip vortices, and thus downwash, determine the amount of induced drag produced by the wing. The closer the aircraft is to the surface, the greater the reduction in induced drag at any given angle of attack. Thus, a low wing aircraft on landing will produce the least amount of Induced Drag. (figure 2)

title: How does the V<sub>A</sub> change if the the aeroplane's mass decreases with 20%?
optionA: Decreases by 10% approximately
optionB: Decreases by 20% approximately
optionC: Increases by 20% approximately
optionD: Increases by 10% approximately
explanationTotal:
Maneuvering Speed (VA) is the speed at which an airplane will stall before exceeding its maximum load limit.

Any stalling speed changes with the square root of the change in mass.

A 20% reduction in mass is a change of mass by a factor of 0.80. Consequently, the stall speed will reduce by a factor of:

  • √0.80 = 0.90
For example, if VA was 100 kt, the new VA (at a lower mass) would be:
  • 100 kt x 0.90 = 90 kt
Which corresponds to a 10% reduction.

title: During a training flight you want to demonstrate engine failures by producing the greatest possible yawing moment. For a twin-engined propeller aeroplane with counter-rotating propellers, you would fail:
optionA: Any engine, as the thrust arm for both engines is equal.
optionB: The left engine, because its thrust arm is longer.
optionC: The left engine, because the thrust arm of the right engine is longer.
optionD: The right engine, because the thrust arm of the left engine is longer.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Asymmetric blade effect (also known as ‘P’ Factor)

Propeller blades are not flat, they are in fact shaped as small wings. As a consequence, as the angle of attack of the airplane increases, the air passing by hits the blades differently:

The down-going blade (viewed from the cockpit) will have a larger angle of attack compared to the up-going blade, generating more thrust. This then means that the down-swinging blade exerts a greater force than the up-going blade. For this reason, the thrust line will be displaced to the right of the engine centre line.
  • Propellers rotating in the same direction (clockwise): if both engines rotate clockwise, the right engine will have a longer thrust arm than the left engine. This difference in thrust will give a yawing moment to the left with a clockwise rotating propeller in a nose-up attitude. The failure of the left-hand engine will result in a larger yaw effect via the operating right-hand engine, rather than vice-versa. The left engine is therefore the critical engine.
  • Counter-rotating propellers: they are called counter-rotating propellers because the propeller on one wing turn in the opposite direction to the one on the other wing. The principle advantage of counter-rotation is to balance propeller torque effects thus eliminating any problems associated with a Critical engine.
=> For both counter-rotating inwards or outwards, the yawing moment will be the same regardless if the right or left engine fails.

title: What could happen if a high-speed aircraft climbs with constant IAS at high altitudes?
optionA: Increased turbulence.
optionB: Engine failure.
optionC: Aileron droop.
optionD: Mach buffet.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
Stall boundaries set a lower limit to the operating speed, according to the load factor. In the case of a high-speed aircraft, there is also an upper limit which is due to the approach of shock stall and the associated buffet which occurs if the aircraft enters the transonic speed range. The limits associated with these effects give the buffet boundaries.

The Mach number is defined as the ratio between the TAS and the LSS (Local speed of sound):

M = TAS ÷ LSS

The speed of propagation of small pressure waves depends upon the temperature of the air ONLY.

Effect on Mach Number of Climbing at a Constant IAS:
- Temperature decreases with increasing altitude, so the speed of sound will decrease as altitude is increased.
- If altitude is increased at a constant IAS, the TAS increases.
- Therefore, the Mach number will increase if altitude is increased at a constant IAS. This is because TAS gets bigger and LSS gets smaller.

As the climb continues, an altitude will be reached at which the flight crew must stop flying at a constant IAS and fly at a constant Mach number, to avoid accidentally exceeding MMO.

title: Select the correct consequence of a right engine failure with flaps extended, when flying a multi engine aircraft:
optionA: Right roll, flaps will increase the roll.
optionB: Left roll, flaps will increase the roll.
optionC: Left roll, flaps will decrease the roll.
optionD: Right roll, flaps will decrease the roll.
explanationTotal:
If a multi-engine aircraft suffers engine failure when airborne, there are two immediate aerodynamic effects:
  • The initial effect is the yawing that occurs due to the asymmetry of the thrust line. 
  • The second effect is roll. This occurs when the aircraft continues to yaw towards the failed engine resulting in a decrease in lift from the retreating wing and a yaw-induced roll towards the failed engine => aircraft will roll to the right.
Flap extended on the left side will increase this right roll => greater lift on the left wing.

title: The calibrated airspeed during the take-off run at which, when the critical engine is suddenly made inoperative, it is possible to maintain control of the aeroplane using the rudder control alone, and the lateral control to the extent of keeping the wings level to enable the take-off to be safely continued using normal piloting skill, is called...
optionA: VMC.
optionB: V2.
optionC: V1.
optionD: V<sub>MCG</sub>.
explanationTotal:
VMCG, the minimum control speed on the ground, is the calibrated airspeed during the takeoff run, at which, when the critical engine is suddenly made inoperative, it is possible to maintain control of the airplane using the rudder control alone (without the use of nose wheel steering) to enable the take-off to be safely continued using normal piloting skill.
The rudder control forces may not exceed 150 pounds (68.1 kg) and, until the airplane becomes airborne, the lateral control may only be used to the extent of keeping the wings level. In the determination of VMCG, assuming that the path of the airplane accelerating with all engines operating is along the center of the runway, its path from the point at which the critical engine is made inoperative to the point at which recovery to a direction parallel to the center line is completed may not deviate more than 30 ft (9.144 m) laterally from the center line at any point. As with VMCA, this must be established with:
  • maximum available take-off power or thrust on the engines.
  • the airplane trimmed for take-off.
  • the most unfavorable CG position.
  • maximum sea level take-off weight.

title:
Refer to figure.
Which of the graphs correctly illustrates how power required changes with increasing altitude?
optionA: Figure 1
optionB: Figure 2
optionC: Figure 3
optionD: Figure 4
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Aeroplane drag is divided into two types at low speeds, parasite drag and induced drag. Parasite drag increases with the square of the speed, induced drag changes with the inverse square of the speed (highest at low speeds). Together, they create the familiar drag curve of an aircraft.

Sometimes, we have to convert that graph again, from drag (thrust required) to something more friendly to propeller aircraft. Propeller aircraft cannot measure thrust output, only power (Power = Thrust x Velocity). This means that it is often useful to change thrust required graphs into power required graphs, by multiplying by speed (TAS) again. The curve looks the same, but if you get to compare them, the power required curve is steeper and a little to the left.

This is where it can get a little complicated, as drag graphs are often created with IAS on the X-axis, for easy usage at all altitudes, but Power = Thrust x True Airspeed. This means that for the same thrust required (drag), an increase in altitude causes a higher TAS and therefore a higher power required.

There we have it then; the power required curve will look almost the same (There is a slight flat section of figure 2 but it is not important, imagine it looks the same as the others), but for each point on the curve, the TAS will be higher (so the curve moves to the right) and therefore the power required will also be higher (so the graph moves upwards). It must be figure 2.

title: Ice build-up on propeller blades...
optionA: increases the propeller’s RPM.
optionB: reduces the generated thrust.
optionC: reduces the propeller’s drag.
optionD: has a neutral effect on propeller efficiency.
explanationTotal:
Ice contamination on the propeller has the same effect as ice on the wings, in that both reduce the efficiency of the airfoils. Leading edge ice on the propeller reduces the generated thrust in the same way the lift of the wing is reduced; by creating turbulent air flow.

In the same way, as the drag of an ice contaminated airplane increases, the resisting force on the propeller increases for a given rpm and blade angle. Ice separating from the propeller blades, as well as vibration due to propeller imbalance, may cause damage to the airplane structure. Since ice on the propeller blades reduces the available thrust, extra power may be required from the engine to overcome the increased drag, decreasing propeller efficiency.

title: The Mean Aerodynamic Chord (MAC) for a given wing of any planform is...
optionA: the chord of an equivalent untwisted, rectangular wing with the same pitching moment and lift characteristics as the actual wing.
optionB: the chord of a equivalent rectangular wing with the same leading and trailing edge positions as the actual wing half way between the wing root and wing tip.
optionC: the average chord of the aeroplane’s wing, which is used to determine the pitching moment and lift characteristic of the whole wing.
optionD: determined by dividing the actual aeroplane’s wing area by the wing span.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Mean Aerodynamic Chord

The chord line that passes through the geometric center of the plan area (the centroid) of an airfoil is the Mean Aerodynamic Chord (MAC) and for any planform is equal to the chord of a rectangular wing having the same wing span and the same pitching moment and lift.
It is usually located at approximately 33% of the semi-span from the wing root. The MAC is often used to reference the location of the center of gravity. It is the primary reference for longitudinal stability.

title: Moving the CG from an aft to a forward position during flight will:
optionA: decrease fuel consumption and decrease the aircraft’s longitudinal stability.
optionB: increase fuel consumption and decrease the aircraft’s longitudinal stability.
optionC: decrease fuel consumption and increase theaircraft’s longitudinal stability.
optionD: increase fuel consumption and increase the aircraft’s longitudinal stability.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
The relationship between your aircraft's performance and CG location is simple: by moving your CG forward and aft, you change the amount of tail down force and lift you need for stable flight.
When you create more lift, you create more induced drag, and your performance goes down.

The aircraft cruises slower with an forward CG location because of increased drag.
The drag is increased because a higher AOA and much downward deflection of the stabilizer are required to support the aircraft and overcome the nose-down pitching tendency. Increased drag means (causes more fuel consumption) degreaded endurance and range.

title: Assuming incompressible flow, when considering streamlines in the vicinity of an aerofoil, which of the following answers is correct?
optionA: Converging streamlines indicate that the speed of the flow is increasing and that the static pressure is decreasing.
optionB: Diverging streamlines indicate that the speed of the flow is decreasing and that the static pressure is decreasing.
optionC: Diverging streamlines indicate that the speed of the flow is increasing and that the static pressure is increasing.
optionD: Converging streamlines indicate that the speed of the flow is decreasing and that the static pressure is increasing.
explanationTotal:
When considering streamlines, we can say that converging streamlines indicate an increasing airflow velocity, and diverging lines indicate a decreasing airflow velocity.

Now when considering the pressure, we know that the total pressure always remains constant in subsonic airflow. Next, knowing that the total pressure is equal to the dynamic pressure plus the static pressure, we know that if one increases, the other must decrease to maintain a constant total pressure.

Now what is the dynamic pressure and what is static pressure:

  • Dynamic pressure is equal to: q = ½ rho V2. Therefore we can say that the dynamic pressure is proportional to the velocity of the airflow.
  • Static pressure is the pressure that any object feels even when not moving. This pressure is caused by the force of gravity forcing particles closer together and pushing against each other and any objects around them.

Knowing that dynamic pressure is basically the velocity of the airflow, we can say that if the velocity increase, hence increasing the dynamic pressure, there has to be a reduction in static pressure.
This is known as Bernoulli’s principle!

What this means for our question is that:

  • Converging streamlines indicate a speed increase
  • Diverging streamlines indicated a speed decrease
  • A decrease in static pressure occurs with an increasing speed
  • And an increase in static pressure occurs with a decreasing speed

title: While performing the “After Engine Start” procedures, the pilots of a commercial jet aircraft forget to set the slats/flaps in the calculated take-off position. What could be a consequence of this action?
optionA: A safe to take-off will be possible as this case is considered in the V<sub>R</sub> calculation.
optionB: After rotation, the aircraft will stall after getting airborne.
optionC: There would be insufficient elevator authority such that the aeroplane will NOT rotate.
optionD: Acceleration will be lower, but a safe take-off will be conducted.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Take-off with lower-than-calculated flap position leads to several possible incidents, since the real stall speed will be higher than the calculated one.

If the pilots happen to think that the flaps are lowered for take-off and they calculated their rotation speed taking the flaps into consideration, then it is an issue. With the flaps, the rotation speed will be lower than that without and the premature take-off will result in a stall. Flaps give more lift at a given speed, hence with flaps the rotation is speed is lower.

There is also risk of tail strike, where the rotation is started before is it possible at lift-off, consequently angle of attack might be increased up to tailstrike.

title: In order to fly a steady co-ordinated horizontal rate one turn at a lower airspeed, the bank angle must be:
optionA: increased and the turn radius will increase.
optionB: decreased and the turn radius will increase.
optionC: increased and the turn radius will decrease.
optionD: decreased and the turn radius will decrease.
explanationTotal:
The formula for turning radius is as follows

r = v2 / ( g * tan(bank angle) )
r = radius
v = velocity
g = gravitational constant (9.81, however in some questions stated to be 10)

From this formula we can derive that the radius of turn decreases with decreasing airspeed.
If we fly at a lower speed and still keep the same bank angle, the rate of turn will increase.
Therefore, if the speed decreases and we still want to achieve the rate one turn (3 degrees per second) we have to decrease our bank angle.

title: For a normal stable aeroplane, the centre of gravity is located:
optionA: between the aft limit and the neutral point of the aeroplane.
optionB: with a sufficient minimum margin ahead of the neutral point of the aeroplane.
optionC: aft of the neutral point of the aeroplane.
optionD: at the neutral point of the aeroplane.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
A variation of CG position can cause large changes in the static longitudinal stability. In the conventional airplane configuration, the large changes in stability with CG variation are primarily due to the large changes in the wing contribution.

As the CG is gradually moved aft, the airplane static stability decreases, then becomes neutral then unstable. The CG position which produces zero slope and neutral static stability is referred to as the “neutral point”. The neutral point may be imagined as the effective aerodynamic center of the entire airplane configuration, i.e. with the CG at the neutral point, all changes in net lift effectively occur at that point and no change in pitching moment results. The neutral point defines the most aft CG position without static instability.

For an airplane to always have positive longitudinal static stability the CG must be ahead of the neutral point, so that the wing-pitching moment always exceeds the tail plane pitching moment. The further aft the neutral point is from the CG the greater is the static longitudinal stability.

title:
Refer to figure.
The line representing the effect of the tail on the longitudinal static stability of an aeroplane is line (1) _____, and it has a (2) _____ contribution.
optionA: (1) Y; (2) stabilising
optionB: (1) Z; (2) stabilising
optionC: (1) Y; (2) destabilising
optionD: (1) Z; (2) destabilising
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
Evidence of static stability is shown by a tendency to return to equilibrium, or “trim”, upon displacement.
Positive static longitudinal stability is indicated by a negative slope of CM versus CL. The degree of static longitudinal stability is indicated by the slope of the curve.

Thus, the tail has a stabilising contribution for stability which is represented by a negative slopped curve Z.

title:
Refer to figure.
The image shows two main forces acting on the propeller blade, what are these forces called?
optionA: (1) Torque Drag; (2) Thrust
optionB: (1) Lift; (2) Thrust
optionC: (1) Thrust; (2) Torque Drag
optionD: (1) Torque Drag; (2) Reverse Thrust
explanationTotal:
A propeller blade is just a wing. Anything that happens to a propeller blade can be translated into our knowledge of how a wing behaves. The main difference is that the air interacting with a propeller blade is partially from ahead of the aircraft, brought in by the TAS (True Airspeed) of the aircraft, and the other component of the incoming air is from the rotational speed of the propeller. This means that the angle of relative airflow will change, depending on the RPM and TAS, and their relationship.

In the case of this diagram, we have one force being created by the propeller blade, split into two components. Number 1 component is opposing the rotation of the propeller, where number 2 component is in the direction of flight. This makes number 2 quite simple, it is the thrust produced. It is quite a similar force vector to the lift created by a fixed wing.

Number 1 is the opposing force of the propeller rotation, and therefore the opposing force to the engine. This means that it is the opposing torque, known sometimes just as "torque" or "torque drag". Torque is the measure of how much force an engine can apply in one rotation, and for an engine at constant RPM, the torque from the engine will match the "torque drag" of the propeller. Notice how, for a wing, number 1 would be closely related to the drag of the wing, hence even easier to remember "torque drag"

title: Where would you expect the forward stagnation point of an aerofoil to be during slow flight?
optionA: Lower surface.
optionB: Leading edge point.
optionC: Upper surface.
optionD: Upper surface, at a location nearly 25% of the chord.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
The lift equation states:

LIFT = ½ρV2SCL

Considering Lift to remain constant, as speed is decreased to achieve slow flight, the angle of attack (CL) is increased in order to keep the equation balanced.

Stagnation Point - A point where streamlines are divided by a body and where the fluid speed is zero, relative to the surface.

As the dividing streamline approaches the aerofoil it slows down, and momentarily comes to rest just below the leading edge, forming a stagnation point.

The greatest positive pressure occurs at the stagnation point where the relative flow velocity is zero. This stagnation point is located somewhere near the leading edge.

As the angle of attack increases from -4°, the leading edge stagnation point moves from the upper surface around the leading edge to the lower surface.

It is at the front stagnation point where the flow divides to pass over and under the section.

As angle of attack increases, the stagnation point moves downwards and backwards around the leading edge.

title: What type of drag is increased when an aerofoil is contaminated by dust and other particles?
optionA: Material drag
optionB: Induced drag
optionC: Wave drag
optionD: Friction drag
explanationTotal:
Total Drag is sub-divided into two main types:
  • Parasite Drag - independent of lift generation, and
  • Induced Drag - the result of lift generation.

PARASITE DRAG is simply caused by the aircraft's shape, construction-type, and material. For instance, an airplane with a rough surface creates more parasite drag than one with a smooth surface. And there are three basic types of parasite drag:

1. Skin Friction Drag is the result of the aircraft's surface being rough. Olympic swimmers wear swim caps on their heads, so hair doesn't create extra drag and they can swim faster through the water => this same principle can be applied to most aircraft, where a smooth skin reduces skin friction drag, improving performance and fuel efficiency.
2. Form Drag is the result of an object's general shape in relation to the relative wind. Resulting from the pressure at the leading edge of a body being greater than the pressure at the trailing edge.
3. Interference Drag is generated by the mixing of airflow streamlines between airframe components such as the wing and the fuselage or the landing gear strut and the fuselage. As air flows around different aircraft components and mixes, a localized shock wave is formed, creating a drag sum greater than the drag that components would have by themselves.

Factors Affecting Parasite Drag:

  • Indicated Airspeed - It varies directly with the square of the Indicated Airspeed. If IAS is doubled, the Parasite Drag will be four times greater - if IAS is halved, the Parasite Drag will be one quarter of its previous value.
  • Configuration - Parasite Drag varies directly in proportion to the frontal area presented to the airflow. If flaps are deployed, the undercarriage lowered, speed brakes selected or roll control spoilers operated, "Parasite Area" is increased and Parasite Drag will increase.
  • Airframe Contamination - Contamination by ice, frost, snow, mud, dust or slush will increase the Parasite Drag Coefficient, and in the case of severe airframe icing, the Parasite Area.

title: While performing a take-off under icing conditions, the pilot rotates the aircraft at the correct speed and rate, but notices that the aircraft does NOT lift off as expected. What could be the cause?
optionA: The angle of attack during rotation exceeds the lower, icing-induced critical angle of attack, preventing the aircraft from becoming airborne.
optionB: Ice can distort the flow of air over the wing, increasing the angle of attack for maximum lift and significantly increasing drag.
optionC: The rotation speed is too fast, significantly increasing drag and preventing the aircraft to lift off.
optionD: The rotation rate is too fast, increasing the critical angle of attack and preventing the aircraft to lift off.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Note: This is a terrible question, and even though it has been reported as seen many times in exams, we are still massively lacking in feedback for its wording and the correct answer. We have recently made a small wording change that we believe might correspond closer to the exam, and this has changed the "correct answer". Beware that this answer is not confirmed, so please send any exam feedback you have to us in the comments, thank you!

We can assume that "the pilot rotates the aircraft at the correct speed and rate" means that the pilot rotates at the VR that was calculated, and at the correct rate of rotation for a clean airframe.

The formation of ice and frost on the airframe will modify the profile of the aerofoil, increase the roughness of the aircraft surface as well as increasing the weight of the aircraft. This reduction in lift and increase in drag drastically affects the flying characteristics of the aircraft. The biggest problem in this scenario is that the disturbance of the airflow causes the wing to stall at a much lower angle of attack, hence the wing has a much lower critical angle of attack, due to the ice accretion.

As this is the take-off rotation, the aircraft is very quickly increasing its angle of attack, and the ice accretion could mean that it quickly passes through the angles of attack that produce lift, and past the critical angle of attack. This means that the aircraft is accelerating down the runway with a nose-up attitude, but the wings are stalled so no lift is created.

Icing or any other type of contaminant does definitely NOT increase the angle of maximum CL. Any contamination degrades aerodynamic performance, by increasing Drag and decreasing Lift and ultimately by DECREASING the angle for maximum CL.

As we mentioned above, this is a terrible question, and this is just one interpretation of it, so be careful whilst reading it if you get it in the exam.

title: In cruising flight, with the centre of gravity forward of main wing centre of pressure, the force on the horizontal tailplane is directed:
optionA: Upward in order to balance the aerodynamic moment about the centre of gravity.
optionB: Upward and is equal to weight.
optionC: Downward which reduces the induced drag.
optionD: Downward in order to balance the aerodynamic moment about the centre of gravity.
explanationTotal:
If the Center of Gravity (CG) is located in front of the Center of Pressure (CP), it means that the lift acts behind the CG.
This causes a nose down movement.
To keep an aircraft level, the two moments from the wing and tailplane will have to cancel each other out.
The CP always points upwards.

This means that if the CP is behind the CG, the nose wants to move downwards.
To cancel this movement, the tailplane generates a downwards moment to keep the nose straight. In this case, the CP is located behind the CG.
To have the nose not move downwards, an downwards moment has to be created by the tailplane, so the tail comes down again and the nose goes up to a 0 angle.

title: Which is the correct statement with regards to Dutch roll?
optionA: A roll damper is used in most aeroplanes to counteract Dutch roll.
optionB: If Dutch roll occurs, try to counteract the oscillations by opposite rudder.
optionC: Dutch roll is usually encountered during an approach in turbulence.
optionD: If the yaw damper is inoperative, consider reducing speed and altitude.
explanationTotal:
Aircraft with a tendency to Dutch roll are fitted with a Yaw Damper. This automatically displaces the rudder proportional to the rate of yaw to damp-out the oscillations.

If the Yaw Damper fails in flight, it is recommended that the ailerons be used by the pilot to damp-out Dutch roll or the speed and altitude to be reduced. Because of the response lag, if the pilot uses the rudder at a high speed, pilot induced oscillation (PIO) will result and the Dutch roll may very quickly become divergent, leading to loss of control.

title: An aeroplane, being manually flown in the speed unstable region, experiences a disturbance that causes a speed reduction. If the altitude is maintained and thrust remains constant, the aeroplane speed will:
optionA: further decrease.
optionB: initially further decrease and thereafter increase.
optionC: initially increase and thereafter decrease.
optionD: increase.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Following a sudden decrease in speed; because we the aircraft is situated in the speed unstable region, the drag will increase, whilst the thrust available will remain the same. A thrust deficit will be created.

This thrust deficit, assuming no change in pitch is made to the aircraft, will result in a further decrease in airspeed until the aircraft cannot maintain altitude and stalls.

title: The calibrated airspeed during approach and landing, with all engines operating, at which, when the critical engine is suddenly made inoperative, it is possible to maintain control of the aeroplane with that engine still inoperative, and maintain straight flight with an angle of bank of not more than 5°, is called...
optionA: VMG.
optionB: VMCL-2.
optionC: VMC.
optionD: V<sub>MCL</sub>.
explanationTotal:
VMCL, the minimum control speed during approach and landing with all engines operating, is the calibrated airspeed at which, when the critical engine is suddenly made inoperative, it is possible to maintain control of the airplane with that engine still inoperative and maintain straight flight with an angle of bank of not more than 5°.

VMCL must be established with:

  • the airplane in the most critical configuration for approach and landing with all engines operating.
  • the most unfavorable CG.
  • the airplane trimmed for approach with all engines operating.
  • the most unfavorable weight.
  • for propeller airplanes, the propeller of the inoperative engine in the position it achieves without pilot action and go-around power or thrust setting on the operating engines(s).
In demonstrating VMCL:
  • the rudder force may not exceed 150 lb.
  • the airplane may not exhibit hazardous flight characteristics or require exceptional piloting skill, alertness, or strength.
  • lateral control must be sufficient to roll the airplane, from an initial condition of steady flight, through an angle of 20° in the direction necessary to initiate a turn away from the inoperative engine(s), in not more than 5 seconds.

title:
Determine the drag for an aircraft that is on a 20º gliding descent, given:

Weight: 100 500 N
Lift: 94 439 N
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The forward component of weight must balance drag. Therefore, Forward Component of Weight = Drag

D = W sin y
D = 100 500 sin 20º
D = 34 373 N

GLIDE

A glide is a basic maneuver in which the airplane loses altitude in a controlled descent with little or no engine power; forward motion is maintained by the weight component along the flight path which balances drag.
There are only three forces that act on an aircraft in a steady glide: Lift, Weight, and Drag.

title: Aircraft certified under CS-23 and CS25 have to be able to show that they can avoid upset situations and unusual attitudes, as well as withstand and recover from them. Consider two identical aeroplanes, one with its CG at the FWD limit, the other with its CG at the AFT limit; which of the following statements is true regarding stability and manoeuvrability?
optionA: Stability increases as the CG moves aft.
optionB: Stability and manoeuvrability are not affected by CG position.
optionC: Stability decreases as the CG moves forward.
optionD: Manoeuvrability reduces slightly with a FWD CG compared to an AFT CG.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Stability of an aeroplane is its tendency to return to an original point after a disruption. Manoeuvrability is the exact opposite, it is how easy it is to change an aircraft's attitude or direction. With high stability comes low manoeuvrability (think large jet aircraft) and with low stability comes high manoeuvrability (fighter jets or aerobatic display aircraft).

The movement (forward/aft) of the CG is incredibly important to longitudinal stability (stability in pitch movements), as having a forward CG means that the CG is further in front of the neutral point. This means greater stability, and therefore lower manoeuvrability.

The neutral point is the place on an aeroplane that the CG must be in front of to make the aircraft stable in a particular axis. Its location is decided by the aerodynamic surfaces and qualities of the aircraft only. The distance between the neutral point and the CG is called the static margin. The larger the static margin, the greater the stability, (and lower the manoeuvrability).

Therefore, now we know that manoeuvrability is higher with an AFT CG, and lower with a FWD CG, there is only one correct answer left.

title:
Given the following information, calculate the Thrust vector in a straight and steady power-on descent with an angle of 30°.

Mass: 9 450 kg
Lift: 92 500 N
Drag: 93 500 N
g: 10 m/s2
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The balance of forces in steady climb show thrust is partly acting upwards and weight is partly adding to the drag. Because the thrust is now assisting lift, there is less lift required than in level flight.
For steady speed, the thrust and two effects of aerodynamic drag and weight must be equal.

  • T= D + W sin(gamma)
    Where, T = Thrust, W = Weight and D = Drag

This means that the climb angle (sin gamma) depends on excess thrust and weight.

In descent the formula will become T= D – W sin(gamma)

As the lift is now decreased and the load factor in straight and level flight is 1, the load factor will now be less than 1.

Solving this excercise:

Pay attention to the units. Start by converting Mass into Weight: 9 450 kg x 10 = 94 500 N

  • Thrust = drag - (W * sin(angle) )
    Thrust = 93 500 - (94 500 * sin (30) )
    Thrust = 46 250 N

title: Extending flaps will (1)_____ the wing’s effective camber and, consequently, (2) _____ the stall speed.
optionA: (1) decrease; (2) decrease.
optionB: (1) increase; (2) decrease.
optionC: (1) increase; (2) increase.
optionD: (1) decrease; (2) increase.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.

EFFECT OF FLAPS ON LANDING/TAKE-OFF RUN AND CLIMB GRADIENT

The use of high life devices (Flaps) will have an impact on the take-off and Landing roll and climb gradient.
For a given runway length and airplane weight, selecting a greater flap setting will increase the wing’s effective camber and the lift coefficient, which reduces the stalling speed.
  • As a consequence, the take-off speeds are reduced (the same lift will be created at smaller air speed due to greater lift coefficient). This will reduce the take-off run.
  • Flap extension during landings provides several advantages by:
producing greater lift and permitting lower landing speed;
producing greater drag, permitting a steep descent angle without airspeed increase.
=> Reducing the length of the landing roll.

The down side of the use of flaps is that it generates more parasite drag:

We get our best angle of climb and, therefore, our best gradient where there is the biggest gap between the thrust available and thrust required. The parasite drag from the extended flap closes the gap and the climb angle and climb gradient will reduce => go around performance is deteriorated. Hence as soon as we can after take off we accelerate and retract the flap and climb clean.

title: To reduce friction drag, some aeroplanes are equipped with modified wing designs to:
optionA: Delay the transition point and have a larger laminar flow.
optionB: Accelerate separation and have a larger turbulent flow.
optionC: Increase the effective angle of attack.
optionD: Increase wing lift.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Friction drag represents the energy dissipated due to friction within the boundary layer. Within the boundary layer, the laminar layer is the thinnest and generates the least friction. However, as this laminar layer progresses toward the transition point, it transitions into the turbulent layer. This turbulent layer is thicker and contributes to higher friction drag. To enhance aerodynamic performance, certain aerofoils are engineered to delay this transition, allowing it to occur further downstream. This strategy increases the extent of laminar flow, reducing overall friction drag.

For instance, vortex generators may be used to extend the laminar flow by energizing the boundary layer and creating turbulent flow, which does cause more drag indeed, but that's how separation is delayed which is actually more important when you look at the big picture. Vortex generators are located on the upper surface of a wing to create a slightly disturbed airflow perpendicular to the leading edge of the wing. The higher energy level delays the boundary layer separation (resulting in an extended laminar flow section), which reduces the stall speed.

title:
Which statements about an aeroplane leaving ground effect are correct or incorrect?

1) The downwash angle increases.
2) The induced angle of attack increases.
optionA: 1) is correct, 2) is incorrect.
optionB: 1) is incorrect, 2) is incorrect.
optionC: 1) is correct, 2) is correct.
optionD: 1) is incorrect, 2) is correct.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
When an airplane flies at a height equal to or less than the length of its wingspan the efficiency of its wings is considerably improved. A low wing airplane, just before touchdown, experiences a 50% reduction of its total drag. This phenomenon is ground effect.
Ground effect occurs because the surface alters the airflow pattern around the wings. Primarily, the surface restricts the formation of the wingtip vortices.
When an aircraft enters ground effect during the landing phase of flight, the sudden increase in lift and reduction in drag cause it to experience a floating tendency. The aircraft also tends to pitch nose-down due to the reduction in download on the tail plane.
The magnitude of the wing tip vortices, and thus downwash, also determine the amount of induced drag produced by the wing. The closer the aircraft is to the surface, the greater the reduction in induced drag at any given angle of attack.

Aircraft entering ground effect:

  • Downwash decreases.
  • The effective angle of attack increases.
  • Increased lift during landing if the angle of attack remains constant.
  • The induced angle of attack decreases.
  • Induced drag decreases.
Aircraft leaving ground effect:
  • The effective angle of attack decreases.
  • Decreased lift during take-off if the angle of attack remains constant.
  • Induced drag increases.
  • Downwash increases. Therefore, statement 1 is correct.
  • The induced angle of attack increases. Therefore, statement 2 is correct.

title:
During a straight and level flight the pilot eases back on the control column to gain altitude. What effect will this have on the stagnation point of the aerofoil, and the angle of attack?

The leading edge stagnation point of the aerofoil moves towards the _____ surface of the aerofoil as the angle of attack _____.
optionA: Lower, increases.
optionB: Upper, increases.
optionC: Lower, decreases.
optionD: Upper, decreases.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The stagnation point is that point on an airfoil at which the approaching airflow becomes stationary.

It is located on the leading edge of the airfoil just below the maximum point of curvature and moves downward and aft along the lower surface of the airfoil profile as the angle of attack increases. The stagnation pressure, the pressure necessary to stop the airflow at the stagnation point, is equal to the dynamic pressure plus the static pressure.

title: What happens to parasite drag if the true airspeed of an aircraft is multiplied by two, and all other parameters are kept constant? The parasite drag...
optionA: is unaffected by speed.
optionB: will be multiplied by four.
optionC: will be divided by two.
optionD: will be multiplied by two.
explanationTotal:
The formula for parasite drag is described as follows;

Parasite drag = ½ * ρ * S * V^2 * CD0 (parasite drag coefficient)

If TAS (V) is multiplied by 2, the total parasite drag will increase with 2^2= 4.

title: How is the design manoeuvring speed (V<sub>A</sub>) affected by changes in aircraft mass (weight)?
optionA: A decrease in aircraft mass results in an increase in VA.
optionB: A decrease in aircraft mass results in a decrease in V<sub>A</sub>.
optionC: Aircraft mass has no effect on V<sub>A</sub>.
optionD: An increase in aircraft mass results in a decrease in VA.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Design Manoeuvring Speed (VA): Is the design manoeuvring speed and is the maximum speed at which it is possible to safely use maximum up elevator; if this speed is exceeded with the elevator deflected fully upward then the aeroplane may suffer permanent distortion.

VA is the highest speed at which the aeroplane will stall before exceeding the manoeuvre maximum load factor and does not need to exceed VC.

The stall speed depends on the weight of the aircraft. The line OA (in V-n diagram) is drawn for the maximum design weight (takeoff). Lower weights will have a lower stall speed. For the same limit load factor, VA decreases with a decrease in weight.

VA = VAmax x √ (WActual ÷ Wmax)

title:
Which statement is correct regarding the gyroscopic effect of a clockwise rotating propeller on a single engine aeroplane?

I. Pitch up produces right yaw.
II. Right yaw produces pitch up.
optionA: I is correct, II is incorrect.
optionB: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
optionC: I is correct, II is correct.
optionD: I is incorrect, II is correct.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
On take-off, rotation of a single-engine propeller causes an aircraft to swing to one side, particularly those fitted with a tail-dragger undercarriage. The main causes of this are:

  • Slipstream effect
  • Torque reaction
  • Gyroscopic effect
  • Asymmetric blade effect

Gyroscopic Effect

A rotating propeller has the properties of a gyroscope - rigidity in space and precession. The characteristic which produces “gyroscopic effect” is precession. Gyroscopic precession is the reaction that occurs when a force is applied to the rim of a rotating disc. When a force is applied to the rim of a propeller, the reaction occurs 90° ahead in the direction of rotation and in the same direction as the applied force. As the aircraft is pitched up or down or yawed left or right, a force is applied to the rim of the spinning propeller disc.

Note: Gyroscopic effect only occurs when the aircraft pitches and/or yaws.

For a clockwise rotating propeller:

Pitch down - forward force on the top, force emerges 90° clockwise, left yaw.
Left yaw - forward force on the right, force emerges 90° clockwise, pitch up.
Pitch up - forward force on the bottom, force emerges 90° clockwise, right yaw. Therefore, statement 1 is correct.
Right yaw - forward force on the left, force emerges 90° clockwise, pitch down. Therefore, statement 2 is incorrect.

title: When an aeroplane with the centre of gravity forward of the centre of pressure of the combined wing / fuselage is in straight and level flight, the vertical load on the tailplane will be:
optionA: zero because in steady flight all loads are in equilibrium.
optionB: upwards.
optionC: downwards.
optionD: downwards because it is always negative regardless of the position of the centre of gravity.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The tail plane is able to supply the necessary force to balance any residual pitching moments because it is positioned some distance from the aircraft's center of gravity and has a large moment arm.

If the CG is in front of the CP, giving a nose-down pitching moment and there is no thrust/drag moment to oppose it, the tail plane must provide a download to maintain equilibrium. Lift must be increased to maintain an upwards force equal to the increased downwards force.

title: An aeroplane in straight and level flight at 100 kt is subjected to a sudden disturbance in speed. Assuming the angle of attack remains constant initially and the load factor reaches a value of 1.96:
optionA: the speed will have increased by 20 kt.
optionB: the speed will have decreased by 40 kt.
optionC: the speed will have decreased by 20 kt.
optionD: the speed will have increased by 40 kt.
explanationTotal:
Load Factor is the ratio of the weight of an aircraft to the load imposed by lift: Load Factor = Lift / Weight
Lift is propotional to V2: L= CL × ½ rho × V2 × S

Therefore, n is proportional to V2 . An increase in "n" to 1.96 means lift has increased by a factor of 1.96. Consequently, "V" must change by a factor of √1.96 = 1.4.

The speed has increased to: 100 x 1.4 = 140 kt (= an increase of 40 kt)

title: Regarding downwash, which of the following answers is correct?
optionA: Downwash is caused by the lower surface of the aerofoil deflecting the airflow downwards, producing lift upwards.
optionB: The greater the downwash, the less lift is being produced by the aerofoil due to energy loss.
optionC: Downwash is caused by the converging airflow above the aerofoil.
optionD: The greater the downwash, the greater the lift being generated by the aerofoil.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Please note that downwash can mean two slightly different things. Downwash is the effect of a wing changing the local relative airflow (primarily due to 3D airflow and wingtip vortices). It is also the term for the air being forced downwards behind a wing as part of lift generation. The terms are very closely linked, and often refer to the same thing, in fact, but there are some differences to how we view them in different contexts as part of the syllabus.

The two similar terms do not cause a problem in this question, and the correct answer remains the same.

The main wing generates downwash as a by-product of lift generation; the magnitude of downwash is proportional to the lift created. Think of the momentum change in the airflow as being the 'equal and opposite reaction' to the lift force, in order to satisfy Newton's 2nd law of motion. Therefore, one can say that the greater the downwash, the greater the lift being generated by the aerofoil.

  • If the aerofoil is producing more lift, its angle of attack will be greater, and downwash will be greater, especially towards the wingtip where vortices are stronger. If we observe a lot of downwash, we can conclude that a lot of lift is being generated.

title:
Refer to figure.
The same wing is shown in two distinct configurations in the figure in the annex. Curve A is the CL curve in clean configuration. The wing profile is (1) _____, and line B depicts the effect of (2) _____ edge flaps.
optionA: (1) symmetrical; (2) trailing
optionB: (1) asymmetrical; (2) leading
optionC: (1) symmetrical; (2) leading
optionD: (1) asymmetrical; (2) trailing
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
Symmetrical Aerofoil

The change in pressure distribution with angle of attack for the symmetrical aerofoil is visualized, i.e., with zero angle of attack, the upper and lower surface forces are equal and located at the same point, thus lift is equal to zero. If the angle of attack increases, the upper surface force increases, while the lower surface force decreases.

Trailing-Edge Lift Augmentation

A flap is a hinged portion of the trailing or leading-edge, which can be deflected downwards and produce an increase of camber. For low speed aerofoils, the flaps will be on the trailing edge only.

When the flaps are lowered, CLMAX is increased, but the stalling angle is reduced. This is because lowering the flap increases the effective angle of attack due to the changed camber.

title:
A flight instructor is demonstrating stall and stall recovery during a lesson. As a part of the exercise, the instructor demonstrates the use of excessive pitch-down stick input during the initial portion of the recovery. Recovering from the dive, the pilot applies excessive back force on the stick, which forces the aeroplane to enter a secondary (accelerated) stall. Considering the aeroplane limitations given below, what speed range should the aeroplane be operated in order to safely carry out this demonstration?

VS: 45 kt
VA: 100 kt
VNO: 125 kt
VNE: 160 kt.
optionA: 45 kt to 100 kt.
optionB: 100 kt to 125 kt.
optionC: 45 kt to 125 kt.
optionD: 100 kt to 160 kt.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
COLOUR CODING OF THE ASI

White arc

This arc extends from VSO (stall full flap) to VFE (maximum speed with flaps extended), and marks the flap operating speed range.

Green arc

This arc extends from VSI (stall clean) to VNO (normal operating speed), and is the normal operating speed range.

Yellow

This arc extends from VNO to VNE (never exceed speed), and denotes the cautionary speed range. Operations within this speed range should not be carried out except in smooth air.

Red Radial line

This line marks VNE.

MANOEUVERING SPEED (VA) (figure 2)

VA - Maximum design manoeuvring speed and is the highest speed where the aircraft will stall before it exceeds the maximum load factor

THE STALL

The CL of an aerofoil increases with angle of attack up to a maximum (CLMAX). Any further increase above this stalling angle, or critical angle of attack, will make it impossible for the airflow to smoothly follow the upper wing contour, and the flow will separate from the surface, causing CL to decrease and drag to increase rapidly.

A stall is caused by airflow separation. Separation can occur when either the boundary layer has insufficient kinetic energy or the adverse pressure gradient becomes too great.

STALL RECOVERY

To recover from a stall or prevent a full stall, the angle of attack must be decreased to reduce the adverse pressure gradient. This may consist of merely releasing back pressure, or it may be necessary to smoothly move the pitch control forward, depending on the aircraft design and severity of the stall.

Allow airspeed to increase and recover lost altitude with moderate back pressure on the pitch control.

Pulling too hard could trigger a secondary stall, or worse, could exceed the limit load factor and damage the aircraft structure.

At low airspeeds the stall may occur before reaching the limit load factor. That is why, when pulling from a stall recovery, keeping the speed between VS and VA will allow us to not stall again due to the increased load factor.

As angle of attack reduces below the critical angle, the adverse pressure gradient will decrease, airflow will re-attach, and lift and drag will return to their normal values.

title: Artificial feel is required:
optionA: when the flight control surfaces are fitted with control tabs or trim tabs.
optionB: with power assisted flight controls.
optionC: with fully powered flight controls.
optionD: when there is a trimmable stabiliser.
explanationTotal:
Powered Flying Controls
In a fully powered system, aerodynamic loads on aircraft control surfaces are not felt on the cockpit controls (pilot receives no feedback), because there is no physical connection between the pilot's controls and the control surface. In the same way, aerodynamic loads cannot move the controls.
