  • This is known as an Irreversible control and requires some form of artificial feel to relay how much force is being applied.

title:
Choose the correct statements with regard to the forces acting parallel and perpendicular to the flight path, for an aeroplane in a straight and steady power-on descent. (L = Lift, D = Drag, T = Thrust, W = Weight, y = descent angle, x = multiplied by)

1. L and (W x cos y) act perpendicular to the flight path.
2. L and W act perpendicular to the flight path.
3. T, D and (L x cos y) act parallel to the flight path.
4. T, D and (W x sin y) act parallel to the flight path.
optionA: 1 and 3
optionB: 2 and 3
optionC: 2 and 4
optionD: 1 and 4
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Figure 1 illustrates the forces in a steady Power-on descent.
The force of Weight is split into two components. One component (W cos γ) acts perpendicular to the flight path and is balanced by Lift, while the other component (W sin γ) acts forward along the flight path and ‘adds’ to the Thrust to balance Drag. If the nose of the aircraft is lowered with a constant Thrust setting, the increased component of Weight acting forward along the flight path will cause an increase in IAS. The increased IAS will result in an increase in Drag which will eventually balance the increased forward force of Weight and equilibrium will be re-established.
If the throttle is closed, the force of Thrust is removed, and a larger forward component of Weight must be provided to balance Drag and maintain a constant IAS. This is accomplished by lowering the nose of the airplane to increase the descent angle (γ).

In a descent Lift is less than Weight. This is because Lift only has to balance the component of Weight perpendicular to the flight path (W cos γ).
L = W cosγ

In a descent Thrust is less than Drag. This is because Weight is giving a forward component in the same direction as Thrust (W sin γ).
D = T + W sinγ

title:
Refer to figure.
The force vector which correctly represents Thrust force is:
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
Propeller thrust is a component at right angles to the plane of rotation. The thrust force will vary along the length of each blade, reducing at the tip where the pressures equalize and towards the root where the rotational velocity is low. Thrust will cause a bending moment on each blade, tending to bend the tip forward.

title: In the event of a dual-channel failure of the Mach trim system in flight, what is the appropriate course of action?
optionA: It is solely up to the Commander to decide if the aircraft may be flown.
optionB: The aircraft may be flown at or below a specified lower altitude.
optionC: The aircraft may be flown at or below a specified lower Mach number.
optionD: The aircraft cannot fly passengers, however it may be flown to a maintenance facility at a lower speed, at or below the changeover altitude.
explanationTotal:
As speed increases beyond the Critical Mach number (MCRIT), shock wave formation at the root of a swept-back wing will:

  • reduce lift forward of the CG (CP moves rearward), and
  • reduce downwash at the tail plane.

Together, these factors will generate a nose-down pitching moment.

At high Mach numbers, an aircraft will become unstable with respect to speed; instead of an increasing push force being required as speed increases, a pull force becomes necessary to prevent the aircraft accelerating further.

A small increase in Mach number will give a nose-down pitch which will further increase the Mach number. This in turn leads to a further increase in the nose-down pitching moment. This unfavourable high-speed characteristic, known as “Mach Tuck”, “High Speed Tuck” or “Tuck Under” would restrict the maximum operating speed of a modern high-speed jet transport aircraft.

To maintain the required stick force gradient at high Mach numbers, a Mach trim system must be fitted. It is operational at high Mach numbers in the transonic speed range. In the event of this equipment failing, the speed is limited to specified Mach number.

title: When you pull the yoke backwards, what happens?
optionA: Elevator goes up and increases the tailplanes negative angle of attack
optionB: Elevator goes up and increases the tailplanes positive angle of attack
optionC: Elevator goes down and increase the tailplanes negative angle of attack
optionD: Elevator goes down and increase the tailplane positive angle of attack
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
ELEVATORS. When the elevators are used, they produce a pitching moment about the lateral axis.

  • When you push the yoke forward, the elevator goes down, forcing the tail up, and the nose goes down.
  • When you pull the yoke back, the elevator goes up, forcing the tail down, and the nose goes up. The camber of the horizontal stabiliser is altered and the negative angle of attack of the tailplane is increased.

title: An aeroplane is at risk of a low speed stall under the following circumstances:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Descending at a constant Mach number.
optionB: Descending in “vertical speed” mode.
optionC: Climbing in “vertical speed” mode.
optionD: Climbing at constant IAS.
explanationTotal:
The autopilot's vertical speed mode allows you to perform constant-rate climbs and descents. In this mode, the vertical speed is prioritised over airspeed. When you engage the vertical speed mode, the FD/autopilot will attempt to maintain the specified vertical speed until you choose a different setting in autopilot, the aircraft reaches an assigned altitude set into the assigned altitude selector/alerter, or the autopilot is disconnected.

As altitude increases and the air gets thinner, the IAS will reduce for a given pitch setting. Consequently, the angle of attack also reduces. As a result, the vertical speed will reduce for a certain pitch attitude. The autopilot will therefore chase the selected vertical speed by pitching up. This results in further decreased IAS. Ultimately, this could lead to a stall.

title:
Parasite Drag can be divided into:

1. Tip-vortex drag
2. Interference drag
3. Pressure drag
4. Friction drag

The combination that regroups all of the correct statements is:
optionA: 1 only
optionD: 3 and 4
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Drag is the force which resists the forward motion of the aircraft. Drag acts parallel to and in the same direction as the relative airflow (in the opposite direction to the flight path).

Total Drag is sub-divided into two main types:

INDUCED DRAG - the result of lift generation.
PARASITE DRAG - independent of lift generation.

Parasite drag is further sub-divided into:

- Skin Friction Drag
- Form (Pressure) Drag
- Interference Drag

title: Compared to a turbulent boundary layer, a laminar boundary layer:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Generates less skin friction.
optionB: Produces more drag.
optionC: Is more resistant to separation.
optionD: Has a higher level of kinetic energy within it.
explanationTotal:
Boundary layers are not only important to calculate drag, but stall is caused by separation of the boundary layer. Basically, there are two types of boundary layers:

  • Laminar

  • Turbulent

Boundary Layers

Laminar

Turbulent
Layers slip on each other, there is no mixing.
Various particles having different speeds which result in mixing.
Drag is smaller
Drag is higher
Is thinner
Is thicker
Lower level of kinetic energy
Higher level of kinetic energy
Separates easily from the surface.
Separation occurs much later.

The increased rate of change in velocity at the surface in the turbulent flow will give more skin friction than the laminar flow. A turbulent boundary layer also has a higher level of kinetic energy than a laminar layer.

title: Flying an aircraft with a joystick, if a small displacement of the joystick results in a large change in pitch/bank angle, the aeroplane is decribed as being...
optionA: very stable.
optionB: highly manoeuvrable.
optionC: nose heavy.
optionD: very stable and very manoeuvrable.
explanationTotal:
An aircraft's stability affects many aspects of its flight characteristics. For an aircraft to be considered statically stable, it must initially begin to return to its original position/orientation after some sort of displacement. Think of placing a ball in a bowl, it will always begin to roll back to the bottom of the bowl, the equilibrium point. An aircraft can have stability in all three axes, pitch (longitudinal stability), yaw (directional stability) and roll (lateral stability).

The opposite of stability is manoeuvrability, and if the aircraft is very stable, it is not very manoeuvrable, and vice-versa. The less stable (more manoeuvrable) we make an aircraft, the more easily it will change orientation. This is why aerobatic aircraft have very light controls, meaning that even small stick forces will cause a large aircraft movement, whereas stable aircraft, such as transport jets, are very stable, and will require much larger stick movements, and more stick force, to provide the same amount of aircraft movement. This is called stick force stability, which is a measure of how much input force is required to cause a 1G change.

This question is asking about stick displacement, but it is largely the same thing. It is the reason that you would not want to cruise a highly aerobatic aircraft for long distances, as the fineness of control is difficult to achieve when the controls are so light and tiny movements cause huge changes. To answer the question, if small movements of the stick create large pitch/roll changes, the aircraft must be highly manoeuvrable.

Interestingly, modern fighter aircraft, such as the Eurofighter Typhoon, are designed to be statically unstable for highest manoeuvrability, and have very responsive fly-by-wire controls making sure that the aircraft does not become unstable during flight. Excellent for air-to-air combat, terrible if they lose their FBW system.

title:
Refer to figure.
During the approach, the pilot retracts the flaps. Due to a malfunction, the flaps are retracted as in the figure. How should the pilot react?
optionA: Roll to the right and left rudder.
optionB: Roll to the left and right rudder.
optionC: Roll to the right and right rudder.
optionD: Roll to the left and left rudder.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
ASYMMETRY OF HIGH LIFT DEVICES

Deployment of high lift devices can produce large changes of lift, drag and pitching moment. If the movement of the devices is not symmetrical on the two wings, the unbalanced forces could cause severe roll control problems.

On many flap control systems, the deflection on the two sides is compared while the flaps are moving, and if one side should fail, movement on the other side is automatically stopped. However, on less sophisticated systems a failure of the operating mechanism could lead to an asymmetric situation.

The difference in lift will cause a rolling moment which must be opposed by the ailerons, and the difference in drag will cause a yawing moment which must be opposed by the rudder.

Whether the controls will be adequate to maintain straight and level flight will depend on the degree of asymmetry and the control power available.

title: A pilot plans a flight with the CG at the aft limit. During the flight, the aircraft burns 400 kg of fuel, and the CG moves forward. How will this affect the stick force stability?
optionA: Increased stick force stability due to the CG movement.
optionB: Decreased stick force stability due to the CG movement.
optionC: Increased stick force stability due to the reduced weight.
optionD: Stick force stability doesn’t change since the centre of gravity stays within its limit.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
Note: The feedback for this question has been limited so far, so we are requesting any further feedback to verify the options and the question wording. Thank you!

LONGITUDINAL STABILITY (figure 1)
Longitudinal stability is motion about the lateral axis. An aircraft will exhibit static longitudinal stability if it tends to return towards the trim angle of attack when displaced by a gust OR a control input.

If the tail moment is greater than the wing moment, the sum of the moments will not be zero and the resultant nose-down moment will give an angular acceleration about the CG. The nose-down angular acceleration about the CG will return the aircraft towards its original position of equilibrium. The greater the tail moment relative to the wing moment, the greater the rate of acceleration towards the original equilibrium position.

The length of both arms is dependent upon CG position. If the CG is considered in a more forward position, the tail arm is larger and the wing arm is smaller. A more forward CG position increases static longitudinal stability.

STICK FORCE STABILITY (STICK FORCE PER G) (figure 2)
The force on the stick required to change the aircraft's load factor by 1 G.

One of the biggest factors for changing stick force stability is the change of stability from a movement of the CG. Moving the CG forwards increases the stability of the aircraft, thereby reducing manoeuvrability, and increasing stick force stability, as seen by the steeper line on figure 2 when the CG is at 10% MAC (far forward CG = higher stick force per G).

The change in mass on its own causes an unknown change to the stick force per G without in-depth analysis into the particular aircraft (so we assume no change), and the only change in stick force stability comes from the CG movement.

title:
Which of these statements about the strength of wing tip vortices are correct or incorrect?

I. Assuming no flow separation, the strength of wing tip vortices increases as the angle of attack increases.
II. The strength of wing tip vortices increases as the aspect ratio increases.
optionA: I is correct, II is correct.
optionB: I is incorrect, II is correct.
optionC: I is correct, II is incorrect.
optionD: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
explanationTotal:
Wing tip vortices are a byproduct of lift. They are caused by the pressure differential between the top and bottom of the wing, which causes an updraft of high pressure air around the tip of the wing. This updraft turns into a downdraft behind the wing, creating a vortex. The higher the pressure difference between the top and bottom of the wing, the stronger the vortices.

This question is specifically asking for:

  • Angle of attack: The strength of the vortices (and therefore also induced drag) is proportional to the angle of attack. Therefore; the strength of the vortices increase as the angle of attack increases, hence statement 1 correct!
  • Aspect ratio: The strength of the vortices is inversely proportional with the aspect ratio. Meaning that the strength of the wing tip vortices decreases as the aspect ratio increases, hence statement 2 is incorrect!

title: The following unit of measurement: kgm/s<sup>2</sup> is expressed in the SI-system as...
optionA: newton.
optionB: pascal.
optionC: watt.
optionD: joule.
explanationTotal:
NEWTON'S FIRST LAW OF MOTION
States that every body remains in a state of rest or uniform motion unless compelled to change its state by an applied force. Bodies at rest or in a state of steady motion are said to be in equilibrium and have the property of inertia.

The magnitude of the acceleration (a) for any given mass (m) is directly proportional to the size of the force (F) applied (i.e. when a force of 1 N is applied to a mass of 1 kg, it will accelerate at 1 m/s2).

F (N) = m (kg) x a (m/s2)

title: The value of the parasite drag in straight and level flight at constant weight varies linearly with the:
optionA: square of the speed.
optionB: angle of attack.
optionC: speed.
optionD: square of the angle of attack.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The force directly opposing the forward movement of the airplane through the air is referred to as drag. It is the resistance to forward motion and is assumed to act along a line parallel to the longitudinal axis. The total drag may act through a line above or below the thrust line depending on the position of the engines. There are two major components that make up the total drag acting on an airplane. They are parasite drag, and induced drag.
Parasite drag is that which is produced even when lift is not produced, and induced drag is that which is caused when the airplane’s airfoils are producing lift. The lift and drag forces acting on an airfoil depend on the pressure distribution around the airfoil.
Parasite drag is sub-divided into:

  • Skin Friction Drag.
  • Form (Pressure) Drag.
  • Interference Drag.

Parasite can be defined by:

DP = 1/2 ρV2SCDP

Where:

DP - Parasite Drag
Ρ – Air density
V – True Air Speed
S – Surface Area
CDP – Parasite Drag Coefficient

title: An aeroplane with a mass of 2000 kg, is performing a co-ordinated level turn at a constant TAS of 160 kt and the bank angle is 60°. The lift is approximately:
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
In level flight, any turn will be coordinated or uncoordinated. A coordinated turn is one in which the only acceleration is along the normal axis of the airplane, towards the center of the turn, and the angle of bank is precisely correct for the aircraft speed and the radius of turn. If not all these factors are present, the turn will be uncoordinated and there will be a lateral acceleration either towards or away from the center of the turn. The total lift of a balanced turn provides the centripetal force and the force that opposes the mass of the airplane.
If there is acceleration towards the center of the turn the airplane is slipping and if it is away from the center of the turn the airplane is skidding. Either condition will be indicated on the turn and slip indicator. An overbanked airplane will slip into the turn and requires an increase of speed or a reduction in bank angle to correct this condition. An underbanked airplane will skid out of the turn, which requires a decreased speed or an increased bank angle to correct this condition. These are indicated on the turn and slip indicator by the needle one-way and the ball the other.
To maintain altitude and airspeed when executing a turn both the angle of attack and the thrust have to be increased above their level flight values.

In a turn, the load factor (n) is defined by:

n = L/W = 1/cos Φ

On a 60° bank turn, to maintain the same lift as in straight and level flight, with a weight of 20000 N,

L/20000 = 1/cos 60
L = 20000 * 1/cos⁡ 60
L = 40000 N
Lift is equal to 40000 N.

title: A light aircraft has a demonstrated stall speed (V<sub>S</sub>) in straight and level flight of 154 kt. If the same aircraft is flown with a 60 degree bank angle, by how much does V<sub>S</sub> change?
optionA: V<sub>S</sub> decreases by 77 kt.
optionB: V<sub>S</sub> decreases by 45 kt.
optionC: V<sub>S</sub> increases by 64 kt.
optionD: V<sub>S</sub> increases by 154 kt.
explanationTotal:
In a turn, the load factor (n) is equal to:

n = 1/cos(ø), where ø is the bank angle.

n = 1/cos(60º) = 2 g

The Stall Speed in the turn (VSNEW) is calculated by:

VSNEW = √n x VSOLD

VSOLD = 154 kt

VSNEW = √2 x 154 = 218 kt

To know by how much VS has changed, we should find the difference between VSNEW and VSOLD:

VSNEW - VSOLD = 218 - 154 = 64 kt

On a turn with 60º, the Stall Speed increases by 64 kt.

title:
Refer to figure.
Which of the following graphs illustrate the power change with decreasing altitude?
optionA: Figure 1
optionB: Figure 4
optionC: Figure 2
optionD: Figure 3
explanationTotal:
The constituent parts of the total power required curve are the induced power required and the parasite power required, just as the total drag curve is made up of induced drag and parasite drag.

The left scale of the graph is power required and the bottom scale is TAS. Decreasing altitude or temperature, TAS decreases, which clearly affects the value of the total power required, because the power required is: DRAG x TAS.

The total power required curve moves down and left along the tangent to the origin (in other words the minimum value of drag stays the same).

Since, the total power required decreases, VMP (the lowest point of the power required curve), expressed as a TAS, also decreases.

title:
Refer to figure.

The pilot currently follows flight path 2 but desires to follow flight path 3. Despite having a bank angle of 25 degrees, the operator restricts the bank angle to 30 degrees for passenger comfort. What action should the pilot take?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Increase the bank angle to 30º and decrease speed to have a smaller radius.
optionB: Increase the bank angle to 30º and pull back on the stick.
optionC: Maintain bank angle 25º to maintain a margin but increase speed to increase the rate of turn.
optionD: Reduce bank angle to 15º to maintain a margin but increase speed to increase the rate of turn.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The formula for turn radius R is given by R = V2 / (g x tan Φ), where V is the true airspeed, g is the acceleration due to gravity, and Φ is the bank angle.

The radius of turn at any given airspeed is inversly proportional to the bank angle, which means that a larger angle of bank will result in a smaller turn radius. The turn radius is dependent solely on the TAS for a given bank angle.

To reduce the turn radius along flight path 3, the TAS can be decreased while maintaining the bank angle, or the bank angle can be increased while keeping the TAS constant.

  • "bank 30 and pull back on stick" This option is partially correct. By increasing the bank angle, the turn radius will reduce. If we increase the bank angle, a pull force on the stick will be required to maintain the same altitude. However, if no action is taken to maintain the airspeed, it will decrease and may lead to a stall.

  • "bank 25 degrees to maintain a margin but increase speed to increase the rate of turn" This option is incorrect. Maintaining the same bank angle while increasing speed will actually increase the turn radius.

title: Which stall-detection device uses the movement of the leading-edge stagnation point to detect a stall?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: A flapper switch.
optionB: A stick shaker.
optionC: An angle of attack vane.
optionD: An angle of attack probe.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
To augment pre-stall buffet, light aircraft normally have an audible stall-warning device that operates just before the stall. This device is activated by a moving vane (Flapper Switch), positioned approximately midway along the wing, just below the leading edge as seen in figure 1.

Airflow holds down the vane at normal operating angles of attack, but just before the wing stalls, movement of the stagnation point around the leading edge lifts the vane (figure 2).

This closes a micro-switch and sounds a buzzer in the cockpit, giving warning of an impending stall. On some light aircraft, a flashing red light on the instrument panel replaces the aural warning. On aircraft cleared to operate in icing conditions, the sensing device is electrically heated. Stall warning normally activates 5 to 10 knots above the stalling speed.

title: How do ventral fins typically affect the longitudinal stability of an aircraft?
optionA: Ventral fins improve the longitudinal stability of the aircraft.
optionB: Ventral fins decrease the longitudinal stability of the aircraft.
optionC: Ventral fins increase the lateral stability of the aircraft.
optionD: Ventral fins have no impact on the aircraft's longitudinal stability.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

The aircraft fin is a very powerful stabilising element of an aircraft, and contributes to positive stability both directionally (stability in yaw), and laterally (stability in roll). Some aircraft have more complex aerodynamical needs though, leading to the use of dorsal and/or ventral fins as well as the main tail fin.

Dorsal fins are effectively just an extension to the main fin, extending forwards to provide some benefits such as the blending with the fuselage, reducing drag, providing better stability at high sideslip angles, etc. They therefore have a positive effect on directional and lateral stability.

Ventral fins (sometimes called strakes), however, are placed under the fuselage, and provide a further increase in directional stability (yaw), but have the opposite effect to the main and dorsal fins when it comes to lateral stability, they are de-stabilising. Ventral fins are very useful for improving the stall/spin characteristcs of aircraft where the fuselage and wings may render the main fin less effective at high angles of attack (similar to a deep stall, but for stability). Their main limitation is ground clearance.

None of these items have any effect on longitudinal stability, which is stability in pitch, as a pitch change will not cause any angle of attack change to these components.

Some ventral fins/strakes are actually angled outwards, so they are not perfectly vertical. Now this would give very slightly increased longitudinal stability due to their location at the rear of the aircraft, however, the majority of ventral fins (as is the primary intention of them) have no effect on longitudinal stability.

title: For a given airplane that is travelling at 1.4 V<sub>A</sub>. When V<sub>A</sub> decreases to 1.1. By what % has C<sub>L</sub> increased if the aircraft is to maintain straight and level flight?
explanationTotal:
L = ½ p x CL x V2 x S
  • ½ p and S will remain constant. Lift will also be unchanged in straight and level flight. Therefore, we have:
    CL = 1 / V2

According to the above formula, to maintain constant lift, if V decreases => CL must increase.
In this case, speed decreases by:

((1.1 - 1.4) / 1.4) * 100 = -21.43%

V has decreased by a factor of 0.786, so:

V2 decreased by a factor of (0.786)2 = 0.618

To keep lift constant, CL must increased by the same amount:

So new value of CL will be CL = 1/0.62 = 1.62 = 62%

Alternatively, the following method could be used:

NEW VA / OLD VA = √(CLOLD / CLNEW)
(NEW VA / OLD VA)2 = (CLOLD / CLNEW)
(1.1/ 1.4)2 = (CLOLD / CLNEW)
0.62 = (CLOLD / CLNEW)
CLNEW = (1/.62)CLOLD
CLNEW = 1.62CLOLD

Which equals a 62% increase.

title: The purpose of a dorsal fin is to:
optionA: stabilise forebody vortices.
optionB: maintain static directional stability at large sideslip angles.
optionC: reduce tendency for spiral instability.
optionD: provide pitch and yaw control.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
To improve and maintain static directional stability at large sideslip angles, aircraft manufacturers benefit the use of dorsal and ventral fins (also called strakes).

A dorsal fin is a small surface extension installed at the leading edge of the vertical stabilizer.
It adds stability and prevents a condition called rudder lock, which is when the vertical stabilizer stalls and the rudder suddenly reverses, which may leave the pilot unable to center it.

A ventral fin is placed on the underside of the aircraft’s fuselage.
Any fin placed on the underside of the fuselage is called a ventral fin, it improves static directional stability and reduces lateral stability.

title: Which of the following situations is the worst for aircraft handling in the event that a twin-engined aircraft is flying with one engine inoperative?
optionA: At high altitude with full passengers.
optionB: Empty aircraft at low altitude.
optionC: Performing a go-around with full passengers.
optionD: Empty aircraft performing a go-around.
explanationTotal:
Note: We had a very small amount of feedback for this question, and we had to make a judgement as to whether the examiner means performance or handling (our feedback did not make it clear, and the answers are the exact opposite of each other); we chose handling based on the other questions we have. It is therefore vital to fully read the question in the exam, and please let us know anything you can remember if you do see this question in your exam, so we can make it more precise, thank you!

Refer to figure.
ENGINE FAILURE

If one engine on a conventional twin-engine aircraft fails in flight, it adversely affects its performance and controllability.

With both engines operating at the same power setting on a twin-engine aircraft, the amount of thrust produced by each engine is identical and their lines of action are symmetrically displaced about the aircraft's normal axis.

If one engine fails in flight, the remaining thrust forces are asymmetrically displaced and the aircraft yaws in the direction of the failed engine.

YAWING MOMENT

The yawing moment is the product of thrust from the operating engine multiplied by the distance between the thrust line and the CG (thrust arm), (plus the drag from the failed engine multiplied by the distance between the engine centre line and the CG).

The strength of the yawing moment will depend on:
- how much thrust the operating engine is developing (throttle setting and density altitude).
- the distance between the thrust line and the CG (thrust arm).
- how much drag is being produced by the failed engine.

The rudder moment, which balances the yawing moment, is the result of the rudder force multiplied by the distance between the fin CP and the CG (rudder arm)

The ability of the pilot to counteract the yawing moment due to asymmetric thrust will depend on:
- rudder displacement (affecting rudder force).
- CG position (affecting rudder moment arm).
- the IAS (affecting rudder force).

This question is asking us which scenario is worst for controllability, which is where there is a high yawing moment, and our rudder has a low balancing moment. This would be at low altitude, high thrust settings, and low airspeed. This is because the high thrust creates a large asymmetry, and there is not much airflow over the rudder to fight against it.

A further decrease in controllability comes when the aircraft is at a low weight. The pilot can use a small bank angle onto the side of the live engine to reduce the aircraft's sideslip, and therefore its rudder deflection. This "banking technique" uses the aircraft's weight, and a heavier aircraft (counter-intuitively) is actually better for controllability.

Therefore, the worst scenario here is during a go-around with an empty aircraft.

title:
Refer to figure.
Line 1 shows the CL vs Alpha graph of an aerofoil in clean configuration. What can we say about the aerofoil and the configuration represented by line 2?
optionA: Symmetrical airfoil with trailing edge flaps.
optionB: Symmetrical airfoil with leading edge flaps.
optionC: Asymmetrical airfoil with leading edge flaps.
optionD: Asymmetrical airfoil with trailing edge flaps.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The graph in the question annex is the CL vs Alpha graph (Lift Coefficient vs Angle of Attack[AoA]) for a three different configurations of wing.

Knowing that line 1 is a clean aerofoil, we can see that line 2 has a slightly higher CL at all angles of attack, and a slight increase in critical angle of attack. Assuming that they are the same wing with the addition of an aerodynamic device, that would fit the profile of a leading edge flap.

Again, assuming that the same wing is being used, then line 3 is a significant increase in CL for the same AoA, with a lower critical angle of attack, which would indicate the presence of trailing edge flaps.

Another common line to see is that of slats, which follows the clean wing line, but continue on the same angle above the clean CLMAX, delaying the stall to a higher critical AoA. This is added here in green, and is very commonly asked.

We do also need to spot that line 1 crosses through the origin. This means that at 0º AoA, the lift is zero, which means that the aerofoil is symmetrical. If the line crosses the Y-axis above the origin, then the aerofoil has positive camber.

We can assume from the question text that the other lines represent different configurations of the same aerofoil, so our answer is symmetrical aerofoil with leading edge flaps extended.

title: In addition to ailerons, spoilers might be used at the same time to assist in lateral control. When doing so, how will the spoilers behave?
optionA: Down-going wing rise proportionally to aileron input, disturbing the airflow over the wing, reducing lift, and creating a roll moment.
optionB: Down-going wing fully rise with aileron input, disturbing the airflow over the wing, reducing lift, and creating a roll moment.
optionC: Up-going wing rise proportionally to aileron input, locally increasing drag, assisting to counteracting adverse yaw.
optionD: Up-going wing fully rise with aileron input, increasing total drag, reducing lift, and creating a roll moment.
explanationTotal:
Spoilers are panels on the upper wind surface that are movable. They are hinged at the forward edge and is used to disturb the airflow over the wing to reduce lift. It will also increase drag on the wing that it is raised.

When turning, the down going wing will experience a decrease of lift with an up going aileron. That decrease of lift can be assisted by raising the spoiler as well. Raising the spoiler on the down going wing also increases drag on that wing which helps to counter adverse yaw. The degree of spoiler that needs to be raised varies proportionally to the aileron input, so as to remain versatile with respect to the addition of drag and decrease in lift. At the same time the spoiler on the up going wing will remain flushed.

title: The sensor of a stall warning system can be activated by a change in the location of the:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: centre of gravity.
optionB: centre of lift.
optionC: stagnation point.
optionD: transition region.

optionA: speed = 0, load factor = +1.
optionB: speed = V<sub>S</sub>, load factor = 0.

title: You are the pilot flying a light aeroplane with a clockwise turning propeller. While you are distracted by having to deal with a minor equipment failure, the stall warning horn activates. Which of the following would indicate that the aircraft had entered a full stall, if you do NOT respond to the warning and try to maintain level flight using the elevator?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: The nose pitching down with a full pitch-up elevator.
optionB: The aileron controls give a feeling of a heavy buffet.
optionC: The effect of the rudder control being reversed.
optionD: The nose yaws to the right regardless of the rudder input.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
When the lift developed by an aeroplane wing is no longer sufficient to sustain the mass of the aeroplane in flight, in the configuration being considered, the wing is stalled.

A stall is caused by airflow separation. Separation can occur when either the boundary layer has insufficient kinetic energy or the adverse pressure gradient becomes too great.

STALLING ANGLE OF ATTACK
At a constant mass and air density, the coefficient of lift (CL), and consequently the total amount of lift, is dependent on the angle of attack.

Graphically, lift increases almost linearly from an angle of attack of 0º to 4º, and then at an increasing rate to 15º. Lift cannot be obtained without incurring the penalty of drag.

At a specific angle of attack, depending on circumstances, the lift generated is insufficient to sustain the aircraft in level flight. The angle of attack at which this occurs is the stalling angle or critical angle and is the point at which CLMAX is attained. An aeroplane will not stall unless the critical angle is exceeded.

The aeroplane may be considered stalled when the behaviour of the aeroplane gives a clear distinctive indication of an unacceptable nature to the pilot that the aeroplane is stalled.

Acceptable indications of a stall, occurring either individually or in combination are:
a. A nose-down pitch that cannot be readily arrested.
b. Buffeting, of a magnitude and severity that is a strong and effective deterrent to further speed reduction.
c. The pitch control reaches the aft stop and no further increase in pitch attitude occurs when the control is held full aft for a short time before recovery is initiated.
d. Unresponsive flight controls.

title:
Assuming ISA conditions and a climb above the tropopause at constant Mach number and aeroplane mass, the:
(note: assume maintaining constant thrust)
optionA: lift coefficient increases.
optionB: IAS increases.
optionC: lift coefficient decreases.
optionD: TAS decreases.
explanationTotal:
Mach Number equals True Airspeed (TAS) divided by the local speed of sound (LSS). LSS is a function of temperature only and equals 38.95 x √K.

Above the tropopause, temperature remains constant. Consequently, LSS will also remain unchanged. In order to maintain a constant Mach number, TAS must also remain unchanged.

With increasing altitude, pressure continues to fall. This causes density to reduce with increasing altitude. IAS is a measurement of dynamic pressure.

  • Dynamic pressure = 1/2 p V2, where V equals TAS.
  • With a decreasing density (p) and constant TAS, IAS decreases.

Now let's take a look at the lift formula:

  • L = 1/2 p V2 S CL

A decrease in IAS, with all remaining variables being the same would result in a decrease in lift. To maintain a climbing situation, lift must increase to its original value. Therefore, lift coefficient must be increased (by increasing AOA.

title: An aircraft has a mass of 304 tonnes which includes 75 tonnes of fuel at take-off. The aircraft lands with 8.5 tonnes of fuel remaining. On take-off, its stalling speed was 100 kt. Determine the stalling speed on landing:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
explanationTotal:
The aircraft has burnt 75 - 8.5 = 66.5 tonnes of fuel.
Landing Mass = 304 - 66.5 = 237.5 tonnes

This exercise can be solved applying the following formula:

New VS = Old VS √Change in Mass
New VS = 100 √(237.5 / 304)
New VS = 88.4 kt

title: Which of the following configurations will give the highest Lift/Drag ratio?
optionA: Clean wing.
optionB: Leading edge devices extended.
optionC: Trailing edge devices extended.
optionD: Both leading and trailing edge devices extended.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
THE CL v CD POLAR DIAGRAM

The polar curve of an aerofoil is the graphical relationship of the coefficients of lift and drag plotted against each other, the resulting graph is as shown in the attached figure.

LIFT/DRAG RATIO

For any given mass and altitude, level flight can be maintained at any speed, between the maximum and minimum limits, by adjusting the angle of attack to keep the lift formula in balance, to ensure the lift developed is equal to the mass.

As the angle of attack increases so does the induced drag, this increases the total drag. To counteract the increased total drag a greater amount of thrust is required. This will increase the fuel consumption and is clearly an inefficient way to maintain level flight.

The most efficient manner in which to fly an aeroplane is with an angle of attack that creates the greatest amount of lift whilst causing the least amount of drag.

The most efficient angle of attack is that which produces the highest lift/drag ratio. This angle of attack is the same for all masses and altitudes and is usually 4º.

The EAS at which this occurs is the most economical cruise EAS and varies in direct proportion to the gross mass of the aeroplane.

THE EFFECT OF FLAPS

Although lift increases with greater flap angles so also does drag, but to a much greater extent, particularly at angles of attack above that which produces the best lift/drag ratio.

Lowering flaps usually decreases the lift/drag ratio and, although it is possible to fly at a lower speed, the thrust required increases. Selecting the largest flap angle causes the greatest negative influence on the lift/drag ratio.

title: Total pressure is: (rho = density)
optionA: is ½ rho V².
optionB: static pressure minus dynamic pressure.
optionC: measured at a small hole in a surface, parallel to the local stream.
optionD: static pressure plus dynamic pressure.
explanationTotal:
Bernoulli's equation (theorem) states:

Total Pressure = Dynamic Pressure (½ ρ V2) + Static Pressure = Constant.

title: The use of flaps allows an aircraft to produce (1) _____ lift at a (2) _____ speed, and with (3) _____ drag.
optionA: (1) less; (2) higher; (3) lower
optionB: (1) more; (2) lower; (3) higher
optionC: (1) the same; (2) the same; (3) lower
optionD: (1) the same; (2) lower; (3) higher
explanationTotal:
Flaps are called high-lift devices, and are primarily used to allow an aircraft to fly slower without stalling, useful for take-off and landing. Their other uses are for increased drag; modern jet aeroplanes are particularly "slippery" these days, and sometimes struggle to lose energy, so flaps can be used to help with this. Flaps also change the chord line of the wing, allowing a more nose-down attitude for better pilot visibility and easier landings.

Flaps increase lift by increasing the camber of the wing, and often also increasing the wing area, depending on the style of flaps. This helps the aircraft gain more lift for the same airflow. An aircraft only needs enough lift to counteract its own weight in normal operations (and a little more in turns), so there is no need for more lift, only to fly slower, with the same amount of lift.

The increased drag also comes from the increased camber and wing area, as this makes the wing less efficient, with a lower lift-to-drag ratio. The steeper the flap angle, the higher the drag they will produce, and this is parasite drag, which increases with the square of the speed.

title: Why is there a limit on the full rudder deflection as airspeed (IAS) increases on transport aeroplanes?
optionA: To reduce the directional stability at high airspeed.
optionB: Full rudder deflection is not to be limited on transport aeroplanes as airspeed increases.
optionC: Because full rudder deflection could create an excessive load on the structure.
optionD: To reduce the risk of entering a spiral divergence in cruise.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
With a simple control system, full rudder pedal movement will provide full rudder deflection.

With high speed aircraft, while it is necessary to have large rudder deflections available at low speed, when flying at high speed, full rudder deflection would cause excessive loads on the structure.

To prevent this occurring, a gear change system can be incorporated into the rudder control system. This may be a single gear change which gives a smaller rudder deflection for full pedal movement above a certain speed, or a progressive gear change which gives a decreasing rudder deflection with full pedal movement as speed increases.

title:
Refer to figure.
During a go-around, how will each aircraft react?
optionA: A tends to pitch down on application of TOGA.
optionB: B will just accelerate if no pull force is applied.
optionC: A requires more pull force than B.
optionD: A is more likely to over rotate.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

Go-around with underslung engines (A)

If the engine is located well below the CG (figure A, like most modern jets), adding maximum thrust (TOGA) produces a strong pitch-up moment. This pitch-up moment – depending on aircraft geometry – can be so pronounced, that from a trimmed approach condition, the aircraft pitches up until stall unless acted against by the pilot by pushing the control column

Go-around with tail mounted engines (B)

If the engine is mounted in the tail, the thrust line is above the CG (figure B) this is the opposite of the above and a thrust increase will produce a nose down moment (negative moment). B requires more pull force than A.

title:
Determine the thrust in N if you are in a 30 degree climb, given:

Lift: 127 436 N
Drag: 120 500 N
Weight: 15 000 kg
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Consider an aircraft in a straight steady climb along a straight flight path inclined at an angle (γ) to the horizontal. γ (gamma) is the symbol used for climb angle. The forces on the aircraft consist of Lift, normal to the flight path; Thrust and Drag, parallel to it; and Weight, parallel to the force of gravity.

Weight is resolved into two components: one opposite Lift (W cos γ) and the other acting in the same direction as Drag (W sin γ), backwards along the flight path. The requirements for equilibrium are:

  • Thrust must equal the sum of Drag plus the backwards component of Weight (T = D + W sin γ); and
  • Lift must equal its opposing component of Weight (L = W cos γ)
For equilibrium at a greater angle of climb, the Lift required will be less, and the backwards component of Weight will be greater.

With regards to this question,

  • W = 15 000 kg x 9.81 m/s2 = 147 150 N
  • T = D + W sin γ
    T= 120 500 + 147 150 sin (30º) = 194 075 N

title: Bernoulli’s equation can be written as:(pt = total pressure, ps = static pressure, q = dynamic pressure)
optionA: pt + ps = q.
optionB: pt - q = ps.
optionC: pt = q - ps.
optionD: pt = ps - q.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
A venturi works on the principle of pressure, speed and airflow.
Air comes in under constant pressure (which we will call X from this point onwards) and is directed through the tube.
At a certain point in time, the tube starts becoming tighter.
However, the same amount of air still has to travel through this (now tighter) tube (we call this airflow Y).
It does so by flowing faster than before.
This increased airspeed creates a lower pressure at the tighter part of the venturi, while the wider part still has its original pressure and airspeed.
After the tightening, the tube becomes wider again and the air returns to its original static pressure and airspeed (airflow Z).
It now has the properties of airflow X again.

Before the venturi (airflow X)

  • Static Pressure normal
  • Speed of the airflow normal
In the throat (airflow Y)
  • Total pressure same as airflow X and Z
  • Static Pressure low
  • Speed of the airflow increased
After the venturi (airflow Z)
  • Static Pressure normal
  • Speed of the airflow normal
The venturi works on Bernoulli’s principle.
Bernoulli’s principle states that in increase in speed of a fluid occurs simultaneously with a decrease in the fluid’s static pressure.
The formula for this principle = Total pressure = static pressure + dynamic pressure.
If airspeed increases, the static pressure decreases and dynamic pressure increases, keeping total pressure the same.

title: Assuming all other factors remain the same, which of the following wing designs would have the least effective high lift devices?
optionA: A wing without any sweep angle.
optionB: A wing with a sweepback angle of 15°.
optionC: A wing with a sweepback angle of 25°.
optionD: The sweep angle of the wing does not influence the effectiveness of high lift devices.
explanationTotal:
Learning Objective 081.02.05.01.02: Describe the influence of the angle of sweepback at subsonic speed on: CLMAX; efficiency of and requirement for high-lift devices; pitch-up stall behaviour.

Swept wings can be very useful for high speed flight, as the effectively lengthen the chord of the wing, so therefore decrease the thickness-to-chord ratio, effectively making the wing behave like a thinner wing and having a higher MCRIT.

Swept wings do pay for this in other areas though, such as low speed flight, where they have a tendency to stall at the tips first, as well as lower lift for the same angle of attack, and less effective high lift devices.

High lift devices are less effective on swept wings, take trailing edge flaps for example, simply because the hinge line is not perpendicular to the airflow, and this puts the flaps at an angle, which decreases their effectiveness. The steeper the sweep angle, the stronger this effect. Therefore, the worst wing type from these options is the one with the greatest sweepback of 25°.

title: The Lift Coefficient versus Angle Of Attack curve of a negatively cambered aerofoil section intersects the horizontal axis of the graph...
optionA: at the origin.
optionB: at no point.
optionC: to the left of the origin.
optionD: to the right of the origin.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
Camber is the asymmetry between two acting surfaces on an airfoil. For an aircraft, this is the top and the bottom of the wing.
Positive camber means that a wing is thicker on the top end of the wing, than on the bottom if looked at from the chord.
In case of positive camber, a wing will generate lift with airspeed, as the air on top of the airfoil will get accelerated more than on the bottom, creating a low pressure on the top and high pressure at the bottom.
This is “pushing” the wing up into the air as the pressure difference wants to restore itself to 0 difference.
In case of negative camber, the exact opposite happens and the lift coefficient for a certain speed is lower than for a positively cambered wing.

A completely symmetrical airfoil will intersect the vertical axis of the graph at the origin (0).
A positively cambered airfoil will generate more lift at the same speed (and therefore has a higher CL) than a symmetrical airfoil and therefore intersects the vertical axis above and left of the origin.
A negatively cambered airfoil will generate less lift at the same speed (which translates into a lower CL at a certain speed) and therefore intersects the vertical axis below and right of the origin.

title: What causes the separation of the boundary layer at high Mach numbers?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Shockwave
optionB: A higher angle of attack
optionC: Increases buffet on the controls which make the boundary layer to separate
optionD: Due to a higher Mcrit and reduced static pressure
explanationTotal:
Normal shock waves are disadvantageous as they provide high force against motion (i.e. drag). Shock waves cause turbulent airflow behind it, there is a large increase in pressure which results in airflow separation. The separation of airflow will cause buffet.

  • At high speed, the angle of attack is low.
  • MCRIT is the speed above which the shockwave appears.

title: An aeroplane performs a steady horizontal, co-ordinated turn with 45 degrees of bank at 230 kt TAS. The same aeroplane with the same bank angle and speed, but at a higher mass:
optionA: will turn with the same radius, but might stall.
optionB: will have a higher rate of turn.
optionC: will turn with a larger turn radius.
optionD: will turn with a smaller turn radius.
explanationTotal:
The Turn radius varies with changes in either speed or bank:
  • Turn Radius = TAS2 ÷ (g x tan ɸ)

Therefore, if both aircraft have the same speed and bank angle, they will have the same turn radius.

However, an increase in mass requires an increase in lift. The question states that speed and bank angle remain the same, therefore lift can only be increased by increasing angle of attack which is represented by coefficient of lift (CL):

  • L = 1/2 p V2 S CL
If the angle of attack increases too much, beyond the critical angle of attack, the aircraft may stall.

title:
The Cm (pitching moment) vs alpha (angle of attack) graph is mainly determined by aerofoil and aircraft design, and dictates aircraft longitudinal stability. Which of the following factors can the pilot influence whilst in flight?

1. The centre of pressure, by changing the flap setting.
2. The neutral point, by varying alpha.
3. The centre of pressure, by varying alpha.
4. The centre of gravity, which influences the degree of pitching moment.
optionA: 1 and 4
optionB: 1 and 3
optionC: 2 and 3
optionD: 2 and 4
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The CM (pitching moment) vs alpha (Angle of Attack) graph is a graph depicting the longitudinal stability of an aircraft. As a very short explanation, the point where the line crosses the X-axis (Angle of Attack) is the trim position, where no pitching moment exists. As long as the gradient of the graph is negative, whenever the aircraft has a nose-up disturbance, the AoA will decrease to correct for this, and vice versa. That means that a negative gradient gives positive static longitudinal stability. The more negative the gradient of the line is, the stronger the stability. The line is not usually straight, it changes gradient due to the aircraft's design and window of stability.

The CM vs alpha graph is affected by various things in the aircraft's design, including the locations of the wings and the shape of aerofoils, size of wings, etc. The CG location also massively affects the CM vs alpha graph, of course.

The question is terribly worded, but really we only have to be able to say which factors a pilot can change in flight, and make sure that they actually do affect stability, and the CM vs alpha graph. Whilst the question is terrible, the answer isn't too bad.

  1. "The centre of pressure, by changing the flap setting."
    • Yes, the centre of pressure is one of the key factors determining the CM and it can be changed by changing flap setting, which is something we can do in the air. This would likely change the CM vs alpha graph completely.
  2. "The neutral point, by varying alpha."
    • The neutral point is a set location in the aircraft, determined by things such as the wing sizes and moment arms, and cannot be changed in flight.
  3. "The centre of pressure, by varying alpha."
    • Yes, again, the centre of pressure does affect the CM, and changing the angle of attack changes the CM and the gradient, strength of stability, etc., and is something that we can do in flight, of course.
  4. "The centre of gravity, which influences the degree of pitching moment."
    • This is where the question gets a bit more difficult. We are assuming that the pilot cannot change the CG during flight, but of course, some aircraft have trim tanks for that possibility, and we know that fuel burn does alter the CG, but not in a way the pilot can meaningfully control. The second part, the "degree of pitching moment" is also incredibly vague, and given the vague question, we agree that this option is incorrect.

title: Assuming no flow separation and no compressibility effects the location of the centre of pressure of a positively cambered aerofoil section:
optionA: moves backward when the angle of attack decreases.
optionB: is at approximately 25% chord irrespective of angle of attack.
optionC: moves forward when the angle of attack decreases.
optionD: is independent of angle of attack.
explanationTotal:
Refer to the figure.
The centre of pressure is the theoretical point through which we assume all the lift to act.

For cambered aerofoils, we know that the centre of pressure moves forwards as angle of attack increases, and moved backwards as the angle of attack decreases.
For symmetrical aerofoils, the centre of pressure is at a fixed and does not move with changes in angle of attack.

In the figure you can see how the centre of pressure moves with decreasing angle of attack.

title: Regarding wake turbulence, choose the correct sentence.
optionA: As an aircraft’s angle of attack increases to a high angle, the wake turbulence becomes weaker.
optionB: Heavy aircraft produce stronger wake turbulence than lighter ones.
optionC: Aircraft mass does NOT influence wake turbulence.
optionD: Wake turbulence is stronger behind a light aircraft than a heavier aircraft.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
WAKE TURBULENCE

The strength and size of the vortices produced by an aeroplane are dependent on the amount of lift produced. Strong vortices are produced by large transport aeroplanes that create a significant amount of turbulence behind the aeroplane along the path of the aircraft.

The disturbance so caused can extend for a considerable distance and last for several minutes. This is wake turbulence that can seriously affect the controllability of following aeroplanes if they are too close.

The severity of the turbulence so created is categorised to enable following pilots to assess the difficulties that may be encountered. The larger, heavier aeroplanes create the worst turbulence that will cause problems to following pilots particularly when close to the ground during take-off or landing. Pilots are advised by the aviation authorities of the minimum distance and/or time separation from the aeroplane ahead deemed to be safe, to avoid having control problems.

The minimum separation distance and/or time is based on the relative sizes of the aeroplanes concerned. Wake turbulence is affected by the height of the aeroplane and the prevailing wind conditions. The downwash of the airflow behind the aeroplane causes the vortices to descend to one thousand feet below the aeroplane. However, at low height, when the aeroplane is in ground effect, the vortices move outward from the path of the aeroplane over the ground. But any cross wind between 5 kt and 10 kt will prevent this happening to the upwind vortex and will keep it on the aircraft’s track. It is particularly important during the take-off phase that the following aircraft complies with the advised separation because of this.

Aircraft mass, speed, aspect ratio and trailing-edge flap setting influence the strength of the vortices. The vortex strength is greatest for heavy aeroplanes at low airspeed and in the clean configuration, which is just after rotation at take-off. Vortices only cease when the nose-wheel touches down during landing ground run.

title: When operating at a constant RPM, the engine torque is _____ the propeller torque.
optionA: lower than
optionB: the same as
optionC: independent of
optionD: higher than
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The purpose of the propeller is to convert the power output from the engine into thrust. The power developed is transmitted to the propeller shaft as engine torque and rotates the propeller.

The rotation of a propeller creates a total reactive force at right angles to the chordline of the propeller blade. This can be divided into two components, that which is perpendicular to the relative airflow, the lift, and that which is parallel to the relative airflow, the drag.

Thrust acts parallel to the direction of flight, whilst propeller torque (the resistance to the motion in the plane of rotation) acts perpendicular to the direction of flight. The propeller torque must thus be overcome or balanced by engine torque for a propeller section to provide thrust.

Engine torque will rotate the propeller and the propeller, while creating thrust (propeller lift) will resist the engine torque with propeller torque (propeller drag). If the engine and propeller torque are in balance, the engine RPM is constant (Newton’s first law of motion)

title:
Refer to figure.
What is the effect of spoilers on the angle of attack and stall speed at a constant mass?
optionA: With increasing spoilers, the angle of attack increases and the stall speed decreases.
optionB: With decreasing spoilers, the angle of attack decreases and the stall speed increases.
optionC: With increasing spoilers, both the angle of attack and stall speed decrease.
optionD: With increasing spoilers, both the angle of attack and stall speed increase.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Spoilers can be used for roll control or as speedbrakes.
In either case they:
- increase drag
- decrease CLMAX
- increase stall speed
- for a constant CL, increase the angle of attack

title: Which of the following is the design speed for maximum gust intensity?
optionA: V<sub>A</sub>
optionB: V<sub>B</sub>
optionC: V<sub>C</sub>
optionD: V<sub>NE</sub>
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
All aircraft have limitations to their speed and the loads that they can sustain at those speeds. In particular, we have to know about the load/speed diagram for CS-25 (large) aeroplanes. There is a diagram for the maximum load factors (positive and negative) that an aircraft can sustain, whether that limit was to do with a stall limit, or a structural load factor limit. There is also a limiting gust envelope diagram for the maximum gusts an aircraft must be able to handle at various speeds, see annex above.
This creates some set design speeds for the aircraft, such as VA, VB, VC and VD.
  • VA - Manoeuvring Speed, the speed where the aircraft will stall at exactly the limiting load factor (2.5 G for CS-25 aircraft).
  • VB - Design Speed for Maximum Gust Intensity, the speed where an aircraft must be able to manage a gust of up to 66 fps.
  • VC - Design Cruise Speed, the maximum speed an aircraft is able to cruise at, giving sufficient safety margin to VD, and means the aircraft will not exceed VD if a particular disturbance occurs when cruising at VC. It is also the point where gusts of up to 50 fps should be managed by the airframe. VC should not be more than 0.8 x VD.
  • VD - Design Dive Speed, the maximum speed that the aircraft can handle in a dive, often limited by vibrations, buffet or flutter. This is the absolute speed limit of the airframe, and the aircraft should be able to manage 25 fps gusts at this speed.

title: While a multi engine aeroplane is taking of on a wet runway, the aeroplane starts becoming uncontrollable with significant yaw. This is due to...
optionA: the slipstream effect.
optionB: the gyroscopic effect.
optionC: the CG being close to the forward limit.
optionD: asymmetric thrust.
explanationTotal:
Note: This question was created from broken feedback. Please send any further exam feedback to us in the comments or email it to info@atplquestions.com, thank you.

The clues for this one were the wet runway, and the uncontrollability. If a multi-engine aircraft loses an engine during take-off, the remaining engine will produce a significant amount of asymmetry, causing a strong yawing moment towards the dead engine. This can be fought against by using the rudder, and helped also by a little nosewheel steering. However, on a wet runway, the nosewheel steering may not be effective, as hydroplaning could drastically reduce the traction of the front tyre(s) and therefore turning the nosewheel would not help the situation.

This is partly why the VMCG (minimum control speed on the ground) can only be calculated using force from the rudder, as the rudder will not be affected by a wet surface, but the nosewheel might be. We have not been told if we are above VMCG or not here, but you could assume that we are not if the aircraft is "uncontrollable". This would result in a rejected take-off, as we are certainly below V1.

Any significant yaw on take-off is usually from an engine problem. Possibly from a tyre blowout also, but that is not one of the options. Some of the other options were possibilities for causing yaw, particularly in a propeller aircraft, but they did not fit the conditions nearly as well as asymmetric thrust.

title:
Refer to figure.
Which force do lines 1 and 2 represent?
optionA: (1) Thrust, (2) torque.
optionB: (1) Torque, (2) Thrust.
optionC: (1) Lift, (2) drag.
optionD: (1) Drag, (2) lift.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The purpose of the propeller is to convert the power output from the engine into thrust. The power developed is transmitted to the propeller shaft as engine torque and rotates the propeller.

The rotation of a propeller creates a total reactive force at right angles to the chordline of the propeller blade. This can be divided into two components, that which is perpendicular to the relative airflow, the lift, and that which is parallel to the relative airflow, the drag.

Thrust acts parallel to the direction of flight, whilst propeller torque (the resistance to the motion in the plane of rotation) acts perpendicular to the direction of flight.

The propeller torque must thus be overcome or balanced by engine torque for a propeller section to provide thrust.

title: What speed will be limiting with a descent at constant mach?
optionA: M<sub>MO</sub>
optionB: V<sub>MO</sub>
optionC: V<sub>S</sub>
optionD: V<sub>NE</sub>
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
At sea level, the TAS is comparitively low and the speed of sound is quite high. At high altitude (for a given CAS), the TAS is much higher, because the air is thin and the local speed of sound (LSS) is less, because it is colder.
Because the Mach number is TAS divided by LSS, this means in turn that at altitude, your Mach number is higher for a given CAS, than it is at low level.

The result of this is that, as you climb, the maximum speed is controlled at low level by CAS and VMO, and at altitude you reach your limiting Mach number MMO , before you reach VMO and therefore your maximum speed is controlled by MMO.

In the descent the reverse is true. Your maximum speed is controlled by MMO first, and then by VMO at lower altitudes.

Alternatively, LSS increases during the descent, due to the rising temperature. Therefore, TAS must increase during descent to maintain constant Mach No.
IAS is also increasing and will eventually reach its limit. VMO ("max operating") is the term for the maximum certified IAS.

NOTE: You can also advice the ECTM lines to show that IAS increases with constant Mach.

title: In an aircraft that has positive stick force stability, whilst remaining in straight and level flight and without retrimming, the elevator stick force required when accelerating from 70 to 75 kt will be _____ than the force required when accelerating from 100 to 105 kt.
optionA: greater than
optionB: less than
optionC: close to zero, and the same as
optionD: very large, and the same as
explanationTotal:
IMPORTANT NOTE: We believe that "greater than" is the correct answer here (and most recent feedback seems to agree), but we have varying feedback about the correct answer over the past few months. Please let us know in the comments if you see this question in the real exam, thanks.

Also please note that this is a very different question to 811457, as many people (understandably) have connected the two. This question is about stick force stability, the force required to hold a different airspeed, whereas 811457 is about stick force stability, the force required to pull a particular G-force, so they are very different.

Refer to figure.

Figure 1 indicates the variation of stick force with airspeed and illustrates the effect of tab setting on stick force.

You can see from the graph, that dependent on EAS (Equivalent Air Speed) and trim tab setting, the stick force to hold a 1 kt change in airspeed from the trimmed speed DECREASES as the trimmed speed increases. There are a few factors at play that cause this, including the change to elevator displacement, effect of the trim tab, dynamic pressure change, etc.

This means that holding the aircraft 10 kts from its trimmed speed requires less stick force at a high trimmed speed than if it were trimmed at low speed.

Therefore, holding a 5 kt difference from 70 kts would required a greater force than holding a 5 kt difference from 100 kt.

Stick position stability exists when the aircraft responds "correctly" to a push or pull. For example, pushing the stick causes a pitch down and an airspeed increase (this is binary, an aircraft either has stick position stability or it doesn't).

Stick force stability is a further continuation of that, and in an aircraft that has positive stick force stability, a greater push force produces a greater increase in airspeed (it is a bit more nuanced than this, but this is all we need to know here). The level of stick force stability is proportional to the slope of the curve of stick force vs. speed (annex above). The steeper the curve, the higher the stick force stability (i.e. a 1 kt change to airspeed requires more force).

title: After take-off, the pilot monitoring retracts the flaps prematurely instead of the landing gear. Which of the following speed limitations may be broken?
optionA: V<sub>MO</sub>
optionB: V<sub>FE</sub>
optionC: V<sub>S</sub>
optionD: V<sub>LE</sub>
explanationTotal:
Learning Objective 081.01.09.01.09: Explain the effects of flap-setting errors, such as mis-selection and premature/late extension or retraction of flaps, on: take-off and landing distance and speeds; climb and descent performance; stall buffet margins.

The use of flaps on take-off is to allow the aircraft to maintain flight at lower speeds, therefore using less runway whilst accelerating. After take-off, the flaps just increase the aircraft's drag, so reduce the climb capability of the aircraft. Therefore, quite early into the take-off climb, the pilots will retract the flaps, in order to accelerate further and reduce drag.

If the flaps are retracted too early, the aircraft may not be flying fast enough to gain sufficient lift with a clean wing, and the aircraft will therefore stall. If the flaps are retracted too late, the aircraft may accelerate past the VFE for that flap setting (maximum speed with flaps extended).

Therefore, in this question, where the pilot monitoring has retracted the flaps prematurely (early), there is a potential for the aircraft to be below the new VS, thereby stalling the aircraft.

title: When a wing’s angle of attack increases, the pressure differential (1) _____, leading to a/an (2) _____ in the intensity of the wing tip vortices.
optionA: (1) increases; (2) increase
optionB: (1) increases; (2) decrease
optionC: (1) decrease; (2) decrease
optionD: (1) decrease; (2) increase
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
Bernoulli’s theorem when applied to the airflow past an aerofoil at less than Mach 0.4 shows that the total pressure is equal to the sum of the dynamic pressure (the pressure caused by the movement of the air) and the static pressure(the pressure of the air not associated with its movement) and can be expressed as the following equation:

Total Pressure (pt) = Dynamic Pressure (q) + Static Pressure (ps)

The total pressure is constant along a streamline flow. Therefore, if dynamic pressure increases then static pressure decreases and vice versa.

If the static pressure on one side of a body is reduced more than on the other side, a pressure differential will exist.

The actual pressure distribution over the upper and lower surfaces varies with changes in angle of attack, as does the pressure differential and the amount of lift developed.

As the angle of attack increases, the low pressure above the aerofoil deepens and the suction peak moves forward. This results in the lift increasing and more of the lift being generated further forward.

INDUCED DRAG
Whenever a wing produces lift, concentrated vortices form at the wing tips. The vortices are strongest at the wingtips and become progressively weaker toward the centre-line of the aircraft.

It is the production of lift itself which reduces the magnitude of the lift force being generated. To replace the lift lost by the increased downwash, the aircraft must be flown at a higher angle of attack. This increases drag. This extra drag is called induced drag.

The stronger the vortices, the greater the induced drag.

The induced drag decreases with airspeed (with a rate of 1/V²) and increases with angle of attack and increasing weight.

INDUCED DRAG COEFFICIENT

CDI = CL2 / π * AR

Increasing the angle of attack increases CL. From the formula we can deduct that Induced drag is directly proportional to CL squared.
So, increasing the angle of attack increases CL, which increases Induced drag.

title: The effects of the yawing moment caused by an engine failure in a twin-engine aeroplane will be greater when the distance between the operating engine and the CG (thrust arm) is...
optionA: greater than the distance between the rudder and the CG.
optionB: greater.
optionC: less than the distance between the rudder and the CG.
optionD: less.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
When an engine fails on a multi-engine aircraft there will be a decrease in thrust and an increase in drag on the side with the failed engine:

  • airspeed will decay.
  • the nose will drop and.
  • most significantly, there will be an immediate yawing moment towards the failed engine.
The forces and moments acting on an aircraft following failure of the left engine are shown in figure 1. The aircraft has a yawing moment towards the dead engine. The pilot has applied rudder to stop the yaw. The vital action when an engine fails is to stop the yaw.
The rolling and yawing moments and the power of the flight controls to balance them will determine the controllability of an aircraft with asymmetric thrust. Rolling and yawing moments with asymmetric thrust are affected by:
  • Thrust on the live engine
  • Altitude
  • Drag from the dead engine and propeller
  • Asymmetric blade effect (also known as ‘P’ Factor)
  • CG position
The fore and aft CG location has no effect on the yawing moment from a failed engine, but will influence the rudder arm, hence the rudder moment. CG on the aft limit will give the smallest rudder arm and the least ability to oppose the yawing moment from a failed engine.
  • Torque reaction
  • Difference in lift due to slipstream
  • Rolling moment due to sideslip
  • Weight
  • Airspeed

title:
Refer to figure.
The line representing the effect of the tail on the longitudinal static stability of an aeroplane is line (1) _____, which has the same effect as a (2) _____ CG.
optionA: (1) Y; (2) forward
optionB: (1) Z; (2) forward
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
Evidence of static stability is shown by a tendency to return to equilibrium, or “trim”, upon displacement.
Positive static longitudinal stability is indicated by a negative slope of CM versus CL. The degree of static longitudinal stability is indicated by the slope of the curve.

Thus, the tail has a stabilising contribution for stability which is represented by a negative slopped curve Z.

Position of the Centre of Gravity
Variations in the position of the centre of gravity greatly affect the static longitudinal stability of an aircraft.

Generally, the further forward the centre of gravity the greater the stability.

Note:
Tail effect: The downward force moment at the tail causes the aircraft to pitch up.

When the center of gravity (Cg) is positioned forward, it creates a pitch-down moment at the nose of the aircraft.

title: Which statement is correct regarding the Drag Divergence Mach number (MDRAG DIVERGENCE)?
optionA: Drag Divergence Mach number is close to, and always less than M<sub>CRIT</sub>.
optionB: Drag Divergence Mach number is greater than M<sub>CRIT</sub>, except for supercritical wings where it is slightly less than M<sub>CRIT</sub>.
optionC: Drag Divergence Mach number is slightly less than M<sub>CRIT</sub>, except for supercritical wings where it is greater than M<sub>CRIT</sub>.
optionD: Drag Divergence Mach number is close to, and always greater than M<sub>CRIT</sub>.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
As speed increases above MCRIT shock waves begin to form and drag increases more rapidly than it would have done without the shock waves. The additional drag is called wave drag and is due to energy drag and boundary layer separation.

The Mach number at which the aerodynamic drag begins to increase rapidly is called the Drag Divergence MachNumber.

The Drag Divergence Mach Number is usually close to, and always greater than, the Critical Mach Number.

title: An aircraft is flying near the ITCZ and suffers buffeting due to clear air turbulence? What should be done?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Climb to a higher altitude.
optionB: Extend the flaps and slow the aircraft to V<sub>S</sub>.
optionC: Descend to a lower altitude and fly at the turbulence penetration speed.
optionD: Continue flying at present speed and altitude, CAT is temporary in the ITCZ.
explanationTotal:
The ITCZ (Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone) is an area of very large uplift and often violent thunderstorms due to converging air at the surface. It is also a region where the tropopause will be incredibly high, sometimes in the region of 55-60,000ft. This makes it often impossible to climb away from the Clear Air Turbulence experienced in that region.

The Clear Air Turbulence is causing us to go into either high or low speed buffet at our current altitude, so we should instead descend to a lower altitude, out of “coffin corner” and fly at turbulence penetration speed to get the best safety margin for turbulence.

title: Why is it bad to have too much lateral stability?
optionA: Less aileron deflection required during crosswind landing
optionB: More aileron deflection required during crosswind landing
optionC: Constant aileron deflection required during crosswind landing
optionD: About the same deflection required as normal landing
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
During a crosswind landing, normally wind coming from the side tends to lift the wing in that direction and roll the aircraft to other side. To avoid this unwanted roll inner wing is kept lower to reduce its angle of attack.
The outer wing will have more angle of attack, hence more lift to balance this tendency.
High lateral stability would oppose this and try to make wings level, therefore more aileron deflection would be needed.

title:
Refer to figure.
What is the correct combination of letters identifying the airfoils with the corresponding numbers from the CD graphic?
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Aerofoils with high camber will produce the highest lift and, consequently, the greatest induced drag.

Aerofoils with greater frontal areas will produce the most parasite drag.

Less lift and induced drag will be produced by thinner aerofoils and shapes with little camber.

Let’s examine each aerofoil:

  • “a” and “d” have high camber.

  • “d” has a larger frontal area (and nose radius), therefore it will produce more drag than “a”.

  • “b” and “c” have little camber.

  • “b” is thinner than “c”. Thus “b” will produce less drag than “c”.

We get the following combinations: 1 – d, 2 – a, 3 – c, 4 – b

title: How does the speed of sound change with changing altitude in International Standard Atmosphere (ISA) conditions? As the altitude increases, the speed of sound...
optionA: increases in the troposphere.
optionB: decreases in the lower part of the stratosphere.
optionC: increases in the lower part of the stratosphere.
optionD: decreases in the troposphere.
explanationTotal:
Because air is compressible the changing air pressure created by the movement of the airplane is accompanied by a change of air temperature and a change of air density. Owing to this, the speed of movement generated by the pressure wave is equal to the speed of sound. Sound waves are audible pressure waves travelling at the speed of sound.

The Local Speed of Sound is defined by:
LSS=38.95∗√(T(K))

The speed of propagation of small pressure waves depends upon the temperature of the air ONLY.
In the troposphere, as altitude increases, the temperature decreases, therefore the LSS also decreases.

title: What will happen to the stall speed, stalling Angle Of Attack (AOA) and controllability of an aircraft in flight due to icing?
optionA: Stall speed, stalling AOA and controllability will all decrease.
optionB: Stall speed will increase but stalling AOA and controllability will both decrease.
optionC: Stall speed will decrease but stalling AOA and controllability will both increase.
optionD: Stall speed, stalling AOA and controllability will all increase.
explanationTotal:
