• Stalling angle of attack: as ice builds up, the aerodynamic efficiency of the wing and its ability to prevent separation of the airflow and therefore stall is highly reduced. Ice will lead to sooner separation, smaller stalling angle of attack, therefore causing a lower CLMAX.
  • Stall speed: referring to the lift equation, and assuming all other factors stay the same, ice buildup decreases the CLMAX and increases the mass of the aircraft in flight. Firstly just by itself an increase in mass causes an increase in stall speed. Secondly, a smaller CLMAX means that a higher speed will have to be maintained in order to maintain the same lift. Therefore our stall speed will have increase due to ice accretion.
  • Controllability: on top of the fact that an increase in weight will mean that any input in the control surfaces will lead to a slower reaction by the aircraft, icing can also get stuck between the control surfaces and or completely nullify their effect. For example, icing on the horizontal stabilizer will occur before the main wing, and seeing as the tail is normally producing a downwards force, a stall of the tail plane will lead to a drop of the nose of the aircraft and controllability over the longitudinal axis will have been completely lost. Therefore controllability will decrease in icing conditions.

title: An aeroplane is fitted with an external piece of scientific equipment. Which of the following factors will minimise the increase in form (pressure) drag?
optionA: An aerodynamically-shaped fairing.
optionB: A smooth or shiny surface that is kept clean.
optionC: A shape-minimising formation of shockwaves.
optionD: Minimising the weight of the equipment and fitting.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
Fairing - A secondary structure added to any part to reduce its drag.

Drag is the force which resists the forward motion of the aircraft. Drag acts parallel to and in the same direction as the relative airflow (in the opposite direction to the flight path).

Total Drag is sub-divided into two main types:

INDUCED DRAG - the result of lift generation.
PARASITE DRAG - independent of lift generation.

Parasite drag is further sub-divided into:

- Skin Friction Drag
- Form (Pressure) Drag
- Interference Drag

FORM DRAG

Form drag is produced whenever the streamline airflow passing over an aircraft separates from the surface and becomes turbulent. An example of extreme form drag is the effect of a flat plate placed at right angles to the airflow.

The pressure immediately in front of the plate is above atmospheric, whilst the pressure behind the plate is below atmospheric. This results in a sucking effect behind the plate and the formation of vortices. The more rapidly the airflow changes direction, the greater the pressure gradient, the earlier the separation, and the higher the form drag.

Changing the shape, or streamline, of a given object reduces drag by delaying the point at which the airflow separates.

On aircraft, for example, a fairing is often fitted around a fixed undercarriage leg to reduce form drag to an acceptable level.

title: The neutral point of an aeroplane is the point where:
optionA: assuming no flow separation, the pitching moment coefficient does not change with varying angle of attack.
optionB: the boundary layer changes from laminar to turbulent.
optionC: the velocity of the relative airflow is reduced to zero.
optionD: the aeroplane becomes longitudinally unstable when the CG is moved beyond it in an aft direction.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
The point where an aircraft’s total sum of a pressure field is acting upon the body is called the Center of Pressure (CP).
This is the point where the resultant vector of lift is said to be operating.
As the airfoil or Angle of attack changes (thus changing the lift coefficient), this pressure field will change and so will the center of pressure.

Aircraft longitudinal stability is directly related to Centre of Gravity (CG) position.
An aircraft with a more forward CG is more longitudinally stable than an aircraft with a more aft CG.
Placing the CG beyond the forward limit can cause an unacceptably high value of longitudinal stability, decreasing manoeuvrability by a significant amount.
Place the CG beyond the aft limit and the aircraft is too unstable, having excessive manoeuvrability.

If an aircraft is longitudinally stable, an increase in Angle of Attack (α) results in a negative pitching moment.
The nose will slightly fall down, decreasing the Angle of Attack.

If this aircraft has a decrease of Angle of Attack, the nose will come slightly upwards again, creating a positive pitching moment again by slightly raising the nose.
The point where the aircraft does not have any positive or negative static longitudinal stability, and therefore is static longitudinally neutral, is called the neutral point.
Placing the CG aft of this point makes the aircraft unstable, placing the CG forward of this point makes the aircraft stable.

title: Shock induced separation can occur...
optionA: at high Mach numbers, only at high angles of attack.
optionB: at high Mach numbers, only at low angles of attack.
optionC: behind a strong, normal shock wave, ranging from low to high angles of attack.
optionD: in supersonic flow only.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
Critical Mach Number: (MCRIT) The critical Mach number is the Mach number of the aircraft when the speed of the airflow over some part of the aircraft first reaches the speed of sound.

At high altitude, a large high-speed jet transport aircraft will be cruising at a speed marginally above its critical Mach number, and it will have a small shock wave on the wing. If such an aircraft overspeeds, the shock wave will rapidly grow larger, causing the static pressure to increase sharply in the immediate vicinity of the shock wave. The locally increased adverse pressure gradient will cause the boundary layer to separate immediately behind the shock wave. This is called a ‘shock stall’ because it results from a separated boundary layer just as the low speed stall does.

In the transonic range, the ‘shock stall’ is the separation of the boundary layer from the upper surface of the wing behind a shockwave. This causes the total lift generated to decrease.

Unlike the normal high-incidence angle stall, the ‘shock stall’ occurs at low angles of attack and at an unexpectedly high IAS. For swept-wing airplanes because the wing-tips stall first the airplane has a nose-up pitch tendency.

The angle of attack of the high-speed shock stall decreases as the Mach number increases and CLMAX decreases in a similar manner. Because the turbulent airflow behind a shockwave results in an increased loss of lift, any large rapid increase of speed can induce a premature stall.

title: On a jet aeroplane (engines mounted below the low wing) the thrust is suddenly increased. Which of these statements is correct about the elevator deflection required to maintain zero pitching moment?
optionA: The amount of elevator deflection is independent of CG location.
optionB: The elevator must be deflected downward.
optionC: No elevator deflection be will required because the thrust line of the engines remains unchanged.
optionD: The elevator must be deflected upwards.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The vertical location of the thrust line defines one of the direct contributions to stability.

  • If the thrust line is below the CG (the case of most airliners with underwing engines), a thrust increase will produce an added pitch-up moment => this will cause the airplane to slow down more than necessary (despite the added thrust). Creating an unstable situation. To counteract this, a pitch-down moment must be created. Therefore, the elevator must be deflected downwards.
  • If the thrust line is above the CG, this is the opposite of the above and a thrust increase will produce a nose down moment (negative moment), and, in moderate amounts, can have a stabilising effect. The airplane will settle at a higher speed, which is presumably what the pilot wants (despite the "power controls altitude" mantra). When the line is too high, the airplane may even descend and accelerate more than necessary, until the aerodynamic moment balances out the thrust moment, but overall the condition is stable.
  • Thrust is in line with CG. The airplane will start to climb (or reduce descent) and will settle on the same AoA and roughly the same speed.

title:
Refer to figure.
A rotating propeller blade element produces an aerodynamic force F that may be resolved into two components:

a force T perpendicular to the plane of rotation (thrust).
a force R generating a torque absorbed by engine power.

The diagram representing a rotating propeller blade element during reverse operation is:
optionA: diagram 1.
optionB: diagram 3.
optionC: diagram 4.
optionD: diagram 2.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Some airplanes have a manual override to the constant-speed mechanism to enable the pilot to reverse the pitch angle and thereby reverse the thrust. Utilization of this facility decreases the length of the ground run during a landing or an abandoned take-off and saves the wear on the brakes and tires.
For the propeller to produce thrust opposite to the direction of travel the propeller blades have to be rotated through the fine pitch stop to the ‘braking’ position.
The propeller blades have a negative angle of attack and will produce the required negative thrust. The drag so produced will decrease the length of the landing ground run or in the event of an abandoned take-off decrease the distance required to bring the airplane to a halt.

title: A light aircraft has a lift to drag ratio of 25 (L / D = 25). What is the maximum gliding distance from a height of 1000 m?
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
LIFT/DRAG RATIO

An appreciation of the efficiency of lift production is gained from studying the ratio between lift and drag, a high L/D ratio being more efficient.

For maximum efficiency, the wings should produce maximum lift with the least possible drag.

The L/D ratio increases with angle of attack up to a maximum at about 4°; this is called the “optimum” angle of attack. The L/D ratio then decreases with increasing angle of attack until CLMAX is reached.

ANGLE OF DESCENT IN THE GLIDE

Glide angle is a function ONLY of the L/D ratio. The descent (glide) angle will be least when the L/D ratio is the greatest.

L/D ratio is a maximum at the optimum angle of attack, and this also corresponds to the minimum drag speed (VMD). At speeds above or below VMD the glide angle will be steeper.

Maximum distance in a glide can be achieved when the aircraft is flown at (L/D)MAX (VMD).

EFFECT OF WIND

The glide angle will determine the distance that the aircraft can glide for a given change of height.

GLIDE DISTANCE = HEIGHT LOSS × (LIFT / DRAG)

This distance would only be achieved in still air. If there is a wind, the ground speed will change, and so the distance over the ground will change. In a headwind the ground distance will be decreased, and in a tailwind it will be increased.

In this question, using the above formula, where:

Height Loss = 1000m
Lift/Drag = 25

GLIDE DISTANCE = HEIGHT LOSS × (LIFT / DRAG) = 1000 x 25 = 25000m

GLIDE DISTANCE = 25000m.

title: The contribution of wing sweep back to static directional stability is:
optionA: positive
optionB: zero
optionC: negative
optionD: positive or negative depending on sweepback angle
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Sideslip develops whenever an aircraft rolls away from wings level.

With a swept wing in a sideslip, the low wing will have an increase in CL, because the low wing effectively becomes a straight wing, while the high wing effectively becomes more swept. To add to that, the low wing increases in AR (Aspect Ratio), while the high wing decreases in AR.
Both of these will increase the lift on the low wing, and restore the aircraft to level flight, hence the high static lateral stability of swept wing aircraft.

  • We also know that if you increase the lift, you increase the drag. So, it will have a slight tendency to yaw into the relative airflow (as there is more drag on the low wing), thereby contributing to static directional stability.
This is a very small factor compared to the directional stability provided by the vertical fin but it does contribute to it. So it is positive.

title: Which definition of propeller parameters is correct?
optionA: Helix angle is the angle between the actual path of the propeller and the propeller axis.
optionB: Geometric pitch is the actual distance a propeller would advance in one revolution.
optionC: Propeller angle of attack is the angle between the blade chord line and the relative airflow.
optionD: Blade angle is the angle between the blade chord line and the propeller axis.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The Blade Angle

Sometimes called the pitch angle, is the angle subtended between the plane of rotation and the chord line of the propeller blade, which may be fixed or variable. When the airplane is moving it comprises two parts, the angle of attack and the helix angle, but when it is stationary the blade angle is equal to the angle of attack.

The Helix Angle

The angle that the actual path of the propeller makes to the plane of rotation.

Angle of Attack

The path of the propeller through the air determines the direction of the relative airflow. The angle between the blade chord and the relative airflow is the angle of attack (α).
The angle of attack (α) is the result of propeller rotational velocity (RPM) and aircraft forward velocity (TAS).

title: In a co-ordinated horizontal turn, the magnitude of the centripetal force at 45 degrees of bank:
optionA: is equal to the lift of the aeroplane.
optionB: has a vertical component.
optionC: is equal to the weight of the aeroplane.
optionD: is greater than the lift of the aeroplane.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
In level flight, any turn will be coordinated or uncoordinated. A coordinated turn is one in which the only acceleration is along the normal axis of the airplane, towards the center of the turn, and the angle of bank is precisely correct for the aircraft speed and the radius of turn. If not all these factors are present, the turn will be uncoordinated and there will be a lateral acceleration either towards or away from the center of the turn. The total lift of a balanced turn provides the centripetal force and the force that opposes the mass of the airplane.
If there is acceleration towards the center of the turn the airplane is slipping and if it is away from the center of the turn the airplane is skidding. Either condition will be indicated on the turn and slip indicator. An overbanked airplane will slip into the turn and requires an increase of speed or a reduction in bank angle to correct this condition. An underbanked airplane will skid out of the turn, which requires a decreased speed or an increased bank angle to correct this condition. These are indicated on the turn and slip indicator by the needle one-way and the ball the other.
To maintain altitude and airspeed when executing a turn both the angle of attack and the thrust have to be increased above their level flight values.

In a turn, the centripetal force is defined as:

CF = L * sinΦ

And Weight is defined by:

W = L * cosΦ

Dividing one by the other, we get:

(L∗ sinΦ)/(L∗ cosΦ) = CF/W

Then:

tanΦ = CF/W
W * tanΦ = CF

For a 45° bank angle where tan 45° = 1 , CF = W.

title: If an aeroplane exhibits insufficient stick force per g, this problem can be resolved by installing:
optionA: a bobweight in the control system which pulls the stick backwards.
optionB: a spring which pulls the stick backwards.
optionC: a spring which pushes the stick forwards.
optionD: a bobweight in the control system which pulls the stick forwards.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
There is an increment of force dependent on the trim tab setting which varies with the dynamic pressure or the square of equivalent airspeed. Figure 1 indicates the variation of stick force with airspeed and illustrates the effect of tab setting on stick force.

To trim the airplane at point (1) a certain amount of up elevator is required, and zero stick force is obtained with the use of the trim tab. To trim the airplane for higher speeds corresponding to points (2) and (3), less and less aircraft nose-up tab is required.

Note that when the airplane is properly trimmed, a push force is required to increase airspeed and a pull force is required to decrease airspeed. In this manner, the airplane would have positive stick force stability with a stable “feel” for airspeed.

Irrespective of the speed or the deflection of the elevators, by modifying the forces acting on the control column such that a greater pull and push force is necessary, stick-force stability is obtained.

There are two devices that achieve this aim, they are the down spring (figure 2) and the bobweight (figure 3). Either of them can be introduced in the control system between the control column and the elevators.

title: An aeroplane flying at 200 kt in straight and level flight is subjected to a disturbance that suddenly increases the speed by 80 kt. Assuming the angle of attack remains constant, the load factor will initially:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: remain unchanged, since the angle of attack does not change.
optionB: increase to 1.4.
optionC: increase to 1.96.
optionD: increase to 1.8.
explanationTotal:
Load factor is defined as:

n = Lift / Weight

Expanding the Lift Formula:

L = ½ x ρ x V2 x S x CL

n = (½ x ρ x V2 x S x CL) / W

By removing all the constants, we can say that:

n ∝ V2

To find the change in load factor (nΔ), we have to divide nNEW by nOLD:

nΔ = nNEW / nOLD

nΔ = VNEW2 / VOLD2

Where, VNEW = 200 kt + 80 kt = 280 kt and VOLD = 200 kt

nΔ = 2802 / 2002

nΔ = 1.96 g

Knowing now that accelerating from 200 kt to 280 kt, we can conclude that after passing the disturbance the load factor increased to 1.96 g.

title: Considering an aeroplane’s manoeuvrability in pitch, the further forward the centre of gravity...
optionA: the less the manoeuvrability due to the increased static longitudinal stability.
optionB: the less the manoeuvrability due to the increased dynamic longitudinal stability.
optionC: the greater the manoeuvrability due to the increased elevator forces that can be achieved.
optionD: the greater the manoeuvrability due to a longer elevator to CG arm, which increases the pitching moment.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
An aircraft is said to be trimmed (in trim) if all moments in pitch, roll, and yaw are equal to zero.

The term controllability refers to the ability of the aircraft to respond to control surface displacement and achieve the desired condition of flight. Adequate controllability must be available to perform take-off and landing and accomplish the various maneuvers in flight.

A contradiction exists between stability and controllability. A high degree of stability gives reduced controllability. The relationship between static stability and controllability is demonstrated by figure 1 and 2.

The effect of increased static stability (forward CG movement) on controllability is illustrated by the ball in a steeper trough (figure 2). A greater force is required to “control” the ball to the same position of displacement when the static stability is increased. In this manner, a large degree of static stability tends to make the aircraft less controllable. It is necessary to achieve the proper proportion between static stability and controllability during the design of an aircraft because too much static stability (forward CG position) reduces controllability. The forward CG limit is set to ensure minimum controllability.

title: When flaps are retracted at constant angle of attack the lift coefficient will:
optionA: vary as the square of IAS.
optionB: decrease.
optionC: remain the same.
optionD: increase.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
As you can see in the graph, when retracting flaps at a constant angle of attack, the coefficient of lift will decrease. CL CLEAN < CL FLAPS DOWN.

title:
Refer to figure.
The correct sequence of cross-sections representing propeller blade twist is:
optionA: sequence 3.
optionB: sequence 4.
optionC: sequence 2.
optionD: sequence 1.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Blade Twist

Sections near the tip of the propeller are at a greater distance from the propeller shaft and travel through a greater distance. Tip speed is therefore greater. The blade angle must be decreased towards the tip to give a constant geometric pitch along the length of the blade.

title: Which statement about a primary control surface controlled by a servo tab, is correct?
optionA: Due to the effectiveness of the servo tab the control surface area can be smaller.
optionB: The servo tab can also be used as a balance tab.
optionC: The control effectiveness of the primary surface is increased by servo tab deflection.
optionD: The position is undetermined during taxiing, in particular with tailwind.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The force required to operate the primary control surfaces, even using balance tabs, is often too great to be acceptable. To relieve the pilot of the need to apply so much force to operate the controls servo-tabs are fitted to carry out this function.

The servo-tab is a small tab hinged on the trailing edge of the primary control surface and linked directly to the control column. There is no direct link between the control column and the primary control surface.

The function and operation of the servo-tab is the same as the balance tab and moves the trim tab in the opposite direction to the movement of the primary control surface. However, at low IAS the servo-tab makes the main control surface less effective. The position of a servo-controlled primary control surface cannot be determined until a positive pressure is applied to the servo-tab by the airflow.

title: What happens when an aeroplane climbs at constant IAS before the crossover altitude?
optionA: Lift coefficient increases.
optionB: Lift coefficient decreases.
optionC: Lift coefficient remains unchanged.
optionD: Lift coefficient increases and then decreases.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
L = 1/2 rho V2 S CL

Where “1/2 rho V2” stands for dynamic pressure.
L = (1/2 rho V2) S CL

The climb is carried out with a constant IAS till crossover altitude. As IAS is a direct measurement of dynamic pressure, this tells us that the dynamic pressure (1/2 rho V2) is unchanged. As the wing area (S) does not change, of course, and our Lift (L) does not change (there is a slight change in weight due to fuel burn but this is ignored for a theoretical question such as this), then all known parts of the equation are staying the same.

If all other parts of the equation are staying the same, then the Coefficient of Lift (CL) must remain the same, as any change would "unbalance" the equation.

title: Airflow separation is characterised by:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: The transition from laminar to turbulent boundary layer.
optionB: Airflow reversal on the surface of the body.
optionC: A reduction in form drag.
optionD: Increased velocity on the surface of the body.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Airflow separation is where the boundary layer does not have enough energy to resist the adverse pressure gradient. It then releases from the surface and causes flow reversal along the top of the surface of the wing. The earlier the separation, the larger area is covered with reversal flow, meaning less off the wing is producing lift.

Do not confuse separation point with the transition point!
Transition point is that where the boundary layer goes from laminar to turbulent. See the difference in the figure.

title:
Refer to figure.
The image illustrates the same aeroplane flying at two different angles of attack (AOA), 2° and 12°, and a simplified representation of the streamlines in the 3D airflow around the wing. The pilot of the aeroplane reduces airspeed while increasing pitch from an AoA of 2° to an AoA of 12° in order to maintain straight and level flight. At the end of the speed reduction, the lift vector will have...
optionA: changed direction by a value greater than 10°, with the lift vector pointing more rearwards because of a larger induced AOA.
optionB: changed direction by a value smaller than 10°, with the lift vector pointing more forwards because of a smaller induced AoA.
optionC: maintained its direction referenced to the chord line because the direction of the vector follows any changes to the AOA.
optionD: increased its magnitude while maintaining its vertical direction because the direction of the lift vector is independent of the AOA.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Note: This question appears to have different answers with different authorities. We think that the question has no correct answer in its current form. Please send us any exam feedback you have about this question so we can get it as representative as possible of the question in the exam quickly, thank you!

As far as we currently know, the following authorities are considering the following options to be correct.

Authority Reported Answer
Latvia C (maintained its direction...)
Poland Not C
Austro Not C
Spain A (greater than 10°...)

We would say if your country is "Not C", go for A "greater than 10 degrees".

A wing creates a force from the air flowing over it, and the direction and magnitude of that "resultant force" change based on the speed of the airflow, density of the air, and angle of attack (AoA) of the wing.

This resultant force is split into two forces we know very well. Lift and Drag. Lift is the component of the resultant force that acts at 90º to the relative airflow (dictated by the speed and direction of the air approaching the wing - not yet affected by the presence of the wing or the aircraft), whereas drag is the force parallel to the relative airflow.

This is the basics of "2D airflow", but gets a bit more complicated when we include "3D airflow", the existence of induced drag, wingtip vortices, etc. When flying at higher angles of attack, the effects of wingtip vortices introduce upwash ahead of the wing and downwash behind it, and this changes the "effective" angle of attack, which is the angle of air as it hits the wing, and is approaching from higher up than the relative airflow. The "effective lift vector" is at 90º to this "effective" angle of attack. Because this "effective" lift vector points slightly backwards, some of this "effective lift" is turned into drag. We call that "induced drag".

The angle of "tilt" of the effective lift vector is the same angle that our angle of attack changes by (from actual AoA to effective AoA), and this angle of attack that we "lose" is called the induced angle of attack. This is particularly useful knowledge for questions about ground effect.

Now to look at this question. When the aircraft slows down and increases its angle of attack to remain straight and level, the actual lift vector (90º to the relative airflow - so directly upwards) must stay the same direction and magnitude, to counteract the weight of the aircraft. The increase in AoA causes an increase in the strength of the wingtip vortices, and therefore the upwash ahead of the wing, thus increasing the induced AoA (the angle of attack that is lost). This means that the "effective lift vector" of the wings tilts back somewhat and increases in magnitude (to keep the actual lift constant), creating more induced drag. This "angle of tilt" (the induced AoA) is much less than the change in total AoA of 10º. Using normal wings, it would be in the region of 3º change.

Therefore, the "effective lift vector" would tilt back by around 3º (less than 10º) and increase in magnitude, due to the larger induced AoA.

Now that actually doesn't leave us with a correct answer. That is because none of the answers are correct. Even with a question that can be interpreted 2 ways, there is still no correct answer.

If you take the question as literally as possible, then the actual lift vector (vertical) does not change in direction or magnitude, remaining vertical and equal to the weight force (option D is therefore wrong due to the magnitude).

If you take the question to mean the "effective lift vector", then the correct answer would be "changed direction by a value smaller than 10°, with the lift vector pointing more rearwards because of a larger induced AOA.". None of the other answers fit this. Answer C says that it stays in the same direction with relation to the chord line, meaning that the effective lift vector moves by 10°, the same as the AoA change, which is not correct.

​

title: Flaperons are controls, which combine the function of:
optionA: ailerons and elevator.
optionB: ailerons and flaps.
optionC: flaps and speed brakes.
optionD: flaps and elevator.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Flaperon comes from the names flap and aileron. In that case, if needed, flaperons are lowered on the whole wingspan and at the wing tip part they move relative to that deflection.

title: Slats are...
optionA: More beneficial than the flaps regarding the effect on the stall speed.
optionB: Located at the trailing edge of the wing.
optionC: High lift devices which decrease the stalling angle of attack.
optionD: Less beneficial than the flaps regarding the effect on the stall speed.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
It can be seen that the contrivution to CL is very high and the greatest aong leading and trailing edge devices. In practice, they increase critical angle of attack as well.

When the aircraft is at lower angles of attack (i.e. 5 degrees) the diagram shows that deployment of Trailing Edge (TE) flaps increases CL by much more than LE devices. This is because TE flap deployment increases local alpha, whereas LE devices reduce local alpha on the part of the wing where they are deployed. However, CL is still boosted a little, because LE devices increase camber and also increase the mass flow over the upper surface of the wing. This means that the airflow over the top of the wing has more kinetic energy, and the forward movement of the separation point at high alpha will be delayed.

Therefore, we can increase AOA and CL beyond the point at which airflow over the wing without LE devices would have separated and we would stall.

  • LE devices enable aircraft alpha to increase to a higher value before the stall, at which point CLMAX has a higher value than when TE flaps are deployed.

title: In straight and level flight, which sentence is correct regarding the CL/CD ratio?
optionA: It depends on the angle of attack.
optionB: The C<sub>L</sub> is higher than C<sub>D</sub>.
optionC: The C<sub>D</sub> is higher than C<sub>L</sub>.
optionD: C<sub>L</sub> equals C<sub>D</sub>.
explanationTotal:
The Lift to Drag ratio (CL/CD) is a measure of how much lift an aircraft produces per unit of drag. So an aircraft with a Lift to Drag ratio of 10/1 is producing 10 times more lift than it is producing drag.

The lift to drag ratio depends on the angle of attack. The angle of attack of a clean wing decides its lift coefficient, and its drag coefficient, then you can compare those two to get the lift/drag ratio.

In reality, the lift is often much higher than the drag, so the L/D ratio is usually over 1. If an aircraft could fly fast enough to run at a very low (or negative) angle of attack, then its lift produced (which will equal its weight in straight and level flight) could be less than the drag (and therefore thrust - if the aircraft is at a constant speed). It is a bit of a crazy notion for civilian pilots, as the aircraft would have to have a higher thrust than its own weight, but this is quite common in fighter jets, especially modern jets or VTOL jets. We can see that by the fact that they can accelerate vertically upwards.

title: Which statement is correct about an aeroplane, that has experienced a left engine failure and continues afterwards in straight and level cruise flight with wings level?
optionA: turn indicator left of neutral, slip “ball” neutral.
optionB: turn indicator left of neutral, slip “ball” left of neutral.
optionC: turn indicator neutral, slip “ball” left of neutral.
optionD: turn indicator neutral, slip “ball” neutral.
explanationTotal:
When maintaining straight and level flight with wings level, turn and slip indicators will be neutral.

Flying as described, symmetrically straight and level, would probably require enormous rudder and aileron deflections, but once reached, the turn and the slip indicator will be neutral.

title: When comparing a stabiliser trim system with an elevator trim system, which of these statements is correct?
optionA: a stabiliser trim is more sensitive to flutter.
optionB: an elevator trim is less suitable for aeroplanes with a large CG range.
optionC: an elevator trim is able to compensate larger changes in pitching moments.
optionD: an elevator trim is able to compensate larger changes in airspeed.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
The forces on a jet transport aeroplane are very high in flight.
The wing surfaces are large and travel at high speeds, generating lots of lift.
A trim tab is an easy solution in general aviation aircraft, as the forces are much smaller and it’s a lot cheaper and lighter than a stabilizer.

However, the trim tab is not able to withstand the forces at very high speeds and is not powerful enough to generate the loads required for a change in configuration.
A stabilizer is powerful enough and is able to cope with larger CG ranges, because the forces required with a CG change will change drastically.
Therefore the stabilizer is the best suitable option for transport jet aeroplanes.

title: Aircraft A and Aircraft B are climbing in a standard atmosphere with the same pitch angle. Aircraft A climbs with M0.75 and Aircraft B with M0.73. Disregarding compressibility effects, which of the following statements is correct?
optionA: Aircraft A has a better rate of climb than B.
optionB: Aircraft B has a better rate of climb than A.
optionC: Aircraft A and B have the same rate of climb.
optionD: To compare TAS is needed.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The Mach Number can be defined by the relation between True Airspeed (TAS) and Local Speed of Sound (LSS) as follows:

M = TAS ÷ LSS

or,

TAS = M x LSS

From the above equation, and considering that outside conditons remain the same, the aircraft with higher (faster) Mach Number will have the higher TAS.

RATE OF CLIMB

The rate of climb is the vertical speed of an aeroplane, which is usually specified in feet per minute (fpm) and is the vertical component of the forward speed of the aeroplane along the climb path. I can be expressed by:

Rate of climb = Angle of climb x TAS

Therefore, if TAS increases, the Rate of Climb increases as well.

Note: rate of climb depends on weight and excess power.

title:
Refer to figure.
X, Y and Z correspond to:
optionA: Climb angle, pitch angle, angle of attack.
optionB: Pitch angle, climb angle, angle of attack.
optionC: Angle of attack, climb angle, pitch angle.
optionD: Angle of attack, pitch angle, climb angle.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
ANGLE OF ATTACK

Angle of attack is the difference between pitch attitude and flight path angle.

It is defined as the angle between the chord of an airfoil and the relative wind.

FLIGHT PATH ANGLE

Flight path angle is the angle between the horizon and the flight path (speed vector). Also called climb or descent angle.

PITCH ANGLE

Pitch angle is the angle between the horizon and longitudinal axis of the aircraft, it is equal to Flight path angle + Angle of attack.

title: VC is...
optionA: a specially recommended penetration speed for severe turbulence.
optionB: the maximum tested airspeed where the aircraft is free from any signs of dynamic pressure overload, flutter, and/or control reversal.
optionC: a speed selected by the designer and used to assess the strength requirements in cruise.
optionD: the highest speed at which sudden, full elevator deflection (nose up) can be made without exceeding the design limit load factor.
explanationTotal:
VC - is the design cruising speed. The minimum value of VC must exceed VB by a sufficient margin to allow for inadvertent speed increases that may be caused by severe turbulence.
This is a speed selected by the designer and used to assess the strength requirements in the cruise. Its value is determined by the requirements CS-25.335 and CS-23.335.

title: Which combination of bank and slip gives the lowest V<sub>MC</sub>?
optionA: 5º bank into the live engine and ½ ball out to the live engine.
optionB: 5º bank into the dead engine and ½ ball out to the live engine.
optionC: 5º bank into the dead engine and ½ ball out to the dead engine.
optionD: 5º bank into the live engine and ½ ball out to the dead engine.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
ENGINE FAILURE

If one engine on a conventional twin-engine aircraft fails in flight, it adversely affects its performance and controllability.

With both engines operating at the same power setting on a twin-engine aircraft, the amount of thrust produced by each engine is identical and their lines of action are symmetrically displaced about the aircraft's normal axis.

If one engine fails in flight, the remaining thrust forces are asymmetrically displaced and the aircraft yaws in the direction of the failed engine.

YAWING MOMENT

The yawing moment is the product of thrust from the operating engine multiplied by the distance between the thrust line and the CG (thrust arm), plus the drag from the failed engine multiplied by the distance between the engine centre line and the CG.

The strength of the yawing moment will depend on:
- how much thrust the operating engine is developing (throttle setting and density altitude).
- the distance between the thrust line and the CG (thrust arm).
- how much drag is being produced by the failed engine.

The rudder moment, which balances the yawing moment, is the result of the rudder force multiplied by the distance between the fin CP and the CG (rudder arm)

The ability of the pilot to counteract the yawing moment due to asymmetric thrust will depend on:
- rudder displacement (affecting rudder force).
- CG position (affecting rudder arm).
- the IAS (affecting rudder force).

Rudder to Stop Yaw - Bank Towards Live Engine
It is more aerodynamically efficient to balance the rudder sideforce by banking towards the live engine, so that lift gives a sideways component opposite to the rudder force. The angle of bank must not exceed 5°, to prevent excessive loss of vertical lift component.

Banking towards the live engine also reduces the side force on the fin from sideslip, which minimizes VMC, effectively reduces the yawing moment and gives more rudder authority to stop the yaw.

The cockpit indication will be the turn needle central with the slip indicator (ball) one half diameter displaced towards the live engine. The ‘ball’ is not centred, but the aircraft is not sideslipping.

This method produces minimum drag and gives the best ability to climb and is therefore the preferred method of putting the aircraft in equilibrium following engine failure.

title:
Refer to figure.
Assuming all bodies have the same cross-sectional area and are in motion, place these bodies in order of decreasing pressure drag.The correct answer is:
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Total Drag is sub-divided into two main types:
Parasite Drag - independent of lift generation, and
Induced Drag - the result of lift generation.

Parasite drag is further sub-divided into:

  • Skin Friction Drag
  • Form (Pressure) Drag, and
  • Interference Drag

NOTE: Skin Friction and Form Drag are together known as PROFILE DRAG.

Form drag is produced whenever the streamline airflow passing over an aircraft separates from the surface and becomes turbulent. An example of extreme form drag is the effect of a flat plate placed at right angles to the airflow.
The pressure immediately in front of the plate is above atmospheric, whilst the pressure behind the plate is below atmospheric. This results in a sucking effect behind the plate and the formation of vortices. The more rapidly the airflow changes direction, the greater the pressure gradient, the earlier the separation, and the higher the form drag.
Changing the shape, or streamline, of a given object reduces drag by delaying the point at which the airflow separates.

title: A shockwave is formed both on the upper and lower surface of the wing. Mach number is increased. Where is the lower surface shock wave in relation to the upper surface?
optionA: More forward.
optionB: More aft.
optionC: At the same position.
optionD: Impossible to say.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
When an aircraft approaches the speed of sound, the airflow over the wing reaches supersonic speed before the airplane itself does, and a shock wave forms on the upper surface of the wing. As the aircraft speed is further increased, the region of supersonic flow on the upper surface extends, and the shock wave marking the end of the supersonic region moves rearwards. A similar sequence of events will occur on the lower surface although the shock wave will usually form at a higher aircraft speed because the lower surface usually has less curvature so the air is not accelerated so much.

The shock wave on the lower surface usually forms at a higher free stream Mach number than the upper surface shock, but it reaches the trailing edge first. The lower shock wave appears at higher speed and moves quicky to aft as mach number increases and reaches trailing edge before the upper one.

Note: This question was created based on incomplete feedback, please let us know if you come across it in your official exam.

title: The limiting load of a:
optionA: Light aircraft will be reached at a lower load factor as that of a heavier aircraft.
optionB: Light aircraft will be reached at the same value as that of a heavier aircraft.
optionC: Heavy aircraft will be reached at a lower value than that of a lighter aircraft.
optionD: Heavy aircraft will be reached at a higher value than that of a lighter aircraft.
explanationTotal:
This question is ambiguous and the answer depends on the interpretation of the question text. There are two possible scenarios:

  1. If the question is referring to different aircraft classes (CS 25 vs CS 23), then a light aircraft (CS 23) has a maximum limiting load factor of 3.8 g, whereas a heavy aircraft (CS 25) has a maximum limiting load factor of 2.5 g. In this case, the heavy aircraft will reach its limiting load at a lower value than that of a lighter aircraft.

  2. If the question is referring to the same aircraft with a change in mass (for instance, due to fuel consumption), then the limiting load factor is attained at the same value regardless of mass. This is most likely what the question is referring to.

    Let's consider the following scenario: A Boeing 737 (CS 25) takes off with a mass of 200 tonnes and is limited to a maximum load factor of 2.5 g, which would create a certain amount of stress on the wings if applied. After several hours and using most of its fuel, the aircraft's mass is reduced to 100 tonnes. Applying 2.5 g at this lower mass would create a lower amount of stress on the wings. In theory, the lighter aircraft could withstand more "g" before the stress reached the same level as during takeoff. However, in practice, a CS25 aircraft is certified to a maximum load factor of 2.5 g regardless of its mass. Therefore, the limiting load factor is still 2.5 g, regardless of the aircraft's current mass.

For the CS-25 category, the maximum positive and minimum negative limitation of load factor is:
nMAX = 2.5; nMIN = -1 in clean configuration (high lift devices not extended)

The CS-23 category includes three subparts:

Normal [N] nMAX = 3.8 nMIN = -1.52
Utility [U] nMAX = 4.4 nMIN = -1.76
Aerobatic [A] nMAX ≥ 6

nMIN ≤ 3

title: Which speed should you fly if you want to stay in the air for the longest time possible?
optionA: V<sub>MP, </sub>becauses it is the speed for minimum rate of descent.
optionB: Minimum clean speed.
optionC: Minimum glide speed.
optionD: V<sub>MP</sub>, because is the speed for best range.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
In a condition where fuel saving is a priority, the knowledge of the maximum endurance is a determining factor. As a result, it is important to try to minimize fuel consumption versus time as much as possible, or to simply minimize fuel flow (kg or lb per hour).

SPEED FOR MINIMUM RATE OF DESCENT

Rate of descent depends on both the angle of descent and the speed down the flight path. Rate of descent is not minimum at VMD, where the angle of descent is minimum, because the speed is moderately fast.

Rate of descent is actually minimum at VMP (the velocity for minimum power). This means that maximum endurance (maximum time in the air) is achieved at VMP.

The attached figure shows two aeroplanes descending, one at VMD and the other at VMP. Although the aeroplane descending at VMP has a slightly steeper angle of descent, the much slower speed (76% of the speed at VMD) results in a lower (minimum) rate of descent.

title: During cruise flight, a continuous stall warning is activated. The initial pilot’s action should be:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Check for another indication that the aircraft has actually stalled.
optionB: Immediately lower the nose to reduce alpha, in all circumstances.
optionC: Immediately apply full power whilst simultaneously reducing alpha.
optionD: Immediately apply full power and raise the nose to stop any descent.
explanationTotal:
NUISANCE STALL WARNING

A nuisance stall warning event is one in which the stall warning activates although the airplane is not near a stall condition.

Some in-service incidents have revealed corners of the operating envelope where turbulence or additional manoeuvre loads can result in momentary nuisance stall warning events.

Most of the conditions leading to nuisance stall warning events are related to moderate to severe turbulence when operating at or near the Maximum Operating Altitude.

In this scenario, the crew should confirm the stall with other indications and flight instruments such as airspeed, altitude and attitude.

In general, every stall warning should be taken seriously and the response appropriate to the phase of flight and flight conditions.

title: Which of the following creates induced drag on a wing?
optionA: Angle of attack.
optionB: Ground effect.
optionC: Airflow around the fuselage and wing root meeting.
optionD: Turbulence.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Total Drag is sub-divided into two main types:

  • Parasite Drag - independent of lift generation, and

  • Induced Drag - the result of lift generation.

Induced drag is caused when an object redirects the airflow. A wing produces lift by creating a pressure difference. This pressure difference is caused by the shape of the airfoil, causing the airflow on top to accelerate, creating a low pressure on top of the wing and high pressure below the wing. This pressure difference naturally wants to restore towards a uniform pressure, which creates vortices around the wingtip. These vortices are deflected downwards, this phenomenon is also called downwash. The induced drag decreases with airspeed (with a rate of 1/V2) and increases with angle of attack and increasing weight.

  • CDI = CL2 / π * AR

Where, CDI – Induced Drag Coefficient; CL2 – Lift Coefficient squared; AR – Aspect Ratio

Increasing the angle of attack increases CL. From the formula we can deduct that Induced drag is directly proportional to CL squared.
So, increasing the angle of attack increases CL, which increases Induced drag.

title: What is the relationship between speed of sound and absolute temperature?
optionA: Directly proportional to square of temperature.
optionB: Directly proportional to square root of temperature.
optionC: Inversely proportional to square of temperature.
optionD: Inversely proportional to square root of temperature.
explanationTotal:
LOCAL SPEED OF SOUND (LSS)

The speed at which pressure waves propagate is proportional to the square root of the absolute temperature of the air. The higher the temperature, the higher the speed of propagation.

  • LSS = 38.95 x √ (K)
    where LSS = Local Speed of Sound (kt) and K = Absolute temperature (Kelvin)

title: A scheduled flight is heavily delayed due to maintenance. During this time, the Outside Air Temperature increases significantly. What impact does this temperature change have on V<sub>MCG</sub>?
optionA: V<sub>MCG</sub> decreases, due to the decreasing thrust.
optionB: V<sub>MCG </sub>decreases due to the increasing density.
optionC: V<sub>MCG</sub> remains constant for the same configuration.
optionD: V<sub>MCG</sub> increases due to decreasing rudder effectiveness.
explanationTotal:
When a multi-engine aircraft suffers an engine failure several variables affect both the yawing moment and the rudder moment which is used to oppose it.

There is a minimum IAS (VMC), below which it is impossible for the pilot to maintain directional control with asymmetric thrust.

VMCG, the minimum control speed on the ground, is the calibrated airspeed during the takeoff run, at which, when the critical engine is suddenly made inoperative, it is possible to maintain control of the aeroplane using the rudder control alone (without the use of nose wheel steering) to enable the take-off to be safely continued using normal piloting skill.

Airworthiness Authorities, in this case the EASA, have laid down conditions which must be satisfied when establishing the minimum airspeeds for inclusion in the Flight Manual of a new aircraft type. As in most other cases, the conditions under which the minimum control airspeeds are established are ‘worst case’.

VMC is affected by the amount of thrust being developed by the operating engine. As altitude and/or temperature increases, the thrust from an unsupercharged engine will decrease.

VMC decreases with decreasing density.

Air density will be lowest when the aerodrome pressure altitude is highest (low atmospheric pressure), the air temperature is highest and the water-vapour content of the air is highest.

title: Why is a propeller blade twisted from root to tip?
optionA: To ensure the angle of attack is greatest at the tip.
optionB: To ensure that the tip produces most thrust.
optionC: To ensure that the root produces most thrust.
optionD: To maintain a constant angle of attack along the whole length of the propeller blade.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The angle between the blade chord and the plane of rotation.
Sections near the tip of the propeller are at a greater distance from the propeller shaft and travel through a greater distance. Tip speed is therefore greater. The blade angle must be decreased towards the tip to give a constant geometric pitch along the length of the blade.
The blades twist more at the root than the tip to maintain a constant angle of attack along the complete blade.
The blade angle determines the geometric pitch of the propeller. A small blade angle is called “fine pitch”, a large blade angle is called “coarse pitch”.

title:
Refer to figure.
What will be the consequence on the speed of the aircraft while going from Point B to Point C and maintaining steady, straight and level flight?
optionA: The aircraft will be flown at a slower speed.
optionB: The aircraft will be flown at a faster speed.
optionC: The aircraft’s speed remains unchanged.
optionD: The aircraft will stall.
explanationTotal:
As we can see from the CL alpha graph given in the figure, when moving from point B to point C, we are clearly experiencing an increase in the coefficient of lift.

Knowing that the lift formula is:

L = CL ½ rho V2 S

As the question states, we want to remain in straight and level flight, therefore we know that our lift must remain equal. To maintain the same lift with an increasing coefficient of lift, we will either have to:

  • Decrease the air density
  • Decrease the velocity of the aircraft
  • Decrease the surface area of the wing
Of the given answers, the only one that fits is to fly at a slower speed.

title:
Refer to figure.
Which of the four points in the attached graph depicts the maximum lift to drag ratio?
optionA: Point 4
optionB: Point 3
optionC: Point 1
optionD: Point 2
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
An appreciation of the efficiency of lift production is gained from studying the ratio between lift and drag, a high L/D ratio being more efficient.
The proportions of CL and CD can be calculated for each angle of attack.
In general, we can say that the L/D ratio increases with angle of attack up to a maximum at about 4°; this is called the “optimum” angle of attack. The L/D ratio then decreases with increasing angle of attack until CLMAX is reached.

title:
You are in a power-on descent with a glide angle of 30º. Determine the thrust vector in kg, given:

Weight: 11 000 N
Drag: 8 500 N
Lift: 10 500 N
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Power-on descent

Weight is split into 2 components:

  • W cos y acts perpendicular to the flight path and balances lift;
  • W sin y acts forward along the flight path, adding to Thrust to balance drag.

Lift is less than Weight: Lift only has to balance the component of weight which acts perpendicular to the flight path (L = W cos y).
Thrust is less than drag: Weight gives a forward component in the same direction as thrust.

For a power-on descent, we get the following formulas:

D = T + W sin y
T = D – W sin y
L = W cos y

With regards to this question:
  • T = D – W sin y
    T = 8 500 N – 11 000 sin 30
    T = 3000 N
  • Assuming G = 9,81 m/s2
    T = 3 000 / 9,81
    T = 306 kg

title:
Which statement is correct?

I. A propeller with little blade twist is referred to as being in fine pitch.
II. A propeller with a large blade angle is referred to as being in coarse pitch.
optionA: I is incorrect, II is correct.
optionB: I is correct, II is correct.
optionC: I is correct, II is incorrect.
optionD: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The blade angle, sometimes called the pitch angle, is the angle subtended between the plane of rotation and the chord line of the propeller blade, which may be fixed or variable. When the airplane is moving it comprises two parts, the angle of attack and the helix angle, but when it is stationary the blade angle is equal to the angle of attack.
It is usually referenced at 75% of the blade radius measured from the center of the shaft.
A small blade angle is called “fine pitch”. Therefore, statement 1 is incorrect.
A large blade angle is called “coarse pitch”. Therefore, statement 2 is correct.

title:
Refer to figure.
At a mass of 130 tons:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: the buffet free range in 1 g flight at FL410 is from approximately M = 0.76 to M = 0.83.
optionB: buffet free flight is possible at M = 0.80 only.
optionC: buffet free flight at 1 g at FL410 is possible without any Mach number restriction.
optionD: the buffet free range in a level 30 degree bank turn at FL360 is from approximately M = 0.75 to M = 0.84.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
In the same way that separated airflow prior to a low speed stall can cause airframe buffet, shock induced separation (shock stall) at high speed can also cause buffeting.

Aerodynamic buffet is a valuable stall warning, but it can damage the aircraft structure. Because of the higher dynamic pressure when an aircraft is operating in the transonic speed region, any shock induced buffet will have a greater potential for severe airframe damage.

High speed buffet must be completely avoided. The aircraft must therefore be operated in such a manner that a (safety) margin exists before aerodynamic buffet will occur.

If the variables which affect both high speed and low speed stall are considered it will be possible to identify the conditions under which buffeting will occur and a chart can be drawn to show all the factors involved.
This is called a ‘Buffet Onset’ chart which is used by flight crews to ensure their aircraft is always operated with a specified minimum buffet margin.

In this exercise:

  • Start by drawing a line from de 1g load factor that intersects the 130-ton curve.
  • From here, draw a straight line from right to left that intersects the FL410 curve.
  • The goal is to have to intersection points, which correspond to the lowest and highest limits of the buffet boundaries. In this case, the low speed boundary is M0.76 and the high-speed boundary is M 0.83

title:
Given a constant load factor, which of these statements about the variation of induced drag with changes of speed and mass are correct or incorrect?

1. When speed increases, induced drag increases.
2. When mass increases, induced drag increases.
optionA: 1 is correct, 2 is correct.
optionB: 1 is incorrect, 2 is correct.
optionC: 1 is correct, 2 is incorrect.
optionD: 1 is incorrect, 2 is incorrect.
explanationTotal:
Induced drag is created as a byproduct of lift. The pressure differential between the top and bottom of the wing creates a upwash around the tip of the wing that turns into a downwash behind the wing. This is known as a vortex, which creates a rearward force known as induced drag.

This question is asking for the effect of:

  • Speed: The induced drag is inversely proportional to the speed. Therefore, induced drag increases as the speed decreases, and, induced drag decreases and the speed increases.
This is because, to maintain lift constant, as the velocity decreases, the coefficient of lift will have to be increased. At higher coefficients of lift, the pressure differential between the top and bottom of the wing will be greater and therefore produce stronger vortices = stronger induced drag. (and vice versa)
  • Changing mass: Induced drag is proportional to the mass. Therefore, induced drag increases with increasing aeroplane mass, and, induced drag decreases with decreasing aeroplane mass.

This is because, as the aircraft get heavier, the lift that the wings will have to produce increases. To achieve that, the coefficient of lift will have to increase, meaning a higher AoA, which creates stronger vortices. (and vice versa)

Summary:

  • Higher AR = Lower induced drag
  • Higher AoA = higher induced drag
  • Higher weight = higher AoA = higher induced drag
  • Higher speed = lower AoA = lower induced drag
  • Winglets = lower induced drag.

title: Which one of the following statements is true regarding icing on a propeller?
optionA: Icing will first form on different parts of the airplane before it forms on the propellers.
optionB: Icing does not affect the propeller's efficiency.
optionC: Icing first forms on the tips of the propeller.
optionD: Thrust is decreased by 20%.
explanationTotal:
Ice on an aerofoil changes its properties, reducing lift and increasing drag for a given angle of attack. Ice on a propeller blade reduces the efficiency of the propeller and reduces thrust.

In the same way, as the drag of an ice contaminated airplane increases, the resisting force on the propeller increases for a given rpm and blade angle. Ice separating from the propeller blades, as well as vibration due to propeller imbalance, may cause damage to the airplane structure. Since ice on the propeller blades reduces the available thrust, extra power may be required from the engine to overcome the increased drag, decreasing propeller efficiency.

Note: Propeller icing can be expected to reduce propeller efficiency by up to 10% normally, but could up to 20% in very severe icing.

Propeller icing occurs on the leading edge, but is least at the tip of the blade, where the high rotational speed tends to shed the ice more easily.

For that reason, icing will be reduced by INCREASING propeller rpm, not reducing it.

The loss of aircraft performance in icing conditions is mainly due to ice formation on the rest of the wings and airframe, with a smaller contribution coming from the propeller icing.

title: Excessive static lateral stability is an undesirable characteristic for a transport aeroplane because:
optionA: performing co-ordinated turns would be very difficult.
optionB: it would impose excessive demands on roll control during a sideslip.
optionC: it would result in excessive wing loading during a co-ordinated turn.
optionD: it would result in a proportional decline in static directional stability.
explanationTotal:
Lateral stability refers to stability about the longitudinal axis. An aircraft is considered to be laterally stable, if in case of unexpected bank angle, the aircraft wants to reduce it to 0. The value of lateral stability should not be too low, nor too high.
  • Lateral stability too low: If lateral stability is lower than adequate, the aircraft simply does not get back to 0º bank angle in time, thus deviation from the position and altitude is excessive.
  • Lateral stability too high: An excessive lateral stability can cause problems during crosswind landings/take-offs. A high static lateral stability reduces controllability in roll, therefore to hold a sideslip angle, the control force must be increased.

title: An aeroplane performs a steady horizontal, co-ordinated turn with 20 degrees of bank at 150 kt TAS. The same aeroplane with the same bank angle and speed, but at a lower mass will have:
optionA: The same turn radius.
optionB: A smaller turn radius.
optionC: A larger turn radius.
optionD: A smaller turn radius and a higher turn rate.
explanationTotal:
Turn radius (R) is (TAS2 ÷ (g × tan Φ)), where Φ is the bank angle.
Since this expression is independent on aircraft weight, the same speed and bank angle gives the same radius.

title: Which plane and situation experiences the least amount of lift reduction?
optionA: High wing on take-off
optionB: Low wing on take-off
optionC: High wing on landing
optionD: Low wing on landing
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
Ground effect occurs because the surface alters the airflow pattern around the wings. Primarily, the surface restricts the formation of the wingtip vortices.

This results in a reduction in the amount of induced downwash behind the wing and increases the wing’s effective angle of attack.

It also alters the pressure distribution around the wing and the amount of lift developed. This occurs because the change in effective angle of attack increases the wing’s coefficient of lift (CL) and thus its lifting capability at any given angle of attack.

The magnitude of the wing tip vortices, and thus downwash, also determine the amount of induced drag produced by the wing. The closer the aircraft is to the surface, the greater the reduction in induced drag at any given angle of attack. (figure 2)

THE INFLUENCE OF GROUND EFFECT ON LANDING
When an aircraft enters ground effect during the landing phase of flight, the sudden increase in lift and reduction in drag cause it to experience a floating tendency. The aircraft also tends to pitch nose-down due to the reduction in download on the tailplane.

THE INFLUENCE OF GROUND EFFECT ON TAKE-OFF
During the take-off phase of flight, as the aircraft leaves ground effect the wing tip vortices rapidly grow in magnitude producing an increase in downwash behind the wing. This causes a reduction in the lift produced at a given angle of attack and the associated rapid increase in induced drag may prevent a successful take-off. The increased downwash acting on the tailplane increases the download, resulting in a nose-up pitching moment.

The high wing aircraft will still experience ground effect, but because the wing is several feet farther from the runway, the total effect on the aircraft is greatly reduced, as ground effect decreases exponentially with difference from the runway surface.

Thus, a high wing on take-off is the configuration with the least reduction in lift.

title: Aeroplane manoeuvrability decreases for a given control surface deflection when:
optionA: the CG moves aft.
optionB: IAS increases.
optionC: flaps are retracted at constant IAS.
optionD: IAS decreases.
explanationTotal:
Control surfaces produce lift or drag. Lift and drag increase and decrease with increasing and decreasing speed. Therefore, only small deflections are necessary when flying with high airspeeds and larger deflections at lower speeds.

The lift equation states:

LIFT = ½ρV2SCL

  • CL = coefficient of lift. This represents angle of attack of the airfoil and the shape of the airfoil. This described in terms of thickness/chord ratio and a camber and can be altered in flight, for example, by lowering the flaps.
  • ρ = The density of the air. For any given altitude during subsonic flight, the density may be considered to be constant.
  • V2 = The velocity of the aircraft, squared.
  • S = The wing area.

The lift formula can also be rearranged and written as: LIFT = q × S × CL (q = dynamic pressure, i.e. ½ρ × V2).

In the lift equation all factors except density and speed (TAS) are constant. At higher altitude ρ is reduced; therefore TAS (V) must be increased to maintain the same lift (= weight).

Drag equation states that:

DRAG = ½ρV2SCD

  • ρ = the mass density of the fluid (rho),
  • V = the velocity of the object relative to the air,
  • S = the reference area,
  • CD = the drag coefficient - a dimensionless constant.

The drag formula can be rearranged and written as:

DRAG = CD × ½ρ × V2 × S

From the drag equation it is clear that drag is directly proportional to the frontal area: if it increases by a factor of e.g. 3 the drag will be increased by the same factor.

title: Upon extension of a wing spoiler, if the angle of attack remains constant:
optionA: C<sub>D</sub> increases and C<sub>L</sub> decreases.
optionB: C<sub>L</sub> decreases but C<sub>D</sub> remains unaffected.
optionC: C<sub>D</sub> increases but C<sub>L</sub> remains unaffected.
optionD: both C<sub>L</sub> and C<sub>D</sub> increase.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
SPOILERS
Spoilers are flap type control surfaces, normally located on the upper surface of the wing, just in front of the trailing edge flaps.

These surfaces individually hinge at their leading edges and are actuated by hydraulic power supplied by dedicated power control units. The main purpose of the surfaces is to disturb the smooth airflow over the top of the wing, thereby reducing the wings lifting capability. When fully extended, they considerably increase aircraft drag.

The maximum deflection angles are greater in the ground mode than the flight mode. With the spoilers in their fully extended position, approximately 80% of the wing/flap lift is destroyed and the aerodynamic drag of the aircraft more than doubles.

title:
Refer to figure.
Given the wing planform represented in the diagram and the following dimensions: Span 12.5 m Root chord 1.5 m Tip chord 1.0 m. The correct values of wing area and taper ratio or aspect ratio are:
optionA: Wing area: 18.75 m<sup>2</sup> Aspect ratio: 10
optionB: Wing area: 15.625 m<sup>2</sup> Aspect ratio: 12.5
optionC: Wing area: 18.75 m<sup>2</sup> Taper ratio: 1.5
optionD: Wing area: 15.625 m<sup>2</sup> Taper ratio: 0.666
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Wing Area

The plan surface area of the wing. Although a portion of the area may be covered by fuselage or engine nacelles, the pressure carryover on these surfaces allows legitimate consideration of the entire plan area.

S=b*c
S - Wing Area
b - Span
c - Average Chord = (Root Chord + Tip Chord) /2

Taper ratio

The ratio of the tip chord to the root chord. The taper ratio affects the lift distribution and the structural weight of the wing. A rectangular wing has a taper ratio of 1.0 while the pointed tip delta wing has a taper ratio of 0.

TR= CT/CR
TR - Taper Ratio
CT - Tip Chord
CR - Root Chord

Aspect ratio

The aspect ratio of the wing determines the aerodynamic characteristics and structural weight. Typical aspect ratios vary from 35 for a high-performance sailplane to 3 for a jet fighter. The aspect ratio of a modern high-speed jet transport is about 12.

AR= b/c or,
b2 /S
AR - Aspect Ratio
b - Span
c - Average Chord
S - Wing Area

In this example, we are given a Span (b) of 12.5 m, a Tip Chord of 1.0 m and a Root Chord of 1.5 m (or an Average Chord of 1.25 m):

Wing area (S) = 12.5 x 1.25 = 15.625 m2
Taper Ratio (TR) = 1.0 / 1.5 = 0.666(6)
Aspect Ratio (AR) = 12.5 / 1.25 = 10

title: High aspect ratio, as compared with low aspect ratio, has the effect of:
optionA: increasing lift and drag.
optionB: increasing lift and critical angle of attack.
optionC: increasing induced drag and decreasing critical angle of attack.
optionD: decreasing induced drag and critical angle of attack.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The aspect ratio of a wing is defined as being the proportion of the span and the average chord. In other words AR = b/c. “b” being the wingspan, and “c” being the chord. Gliders, with very large wingspans and small chords, have a very high aspect ratio, whilst jets, with very small wingspans with relation to their large chord, have a very low aspect ratio.

Firstly, the higher the aspect ratio of a wing, the lower the induced drag. This is the main reason why gliders fly so efficiently.

Secondly, as you can see in the figure, a higher aspect ratio means a smaller range of usable angles of attack, and also consequently a smaller critical angle of attack.

title: In comparison to a clean configuration, flying straight and level with flaps extended will cause the lift force to (1)_____, the stall speed will (2)_____ and the drag will be (3)_____.
optionA: (1) stay the same; (2) decrease; (3) increased
optionB: (1) increase; (2) decrease; (3) the same
optionC: (1) increase; (2) stay the same; (3) decreased
optionD: (1) decrease; (2) increase; (3) increased
explanationTotal:
Flaps are high-lift devices, primarily used to allow flight at slower airspeeds for take-off and landing. Flaps also increase aircraft drag, which can be useful for energy management, particularly on large jets.

Flaps increase the camber of the wing, and sometimes extend backwards to increase the wing are too. Increasing the camber leads to an increased coefficient of lift (CL), which allows a higher lift force to be produced from the same airflow. This means that an aircraft can fly slower without stalling, as the same amount of lift required to balance out the aircraft weight will be created at lower indicated air speeds. It is important to note that in level flight, the lift force equals weight, and therefore lift does not change just by extending flaps. All that will change is how slow we can fly and still gain that same lift force (stall speed).

We do not use flaps all the time because they also greatly increase the coefficient of drag (CD), so increase the drag force.

title:
Refer to figure.
Arrange the flaps in order of increasing L/D ratio:
explanationTotal:
The correct order is as follows:

(1) Plain Flap: The rear portion of the wing aerofoil rotates downwards on a simple hinge arrangement mounted at the front of the flap. Provides good increase in CLMAX, but with fairly high drag.

(4) Split Flap: The rear portion of the lower surface of the wing aerofoil hinges downwards from the leading edge of the flap, while the upper surface remains immobile. These produce more lift (especially at higher angles of attack) than Plain flaps but still produce high drag.

(2) Slotted Flap: Similar to a Plain Flap but incorporates a gap between the flap and the wing to force high pressure air from below the wing over the upper surface of the flap. This helps reduce boundary layer separation and allows the airflow over the flap to remain laminar. The slotted flap gives a bigger increase in CLMAX than the plain or split flap and much less drag.

(3) Fowler Flap: A split flap that slides rearwards level for a distance prior to hinging downwards. It thereby first increases chord (and wing surface area) and then increases camber. The Fowler flap gives the greatest increase in lift of the flaps considered and also gives the least drag because of the slot and the reduction of thickness

title: During cruise flight, one engine suddenly fails. Which of the options below reflects the worst combination?
optionA: Empty fuel tank at high altitude.
optionB: Empty fuel tank at low altitude.
optionC: Full fuel tank at low altitude.
optionD: Full fuel tank at high altitude.
explanationTotal:
In a condition where fuel saving is a priority, the knowledge of the maximum endurance is a determining factor. As a result, it is important to try to minimize fuel consumption versus time as much as possible, or to simply minimize fuel flow (kg or lb per hour).

SPEED FOR MINIMUM RATE OF DESCENT

Rate of descent depends on both the angle of descent and the speed down the flight path. Rate of descent is not minimum at VMD, where the angle of descent is minimum, because the speed is moderately fast.

Rate of descent is actually minimum at VMP (the velocity for minimum power). This means that maximum endurance (maximum time in the air) is achieved at VMP.

From the options given, flying at low altitude and without fuel is definitely the worse situation as we cannot trade altitude for speed/ground distance and adding to that no having fuel greatly reduces our options.

title: The wing of an aeroplane will never stall at low subsonic speeds as long as...
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: the angle of attack is smaller than the value at which the stall occurs.
optionB: the IAS exceeds the power-on stall speed.
optionC: there is a nose-down attitude.
optionD: the CAS exceeds the power-on stall speed.
explanationTotal: There is a certain angle of attack (AOA), at which the flow cannot follow the shape of the profile, the flow separates from the surface and vortices are created. This results in a smaller suction, smaller lift and high drag. If AOA is increased further beyond this AOA, lift will reduce. This angle of attack is called critical angle of attack. The critical angle of attack will remain the same regardless of gross weight. A given wing will always stall at the same AOA, regardless of weight, load factor, density altitude and airspeed. However, increased weight, a higher load factor and increased density altitude do increase the airspeed at which the aircraft reaches its critical AOA.

title:
Which statement about an aeroplane leaving ground effect is correct?

I. The downwash angle decreases.
II. The induced angle of attack increases.
optionA: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
optionB: I is incorrect, II is correct.
optionC: I is correct, II is correct.
optionD: I is correct, II is incorrect.
explanationTotal:
For a fixed wing aircraft, ground effect is the increased lift and decreased drag that the wings generate when they are close to the ground.
Upon landing, ground effect can give the effect of floating. The stall speed may be temporarily reduced due to ground effect.

Ground effect is effective from the ground to approximately half the aircraft’s wingspan above ground.
The effect is caused by the ground interrupting the wingtip vortices, decreasing the downwash angle.

Below the airfoil, a higher pressure than if an airfoil travels at higher altitude is created, as the air below the airfoil is trapped in between the wing and the ground.
This means that the aircraft needs a lower angle of attack for a certain amount of lift.
This results in lower induced drag (decreasing induced angle of attack).

title: if the Mach number is 0.8 and the TAS is 480 kt, what is the speed of sound?
explanationTotal:
The Mach number is defined as the ratio between the TAS and the LSS (Local speed of sound).
It is an indication of how fast an aircraft is travelling with relation to the sound waves that surround it.

The Mach number may be calculated as follows:
M=TAS/LSS=(TAS(kt))/(38.95∗√(T(K)))

The speed of propagation of small pressure waves depends upon the temperature of the air ONLY.
In this exercise:

0.8=480/LSS⇔LSS=480/0.8⇔LSS=600kt
Local Speed of Sound (LSS) is equal to 600 knots.

title: The lift coefficient of a symmetrical aerofoil section at zero angle of attack is:
optionA: positive.
optionB: positive, if the centre of pressure coincides with the centre of gravity.
optionC: negative.
optionD: zero.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
The distribution of pressure is important in aerodynamics, since it determines:
- The amount of lift generated
- Any pitching moments
- The form drag of an aerofoil section

The lift and drag forces of a wing cross-section are dependent on the pressure distribution around the wing. The pressure distribution around an aerofoil is the resultant of the angle of the aerofoil chordline to the oncoming airflow, the angle of attack.

If a symmetrical aerofoil section is in a steady airstream at zero degrees Angle of Attack, a stagnation point forms on the leading edge.

The airflow velocity above and below the aerofoil increases by an equal amount and the static pressures reduce by an equal amount. Consequently, no pressure differential exists, and no net lift is created.

title:
Refer to figure.
The aircraft with a higher aspect radio is (1)______ and it has (2) ______ induced drag.
optionD: (1) 2; (2) higher.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
At any given lift coefficient, an increased aspect ratio results in a reduced wing drag coefficient. This relationship is due to the fact that the induced drag coefficient varies inversely with the aspect ratio. When the aspect ratio is elevated, the induced drag experiences only minor fluctuations as lift varies. Conversely, at high lift coefficients, particularly at low indicated airspeeds (IAS), the induced drag becomes significant and exhibits a rapid increase as the lift coefficient rises. When examining the lift and drag curves for a wing with a high aspect ratio, they reveal a pronounced and consistent increase in lift coefficient with respect to angle of attack (α) until reaching the point of stall. Significant alterations in drag coefficient (CD) are primarily observed in the vicinity of the stall point.

title:
Refer to figure.
Which of these curves would result in the greatest load factor for a certain gust?
optionA: Curve 3
optionB: Curve 2
optionC: Curve 4
optionD: Curve 1
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
For a given gust speed and TAS, the increment of the load factor depends on the increase in CL per change in angle of attack due to the gust (the slope of the lift curve). If the lift curve has a steep slope, the g increment will be greater per change in angle of attack. Factors which affect the lift curve are aspect ratio and wing sweep.

Wings with a low aspect ratio or sweep will have a flatter lift curve slope. This results in a smaller change in CL or g due to a given gust at a certain TAS.

title: The load factor is less than 1 (one):
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: when lift is greater than weight.
optionB: during a steady horizontal turn.
optionC: during a wings level stall before recovery.
optionD: in steady wings level horizontal flight.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The balance of forces in steady climb show thrust is partly acting upwards and weight is partly adding to the drag.
