Because the thrust is now assisting lift, there is less lift required than in level flight.
For steady speed, the thrust and two effects of aerodynamic drag and weight must be equal.

T= Thrust
W= Weight
D= Drag
T= D + W sin(gamma)

This means that the climb angle (sin gamma) depends on excess thrust and weight.
In descent the formula will become T= D – W sin(gamma)
The load factor is the relationship between lift and weight.
As the lift in a stall is decreased and the load factor in straight and level flight is 1, the load factor will now be less than 1.

title: How does VMCL change with an increase of density altitude?
optionA: It increases due to the increased rudder force.
optionB: It decreases due to the decreased rudder force.
optionC: It increases due to the increased engine thrust.
optionD: It decreases due to the decreased engine thrust.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
VMCL, the minimum control speed during approach and landing with all engines operating, is the calibrated airspeed at which, when the critical engine is suddenly made inoperative, it is possible to maintain control of the airplane with that engine still inoperative and maintain straight flight with an angle of bank of not more than 5°.

VMCL is very similar to the other two minimum control speeds, in that it mainly is set by the thrust asymmetry vs the rudder force available. The asymmetry caused by running one engine at maximum power/thrust with the other engine failed/windmilling can be huge, and causes a very large yawing moment towards the dead engine. This must be counteracted by the rudder force, to stop the aircraft becoming uncontrollable.

At high speeds, this is fine, as the rudder has plenty of airflow over it and therefore can counteract the thrust asymmetry just fine, but at lower speeds, this is not the case.

There is a speed, below which the rudder does not have the available force to counteract the thrust asymmetry of a failed engine at maximum thrust. This would be because the rudder does not have a fast enough airflow over it, and has reached its maximum deflection angle. Below this speed, even at maximum rudder deflection, the aircraft will yaw towards the dead engine. This speed is called the minimum control speed.

Minimum control speeds change with the density altitude, but not because of the airflow over the rudder (this has a small effect), instead due to the difference in thrust available from the engine. At lower density altitudes (higher air densities), there is more air to be mixed with fuel and burnt, so the thrust is higher, and therefore the thrust asymmetry with a failed engine is higher, and the rudder needs more airflow to counteract this higher moment, so the minimum control speed is higher.

Therefore, at an increased density altitude, the thrust is lower, so the VMCL is decreased also.

title: In straight and steady flight on descent, Thrust is:
optionA: Less than drag.
optionB: Equal to drag.
optionC: Greater than drag.
optionD: Equal to lift.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Power-on descent

Weight is split into 2 components:

  • W cos y acts perpendicular to the flight path and balances lift;
  • W sin y acts forward along the flight path, adding to Thrust to balance drag.
Lift is less than Weight: Lift only has to balance the component of weight which acts perpendicular to the flight path (L = W cos y).

Thrust is less than drag: Weight gives a forward component in the same direction as thrust.

For a power-on descent, we get the following formulas:

D = T + W sin y
T = D – W sin y
L = W cos y

title: Compared with a level, co-ordinated turn, in order to maintain constant speed during straight and level flight, the pilot must:
optionA: decrease angle of attack and keep thrust unchanged.
optionB: decrease thrust and keep angle of attack unchanged.
optionC: decrease thrust and angle of attack.
optionD: decrease thrust and increase angle of attack.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
In level flight, any turn will be coordinated or uncoordinated. A coordinated turn is one in which the only acceleration is along the normal axis of the airplane, towards the center of the turn, and the angle of bank is precisely correct for the aircraft speed and the radius of turn. If not all these factors are present, the turn will be uncoordinated and there will be a lateral acceleration either towards or away from the center of the turn. The total lift of a balanced turn provides the centripetal force and the force that opposes the mass of the airplane.
If there is acceleration towards the center of the turn the airplane is slipping and if it is away from the center of the turn the airplane is skidding. Either condition will be indicated on the turn and slip indicator. An overbanked airplane will slip into the turn and requires an increase of speed or a reduction in bank angle to correct this condition. An underbanked airplane will skid out of the turn, which requires a decreased speed or an increased bank angle to correct this condition. These are indicated on the turn and slip indicator by the needle one-way and the ball the other.
To maintain altitude and airspeed when executing a turn both the angle of attack and the thrust have to be increased above their level flight values. In a turn, Thrust is equal to Drag.

title: Whilst flying at a constant IAS and at n = 1, as the aeroplane mass increases, the value of M<sub>CRIT</sub>:
optionA: increases.
optionB: remains constant.
optionC: is independent of the angle of attack.
optionD: decreases.
explanationTotal:
Critical Mach number (MCRIT) is the free stream Mach number at which local speed of the airflow somewhere around the aircraft reaches local sonic speed (M = 1).

MCRIT of the wing depends on (for a given configuration), amongst other, profile shape:

MCRIT ≈ 1 – 0.7 √t – 3.2 t √(3/CL)
Where “t” is the relative thickness.

From the formula, we can conclude that:

  • If relative thickness is higher, MCRIT is lower.
  • If CL is higher, MCRIT is lower. Since CL is a direct function of angle of attack, if angle of attack is increased, MCRIT reduces.
Consequently, if mass and/or load factors (i.e. turn) increases, CL has to increase, thus MCRIT reduces.

title: A multi engined commercial jet with underslung wing mounted engines is flying at the stall speed with idle power. If power is increased, C<sub>LMAX</sub> will (1) _____ and the stall speed will (2) _____.
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: (1) remain the same; (2) decrease
optionB: (1) remain the same; (2) increase
optionC: (1) increase; (2) remain the same
optionD: (1) decrease; (2) remain the same
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
STALLING SPEED (VS)

The stalling speed is defined as the calibrated stalling speed, or the minimum steady flight speed, in knots at which the aircraft is still controllable and is represented by the formula:

VS = √(2×Mass) ÷ (CLMAX × ρ × S)

The stalling speed depends on the amount of lift a wing needs to generate, as determined by the following factors:

- Weight
- Aircraft Configuration
- Manoeuvres
- Wing Loading
- Wing Contamination
- Power:

Approaching the stalling angle with power on, a component of thrust partially supports the weight of the aircraft. The wings become slightly off-loaded, and produce less lift, which results in the aircraft stalling at a lower indicated airspeed.

Changes in power have no direct effect on the CLMAX.

title: An aeroplane flying at 200 kt in straight and level flight is subjected to a disturbance that suddenly increases the speed by 60 kt. Assuming the angle of attack remains constant, the load factor will initially:
optionA: increase to 1.6.
optionB: increase to 1.69.
optionC: remain unchanged, since the angle of attack does not change.
optionD: increase to 1.3.
explanationTotal:
Load Factor is the ratio of the weight of an aircraft to the load imposed by lift: Load Factor = Lift / Weight
Lift is propotional to V2: L= CL × ½ rho × V2 × S

Therefore, n is proportional to V2 . An increase in "n" means lift has increased by a factor "n".

  • In this case, speed has increased by a factor of: 260/200 = 1.30

Consequently, lift has changed by a factor of: 1.302 = 1.69 ⇒ Load factor is now 1.69.

title: If the thrust line is located below an aeroplane’s CG, it will create a:
optionA: Positive pitch moment that is stabilising.
optionB: Positive pitch moment that is destabilising.
optionC: Negative pitch moment that is destabilising.
optionD: Negative pitch moment that is stabilising.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
POWER EFFECTS

Its effects may cause significant changes in trim left coefficient and static longitudinal stability.
The vertical location of the thrust line defines one of the direct contributions to stability.

  • If the thrust line is below the CG (the case of most airliners with underwing engines), a thrust increase will produce an added pitch-up moment (positive moment) => this will cause the airplane to slow down more than necessary (despite the added thrust). Creating an unstable situation. Therefore, the effect is destabilizing.
  • If the thrust line is above the CG, this is the opposite of the above and a thrust increase will produce a nose down moment (negative moment), and, in moderate amounts, can have a stabilising effect. The airplane will settle at a higher speed, which is presumably what the pilot wants (despite the "power controls altitude" mantra). When the line is too high, the airplane may even descend and accelerate more than necessary, until the aerodynamic moment balances out the thrust moment, but overall the condition is stable.
  • Thrust is in line with CG. The airplane will start to climb (or reduce descent) and will settle on the same AoA and roughly the same speed.

title: An aeroplane maintains straight and level flight while the IAS is doubled. The change in lift coefficient will be:
explanationTotal:
Lift can be calculated as follows:
L= CL × ½ rho × V2 × S

Where:

  • CL is lift coefficient (without dimension)
  • p is density
  • V is velocity [m/s] (velocity is TAS)
  • S is surface area [m2]
  • L is lift [N]
⇒ If the velocity doubles, lift increases by a factor of 22 = 4. To maintain lift constant (straight and level flight), lift coefficient (CL) must be 0.25 of the old CL (x 0.25).

title: Which definition of propeller parameters is correct?
optionA: Blade angle is the angle between the blade chord line and the propeller axis.
optionB: Angle of attack is the angle between the blade chord line and the propeller vertical plane.
optionC: Helix angle is the angle between the actual path of the propeller and the plane of rotation.
optionD: Geometric pitch is the actual distance a propeller would advance in one revolution.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The Blade Angle

Sometimes called the pitch angle, is the angle subtended between the plane of rotation and the chord line of the propeller blade, which may be fixed or variable. When the airplane is moving it comprises two parts, the angle of attack and the helix angle, but when it is stationary the blade angle is equal to the angle of attack.

The Helix Angle

The angle that the actual path of the propeller makes to the plane of rotation.

Angle of Attack

The path of the propeller through the air determines the direction of the relative airflow. The angle between the blade chord and the relative airflow is the angle of attack (α).
The angle of attack (α) is the result of propeller rotational velocity (RPM) and aircraft forward velocity (TAS).

title: Compared to a conventional aerofoil at a given flight level, the MCRIT of a supercritical aerofoil will be...
optionA: lower.
optionB: the same at lower speeds and higher at transonic speeds.
optionC: higher.
optionD: the same.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
A supercritical wing is one that has been designed with specific streamwise segments to delay the onset of the adverse effects of the shockwave, i.e. wave drag and its severity and decreased lateral stability, when the airplane is flying in the transonic speed range or just above MCRIT. It increases the cruise Mach number, the range, and the endurance of the airplane. The main features of a supercritical wing are:

The upper surface is flattened but the lower surface is reflex cambered towards the trailing edge. Thus, the airflow over the upper surface is not accelerated as much as conventional airfoils, which delays the formation of the shockwave to a higher speed.

Compared with a conventional airfoil section it has a larger leading-edge radius, a flatter upper surface and both positive and negative camber and enables a relatively thick wing to be used for approximately the same cruise Mach number.

The curved lower surface increases the lift generated by the aft end of the airfoil and replaces some of the lift lost from the flat upper surface. Because of the rear-loaded lift generation it is often called an aft-loaded wing.

The leading edge of the supercritical wing has a greater radius than traditional airfoils that suffer from excessive wave drag and the loss of longitudinal stability (tuck under). By ensuring that its profile is carefully designed any expansion waves will be reflected from the subsonic boundary back to the shockwave, thereby weakening its intensity.

title: What is the significance of the maximum allowed cruising altitude, based on the 1.3 g margin? At this altitude:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: exceeding a load factor of 1.3 will cause permanent deformation of this aeroplane.
optionB: a manoeuvre with a load factor of 1.3 will cause a Mach number at which accelerated low speed stall occurs.
optionC: a manoeuvre with a load factor of 1.3 will cause M<sub>CRIT</sub> to be exceeded.
optionD: a manoeuvre with a load factor of 1.3 will cause buffet onset.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Stall boundaries set a lower limit to the operating speed, according to the load factor. In the case of a high-speed aircraft, there is also an upper limit which is due to the approach of shock stall and the associated buffet which occurs if the aircraft enters the transonic speed range. The limits associated with these effects give the buffet boundaries.

The margin between the two types of stall narrows with increasing altitude. Notably the true airspeed of the low-speed stall increases with increasing altitude for a given indicated airspeed, whilst the true airspeed of the shock stall reduces up to the base of the tropopause, above which it remains constant.

The point at which the two stalls coincide is referred to as the 'coffin corner'. The altitude at which an aircraft can fly at one airspeed in a 1g maneuver is called the aerodynamic ceiling.

For any given combination of mass, center of gravity position and airspeed, the maximum operating altitude is that altitude at which a normal positive acceleration increment of 0.3g, without exceeding the buffet onset boundary, is possible.
It is, therefore, common practice to draw the ‘buffet-onset boundary chart’ for a range of cruise masses at 1.3g. Any maneuver having a load factor exceeding 1.3g will initiate the buffet onset.

title: You have an engine failure in a single-engined aircraft and need to glide 5 km to a safe landing site. With an engine out, the glide ratio is 10/1. What is the minimum height the aircraft must be at for this to be possible?
optionA: 500 km
explanationTotal:
Glide ratio is the measure of how far (horizontally) an aircraft can glide, per vertical height lost. So a glide ratio of 10/1 means that the aircraft can go 10 m laterally for each 1 m of height lost.

This is a simple calculation then, if the horizontal distance to cover is 5 km (5 000 m), which is worth 10 units, then the height we must be at (worth 1 unit), need only be 5 000 / 10 = 500 m.

title: Which of the following scenarios causes a worse effect on aeroplane controllability with an engine failure?
optionA: A light aircraft during go-around.
optionB: A heavy aircraft during go-around.
optionC: A heavy aircraft in the cruise.
optionD: A light aircraft in the cruise.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
When an engine fails on a multi-engine aircraft there will be a large decrease in thrust and an increase in drag on the side with the failed engine:

  • airspeed will decay.
  • the nose will drop and.
  • most significantly, there will be an immediate yawing moment towards the failed engine.

The forces and moments acting on an aircraft following failure of the left engine are shown in figure 1. The aircraft has a yawing moment towards the dead engine. The pilot has applied rudder to stop the yaw. This is the vital action when an engine fails, to stop the yaw.
Any increase in weight ultimately reduces the aircraft’s overall performance, but in a banked condition, the extra weight induces a greater side force, which removes the need for sideslip, allowing for a reduction in the rudder application, thereby making the aircraft more controllable in one-engine-inoperative flight. Also, the extra momentum and rotational momentum means the aircraft reacts less strongly when an engine fails when at high mass.

Therefore, increased weight is somewhat beneficial to controllability in the event of an engine failure. It is important to note, though, that in reality, this benefit is insignificant compared to the performance penalties associated with any additional weight.

title: The critical Mach number of a conventional aerofoil section increases if:
optionA: its camber is increased.
optionB: it is flown at lower angles of attack.
optionC: its thickness to chord ratio is increased.
optionD: its leading edge radius is increased.
explanationTotal:
The critical Mach number (MCRIT) is the lower limit of a speed band, known as the transonic range, in which the local Mach number may be either subsonic or supersonic. Its value varies with the angle of attack and is the free-stream Mach number at which sonic speed is reached over the upper surface of a wing. In other words, it is the speed at which the local Mach number is equal to the free-airstream Mach number. It is also the highest speed possible without supersonic flow over the wing.

The critical Mach number is inversely proportional to the angle of attack, i.e. MCRIT decreases with increasing angle of attack and vice versa. This is because, as the angle of attack increases the local peak velocity of the airflow over the wing also increases. It therefore reaches Mach 1 sooner than it would have done at a lower angle of attack; thus, the critical Mach number is less.

title: A swept-back wing compared to a straight wing of the same dimensional thickness and free stream velocity increases MCRIT because sweeping the wing back...
optionA: reduces the effective chord.
optionB: increases the local velocity.
optionC: increases the effective aspect ratio.
optionD: increases the effective chord.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
One of the most used methods of increasing MCRIT is to sweep the wing back.

As shown in figure 1, it can be considered that compared to a straight wing, a swept-back wing of the same airfoil section has a smaller effective thickness chord ratio. Sweeping the wing back increases the effective aerodynamic chord for the same dimensional thickness.

The local velocity will be lower for a given free stream velocity. In this way, the MCRIT of a swept wing will be higher and the transonic drag rise will be delayed.

title: What should you do if you encounter a thunderstorm during your cruise that you cannot circumnavigate?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Climb above the thunderstorm.
optionB: Descend to a lower altitude to avoid the thunderstorm.
optionC: Fly at turbulence penetration speed.
optionD: Increase airspeed to pass through the thunderstorm quickly.
explanationTotal:
Turbulence Penetration Speed

For flight in turbulence an airspeed must be chosen to give margin against stalling and overstressing the aircraft structure. This speed is VRA/MRA (the rough-air speed) or turbulence penetration speed. VRA/MRA will give adequate protection from over-stressing the aircraft with maximum protection from an inadvertent stall.

Thunderstorms should be circumnavigated and preferably upwind. Extensive use of weather radar scanning is useful. A turbulence penetration speed should be selected to minimise the gust loads on the aircraft. When possible, descent to a lower altitude should be considered as it gives more performance and buffet margin to cope with gusts.

title: According to the equation of continuity, the constant mass flow in a stream tube is dependent on the following for a low subsonic flow, assuming that the air is incompressible:
optionA: Velocity of the air only
optionB: Velocity of the air and cross-sectional area of the stream tube
optionC: Mass of the air only
optionD: Density of the air only
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
To demonstrate the effect the Principle of Continuity has on aerodynamic theory, we consider a streamline flow of air through a tube, which has a reduced cross-sectional area in the middle.

The air mass flow, or mass per unit time (kg/m3), through the tube will be the product of the cross-sectional area (A), the airflow velocity (V), and the air density (ρ). Mass flow will remain a constant value at all points along the tube. The equation of continuity is:

A x V x ρ = Constant

Because air is a compressible fluid, any pressure change in the flow will affect the air density. However, at low subsonic speeds (< M 0.4 or Mach 0.4, i.e., aircraft speed is 40% of the local speed of sound), density changes will be insignificant and can be disregarded. The equation of continuity can now be simplified to:

A x V = Constant ⇒ V ≈ 1/A

Because the mass flow must remain constant, it can be seen from the equation of continuity that the reduction in the tube’s cross-sectional area results in an increase in velocity, and vice versa.

title:
Refer to figure.
Assuming all bodies have the same cross-sectional area and are in motion, place these bodies in order of increasing pressure drag.The correct answer is:
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

Total Drag is sub-divided into two main types:
Parasite Drag - independent of lift generation, and
Induced Drag - the result of lift generation.

Parasite drag is further sub-divided into:

  • Skin Friction Drag
  • Form (Pressure) Drag, and
  • Interference Drag

NOTE: Skin Friction and Form Drag are together known as PROFILE DRAG.

Form drag is produced whenever the streamline airflow passing over an aircraft separates from the surface and becomes turbulent. An example of extreme form drag is the effect of a flat plate placed at right angles to the airflow.
The pressure immediately in front of the plate is above atmospheric, whilst the pressure behind the plate is below atmospheric. This results in a sucking effect behind the plate and the formation of vortices. The more rapidly the airflow changes direction, the greater the pressure gradient, the earlier the separation, and the higher the form drag.
Changing the shape, or streamline, of a given object reduces drag by delaying the point at which the airflow separates.

title:
Which of the following methods can be applied to counter "Mach Tuck"?

I. Shifting CG backwards.
II. Shifting CG forwards.
III. Automatic pitch trim to pitch nose up.
IV. Automatic pitch trim to pitch nose down.
optionA: II and III.
optionB: I and III.
optionC: I and IV.
optionD: II and IV.
explanationTotal:
MACH TUCK is a nose down pitch tendency due to a rearward CP movement with increasing Mach number in the transonic region.

A further factor contributing to the nose-down pitching moment is decreased downwash at the tail resulting from reduced lift at the wing root. If the tailplane is situated in the downwash, its effective angle of attack is increased, giving an increase in the nose-down pitching moment.

To overcome the above described phenomenon, a Mach trim system is fitted. This device, sensitive to Mach number, may:

  • deflect the elevator up (pitch nose up).
  • move the CG rearwards, i.e. by transferring fuel from the wings to a rear trim tank.
  • decrease the incidence of the variable incidence trimming tailplane.

title: Wave drag above MCRIT consists of:
optionA: Energy drag and boundary layer separation.
optionB: Shock drag.
optionC: M<sub>CRIT</sub> and wave drag.
optionD: Induced drag and parasite drag.
explanationTotal:
WAVE DRAG

Wave drag describes the extra drag encountered when, at high speed, shock waves form on an aircraft. As speed increases above MCRIT shock waves begin to form and drag increases more rapidly than it would have done without the shock waves. The additional drag is called wave drag and is due to energy drag and boundary layer separation.

  • Heat is created at a shock wave. Energy has to be used to provide this temperature rise across the shock wave and this energy loss is drag on the aircraft – Energy Drag.
  • The high pressure found at the shock wave creates a strong adverse pressure gradient on the aircraft surface. This turbulence represents energy lost to the flow and contributes to the drag – Separation Drag.

title: A plane is flying at 1,8 V<sub>S</sub>, what % of C<sub>LMAX</sub> is that?
explanationTotal:
Formula:

L = 1/2 p V2 S CL
Lift should stay constant as weight stays constant. So let's write the equation for CLMAX too. Then find our CL value in CLMAX.

1/2 p V2 S CL = 1/2 p VS2 S CLMAX
V2 CL = VS2 CL MAX

Remember that V = (1.8) VS,
(1.8)2 CL = CL MAX
CL = 1 / (1.8)2
CL = 0.308 CL MAX

  • 31% of CLMAX

title: An aerofoil with reduced camber compared to one with increased camber at high subsonic speed, at the same level and configuration will...
optionA: be more sensitive to gust turbulence.
optionB: produce more lift.
optionC: have a lower MCRIT.
optionD: have a higher M<sub>CRIT</sub>.
explanationTotal:
The critical Mach number (MCRIT) is the lower limit of a speed band, known as the transonic range, in which the local Mach number may be either subsonic or supersonic. Its value varies with the angle of attack and is the free-stream Mach number at which sonic speed is reached over the upper surface of a wing. In other words, it is the speed at which the local Mach number is equal to the free-airstream Mach number. It is also the highest speed possible without supersonic flow over the wing.

The critical Mach number is inversely proportional to the angle of attack, i.e. MCRIT decreases with increasing angle of attack and vice versa. This is because, as the angle of attack increases the local peak velocity of the airflow over the wing also increases. It therefore reaches Mach 1 sooner than it would have done at a lower angle of attack; thus, the critical Mach number is less.

At the design stage of an airplane the inclusion of some characteristics will increase the value of the critical Mach number:

A thin airfoil cross-section (low thickness to chord ratio).

Generally, a thicker wing with a large amount of camber has a lower critical Mach number than a thin wing with little camber because the airflow over its upper surface accelerates to a higher speed than it would over a thin wing. Therefore, an airfoil with reduced camber will have a higher MCRIT.

title: If the density altitude increases, what happens to the Minimum Control Speed (VMC)?
optionA: As thrust increases, VMC increases.
optionB: As density increases, VMC decreases.
optionC: As thrust decreases, VMC decreases.
optionD: As density decreases, V<sub>MC</sub> increases.
explanationTotal:
VMCA is the calibrated airspeed at which, when the critical engine is suddenly made inoperative, it is possible to maintain control of the airplane with that engine still inoperative and maintain straight flight with an angle of bank of not more than 5°.

VMCA may not exceed 1.13VSR with:

  • maximum available take-off power or thrust on the engines.
  • the airplane trimmed for take-off.
  • the most unfavorable CG position.
  • maximum sea level take-off weight.
  • the airplane in its most critical take-off configuration (but with gear up); and
  • the airplane airborne and the ground effect negligible; and
  • if applicable, the propeller of the inoperative engine:
    • wind milling
    • feathered, if the airplane has an autmatic feathering device.
  • The rudder forces required to maintain control at VMCA may not exceed 150 lb. nor may it be necessary to reduce power or thrust on the operative engines.

Note: There is no performance requirement, just directional control.

Banking towards the live engine reduces the rudder deflection required and so allows a lower VMCA. The magnitude of VMCA increases with increased bank angle from 0° to 5°. The maximum limit is set at 5° because there is an increasing risk of fin stall above this limit.
VMCA is affected by the amount of thrust being developed by the operating engine. As altitude and/or temperature increases, the thrust from an unsupercharged engine will decrease. Therefore, VMCA decreases with an increase in altitude and/or temperature.

title: What could be the cause of a periodic yawing motion whilst flying at transonic speeds?
optionA: Minor control surface flutter.
optionB: Dutch roll.
optionC: Shockwave formation.
optionD: Dutch roll caused by shockwave formation.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
Learning Objective 081.04.06.03.03: Describe how the asymmetric nature of shock waves on both wings, at high Mach numbers, can lead to Dutch roll.

Dutch Roll

Dutch roll is a coupled lateral and directional oscillation which is undesirable because of the oscillatory nature. Dutch roll can occur when the static lateral stability (caused by dihedral, etc.) is high in comparison to the static directional stability (caused by the tail fin, etc.)

Asymmetric shockwaves

Modern transport jet aircraft tend to cruise at high altitudes with high Mach numbers, very close to - or just inside - the transonic regime. This is the range of speeds (At and above MCRIT) where some of the aircraft experiences supersonic airflow, but not all the aircraft does. This brings rise to shockwaves, first on the upper wing surfaces near the roots, then spreading to other areas of the aircraft. Shockwaves produce quite high drag forces, classed as "wave drag".

If the shockwaves form asymmetrically on the aircraft, whether due to different airflow patterns over the wings, small differences in the aircraft structure, control surfaces, etc., then the different drag forces can cause a yawing motion, which sets off the oscillation known as Dutch roll. This Dutch roll would be made worse by the shockwaves forming on the faster wing, reducing lift and increasing drag to drop it down and drag it back, exacerbating the Dutch roll.

title: The pitch up effect of an aeroplane with swept-back wing in a stall is due to the:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: wing root stalling first.
optionB: wing tip stalling first.
optionC: forward movement of the centre of gravity.
optionD: aft movement of the centre of gravity.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
As we can see in the diagram, aircraft with swept wings have the tendency to pitch up during or when approaching a stall because of the movement of the centre of pressure. As the tip stalls the centre of pressure will move more towards the root of the wing, and more towards to nose of the aircraft. This will cause a deviation from the trimmed/stable position and lead to a nose up reaction.

title: Excluding constants, the coefficient of induced drag (C<sub>DI</sub>) is the ratio of:
optionA: C<sub>L</sub>² and AR (aspect ratio).
optionB: C<sub>L</sub> and b (wingspan).
optionC: C<sub>L</sub>² and S (wing surface).
optionD: C<sub>L</sub> and C<sub>D</sub>.
explanationTotal:
The induced drag can be defined by:

CDI = CL2 / π * AR

Where,
CDI – Induced Drag Coefficient
CL2 – Lift Coefficient squared
AR – Aspect Ratio

title:
Which of the following statements are correct with regards to fin angle of attack, sideslip, and rudder effectiveness, following an engine failure?

1. The greater the sideslip, the greater the fin angle of attack.
2. Excessive sideslip may cause fin stall.
3. The greater the sideslip, the greater the rudder effectiveness.
4. Excessive sideslip may cause fin stall, but only at a low aeroplane mass.
optionA: 1 and 2
optionB: 1 and 4
optionC: 2 and 3
optionD: 3 and 4
explanationTotal:
"1. The greater the sideslip, the greater the fin angle of attack." Correct.

In a sideslip the fin will experience a change in angle of attack - sideslip gives the fin an angle of attack. The change in lift (side force) on the fin creates a yawing moment about the centre of gravity which tends to yaw the aeroplane into the relative airflow.

"2. Excessive sideslip may cause fin stall." Correct.
An excessive sideslip can create an angle of attack greater than the fin's critical angle of attack, causing it to stall.
"3. The greater the sideslip, the greater the rudder effectiveness." Incorrect.
An increased sideslip will result in a reduced rudder effectiveness in the task of preventing the aircraft from yawing out of control. The sideslip will create extra yawing moments in the same direction as the asymmetric thrust (increasing the moments that the rudder must oppose).
"4. Excessive sideslip may cause fin stall, but only at a low aeroplane mass." Incorrect.
An excessive sideslip can create an angle of attack greater than the fin's critical angle of attack, causing it to stall at any mass.

title: Swept wings have the following properties:
optionA: More affected by turbulence and steeper slope of lift curve vs AOA.
optionB: Less affected by turbulence and steeper slope of lift curve vs AOA.
optionC: Less affected by turbulence and shallower slope of lift curve vs AOA.
optionD: More affected by turbulence and shallower slope of lift curve vs AOA.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Swept-wings experience poor lift qualities because the sweep-back design has the effect of reducing the lift capabilities of the wing. Consequently, it will have a shallower slope of lift curve vs AOA, as you can see in the attached figure.

The advantages a jet aircraft gains from the swept wing are high Mach cruise speeds and stability in turbulence.

  • Stability in turbulence. Ironically, a disadvantage of the swept wing is its poor lift qualities, which lends itself to an advantage in that it is more stable in turbulence compared with a straight-winged aircraft. This is so because the swept wing produces less lift and therefore is less responsive to updraughts, which allows for a smoother, more stable ride in gusty conditions.

title: Some aircraft have design options often referred to as the "waistline" or "coke bottle shape", mainly characterised by the reduction of the fuselage cross-section. What is the purpose of these designs?
optionA: Reduce friction drag by reducing surface areas
optionB: Improve airflow to the engine air inlet
optionC: Reduce wave drag through application of the area rule
optionD: Improve aerodynamic stability
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
At the design stage of an aeroplane the name given to the principle adopted when matching parts of an aeroplane together so that they produce the minimum total drag is the ‘area rule’.

The area rule states that provided the cross-sectional area of the aeroplane is similar to that of the ideal shape, the wave drag of the aeroplane will be similar to that of the ideal shape, irrespective of its actual shape. Wave drag is related to the curvature of the distribution of the volume of an aeroplane. The smoother the curvature the less is the magnitude of the wave drag.

Large volumes of the airframe, such as the wings, are usually positioned at the widest part of the fuselage and other necessary features such as the cockpit, the tailplane and engine intakes have to be spread out along the fuselage to maintain the cross-sectional area distribution as near perfect as possible.

For transonic aeroplanes it was discovered that indenting the fuselage to produce a waist and adding more volume to the rear of the aeroplane minimised transonic wave drag. Thus, the volume of the fuselage has to be decreased wherever a projection such as the wings and tailplane are positioned so that the cross-sectional area distribution changes smoothly with no discontinuities. This is sometimes referred to as the ‘coke bottle’ effect.

title: The speed V<sub>C </sub>in gust diagram...
optionA: equals 50 ft/s.
optionB: equals 66 ft/s.
optionC: equals 55 ft/s.
optionD: equals 25 ft/s.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
It is a design requirement of CS25 (old JAR25) that an airframe structure must be strong enough to withstand gusts both positive and negative that would cause a change of angle of attack so increasing load factor at three specified design speeds.

  • Speed VB (max gust intensity speed): +/- 66 ft/sec
  • Speed VC (design cruise speed): +/- 50 ft/sec
  • Speed VD (design dive speed): +/- 25 ft/sec.

VB is quite a low airspeed so the aircraft would be flying at high alpha and it would take some time for an aircraft to slow from VC (the design cruising speed) to VB if it flew into turbulence. Therefore, another design strength requirement is for the aircraft also to be strong enough to withstand a vertical gust of 50 ft/ sec at VC.

title: For an aeroplane in straight and level flight, lowering the flaps (1) _____ wing tip vortices, because the production of lift moves closer to the (2) _____.
optionA: (1) decreases; (2) tip
optionB: (1) decreases; (2) root
optionC: (1) increases; (2) root
optionD: (1) increases; (2) tip
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
INDUCED DRAG

Whenever a wing produces lift, concentrated vortices form at the wing tips. The vortices are strongest at the wing tips and become progressively weaker toward the centre-line of the aircraft.

It is the production of lift itself which reduces the magnitude of the lift force being generated. To replace the lift lost by the increased downwash, the aircraft must be flown at a higher angle of attack. This increases drag. This extra drag is called induced drag.

The stronger the vortices, the greater the induced drag.

WING TIP VORTICES vs. FLAPS

A stronger pressure differential above and below the wing generates stronger wing tip vortices. This may be achieved by flying at a higher angle of attack (flying a heavier airplane or flying slower).

Vortex strength is greatest with aircraft in a “clean” configuration (for a given speed and weight). This is because, with flaps extended the outboard portion of extended flaps offer another opportunity for higher-pressure air below the wing to move up.

With flaps extended, the aircraft generates four main vortices, weakening their overall effect. With the flaps retracted, those four vortices become two stronger ones.

title: In straight and level flight at a speed of 2 V<sub>S</sub>, the lift coefficient, expressed as a percentage of its maximum C<sub>LMAX</sub>, would be:
explanationTotal:
To solve this question, we either need to know the relationship by heart, or know how to get to it. If remembering works better for you, skip the italic part, if you prefer understanding where the relationship comes from, see the italic part.

Knowing that:

L = CL ½ rho v2 S

If we re-organize to make the coefficient of lift (CL) the subject of the equation:

CL = L ÷ (½ rho v2 S)

Therefore, removing the constant from the equation, we can say that:

CL ∝ 1 ÷ v2

Now that we know the relationship, and knowing that v = 2 VS , we can solve the question:

CL = 1 ÷ 22

CL = 0.25

With that information we know that our coefficient of lift at 2 VS will be 0.25 (25%) of the coefficient at VS.

title: A windmilling propeller:
optionA: has a greater blade angle than a feathered propeller.
optionB: produces drag instead of thrust.
optionC: produces neither thrust nor drag.
optionD: improves the glide performance of an aeroplane.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
In the event of an engine failure both the engine and the propeller will slow down. The CSU will attempt to maintain the selected RPM by driving the propeller blades to a fine position that will continue until reaching the fine pitch stop.
Despite the engine failing the airplane still has forward speed, for a single-engine airplane due to the glide descent the forward speed causes the propeller to have a negative angle of attack due to the direction of the relative airflow. This angle of attack generates sufficient torque to rotate the unpowered propeller in the normal direction of rotation.
The component of the force at right angles to the plane of rotation now acts rearwards and is no longer thrust but is now drag and presents a flat disc to the direction of travel.
Because the propeller is being driven only by the relative airflow it is said to be wind milling. As such, it causes a considerable amount of drag, reduces the IAS, reduces the Lift/Drag ratio and increases the rate of descent.

title:
Refer to figure.
Which device could you use to change from curve 1 to curve 2?
optionA: Trailing edge flaps
optionB: Leading edge flaps
optionC: Slats
optionD: Speed brakes
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
SPOILERS
Spoilers are flap type control surfaces, normally located on the upper surface of the wing, just in front of the trailing edge flaps.

These surfaces individually hinge at their leading edges and are actuated by hydraulic power supplied by dedicated power control units. The main purpose of the surfaces is to disturb the smooth airflow over the top of the wing, thereby reducing the wings lifting capability. When fully extended, they considerably increase aircraft drag.

The maximum deflection angles are greater in the ground mode than the flight mode. With the spoilers in their fully extended position, approximately 80% of the wing/flap lift is destroyed and the aerodynamic drag of the aircraft more than doubles.

Although Flaps increase Drag, they also increase Lift. From the options given, the only which causes both Lift to decrease and Drag to increase are the Speed Brakes.

title: The lift- and drag forces, acting on an aerofoil:
optionA: are proportional to each other, independent of angle of attack.
optionB: vary linearly with the angle of attack.
optionC: are normal to each other at just one angle of attack.
optionD: depend on the pressure distribution around the aerofoil.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
The distribution of pressure is important in aerodynamics, since it determines:
- The amount of lift generated
- Any pitching moments
- The form drag of an aerofoil section

The actual pressure distribution over the upper and lower surfaces varies with changes in angle of attack, as does the pressure differential and the amount of lift developed.

The lift and drag forces of a wing cross-section are dependent on the pressure distribution around the wing. The pressure distribution around an aerofoil is the resultant of the angle of the aerofoil chordline to the oncoming airflow, the angle of attack. The pressure distribution varies with the angle of attack.

title: Which of these statements about boundary layers is correct?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: A laminar boundary layer is thicker than a turbulent one.
optionB: A turbulent boundary layer produces less friction drag than a laminar one.
optionC: A turbulent boundary layer becomes laminar at the transition point.
optionD: Compared with a laminar boundary layer, a turbulent boundary layer is better able to resist a positive pressure gradient before it separates.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Due to the higher average velocity of the turbulent boundary layer compared to the laminar boundary layer, the turbulent boundary layer has more energy that will better able to resist the adverse pressure gradient. Therefore the turbulent layer separates much later than the laminar boundary layer.
This is why vortex generators are commonly used on general aviation aircraft to create a larger area of turbulent air on the wing. This will lead to an increase in critical angle of attack and decrease the stall speed.

The other answers were incorrect because:

  • “Laminar boundary layer is thicker than a turbulent one” is incorrect because as you can see in the diagram, the turbulent boundary layer is thicker.
  • “A turbulent boundary layer produces less friction drag than a laminar one” is incorrect because a turbulent boundary layer produces more friction than a laminar boundary layer.
  • “A turbulent boundary layer becomes laminar at the transition point” is incorrect because turbulent air will not by nature turn into laminar air. However, laminar air does turn into turbulent air at the transition point as seen on the diagram.

title: An aeroplane flying at 200 kt in straight and level flight is subjected to a disturbance that suddenly increases the speed by 20 kt. Assuming the angle of attack remains constant, the load factor will initially:
optionA: increase to 1.20.
optionB: increase to 1.10.
optionC: remain unchanged, since the angle of attack does not change.
optionD: increase to 1.21.
explanationTotal:
Let’s start by identifying the equations used to answer the question.

Load factor is defined as:

n = L/W

Now we replace the lift with the full equation:

L = CL ½ rho V2 S
n = (CL ½ rho V2 S) / W

By removing all the constants, we can say that:

n = (CL ½ rho V2 S) / W

n ∝ V2

To find the change in load factor (nΔ), we have to divide nNEW by nOLD:

nΔ = nNEW / nOLD

nΔ = VNEW2 / VOLD2

For those who prefer remembering equations, remember the above

nΔ = 2202 / 2002

nΔ = 1.21

This means that the initial change in load factor due to the increase in airspeed of 20kt is 1.21.

title:
Refer to figure.
Which of the following graphs illustrate the movement of the total drag curve as density altitude decreases?
optionA: Figure 1
optionB: Figure 4
optionC: Figure 2
optionD: Figure 3
explanationTotal:
Decreasing density altitude implies an increase in air density, typically occurring during descent. Consequently, TAS decreases while drag remains constant. If density increases, TAS must decrease to maintain a constant dynamic pressure (Q). Drag values remain unchanged, occurring at a lower TAS. A decrease in pressure altitude or an increase in density results in a leftward shift of the total drag graph (lower TAS for a given drag). With increased density, the minimum drag speed (VDmin) in TAS decreases while the minimum drag value remains constant.

  • The graph which shows a decrease in TAS, with the drag curve moving horizontally left, is Figure 2.

title:
What is the Lift force in a steady wings level descent at 30 degrees? Given:

Weight: 104500 N
Thrust: 85000 N
Drag: 110230 N
Gravity constant: 10 m/s2
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Steady Descent

Weight is split into 2 components:

  • W cos y acts perpendicular to the flight path and balances lift;
  • W sin y acts forward along the flight path, adding to Thrust to balance drag.
Lift is less than Weight: Lift only has to balance the component of weight which acts perpendicular to the flight path (L = W cos y).

Thrust is less than drag: Weight gives a forward component in the same direction as thrust.

For a power-on descent, we get the following formulas:

D = T + W sin y
T = D – W sin y
L = W cos y

With regards to this question,
  • L = W cos y
  • L = 104 500 N x cos 30 = 90 500 N

title: During a straight steady vertical descent (dive):
optionA: weight is less than thrust.
optionB: lift is equal to the sum of weight and drag.
optionC: drag is equal to the sum of weight and thrust.
optionD: lift is greater than drag.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
A standard descent would not be like this, of course, and in a normal aircraft descent, the weight has a component that acts with the thrust vector, and the thrust plus the weight's forward component are both balanced by the aircraft's drag.

In this situation, however, both thrust and weight are acting completely downwards, and the only upwards force on the aircraft is drag, which will increase as the aircraft accelerates until it balances out the downwards forces, at which point the aircraft will remain at a constant speed (terminal velocity).

As for the lift force, there technically isn't any lift force present here, as that would cause the aircraft to begin to pull out of the dive.

title: You are flying at a constant CAS in the unstable speed region and encounter a wind shear which changes a headwind into a tailwind. What will happen?
optionA: Nothing will happen, but should fly carefully from this point and forward
optionB: Airspeed will decrease because the total drag is more
optionC: Airspeed will increases because the total drag is less
optionD: The aeroplane will stall due to insufficient lift
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
During flight, an aircraft will experience Parasite Drag (proportional to IAS2, increases with increasing “Parasite Area” => flaps, undercarriage or speed brakes) and Induced Drag (inversely proportional to IAS2, increases with increasing weight). The sum of Parasite Drag and Induced Drag is the Total Drag.

  • The Total Drag will be minimum at the IAS where Parasite Drag = Induced Drag. This speed is called Minimum Drag Speed (VMD);
    => Flying at a slower or faster speed than VMD will generate more drag.

When flying at a slower speed than VMD (back side), the aircraft will be in the unstable speed region. Any loss of speed will result in an increase in drag and further speed loss (which must be corrected by an increase in thrust). The sudden change to a tailwind will cause a loss of airspeed.

title: With a nose heavy aircraft (CG moves forward), the negative force produced by the horizontal stabiliser...
optionA: increases.
optionB: decreases.
optionC: remain the same.
optionD: the tailplane never produces a negative force.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Longitudinal stability is motion about the lateral axis.

Static Longitudinal stability is the aircraft's natural tendency when disturbed in pitch, to return to its former trimmed angle of attack without pilot input, and is desirable throughout the aircraft's complete speed range.

For the study of stability, we consider the changes in magnitude of lift force due to changes in angle of attack, acting through a stationary point, the aerodynamic centre (AC).

There are two moments to consider: the wing moment and the tail moment:

- The wing moment is a function of the change in wing lift multiplied by an arm (distance from wing CP to CG).
- The tail moment is a function of the change in tailplane lift multiplied by arm (distance from tailplane CP to CG).

The length of both arms is dependent upon CG position. If the CG is considered in a more forward position, the tail arm is larger and the wing arm is smaller. A more forward CG position increases static longitudinal stability.

The position of the CG directly affects the magnitude of the longitudinal static stability, the tailplane downforce and the stalling speed because its position determines the length of the arm of any restoring moment.

A forward movement of the CG increases the positive longitudinal static stability of an aircraft but decreases the manoeuvrability and control response because the moment arm is increased in length and increases the nose-down pitching moment. Thus, the required downforce on the tailplane increases.

title: On a jet transport aircraft flying at (1) _____ speeds, the outboard ailerons are (2) _____ to prevent (3) _____.
optionA: (1) low; (2) locked; (3) geometric washout
optionB: (1) low, (2) unlocked; (3) geometric washout
optionC: (1) high; (2) locked; (3) control reversal
optionD: (1) high; (2) unlocked; (3) control reversal
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Ailerons are the control surface on an aircraft that controls roll. They are usually mounted at the tips of the wings, to create the largest moment arm between them and the centre of gravity, for greater effectiveness.

This can become problematic, particularly at high speeds. At high speeds, the forces on a control surface are so great that they can actually twist the wing they are connected to. The further outboard the ailerons are, the easier it is to cause the wing to twist, as it has less stiffness. Imagine a down-going aileron, used to increase the lift of the wing and make the wing rise. This would also twist the wing so its trailing edge was up, and therefore the leading edge goes down, causing the wing to lose lift, and the wing would drop, instead of rising. We call this aileron reversal, shown in the annex above.

This is why many high speed aircraft often have secondary ailerons, which are called inboard ailerons, much closer to the fuselage, that are used during high speed flight, and the outboard ailerons are locked in place to avoid control reversal, flutter, and other structural issues due to the high aerodynamic forces. Some aircraft use roll spoilers also.

There is also a low speed aileron reversal that happens near the stall, so be aware of the similar names.

title: The effects of very heavy tropical rain on the aerodynamic characteristics of an aeroplane are:
optionA: increase of C<sub>LMAX</sub> and decrease of drag
optionB: increase of C<sub>LMAX</sub> and increase of drag.
optionC: decrease of C<sub>LMAX </sub>and increase of drag.
optionD: decrease of C<sub>LMAX</sub> and decrease of drag.
explanationTotal: Rain on an airfoil will distort the wing surface and therefore the air around it. The wing won’t operate in its maximum performance. Therefore C<sub>LMAX</sub> will decrease and drag will increase.

title:
Refer to figure.
The helix or advance angle of a rotating propeller blade element shown in the annex is:
optionA: angle 2.
optionB: angle 3.
optionC: angle 1.
optionD: not correctly indicated in the diagram.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The Blade Angle

Sometimes called the pitch angle, is the angle subtended between the plane of rotation and the chord line of the propeller blade, which may be fixed or variable. When the airplane is moving it comprises two parts, the angle of attack and the helix angle, but when it is stationary the blade angle is equal to the angle of attack.

The Helix Angle

The angle that the actual path of the propeller makes to the plane of rotation.

Angle of Attack

The path of the propeller through the air determines the direction of the relative airflow. The angle between the blade chord and the relative airflow is the angle of attack (α).
The angle of attack (α) is the result of propeller rotational velocity (RPM) and aircraft forward velocity (TAS).

title: An example of differential aileron deflection during initiation of left turn is:
optionA: Left aileron: 2° up. Right aileron: 5° down.
optionB: Left aileron: 2° down. Right aileron: 5° up.
optionC: Left aileron: 5° up. Right aileron: 2° down.
optionD: Left aileron: 5° down. Right aileron: 2° up.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
During a bank, the upgoing wing effectively experiences a decreased angle of attack whilst the effective angle of attack of the down going wing increases. Consequently, the slope of the total lift vector generates a rearward component on the upgoing wing and a forward component on the down going wing. These are yaw moments but in the opposite direction to that of the roll caused by the difference of the induced drag of each wing. This is adverse yaw, which is particularly significant at low airspeeds because of the large aileron deflection necessary to achieve the same rate of roll as at higher speeds with less deflection.

Adverse yaw may be counteracted by any one of the following devices:

  • rudder/aileron coupling.
  • slot/aileron coupling.
  • spoiler/aileron coupling.
  • frise ailerons.
  • differential aileron deflection.

title: If the elevator trim tab is deflected up, the cockpit trim indicator shows:
optionA: neutral.
optionB: nose down.
optionC: nose up.
optionD: nose left.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
When the elevator trim is moved up, it will force the elevator to move down and thus decreasing the down force from the stabiliser. This will cause a nose down moment from the wing lift, so the cockpit trim indicator should show nose down.

title:
Consider the ‘’CL vs angle of attack’’ graph of a non-symmetrical airfoil with the X axis representing angle of attack, and the Y axis representing CL.
The angle of attack at which the aerofoil achieves CLMAX can be found on the graph…
optionA: at the point where it crosses the X axis.
optionB: at its highest X value.
optionC: at the point where it crosses the Y axis.
optionD: at its highest Y value.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

Lift coefficient increases with angle of attack up to a maximum (CLMAX). The angle at which the maximum value of CL is reached is called the stalling angle or critical angle of attack. If the angle of attack is increased beyond this point, the airflow will no longer maintain its smooth flow over the upper surface and, consequently, the lift will reduce. This is depicted in the attached figure.
With regards to this question, assuming the X axis represents the angle of attack and the Y axis is the CL, CLMAX will be found at the highest Y value (= highest CL).

title: An aeroplane maintains straight and level flight at a speed of 1.8 V<sub>S</sub>. A vertical gust causes a load factor of 1.9. Determine the load factor n caused by the same gust at a speed of 2V<sub>S</sub>:
optionD: Not relevant. The gust at 1.8 V<sub>S </sub>would cause a stall.
explanationTotal:
An aircraft travelling at a certain speed (Vold) encounters a vertical gust which increases its load factor (nold) to a certain amount.
The goal is to compare the effect of the same gust on an aircraft travelling at a different speed (Vnew, in blue) and assessing the resultant load factor (nnew).

Vold = 1.8VS
nold = 1.9g
Vnew = 2VS
nnew =?

The first thing we should do is check if in the first situation the aircraft is stalled, by comparing the two VS0:

VS1 = VS0 x √(nold)
VS1 = √1.9 x VS0 = 1.38VS0
1.38VS0 < 1.8VS0

  • Therefore, the aircraft is not stalled!

As the aircraft does not stall in the first situation, we can calculate the load factor resulting from the same gust on an aircraft travelling at Vnew using a direct proportion:

Vold x (nnew−1) = Vnew x (nold−1)
nnew = ((Vnew x (nold−1)) / Vold) +1
nnew = ((2VS x (1.9−1)) / 1.8VS) +1
nnew = 2.00g

  • Encountering the same gust with a speed of 2VS the load factor will be 2.00g.

The last step of the exercise is to assess the limiting load factor at which the aircraft would stall and conclude if the new load factor calculated would be reached or the aircraft would stall before that.
To do this, let us compare Vnew with the stall speed (VS) and load factor in straight and level flight (n1g):

Vnew = VS * √(n1g

From here results that our limiting load factor is:

n1g = V2new
n1g = 4.00g

As our limiting load factor is higher than the new. In this case encountering the gust the aircraft would have its load factor increased to 2.00g without stalling.

title:
Refer to figure.
Consider the four glide flight paths represented in the annex. If the aeroplane is flying path 2 and the pilot extends the flaps, what would be the new flight path (the corresponding endurance times are shown on the annex)?
optionA: Path 2
optionB: Path 1
optionC: Path 3
optionD: Path 4
explanationTotal:
A descent may be with or without power. A descent without power is a glide descent and has no thrust vector. The remaining force vectors, lift, mass and drag.

There are three variables in a glide descent, the IAS, the configuration and the glide angle that can be manipulated to achieve either of two goals, maximum range or maximum endurance.

Glide for maximum range
The use of flap is restricted to the period of the descent when the IAS has fallen below the maximum speed for lowering flap (VLO). It is, therefore, limited to the final approach path. Using flap increases parasite drag, decreases the Lift/Drag ratio, increases the effective angle of attack and decreases the maximum glide range.

Increased flap decreases range because of the increased pitch angle

Glide for maximum endurance
The speed used during the descent is the rate of movement of the aeroplane along the descent path and is divided into two components: horizontal and vertical. The horizontal component is the aeroplane’s forward movement across the ground, its groundspeed, and the vertical component is its rate of descent.

It is essential to reduce the vertical component to a minimum to produce the maximum endurance.

The power required is the product of the TAS and the drag. Therefore, the lowest rate of descent is attained at the speed for which the least power is required.

Increased flap decreases endurance because of the increased drag.

To complete this exercise we are looking for the descent path which displays both a decrease in range and endurance. That is path number 4.

title: A normal, cambered aerofoil accelerates to transonic speeds: the lower shockwave moves aft...
optionA: More quickly than the upper.
optionB: But remains ahead of the upper shockwave.
optionC: To the location of the upper shockwave than remains static.
optionD: It is not possible to say.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The curvature of the underside of a wing is usually less than that of the upper surface, therefore the acceleration of the airflow is less, consequently the airflow does not become sonic until the aeroplane is travelling at a higher airspeed.

At lower airspeeds the only shockwave occurs on the upper surface and first appears at the wing root. At speeds above this, a shockwave forms beneath the lower surface of the wing ahead of the upper surface shockwave.
The shock wave on the lower surface usually forms at a higher free stream Mach number than the upper surface shock, but it reaches the trailing edge first.

The meeting point of the two pressure waves occurs nearer the trailing edge.

title: An aeroplane with a mass of 1 550 kg has a stall speed of 73 kts. The same aeroplane with a basic empty mass of 1 000 kg, a pilot with baggage with a mass of 102 kg and 120 litres of fuel (specific gravity 0.77) is performing a turn with a bank of 45 degrees. Calculate the stall speed:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: 71 kts
optionB: 76 kts
optionC: 64 kts
optionD: 67 kts
explanationTotal:
The stall speed is defined by:

VS = √((2∗W) / (ρ∗S∗CLMAX))

In this exercise there is a decrease in mass and an increase in load factor due to the turn, therefore:

mNEW = 1000 + 102 + (120 * 0.77) ⇔ mNEW = 1194 kg
mOLD = 1550 kg
VS OLD = 73 kt
nNEW = 1/cos(45°)

Lets first calculate the new VS in straight and level flight (VS NEW 1G):

VS NEW 1G = √(mNEW /mOLD) * VS OLD = √(1194 /1550 ) * 73 = 64 kt

Finaly, the new VS with an angle of bank of 45°:

VS NEW = √(nNEW) * VS NEW 1G = √(1/cos(45°)) * 64 = 76 kt

VS NEW ≈ 76 kt

The new stall speed with decreased weight and increased load factor is 76 knots.

title: Using conventional flight controls, you are manually piloting a jet transport aircraft as you decelerate from M0.76 to M0.73. A supercritical wing design is used on the aircraft. To maintain altitude as the plane decelerates, you must continuously apply a small nose-down trim. As you decrease your speed through M 0.73, you find that there is a need for progressive nose-up trim. This could have several causes, including...
optionA: that the shock waves are increasing in strength, creating an increased nose down pitching moment, which requires a greater nose-up trim
optionB: the slight pitch down moment due to shock waves reduces and the airplane returns to normal trim behavior below MCRIT
optionC: shock waves forming at the rear of aerofoil creating increased lift at the back of the profile and therefore a nose down pitch moment
optionD: all the speed reduces below MCRIT, the shock waves increase in strength and create a nose-down pitching moment
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The centre of pressure of an aerofoil is determined by the pressure distribution. As the speed increases through the transonic region, the pressure distribution changes and the centre of pressure will move.

Above the MCRIT, the upper surface pressure continues to drop on the wing until the shock wave is reached. This means that a greater proportion of the suction pressure will come from the rear of the wing and the centre of pressure is further aft.

The aerodynamic centre moves back to the 50% chord position during transonic flight.

As speed increases beyond MCRIT, shock wave formation will generate a nose-down pitching moment because there is less lift forward of the CG, and downwash on the tailplane is reduced. At high Mach numbers, an aircraft tends to become speed unstable. Instead of an increasing push force being required as speed increases, a pull force becomes necessary to prevent the aircraft accelerating further.

When decelerating, the effect is reversed. The decreased shockwave formation will ease the nose-down pitch, and a decrease in speed will eventually require a nose-up trim.

title: When approaching to land, the pilot forgets to lower the flaps. What is going to happen to the LDR, drag and speed at threshold?
optionA: Increases, decreases, increases (respectively).
optionB: Increases, decreases, decreases (respectively).
optionC: Decrease, increases, increases (respectively).
optionD: Decreases, increases, decreases (respectively).
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
When you extend the flaps on your plane, you lower your aircraft's stall speed, and at the same time, increase drag. When you're landing, you typically extend your flaps close to maximum setting. By putting the flaps out all the way, you maximize the lift and drag that your wing produces.

Flap extension during landings provides several advantages by:

• Producing greater lift and permitting lower landing speed (due to the slower stall speed).
• Producing greater drag, permitting a steep descent angle without airspeed increase.
• Reducing the length of the landing roll.

In this case, for a clean configuration (in comparasion to a full flap configuration):

- Drag is reduced;
- Speed at threshold is greater; and
- Landing distance is increased.

title:
Refer to figure.
The correct sequence that represents the ordering of the aerofoils by increasing CL is:
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The attached figure shows aerofoil sections with different thickness and camber combinations producing specific Lift Coefficient (CL) against Angle of Attack (α) plots.

- An increase in the thickness of a symmetrical aerofoil gives a higher CLMAX.
- The introduction of camber also has a beneficial effect on CLMAX.

The importance of maximum lift coefficient is that the greater the CLMAX , the lower the minimum flight speed (stall speed). If an aerofoil section of greater camber is used to give a lower minimum flight speed, the efficient cruise speed will be lower due to o the generation of excessive drag. It is better to use an aerofoil section that is efficient at high cruise speed, with the ability to temporarily increase the camber of the wing when it is necessary to fly slowly.

In the figure is also dipected that the CL increases with increasing Angle of Attack until the point of CLMAX, where an increase in Angle of Attack leads to a decrease in CL.

In this exercice there are two airfoils:
- airfoil 1 and 2 are identical, with airfoil 2 at a higher angle of attack
- airfoil 3 and 4 are identical, with airfoil 4 at a higher angle of attack

Airfoil 1 and 2 have a higher thickness and camber when compared to airfoil 3 and 4.

From this we can conclude that:
- Airfoil 3 is producing the least CL as it has the least camber, thickness and angle of attack;
- Airfoil 4 produces more CL than airfoil 3 because it has a higher angle of attack
- Airfoil 1 prduces more CL than the previous ones due to its camber and thickness
- Airfoil 2 produces the most CL because of its camber, thickness and higher angle of attack.

Knowing this, we can select the correct option: 3, 4, 1, 2.

title: What is correct about the buffet margin?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Decreases during a descent with a constant Mach number.
optionB: Is always greatest after a stepclimb has been executed.
optionC: Is always positive at Mach numbers below M<sub>MO</sub>.
optionD: Increases during a descent with a constant IAS.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The buffet onset boundary chart has both high speed and low speed buffet limits. Where the low speed buffet boundary marks the onset of the pre stall buffet and the high speed buffet boundary marks the onset of high speed buffeting. The speeds for high and low speed buffeting are dependent on weight, altitude, load factor and CG position. On the buffet onset boundary chart we will find the variables for altitude, weight and load factor.

For each mass and altitude, a low and high speed buffet will be identified, which will then limit the range of speeds for the specific mass and altitude.

  • In this case, during a descent, if IAS is kept constant, the Mach number is steadily decreasing. Consequently, the difference between the Mach number at which buffet is encountered increases.

title: A line connecting the leading and trailing edge midway between the upper and lower surface of an aerofoil, is the definition of the...
optionA: upper camber line.
optionB: mean aerodynamic chord line.
optionC: chord line.
optionD: camber line.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The line joining points that are equidistant from the upper and lower surfaces of an airfoil is the mean camber line. Maximum camber occurs at the point where there is the greatest difference between the mean camber line and the chordline. When the mean camber line is above the chordline the airfoil has positive camber.

title: In a sideslip, rudder effectiveness may be reduced. Deflection of which control surface will aid, through secondary or couple aerodynamic effects, the rudder yawing moment?
optionA: Slats
optionB: Flaps
optionC: Ailerons
optionD: Elevators
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
During a bank, the upgoing wing effectively experiences a decreased angle of attack whilst the effective angle of attack of the down going wing increases. Consequently, the slope of the total lift vector generates a rearward component on the upgoing wing and a forward component on the down going wing. These are yaw moments but in the opposite direction to that of the roll caused by the difference of the induced drag of each wing. This is adverse yaw, which is particularly significant at low airspeeds because of the large aileron deflection necessary to achieve the same rate of roll as at higher speeds with less deflection.

title: In high speed flight, as an aeroplane exceeds the drag divergence Mach number, it becomes (1) _____ stable with respect to speed, because of the (2) _____ movement of the centre of pressure.
optionA: (1) less; (2) forward
optionB: (1) less; (2) rearward
optionC: (1) more; (2) rearward
optionD: (1) more; (2) forward
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
The Mach number at which the aerodynamic drag begins to increase rapidly is called the Drag Divergence Mach Number. The Drag Divergence Mach Number is usually close to, and always greater than, the Critical Mach Number.

As the aircraft accelerates and shockwaves begin to develop on the airfoil, the CP (centre of pressure) moves rearward.

Whilst the nose-down pitching moment that the rearward movement of CP causes increases longitudinal stability, in terms of speed/velocity, the stability is reduced due to the mach tuck effect.

title: What is the position of the elevator in relation to the trimmable horizontal stabiliser of an aeroplane with fully hydraulically operated flight controls that is in trim?
optionA: Elevator deflection is zero.
optionB: The elevator is always deflected slightly downward in order to have sufficient remaining flare capability.
optionC: At a forward CG, the elevator is deflected upward and at an aft CG, it is deflected downward.
optionD: The position depends on speed, the position of flaps and slats and the position of the centre of gravity.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
A trimmable horizontal stabilizer serves as both a stabilizer and a trim device. It allows for the adjustment of the angle of incidence during flight to trim the aircraft.

In a power-assisted airplane, the stabilizer's position is influenced by factors such as speed, the configuration of slats and flaps, and the center of gravity. The elevator deflection, in relation to the stabilizer position, may not always be zero because the control force on the control column needs to be balanced in a trimmed position.

In a fully powered airplane, achieving a perfectly trimmed position for the elevator is not essential to zero out the force on the control column or stick in the cockpit. The artificial feel unit sets only the force on the controls to zero, while the elevator deflection is maintained at zero in comparison to the stabilizer position.

title: The positive manoeuvring limit load factor for a light aeroplane in the normal category in the clean configuration may not be less than:
explanationTotal:
EASA regulations for flight manoeuvring envelope
The load factor and speed limits for a given aircraft are strictly regulated by EASA. The requirements are described in CS-25 (Certification Specification 25) for transport aircraft MTOW > 5 700 kg and in CS-23 for smaller aircraft MTOW < 5 700 kg.

Note: This is not the full description of classification of CS-23 and CS-25 aircraft but it is enough for us to know.

For the CS-25 category, the maximum positive and minimum negative limitation of load factor is:
nMAX = 2.5; nMIN = -1 in clean configuration (high lift devices not extended)

The CS-23 category includes three subparts:

Normal [N] nMAX = 3.8 nMIN = -1.52
Utility [U] nMAX = 4.4 nMIN = -1.76
Aerobatic [A] nMAX ≥ 6

nMIN ≤ 3

If flaps are deployed nMAX = 2; nMIN = 0 are the required limits for both categories.

title: When a profile reaches the speed of sound, what kind of shock wave is produced at the point of maximum speed?
optionA: Mach shock wave
optionB: Oblique shock wave
optionC: Straight/right shock wave
optionD: Conformal shockwave
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
During high-speed flight, significant changes occur in the flow and pressure distributions around the aircraft, which result in a loss of lift and an increase in drag. This is caused by the formation of shock waves, which adversely affect the stability and control characteristics of the aircraft.

The speed of sound is defined as the rate at which small pressure disturbances are propagated through the air, which is solely a function of air temperature.

THE DEVELOPMENT OF SHOCK WAVES
When aircraft fly through the air, every part of them sets up tiny pressure disturbances, which radiate outward at the speed of sound in all directions.

As Mach number increases, the flow over the wing continues to accelerate and eventually reaches a sonic value at a particular point on the wing, normally the point of maximum thickness.

With increasing Mach number, this point grows into an area of supersonic flow, so the air moving over the upper surface will be moving rearward faster than the pressure disturbances can move forward. These disturbances consequently pile up on each other and form a shock wave.

The shock wave acts perpendicular, or normal, to the surface, and is more commonly referred to as a normal shock wave. Notably, this occurs where the flow changes from supersonic back to subsonic.

title: What is the effect on an aeroplane's characteristics of extending Fowler flaps to their fully extended position?
optionA: C<sub>D</sub> remains constant for a given angle of attack.
optionB: wing area and camber increase.
optionC: wing area remains constant but camber increases.
optionD: C<sub>LMAX</sub> occurs at a higher angle of attack.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The Fowler flap moves rearwards and then down, initially giving an increase in wing area and then an increase in camber. The Fowler flap may be slotted.

title: On the base leg of a a circuit to land, the pilot is distracted by the warning of an alternator failure, but elects to continue the approach, immediately turning onto final. During the final turn the pilot feels that the aircraft bank angle is difficult to maintain, that the ailerons and elevator are lighter and NOT as effective as usual. These symptoms are most likely related to…
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: a sign of loose control lines.
optionB: caused by the engine losing power.
optionC: an indication of a control restriction.
optionD: a warning of an incipient stall.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
When the lift developed by an aeroplane wing is no longer sufficient to sustain the mass of the aeroplane in flight, in the configuration being considered, the wing is stalled.

A stall is caused by airflow separation. Separation can occur when either the boundary layer has insufficient kinetic energy or the adverse pressure gradient becomes too great.

STALLING ANGLE OF ATTACK
At a constant mass and air density, the coefficient of lift (CL), and consequently the total amount of lift, is dependent on the angle of attack.

Graphically, lift increases almost linearly from an angle of attack of 0º to 4º, and then at an increasing rate to 15º. Lift cannot be obtained without incurring the penalty of drag.

At a specific angle of attack, depending on circumstances, the lift generated is insufficient to sustain the aircraft in level flight. The angle of attack at which this occurs is the stalling angle or critical angle and is the point at which CLMAX is attained. An aeroplane will not stall unless the critical angle is exceeded.

The aeroplane may be considered stalled when the behaviour of the aeroplane gives a clear distinctive indication of an unacceptable nature to the pilot that the aeroplane is stalled.

Acceptable indications of a stall, occurring either individually or in combination are:
a. A nose-down pitch that cannot be readily arrested.
b. Buffeting, of a magnitude and severity that is a strong and effective deterrent to further speed reduction.
c. The pitch control reaches the aft stop and no further increase in pitch attitude occurs when the control is held full aft for a short time before recovery is initiated.
d. Unresponsive flight controls.

title: Which situation will be taken into account when defining V<sub>MCL</sub>? The aeroplane trimmed for...
optionA: approach with all engines operating.
optionB: take-off with all engines operating.
optionC: take-off with one engine out.
optionD: approach with one engine out.
explanationTotal:
VMCL, the minimum control speed during approach and landing with all engines operating, is the calibrated airspeed at which, when the critical engine is suddenly made inoperative, it is possible to maintain control of the airplane with that engine still inoperative and maintain straight flight with an angle of bank of not more than 5°.
VMCL must be established with:
  • the airplane in the most critical configuration for approach and landing with all engines operating.
  • the most unfavorable CG.
  • the airplane trimmed for approach with all engines operating.
