  • the most unfavorable weight.
  • for propeller airplanes, the propeller of the inoperative engine in the position it achieves without pilot action and go-around power or thrust setting on the operating engines(s).
In demonstrating VMCL:
  • the rudder force may not exceed 150 lb.
  • the airplane may not exhibit hazardous flight characteristics or require exceptional piloting skill, alertness, or strength.
  • lateral control must be sufficient to roll the airplane, from an initial condition of steady flight, through an angle of 20° in the direction necessary to initiate a turn away from the inoperative engine(s), in not more than 5 seconds.

title: Consider a fixed-pitch propeller aeroplane at take-off. When the aeroplane accelerates during the take-off run phase, the blade angle of attack will (1) _____ and the thrust produced by the propeller will (2) _____.
optionA: (1) increase; (2) increase
optionB: (1) decrease; (2) increase
optionC: (1) increase; (2) decrease
optionD: (1) decrease; (2) decrease
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The figure shows the changes that take place as the aircraft speed (TAS) increases. Assuming that propeller RPM and blade pitch angle remains constant, at a low speed the angle of attack will be large, giving a lot of thrust. Alpha will reduce with increasing speed and at about 4 degrees the blade will be operating at its best lift/drag ratio, i.e. the propeller is achieving its highest efficiency.

Higher speeds (maybe in a dive) will reduce the blade angle of attack to its zero lift value of about minus 4 degrees. At this point, the propeller will be producing zero thrust.

The thrust that is produced by the propeller depends on the angle of attack of the blade. The angle of attack of the blade depends in turn on the airspeed and induced airflow through the propeller. At low airspeeds the angle of attack will be large, near the stall, and thrust will be at its maximum. As forward speed increases, the angle of attack decreases and thrust reduces.

That means that the maximum thrust produced by a propeller driven aircraft, also occurs at zero forward airspeed and reduces with forward speed.

A fixed propeller can only have one optimum combination of forward airspeed and engine RPM and only one optimum propeller efficiency. At all other combinations it operates less efficiently. This effect can be offset to an extent by using a variable pitch propeller, coarsening the blade angle at higher speeds to maintain the optimum angle of attack.

title: Whilst in straight and level flight with the autopilot engaged, the aircraft begins to pick up some autopilot-induced oscillations. Which of the following will happen if the pilot does not intervene?
optionA: Dutch Roll.
optionB: Fuel starvation.
optionC: Unwanted pitch and/or roll.
optionD: Engine stall.
explanationTotal:
Note: This question is based on incomplete feedback, so may be slightly different than seen in the exam. Please put any further exam feedback you can remember in the comments or send by email to info@atplquestions.com, thank you very much.

Pilot-induced oscillations are where the pilot "over-controls" the aircraft, and therefore, will not only correct for an incorrect attitude, altitude, speed, etc., but will over-correct, and go through the equilibrium, ending up in the opposite scenario. This can often be seen on a pilot's first few ILS approaches when they begin to get very accurate near the runway, or during the flare, when pilots sometimes over-flare, and end up porpoising (up and down) along the runway. It is very common in many stages of flight, and something to try and avoid.

Autopilots can perform self-induced oscillations too, if they are not quick enough to catch the overcontrolling with their feedback loop, for example. This could be in pitch, or in yaw and roll (which could lead to Dutch roll).

This question is very vague, it does not tell us what oscillations we are feeling, nor much about how they have been formed, so we have chosen the most vague answer that is correct (it could also be Dutch roll, but we would have to make a lot more assumptions, so we think that "Dutch roll" is not as correct).

title: Icing on the wing can lead to the absence of a stall warning by...
optionA: decreasing the critical angle of attack.
optionB: increasing the critical angle of attack.
optionC: freezing the device in place preventing it from moving at high angles of attack.
optionD: causing the stall warning device to deflect in the opposite direction thus causing no stall warning.
explanationTotal: Icing can reduce total available lift by as much as 50 percent. With less lift, you need a higher angle of attack (AOA) to maintain level flight, which means you will be cruising closer to stall. Additionally, the ice causes the wing to stall at a lower AOA. That means the plane will stall before your stall horn goes off, since it’s set to a different AOA. Alpha is a necessary input for many stall warning systems. With icing, a wing will stall before the angle of attack reaches the value at which these warnings are triggered.

title: Which of the following statements is correct regarding the speeds VMO and VC?
optionA: V<sub>MO</sub> must be equal to V<sub>C</sub>.
optionB: V<sub>MO</sub> must be equal to or greater than V<sub>C</sub>.
optionC: V<sub>MO </sub>must NOT be greater than V<sub>C</sub>.
optionD: V<sub>MO</sub> must NOT be greater than 0.8 x V<sub>C</sub>.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
Learning Objective 081.06.02.01.05: Describe the relationship between VMO or VNE and VC.

All aircraft have limitations to their speed and the loads that they can sustain at those speeds. In particular, we have to know about the load/speed diagram for CS-25 (large) aeroplanes. There is a diagram for the maximum load factors (positive and negative) that an aircraft can sustain, whether that limit was to do with a stall limit, or a structural load factor limit. There is also a limiting gust envelope diagram for the maximum gusts an aircraft must be able to handle at various speeds, see annex above.

This creates some set design speeds for the aircraft, such as VA, VB, VC and VD.

  • VA - Manoeuvring Speed, the speed where the aircraft will stall at exactly the limiting load factor (2.5 G for CS-25 aircraft).
  • VB - Design Speed for Maximum Gust Intensity, the speed where an aircraft must be able to manage a gust of up to 66 fps.
  • VC - Design Cruise Speed, the maximum speed an aircraft is able to cruise at, giving sufficient safety margin to VD, and means the aircraft will not exceed VD if a particular disturbance occurs when cruising at VC. It is also the point where gusts of up to 50 fps should be managed by the airframe. VC should not be more than 0.8 x VD.
  • VD - Design Dive Speed, the maximum speed that the aircraft can handle in a dive, often limited by vibrations, buffet or flutter. This is the absolute speed limit of the airframe, and the aircraft should be able to manage 25 fps gusts at this speed.
To keep the aircraft within safe operation, the VMO (maximum operating speed) must be kept below VC. This is still very fast, and should not be exceeded in normal operations.

title: Aircraft certified under CS-23 and CS-25 must be able to show that they are able to retain control at and just after the critical angle of attack. Which of the following design features may influence this controllability and why?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Aft mounted engines, as an increase in thrust produces a nose down moment.
optionB: Position of horizontal stabiliser, e.g. a T-tail makes it harder to recover from a stall.
optionC: Supercritical wings increase nose up tendency in a stall.
optionD: Using roll spoilers increases the chance of aileron reversal near the stall.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Note: The feedback for this question is quite limited, and there is another option that is very close to being correct, but we are happy with our choice of correct answer. Please send us any further exam feedback you have about this question, thank you!

The vast majority of aircraft are never meant to stall, but it is always a possibility, no matter how many measures the designers put in to stop it occurring. This is why aircraft must be made to be controllable and predictable at stalling. In particular, we want the aircraft to have a nose down moment at the stall, and we want the controls to be effective at the stall.

One way the controls could become ineffective at the stall is with a T-tail horizontal stabiliser design. Whilst a T-tail design usually takes the horizontal stabiliser away from the wake of the main wing, when the aircraft is pitched at the stalling angle of attack, often the horizontal stabiliser is in the zone of stalled airflow, where little to no lift can be gained. This is called a "deep stall" (or a super-stall) and makes the elevators quite useless, and even an all moving tailplane (which you would not usually find in a T-tail configuration) would be quite useless too.

This is why most T-tail aircraft have a stall prevention device fitted called a stick pusher, which will put in a very strong pitch down control force just before the "deep stall" is reached.

As we have already mentioned, there is another option present that is very close to correct...

  • "Aft mounted engines, as an increase in thrust produces a nose down moment."
    • We call this a stabilising thrust line, because the addition of thrust helps us gain airspeed by causing a pitch down moment as well as an increase in thrust. In our opinion it would be useful to have during stall. However, the controllability during and after the stall would not strictly be affected by this, only the ability to recover from the stall. If you interpret the question slightly differently, then this could be considered correct, but we would say it is not quite correct.
  • "Position of horizontal stabiliser, e.g. a T-tail makes it harder to recover from a stall."
    • As discussed above, this makes a huge difference to stall controllability, especially due to the ability of a T-tail design to go into a "deep stall".
  • "Supercritical wings increase nose up tendency in a stall."
    • Supercritical wings do stall slightly differently (much faster and less gradual), but this does not really relate to a nose up tendency. Also, this option does not really answer the question above, so it is incorrect.
  • "Using roll spoilers increases the chance of aileron reversal near the stall."
    • This one filled in incomplete feedback. Do not expect it in the exam. Aileron reversal (low speed) can happen if an aileron drops near the stall, increasing the AoA passed the stalling AoA and causing a reversal of the requested turn direction.

title: Assuming constant IAS, when an aeroplane leaves ground effect:
optionA: the effective angle of attack increases.
optionB: induced drag decreases.
optionC: downwash does not change.
optionD: downwash increases.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The decreased downwash upon entering the ground effect gives an increase in the effective angle of attack and thus reduces the induced angle of attack (see illustration). A smaller induced angle of attack means a decrease in induced drag. When leaving ground effect it's the other way around.

title: An aeroplane's pitch angle is defined as the angle between its:
optionA: longitudinal axis and the horizontal plane.
optionB: speed vector and its longitudinal axis.
optionC: lateral axis and the horizontal plane.
optionD: speed vector and the horizontal plane.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

Angle of attack is the difference between pitch attitude and flight path angle.
It is defined as the angle between the chord of an airfoil and the relative wind.
Flight path angle is the angle between the horizon and the flight path. Also called climb or descent angle.
Pitch angle is the angle between the horizon and longitudinal axis of the aircraft, it is equal to Flight path angle + Angle of attack.

title:
Which statement about propeller icing is correct?

I. Propeller icing increases blade element drag and reduces blade element lift.
II. Propeller icing reduces propeller efficiency.
optionA: I is correct, II is incorrect.
optionB: I is incorrect, II is correct.
optionC: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
optionD: I is correct, II is correct.
explanationTotal:
Ice contamination on the propeller has the same effect as ice on the wings, in that both reduce the efficiency of the airfoils. Leading edge ice on the propeller reduces the generated thrust in the same way the lift of the wing is reduced; by creating turbulent air flow. Therefore, statement 1 is correct.
In the same way, as the drag of an ice contaminated airplane increases, the resisting force on the propeller increases for a given rpm and blade angle. Ice separating from the propeller blades, as well as vibration due to propeller imbalance, may cause damage to the airplane structure. Since ice on the propeller blades reduces the available thrust, extra power may be required from the engine to overcome the increased drag, decreasing propeller efficiency. Therefore, statement 2 is correct.

title: During a take-off roll with a strong crosswind from the left, a four-engine jet aeroplane with wing-mounted engines experiences an engine failure. The failure of which engine will cause the greatest control problem?
optionA: The left outboard engine.
optionB: The right inboard engine.
optionC: The left inboard engine.
optionD: The right outboard engine.
explanationTotal:
During a crosswind take-off, an airplane tends to weathercock into wind (yaw into the wind), due to the wind acting on the fin which produces a yaw moment.

In this case, with a crosswind from the left, the aircraft will tend to yaw left.
  • If a right engine fails, the left side will produce much more thrust than the right side, resulting in a right-yaw. This will oppose the yaw-left moment.
  • If a left engine fails, the right side will produce more thrust than the left side, resulting in a left-yaw. This will add to the left-yaw moments.

The engine's distance to the CG is greatest for outboard engines, which means that they have the largest moment arms. The loss of an outboard engine will result in the strongest yaw tendency.

Therefore, the failure of the outboard engine on the windward side of the airplane is the most difficult to counteract.

title: The load factor is less than 1 (one):
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: in steady wings level horizontal flight.
optionB: during a steady horizontal turn.
optionC: during recovery after a wings level stall.
optionD: when lift is less than weight.
explanationTotal:
Load factor is known as the lift divided by the weight:

n = L / W

During straight and level flight, load factor is equal to 1 as the lift will equal the weight of the aircraft.

To have a load factor of less than 1, lift would have be less than the weight.

The other answers are incorrect because:

  • In a turn the load factor is increased because the lift will have to higher than the weight to compensate for the bank angle.
  • In steady level horizontal flight the load factor is 1.
  • During a recovery from a stall lift, the aircraft would have to pitch up from a dive, therefore the lift has to exceed the weight.

title: How are the angle of attack and the margin to the stall affected by the extension of spoilers?
optionA: Angle of attack increases: margin to stall increases
optionB: Angle of attack is unaffected; margin to stall reduces
optionC: Angle of attack decreases; margin to stall increases
optionD: Angle of attack is unaffected; margin to stall is unaffected
explanationTotal:
Spoilers are aerodynamic surfaces that exist on the top surface of some wings, and are used for many reasons. They are primarily used to increase drag and "dump" lift. (If they are just for drag then they are called speedbrakes, but aircraft manufacturers do blur these distinctions).

They are called spoilers because they "spoil" the airflow, sticking up into the airflow, causing a lift reduction similar to an up-going aileron and a similar drag increase to that of a split flap.

Of course, the spoiled airflow is not as effective at producing lift, and the stall speed therefore increases. This means that the margin to the stall immediately reduces, as the aircraft is flying closer to the new stall speed. There is, however, a counter-intuitive rise in the critical angle of attack, but that is not asked about in this question.

The question does ask about the angle of attack of the wing. As the angle of attack is the angle between the incoming airflow and the chord line, there is actually no change to the angle of attack. The chord line is the straight line between the wing's leading edge and trailing edge, and is not changed by extension of spoilers. Of course, after some time with spoilers extended, the angle of attack may change depending on pilot or autopilot input to remain level, descend, etc., but initially, the angle of attack is unaffected by spoiler extension.

title: You are flying a crop duster in the utility category with a VSO of 45 kts and a VS1 of 58 kts. What is the VA speed?
optionA: 66 kt
optionB: 113 kt
optionC: 122 kt
optionD: 94 kt
explanationTotal:
VA = VS1 x √limiting load

EASA CS23, load limits for utility:

Maximum +4.4g
Minimum -1.76g

  • VA = 58 x √4.4
  • VA = 122 kt

title: As well as VLE, sometimes an aircraft may have another limitation speed called VLO. This will be implemented if at the (1) _____ speed, the aerodynamic loads could make operation of the (2) _____ unsafe.
optionA: (1) V<sub>LO</sub> ; (2) landing gear
optionB: (1) V<sub>LE</sub> ; (2) landing gear
optionC: (1) V<sub>LO</sub> ; (2) leading edge devices
optionD: (1) V<sub>LE</sub> ; (2) leading edge devices
explanationTotal:
Learning Objective 081.06.01.03.01: Describe the reason for flap/landing gear limitations. Define ‘VLO’. Define ‘VLE’.

VLO and VLE refer to landing gear:

VLE - Maximum landing gear extended speed. The maximum IAS that should be flown if the landing gear are extended.
VLO - Maximum landing gear operating speed. The maximum IAS at which the landing gear should be extended or retracted (sometimes there are separate speed for extension and retraction).

The operation of the landing gear is often more susceptible to input from the aerodynamic loads than when the gear is fully extended and locked. In particular, the gear doors may have to move within the airflow, or the gear may have to be raised or lowered into the oncoming airflow.

For example, in the common multi-engine trainer, the DA42, the nose gear extends backwards, and raises forwards into the airflow. The VLE and VLO (extend) are the same, but the VLO (retract) is around 40 kts lower, as the aerodynamic loads would be working against the hydraulic system when raising into the airflow.

title: For a fixed-pitch propeller in flight at a given TAS, the blade angle of attack will:
optionA: remain constant if RPM increases.
optionB: remain constant if RPM decreases.
optionC: increase if RPM increases.
optionD: decrease if RPM increases.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
The blade angle of a fixed-pitch propeller is constant, but the helix angle and the angle of attack will vary according to its forward speed. To ensure its efficient operation the blade angle of attack of a fixed-pitch propeller must be close to the optimum and is that which produces the greatest excess of horizontal lift (thrust) over drag.
Figure 1 shows a “fixed pitch” propeller at constant RPM. Increasing TAS (during take-off, for example) decreases the angle of attack of the propeller. Figure 2 shows a “fixed pitch” propeller at a constant TAS. Increasing RPM increases the angle of attack of the propeller.

title: An aircraft decelerates from 1.4 V<sub>S</sub> to 1.05 V<sub>S</sub>. What is the percentage increase in the lift coefficient (expressed as a percentage of C<sub>LMAX</sub>)?
explanationTotal:
Lift = 1/2 x ρ x V2 x CL x S

As weight is to be assumed constant, lift should be constant as well.
VS2CL = VS2CLMAX

(1) Start by finding the percentage of CLMAX at 1.4 VS:
VS2CL = VS2CLMAX
(1.4VS)2 CL = VS2CLMAX
Cancel "VS" on both sides:
(1.4)2 CL = CLMAX
CL = 1 ÷ (1.4)2 CLMAX
CL = 0.51 CLMAX ⇒ 51%

(1) Find the percentage of CLMAX at 1.05 VS:
VS2CL = VS2CLMAX
(1.05VS)2 CL = VS2CLMAX
Cancel "VS" on both sides:
(1.05)2 CL = CLMAX
CL = 1 ÷ (1.05)2 CLMAX
CL = 0.91 CLMAX ⇒ 91%

As percentage of CLMAX, the increase equals: 40%.

title: By what percentage does the lift increase in a level turn at 45° angle of bank, compared with straight and level flight?
optionA: 52%
optionB: 31%
optionC: 41%
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
In level flight, any turn will be coordinated or uncoordinated. A coordinated turn is one in which the only acceleration is along the normal axis of the airplane, towards the center of the turn, and the angle of bank is precisely correct for the aircraft speed and the radius of turn. If not all these factors are present, the turn will be uncoordinated and there will be a lateral acceleration either towards or away from the center of the turn. The total lift of a balanced turn provides the centripetal force and the force that opposes the mass of the airplane.
If there is acceleration towards the center of the turn the airplane is slipping and if it is away from the center of the turn the airplane is skidding. Either condition will be indicated on the turn and slip indicator. An overbanked airplane will slip into the turn and requires an increase of speed or a reduction in bank angle to correct this condition. An underbanked airplane will skid out of the turn, which requires a decreased speed or an increased bank angle to correct this condition. These are indicated on the turn and slip indicator by the needle one-way and the ball the other.
To maintain altitude and airspeed when executing a turn both the angle of attack and the thrust have to be increased above their level flight values.

In a turn, the load factor (n) is defined by:
n = L/W = 1/ cos Φ

On a 45° bank turn, to maintain the same lift as in straight and level flight,

L/W = 1/cos 45
L = W * 1/ cos⁡ 45
L= 1.41 * W
Lift must be increased 1.41 times, or 41%.

title: In a coordinated banked turn, the centripetal force is equal to...
optionA: L x sin(bank angle)
optionB: W x sin(bank angle)
optionC: L x cos(bank angle)
optionD: W x cos(bank angle)
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
In a turn, the lift vector of the aircraft is moved from vertical to being up and towards the direction of turn, as shown in the diagram above. That means that some of the lift goes into becoming a "turning force", sometimes called the "turning lift", but the technical name for it is centripetal force. Centripetal force is the force towards the centre of a circle that must be exerted to make an object turn.

In this case, you can see in the diagram above that the lift vector is split into 2 components, one creating "effective lift" to counter the aircraft's weight, and the other creating centripetal force to cause the turn. The centripetal force is the opposite side to the angle, so using trigonometry, the centripetal force is Lift x sin(Bank Angle). Bank angle is shown as Φ (Greek capital letter Phi) in the diagram, as is common for bank angles.

Notice also that the amount of total lift required to maintain height (effective lift = weight) is more in the turn, as the total lift vector is being split. This is asked about in many questions.

title:
Which of these statements about a steady subsonic flow are correct or incorrect?

1. The static pressure decreases as the streamlines diverge.
2. The velocity increases as the streamlines diverge.
optionA: 1 is correct, 2 is incorrect.
optionB: 1 is incorrect, 2 is incorrect.
optionC: 1 is correct, 2 is correct.
optionD: 1 is incorrect, 2 is correct.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
To understand the venturi effect, we must first introduce two conditions: The conservation of mass (Continuity Equation) and the Conservation of Energy (Bernoulli’s Theorem).

Conservation of Mass (Continuity Equation)

The mass of air entering the pipe, in each unit of time, equals the mass of air leaving the pipe, in the same unit of time. The mass flow through the pipe must remain constant.

The mass air flow 'm' is the product of the density, the area and the velocity:

m= ρ*A*V

Continuity equation:

m1= m2= m3= ρ1* A1* V1= ρ2* A2* V2= ρ3* A3* V3=constant

The continuity equation explains the relationship between velocity and cross-sectional area: The speed is inversely proportional to the cross-sectional area.

Conservation of Energy (Bernoulli’s Theorem)

The total energy of an airstream comes in two forms: potential energy (static pressure) and kinetic energy (dynamic pressure).
The total pressure of the airstream is the sum of the static pressure and the dynamic pressure and must remain constant, according to the law of conservation of energy.
Thus, an increase in one form of pressure, must result in a decrease in the other.

Dynamic pressure (q) is expressed by:

q= 1/2* ρ* V2

Assuming the total pressure to be constant, the static pressure and the dynamic pressure vary inversely: If one increases the other decreases and vice-versa.
As an airfoil (wing) moves through the air, varying changes in velocity occur on its surfaces. Air particles move around it in specific trajectories. These trajectories are called streamlines.
Diverging streamlines mean a decrease in airspeed.
Converging streamlines imply an increase in airspeed.

In Conclusion:

With an increase in section area (from station 2 to station 3), flow speed decreases, decreasing dynamic pressure (streamlines diverge). If dynamic pressure decreases, static pressure increases. Statement 1 is therefore incorrect.
With an increase in section area (from station 2 to station 3), flow speed decreases, decreasing dynamic pressure (streamlines diverge). Statement 2 is therefore incorrect.

title: When is a turn co-ordinated?
optionA: If no rudder deflection is required during the turn.
optionB: When the longitudinal axis of the aeroplane at the CG is tangential to the flight path.
optionC: If no aileron deflection is required during the turn.
optionD: When only minor elevator pull force is required.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
A co-ordinated turn means that the aircraft is flying a perfect circle (flight path) when looking from above or below. The tangent (longitudinal axis of the aeroplane) is a straight line that touches the circle at one point. As the tangent passes through the point, the tangent line is "going in the same direction" as the curve and is perpendicular to line representing the radius at that point. Imagine or try to visualize, that during a co-ordinated turn, the heading permanently changes and therefore the tangent will move around the circle.

title:
Which statement is correct?

I. Stick force per g is independent of altitude.
II. Stick force per g increases when the centre of gravity moves forward.
optionA: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
optionB: I is correct, II is correct.
optionC: I is incorrect, II is correct.
optionD: I is correct, II is incorrect.
explanationTotal:
1. At a constant IAS, stick force per g reduces with altitude, as aerodynamic damping reduces with the increasing TAS
2. When C of G moves forward stability increases and stick forces increase.

title: A transport aircraft must display adequate stability in each of the three axes to comply with CS 25 standards. What is the main reason behind this requirement?
optionA: To simplify aircraft design.
optionB: To prevent it from entering dangerous situations potentially unrecoverable.
optionC: To reduce fuel consumption.
optionD: To decrease the aircraft's takeoff distance.
explanationTotal:
CS 25.171 General

The aeroplane must be longitudinally, directionally and laterally stable in accordance with the provisions of CS 25.173 to 25.177. In addition, suitable stability and control feel (static stability) is required in any condition normally encountered in service, if flight tests show it is necessary for safe operation.

Stability is the tendency of an aircraft to return to a steady state of flight (equilibrium) without any help from the pilot, after being disturbed by an external force.

An aircraft must have the following qualities:

  • Adequate stability to maintain a uniform flight condition
  • The ability to recover from various disturbing influences
  • Sufficient stability to minimize the workload of the pilot
  • Proper response to the controls so that it may achieve its design performance with adequate manoeuvrability

title: Which definition of propeller parameters is correct?
optionA: Helix angle is the angle between the actual path of the propeller and the propeller axis.
optionB: Blade angle is the angle between the blade chord line and the propeller axis.
optionC: Angle of attack is the angle between the blade chord line and the propeller vertical plane.
optionD: Geometric pitch is the theoretical distance a propeller would advance in one revolution at zero blade angle of attack.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The geometric pitch is the distance the propeller would travel forward in one complete revolution if it were moving through the air at the blade angle.

title:
Which of these statements about VMCG determination are correct or incorrect?

I. VMCG may be determined using both lateral and directional control.
II. During VMCG determination, the lateral deviation from the runway centreline may be not more than half the distance between the runway centreline and runway edge.
optionA: I is correct, II is incorrect.
optionB: I is correct, II is correct.
optionC: I is incorrect, II is correct.
optionD: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
explanationTotal:
According to CS 25.149 and CS 23.149 - Minimum Control Speed:

Minimum Control Speed on the ground (VMCG) is defined as the calibrated airspeed during the take-off run at which, when the critical engine is suddenly made inoperative, it is possible to maintain control of the aeroplane using the primary aerodynamic control (rudder control) alone (without the use of nosewheel steering), as limited by 667 N of force (150 lbf), and the lateral control to the extent of keeping the wings level to enable the take-off to be safely continued using normal piloting skill.

In the determination of VMCG, assuming that the path of the aeroplane accelerating with all engines operating is along the centreline of the runway, its path from the point at which the critical engine is made inoperative to the point at which recovery to a direction parallel to the centreline is completed, may not deviate more than 9.1 m (30 ft) laterally from the centreline at any point.

title: If the aircraft's mass changes, the V<sub>MD</sub> (1)_____ and the induced drag (2)_____.
optionA: (1) varies; (2) remains constant.
optionB: (1) remains constant; (2) remains costant.
optionC: (1) remains constant; (2) varies.
optionD: (1) varies; (2) varies.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
For instance, as the weight of the aircraft decreases, it will require less lift (resulting in a lower coefficient of lift, CL). This, in turn, will lead to a reduction in induced drag. Consequently, the total drag experienced by the aircraft will be diminished, causing the VMD to occur at a lower indicated airspeed (IAS).

title:
Refer to figure.
Which line in the annexed CM versus angle of attack graph shows a statically stable aeroplane?
optionA: Line 1.
optionB: Line 3.
optionC: Line 4.
optionD: Line 2.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Static longitudinal stability depends upon the relationship of angle of attack and pitching moment (CM).

A variation of CG position can cause large changes in the static longitudinal stability. In the conventional airplane configuration, the large changes in stability with CG variation are primarily due to the large changes in the wing contribution. If the incidence of all surfaces remains fixed, the effect of CG position on static longitudinal stability is typified by the chart in figure 1:

As the CG is gradually moved aft, the airplane static stability decreases, then becomes neutral then unstable. The CG position which produces zero slope and neutral static stability is referred to as the “neutral point”. The neutral point defines the most aft CG position without static instability.

Positive static stability is indicated by the curve with negative slope. Moving the CG forward, will increase static longitudinal stability and this is represented by a (steeper) negative slope.

Neutral static stability would be the result if the curve had zero slope. If neutral stability existed, the airplane could be disturbed to some higher or lower lift coefficient without change in pitching moment coefficient.

An airplane which demonstrates a positive slope of the CM versus CL curve would be unstable.

title: On a wing fitted with a "Fowler" type trailing edge flap, the "Full extended" position will produce:
optionA: an unaffected C<sub>D</sub>, at a given angle of attack.
optionB: an increase in wing area and camber.
optionC: an unaffected wing area and increase in camber.
optionD: an increase in wing area only.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The fowler flap is a construction that normally is not noticeable when it is retracted. It forms part of the wing. If the fowler flap is extended, it will move outwards and then downwards, increasing wing area and camber, increasing CL and CD. Due to the increased wing area, the plane produces even more lift and is therefore able to fly at a lower angle of attack or lower speed. It is the only flap that increases wing area and is therefore the most effective flap system.

title: The wing angle of incidence usually varies from root to tip. This is called wing washout and its purpose is...
optionA: to increase lift at the tip, thus equalising lift across the wing.
optionB: to ensure that stall occurs at the root first, maximising controllability.
optionC: to reduce induced drag caused by wing tip vortices.
optionD: to reduce lift at the tip, thus equalising lift across the wing.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
In some wing designs, separation tends to occur first in the region of the tip, reducing lift in those areas. If an actual wing were allowed to stall in this way, stalling would give aileron buffet and perhaps violent wing drop.

To give favourable stall characteristics, a tapered wing must be modified using one or more of the following:

Geometric twist (washout), a decrease in incidence from root to tip. This decreases the angle of attack at the tip, and the root will tend to stall first.

The aerofoil section may be varied throughout the span such that sections with greater thickness and camber are located near the tip. The higher CLMAX of such sections delays stall so that the root will tend to stall first.

title: The effect of a ventral fin on the static stability of an aeroplane is as follows: (1=longitudinal, 2=lateral, 3=directional)
optionA: 1: no effect, 2: negative, 3: positive.
optionB: 1: positive, 2: negative, 3: negative.
optionC: 1: negative, 2: positive, 3: positive.
optionD: 1: no effect, 2: positive, 3: negative.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

To overcome the instability in the fuselage it is possible to incorporate into the overall design dorsal or ventral fins. A dorsal fin is a small aero foil, of very low aspect ratio, mounted on top of the fuselage near the rear. A ventral fin is mounted below.

If the aircraft is yawed to the right, the dorsal and ventral fins will create a side force to the right. The line of action of this force is well aft of the aircraft CG, giving a yawing moment to the left (a stabilizing effect). However, at small angles of yaw they are ineffective.

Dorsal and ventral fins become more effective at relatively high sideslip angles. Due to their low aspect ratio, they do not tend to stall at any sideslip angle which an aircraft is likely to experience in service.

While dorsal and ventral fins contribute positively to directional static stability, a dorsal fin contributes positively to lateral static stability, while a ventral fin is destabilizing in this mode and has no effect on longitudinal stability. It creates lift below CG in the direction of the roll.

title: Approximately how long does it take to fly a complete circle during a horizontal steady co-ordinated turn with a bank angle of 45° and a TAS of 380 kt?
optionA: 125 s.
optionB: 65 s.
optionC: 95 s.
explanationTotal:
Turn radius = V^2 /( g * tan(bank angle) )
V = velocity in m/s. To get m/s, multiply the speed in knots by 0.514
Turn radius = (380*03514)^2 / (9.81 * tan(45) = 3888.89 m

Circumference = 2 * π * r
Circumference = 2 * 3.14 * 3888.89 = 24422.17 m

380*0.514= 195.32 m/s
Time = distance / speed
Time = 24422.17 / 195.32 = 125 s

title: A crew plan for a full flap landing (30⁰) but, due to distraction, fail to extend flaps from the approach to the landing setting until a few seconds before touchdown. Which of the following statements is correct assuming the correct glidepath was flown to touchdown?
optionA: The aircraft is likely to float and touch down further along the runway.
optionB: There is no problem if the aircraft attitude is not changed.
optionC: There is less risk of a hard landing.
optionD: A go-around is unnecessary.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
Note: There are quite a few factors which affect an aircraft's landing performance and handling. The question and available options do not take into account these different factors. That is to say that the examiner has been very closed minded in writing this question, using a "tunnel vision" approach.

The current correct option is simply the only answer that makes any sense. It is the "most correct" out of a bad bunch, and in itself is arguable, but depending on the circumstances we have not been told, may be true, whereas the other answers are not true in any circumstance.

For a given runway length and airplane weight, selecting a greater flap setting will increase the wing’s effective camber and the lift coefficient, which reduces the stalling speed.
  • As a consequence, the take-off speeds are reduced (the same lift will be created at smaller air speed due to greater lift coefficient). This will reduce the take-off run.
  • Flap extension during landings provides several advantages by:
  • producing greater lift and permitting lower landing speed;
  • producing greater drag, permitting a steep descent angle without airspeed increase, therefore Reducing the length of the landing roll.

Therefore, the answer here is that using less flaps than expected will cause significantly less drag than expected, so the aircraft may float for a while longer, and therefore have a longer landing roll (that is assuming that the pilot rotates enough during the flare, which has not been specified in the question).

As mentioned above, none of the other answers could be correct:

  • There will be a large difference to the handling characteristics, even if the attitude remains the same.
  • There is arguably a higher risk of a hard landing due to the lower "cushioning" effect of the lower flap setting. This one takes longer to explain but most pilots know it naturally from experience.
  • A go-around is very much advised if you realise the flaps are incorrectly set at a low altitude where this cannot be fixed.

title: Flying in icing conditions may result in the stall warning system failing to trigger. This is due to the aeroplane stalling at a lower _____, because of premature boundary layer separation.
optionA: Angle of Attack
optionB: Attitude
optionC: Indicated Air Speed (IAS)
optionD: True Air Speed (TAS)
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The formation of ice and frost on the airframe will:
- modify the profile of the aerofoil.
- increase the roughness of the aircraft surface.
- increase the weight of the aircraft.

Ice will normally form on and behind the leading edges of wings and tailplane and can result in severe distortion of the leading edge profile. This will give a large increase in drag and a substantial decrease in CLMAX.

The skin friction drag will increase and the boundary layer will have an earlier separation, giving a reduced critical angle of attack.

The reduced CLMAX of the wing will give a higher stalling speed.

title: The centre of pressure of your wing moves. Which statement is correct?
optionA: Movement of the centre of pressure affects pitch moment, but does not cause stabiliser movement.
optionB: The centre of pressure moving does not cause a pitch moment, even if the pilot doesn't correct.
optionC: Movement of the centre of pressure affects pitch moment and stabiliser movement.
optionD: Only movement of the centre of gravity affects stabiliser movement.
explanationTotal:
The pitching moment is the force that causes an aeroplane to move about its lateral axis. The force in this case is the lift and is applied through the CP. The arm is the distance of the CP from a specified position. As the CP moves with the changing angle of attack, the moment about a point will also change as the angle of attack changes.

On a cambered aerofoil even though the centre of pressure (CP) moves with the changing angle of attack, the lift is assumed to act through the aerodynamic centre (AC). The combination of the AC and the pitching moment coefficient are required for the analysis of the longitudinal stability of an aeroplane.

The tailplane is a major contributor to the longitudinal stability of an aeroplane. To maintain a particular angle of attack a specific deflection of the elevator is established that will maintain this requirement.
Thus, the movement of CP has an effect on both the pitching moment and stabilizer movement.

title:
Which of the following may cause buffeting when flying through Clear Air Turbulence?

1. Mach variations,
2. Precipitation distorting the airflow,
3. Reduced mach margins at altitude,
4. Autopilot disengagement.
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: 1 and 3
optionB: 3 and 4
optionC: 2 and 4
optionD: 1 and 2
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
In the same way that separated airflow prior to a low speed stall can cause airframe buffet, shock induced separation (shock stall) at high speed can also cause buffeting.

Aerodynamic buffet is a valuable stall warning, but it can damage the aircraft structure. Because of the higher dynamic pressure when an aircraft is operating in the transonic speed region, any shock induced buffet will have a greater potential for severe airframe damage.

High speed buffet must be completely avoided. The aircraft must therefore be operated in such a manner that a (safety) margin exists before aerodynamic buffet will occur.

If the variables which affect both high speed and low speed stall are considered it will be possible to identify the conditions under which buffeting will occur and a chart can be drawn to show all the factors involved.

This is called a ‘Buffet Onset’ chart which is used by flight crews to ensure their aircraft is always operated with a specified minimum buffet margin.

For any given combination of mass, center of gravity position and airspeed, the maximum operating altitude is that altitude at which a normal positive acceleration increment of 0.3 g, without exceeding the buffet onset boundary, is possible.

Note: Flying in turbulent conditions may cause sudden changes in speed and load factor. Looking at the buffet margin graph attached, we can conclude that both speed/mach variations and changes in load factor may bring the aircraft closer to one of the buffet margins.

title: What is the reason for the stagnation point at the leading-edge moving from the upper surface to the lower surface?
optionA: Due to reduced angle of attack.
optionB: Due to increased angle of attack.
optionC: Due to increased total pressure.
optionD: Due to ice on the leading edge.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The stagnation point is the point on the leading edge of the wing where the speed is reduced to zero, where the air comes to a complete standstill.

The point of lowest static pressure is equal to the point of highest dynamic pressure. The point along the profile where the speed is highest is along the upper side of the wing, and moves forward as the angle of attack increases, and backwards when the angle of attack decreases.

Therefore as the angle of attack increases:

  • The stagnation point will move down
  • The point of lowest static pressure moves forward

title: The pilots prepare and trim the aircraft for take-off, setting the trim for a CG position at 24% of the MAC. But due to an error, the real position of the CG is at 12% of the MAC. What could this cause?
optionA: The length of the runway may not be sufficient to take-off.
optionB: Large stick forces are required to achieve rotation.
optionC: Risk of over rotation that can lead to a tail strike.
optionD: Reduced climb performance after take-off.
explanationTotal:
When the CG is located further forward than intended, it shifts the aircraft's balance towards the nose. In this case, during takeoff, the aircraft would tend to have a tendency to pitch down, making it harder to rotate and lift off the runway. The pilots would need to apply significant backpressure on the control stick to raise the nose and achieve the desired rotation angle. This would result in large stick forces being required to initiate the rotation.

The risk of over rotation and tail strike (option c) would not be a concern in this scenario since the CG is forward rather than aft. The other options, a) and d), are not directly affected by the CG position and are not applicable in this situation.

Therefore, if the actual CG position is at 12% (as opposed to 24%) of the MAC, the correct answer would be b) Large stick forces are required to achieve rotation.

title: In a slipping turn (nose pointing outwards), compared with a co-ordinated turn, the bank angle (i) and the "ball" or slip indicator (ii) are respectively:
optionA: (i) too small, (ii) displaced towards the high wing.
optionB: (i) too large, (ii) displaced towards the low wing.
optionC: (i) too large, (ii) displaced towards the high wing.
optionD: (i) too small, (ii) displaced towards the low wing.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
A coordinated turn is a turn where there is no sideslip or skid, this is the most effective and therefore preferable way to turn.
In a coordinated turn, the turn and bank indicator in the plane shows the ball in the center.
If the turn is not coordinated, you’re either in a slip or a skid.
These two things are different and shall therefore be eliminated differently.

A slipping turn is a turn where the aircraft’s nose is outside of the turning radius and the tail is in the turn radius.
A slip is caused by using too much bank and too little rudder.
The slip indicator (ball) will point towards the low wing.

A skidding turn is a turn where the aircraft’s nose is inside of the turning radius and the tail is outside of the turn radius.
A skid is caused by using too much rudder and not enough bank.
The ball will point towards the high wing.

title: The lift to drag ratio is highest when the flight speed is:
optionA: At its maximum.
optionB: Equal to cruising speed.
optionC: Equal to best glide speed.
optionD: At its minimum.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The polar curve of an airfoil is the graphical relationship of the coefficients of lift and drag plotted against each other, the resulting graph is as shown in figure 1. It reveals that the total lift and total drag increase from point A to a maximum at point D, thus the angle of attack of the wings increases in the same manner. Therefore, the speed decreases from a maximum at point A to a minimum at point D.
Point B is the point at which a tangent from the origin touches the polar curve, which is at the point at which the total drag is minimum, the lift/drag ratio is maximum and the IAS in level flight is VMD. This is also the speed at which the longest glide distance will be achieved.

title:
Refer to annex.
A jet transport aeroplane with a mass of 100 tons carries out a steady level 50 degree bank turn at FL320. The buffet free speed range extends approximately from:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

    1. Enter the diagram at the 50º of bank mark in the bottom right hand corner of the diagram.

    2. Draw a line up to the 100 tones mass line.

    3. Draw a horizontal line to the left to cut the FL320 curve.

    4. At this point read off the Indicated Mach No on the bottom left hand scale of the diagram = 0.65. This is the point at which Low speed buffeting will begin.

The horizontal line we drew does not cut the FL320 line as it slopes down at the right-hand side of the Indicated Mach No scale. This means that we cannot determine the high-speed buffeting Mach No because it is off the scale. All we can say is that it will occur at a greater Mach No than the 0.84M where the scale ends.

Mach 0.84 is the aircraft’s MMO, which is the speed limit set to avoid High Speed Buffet.

title: In the transonic region, the coefficient of drag:
optionA: First decreases and then increases.
optionB: Increases with increasing Mach number.
optionC: Decreases with increasing Mach number.
optionD: Varies depending on Mach number.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

As you can see in the attached figure, with increasing mach number, in the transonic range, the coefficient first increases and then decreases.

title:
What is the effect of icing or other airframe contaminants on the value of CLMAX, stall speed, and critical angle of attack?
The CLMAX…
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: increases, stall speed increases, and critical angle of attack decreases.
optionB: increases, stall speed decreases, and critical angle of attack increases.
optionC: decreases, stall speed increases, and critical angle of attack decreases.
optionD: remains unchanged, stall speed increases, and critical angle of attack decreases.
explanationTotal:
Ice will normally form on and behind the leading edges of wings and tailplane and can result in severe distortion of the leading edge profile. This will give a large increase in drag and a substantial decrease in CLMAX.
The skin friction drag will increase and the boundary layer will have an earlier separation, giving a reduced critical angle of attack.
The reduced CLMAX of the wing will give a higher stalling speed.

title: The positive manoeuvring limit load factor for an aeroplane with flaps extended is:
explanationTotal:
EASA regulations for flight manoeuvring envelope
The load factor and speed limits for a given aircraft are strictly regulated by EASA. The requirements are described in CS-25 (Certification Specification 25) for transport aircraft MTOW > 5 700 kg and in CS-23 for smaller aircraft MTOW < 5 700 kg.

Note: This is not the full description of classification of CS-23 and CS-25 aircraft but it is enough for us to know.

For the CS-25 category, the maximum positive and minimum negative limitation of load factor is:
nMAX = 2.5; nMIN = -1 in clean configuration (high lift devices not extended)

The CS-23 category includes three subparts:

Normal [N] nMAX = 3.8 nMIN = -1.52
Utility [U] nMAX = 4.4 nMIN = -1.76
Aerobatic [A] nMAX ≥ 6

nMIN ≤ 3

If flaps are deployed nMAX = 2; nMIN = 0 are the required limits for both categories.

title: How does VA (EAS) alter when the aeroplane’s mass decreases by 19%?
optionA: No change.
optionB: 10% reduction.
optionC: 19% reduction.
optionD: 4.36% reduction.
explanationTotal:
VS1g NEW = VS1g OLD √(new weight / old weight)
VA = VS1g √n

Since the load factor “n” is the same for both weights, therefore we have New VA:
VA NEW = VA OLD √(new weight / old weight)
VA NEW = VA OLD √(0.81 / 1)
VA NEW = VA OLD 0.9 => This equals a 10% reduction.

title: A negative contribution to the static longitudinal stability of conventional jet transport aeroplanes is provided by:
optionA: a fixed elevator deflection.
optionB: the fuselage.
optionC: the tail.
optionD: a fixed trim position.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The longitudinal static stability of an airplane is its ability to return to its original pitch attitude with no outside assistance, after the disturbance that caused a nose-up or a nose-down movement has ceased.

The main factors that affect the longitudinal static stability are the design of the tail plane and the position of the CG relative to the position of the CP because they determine the direction of the additional wing-pitching moment.

The tail plane and elevators act as a horizontal stabilizer and the degree of positive longitudinal static stability that they provide is dependent on the size of the restoring moment they can attain; nevertheless, they do make the largest contribution to the longitudinal static stability. The tail plane design and the length of the moment arm from the tail plane CP to the CG condition the magnitude of the restoring moment.

The effect that the fuselage, and to a lesser extent wing-mounted the engine nacelles, has on the airplane’s longitudinal static stability is normally a destabilizing influence, a negative contribution. If the fuselage aerodynamic center is ahead of the wing aerodynamic center, the aerodynamic center of the wing–fuselage combination is further forward than it would normally be. If such is the case the aircraft CG will be further aft than is normal and the aircraft longitudinal static stability is decreased.

title: Rotation about the longitudinal axis of an aeroplane can be achieved by:
optionA: aileron deflection and/or rudder deflection.
optionB: symmetrical spoiler deflection and/or elevator deflection.
optionC: speed brake extension or wing flap deflection.
optionD: elevator deflection and/or slat extension.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.

The three axes of an airplane intersect at the center of gravity (CG) and are those about which an airplane moves in flight. They are the longitudinal, the lateral and the
normal axes. If the forces about any axis are not balanced there will be an angular acceleration and the airplane will rotate about that axis.

The horizontal straight line joining the most forward point of the fuselage of the airplane, the center of the nose, to the center of the most rearward point of the airplane’s fuselage is the longitudinal axis. It is often referred to as the roll axis because the airplane, in response to a control input by the pilot or as the result of an external disturbance, drops one wing and raises the other. Thus, it rotates or rolls about the longitudinal axis.

The flight controls enable the pilot to rotate the airplane about its three axes. The ailerons and the rudder cause the airplane to roll about its longitudinal axis, the elevators enable the airplane to pitch around its lateral axis and the rudder allows the airplane to yaw around its normal axis.

title: For a given RPM of a fixed pitch propeller, the blade angle of attack will:
optionA: remain constant when the TAS decreases.
optionB: remain constant when the TAS increases.
optionC: increase when the TAS decreases.
optionD: decrease when the TAS decreases.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
The blade angle of a fixed-pitch propeller is constant, but the helix angle and the angle of attack will vary according to its forward speed. To ensure its efficient operation the blade angle of attack of a fixed-pitch propeller must be close to the optimum and is that which produces the greatest excess of horizontal lift (thrust) over drag.
Figure 1 shows a “fixed pitch” propeller at constant RPM. Increasing TAS decreases the angle of attack of the propeller. Figure 2 shows a “fixed pitch” propeller at a constant TAS. Increasing RPM increases the angle of attack of the propeller.

title:
Given the following information, calculate the lift coefficient for an aircraft in straight and level flight, flying in a clean configuration just above the clean stall speed.

Density: 1.225 kg/m³
TAS: 73 kt
Mass: 7 300 kg
Wing area: 49 m2
G: 9.81 m/s2
optionA: C<sub>L</sub> = 0.045
optionB: C<sub>L</sub> = 0.17
optionC: C<sub>L</sub> = 0.45
optionD: C<sub>L</sub> = 1.69
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
This question requires use of the lift formula.

Lift = 1/2 x ρ x V2 x CL x S

Where;
ρ = Air Density,
V = Velocity (true air speed),
CL = Coefficient of Lift,
S = Wing Area.

To use the formula above, we need everything in the correct units. That means that we have to convert the velocity (TAS) from knots into m/s. As 1 knot is one nautical mile per hour, we have to multiply by the amount of metres in a nautical mile (1852) and then divide by the amount of seconds in an hour (3600).

Velocity = 73 kt x 1852/3600 = 37.55 m/s

We are going to rearrange the formula to find the CL, and that means we need to have a value for the lift produced by the wing. As we are in straight and level flight, Lift = Weight, so we just need the weight of the aircraft. Weight = Mass x Acceleration due to gravity (G). Therefore;

Lift = Weight = 7300 x 9.81 = 71613 N

Referring to the rearranged equation in the annex above;

CL = (2 x 71613) / (1.225 x (37.55)2 x 49) = 1.69

title: What is the most effective flap system?
optionA: Plain flap.
optionB: Single slotted flap.
optionC: Fowler flap.
optionD: Split flap.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

The fowler flap is a construction that normally is not noticeable when it is retracted. It forms part of the wing. If the fowler flap is extended, it will move outwards and then downwards, increasing wing area and camber, increasing CL and CD. Due to the increased wing area, the plane produces even more lift and is therefore able to fly at a lower angle of attack or lower speed. It is the only flap that increases wing area and is therefore the most effective flap system.

title: Stagnation Point moves up, what is the cause?
optionA: Lower Angle of Attack.
optionB: Higher Angle of Attack.
optionC: Ice on the leading edge.
optionD: Decrease in flap settings
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The stagnation point is the point on the leading edge of the wing where the speed is reduced to zero, where the air comes to a complete standstill.

The point of lowest static pressure is equal to the point of highest dynamic pressure. The point along the profile where the speed is highest is along the upper side of the wing, and moves forward as the angle of attack increases, and backwards when the angle of attack decreases.

Therefore as the angle of attack decreases:

  • The stagnation point will move up
  • The point of lowest static pressure moves aft
