Refer to figure.
The two aircraft have different designs, but are of similar size and passenger capacity. What could be said with regards to the certification of the 2 aeroplanes?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Aircraft A needs fly-by-wire flight controls to ensure that it will not over-rotate during the go-around.
optionB: Aircraft B requires fly-by-wire flight controls to avoid the stall from uncommanded pitch up during the go-around.
optionC: Aircraft B needs a stick pusher system to avoid reaching an angle of attack that is too high, due to the potential for unwanted behaviour in the stall.
optionD: Aircraft A requires a mach trimmer but aircraft B would be immune to mach tuck, so does not.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Note: Beware that the aircraft options in the exam may be flipped, in that aircraft 2 may have underslung engines, and aircraft 1 have tail mounted engines. We also only know 2 options, the correct one and one incorrect one, and the other two incorrect options are likely to be different in the exam.

DEEP STALL
A deep stall is a dangerous phenomenon that occurs when the turbulence created by the main wing encompasses the horizontal stabilizer of the aircraft, preventing the aircraft from recovering from the stall.

T-tail aircraft are most likely to have deep stall characteristics. When the main wing stalls, the stabilizer becomes ineffective because it is situated in the separated turbulent flow of the wing and sometimes the fuselage. This can lead to a very dangerous scenario where the aircraft can sit stable in the deep stall, with no control surface left working to get out of the situation.

A common way to prevent deep stall in these types of aircraft is a stick pusher device, which detects high angles of attack, approaching the stall, and instead of notifying the pilots of this (a stick shaker, stall warner, etc.), it actually pushes the stick forwards without any pilot intervention.

title: Positive static stability of an aeroplane means that following a disturbance from the equilibrium condition:
optionA: the initial tendency is to return towards its equilibrium condition.
optionB: the tendency is to move with an oscillatory motion of decreasing amplitude.
optionC: the initial tendency is to diverge further from its equilibrium condition.
optionD: the tendency is to move with an oscillatory motion of increasing amplitude.
explanationTotal:
An aircraft is in a state of equilibrium (trim) when the sum of all forces is zero and the sum of all moments is zero; there are no accelerations and the aircraft will continue in steady flight.

If equilibrium is disturbed by a gust, or deflection of the controls, the aircraft will experience accelerations due to an unbalance of moments or forces.
The type of static stability an aircraft possesses is defined by its initial tendency, following the removal of some disturbing force.

  • Positive static stability (or static stability) exists if an aircraft is disturbed from equilibrium and has the tendency to return to equilibrium.
  • Neutral static stability exists if an aircraft is subject to a disturbance and has neither the tendency to return nor the tendency to continue in the displacement direction.
  • Negative static stability (or static instability) exists if an aircraft tends to continue in the direction of disturbance.

title: While increasing the angle of attack, the leading edge stagnation point of the aerofoil moves towards the…
optionA: upper side of the aerofoil.
optionB: lower side of the aerofoil.
optionC: neutral position.
optionD: first upper then lower side of aerofoil.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
The lift equation states:

LIFT = ½ρV2SCL

Considering Lift to remain constant, as speed is decreased to achieve slow flight, the angle of attack (CL) is increased in order to keep the equation balanced.

Stagnation Point - A point where streamlines are divided by a body and where the fluid speed is zero, relative to the surface.

As the dividing streamline approaches the aerofoil it slows down, and momentarily comes to rest just below the leading edge, forming a stagnation point.

The greatest positive pressure occurs at the stagnation point where the relative flow velocity is zero. This stagnation point is located somewhere near the leading edge.

As the angle of attack increases from -4°, the leading edge stagnation point moves from the upper surface around the leading edge to the lower surface.

It is at the front stagnation point where the flow divides to pass over and under the section.

As angle of attack increases, the stagnation point moves downwards and backwards around the leading edge.

title: In which phase of the take-off is the aerodynamic effect of ice located on the wing leading edge most critical?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: The take-off run.
optionB: The rotation.
optionC: During climb with all engines operating.
optionD: All phases of the take-off are equally critical.
explanationTotal:
As ice accumulates on a wing's profile, it modifies its shape and negatively impacts the maximum lift coefficient (CLMAX). This, in turn, reduces the critical angle of attack necessary for lift, thereby causing the wing to stall at a lower angle of attack. During the rotation phase of takeoff, the angle of attack is increased, and it may surpass the critical value, resulting in a stall of the wing.

Further information:
ICE ACCRETION

The formation of ice on the surface of an aeroplane has a dramatically adverse effect on its performance. The most dangerous type of ice accretion is that which occurs when flying through cumulo-nimbus cloud or through supercooled water droplets ahead of a warm front because of its rapid accumulation.

The effect that ice accretion has on an aeroplane’s performance includes:

- increased mass;
- decreased total lift;
- decreased CLMAX (that is the most serious effect);
- increased total drag;
- up to 25% increased stalling speed;
- reduced stalling angle;
- changed aerofoil shape;
- abnormal stalling characteristics.

For an aeroplane in the take-off or landing configuration, ice accretion is extremely dangerous because of the close proximity of the normal operating speed to the stalling speed. Consequently, there is a very high risk of the aeroplane stalling when it is close to the ground.

title: A laminar boundary layer is a layer, in which:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: the temperature varies constantly.
optionB: no velocity components exist, normal to the surface.
optionC: the velocity is constant.
optionD: the vortices are weak.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The boundary layer is the layer of fluid (in our case this fluid is the atmosphere) in the immediate surface of a bounding surface (the airfoil) where the effects of viscosity are significant.There are two types of boundary layer; the laminar and the turbulent boundary layer.

In the laminar boundary layer, the flow moves parallel to the surface over which it flows.In the laminar boundary layer, the air flows very smoothly.The velocity increases with distance from the airfoil and there is no movement of air perpendicular to the surface of the airfoil.Laminar flow creates less friction drag than the turbulent flow, but is less stable.

At a distance from the leading edge of the airfoil, the air transitions from a laminar flow to a turbulent flow.This air does not flow smoothly, it contains swirls.There is flow in parallel and perpendicular direction.This air creates more drag than the laminar air flow, but breaks down less easily and is therefore more stable.

title: Which of the following statements is true regarding ground effect?
optionA: The ground effect over an aeroplane is decreased when the temperature increases.
optionB: The ground effect over an aeroplane is greater on a hotter day.
optionC: The ground effect is not affected by temperature.
optionD: The colder the temperature the greater the ground effect.
explanationTotal:
Ground Effect is the name given to the positive influence on the lifting characteristics of the horizontal surfaces of an aircraft wing when it is close to the ground. It is important to note that temperature has no effect on ground effect itself. However, it adds to the ground effect.

But how will an increased temperature add to the ground effect? It's simple, convective currents from a warm runway will add to the upward forces caused by the ground effect, increasing the tendency of the aircraft to float beyond the touchdown point.

title: Low speed pitch up can be caused by the:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: outward drift of the boundary layer on a swept-back wing.
optionB: dihedral effect.
optionC: boundary layer separation at the wing tip of a forward swept wing.
optionD: wing tip vortices on high aspect ratio wings.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The lift from a wing is generated by airflow over it from front to back. If the span-wise flow increases, the boundary layer on the wing surface travels for longer. This causes them to be thicker and more susceptible to transition to turbulence or flow separation. The normal tip vortice on a swept wing joins up with a leading edge separation bubble, creating a larger vortex called the Ram’s horn vortex. This vortex goes inboard along the wing’s leading edge. The downward flow from the vortex induces pressure on the boundary layer at the wingtip, whereas on straight wings the exact opposite occurs. With a swept wing, this creates a slow-moving layer of air at the wing tip. This slow-moving air will separate into disturbed flow and will then stall the tip.

As the wingtips for a swept wing are positioned aft of the center of pressure (CP), the center of pressure upon a wing tip stall will move forward, creating a nose up moment. This nose up moment will further increase the Angle of Attack if not corrected in time, increasing the layer of slow-moving air, worsening the situation. Due to the decreased downwash on the elevator, the elevator could be less responsive, creating a so called deep stall. Unswept wings do not have this problem.

The pitch up phenomenon is a dangerous characteristic of swept wing aircraft (with a T-tail) that move at high speed. It could result in a quickly worsening stalling situation, making it very hard to recover.

title: Assuming ISA conditions and a descent below the tropopause at constant Mach number and aeroplane mass, the:
optionA: lift coefficient remains constant.
optionB: lift coefficient increases.
optionC: TAS increases.
optionD: IAS decreases.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

The Mach number is defined as the ratio between the TAS and the LSS (Local speed of sound).
It is an indication of how fast an aircraft is travelling with relation to the sound waves that surround it.

The Mach number may be calculated as follows:

M=TAS/LSS=(TAS(kt))/(38.95∗√(T(K)))

The speed of propagation of small pressure waves depends upon the temperature of the air ONLY.

Effect on TAS of descending at a constant Mach Number:

  • Temperature increases with decreasing altitude, so the speed of sound will increase as altitude is decreased.
  • If altitude is decreased at a constant Mach Number, the TAS increases. This is because LSS gets bigger.

title: A single engine aeroplane with a clockwise rotating propeller drifted to the left during the acceleration for take-off on a wet runway. The most probable cause is...
optionA: spiralling slipstream.
optionB: propeller drag.
optionC: gyroscopic precession.
optionD: asymmetric blade effect.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The high-speed rotation of an aircraft propeller gives a corkscrew or spiraling rotation to the slipstream. At high propeller speeds and low forward speed (as in the take-offs and approaches to power-on stalls), this spiraling rotation is very compact and exerts a strong sideward force on the aircraft’s vertical tail surface.

When this spiraling slipstream strikes the vertical fin, it causes a yawing moment about the aircraft’s vertical axis.The more compact the spiral, the more prominent this force is.

As the forward speed increases, however, the spiral elongates and becomes less effective. The corkscrew flow of the slipstream also causes a rolling moment around the longitudinal axis.

title: Which of the following statements is correct with regards to aircraft certified under CS-23 and CS-25?
optionA: Only jet aeroplanes have a V<sub>MO</sub>.
optionB: V<sub>NE</sub> applies to all aircraft with an MTOW less than 5 670 kg.
optionC: V<sub>NE</sub> only applies to CS-23 aircraft but NOT to CS-25 aircraft.
optionD: V<sub>MO</sub> only applies to CS-25 aircraft but NOT to CS-23 aircraft.
explanationTotal:
Note: You may see this question with VMO or MMO used interchangeably, either can be used, it does not change the answer. Please let us know which you get in the exam, by placing feedback in the comments or by email to info@atplquestions.com, thank you!

Aircraft can be certified under 2 different certification specifications; CS-23 or CS-25.

CS-23 covers "small aircraft". This includes aircraft with MTOW of 5670 kg or less and a maximum operational passenger seating configuration (MOPSC) of 9 or fewer. CS-23 also covers commuter category aircraft up to 8618 kg MTOW and a MOPSC of 19 or fewer. This means that there are CS-23 aircraft with an MTOW above 5670 kg.

CS-25 covers "large aircraft". Specifically, "turbine powered Large Aeroplanes". This includes turboprop aircraft as well as turbojet/turbofan (jet aircraft).

There is a difference between the limiting flight airspeeds, VNE and VMO/MMO. Some aircraft (usually smaller, slower aircraft) use VNE - the never exceed speed, and a corresponding VNO, the normal operating speed, which should only be exceeded in smooth air (bottom of the yellow arc). Larger/faster aircraft use VMO/MMO - the maximum operating speed/maximum operating Mach number. This is calculated a little differently to VNE, and is a speed that should not be exceeded during normal operations. An aircraft either has VNE or VMO/MMO, never both. If an aircraft uses VMO, it will also have a corresponding MMO, but this is not mentioned in this question

CS-23 aircraft mostly use VNE, but turbine powered aeroplanes and those with a particular design dive speed instead use a VMO/MMO (CS 23.1505). Therefore, CS-23 aircraft can use either VNE or VMO/MMO, depending on the particular aircraft.

CS-25 aircraft only use VMO/MMO.

Now we have enough information to go through each option:

  • "Only jet aeroplanes have a VMO."
    • No, there are turboprop aircraft within CS-25 (and CS-23) that also have VMO, and even the possibility for piston aircraft to have VMO under CS-23 in some cases (CS 23.1505).
  • "VNE applies to all aircraft with an MTOW less than 5 670 kg."
    • No, there are aircraft under 5 670 kg with more than 9 passenger seats that would be under CS-25 (and therefore have a VMO) and there are also aircraft within CS-23 that use VMO (CS 23.1505).
  • "VNE only applies to CS-23 aircraft but NOT to CS-25 aircraft."
    • Yes, the majority of CS-23 aircraft use a VNE (but not all), and CS-25 aircraft only use VMO, so do not use VNE at all.
  • "VMO only applies to CS-25 aircraft but NOT to CS-23 aircraft."
    • No. Whilst all CS-25 aircraft do use a VMO, so do some aircraft certified under CS-23 (turbines and certain piston aircraft [CS 23.1505])

title: How does VMCG change with an increase in field elevation and temperature? VMCG...
optionA: decreases, because the amount of thrust developed by the operating engine is reduced.
optionB: increases, because at a lower density a larger IAS is necessary to generate the required rudder force.
optionC: decreases, because VMCG is expressed as an IAS and that decreases with decreasing density.
optionD: increases, because V<sub>MCG</sub> is related to V? and that increases when the density decreases.
explanationTotal:
VMCG, the minimum control speed on the ground, is the calibrated airspeed during the takeoff run, at which, when the critical engine is suddenly made inoperative, it is possible to maintain control of the airplane using the rudder control alone (without the use of nose wheel steering) to enable the take-off to be safely continued using normal piloting skill.
The rudder control forces may not exceed 150 pounds (68.1 kg) and, until the airplane becomes airborne, the lateral control may only be used to the extent of keeping the wings level. In the determination of VMCG, assuming that the path of the airplane accelerating with all engines operating is along the center of the runway, its path from the point at which the critical engine is made inoperative to the point at which recovery to a direction parallel to the center line is completed may not deviate more than 30 ft (9.144 m) laterally from the center line at any point. As with VMCA, this must be established with:
  • maximum available take-off power or thrust on the engines.
  • the airplane trimmed for take-off.
  • the most unfavorable CG position.
  • maximum sea level take-off weight.
VMCG is affected by the amount of thrust being developed by the operating engine. As altitude and/or temperature increases, the thrust from an unsupercharged engine will decrease. Therefore, VMCG decreases with an increase in altitude and/or temperature.

title: How would the TODR (take-off distance required) for a fixed wing aircraft vary with increasing flap settings (from retracted to full flaps)?
optionA: It would decrease.
optionB: It would increase.
optionC: It would decrease and then increase.
optionD: It would increase and then decrease.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Learning Objective 081.01.09.01.09: Explain the effects of flap-setting errors, such as mis-selection and premature/late extension or retraction of flaps, on: take-off and landing distance and speeds; climb and descent performance; stall buffet margins.

Flaps increase the camber (and sometimes the area) of the wing, which increases the amount of lift that can be produced by the wing, for the same IAS (indicated airspeed). They also increase the drag of the wing, by more than they increase lift. This means that the aircraft will always fly more efficiently (better L/D ratio) without flaps, hence why they are not used in the cruise, or the climb, when possible.

Flaps are primarily used for take-off and landing. For take-off, we can rotate at a lower speed, using less runway, and maintain a lower flying speed on the initial climb out. For landing, we can approach at a slower speed (with a higher approach angle if necessary, due to the extra drag), and therefore land in a shorter distance.

For take-off, using flaps is a trade-off between runway length and climb requirements. Flaps are bad for climbing, as they produce more drag, but they will get us off the runway earlier. Therefore, if there is a long runway and high obstacles around, lower (or no) flaps should be used, whereas a short field take-off with few obstacles should use higher flap settings. If there is a short field with obstacles, run the performance calculations carefully for both, and use whichever is better.

In terms of this question, the take-off distance will obviously reduce from no flaps (clean) to some flaps, due to the lower distance to rotation, but will begin to increase again towards full flaps, as the aircraft have so much drag that even if it does leave the ground early, it will struggle to climb to the screen height. Many aircraft would not be able to sustain a climb at all with full flaps set, and the final stage of flaps often produces little extra lift than the last stage, but produces lots more drag.

title:
Refer to figure.
Choose the correct statement:
optionA: Aerofoil 1 corresponds to line 4.
optionB: Aerofoil 4 corresponds to line 1.
optionC: Aerofoil 3 corresponds to line 2.
optionD: Aerofoil 4 corresponds to line 2.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

A completely symmetrical airfoil will intersect the vertical axis of the graph at the origin (0).
A positively cambered airfoil will generate more lift at the same speed (and therefore has a higher CL) than a symmetrical airfoil and therefore intersects the vertical axis above the origin (and generates 0 lift at a negative angle of attack).
A negatively cambered airfoil will generate less lift at the same speed (which translates into a lower CL at a certain speed) and therefore intersects the vertical axis below the origin.

An increased camber generates a higher value of CL at the same Angle of Attack.

Therefore, we have the following combinations:

  • Aerofoil 1 corresponds to line 3.
  • Aerofoil 2 corresponds to line 4.
  • Aerofoil 3 corresponds to line 1.
  • Aerofoil 4 corresponds to line 2.

title: What happens if a pilot flying a clockwise rotating propeller performs a go around?
optionA: Asymmetric thrust is generated, leading to an increased left yaw.
optionB: Asymmetric thrust is generated, leading to an increased right yaw.
optionC: Symmetrical thrust is generated, leading to an increased right yaw.
optionD: Symmetrical thrust is generated, leading to an increased left yaw.
explanationTotal:
Asymmetric blade effect (also known as ‘P’ Factor)

Propeller blades are not flat, they are in fact shaped as small wings. As a consequence, as the angle of attack of the airplane increases, the air passing by hits the blades differently:

The down-going blade (viewed from the cockpit) will have a larger angle of attack compared to the up-going blade, generating more thrust. This then means that the down-swinging (right) blade exerts a greater force than the up-going blade. For this reason, the thrust line will be displaced to the right of the engine centre line. If both engines rotate clockwise, the right engine will have a longer thrust arm than the left engine.
  • This difference in thrust will give a yawing moment to the left with a clockwise rotating propeller in a nose-up attitude. This effect will be greatest at full power and low airspeed.

title: The pilot flying an aircraft extends the trailing edge flaps. This will allow for a (1) _____ lift, with (2) _____ speed and (3) _____ drag.
optionA: (1) same; (2) less; (3) higher
optionB: (1) higher; (2) higher; (3) less
optionC: (1) higher; (2) less; (3) equal
optionD: (1) less; (2) higher; (3) less
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
CLMAX AUGMENTATION

One of the main factors which determine the CLMAX of an aerofoil section is the camber. Increasing the camber of an aerofoil section increases the CL at a given angle of attack and increases CLMAX.

TRAILING EDGE FLAPS

Aircraft are fitted with high lift devices to reduce the take-off and landing distances and when low airspeeds are beneficial. This permits operation at greater weights from given runway lengths and enables greater payloads to be carried.

Returning the flaps to their neutral position when no longer required, returns the wing to its former aerodynamic characteristics.

The increase in lift comes mainly from the variation in effective camber that occurs when the flaps are deflected.This alters the lift curve and also produces a higher maximum coefficient of lift.

In some instances, the trailing edge flaps may also increase the wing's surface area. Extending the trailing edge flaps alters the pressure distribution around the wing.

Any amount of flap increases drag. Parasite Drag varies directly in proportion to the frontal area presented to the airflow. If flaps are deployed, the undercarriage lowered, speed brakes selected or roll control spoilers operated, "Parasite Area" is increased and Parasite Drag will increase.

title: Determine the new V<sub>S</sub>, given the following information: An airplane of 305 t and a V<sub>S</sub> of 175 kt departs with 75 t of fuel aboard. Upon landing there is 8.5 t of fuel remaining.

optionA: 155 kt
optionB: 175 kt
optionC: 137 kt
optionD: 173 kt
explanationTotal:
Use the following equation:
VS NEW = VS OLD x √(New Mass ÷ Old Mass)
  • Fuel burnt = 75 t - 8.5 t = 66.5 t
    New Mass = 305 t - 66.5 t = 238.5 t

title:
What should a pilot do when exceeding VMO/MMO?

1. Reduce power to idle
2. Use the pitch trim
3. Give a nose-up input

The combination regrouping all correct statements is
explanationTotal:
When the flight warning system (FWS) identifies an overspeed condition (airspeed exceeding VMO/MMO), it generates a warning message (visual and aural). This warning system is mandatory in order to prevent inadvertent excursions beyond the limit speeds.

To stop the warning generated by an overspeed warning system, the pilot must reduce the airspeed without any further delay. This will be achieved by reducing the power to idle and pulling the nose up. The Overspeed protection function can even send automatically a pitch up order (on some aircraft types). Since the correct recovery maneuver to get out of an overspeed condition is to pitch the aircraft’s nose up, an inhibition logic could be used to prevent the pilot from pitching down.

title: An aircraft has a mass of 305 tonnes. The aircraft has burnt 63 tonnes of fuel when it starts the approach to land. On take-off, its stalling speed was 140 kt. Determine the stalling speed at the start of the approach:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: 88 kt
optionB: 111 kt
optionC: 125 kt
optionD: 157 kt
explanationTotal:
Landing Mass = 305 - 63 = 242 tonnes

This exercise can be solved applying the following formula:

New VS = Old VS √Change in Mass
New VS = 140 √(242 / 305)
New VS = 124.7 kt

title: What happens to the pressure coefficient (CP) when the flow velocity (Mach number) is higher than the critical Mach number (M<sub>CRIT</sub>)?
optionA: CP decreases
optionB: CP remains constant
optionC: CP increases
optionD: CP fluctuates rapidly
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
During high-speed flight, significant changes occur in the flow and pressure distributions around the aircraft, which result in a loss of lift and an increase in drag. This is caused by the formation of shock waves, which adversely affect the stability and control characteristics of the aircraft.

The speed of sound is defined as the rate at which small pressure disturbances are propagated through the air, which is solely a function of air temperature.

THE DEVELOPMENT OF SHOCK WAVES
When aircraft fly through the air, every part of them sets up tiny pressure disturbances, which radiate outward at the speed of sound in all directions.

As Mach number increases, the flow over the wing continues to accelerate and eventually reaches a sonic value at a particular point on the wing, normally the point of maximum thickness.

With increasing Mach number, this point grows into an area of supersonic flow, so the air moving over the upper surface will be moving rearward faster than the pressure disturbances can move forward. These disturbances consequently pile up on each other and form a shock wave.

The overall direction of the airflow remains the same, but as it passes through the shock wave, the following changes take place:
- The flow is rapidly decelerated to a subsonic Mach number.
- Static pressure increases.
- Temperature increases.
- Density increases.
- The energy of the airstream (total pressure) is greatly reduced.

In fluid dynamics, the pressure coefficient is a dimensionless number that describes the relative pressures throughout a flow. The increase in pressure due to the compressibility effects created by the presence of shockwaves will lead to an increase in the pressure coefficient.

title: What is the effect of winglets on the drag of the wing?
optionA: Increase friction drag, decrease form drag.
optionB: Increase parasite drag, decrease induced drag.
optionC: Increase induced drag, decrease friction drag.
optionD: Increase induced drag, decrease interference drag.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Winglets increase an aircraft's operating efficiency by reducing what is called induced drag at the tips of the wings. By significantly reducing the size of the wingtip vortex, winglets reduce induced drag—the aerodynamic drag created by an airfoil when it is producing lift. However, the added wetted surface area increases the parasite drag.

title:
(For this question use annex 081-013 issue date November 2005).
The angle of attack of a rotating propeller blade element shown in the annex is:
optionA: angle 3.
optionB: angle 2.
optionC: not correctly indicated in the diagram.
optionD: angle 1.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The Blade Angle

Sometimes called the pitch angle, is the angle subtended between the plane of rotation and the chord line of the propeller blade, which may be fixed or variable. When the airplane is moving it comprises two parts, the angle of attack and the helix angle, but when it is stationary the blade angle is equal to the angle of attack.

The Helix Angle

The angle that the actual path of the propeller makes to the plane of rotation.

Angle of Attack

The path of the propeller through the air determines the direction of the relative airflow. The angle between the blade chord and the relative airflow is the angle of attack (α).
The angle of attack (α) is the result of propeller rotational velocity (RPM) and aircraft forward velocity (TAS).

title: Which of the following statements about static lateral and directional stability is correct?
optionA: The effects of static lateral and static directional stability are completely independent of each other because they take place about different axes.
optionB: Static directional stability can be increased by installing more powerful engines.
optionC: An aeroplane with an excessive static directional stability in relation to its static lateral stability, will be prone to spiral dive (spiral instability).
optionD: An aeroplane with an excessive static directional stability in relation to its static lateral stability, will be prone to “Dutch roll”.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
An airplane may display spiral instability in case it has strong directional stability relative to its lateral stability. It looks similar to a spin, however, the wings are not stalled here.

When a wind gust makes an airplane with spiral instability to side-slip, powerful directional stability tends to yaw the airplane back into alignment with the relative wind. In this case the outside wing will generate more lift as it travels faster. This tends to roll the airplane in the direction of the yaw. The rolling force overcomes the weak dihedral effect, allowing further roll. As the vertical component of lift decreases, the relative wind has an upward component with the airplane swinging in alignment with the air stream, the nose begins to drop. This results in a gradually increasing spiral dive.

title:
In a fly-by-wire aircraft, what are the two main parameters that might be maintained with the control wheel or stick neutral, in Pitch Normal Control Law?

1. Maintain the Speed
2. Maintain the Attitude
3. Maintain the thrust
4. Maintain the fuel flow
optionA: 1 and 2.
optionB: 1 and 3.
optionC: 2 and 3.
optionD: 3 and 4.
explanationTotal:
In all of the computations performed by the autopilot computer (the signals processor) “control laws” are taken into account. These determine how the control demands are translated into control movements - in other words the translation of computer input data to computer output control surface deflection data. Among control laws there are for example: high angle of attack, high speed, pitch attitude (30° pitch-up & 15° pitch-down), bank angle, load factor.

With the control Wheel or stick neutral, there are two main parameters that main be maintained: Speed and Attitude.

title: Which of the following aircraft design characteristics is desirable during a flight with a long time spent in straight and level flight and only gentle manoeuvring?
optionA: An aeroplane with neutral stability to reduce the workload of the pilot, since flying requires lower control forces.
optionB: An aeroplane with neutral stability, because it will tend to move less in turbulence since it will remain in its new attitude.
optionC: A statically stable aeroplane where the aeroplane shows a natural tendency to return to its pre-disturbed position.
optionD: A statically unstable aeroplane to reduce the workload of the pilot with lower control forces to maintain an attitude.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
An aircraft is in a state of equilibrium (trim) when the sum of all forces is zero and the sum of all moments is zero; there are no accelerations and the aircraft will continue in steady flight.

If equilibrium is disturbed by a gust, or deflection of the controls, the aircraft will experience accelerations due to an unbalance of moments or forces.

The type of static stability an aircraft possesses is defined by its initial tendency, following the removal of some disturbing force.

Positive static stability (or static stability) exists if an aircraft is disturbed from equilibrium and has the tendency to return to equilibrium.

Neutral static stability exists if an aircraft is subject to a disturbance and has neither the tendency to return nor the tendency to continue in the displacement direction.

Negative static stability (or static instability) exists if an aircraft tends to continue in the direction of disturbance.

title: On an aircraft equipped with a Fly-by-wire control system, the pilot…
optionA: never override soft and hard protections.
optionB: can override hard protections only.
optionC: can override soft protections only.
optionD: can override soft and hard protections.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
FLY-BY-WIRE (FBW)

Fly-by-wire aeroplanes function differently to conventional aeroplanes in that the pilot or autopilot input is via a flight control computer.

The computer translates this input into an aircraft attitude using all three axes, which it will then maintain until another input is made.

CONTROL LAWS - NORMAL LAW

The fly-by-wire system was designed and certified to render the new generation of aircraft even more safe, cost effective, and pleasant to fly.

Flight control surfaces are all :
‐ Electrically-controlled
‐ Hydraulically-actuated.

Computers interpret pilot input and move the flight control surfaces, as necessary, to follow their orders. However, when in normal law, regardless of the pilot’s input, the computers will prevent excessive manoeuvres and exceedance of the safe envelope in pitch and roll axis.

One of the PF's primary tasks is to maintain the aircraft within the limits of the normal flight envelope. Some circumstances, due to extreme situations or aircraft mishandling, may provoke the violation of these limits.

Protections are intended to:
- Provide maximum authority to the PF to consistently achieve the best possible aircraft performance in extreme conditions
- Reduce the risks of over-controlling, or over-stressing the aircraft
- Provide PF with an instinctive and immediate procedure to ensure that the PF achieves the best possible result.
The normal law protects the aircraft throughout the flight envelope, as follows:
‐ load factor limitation
‐ pitch attitude protection
‐ high-speed protection.
- bank angle protection
‐ high-angle-of-attack (AoA) protection

One of the hard protections on the Airbus system, in normal law, is the stall protection. Without flight crew input, the F/CTL computers maintain the AOA equal to a defined value.

The AOA can be further increased by flight crew input, up to a maximum value. The AOA will not exceed that maximum value, even if the flight crew gently pulls the sidestick all the way back.

CONTROL LAWS - RECONFIGURATION LAWS

Depending on the failures occurring to the flight control system, or on its peripherals, there are 3 levels of reconfiguration :
‐ Alternate law (There are two levels of alternate law : with and without reduced protections.)
‐ Direct law
‐ Mechanical

ALTERNATE LAW - REDUCED PROTECTIONS

- Load Factor Limitation
- Pitch Attitude Protection
- Low Speed Stability (Soft protection)

An artificial low speed stability replaces the normal angle-of-attack protection. A gentle progressive nose down signal is introduced, that tends to keep the speed from falling below these values. The flight crew can override this demand. In addition, stall warnings are activated at an appropriate margin from the stall condition.

- High Speed Stability (Soft protection)

Above VMO or MMO, a nose up demand is introduced to avoid an excessive increase in speed. The flight crew can override this demand.

In addition, the aural overspeed warning remains available.

title: The aerodynamic contribution to the static longitudinal stability of the nacelles of aft fuselage-mounted engines is...
optionA: only determined by speed.
optionB: always zero.
optionC: always positive.
optionD: always negative.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The effect that the fuselage, and to a lesser extent wing-mounted the engine nacelles, has on the airplane’s longitudinal static stability is normally a destabilizing influence, a negative contribution. If the fuselage aerodynamic center is ahead of the wing aerodynamic center, the aerodynamic center of the wing–fuselage combination is further forward than it would normally be. If such is the case the aircraft CG will be further aft than is normal and the aircraft longitudinal static stability is decreased.

This destabilizing influence is increased by the induced upwash of the airflow ahead of the wing. However, the downwash of the airflow aft of the wing decreases the destabilizing influence caused by areas of the fuselage and nacelles aft of the wing. Rear fuselage-mounted engine nacelles have a positive effect.

title: When large transport aeroplanes are flying at high speed, full rudder deflection would cause excessive loads on the structure. What system is fitted to the rudder to prevent this happening?
optionA: Rudder trim system.
optionB: Fully powered rudder control.
optionC: Rudder ratio or rudder travel changer.
optionD: Yaw damper system.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
With a simple control system, full rudder pedal movement will provide full rudder deflection.

With high speed aircraft, while it is necessary to have large rudder deflections available at low speed, when flying at high speed, full rudder deflection would cause excessive loads on the structure.

To prevent this occurring, a gear change system can be incorporated into the rudder control system. This may be a single gear change which gives a smaller rudder deflection for full pedal movement above a certain speed (Variable Stop), or a progressive gear change which gives a decreasing rudder deflection with full pedal movement as speed increases (Rudder Ratio).

title:
Determine the one engine inoperative climb angle (in degrees) of a twin engine aeroplane, given:

Weight: 2 720 000 N
Drag: 180 000 N
Thrust: 370 000 N per engine
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The formula for climb angle is as follows:

Sin(γ) = (T – D) ÷ W

γ = climb angle (gamma)

All we have to do is replace all the given forces (considering that they were all given in the same unit, Newtons) in the above formula:

Sin(γ) = (370 000 – 180 000) ÷ 2 720 000
Sin(γ) = 0.070
γ = sin-1(0.070) = 4°

title:
Given a constant load factor, which of these statements about the variation of induced drag with changes of speed and mass are correct or incorrect?

1. When speed decreases, induced drag decreases.
2. When mass decreases, induced drag decreases.
optionA: 1 is incorrect, 2 is correct.
optionB: 1 is correct, 2 is correct.
optionC: 1 is incorrect, 2 is incorrect.
optionD: 1 is correct, 2 is incorrect.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

The total drag is the resulting factor if you add induced drag and parasite drag together.

Parasite drag is caused if an airfoil is moving through the air.
It is the result of form drag and skin friction drag.
Form drag arises from the shape of the object.
The more streamlined the object, the less form drag is present.
Shape and size are most important in the amount of form drag resulting.
Form drag increases with increasing velocity, making it very important for high speed aircraft.
Skin friction drag is caused by the friction of the fluid (in case of aircraft this fluid is the atmosphere) against the skin of the object moving through it.
It is directly related to the surface area in contact with the fluid.
Skin friction increases with the square of the velocity.

Induced drag is caused when an object redirects the airflow.
A wing produces lift by creating a pressure difference.
This pressure difference is caused by the shape of the airfoil, causing the airflow on top to accelerate, creating a low pressure on top of the wing and high pressure below the wing.
This pressure difference naturally wants to restore towards a uniform pressure, which creates vortices around the wingtip.
These vortices are deflected downwards, this phenomenon is also called downwash.
The induced drag decreases with airspeed and increases with angle of attack and increasing weight.

In the image we can see that the two vectors (induced and parasite drag) create a resulting vector, the total drag.
Where the induced and parasite drag vectors collide, we have the minimum drag speed (VMD); the speed where the total drag is the lowest.

This leads us to understand that during an acceleration from a total stand still, the total drag first decreases up until the minimum drag speed and then starts increasing again.

title:
Refer to figure.
The plane is performing a (1) _____ turn to the right, according to the instrument in the picture, therefore requiring (2) _____ rudder to coordinate it.
optionA: (1) slipping; (2) left
optionB: (1) slipping; (2) right
optionC: (1) skidding; (2) left
optionD: (1) skidding; (2) right
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
When an aircraft is slipping or skidding, it is said to be in uncoordinated flight. The turn coordinator's inclinometer portion (ball) or the turn and slip indicator provides the pilot with an indication of the sideslip. The rate of turn is indicated by the aeroplane or needle. To maintain coordinated flight, the pilot keeps the ball centered between the reference lines and applies rudder pressure on the side where the ball is deflected.

A slipping turn is a turn where the aircraft’s nose is outside of the turning radius and the tail is in the turn radius.

  • A slip is caused by using too much bank and too little rudder.
  • The slip indicator (ball) will point towards the low wing.

A skidding turn is a turn where the aircraft’s nose is inside of the turning radius and the tail is outside of the turn radius.

  • A skid is caused by using too much rudder and not enough bank.
  • The ball will point towards the high wing.

title: An aeroplane performs a right turn, the slip indicator is right of neutral. One way to co-ordinate the turn is to apply:
optionA: less right rudder.
optionB: more right bank.
optionC: less right bank.
optionD: more left rudder.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
A coordinated turn is a turn where there is no sideslip or skid, this is the most effective and therefore preferable way to turn.In a coordinated turn, the turn and bank indicator in the plane shows the ball in the center.If the turn is not coordinated, you’re either in a slip or a skid.These two things are different and shall therefore be eliminated differently.

A slipping turn is a turn where the aircraft’s nose is outside of the turning radius and the tail is in the turn radius.A slip is caused by using too much bank and too little rudder.

A skidding turn is a turn where the aircraft’s nose is inside of the turning radius and the tail is outside of the turn radius.A skid is caused by using too much rudder and not enough bank.

title:
Refer to figure.
Name the trailling edge devices in the attached figure.
optionA:
1. Plain flap
2. Slotted flap
3. Fowler flap
4. Split flap
optionB:
1. Fowler flap
2. Slotted flap
3. Plain flap
4. Split flap
optionC:
1. Slotted flap
2. Plain flap
3. Fowler flap
4. Split flap

1. Plain flap
2. Split flap
3. Fowler flap

explanationTotal:
1. Plain flap
2. Slotted flap

A plain flap simply lowers the trailing edge of the wing, increasing camber.

A Fowler flap not only extends rearwards but also moves downward, resulting in an increased wing surface area and an amplified camber.

title: The geometric pitch of a propeller is the:
optionA: the angle between the chordline of a blade element and the propeller plane of rotation.
optionB: distance a propeller advances with slippage.
optionC: theoretical distance a propeller would advance in one revolution at zero blade angle of attack.
optionD: distance a propeller would have to advance in one revolution to give no thrust.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The geometric pitch is the distance the propeller would travel forward in one complete revolution if it were moving through the air at the blade angle.

title: An aerobatic aircraft is in steady 60 degree descent. Its weight is 8000 N. Determine the value of lift required:
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The forward component of Weight (W sin γ) is a product of descent angle (γ); the greater the descent angle, the greater the forward component of weight.
The forward component of weight must balance Drag for the aircraft to be in a steady glide.

For a glide descent, we get the following formulas:

D = W sin y
L = W cos y

With regards to this question:

  • L = W cos y
    L = 8 000 cos 60
    L = 4 000 N

title: Which of the following statements is correct in the event of computer failure on a fly-by-wire (FBW) aircraft?
optionA: Some form of back-up mode is required in the event of total computer failure.
optionB: In “Direct Law”, mechanical linkage to all control surfaces remains available.
optionC: Control of the aircraft is lost if the computer system fails completely.
optionD: Any form of computer failure will affect the aircraft handling.
explanationTotal:
The fly-by-wire system has multiple redundancies that offer layered protection:

Normal Law offers all the protections (like stall, load factor etc). This is the system in operation during normal flights. Normal Law operates in different modes depending on the stage of flight. These modes include:

  • Ground Mode

  • Flight Mode

  • Flare Mode

Alternate Law offers limited protection including stability, load factor and stall protections. Basically, it is the reduced mode of operation which provides most features of normal law.

Direct Law is the lowest level of fly-by-wire system and directly transmits the pilot inputs to control surfaces, while still giving stall and load factor warnings

Mechanical back up. In case all of the above fail, the system reverts to mechanical backup, where pitch control is achieved through the horizontal stabilizer and lateral control is accomplished using the rudder pedals. The purpose of the backup system is to allow control of the aircraft following a total loss of electrics, flight control computers, elevators, or ailerons and spoilers
In case of mechanical backup, the system will operate as long as hydraulic power is available. In case of electrical failure, as long as hydraulics are OK, the pilot should be able to control the aircraft.

title: By deploying the spoilers, the rate of descent (1) _____ and aircraft pitch (2) _____ .
optionA: (1) Decreases, (2) Increases
optionB: (1) Increases, (2) Decreases
optionC: (1) Increases, (2) Increases
optionD: (1) Decreases, (2) Decreases
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Speed brakes affecting drag and lift are called spoilers as they spill or spoil part of the lift force. They are movable panels on the upper wing surface, hinged at their forward edge. They are operated hydraulically and controlled electrically. A raised spoiler will disturb the airflow over the wing, thus reducing lift and increasing drag.

The formula for descent gradient is as follows:

Sin(γ) = (D – T) ÷ W

γ = descent angle (gamma)

An increase in drag will increase the descent gradient or angle, which in a descent is observed by an increase in the pitch-down attitude, i.e., a decrease in pitch.

The rate of descent can be expressed by the following formula:

ROD (ft/m) = TAS x Descent Gradient

From the expression above, we can conclude that an increase in the descent gradient increases the rate of descent. Thus, deploying spoilers will allow for an increase in the rate of descent and a decrease in pitch.

title: The Drag Divergence Mach number is…
optionA: equal the critical Mach.
optionB: below the critical Mach.
optionC: just above the critical Mach.
optionD: independent from critical Mach.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
As speed increases above MCRIT shock waves begin to form and drag increases more rapidly than it would have done without the shock waves. The additional drag is called wave drag and is due to energy drag and boundary layer separation.

The Mach number at which the aerodynamic drag begins to increase rapidly is called the Drag Divergence MachNumber.

The Drag Divergence Mach Number is usually close to, and always greater than, the Critical Mach Number.

title: Consider an aircraft flying in unaccelerated level flight in the speed stable region. What would be the result on Indicated Airspeed (IAS) and drag following a sudden decrease in aircraft speed with no change in thrust available?
optionA: IAS would further decrease due to the increased drag.
optionB: IAS would increase due to the increased drag.
optionC: IAS would increase due to the decreased drag.
optionD: IAS would further decrease due to the decreased drag.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
During flight, an aircraft will experience two types of drag:

- Parasite Drag (proportional to IAS2, increases with increasing “Parasite Area”: flaps, undercarriage or speed brakes)

- Induced Drag (inversely proportional to IAS2, increases with increasing weight).

The sum of Parasite Drag and Induced Drag is the Total Drag.

The Total Drag will be minimum at the IAS where Parasite Drag = Induced Drag. This speed is called Minimum Drag Speed (VMD). Flying at a slower or faster speed than VMD will generate more drag.

Flying at a slower speed than VMD (back side), the aircraft will be in the unstable speed region. Any loss of speed will result in an increase in drag and further speed loss (which must be corrected by an increase in thrust). The sudden change to a tailwind (or a decrease in headwind) can cause a loss of airspeed.

Flying at a faster speed than VMD (front side), the aircraft will be in the stable speed region. Any loss of speed will result in an decrease in drag. This decrease in drag will allow the speed to increase and recover the original speed. The sudden change to a tailwind (or a decrease in headwind) can cause a loss of airspeed.

title:
Which of these statements about the equilibrium of forces and moments at VMCA are correct or incorrect?

I. Because VMCA must be determined for the case where the critical engine suddenly fails, there is no need to obtain equilibrium of moments about the normal axis.
II. Equilibrium of forces along the lateral axis does not require any side slip during a wings level condition.
optionA: I is incorrect, II is correct.
optionB: I is correct, II is correct.
optionC: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
optionD: I is correct, II is incorrect.
explanationTotal:
If an engine fails during the take-off of a multi-engine aircraft a significant yawing moment will be experienced due to asymmetric thrust. In order to maintain directional control and keeping the aircraft in equilibrium around the yaw axis, the pilot must apply corrective action. Above a certain speed this will be possible using aerodynamic controls only. If the aircraft is still on the ground this means the use of the rudder, if the aircraft is airborne, the pilot can also apply bank by using the ailerons. The greater the thrust of this operating engine(s), the greater the yawing moment will be and the greater the aerodynamic forces to counteract this yawing moment would be required.

VMCA = Minimum control speed in the take-off configuration with gear up – the minimum calibrated airspeed at which, when the critical engine is suddenly made inoperative, it is possible to maintain control and maintain straight flight using no more than 5° of bank without required exceptional piloting skill or the aeroplane adopting a dangerous attitude or changing heading by more than 20°. An increased bank angle beyond 5°, while keeping the rudder centered, may lead to a fin stall, due to an extreme sideslip angle, but when decreasing the bank angle below 5° to 0°, rudder deflection has to be increased and therefore VMCA will increase, too.

  • Equilibrium of moments about the normal axis (also called yaw or vertical axis) is provided by rudder deflection (yaw)
  • Equilibrium of moments about the lateral axis is provided by elevator deflection (pitch)
  • Equilibrium of moments about the longitudinal axis is provided by aileron deflection (roll)

Note: Forces along the lateral axis is not the same like moments around the lateral axis. Forces along the lateral axis act around the longitudinal axis. Therefore an equilibrium along the lateral axis always requires bank or sideslip.

title: The angle of attack of a fixed pitch propeller blade increases when:
optionA: forward velocity increases and RPM decreases.
optionB: forward velocity decreases and RPM increases.
optionC: forward velocity and RPM decrease.
optionD: forward velocity and RPM increase.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
The blade angle of a fixed-pitch propeller is constant, but the helix angle and the angle of attack will vary according to its forward speed. To ensure its efficient operation the blade angle of attack of a fixed-pitch propeller must be close to the optimum and is that which produces the greatest excess of horizontal lift (thrust) over drag.
Figure 1 shows a “fixed pitch” propeller at constant RPM. Increasing TAS decreases the angle of attack of the propeller. Figure 2 shows a “fixed pitch” propeller at a constant TAS. Increasing RPM increases the angle of attack of the propeller.

title: Drag is in the direction of – and lift is perpendicular to the:
optionA: chord line.
optionB: relative wind/airflow.
optionC: horizon.
optionD: longitudinal axis.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The total drag is the resulting factor if you add induced drag and parasite drag together. It acts in the direction of the relative wind. Lift is perpendicular to the relative wind.
Parasite drag is caused if an airfoil is moving through the air. It is the result of form drag and skin friction drag. Form drag arises from the shape of the object. The more streamlined the object, the less form drag is present. Shape and size are most important in the amount of form drag resulting. Form drag increases with increasing velocity, making it very important for high speed aircraft. Skin friction drag is caused by the friction of the fluid (in case of aircraft this fluid is the atmosphere) against the skin of the object moving through it. It is directly related to the surface area in contact with the fluid. Skin friction increases with the square of the velocity.

Induced drag is caused when an object redirects the airflow. A wing produces lift by creating a pressure difference. This pressure difference is caused by the shape of the airfoil, causing the airflow on top to accelerate, creating a low pressure on top of the wing and high pressure below the wing. This pressure difference naturally wants to restore towards a uniform pressure, which creates vortices around the wingtip. These vortices are deflected downwards, this phenomenon is also called downwash. The induced drag decreases with airspeed (with a rate of 1/V²) and increases with angle of attack and increasing weight.

In the image we can see that the two vectors (induced and parasite drag) create a resulting vector, the total drag. Where the induced and parasite drag vectors collide, we have the minimum drag speed (VMD); the speed where the total drag is the lowest.

This leads us to understand that during an acceleration from a total stand still, the total drag first decreases up until the minimum drag speed and then starts increasing again.

title:
An aircraft equipped with trailing edge flaps and leading-edge slats is about to take-off and extends the devices to the Take-Off Position. Due to a malfunction, the slats on the right wing remain retracted.

If the malfunction goes undetected, the possible consequences are:
optionA: The left wing could stall upon trailing edge flap retraction.
optionB: The right wing could stall shortly after rotation.
optionC: The left wing could stall shortly after rotation.
optionD: The right wing could stall upon trailing edge flap retraction.
explanationTotal:
Leading-edge slats increase the wing's chamber area and mean aerodynamic chord (MAC), thereby increasing its coefficient of lift (CL) maximum, which reduces the aircraft's stall speed. The mass flow over the upper surface is increased and so is its energy when air flows through the venturi-shaped slot.

These effects combine to delay the forward movement of the separation point as angle of attack increases. The stall is delayed until a higher angle of attack is reached.

The wing where the slats did not extend (right) will stall at a lower angle of attack and higher airspeed than the left wing.

title: For a fixed-pitch propeller, the blade angle of attack:
optionA: decreases when the aeroplane speed decreases (with constant engine RPM).
optionB: is always positive during idling descent.
optionC: can become negative during high-speed idle descent.
optionD: is lower in ground run than in flight (with constant engine RPM).
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
For a fixed-pitch-propeller airplane during a glide descent, maintaining a constant IAS with idle thrust, the propeller pitch and lift/drag ratio will decrease but the rate of descent will increase because the TAS gradually increases during the descent.
In the case of a high-speed glide, it is possible that the TAS increases so much that the blade angle of attack becomes negative.

title: The stagnation point is the point:
optionA: where the velocity of the relative airflow is reduced to zero.
optionB: of the intersection of the total aerodynamic force and the chord line.
optionC: relative to which the sum of all moments is independent of angle of attack.
optionD: of the intersection of the thrust vector and the chord line.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
As we can see in the figure, the stagnation point is that point where the airflow goes from freestream speed to a standstill (velocity reduced to zero). Any airstream above will flow over the wing, and any airflow below will pass under the wing.

title: In addition to V<sub>LE</sub>, a V<sub>LO</sub> limit may be added if at (1) _____ the aerodynamic loads would make operation of the (2) _____ unsafe.
optionA: (1) V<sub>LE</sub>; (2) landing gear
optionB: (1) V<sub>LO</sub>; (2) leading edge
optionC: (1) V<sub>LO</sub>; (2) landing gear
optionD: (1) V<sub>LE</sub>; (2) leading edge
explanationTotal:
LANDING GEAR SPEED LIMITATIONS

The landing gear will normally be retracted as soon as possible after take-off to reduce drag and increase the climb gradient. There is no normal requirement for the gear to be operated at high IAS so the retract and extend mechanism together with the attachment points to the structure are sized for the required task.

LANDING GEAR EXTENDED SPEED - VLE

There may be occasions when it is necessary to ferry the aircraft with the gear down, and to do this a higher permissible speed would be convenient. VLE is the speed at which it is safe to fly the aircraft with the landing gear secured in the fully extended position.

LANDING GEAR OPERATING SPEED - VLO

This is the speed at which it is safe both to extend and to retract the landing gear. If the extension speed is not the same as the retraction speed, the two speeds must be designated as VLO (EXT) and VLO (RET).

When the gear is retracted or extended the doors must open first. The doors merely streamline the undercarriage bay and are not designed to take the aerodynamic loads which would be placed on them at high IAS. Consequently VLO is usually lower than VLE.

title:
Refer to figure.
Two airplanes with distinct design configurations are depicted in the illustration. Certain parameters must be taken into consideration in order to certify the aircraft. Which of the following best represents a feature that could need to be incorporated into the designs for the aircraft in order for them to be certified?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Aeroplane 1 requires a stick pusher to prevent the aeroplane from reaching an excessively high AoA as it is likely to display undesirable behaviour during a stall.
optionB: Aeroplane 2 requires an automatic trim system since the large pitch-power couple caused by the location of the engines may overcome the authority of the elevator.
optionC: Aeroplane 1 requires a fly-by-wire system with envelope protection because the design lacks static stability due to the placement of the engines giving an aft CG.
optionD: Aeroplane 2 requires a fly-by- wire system to control the large destabilising pitch-up moment caused by changing engine thrust, expecially during a go-around.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Rear fuselage mounted engines require the tailplane on top of the fin.

Separated airflow from the stalled wing will immerse a high-set tailplane or T-tail in low energy turbulent airflow. Elevator effectiveness is greatly reduced making it impossible for the pilot to decrease the angle of attack.

The aeroplane will become stabilized in a super stall or deep stall condition. This aeroplane design will be equipped with a stick pusher system to avoid stalling. Recovery from a deep stall condition is not possible, with normal flight controls.

title: If the wing area is increased, lift will...
optionA: increase with the square root of the wing area.
optionB: remain constant provided the coefficient of lift remains constant.
optionC: increase in direct proportion to wing area.
optionD: increase with the square of the wing area.
explanationTotal:
Lift can be calculated as follows:
L= CL × ½ rho × V2 × S

Where:

  • CL is lift coefficient (without dimension)
  • p is density
  • V is velocity [m/s] (velocity is TAS)
  • S is surface area [m2]
  • L is lift [N]
From the lift equation, we can see that if wing area increases, lift will increase in the same proportion.

title: When considering a swept-back wing, without corrective design features, at the stall:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: wing root stall will occur first, which produces a rolling moment.
optionB: tip stall will occur first, which produces a nose-up pitching moment.
optionC: tip stall will occur first, which produces a nose-down pitching moment.
optionD: leading edge stall will occur first, which produces a nose-down pitching moment.
explanationTotal:
The lift from a wing is generated by airflow over it from front to back. If the span-wise flow increases, the boundary layer on the wing surface travels for longer. This causes them to be thicker and more susceptible to transition to turbulence or flow separation. The normal tip vortice on a swept wing joins up with a leading edge separation bubble, creating a larger vortex called the Ram’s horn vortex. This vortex goes inboard along the wing’s leading edge. The downward flow from the vortex induces pressure on the boundary layer at the wingtip, whereas on straight wings the exact opposite occurs. With a swept wing, this creates a slow-moving layer of air at the wing tip. This slow-moving air will separate into disturbed flow and will then stall the tip.

As the wingtips for a swept wing are positioned aft of the center of pressure (CP), the center of pressure upon a wing tip stall will move forward, creating a nose up moment. This nose up moment will further increase the Angle of Attack if not corrected in time, increasing the layer of slow-moving air, worsening the situation. Due to the decreased downwash on the elevator, the elevator could be less responsive, creating a so called deep stall. Unswept wings do not have this problem, as the CP for an unswept wing will move backwards as the aircraft approaches and exceeds CLMAX.

The pitch up phenomenon is a dangerous characteristic of swept wing aircraft (with a T-tail) that move at high speed. It could result in a quickly worsening stalling situation, making it very hard to recover.

title: Before take-off, extra fuel is added aft of the CG, on an airliner with stabiliser trim. After adjusting the trim for take-off, how will the stabiliser move?
optionA: The stabiliser does not move, but the elevator will be deflected downwards.
optionB: The leading edge of the stabiliser will be lowered.
optionC: The trailing edge of the stabiliser will be raised.
optionD: The leading edge of the stabiliser will be raised.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

An aeroplane is trimmed when it will maintain its attitude and speed without the pilot having to apply any load to the cockpit controls.

If it is necessary for a control surface to be deflected to maintain balance of the aircraft, the pilot will need to apply a force to the cockpit control to hold the surface in its deflected position. This force may be reduced to zero by operation of the trim controls.

The aircraft may need to be trimmed in pitch as a result of:
- changes of speed.
- changes of power.
- varying CG positions.
- changes of configuration.

VARIABLE INCIDENCE TAILPLANE

The Variable Incidence Horizontal Stabiliser provides pitch trim on most transport category aircraft. Varying the angle of incidence has the same effect as moving the elevator, but is aerodynamically more efficient, particularly at high airspeeds, and can provide a considerable trim range. An actuator near the leading edge varies the angle of incidence of the stabiliser. This normally operates in conjunction with the elevator to produce the least trim drag.

The position of the CG directly affects the amount of trim necessary for the angle of attack required. A forward CG adds to the inherent longitudinal stability of the aeroplane; the pilot may run out of elevator up movement and be unable to maintain the required attitude. An aft CG decreases the longitudinal stability and makes the aeroplane more difficult or impossible to control in pitch.

The CG must remain within the CG safe envelope at all times to ensure that the aeroplane remains controllable in all phases of flight.

The elevator trim or stabiliser trim setting must be preset to a value for take-off and initial climb that will ensure a minimum stick force during this critical stage of flight.

In comparison with a correctly balanced aeroplane during take-off, the position of the stabiliser for a nose-light aeroplane requires nose-down trim from an increased stabiliser angle of incidence.

title: The lift coefficient C<sub>L </sub>versus angle of attack curve of a negatively cambered aerofoil section intersects the vertical axis of the graph:
optionA: at the origin.
optionB: below the origin.
optionC: above the origin.
optionD: nowhere.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Camber is the asymmetry between two acting surfaces on an airfoil.
For an aircraft, this is the top and the bottom of the wing.
Positive camber means that a wing is thicker on the top end of the wing, than on the bottom if looked at from the chord.

In case of positive camber, a wing will generate lift with airspeed, as the air on top of the airfoil will get accelerated more than on the bottom, creating a low pressure on the top and high pressure at the bottom.
This is “pushing” the wing up into the air as the pressure difference wants to restore itself to 0 difference.
In case of negative camber, the exact opposite happens and the lift coefficient for a certain speed is lower than for a positively cambered wing.

A completely symmetrical airfoil will intersect the vertical axis of the graph at the origin (0).
A positively cambered airfoil will generate more lift at the same speed (and therefore has a higher CL) than a symmetrical airfoil and therefore intersects the vertical axis above the origin.
A negatively cambered airfoil will generate less lift at the same speed (which translates into a lower CL at a certain speed) and therefore intersects the vertical axis below the origin.

title: The critical Mach number of a conventional aerofoil section decreases if:
optionA: its leading edge radius is decreased.
optionB: it is flown at lower angles of attack.
optionC: its camber is decreased.
optionD: its thickness to chord ratio is increased.
explanationTotal:
CRITICAL MACH
At the point where the first hint of supersonic air flow occurs above the wing, the aerofoil is said to be at its critical Mach number.
OBTAINING A HIGHER CRITICAL MACH NUMBER
  • In order to obtain a high critical Mach number from an airfoil at some low lift coefficient the section must have:
    1. Low thickness ratio. The point of maximum thickness should be aft to smooth the pressure distribution.
    2. Low camber. The mean camber line should be shaped to help minimize the local velocity peaks.
  • If supersonic flight is a possibility the thickness ratio and leading edge radius must be small to decrease wave drag.

SUMMARY:
Increasing thickness gives a greater air flow so it will reach sonic speed at a lower value of MCRIT.

title: Which of the following is a cause of form drag on an object in high-speed airflow?
optionA: The energy taken from the object to produce vortices at edges and corners.
optionB: The pressure difference between the leading edge and trailing edge.
optionC: The energy taken from the object surface by the boundary layer.
optionD: The pressure change across a shock wave that forms on the surface.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Drag is the force which resists the forward motion of the aircraft. Drag acts parallel to and in the same direction as the relative airflow (in the opposite direction to the flight path).

Total Drag is sub-divided into two main types:

Parasite Drag - independent of lift generation
Induced Drag - the result of lift generation.

Parasite drag is further sub-divided into:
- Skin Friction Drag
- Form (Pressure) Drag
- Interference Drag

FORM DRAG

Form (pressure) drag results from the pressure at the leading edge of a body being greater than the pressure at the trailing edge.

Skin friction, along with the adverse pressure gradient behind the transition will cause a reduction in kinetic energy of the boundary layer.

Separation will occur when the boundary layer does not have sufficient kinetic energy in the presence of a given adverse pressure gradient.

Because of separation, there will be a lower pressure at the trailing edge than the leading edge. An aerodynamic force will act in the direction of the lower pressure - form drag.

When a shock wave forms on the upper surface, the increase of static pressure through the shock wave will create an extreme adverse pressure gradient. If the shock wave is sufficiently strong, separation will occur immediately behind the shock wave.

title: An experimental aircraft has a rectangular wing that is producing a drag value of 867 N, when generating zero lift. Determine the value of drag if the wing area was increased by 10%:
explanationTotal:
Drag can be calculated using the following formula:
  • D = CD x Q x S
  • Where CD stands for Drag Coefficient, Q is the dynamic pressure and S stands for wing area.
Drag is proportional to wing area. Therefore, assuming no other changes, if S (wing area) increases by 10%, drag will increase by 10%.
  • 867 N x (110 / 100) = approx. 954 N

title: Dihedral contributes positively to lateral stability by:
optionA: Increasing the lift on the wing into the wind.
optionB: Increasing lift on the wing away from the wind.
optionC: Increasing drag on the wing into the wind.
optionD: Increasing drag on the wing away from the wind.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
DIHEDRAL
If not corrected, an unstable aeroplane will side slip down when rolled to one side. This effect is not desirable, so how can we reduce it?

By tilting the wingtips upwards, the aeroplane becomes naturally more stable in the lateral plane. This is called dihedral.

Lift acts perpendicular to the relative airflow. If the aeroplane rolls to the side when disturbed by a gust of wind, the lift vector leans to the side with the aeroplane. This creates a resultant sideways facing force that makes the aeroplane side slip in the same direction. As a result of this side slip, the aeroplane is subjected to a sideways component of the relative airflow. Due to dihedral, the lower wing (into the wind) meets the upcoming airflow at a greater angle of attack than the upper wing. Consequently, the lower wing produces more lift and helps the aeroplane roll back to its original position. This is how dihedral improves lateral stability.

title: In transonic flight the ailerons will be less effective than in subsonic flight because:
optionA: behind the shock wave pressure is lower.
optionB: aileron deflection only partly affects the pressure distribution around the wing.
optionC: aileron down deflection moves the shock wave forward.
optionD: aileron deflection only affects the air in front of the shock wave.
explanationTotal:
EFFECTS OF SHOCKWAVE FORMATION
The formation and development of shock waves on the wing have effects on lift, drag, stability and control. Many of these effects are caused by shock induced separation.

As the air flows through the shock wave, the sudden rise in pressure causes the boundary layer to thicken and often to separate. This increases the depth of the turbulent wake behind the wing.

FLYING CONTROLS
The deflection of a conventional hinged-flap type of control creates a force ahead of the control surface that is normally greater than that which the control surface itself produces. When there is a shockwave established on the lifting surface ahead of the control surface this is no longer the case because pressure variations cannot be transmitted forward through the shockwave.

The shockwave moves slightly aft when an aileron is deflected downwards. This effectively diminishes the result of deflecting the control surface because only the airflow passing over the control surface is modified.

This effect is exacerbated when the shockwave reaches the trailing edge of the aerofoil and the control effectiveness is decreased even further. In transonic flight the ailerons are less effective than in subsonic flight because aileron deflection only partially affects the pressure distribution around the wing.

These characteristics have led to the substitution of the tailplane and elevator combination in high-speed aeroplanes with a fully flying horizontal stabiliser. On these aeroplanes the conventional wing-tip ailerons are replaced with differential spoilers and/or inboard ailerons that are for use when the aeroplane is flying at transonic speeds.

Because of the increased input forces required from the pilot during flight at transonic speeds and the large variation of the stick forces encountered during the transition of the shockwave over the control surface, most high-speed aeroplanes are fitted with fully power-operated controls.

title: If you use only ailerons to bank during take-off without utilizing rudder, the aircraft will begin to experience slipping. As a result, the slip indicator will be...
optionA: Displaced towards the low wing.
optionB: Displaced towards the high wing.
optionC: Centred.
optionD: Show no bank/turn.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
When an aircraft is slipping or skidding, it is said to be in uncoordinated flight. The turn coordinator's inclinometer portion (ball) or the turn and slip indicator provides the pilot with an indication of the sideslip. The rate of turn is indicated by the aeroplane or needle. To maintain coordinated flight, the pilot keeps the ball centered between the reference lines and applies rudder pressure on the side where the ball is deflected.

A slipping turn is a turn where the aircraft’s nose is outside of the turning radius and the tail is in the turn radius.

  • A slip is caused by using too much bank and too little rudder.
  • The slip indicator (ball) will point towards the low wing.

A skidding turn is a turn where the aircraft’s nose is inside of the turning radius and the tail is outside of the turn radius.

  • A skid is caused by using too much rudder and not enough bank.
  • The ball will point towards the high wing.

title: While cruising at M 0.78, an airliner receives a TCAS RA climb command. The manoeuvre causes the angle of attack to temporarily increase. What is the effect on critical alpha?
optionA: Critical alpha decreases due to compressibility.
optionB: Critical alpha increases due to compressibility.
optionC: Critical alpha does not change.
optionD: The RA must be ignored, due to the risk of immediate stall.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
The formation and development of shock waves on the wing have effects on lift, drag, stability and control. Many of these effects are caused by shock induced separation.

As the air flows through the shock wave, the sudden rise in pressure causes the boundary layer to thicken and often to separate. This increases the depth of the turbulent wake behind the wing.

As an aircraft flies faster, the streamline pattern around the wing changes. Faster than about four tenths the speed of sound (M 0.4) these changes start to become significant. This phenomenon is known as compressibility.

EFFECT OF SHOCK WAVES ON LIFT

At low subsonic speeds the lift coefficient CL is assumed to be constant at a given angle of attack. With increasing Mach number, however, it will vary.

At speeds above MCRIT a shock wave will have formed on the upper surface. This may cause boundary layer separation aft of the shock wave, causing loss of lift.

Shock stall results from a separated boundary layer just as the low speed stall does. Shock stall occurs when the lift coefficient, as a function of Mach number, reaches its maximum value (for a given angle of attack).

EFFECT OF SHOCK WAVES ON THE LIFT CURVE AND CLMAX

At low speed, the streamline pattern is affected far ahead of the wing and the air has a certain distance in which to upwash. As speed increases, the wing gets closer to its leading pressure wave, and the streamline pattern is affected a shorter distance ahead so must approach the wing at a steeper angle.

This change in the streamline pattern accentuates the adverse pressure gradient near the leading edge and flow separation occurs at a reduced angle of attack. Above M0.4, CLMAX decreases as seen in figure 1.

At a constant angle of attack, the increase of CL as speed increases from about M 0.4 into the low end of the transonic region gives a steeper lift curve slope, i.e. the change of CL per degree angle of attack will increase, as seen in figure 2.

Because of earlier separation resulting from the formation of the shock wave, CLMAX and the stalling angle will be reduced.

title: For a given aeroplane which two main variables determine the value of V<sub>MCG</sub>?
optionA: Airport elevation and temperature.
optionB: Engine thrust and rudder deflection.
