optionC: Engine thrust and gear position.
optionD: Air density and runway length.
explanationTotal:
In simple words, VMCG is established as being the lowest speed at which rudder effect alone is sufficient to regain and maintain directional control after a sudden engine failure.

The major factor that affects VMCG is the difference in engine thrust. VMCG will therefore be lower at higher airport elevations and at a higher OAT, due to the associated lower thrust. Conversely, VMCG will be higher at lower airport elevations and at a lower OAT.

If conditions are hot, high and humid the air is less dense. This reduces thrust and, consequently, when you lose the critical engine on take-off, there is less yawing effect from asymmetric thrust than there would be in denser air.

title:
Refer to figure.
Regarding the Buffet Onset Boundary Chart in the annexe, which of these statements are correct or incorrect?

1. Flying at M = 0.84 provides the optimum margin with respect to buffet onset.
2. The maximum altitude that can be achieved with respect to buffet onset, according to Certification Specifications, is higher at M = 0.82 than at M = 0.75.
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: 1 is correct, 2 is incorrect.
optionB: 1 is correct, 2 is correct.
optionC: 1 is incorrect, 2 is incorrect.
optionD: 1 is incorrect, 2 is correct.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
In the same way that separated airflow prior to a low speed stall can cause airframe buffet, shock induced separation (shock stall) at high speed can also cause buffeting.

Aerodynamic buffet is a valuable stall warning, but it can damage the aircraft structure. Because of the higher dynamic pressure when an aircraft is operating in the transonic speed region, any shock induced buffet will have a greater potential for severe airframe damage.
High speed buffet must be completely avoided. The aircraft must therefore be operated in such a manner that a (safety) margin exists before aerodynamic buffet will occur.

If the variables which affect both high speed and low speed stall are considered it will be possible to identify the conditions under which buffeting will occur and a chart can be drawn to show all the factors involved.

This is called a ‘Buffet Onset’ chart which is used by flight crews to ensure their aircraft is always operated with a specified minimum buffet margin.

For any given combination of mass, center of gravity position and airspeed, the maximum operating altitude is that altitude at which a normal positive acceleration increment of 0.3 g, without exceeding the buffet onset boundary, is possible.
It is, therefore, common practice to draw the ‘buffet-onset boundary chart’ for a range of cruise masses at 1.3 g. Any maneuver having a load factor exceeding 1.3 g will initiate the buffet onset.

In this exercise:

This chart is specific to an aircraft, and shows the relationship of altitude, load factor, cruise data, weight, Mach number, and IAS. The optimum speed can be found by intersecting the top of the altitude curve. In this case it is M0.80, therefore statement 1 is incorrect.

  • Start by drawing a vertical line from M0.82 and M0.75 to the FL410 curve (first altitude curve).
  • From here, draw a straight line from left to right that intersects the weight curves.
  • Finally, draw a vertical up from 1.3 g load factor that intersects the lines drawn in step 2.
As we can see, flying at M0.82 gives us the ability to carry a greater weight. We can then conclude that it also gives us a higher buffet onset margin, therefore statement 2 is correct.

title: You are flying at FL 380 and encounter a thunderstorm up ahead. You can’t fly around it, what do you do?
optionA: Fly at your V<sub>S1</sub> speed
optionB: Fly at your VRA speed
optionC: Fly at your V<sub>NO</sub> speed
optionD: Fly at your V<sub>A</sub> speed
explanationTotal:
Weather Avoidance. Whenever possible, pilots should endeavour to circumnavigate weather which may be considered prejudicial to either the safety of their aircraft or to the comfort of its passengers such as a Thunderstorm, Cumulonimbus (CB) or Towering Cumulus (TCU) and the severe turbulence and hail which may be associated with them.

  • When avoidance can't be achieved and a flight through a TS is inevitable, the aircraft should be flown at the VRA speed when in severe turbulence.

VRA : The operational rough air speed, it is the recommended speed for flying in turbulence. This speed provides the best protection against reaching structural limits due to gust effect

title: The stall speed in a 60° banked turn increases by the following factor:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
explanationTotal:
The increase of lift in a level turn is a function of the bank angle only. The stall speed will increase by a factor of: 1 ÷ √cos a, where "a" is the bank angle.

  • In this case, the aircraft is on a 60º turn, therefore, the stall speed will increase by:
1 ÷ √cos (60º) = 1.41

title: Artificial feel systems are installed in aircraft with (1) _____, which prevent the pilot from (2) _____ the aircraft.
optionA: (1) fully-powered controls, (2) overstressing
optionB: (1) reversable controls, (2) overstressing
optionC: (1) fully-powered controls, (2) stalling
optionD: (1) reversable controls, (2) stalling
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
With a fully powered flying control the pilot is unaware of the aerodynamic force on the controls, so it is necessary to incorporate “artificial feel" to prevent the aircraft from being overstressed.

As shown schematically in the diagram, a device sensitive to dynamic pressure (1⁄2 ρ V2). Pitot pressure is fed to one side of a chamber and static pressure to the other, which moves a diaphragm under the influence of changing dynamic pressure with airspeed. This causes “regulated” hydraulic pressure to provide a resistance or ‘feel’ on the pilot’s input controls proportional to IAS2, just as in a manual control. In addition, stick force should increase as stick displacement increases.

An advantage of artificial feel is that it can be configured to provide envelope protection, which prevents the pilot over stressing the aircraft. The Boeing777 fly- by-wire system employs envelope protection. This feature of the artificial-feel system provides increasingly greater force when the aircraft is pushed to its limits.

title: Aeroplane manoeuvrability increases for a given control surface deflection when:
optionA: flaps are retracted at constant IAS.
optionB: the CG moves forward.
optionC: IAS decreases.
optionD: IAS increases.
explanationTotal:
When a control surface deflection takes place, the lift of an aerodynamic surface changes, generating more or less lift.
This changes the moment from the aerodynamic surface acting on the aircraft, resulting in aircraft pitch, roll or yaw.
The effectiveness of movement of these control surfaces increases with airspeed for a certain deflection.
This happens because the deflection of the control surface changes the CL for the airfoil on which it operates.
The effectiveness of surfaces operates through the lift formula (CL * ½ * ρ * V² * S).

So, if CL increases, lift will also increase. In this question we are talking about a constant deflection, so CL will remain stable.
Therefore, if we increase speed (v), lift will increase and so does the moment resulting from the control surface, increasing aeroplane manoeuvrability..

title: At stalling speed, the stall warning vane on the leading edge of small aeroplanes moves:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Down due to movement of the stagnation point.
optionB: Up due to movement of the stagnation point.
optionC: Down due to movement of the centre of pressure.
optionD: Up due to movement of the centre of pressure.
explanationTotal:
In aerodynamics, the stagnation point is the point in a flow field where the local velocity of the fluid (in our case the atmosphere) is zero.
This point is located on the leading edge of the wing.
Air above the stagnation point will move upwards and air below it will move downwards if looked at from the side.

If we increase the angle of attack, the stagnation point will move down, causing more air to move upwards over the upper side of the wing.
At a certain angle of attack, this air will move the stall warning upwards, letting off an audible warning horn in the cockpit.

title: Given an initial condition in straight and level flight with a speed of 1.4 V<sub>S</sub>. The maximum bank angle attainable without stalling in a steady co-ordinated turn, whilst maintaining speed and altitude, is approximately:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
explanationTotal:
Formulas you need to be familiar with:
  • Load Factor = 1 ÷ cos (bank angle)
  • Limit LF = VS2
In this case, the speed is 1.4 VS, to determine our Limit Load Factor:
  • VS2 = 1.42 = 1.96, so we know that the aircraft would stall at LF 1.96.

Use the above information on the formula Load Factor = 1 ÷ cos (bank angle):

1.96 = 1 ÷ cos (bank angle).
cos (bank angle) = 1 ÷ 1.96
cos (bank angle) = 0.51
bank angle = 59.32° ≈ 60°

Alternatively, we know that the stall speed will increase by a factor of 1 ÷ √cos a (where a is the bank angle):

√cos a = 1 ÷ 1.4
√cos a = 0.714
cos a = (0.714)2
cos a = 0.51
bank angle = 59.32° ≈ 60°

title: The stall speed line in the manoeuvring load diagram runs through a point where the:
optionA: speed = 0, load factor = +1.
optionB: speed = V<sub>B</sub>, load factor = gust load factor.
optionC: speed = V<sub>A</sub>, load factor = limit load factor.
optionD: speed = V<sub>S</sub>, load factor = 0.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
POINTS ON THE FLIGHT ENVELOPE
In the manoeuvring envelope the load factor is plotted against the vertical axis and the speed as an EAS is plotted against the horizontal axis.

  • The stall speed lines originate from a point where speed = 0 and load factor = 0. If load factor (n) is zero, no lift is being produced and the aircraft will not stall.
  • At some point, the stall speed line will run through a point where the speed = VS and load factor = +1. The stall speed lines show the maximum load factor at which the aircraft can fly without stalling. When that figure is 1, the aircraft must be at its minimum horizontal speed (VS).
  • VA is the point where n reaches its maximum value (for commuter category 2.5). VA is the design manoeuver speed, the speed at which the aircraft will stall at the limiting load factor of 2.5g.

title: (1) _____ the mass of an aircraft will lead to a (2) _____ in M<sub>CRIT</sub>.
optionA: (1) Decreasing; (2) decrease
optionB: (1) Increasing; (2) decrease
optionC: (1) Increasing; (2) no change
optionD: (1) Increasing; (2) increase
explanationTotal:
CRITICAL MACH NUMBER

Critical Mach Number (MCRIT): The critical Mach number is the Mach number of the aircraft when the speed of the airflow over some part of the aircraft (usually the point of maximum thickness on the aerofoil) first reaches the speed of sound.

An aerofoil generates lift by accelerating air over the top surface. At small angles of attack the highest local velocity on an aircraft will usually be located at the point of maximum thickness on the wing.

At increased angles of attack the local velocity will be greater and further forward. Also, if the thickness/chord ratio were greater, the local speed will be higher.

Increased thickness/chord ratio and increased angle of attack cause greater accelerations over the top surface of the wing, so the Critical Mach number will decrease with increasing thickness/chord ratio or angle of attack.

If we consider two aeroplanes maintaining a constant flight level and flying at the same IAS, one heavier and one lighter, the heavier aeroplane will be flying at a greater AoA in order to maintain a constant flight level.

As mentioned above, a higher AofA leads to a higher airflow acceleration over the upper wing surface for the heavier aeroplane, even though both are flying at the same speed.

If both aeroplanes accelerate at the same rate, the heavier aeroplane would be the first to get into a situation where the airflow over the upper surface of its wings would locally reach a sonic speed. Therefore, at the same speed, the heavier aeroplane has a lower MCRIT due to the higher AoA.

In conclusion:

Higher mass = lower MCRIT due to a greater AoA to maintain a level flight at a given speed.
Lower mass = higher MCRIT due to a smaller AoA to maintain a level flight at a given speed.

title:
An aircraft is flying straight and level at 280 kt with a CL of 0.3. The crew are warned of turbulence ahead and reduce speed to 220 kts, the turbulence penetration speed for their aircraft.
Determine the new value of CL:
explanationTotal:
Coefficient of lift decreases as speed increases. In other words, it is inversely proportional to the square of the speed change.

The new CL can be calculated using the following formula:

New CL = Old CL x 1 / (change in speed)2
New CL = 0.3 x 1 / (220/280)2
New CL = 0.49

title: Consider an aircraft flying in unaccelerated level flight in the speed stable region. How does the drag change following a sudden increase in CAS with no change in thrust available, and what will happen to the airspeed after this?
optionA: The total drag increases and the airspeed will decrease.
optionB: The total drag increases and the airspeed will further increase.
optionC: The induced drag increases and the airspeed will remain the same.
optionD: The parasite drag decreases and the airspeed will further increase.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
During flight, an aircraft will experience two types of drag:

- Parasite Drag (proportional to IAS2, increases with increasing “Parasite Area”: flaps, undercarriage or speedbrakes)

- Induced Drag (inversely proportional to IAS2, increases with increasing weight).

The sum of Parasite Drag and Induced Drag is the Total Drag.

The Total Drag will be minimum at the IAS where Parasite Drag = Induced Drag. This speed is called Minimum Drag Speed (VMD). Flying at a slower or faster speed than VMD will generate more drag.

Flying at a slower speed than VMD (back side), the aircraft will be in the unstable speed region. Any gain of speed will result in an decrease in drag and further speed increase. The sudden change to a headwind (or a decrease in tailwind) can cause a gain of airspeed.

Flying at a faster speed than VMD (front side), the aircraft will be in the stable speed region. Any increase of speed will result in an increase in drag. This increase in drag will cause the speed to decrease again (unless the thrust has changed). Therefore, a sudden increase in CAS, due to something like an increase in headwind (or a decrease in tailwind) can cause a momentary increase of airspeed, which eventually recues back to the original airspeed.

title: How do you find VMD on a polar curve graph?
optionA: Highest Point of the graph
optionB: Before the origin
optionC: Lowest point of the graph
optionD: Tangent from the origin
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The polar curve of an airfoil is the graphical relationship of the coefficients of lift and drag plotted against each other, the resulting graph is as shown in figure 1. It reveals that the total lift and total drag increase from point A to a maximum at point D, thus the angle of attack of the wings increases in the same manner. Therefore, the speed decreases from a maximum at point A to a minimum at point D.
Point B is the point at which a tangent from the origin touches the polar curve, which is at the point at which the total drag is minimum, the lift/drag ratio is maximum and the IAS in level flight is VMD. This is also the speed at which the longest glide distance will be achieved.

title: The lift coefficient (C<sub>L</sub>) of an aeroplane in steady horizontal flight is 0.35. An increase in angle of attack of 1 degree would increase C<sub>L</sub> by 0.079. If a vertical gust instantly changes the angle of attack by 2 degrees, the load factor will be:
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
A gust is a localized sudden and rapid change to the speed of the air in the atmosphere that can be either horizontal or vertical. The horizontal gust is of little importance because it causes a change to an airplane’s dynamic pressure that results in an insignificant change to the load factor. The vertical gusts are far more important because they change the effective angle of attack, total lift, and the load factor.
The gust load is the extra load imparted to the airplane by vertical gusts or turbulence. Its magnitude is unaffected by increased altitude but is increased with increased aspect ratio and/or decreased mass.
The load factor for any given angle of attack can be derived from the basic load factor for the normal cruise angle of attack because it is increased by the same percentage as the increase of angle of attack.

It can be defined by:

load factor(n) = (Lift(L))/(Weight(W))

In straight and level flight, Lift = Weight, thus n = 1.
In this exercise, the increment in CL from a gust will be of 0.079 for every degree of angle of attack impacted by the gust. We also know that the aircraft encounters a gust which increases its angle of attack by 2°.

In straight and level flight n = 1 or:

n = 0.35/0.35

A 2° increase in angle of attack,

2*0.079 = 0.158

Will give an increment of 0.45 in the CL:

0.35+0.158 = 0.508

A gust which increases the angle of attack by 2° will increase the load factor to:

n = 0.508/0.35 ≈ 1.45 g

title: The relative thickness of an aerofoil is expressed in:
optionA: degrees cross section tail angle.
optionB: meters.
optionC: camber.
optionD: % chord.
explanationTotal:
THICKNESS/CHORD RATIO

The maximum thickness or depth of an aerofoil section expressed as a percentage of the chord, with its location as a percentage of the chord aft of the leading edge. The thickness and thickness distribution of the aerofoil section have a great influence on its airflow characteristics.

title: An aeroplane in straight and level flight at 300 kt is subjected to a sudden disturbance in speed. Assuming the angle of attack remains constant initially and the load factor reaches a value of 1.44:
optionA: the speed will have increased by 30 kt.
optionB: the speed will have increased by 60 kt.
optionC: the speed will have decreased by 30 kt.
optionD: the speed will have decreased by 60 kt.
explanationTotal:
Let’s start by identifying the equations used to answer the question.

Load factor is defined as:

n = L/W

Now we replace the lift with the full equation:

L = CL ½ rho V2 S

n = (CL ½ rho V2 S) / W

By removing all the constants, we can say that:

n = (CL ½ rho V2 S) / W

n ∝ V2

To find the change in load factor (nΔ), we have to divide nNEW by nOLD:

nΔ = nNEW / nOLD

nΔ = VNEW2 / VOLD2

For those who prefer remembering equations, remember the above

This question wants us to find the VNEW so let’s rearrange the formula to make it the subject of the equation:

VNEW = √(nΔ x VOLD2)

VNEW = √(1.44 x 3002)

VNEW = 360 kt

Knowing now that the new speed is 360 and the old speed was 300, we know that there was an increase in airspeed of 60 kt.

title: An aircraft is descending from FL290 at a constant Mach number close to M<sub>MO</sub>. What must the flight crew do to avoid accidentally exceeding V<sub>MO</sub>?
optionA: At the changeover altitude the flight crew must stop flying at a Mach number and fly at an increased IAS.
optionB: At the transition level the flight crew must stop flying at a Mach number and fly at a constant IAS.
optionC: At the transition level the flight crew must stop flying at a Mach number and fly at an increased IAS.
optionD: At the changeover altitude the flight crew must stop flying at a Mach number and fly at a constant IAS.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
If the aircraft keeps descending at a constant Mach, the TAS and IAS will keep increasing, leading to a VMO overspeed situation.
Therefore, at the changeover altitude, the flight crew must stop flying at a Mach number and fly at constant IAS.

If the flight crew would fly at an increasing IAS, another VMO overspeed situation will arise, so the IAS should be kept constant.
Transition level has nothing to do with this question, as it is the altitude where one changes over from the standard altimeter setting to the local QNH.

title:
Refer to figure.
The figure shows a polar diagram of CL vs CD. Extending which of the following devices would cause the line to move from position 1 to position 2?
optionA: Flaps.
optionB: Landing Gear.
optionC: Lift dumpers.
optionD: Slats.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The polar diagram of CL vs CD is a very common one to be used in the exams. It takes every angle of attack of the wing, and plots the corresponding CL and CD values as a point on the graph. It is not as easy to read as a standard (Cartesian) graph, but once you get used to that, it becomes quite simple. The CL is the lift coefficient and the CD is the drag coefficient. Using this, we can see that the point of highest lift coefficient is at the top of the graph, and has quite a high drag coefficient too. That must be CLMAX and is therefore the point just before the stall. Before that point is the best lift to drag ratio, where the CL is highest for the lowest CD (dashed line). We can infer from this that the faster speeds are closer to the origin, and the speeds get slower as the graph continues.

We can therefore imagine what each of the options would do to the graph, and measure that up with the annex in the question.

  • "Flaps"
    • Flaps increase our CLMAX and also increase drag, so the graph would move up and to the right, which is not the same as the annex.
  • "Landing Gear"
    • Landing Gear won't affect our lift, but they will increase drag, so the graph will move to the right only, not downwards like we see in the annex.
  • "Lift dumpers"
    • Lift dumpers such as wing spoilers reduce lift (as per their name) by ruining the airflow over the wing, and increase drag through this very same method, and by putting an obstruction in the airflow. They would cause the graph to go down and to the right, which matches up with the annex.
  • "Slats"
    • Slats allow an increase in the CLMAX as they allow for higher angles of attack to be flown, but they do not increase drag by very much, so the graph would move upwards, with perhaps a slight movement to the right near the top.

title:
Following stall warning activation, what indicates that the warning is not false, and that recovery action is required?

1. Unusually low indicated airspeed on the Captain’s instruments
2. Lack of pitch authority
3. Inability to arrest the rate of descent
4. Unusually low indicated airspeed, confirmed on both sets of instruments
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: 2 and 3.
optionB: 3 and 4.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
STALL

A stall is an aerodynamic condition which occurs when smooth airflow over the airplane’s wings is disrupted, resulting in loss of lift. Specifically, a stall occurs when the AOA—the angle between the chord line of the wing and the relative wind—exceeds the wing’s critical AOA. It is possible to exceed the critical AOA at any airspeed, at any attitude, and at any power setting.

  • Impending Stall—an impending stall occurs when the AOA causes a stall warning, but has not yet reached the critical AOA. Indications of an impending stall can include buffeting, stick shaker, or aural warning.

  • Full Stall—a full stall occurs when the critical AOA is exceeded. Indications of a full stall are typically that an uncommanded nose-down pitch cannot be readily arrested, and this may be accompanied by an uncommanded rolling motion. The flying controls will feel unresponsive or “mushy”. For airplanes equipped with stick pushers, its activation is also a full stall indication.

title: An aeroplane is descending from FL 390 to ground level at maximum speed. The limit(s) in speed is (are):
optionA: M<sub>MO</sub> only during all the descent.
optionB: V<sub>MO</sub> only during all the descent.
optionC: initially M<sub>MO</sub>, then V<sub>MO</sub> below a given flight level.
optionD: initially V<sub>MO</sub>, then M<sub>MO</sub> below a given flight level.
explanationTotal:
In cruise, and generally at higher levels, for the same VMO, the TAS and Mach number increase due to the decrease in density. Therefore, at high levels, it is very unlikely that you reach the VMO. But let’s suppose you’re trying to reach the VMO (just to illustrate this relationship). By accelerating to reach the VMO, which is an IAS, your TAS and your Mach number will increase, and you will most likely reach your MMO before the VMO.

In the same way, at low levels close to the ground, the IAS and the TAS are very close because of the higher density, therefore the VMO becomes the limiting speed. To reach the MMO at a low level, you will need to drastically increase your TAS, which is impossible as you will reach the VMO and damage your structure way before.

title: As the Mach number increases in straight and level flight, a shock wave on the upper surface of the wing will:
optionA: move towards the trailing edge.
optionB: disappear.
optionC: not move.
optionD: move towards the leading edge.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
An airplane does not have to be flying at the local speed of sound for the airflow over the wings to be supersonic. A normal shockwave can develop at any time the airplane is in the transonic speed range. The function of the wing is to accelerate the air passing over its upper surface. The airflow may be subsonic at the leading edge of the wing but can be accelerated to become supersonic by the trailing edge of the wing, despite the fact that the airplane is flying at a speed of less than Mach 1.0. This is transonic flight, which usually occurs between Mach 0.75 and Mach 1.2.

At speeds less than Mach 0.75 all the airflow over the wing is subsonic and as the airplane accelerates the first shockwave will form on the upper surface at the wing root.

When the air over the upper surface of the wing becomes sonic, a shockwave forms because the pressure waves over the rear of wing at the wing root are attempting to move forward and meet the air moving aft from the leading edge at exactly the same speed but in the opposite direction. The meeting point is usually just aft of the point of maximum camber because this is where the air over the upper surface of the wing is accelerating at the greatest rate.

The meeting point of the two air-pressure waves is the shockwave and is where the airflow changes from being sonic or supersonic to become subsonic. Air passing through the shockwave experiences an increase of pressure, temperature, and density. If the airplane speed continues to increase the area of supersonic air on top of the wing spreads backward towards the trailing edge, resulting in the shockwave moving aft.

title: Given two identical aeroplanes with wing mounted engines, one fitted with jet engines and the other with counter rotating propellers, which of these statements is correct about roll behaviour after an engine failure?
optionA: The propeller aeroplane has more roll tendency.
optionB: Both aeroplanes have the same roll tendency.
optionC: The roll tendency on the propeller powered aeroplane is more pronounced when the left engine fails than when the right engine fails.
optionD: The propeller aeroplane has less roll tendency.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
In the event of an engine failure of a multi-engine airplane the strength of the asymmetric yawing moment caused by its failure is dependent on the distance of the failed engine from the CG, measured at right angles to the longitudinal axis. The further outboard the failed engine is located the greater is the induced yawing moment.

Because the engines of a propeller-driven airplane have to be mounted on the wing sufficiently far from the fuselage to account the necessary propeller clearance then these airplanes always experience a large yawing moment when an engine fails that may be difficult to control. This is not so with a jet airplane because the wing-mounted engines on these airplanes can be mounted relatively close to the fuselage thus creating a relatively short moment arm, which produces a small yawing moment that is easier to control. In such a situation the propeller-driven airplane also has a greater tendency to roll than the jet-propelled airplane.

On suffering an engine failure, the unbalanced thrust and drag produces a yawing moment that must be counteracted by the deflection of the rudder. The side force generated by the rudder deflection when multiplied by the moment arm (the distance that the center of pressure of the rudder is from the CG) has to produce a counteracting moment equal to and opposite to the yawing moment.

title: Which of the following provides a positive contribution to static directional stability?
optionA: Moving the centre of gravity aft.
optionB: A low wing as compared with a high wing.
optionC: A dorsal fin.
optionD: A forward swept wing.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
To overcome the instability in the fuselage it is possible to incorporate into the overall design dorsal or ventral fins. A dorsal fin is a small aero foil, of very low aspect ratio, mounted on top of the fuselage near the rear. A ventral fin is mounted below.

If the aircraft is yawed to the right, the dorsal and ventral fins will create a side force to the right. The line of action of this force is well aft of the aircraft CG, giving a yawing moment to the left (a stabilizing effect). However, at small angles of yaw they are ineffective.

Dorsal and ventral fins become more effective at relatively high sideslip angles. Due to their low aspect ratio, they do not tend to stall at any sideslip angle which an aircraft is likely to experience in service.

While dorsal and ventral fins contribute positively to directional static stability, a dorsal fin contributes positively to lateral static stability, while a ventral fin is destabilizing in this mode and has no effect on longitudinal stability.

title: A positively cambered aerofoil will generate:
optionA: zero lift at a positive angle of attack.
optionB: zero lift at zero angle of attack.
optionC: zero lift at a negative angle of attack.
optionD: lift at all angles of attack.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Camber is the asymmetry between two acting surfaces on an airfoil. For an aircraft, this is the top and the bottom of the wing. Positive camber means that a wing is thicker on the top end of the wing, than on the bottom if looked at from the chord. In case of positive camber, a wing will generate lift with airspeed, as the air on top of the airfoil will get accelerated more than on the bottom, creating a low pressure on the top and high pressure at the bottom. This is “pushing” the wing up into the air as the pressure difference wants to restore itself to 0 difference. In case of negative camber, the exact opposite happens and the lift coefficient for a certain speed is lower than for a positively cambered wing.

A completely symmetrical airfoil will intersect the vertical axis of the graph at the origin (0). A positively cambered airfoil will generate more lift at the same speed (and therefore has a higher CL) than a symmetrical airfoil and therefore intersects the vertical axis above the origin (and generates 0 lift at a negative angle of attack). A negatively cambered airfoil will generate less lift at the same speed (which translates into a lower CL at a certain speed) and therefore intersects the vertical axis below the origin.

The camber of an airfoil can be increased with the use of flaps. The end of the wing reaches out and/or downwards, changing the side profile of the wing and moving the CP aft, resulting in a nose down pitching moment. This generates a higher value of CL at the same Angle of Attack. Therefore if flaps are being retracted, the Angle of Attack should be increased.

title: Which one of the following statements is true with regards to the first stage of spin?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Spinning motion and the forces have not been equalized yet.
optionB: The forces have been stabilized.
optionC: Spinning motion decrease and forces stabilize.
optionD: Spinning motion will increase exponentially until the aircraft crashes.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
SPIN. A stall must occur before a spin can take place. A spin occurs when one wing stalls more than the other.

There are three phases of spin:

  1. INCIPIENT phase - exists from the time the aeroplane stalls and rotation starts until the spin is fully developed. During this phrase, the aerodynamic forces are not balanced and the aircraft is more or less tumbling.
  2. DEVELOPED phase - begins when the aerodynamic forces are in balance (the angular rotation rates, airspeed and vertical descent rate are stabilized from one turn to the next). The spin, although chaotic looking from inside the cockpit, has been established and recovery procedures are now necessary to break the spin.
  3. RECOVERY phase - controls are applied to stop spin, recover from the unusual attitude and maintain straight and level.

title:
Choose the correct answers. In a balanced coordinated turn, with the same bank angle, an increase in speed will:

1. Increase Rate of Turn.
2. Decrease Rate of Turn.
3. Increase Radius of Turn.
4. Decrease Radius of Turn.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Radius of turn is dependent on both airspeed and bank angle.

  • Turn Radius = V2 / g tan Ø
    Where V = True Airspeed, g = acceleration of gravity constant of 9.81 m/s2, Ø = angle of bank

The radius of turn at any given bank angle is directly proportional to the square of the airspeed. Which means that doubling the airspeed results in a radius of turn that is four times greater.

Rate of turn is the rate of change of heading or angular velocity of the turn.

  • Rate of turn = g tan Ø / V
Increasing the speed results in a decrease of rate of turn. Whereas increasing bank angle also increases the rate of turn.

title: Ice contamination on a wing will cause (1) _____ in stall speed and (2) _____ critical angle of attack.
optionA: (1) an increase; (2) a decrease
optionB: (1) no change; (2) a decrease
optionC: (1) an increase; (2) no change
optionD: (1) a decrease; (2) an increase
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The formation of ice and frost on the airframe will:
- modify the profile of the aerofoil.
- increase the roughness of the aircraft surface.
- increase the weight of the aircraft.

The CL of an aerofoil increases with angle of attack up to a maximum (CLMAX). Any further increase above this stalling angle, or critical angle of attack, will make it impossible for the airflow to smoothly follow the upper wing contour, and the flow will separate from the surface, causing CL to decrease and drag to increase rapidly.

A stall is caused by airflow separation. Separation can occur when either the boundary layer has insufficient kinetic energy or the adverse pressure gradient becomes too great.

The formation of ice along a wing's leading edge greatly alters its aerodynamic contour and leads to premature separation of the boundary layer. This reduces the wing's stalling angle of attack and also its maximum coefficient of lift by up to 50%

The increase in stall speed due to ice formation is not easy to quantify, as the accumulation and shape of the iceformation is impossible to predict. Ice or frost must never be allowed to remain on any aerodynamic surfaces in flight, nor must ice, frost, snow or other contamination be allowed to remain on the aircraft immediately before flight.

title: Which of the following terms refers to the maximum altitude at which an aircraft can climb at a sustained rate of 100 feet per minute under standard atmospheric conditions?
optionA: Operational Ceiling
optionB: Absolute Ceiling
optionC: Service Ceiling
optionD: Service Ceiling with One Engine Inoperative
explanationTotal:
Absolute ceiling is the highest altitude to which the aircraft can climb, where thrust = drag, so with no excess of thrust the rate (and gradient) of climb is zero.

Service Ceiling The pressure altitude at which the rate of climb is reduced to a specified minimum value of 100 ft/min for propeller aircraft and 500 ft/min for a jet aircraft

Aerodynamic Ceiling is where "coffin corner" comes to a point, and where low speed buffet and high speed buffet meet each other at a single speed that the aircraft can fly, no faster or slower.

Note: We cannot find any suitable learning objectives for this question in Principles of Flight, but reports show that it has been seen in this subject.

title: The maximum cruise altitude can be limited by a 1.3 g load factor because when exceeding that altitude:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: use of normal manoeuvring bank angles may cause the limit load factor to be exceeded.
optionB: turbulence may cause the limit load factor to be exceeded.
optionC: turbulence may induce high speed or low speed buffet.
optionD: high speed buffet will occur immediately after exceeding this maximum altitude.
explanationTotal:
High-speed buffet is the rapid movement of the control surfaces caused by turbulent airflow passing over them. It can only occur when the Mach number is above the critical Mach number and is likely to be accompanied by a tendency for the airplane to pitch nose-down.

The maximum operating altitude of an airplane can be restricted by the load factor. Above that altitude any turbulence may induce Mach buffet, which could cause the airplane to exceed the maximum permitted load factor.

The airflow behind a shockwave is turbulent and can cause a rapid vibrating movement of the horizontal stabilizer surfaces and is often referred to as the ‘shock stall’ and is the primary cause of high-speed buffet. A secondary cause of the rapid movement of the control surfaces, especially with supercritical airfoil sections, is when the wing reaches a speed of MCRIT the relatively weak shockwave that forms moves rapidly backward and forward over the surface of the wing producing similar indications to those of the shock stall.

title: Assuming constant IAS, when an aeroplane leaves ground effect:
optionA: the effective angle of attack increases.
optionB: the induced angle of attack increases.
optionC: the effective angle of attack does not change.
optionD: induced drag decreases.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
When an airplane flies at a height equal to or less than the length of its wingspan the efficiency of its wings is considerably improved. A low wing airplane, just before touchdown, experiences a 50% reduction of its total drag. This phenomenon is ground effect.
Ground effect occurs because the surface alters the airflow pattern around the wings. Primarily, the surface restricts the formation of the wingtip vortices.
When an aircraft enters ground effect during the landing phase of flight, the sudden increase in lift and reduction in drag cause it to experience a floating tendency. The aircraft also tends to pitch nose-down due to the reduction in download on the tail plane.
The magnitude of the wing tip vortices, and thus downwash, also determine the amount of induced drag produced by the wing. The closer the aircraft is to the surface, the greater the reduction in induced drag at any given angle of attack.

Aircraft entering ground effect:

  • Downwash decreases.
  • The effective angle of attack increases.
  • Increased lift during landing if the angle of attack remains constant.
  • The induced angle of attack decreases.
  • Induced drag decreases.
Aircraft leaving ground effect:
  • Downwash increases.
  • The effective angle of attack decreases.
  • Decreased lift during take-off if the angle of attack remains constant.
  • The induced angle of attack increases.
  • Induced drag increases.

title: From a certification point of view, CS-23 and CS-25 state that an aeroplane must be statically stable and possess a certain level of controllability and manoeuvrability. The relationship between stability and manoeuvrability is that an aeroplane…
optionA: must have augmentation systems in order to be statically stable and have an acceptable level of manoeuvrability.
optionB: has the same level of manoeuvrability regardless of the level of static stability coupled with any size of control surfaces.
optionC: that is statically stable will only be manoeuvrable if designed using the principle of relaxed static stability.
optionD: with a given size of control surfaces will have slightly decreasing manoeuvrability with increasing static stability.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Static stability pertains to how a system reacts immediately when disturbed. In a statically stable system, it initially moves back toward its equilibrium state. An aircraft's type of static stability is defined by its initial reaction after some external force is removed. We use the term "static" because we're only concerned with the initial tendency to return to equilibrium, without considering subsequent motion.

Now, let's differentiate between two essential concepts:

  • Controllability: This refers to the pilot's ability to control the aircraft using inputs. It involves the pilot's capacity to guide the airplane effectively.

  • Manoeuvrability: This relates to the aircraft's ability to change its position or attitude in response to pilot inputs, allowing it to perform various maneuvers.

CS-23 and CS-25 are certification requirements that establish standards for aircraft design and performance. These regulations mandate that an airplane must exhibit static stability and meet specific criteria for controllability and manoeuvrability. In general, an aircraft with static stability is easier to control, and its movements are more predictable.

The connection between manoeuvrability and stability is such that as an aircraft's static stability increases, an aircraft equipped with a particular size of control surfaces may experience a slight reduction in manoeuvrability. This is because static stability characterizes the aircraft's capacity to reestablish its initial position following a disturbance. In essence, a statically stable aircraft tends to oppose alterations in its attitude, which can introduce increased challenges when manoeuvring, especially in specific situations.

title: In twin engine aeroplanes with propellers turning clockwise as seen from behind:
optionA: the left engine produces a higher yaw moment if the right engine fails than vice versa.
optionB: the left engine is the critical engine.
optionC: the right engine is the critical engine.
optionD: the ‘minimum control speed’ is determined by the failure of the right engine.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
For a multi-engine airplane, the largest asymmetric thrust moment occurs when an outboard engine fails. That engine failure which most adversely affects the performance is deemed the critical power unit and is used to determine the limiting control speeds that will ensure adequate directional control in such an event.

During a crosswind take-off an airplane tends to weathercock into wind. Because of this the failure of the outboard engine on the windward side of the airplane is the most difficult to counteract and is, therefore, the critical engine for jet-propelled aircraft.

For propeller-driven airplanes the direction of propeller rotation determines the critical engine. Viewed from behind, a clockwise rotation dictates that the outboard left engine is critical.

title: Considering the polar curve of a subsonic aerofoil, the maximum lift-to-drag ratio is determined by...
optionA: drawing a tangent to the curve from the origin.
optionB: the maximum value of the lift coefficient.
optionC: the point where total lift and total drag are equal.
optionD: the minimum value of the drag coefficient.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The polar curve of an airfoil is the graphical relationship of the coefficients of lift and drag plotted against each other, the resulting graph is as shown in figure 1. It reveals that the total lift and total drag increase from point A to a maximum at point D, thus the angle of attack of the wings increases in the same manner. Therefore, the speed decreases from a maximum at point A to a minimum at point D.
Point B is the point at which a tangent from the origin touches the polar curve, which is at the point at which the total drag is minimum, the lift/drag ratio is maximum and the IAS in level flight is VMD. This is also the speed at which the longest glide distance will be achieved.

title: What happens to a wing's critical angle of attack when it enters ground effect?
optionA: Decreases
optionB: Increases
optionC: Remains unchanged
optionD: Increase then decreases
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
GROUND EFFECT

When an aeroplane flies at a height equal to or less than the length of its wingspan the efficiency of its wings is considerably improved. A low-wing aeroplane, just before touchdown, experiences a 50% reduction of its total drag.

This phenomenon is ground effect, which is only experienced for conventional aeroplanes during the initial climb phase after take-off and the final descent phase during landing.

At low airspeeds it is considered that the air is non compressible and, because of the close proximity of the earth’s surface, the upwash of air ahead of the wing is reduced. Thus, because of the diminished negative lift, the downwash over the upper surface of the wing does not have to be as large as it would be normally. This enables the aeroplane to maintain level flight at a lower than usual angle of attack, which decreases the induced drag and improves the efficiency of the wing.

The consequences of operating in ground effect at a constant IAS are:

- Decreased upwash and downwash angles produce smaller wing-tip vortices.
- Increased Cl.
- Significantly decreased induced drag coefficient; by approximately 8% at a height equal to half
wingspan and reduced by considerably more at any lower height.
- Decreased total drag (no effect on parasite drag).
- Decreased angle of attack for a given lift coefficient.
- Increased angle of attack for a constant IAS.
- Decreased stalling angle of attack.
- Decreased induced angle of attack.
- Increased lift, if the pitch attitude remains constant.
- Increased speed for a constant thrust setting.
- Increased float distance on landing, if the angle of attack is constant, increasing the total landing distance.
- The lift vector is inclined forward, which decreases the thrust required.
- Less thrust and power are required to fly at the same speed.

title:
Which of these statements about the limiting value of 5 degrees bank angle during VMCA determination are correct or incorrect?

I. When the bank angle is decreased from 5 degrees to 0 degrees, the value of VMCA will remain approximately constant.
II. When the bank angle is increased beyond 5 degrees, there is a increasing risk of fin stall.
optionA: I is correct, II is correct.
optionB: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
optionC: I is correct, II is incorrect.
optionD: I is incorrect, II is correct.
explanationTotal:
VMCA is the calibrated airspeed at which, when the critical engine is suddenly made inoperative, it is possible to maintain control of the airplane with that engine still inoperative and maintain straight flight with an angle of bank of not more than 5°.

With regards to this question,

  1. When the bank angle is decreased from 5 degrees to 0 degrees, the value of VMCA will remain approximately constant. INCORRECT
When an engine failure occurs during level flight, in order to maintain wings level, a lot of rudder input is necessary. An increase in bank (usually around 2-5º bank angle), reduces the required rudder input, which provides more controllability, decreasing VMCA. But when decreasing the bank angle below 5º (to 0º), rudder deflection has to be increases and, therefore, VMCA will increase too.
  • VMCA is certified with a bank angle of not more than 5º towards the operating engine, because a lower figure can be obtained compared with wings level.
  1. When the bank angle is increased beyond 5 degrees, there is an increasing risk of fin stall. CORRECT
An increased bank angle beyond 5º, while keeping the rudder centred, may lead us to encounter a new dangerous situation – sideslip towards the live engine, which could possibly send the fin’s angle of attack beyond critical alpha, leading to a fin stall. Control of the aircraft will be immediately lost.

title:
You are in a power-on descent with a glide angle of 30º. Given:

Mass: 12 000 kg
Drag: 12 330 N
Thrust: 11 030 N

Calculate the lift.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Power-on descent

Weight is split into 2 components:

  • W cos y acts perpendicular to the flight path and balances lift;
  • W sin y acts forward along the flight path, adding to Thrust to balance drag.

Lift is less than Weight: Lift only has to balance the component of weight which acts perpendicular to the flight path (L = W cos y).
Thrust is less than drag: Weight gives a forward component in the same direction as thrust.

For a power-on descent, we get the following formulas:

D = T + W sin y
T = D – W sin y
L = W cos y

  • With regards to this question:
    L = W cos y
    L = 120 000 N x cos (30) = 103 923 N

title: As angle of attack is increased on a conventional low speed aerofoil at low subsonic speeds, flow separation normally starts on the:
optionA: upper surface near the leading edge.
optionB: upper surface near the trailing edge.
optionC: lower surface near the trailing edge.
optionD: lower surface near the leading edge.
explanationTotal:
The lift from a wing is generated by airflow over it from front to back. If the span-wise flow increases, the boundary layer on the wing surface travels for longer. This causes them to be thicker and more susceptible to transition to turbulence or flow separation. The normal tip vortice on a swept wing joins up with a leading edge separation bubble, creating a larger vortex called the Ram’s horn vortex. This vortex goes inboard along the wing’s leading edge. The downward flow from the vortex induces pressure on the boundary layer at the wingtip, whereas on straight wings the exact opposite occurs. With a swept wing, this creates a slow-moving layer of air at the wing tip. This slow-moving air will separate into disturbed flow and will then stall the tip.

As the wingtips for a swept wing are positioned aft of the center of pressure (CP), the center of pressure upon a wing tip stall will move forward, creating a nose up moment. This nose up moment will further increase the Angle of Attack if not corrected in time, increasing the layer of slow-moving air, worsening the situation. Due to the decreased downwash on the elevator, the elevator could be less responsive, creating a so called deep stall. Unswept wings do not have this problem.

The pitch up phenomenon is a dangerous characteristic of swept wing aircraft (with a T-tail) that move at high speed. It could result in a quickly worsening stalling situation, making it very hard to recover.

title: Considering a commercial jet aircraft, which of the following is a limiting load factor?
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Note: The way the question is built, there are two correct options to choose from because they aren't specific about whether the aircraft is in clean configuration or not. From student feedback, we think that EASA is considering -1g as the correct answer, but if you get this question in your exam with these options, we strongly recommend you appeal this question. Please report back to us with further feedback so we can continue to update the options. Thank you!

title: An aeroplane slows down at high altitude towards the stall. The aircraft might be considered to have stalled even below the critical angle of attack if…
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: maximum continuous thrust is required to remain in level flight.
optionB: control effectiveness reduces, such that large deflection is needed to maintain wings level.
optionC: the coefficient of lift decreases with increased angle of attack.
optionD: buffet is so strong that it deters the pilot from further speed reduction.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
When an airplane is flying, the airflow over the wings creates lift. As the angle of attack (AOA) increases, the lift generated by the wings also increases. However, at a certain AOA, the smooth flow of air over the wings is disrupted, and the airflow separates from the wing's surface. This leads to a sudden loss of lift, which is known as a stall.

Option a) "maximum continuous thrust is required to remain in level flight." is not correct because the need for maximum continuous thrust to maintain level flight is not necessarily an indication of a stall.

Option b) "control effectiveness reduces, such that large deflection is needed to maintain wings level." is also not correct because while control effectiveness may reduce as the AOA increases, it is not a definitive indicator of a stall.

Option c) "the coefficient of lift decreases with increased angle of attack." is a true statement about the coefficient of lift, but it does not necessarily indicate a stall.

Option d) "buffet is so strong that it deters the pilot from further speed reduction." is the correct answer because when an airplane approaches a stall, the airflow over the wings becomes turbulent, which can cause buffeting or vibration of the aircraft. If the buffeting is strong enough, it can deter the pilot from further reducing the speed, as it is an indication that the airplane is approaching a stall. Therefore, strong buffeting is a definitive indicator of an imminent stall.

title: Dividing lift by weight gives:
optionA: load factor.
optionB: aspect ratio.
optionC: lift – drag ratio.
optionD: wing loading.
explanationTotal:
The Load Factor is the ratio of lift compared to weight of the aircraft denoted by "n":

Load Factor (n) = Lift (L) / Weight (W)

The value of load factor in steady wings level horizontal flight is exactly 1(g). Load factors greater or less than one (or even negative) are the result of maneuvers or wind gusts. The value is less than one in a steady wings level climb, because a vertical component of thrust is balancing some of the weight. So the value of wing lift required is less.

  • Turning. In a horizontal coordinated turn, load factor is always higher than 1 (n = 1 / cos Ø).
  • Climb and Descent. In a climb or descent, n < 1 (L = W cos y)

title: Which statement is correct at the speed for minimum drag (subsonic)?
optionA: The gliding angle is minimum (assume zero thrust).
optionB: Propeller aeroplanes fly at that speed at max. endurance.
optionC: The CL/CD ratio is minimum (assume zero thrust).
optionD: Induced drag is greater than the parasite drag.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
In simple words, flying at the minimum drag speed (VMD), maximum lift/drag ratio is obtained. With maximum L/D, gliding angle is minimum.

The polar curve of an airfoil is the graphical relationship of the coefficients of lift and drag plotted against each other, the resulting graph is as shown in the attached graph - where the speed decreases from a maximum at point A to a minimum at point D:

  • Point A: is between VMD and the maximum speed and has the minimum drag coefficient. It therefore approximates VY for a jet airplane.
  • Point B: is the point at which a tangent from the origin touches the polar curve, which is at the point at which the total drag is minimum, the lift/drag ratio is maximum and the IAS in level flight is VMD. This is also the speed at which the longest glide distance will be achieved and Minimum glide angle.
  • Point C: falls between VMD and VS and is approximately VMP, which approximates to the speed of VY for a piston/propeller airplane and indicates the value at which the minimum sink rate will occur. It is the speed that will attain the maximum endurance during a descent.
  • Point D: is where CL and CD are both maximum and the point at which the minimum speed in level flight, the stalling speed, VS is attained.

title:
Given a constant load factor, which of these statements is correct about the variation of induced drag with changes of speed and mass are correct or incorrect?

1. When speed increases, induced drag decreases.
2. When mass increases, induced drag decreases.
optionA: 1 is correct, 2 is correct.
optionB: 1 is incorrect, 2 is incorrect.
optionC: 1 is incorrect, 2 is correct.
optionD: 1 is correct, 2 is incorrect.
explanationTotal:
Induced drag is created as a by product of lift. The pressure differential between the top and bottom of the wing creates a upwash around the tip of the wing that turns into a downwash behind the wing. This is known as a vortex, which creates a rearward force known as induced drag.

This question is asking for the effect of:

  • Speed: The induced drag is inversely proportional to the speed. Therefore, induced drag increases as the speed decreases, and, induced drag decreases and the speed increases.
This is because, to maintain lift constant, as the velocity decreases, the coefficient of lift will have to be increased. At higher coefficients of lift, the pressure differential between the top and bottom of the wing will be greater and therefore produce stronger vortices = stronger induced drag. (and vice versa)
  • Changing mass: Induced drag is proportional to the mass. Therefore, induced drag increases with increasing aeroplane mass, and, induced drag decreases with decreasing aeroplane mass.

This is because, as the aircraft get heavier, the lift that the wings will have to produce increases. To achieve that, the coefficient of lift will have to increase, meaning a higher AoA, which creates stronger vortices. (and vice versa)

Summary:

  • Higher AR = Lower induced drag
  • Higher AoA = higher induced drag
  • Higher weight = higher AoA = higher induced drag
  • Higher speed = lower AoA = lower induced drag
  • Winglets = lower induced drag.

title: Aircraft can be certified under either CS-23 or CS-25 specifications. How do the positive limiting manoeuvring load factors of these two specifications compare to each other?
optionA: They are the same for CS-23 and CS-25.
optionB: CS-23 factors are higher.
optionC: CS-25 factors are higher.
optionD: They depend on the aeroplane's mass, NOT on the CS regulations.
explanationTotal:
Learning Objective 081.06.02.01.06: State all the manoeuvring load-factors limits applicable to CS-23 and CS-25 aeroplanes.

For the CS-25 category, the maximum positive and minimum negative limitation of load factor is:
nMAX = 2.5; nMIN = -1 in clean configuration (high lift devices not extended)

The CS-23 category includes three subparts of aircraft (not including commuter):

Normal [N] nMAX = 3.8 nMIN = -1.52
Utility [U] nMAX = 4.4 nMIN = -1.76
Aerobatic [A] nMAX ≥ 6

nMIN ≤ 3

As you can see above, the lowest level of CS-23 aircraft has a maximum positive limiting load factor of 3.8 g, whereas a CS-25 aircraft has a maximum positive limiting load factor of 2.5 g, so CS-23 limits are higher.

title: In straight and level flight, the spanwise flow on an unswept wing is from the...
optionA: lower surface via the trailing edge to the upper wing surface.
optionB: lower surface to the upper surface via the wing tip.
optionC: upper surface via the trailing edge to the lower wing surface.
optionD: upper surface to the lower surface via the wing tip.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Whenever a wing produces lift, concentrated vortices form at the wing tips. The vortices are strongest at the wing tips and become progressively weaker toward the centerline of the aircraft.

The third dimensional flow is the movement of air laterally as it moves to the aft edge of the airfoil. This is called spanwise flow. As shown in figure 1 the resulting air-pressure distribution around an airfoil, caused by its movement through the air, is that for all positive angles of attack in level flight there is an excess area of low pressure above the upper surface of the airfoil. Thus, air will flow from the relatively high pressure under the lower surface around the wing tip to the lower pressure over the upper surface.

Consequently, the flow of air moves outward from the wing root towards the wing tip on the lower surface and from the tip inwards towards the wing root on the upper surface.

This is spanwise flow and is a slightly diagonal movement of the rearward airflow. Thus, the airflow over the two surfaces
is moving in different directions when they meet at the trailing edge of the airfoil causing vortices to form along its entire length.

title: In asymmetric flight, rudder is used to stop yaw and ailerons to bank towards the live engine. The bank angle must be limited to prevent...
optionA: increasing the side force on the fin from sideslip.
optionB: the possibility of a fin stall or structural failure of the vertical tailplane.
optionC: the rudder from losing authority to stop the yaw.
optionD: excessive loss of the vertical component of lift.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
When an engine fails on a multi-engine aircraft there will be a decrease in thrust and an increase in drag on the side with the failed engine:

  • airspeed will decay.
  • the nose will drop and.
  • most significantly, there will be an immediate yawing moment towards the failed engine.
The forces and moments acting on an aircraft following failure of the left engine are shown in figure 1. The aircraft has a yawing moment towards the dead engine. The pilot has applied rudder to stop the yaw. The vital action when an engine fails is to stop the yaw.
Rudder is used to prevent yaw, and the wings are maintained level with aileron. Yawing towards the live engine gives a sideslip force on the keel surfaces opposite to the rudder force. If the sideslip angle is too large, the fin could stall.
It is more aerodynamically efficient to balance the rudder side force by banking towards the live engine, so that lift gives a sideways component opposite to the rudder force. The angle of bank must not exceed 5°, to prevent excessive loss of vertical lift component.

title: What is correct regarding Minimum glide angle?
optionA: Best distance to change in height ratio.
optionB: Best time to change in height ratio.
optionC: Best distance to fuel ratio.
optionD: Best time to fuel ratio.
explanationTotal:
Minimum Glide Angle = Minimum Angle during Glide

Minimum glide angle corresponds to (CL/CD)MAX. Minimum glide angle is important to determine the maximum range we can glide from a given height.

The tangent (tan) of the glide angle (a) is equal to the change in height (h) divided by the distance flown (d).

title: When the CG position is moved forward, the elevator deflection to achieve an increase in load factor will be:
optionA: unchanged.
optionB: smaller.
optionC: dependent on trim position.
optionD: larger.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

The static longitudinal stability of an airplane is defined by the tendency to return to equilibrium upon displacement. In other words, a stable airplane will resist displacement from trim or equilibrium. The control forces of the airplane should reflect the stability of the airplane and provide suitable reference to the pilot for precise control of the airplane.

The position of the CG not only affects the positive longitudinal static stability, it also affects the pitch handling characteristics. When the elevators are deflected, the pitching moment they produce must be greater than the restoring moment of the airplane’s positive longitudinal static stability.

For any given elevator deflection there is a small response if the aircraft CG is located forward (i.e. stable condition) and a large response for the same angle of deflection when the aircraft CG is located at an aft position (i.e. a less-stable condition). The elevator deflection required to counter a forward CG movement during a maneuver having a load factor greater than one is increased.

title: In the event of failure of the Mach trimmer:
optionA: the aeroplane mass must be limited.
optionB: the centre of gravity must be moved aft.
optionC: the speed must be kept constant.
optionD: the Mach number must be limited.
explanationTotal:
As speed increases beyond the Critical Mach number (MCRIT), shock wave formation at the root of a swept-back wing will:
  • reduce lift forward of the CG (CP moves rearward), and
  • reduce downwash at the tail plane.

Together, these factors will generate a nose-down pitching moment.

At high Mach numbers, an aircraft will become unstable with respect to speed; instead of an increasing push force being required as speed increases, a pull force becomes necessary to prevent the aircraft accelerating further.

A small increase in Mach number will give a nose-down pitch which will further increase the Mach number. This in turn leads to a further increase in the nose-down pitching moment. This unfavorable high-speed characteristic, known as “Mach Tuck”, “High Speed Tuck” or “Tuck Under” would restrict the maximum operating speed of a modern high-speed jet transport aircraft.

To maintain the required stick force gradient at high Mach numbers, a Mach trim system must be fitted. It is operational at high Mach numbers in the transonic speed range. In the event of this equipment failing, the speed is limited to specified Mach number.

title:
Refer to figure.
The attached figure shows an aeroplane in cruise flight suffering an engine failure with significant damage. The pilot knows that if they enter the clouds it will cause significant turbulence making it more difficult to handle the failure. To avoid entering the clouds and to maintain its current flight path tracking, the pilot must apply...
optionA: right rudder to balance any yawing moments and maintain straight flight, and right aileron to generate a sideslip towards the live engine, achieving a net zero sideslip.
optionB: right rudder as this will cause the aeroplane to continue coordinated flight as the rudder will offset the left yawing moment from the live engine.
optionC: right aileron as this will cause the aeroplane to sideslip towards the live engine and offset the yaw created by the live engine as well as achieving coordinated flight.
optionD: left rudder as this will cause the aeroplane to sideslip towards the live engine and reduce the effect of asymmetric thrust along the flight path.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
ENGINE FAILURE

If one engine on a conventional twin-engine aircraft fails in flight, it adversely affects its performance and controllability.

With both engines operating at the same power setting on a twin-engine aircraft, the amount of thrust produced by each engine is identical and their lines of action are symmetrically displaced about the aircraft's normal axis.

If one engine fails in flight, the remaining thrust forces are asymmetrically displaced and the aircraft yaws in the direction of the failed engine.

YAWING MOMENT

The yawing moment is the product of thrust from the operating engine multiplied by the distance between the thrust line and the CG (thrust arm), plus the drag from the failed engine multiplied by the distance between the engine centre line and the CG.

The strength of the yawing moment will depend on:
- how much thrust the operating engine is developing (throttle setting and density altitude).
- the distance between the thrust line and the CG (thrust arm).
- how much drag is being produced by the failed engine.

The rudder moment, which balances the yawing moment, is the result of the rudder force multiplied by the distance between the fin CP and the CG (rudder arm)

The ability of the pilot to counteract the yawing moment due to asymmetric thrust will depend on:
- rudder displacement (affecting rudder force).
- CG position (affecting rudder arm).
- the IAS (affecting rudder force).

Rudder to Stop Yaw - Bank Towards Live Engine
It is more aerodynamically efficient to balance the rudder sideforce by banking towards the live engine, so that lift gives a sideways component opposite to the rudder force. The angle of bank must not exceed 5°, to prevent excessive loss of vertical lift component.

Banking towards the live engine also reduces the side force on the fin from sideslip, which minimizes VMC, effectively reduces the yawing moment and gives more rudder authority to stop the yaw.

The cockpit indication will be the turn needle central with the slip indicator (ball) one half diameter displaced towards the live engine. The ‘ball’ is not centred, but the aircraft is not sideslipping.

title: A large transport jet flying in a busy airspace is cleared to fly at close to its maximum altitude for its current inflight mass. At that altitude the aircraft encounters clear air turbulence, which increases the AOA for a short time with NO change in airspeed or Mach number. What is the effect of the increase in AOA on the low-speed buffet margin?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: It is NOT affected.
optionB: It decreases.
optionC: It is removed.
optionD: It increases.
explanationTotal: The low-speed buffet is caused by flow separation as the aircraft approaches the stalling angle of attack. Increasing the angle of attack will put the aircraft closer to its critical angle of attack. Thus, closer to the point at which low speed buffet is encountered. Consequently, the low speed buffet margin will decrease.

title: Which CG position with respect to the neutral point ensures static longitudinal stability?
optionA: CG and neutral point at the same position.
optionB: CG ahead of the neutral point.
optionC: CG can be ahead of or behind the neutral point as long as the forward or aft CG limits are not exceeded.
optionD: CG behind the neutral point.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.

The point where an aircraft’s total sum of a pressure field is acting upon the body is called the Center of Pressure (CP).
This is the point where the resultant vector of lift is said to be operating.
As the airfoil or Angle of attack changes (thus changing the lift coefficient), this pressure field will change and so will the center of pressure.

Aircraft longitudinal stability is directly related to Centre of Gravity (CG) position.
An aircraft with a more forward CG is more longitudinally stable than an aircraft with a more aft CG.
Placing the CG beyond the forward limit can cause an unacceptably high value of longitudinal stability, decreasing manoeuvrability by a significant amount.
Place the CG beyond the aft limit and the aircraft is too unstable, having excessive manoeuvrability.

If an aircraft is longitudinally stable, an increase in Angle of Attack (α) results in a negative pitching moment.
The nose will slightly fall down, decreasing the Angle of Attack.
If this aircraft has a decrease of Angle of Attack, the nose will come slightly upwards again, creating a positive pitching moment again by slightly raising the nose.
The point where the aircraft does not have any positive or negative static longitudinal stability, and therefore is static longitudinally neutral, is called the neutral point.
Placing the CG aft of this point makes the aircraft unstable, placing the CG forward of this point makes the aircraft stable.

title: As the stability of an aeroplane increases:
optionA: its tendency to tuck under increases.
optionB: its manoeuvrability increases also.
optionC: its manoeuvrability decreases.
optionD: there is no effect on its stability.
explanationTotal:
The point where an aircraft’s total sum of a pressure field is acting upon the body is called the Center of Pressure (CP).
This is the point where the resultant vector of lift is said to be operating.
As the airfoil or Angle of attack changes (thus changing the lift coefficient), this pressure field will change and so will the center of pressure.

Aircraft longitudinal stability is directly related to Centre of Gravity (CG) position.
An aircraft with a more forward CG is more longitudinally stable than an aircraft with a more aft CG.
Placing the CG beyond the forward limit can cause an unacceptably high value of longitudinal stability, decreasing manoeuvrability by a significant amount.

If an aircraft is longitudinally stable, an increase in Angle of Attack (α) results in a negative pitching moment.
The nose will slightly fall down, decreasing the Angle of Attack.
If this aircraft has a decrease of Angle of Attack, the nose will come slightly upwards again, creating a positive pitching moment again by slightly raising the nose.

title: Which of the following could cause a tricycle aircraft with clockwise rotating propellers to slide to the left when taking off (before rotation) from a wet runway?
optionA: Asymmetric effect
optionB: Spiral slipstream
optionC: Gyroscopic effect
optionD: Propeller drags
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The high-speed rotation of an aircraft propeller gives a corkscrew or spiraling rotation to the slipstream. At high propeller speeds and low forward speed (as in the take-offs and approaches to power-on stalls), this spiraling rotation is very compact and exerts a strong sideward force on the aircraft’s vertical tail surface.

When this spiralling slipstream strikes the vertical fin, it causes a yawing moment about the aircraft’s vertical axis.The more compact the spiral, the more prominent this force is. On clockwise-rotating propellers, the spiralling slipstream causes a yawing moment to the left.

As the forward speed increases, however, the spiral elongates and becomes less effective. The corkscrew flow of the slipstream also causes a rolling moment around the longitudinal axis.

title: Consider a manoeuvring-load diagram. Which of the following can you obtain from it?
optionA: Maximum gust load factor
optionB: Best lift to drag ratio speed
optionC: Best lift to drag ratio
optionD: Maximum load factor at stall
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
THE FLIGHT OPERATING ENVELOPE

Each type of aircraft has its own specific flight envelope, within which it can be safely operated in accordance with the EASA Certification Specifications. This is represented on a velocity against load factor, or V-n diagram.

The V-n diagram illustrates the limit load factors and limit speeds that, if exceeded, may result in permanent structural damage. The limit loads vary depending on aircraft type, but for transport category aircraft these are generally +2.5g and -1g.

At low airspeeds the stall may occur before reaching the limit load factor, but at high airspeeds the limit load factor may be reached before the stall. Gusts also affect the load factor, and the additional acceleration forces (g forces) associated with turbulence can result in structural damage (e.g. an up-gust at high airspeeds).

Important reference speeds the pilot should be aware of are

VS - Unaccelerated stall speed in the clean configuration

VA - Maximum design manoeuvring speed and is the highest speed where the aircraft will stall before it exceeds the maximum load factor

title:
Refer to figure.
Which of the figures shows the change in the total drag graph when density altitude is decreased?
optionA: Figure 1
optionB: Figure 2
optionC: Figure 3
optionD: Figure 4
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
When density altitude decreases, the air gets "thicker", meaning that there are more air particles per cubic metre, and therefore more air particles will hit our aircraft and flow over its wings per mile flown. This would increase lift and drag if we were trying to maintain the same TAS. However, to counteract this effect, we fly our aircraft at a constant IAS/CAS (Indicated Airspeed/Calibrated Airspeed), which is a simple measure of dynamic pressure. This value measures the amount of air particles hitting the aircraft, and their speed.

If we fly at a constant IAS, but descend in the atmosphere, the higher air density means that we have to fly slower to get the same amount of dynamic pressure, meaning the same amount of air particles over the wing, etc. This is a decrease in TAS (True Airspeed) for a constant IAS.

IAS directly controls our drag and our lift, as they vary proportionally to dynamic pressure, see the lift or drag equation for the mathematical proof here, it is very easy to spot.

D = (1/2 x ρ x V2)x CD x S

As dynamic pressure is 1/2 x ρ x V2, which is measured by the IAS, then drag is directly proportional to IAS, coefficient of drag, and surface area.

If the graph was for total drag against IAS, then the curve would remain in exactly the same position with decreased altitude.

As the X-axis on the graphs is TAS, not IAS, then with a decrease in altitude, the drag curve will look the same, but will be shifted to the left, due to the decreased TAS for the same IAS at lower altitudes, but as the same forces of drag exist at each point on the curve, the curve will not move up or down. The answer is therefore figure 2, moving to the left.

title: When an aeroplane has zero static longitudinal stability, the pitching moment coefficient Cm versus angle of attack line:
optionA: has a negative slope.
optionB: is horizontal.
optionC: is vertical.
optionD: has a positive slope.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
A variation of CG position can cause large changes in the static longitudinal stability. In the conventional airplane configuration, the large changes in stability with CG variation are primarily due to the large changes in the wing contribution.

As the CG is gradually moved aft, the airplane static stability decreases, then becomes neutral then unstable. The CG position which produces zero slope and neutral static stability is referred to as the “neutral point”. The neutral point may be imagined as the effective aerodynamic center of the entire airplane configuration, i.e. with the CG at the neutral point, all changes in net lift effectively occur at that point and no change in pitching moment results. The neutral point defines the most aft CG position without static instability.

As seen in figure 1, neutral static stability would be the result if the curve had zero slope. If neutral stability existed, the airplane could be disturbed to some higher or lower lift coefficient without change in pitching moment coefficient.

For an airplane to always have positive longitudinal static stability the CG must be ahead of the neutral point, so that the wing-pitching moment always exceeds the tail plane pitching moment. The further aft the neutral point is from the CG the greater is the static longitudinal stability.

title: Consider a graph showing lift coefficient vs angle-of-attack (CL vs α) for a symmetrical aerofoil. Which of the following is defined by the point which crosses the vertical axis of this graph?
optionA: Negative lift.
optionB: Positive lift.
optionC: Maximum lift.
optionD: Zero lift.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
The Coefficient of Lift is part of the total lift formula, and its job is to change the amount of lift produced by a wing, depending on the shape of the aerofoil and the angle of attack, telling us how much lift can be gained from each particle of airflow.

The angle of attack therefore massively affects the coefficient of lift of an aerofoil.
