In the sense that increasing the angle of attack increases the wing's coefficient of lift in a mostly linear fashion, up until the critical angle of attack, when the wing stalls and any further increase in angle of attack causes a steep drop-off in lift coefficient. There is a graph to show this relationship, the CL vs Alpha (AoA) graph.

The X-axis of the graph is the angle of attack (AoA) (α - Greek letter Alpha), and when the AoA is zero, a symmetrical aerofoil will not have any lift (well more precisely, it has both upwards and downwards lift of equal amounts which cancel out). However, a positively cambered aerofoil will produce some lift at zero degrees angle of attack, depending on how much camber is present. The Y-axis of the graph is the coefficient of lift (CL).

This means that the graph for a symmetrical aerofoil will go straight through the origin, as 0º AoA = 0 lift, so CL = 0. A positively cambered aerofoil will have some lift at 0º AoA, so will have a line that crosses the Y axis above the origin.

In this question, then, a symmetrical aerofoil's CL vs Alpha graph will cross the Y-axis and X-axis at the same point, so the question is asking about the origin of the graph, which means zero lift is being produced at that point.

title: All other parameters remaining constant, what happens to V<sub>A</sub> (Design Manoeuvring Speed) if the weight of an aeroplane reduces by 20%?
optionA: V<sub>A</sub> will decrease by approximately 10%.
optionB: V<sub>A</sub> will decrease by approximately 20%.
optionC: V<sub>A</sub> will increase by approximately 10%.
optionD: V<sub>A</sub> will increase by approximately 20%.
explanationTotal:
VA - is the design maneuvering speed. This is the highest speed at which the airplane will stall before exceeding the maximum load factor and does not need to exceed VC. It is not less than the stalling speed with the flaps retracted multiplied by the square root of the limiting load factor at a speed of VC.
VA is not shown on the ASI, but it should be placarded close to the ASI. For a normal category light airplane having a maximum load factor of 3.8g then:

VA = VS1G ∗ √3.8 = 1.95VS1G

If only one value of VA is quoted, then it is the speed at which the airplane will stall at the maneuvering load factor at the MTOM.
Because of this, a change of mass causes the value of VA to alter by a percentage amount equal to approximately half of the percentage mass change. An alternative calculation that may be required because of a mass change is that:

VA(New Mass) = VA(Original Mass) ∗ √( (New Mass) / (Original Mass) )

In this exercise, the ‘New Mass’ is 20% smaller than the ‘Original Mass’, which is the same as saying that New Mass=80% Original Mass .

VA(New Mass) = VA(Original Mass) ∗ √( (0.8∗Original Mass) / (Original Mass) )

VA(New Mass) = VA(Original Mass) ∗ √0.8

VA(New Mass) ≈ 0.9VA(Original Mass)

The new VA with a mass 20% smaller corresponds to 90% of the original VA, i.e. VA will decrease by approximately 10%.

title: What contributes to a tendency to Dutch Roll?
optionA: Asymmetric shock waves on the wings.
optionB: Use of straight wings instead of swept.
optionC: Larger fin area.
optionD: Yaw damper.
explanationTotal:
Learning Objectives reference 081.04.06.03.03: Describe how the asymmetric nature of shock waves on both wings, at high Mach numbers, can lead to Dutch roll.

Dutch roll is an oscillatory instability associated with swept-wing jet aircraft. It is the combination of yawing and rolling motions. When the aircraft yaws, it will develop into a roll. The yaw itself is not too significant, but the roll is much more noticeable and unstable. This is so because the aircraft suffers from a continuous reversing rolling action. Dutch roll occurs when static lateral stability is strong and static directional stability is relatively weak.Yaw dampers prevent Dutch roll on swept-wing aircraft.

Dutch roll is most common at high speed and high altitude. At high altitude and high Mach number, aerodynamic damping decreases. Decreasing both altitude and Mach number should increase damping and stop the oscillation.

The maximum achievable load factor without buffet onset at FL380 at a mass of 104 tons is approximately:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: 1.5 g at M = 0.80.
optionB: 1.75 g at M = 0.80.
optionC: 1 g at M = 0.80.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
We start this question by finding the FL380 line between FL360 and FL400 line.
To obtain maximum load factor achievable we look for a peak that occurs at M.80.
This is possible for 104 tons of weight and we get 1.5 g load factor as maximum.

title:
Determine the Drag in a straight and steady glide descent, with a glide angle of 30 degrees. Given:

Mass: 10450 kg
Lift: 103 405 N
Assume that g = 10 m/s2
optionC: 52 250 N
optionD: 90 500 N
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The forward component of Weight (W sin γ) is a product of descent angle (γ); the greater the descent angle, the greater the forward component of weight.
The forward component of weight must balance Drag for the aircraft to be in a steady glide.

For a glide descent, we get the following formulas:

D = W sin y
L = W cos y

With regards to this question:

  • W = 10 450 kg x 10 m/s2 = 104 500 N

  • D = W sin y
    D = 104 500 sin (30º)
    D = 52 250 N

title: Moving the CG of an aircraft forward will have what effect on the stall speed, VS?
optionA: V<sub>S</sub> decreases, due to an increase in critical angle of attack.
optionB: None, the CG position has NO influence of V<sub>S</sub>.
optionC: Equivalent to the effect of a decrease in mass.
optionD: Equivalent to the effect of an increase in mass.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
In straight and level flight, an aircraft has 4 main forces acting on it. They create "force couples", in that Thrust cancels out Drag and Lift cancels out Weight. Unfortunately, it is not quite that simple, as, taking Lift vs Weight for instance, the two forces do not act through the same point. Weight acts through the CG, and Lift acts through the CP (Centre of Pressure), which is located behind the CG. This creates a nose-down moment (turning force) on the aircraft.

There are a few ways to cancel out this moment, one we regularly see is low-mounted engines. This means that the thrust line will exist below the line of the drag, and will cause a small nose-up moment. That is not usually enough to cancel out the Lift vs Weight nose-down moment though, we need something else.

Our horizontal stabiliser and elevators on the tail can be used to provide another vector of lift, but this time downwards. We often see horizontal stabilisers designed as "upside-down wings" to make them more efficient at producing downforce. This pushes the aircraft tail down, which creates a nose-up moment, big enough to even out the aircraft's pitch moments. Thankfully, we can modulate this by using variable incidence tailplanes and elevator trim to produce the right amount of downforce for stable flight.

The downforce does act with our weight though, and means that our main wing has to produce even more lift to maintain level flight. The further forward the CG, the more downforce is required, and the greater lift. This is why aircraft are more efficient with an aft CG (within limits of course), as the less lift required means less induced drag.

A forward movement of CG is therefore equivalent to an increase in mass on the stall speed (VS)

title: How does V<sub>MCG</sub> change with increasing field elevation and temperature?
optionA: decreases, because V<sub>MCG</sub> is expressed in IAS, which decreases with constant TAS and decreasing density.
optionB: increases, because V<sub>MCG</sub> is related to V<sub>1</sub> and V<sub>R</sub> and those speeds increase if the density decreases.
optionC: increases, because at a lower density a larger IAS is necessary to generate the required rudder force.
optionD: decreases, because the engine thrust decreases.
explanationTotal:
In simple words, VMCG is established as being the lowest speed at which rudder effect alone is sufficient to regain and maintain directional control after a sudden engine failure.

The major factor that affects VMCG is the difference in engine thrust. VMCG will therefore be lower at higher airport elevations and at a higher OAT, due to the associated lower thrust. Conversely, VMCG will be higher at lower airport elevations and at a lower OAT.

If conditions are hot, high and humid the air is less dense. This reduces thrust and, consequently, when you lose the critical engine on take-off, there is less yawing effect from asymmetric thrust than there would be in denser air.

title: A light twin-engine piston aircraft with clockwise rotating propellers has suffered a failure of the right engine in flight. Which of the following situations would give the worst handling characteristics if the aircraft has to perform a balked landing (go-around) after touchdown?
optionA: High weight, crosswind from the right.
optionB: Low weight, crosswind from the right.
optionC: Low weight, crosswind from the left.
optionD: High weight, crosswind from the left.
explanationTotal:
In the very unlikely event of having to go-around with a failed engine after touchdown, we have to think what wind condition will be worse for asymmetric handling. Re-applying full power with only the left engine working would cause a large yawing moment to the right, so we have to work out what side crosswind will also cause a right yawing moment.

When on the ground, during take-off and landing predominantly, the aircraft will naturally want to turn into the crosswind, a process called weathercocking, that is brought on by the stabilising effect of the tail fin. Therefore, a crosswind from the right would increase the yaw of applying full power, so would be worse in this scenario.

In terms of weight, being light is better for climb performance, but a light aircraft has worse single engine handling characteristics, due to its lower momentum and angular momentum. This means that, rather unusually for principles of flight, higher weight is better for single engine handling (also it helps with banking over the live engine in flight, as the higher weight has more of an effect with less bank required).

Note: the clockwise rotating propellers do not matter in this question, the examiner is trying to confuse you with other questions about the critical engine.

title: In the event of a Mach trimmer failure, what is the appropriate course of action?
optionA: The Mach number must be limited.
optionB: The Mach number be increased.
optionC: The Mach number be decreased.
optionD: You should switch to V<sub>MO</sub>.
explanationTotal:
As speed increases beyond the Critical Mach number (MCRIT), shock wave formation at the root of a swept-back wing will:
  • reduce lift forward of the CG (CP moves rearward), and
  • reduce downwash at the tail plane.

Together, these factors will generate a nose-down pitching moment.

At high Mach numbers, an aircraft will become unstable with respect to speed; instead of an increasing push force being required as speed increases, a pull force becomes necessary to prevent the aircraft accelerating further.

A small increase in Mach number will give a nose-down pitch which will further increase the Mach number. This in turn leads to a further increase in the nose-down pitching moment. This unfavorable high-speed characteristic, known as “Mach Tuck”, “High Speed Tuck” or “Tuck Under” would restrict the maximum operating speed of a modern high-speed jet transport aircraft.

To maintain the required stick force gradient at high Mach numbers, a Mach trim system must be fitted. It is operational at high Mach numbers in the transonic speed range. In the event of this equipment failing, the speed is limited to specified Mach number.

title:
A Pilot is testing out the stalling characteristics of his aeroplane close to the stall. Calculate the coefficient of lift?

Wing area: 13.5 m2
Density: 1.225 kg/m3
Speed: 70 kts
Mass: 1300 kg
Assume g = 9.81
optionA: 1.19
optionB: 1.78
optionC: There is not enough information to calculate the coefficient of lift
explanationTotal:
Firstly lets identify the equation that we are going to use:

L = CL ½ ρ V2 S

L = lift (newtons)
In our case is 12753 N (1300 kg x 9.81 m/s2)
CL = coefficient of lift
What we are looking for.
ρ = air density (kg/m3)
Given as 1.225 kg/m3
V = velocity (m/s)
70 kts = 36.01 m/s ((70 x 1852) ÷ 3600)
S = wing Surface area (m2)
Given as 13.5 m2

Next we must re-arrange the equation to make CL the subject of the equation:

CL = (2 x L) ÷ (ρ x V2 x S)

CL = (2 x 12753) ÷ (1.225 x (36.012) x 13.5)

CL = 1.189

title: Which of the following is a definition of the coefficient of drag (C<sub>D</sub>)?
optionA: A dimensionless quantity that is used to quantify the resistance of an object whilst moving through a fluid.
optionB: A dimensionless quantity that is used to quantify the resistance of an object applied by moving against a solid.
optionC: A quantity measured in Newtons (N) of force, is used to quantify the resistance of an object in a fluid environment.
optionD: A dimensionless quantity that is used to quantify the forward propulsion of an object moving through a fluid environment.
explanationTotal:
The coefficient of drag is a generic measure of the amount of drag exerted on an object in a particular fluid flow. It is not a force, it simply dictates "how draggy" an object (a wing or aircraft in our case) is. There are a few technical definitions for it, each one is correct, and explains it in a different way.

To understand it, you must know that it is a way of comparing two objects, and how much drag force acts on them, for a specific size and dynamic pressure. The actual drag force is calculated by the formula
D = 1/2 x ρ x V2 x CD x S

where D = Drag (N)
V = True Airspeed (m/s)
CD = Coefficient of Drag
S = Wing Area (surface area) (m2)

The coefficient of drag is dimensionless, it has no units.

One of its definitions is as follows, "The Drag Coefficient (CD) is a dimensionless number that is used to quantify the resistance of an object as it moves through a fluid.", as eluded to by this question.

title: An aeroplane is flying in steady, straight and level flight at its 1g stall speed. If the pilot intends to turn left using the ailerons, the aeroplane will…
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: bank to the left provided the speed does NOT decrease below the stalling speed.
optionB: bank to the right, because the wing with the down going aileron will exceed the critical angle of attack.
optionC: maintain straight and level flight because the ailerons will be unresponsive due to flow separation.
optionD: Yaw to the left, because of increased drag due to flow separation on the downgoing aileron.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
USE OF FLIGHT CONTROLS CLOSE TO THE STALL

At low speeds normally associated with stalling, dynamic pressure is at a very low value and greater control deflection will be required to achieve the same response; also, the flying controls will feel unresponsive or “mushy”.

If an accidental stall does occur, it is vitally important that the stall and recovery should occur without too much wing drop.

Moving a control surface modifies the chord line and, hence, the angle of attack. An aircraft being flown close to the stall angle may have one wing that produces slightly less lift than the other; that wing will tend to drop.

Trying to lift a dropping wing with aileron will increase its angle of attack, and may cause the wing to stall completely, resulting in that wing dropping at an increased rate.

At speeds close to the stall, ailerons must be used with caution. On straight wing aircraft the rudder should be used to yaw the aircraft just enough to increase the speed of a dropping wing to maintain a wing’s level attitude. Swept wing aircraft basic stall requirements are designed to enable the ailerons to be used successfully up to ”stall recognition”, but small amounts of rudder can be used if smoothly applied and co-ordinated with the ailerons.

If an aileron is lowered when flying at high angles of attack, that wing could possibly stall. In that case the wing will drop instead of rising as intended.

title: Which one of the following statements is true with regard to the operation of a Mach trim system:
optionA: It only operates when the autopilot is engaged.
optionB: It operates to counteract the larger than normal forward movements of the wing centre of pressure at high subsonic airspeeds.
optionC: It only operates above a pre-determined Mach number.
optionD: It operates over the full aeroplane speed range.
explanationTotal:
Mach trim is used to trim the aircraft at high Mach numbers (e.g. B737 from Mach .615). It prevents instability and tuck under (which appears above MCRIT) due to an increased pitch down moment, which is caused the following reasons:
  • CP moves aft
  • shock waves at the wing root
  • reduced effectiveness of the tailplane
Mach trim counteracts (increases pitch up) by one of the following:
  • adjusting stabilizer
  • adjusting elevator
  • trim tank (fuel pumped to the tail)
Outcome:
  • stick force gradient will be maintained
  • longitudinal stability will be increased
  • tuck under will be avoided

Mach Trim System relates to the pitch channel of the Auto Flight Control System (AFCS). It is designed as an AFCS sub-system and is therefore, like the yaw damper, operational irrespective of whether or not the AFCS is active (autopilot engaged or disengaged). The heart of the Mach trim system is the coupler unit. This receives signals, corresponding to Mach number, from the Air Data Computer (ADC). Whenever these signals exceed the pre-set value (for the aeroplane type) the trim coupler unit releases the brake and the speed signal from the ADC is fed to the motor. This causes the stabiliser to move in such a way that the elevators are driven upward, counteracting any tendency to a "Mach Tuck-under". Internal monitoring of the system provides a failure warning in the form of the illumination of a fail indicator light. Although connected to the pitch channel the system is totally independent of the pitch control channel of the AFCS.

In other words, the Mach trim system provides speed stability at higher Mach numbers. It operates (adjusts the elevators with respect to the stabilizer as speed increases) only above certain minimum Mach number - for example on a B737-300 it is above Mach 0.615. With the Mach trim system INOP the maximum speed of the aircraft is typically limited to a lower Mach number than normally.

"Tuck-under" is the phenomena encountered by aeroplanes flying at high subsonic, transonic or supersonic speeds. In these speed regimes there is typically a significant rearward movement of the Centre of Pressure (CP). In order to prevent this becoming an uncontrollable "nose-down" pitching motion, it is necessary to provide some form of compensation. This is done by the use of a Mach Trim System. Or otherwise said the Mach trim system allows to increase the longitudinal static stability of the aircraft by changing the horizontal stabilizer according to the Mach number.

title: Considering the longitudinal stability of an aeroplane, why does the stick force per ‘g’ decrease with pressure altitude, at a given IAS?
optionA: Because increasing pressure altitude produces a smaller aerodynamic damping.
optionB: Because increasing pressure altitude produces a bigger aerodynamic damping.
optionC: Because the aeroplane has a greater longitudinal stability at higher pressure altitude.
optionD: Because the manoeuvring point is in front of the neutral point at a higher pressure altitude.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

The most direct appreciation of the maneuvering stability of an airplane is obtained from a plot of stick force versus load factor.

The airplane with positive maneuvering stability should demonstrate a steady increase in stick force with increase in load factor or “g”. The maneuvering stick force gradient - or stick force per “g” - must be positive but should be of the proper magnitude.

The stick force required is the amount of effort necessary to overcome the longitudinal static stability of the airplane. To fly the airplane at an airspeed different from that for
which it is trimmed the stick force required is dependent on the location of the CG and the size of the tail plane.

The stick force per g must have upper and lower limits to ensure that the airplane always has acceptable control characteristics.

A forward CG position increases longitudinal static stick-force stability. The magnitude of the stick force required decreases as the CG moves aft; therefore, the maximum permitted aft position of the CG is limited by the minimum acceptable value of the stick force per g.

The pitch damping of the airplane is related to air density. At high altitudes, the high TAS reduces the change in tail angle of attack for a given pitching velocity and reduces the pitch damping. Thus, a decrease in maneuvering stick force stability can be expected with increased altitude.

title: If you are flying at the rear of the drag curve and your CAS decreases, what happens to the parasite, induced and total drag?
optionA: Parasite drag increases; Induced drag decreases; Total drag increases
optionB: Parasite drag decreases; Induced drag increases; Total drag decreases
optionC: Parasite drag increases; Induced drag decreases; Total drag decreases
optionD: Parasite drag decreases; Induced drag increases; Total drag increases
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
On the rear of the Drag curve (speeds below minimum drag), with a decrease in CAS:
- Induced Drag increases
- Parasite Drag decreases
- Total Drag increases

title: Why is it bad to have too much lateral stability?
optionA: More prone to deep stall
optionB: More prone to Dutch roll
optionC: More prone to Spiral dive
optionD: More prone to spin
explanationTotal:
With a dominant lateral stability this will, when a yaw is introduced, roll the aircraft due to the lift increase on the wing into the wind. The increased induced drag on the rising wing will yaw the aircraft in the opposite direction, reversing the coupled oscillations. This is called Dutch roll. Dutch roll might occur when the lateral stability is large compared to the directional stability. Therefore, the moments involved are roll and yaw. The CG position has little influence on the lateral stability, but an aft CG will reduce the directional stability because the Moment Arm of the stabilizing moment from the fin will decrease and thus increasing the possibility of Dutch roll.
  • To reduce the aircraft tendency to Dutch roll, either the lateral stability should be decreased or the directional stability increased => anhedral would decrease the lateral stability.

title: An aircraft flying at high altitudes is subject to a(n) (1) _____ in aerodynamic damping, contributing to a(n) (2) _____ in dynamic lateral/directional stability.
optionA: (1) decrease; (2) decrease
optionB: (1) increase; (2) decrease
optionC: (1) decrease; (2) increase
optionD: (1) increase; (2) increase
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
AERODYNAMIC DAMPING

Damping is the suppression of an unwanted oscillation of a system. In an aircraft, it may be achieved manually, by an electrohydraulic system, or by aerodynamic means.

This type of damping is dependent on the viscosity of the air for its success. The denser the atmosphere, the faster the unwanted movement will be extinguished

When we make a control input, for instance a roll to the right, there is a resistance against this input due to "aerodynamic damping", which in this case, is where the down-going (right) wing gains an increased angle of attack as it is travelling down slightly, changing the relative airflow. This increases the lift slightly and resists the roll a little. This effect is influenced by air density, and in the low density of higher altitudes, the aircraft is travelling at a higher TAS, which means that the angle of attack change is smaller. This is a reduction in aerodynamic damping. All the control axes have natural aerodynamic damping in some form. which are reduced at high altitude.

At an ISA altitude of 40 000 ft, aerodynamic damping would be reduced to one-half the ISA sea level value.

High altitude, and consequently low density (high TAS), reduces aerodynamic damping, and therefore reduces dynamic stability on all axes.

title: Where does the boundary layer separation due to shock wave interaction occur on the wing?
optionA: At the leading edge.
optionB: At the trailing edge.
optionC: Along the upper surface of the wing, just before the trailing edge.
optionD: Along the lower surface of the wing, just after the leading edge.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Note: The feedback is not verified for this question, and it could therefore be slightly different in the exam. Please read it carefully in the exam and do let us know if you see it, and any differences to this question, thank you!

When an aircraft accelerates through the transonic speed range and exceeds its Critical Mach number, the air flowing over the upper wing surface will accelerate above Mach 1 first, and to slow down below Mach 1 again, it creates a normal shock wave perpendicular the upper surface of the wing. This is an incredibly thin layer of air where the particles "catch up" to each other, and along with creating the familiar "sonic boom" shockwave, increases the static pressure, temperature and density of the air as it flows through, whilst reducing the velocity of the air considerably. These effects cause the boundary layer above the wing to be very easily disturbed, inducing flow separation behind the shockwave. This separated airflow does not produce lift and this leads to the "shock stall" effect that can occur at these transonic speeds.

As can be seen on the diagram above, initially the shockwave and boundary layer separation occur on the upper surface of the wing, approximately half-way along, then move backwards as the speed increases. A smaller shockwave also occurs on the underside of the wing near the trailing edge at slightly higher speeds, also moving towards the trailing edge as the aircraft accelerates further.

Therefore, the best option here is on the upper surface, just ahead of the trailing edge. We are sceptical about that last bit of wording, but it is certainly the only possibly correct option in our opinion.

title: A Multi-Engine piston (MEP) with inward counter rotating propellers easier to control after an engine failure, when compared to an MEP with clockwise rotating propellers. Why?
optionA: The thrust line is closer to the longitudinal axis.
optionB: The thrust line is further from the longitudinal axis.
optionC: The thrust line is further from the lateral axis.
optionD: The thrust line is closer to the lateral axis.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
ENGINE FAILURE

If one engine on a conventional twin-engine aircraft fails in flight, it adversely affects its performance and controllability.

If one engine fails in flight, the remaining thrust forces are asymmetrically displaced and the aircraft yaws in the direction of the failed engine.

YAWING MOMENT

The yawing moment is the product of thrust from the operating engine multiplied by the distance between the thrust line and the CG (thrust arm), plus the drag from the failed engine multiplied by the distance between the engine centre line and the CG.

The strength of the yawing moment will depend on:
- how much thrust the operating engine is developing (throttle setting and density altitude).
- the distance between the thrust line and the CG (thrust arm).
- how much drag is being produced by the failed engine.

ASYMMETRIC BLADE EFFECT

If both engines rotate clockwise (figure 2), the right engine has a longer thrust arm. Failure of the left engine will give a larger yawing moment.

This effect will be absent on an aircraft with counter-rotating propellers, contra-rotating propellers or jet engines.

RUDDER MOMENT

The rudder moment, which balances the yawing moment, is the result of the rudder force multiplied by the distance between the fin CP and the CG (rudder arm)

The ability of the pilot to counteract the yawing moment due to asymmetric thrust will depend on:
- rudder displacement (affecting rudder force).
- CG position (affecting rudder arm).
- the IAS (affecting rudder force).

title: You are the pilot flying of a medium jet aeroplane and you are using the autopilot to maintain a constant vertical speed and the autothrust is maintaining a constant airspeed (CAS) while flying a Continuous Descent Approach (CDA). As the aeroplane is gradually slowing down from minimum clean speed of 213 kt to 180 kt, you selected approach flaps. Disregarding any other factors, the...
optionA: trajectory will initially become steeper as the flaps are extended but this reduction is offset by the slower airspeed, provided the vertical speed is maintained constant.
optionB: vertical speed must be reduced to maintain the trajectory, and when the approach speed stabilises, the autothrust will demand more thrust to maintain the speed.
optionC: vertical speed must be increased to offset the greater lift produced when the flaps are extended, and the autothrust will demand less thrust due to lower airpeed.
optionD: trajectory will become more shallow as the flaps are extended and the speed reduces, which require a higher vertical speed to be selected.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
RATE OF DESCENT

The rate of descent is the vertical speed of an aeroplane, which is usually specified in feet per minute (fpm) and is the vertical component of the forward speed of the aeroplane along the climb path.

Rate of descent depends on both the angle of descent and the speed down the flight path. The attached graph shows that there is greater excess drag at high speed than at low speeds. The shallowest angle of descent is achieved by staying slow.

This means, that the slower speed requires a lower rate of descent to maintain the same descent path.

V/S AUTOPILOT MODE

Vertical Speed is an autopilot flight guidance vertical mode. In this mode, the Flight Management and Guidance Computer (FMCG) pitch mode guides the aircraft to the target V/S. The corresponding thrust mode is SPEED or MACH.

The increase in drag associated with flap deflection requires an increased power setting in order to maintain a given airspeed and attitude, or a steady rate of descent.

In conclusion: Using the V/S autopilot mode means that the autopilot is keeping a constant rate of descent. By slowing down, the vertical speed becomes excessive and the pilot must reduce the vertical speed to maintain a constant descent path. After slowing down to the approach speed, the added drag from the configuration will demand more power/thrust from the engines to keep the airspeed constant.

title:
Refer to figure.
The image shows a flap position indicator display, which indicates the positions of the left and right trailing-edge flaps. After departure, one of the flaps has jammed during retraction and the flap position indicator displays the above indication. What control inputs are required to maintain straight flight?
optionA: Right aileron and rudder input.
optionB: Left aileron input and opposite rudder.
optionC: Left aileron and rudder input.
optionD: Right aileron input and opposite rudder.
explanationTotal:
High-lift devices are incredibly important for the operation of aircraft. Particularly for large commercial jet aircraft, the use of flaps and slats is essential to allow acceptable take-off distances and land with reasonable speeds. They are incredibly powerful, which causes a massive problem if the flaps operate differently from each other, which we call flap/slat asymmetry.

This is possible for many reasons, but a common one is if a flap extension/retraction system jams, the two flap settings will become different from each other. Flap asymmetry is worse than slat asymmetry. Flaps provide a large increase in coefficient of lift and in drag for the same angle of attack as a clean wing, whereas slats increase drag slightly, but delay the stall greatly, allowing the aircraft to fly at a much higher angle of attack. Therefore, a flap asymmetry will cause a large rolling moment away from the extend flaps. and a strong yaw towards the side of the extended flaps.

Therefore, to counteract this as pilots, we must roll towards the extended side, and yaw away from the extended side.

On this flap indicator, our right-hand flaps are at flap 15 extension, so must have jammed, and our left-hand flaps are retracting through flap 5/flap 2. We must therefore roll to the right and yaw to the left to maintain straight and level flight.

This is a flap display off the Boeing 737 and actually indicates the location of flaps and slats, if you know the order of flap extension/retraction, but the examiner wants to keep things simple by saying it is only trailing-edge flaps.

title: Ignoring downwash effects on the tailplane, extension of Fowler flaps, will produce:
optionA: a nose up pitching moment.
optionB: a nose down pitching moment.
optionC: no pitching moment.
optionD: a force which reduces drag.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

Camber is the asymmetry between two acting surfaces on an airfoil. For an aircraft, this is the top and the bottom of the wing. Positive camber means that a wing is thicker on the top end of the wing, than on the bottom if looked at from the chord. In case of positive camber, a wing will generate lift with airspeed, as the air on top of the airfoil will get accelerated more than on the bottom, creating a low pressure on the top and high pressure at the bottom. This is “pushing” the wing up into the air as the pressure difference wants to restore itself to 0 difference. In case of negative camber, the exact opposite happens and the lift coefficient for a certain speed is lower than for a positively cambered wing.

A completely symmetrical airfoil will intersect the vertical axis of the graph at the origin (0). A positively cambered airfoil will generate more lift at the same speed (and therefore has a higher CL) than a symmetrical airfoil and therefore intersects the vertical axis above the origin. A negatively cambered airfoil will generate less lift at the same speed (which translates into a lower CL at a certain speed) and therefore intersects the vertical axis below the origin.

The camber of an airfoil can be increased with the use of flaps. The end of the wing reaches out and/or downwards, changing the side profile of the wing and moving the CP aft, resulting in a nose down pitching moment. This generates a higher value of CL at the same Angle of Attack. Therefore if flaps are being retracted, the Angle of Attack should be increased.

title: The angle of attack of an aerofoil section is the angle between the...
optionA: camber line and the horizontal.
optionB: chord line and the bottom surface of the aerofoil.
optionC: camber line and the downwash.
optionD: chord line and the relative undisturbed airflow.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The angle subtended between the chord line of an airfoil and the oncoming airflow is the angle of attack.
It is represented by α or alpha and can also be referred to as Aerodynamic Incidence.

title: Which condition is least favourable handling-wise during take-off for a twin engine aircraft with the engines wing mounted, both being right hand props?
optionA: A right engine failure, with a right quartering wind.
optionB: A left engine failure, with a right quartering wind.
optionC: A left engine failure, with a left quartering wind.
optionD: A right engine failure, with a left quartering wind.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The thrust line of a clockwise rotating propeller, when viewed from the rear, is displaced to the right of the engine centre line.
If both engines rotate clockwise, the right engine will have a longer thrust arm than the left engine.
If the left engine fails, the thrust of the right engine acts through a longer thrust arm and will give a bigger yawing moment.

The critical engine is the engine, the failure of which would give the biggest yawing moment.

If we have a crosswind (quartering wind) from the left this acts on the vertical stabilizer increasing even more the yaw moment.

title: Which statement is correct about a spring tab?
optionA: At high IAS it behaves like a fixed extension of the elevator.
optionB: At low IAS it behaves like a servo tab.
optionC: Its main purpose is to increase stick force per g.
optionD: At high IAS it behaves like a servo tab.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
At low airspeeds, for some airplanes, aerodynamic balancing is not considered necessary, however, as the airspeed increases it progressively becomes a necessity because of the increasing aerodynamic load on the main control surface. Towards the leading edge of the primary control top surface is pivoted a lever.

The top of the lever is connected to the control column and the balance tab is connected to the same lever just above the pivot. Thus, movement of the control column is transmitted to the primary control surface but does not directly operate it. To ensure that the balance tab is only effective when it is required, the operating lever of the balance tab system is pivoted through a spring mounted on the elevator main control surface. This is the ‘spring tab.’

When the elevators are operated with at low airspeeds, the control column movement is fed directly to the primary control surface with no deflection of the balance tab so that there is no geometric movement between them. However, at higher speeds, one side of the spring is compressed and changes the geometric position of the balance tab relative to the main elevator control surface.

The spring causes the tab to move in the opposite direction to the main control surface at an ever-increasing angle, which is directly proportional to the increasing airspeed. Thus, the spring tab assists the pilot by reducing the stick force required to operate the main control surface to a similar level for all airspeeds. At high IAS, the spring tab behaves like a servo-tab.

title: The horn balance is used for aerodynamic balancing. It consists...
optionA: of a tab which moves opposite to the movement of the main control surface.
optionB: in locating part of the control surface behind the hinge line to protrude in the airflow.
optionC: in locating part of the control surface ahead of the hinge line to protrude in the airflow.
optionD: of a downspring which contributes to stick force stability.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Any of the control surfaces can be aerodynamically balanced by designing a portion of the control surface to be ahead of the hinge-line. This is the horn balance.
When the control surface is deflected the horn balance will produce an opposing moment to the hinge moment, which reduces the amount of force required to operate the control surface.

title:
Refer to figure.
Which type of flap re-energises the boundary layer?
optionA: 1. Plain Flap
optionB: 2. Slotted Flap
optionC: 3. Split Flap
optionD: 4. Fowler Flap
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The question figure shows 4 types of flaps:

  • Plain flap -The standard for many light aircraft, increases available lift and increases drag. Easy to manufacture
  • Slotted flap - Increases maximum lift by more than plain flaps, due to the slots allowing high velocity air through to re-energise the boundary layers, preventing separation. Increases drag also over plain flaps. Used commonly on large jet aircraft for slow flight and landing (sometimes in conjunction with the fowler flaps below).
  • Split flap - Increases drag heavily due to the open trailing edge. Very easy to manufacture.
  • Fowler flap - Complex to design and fit, but increase lift by a large amount due to the increased wing area and camber. Increase in drag over plain flaps is smaller than the increased lift, so they provide a high L/D ratio, and are often used in conjunction with multiple levels of slotted flaps on larger aircraft.

title: Mass balancing of control surfaces is used to:
optionA: ensure that the control surfaces are in the mid-position during taxiing.
optionB: limit the stick forces.
optionC: increase the stick force stability.
optionD: prevent flutter of control surfaces.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Flutter of control surfaces is a divergent oscillatory motion of a control surface caused by its natural frequency, the interaction of aerodynamic forces, inertia forces and the stiffness of the structure.

To prevent flutter, stiffness should be increased and/or the CG of the control surface should be moved forward of the control hinge by adding a balancing mass in front of the control surface hinge line (the more forward the CG of a control surface is, the more stable it will be).

Note: A low stiffness would make a control surface more susceptible to flutter because a flexible structure will keep vibrating longer after a disruption than a stiff structure.

title: What happens to the blade angle of attack and the thrust produced when the indicated airspeed (IAS) of a fixed-pitch propeller increases while in flight?
optionA: Decrease, increase
optionB: Decrease, decrease
optionC: Increase, decrease
optionD: Increase, increase
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
A fixed pitch propeller determines its relative airflow by the aircraft’s true airspeed (TAS) in the direction of flight and its RPM in the plane of rotation. The operating angle of attack will be the angle between the relative airflow and the chord line of the propeller blade. This chord line will be set at a fix angle to the plane of rotation (i.e., the blade angle or propeller pitch angle). An increase in TAS will reduce the angle of attack, which reduces the aerodynamic resultant.

During the takeoff roll, the RPM is set to maximum and the TAS is low. The angle of attack is optimum and maximum efficiency is obtained. As the aircraft continues to accelerate, the TAS will increase, which decreases the angle of attack of the blades. Less thrust will be generated and less propeller torque.

title:
Which of these statements about the limiting value of 5 degrees bank angle during VMCA determination are correct or incorrect?

I. As the bank angle is decreased from 5 degrees to 0 degrees, the value of VMCA increases.
II. When the bank angle is increased beyond 5 degrees, there is an increasing risk of fin stall.
optionA: I is correct, II is correct.
optionB: I is incorrect, II is correct.
optionC: I is correct, II is incorrect.
optionD: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
explanationTotal:
VMCA is the calibrated airspeed at which, when the critical engine is suddenly made inoperative, it is possible to maintain control of the airplane with that engine still inoperative and maintain straight flight with an angle of bank of not more than 5°.

With regards to this question,

  1. As the bank angle is decreased from 5 degrees to 0 degrees, the value of VMCA increases. CORRECT
When an engine failure occurs during level flight, in order to maintain wings level, a lot of rudder input is necessary. An increase in bank (usually around 2-5º bank angle), reduces the required rudder input, which provides more controllability, decreasing VMCA. But when decreasing the bank angle below 5º (to 0º), rudder deflection has to be increases and, therefore, VMCA will increase too.
  • VMCA is certified with a bank angle of not more than 5º towards the operating engine, because a lower figure can be obtained compared with wings level.
  1. When the bank angle is increased beyond 5 degrees, there is an increasing risk of fin stall. CORRECT
An increased bank angle beyond 5º, while keeping the rudder centred, may lead us to encounter a new dangerous situation – sideslip towards the live engine, which could possibly send the fin’s angle of attack beyond critical alpha, leading to a fin stall. Control of the aircraft will be immediately lost.

title: Which of the following wing planforms produces the lowest induced drag? (assume zero wing twist)
optionA: Tapered.
optionB: Elliptical.
optionC: Rectangular.
optionD: Circular.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
INDUCED DRAG
Whenever a wing produces lift, concentrated vortices form at the wing tips. The vortices are strongest at the wing tips and become progressively weaker toward the centre-line of the aircraft.

It is the production of lift itself which reduces the magnitude of the lift force being generated. To replace the lift lost by the increased downwash, the aircraft must be flown at a higher angle of attack. This increases drag. This extra drag is called induced drag.

The stronger the vortices, the greater the induced drag.

The main factors affecting induced drag are wing planform, aspect ratio, speed, and weight/lift.

The effect of planform is the principal factor affecting induced drag. The size of the wing tip vortex is directly related to the length of the wing tip chord.

A rectangular planform wing produces a much larger vortex than the tapered section. This is because the longer the tip chord, the greater the spillage of air from the lower surface onto the upper surface, and the larger the wing tip vortex.

In aerodynamic terms, the elliptical planform wing is the most aerodynamically efficient because the downwash remains constant across the complete wingspan, giving minimal induced drag.

title: Which of these statements about weight or mass is correct?
optionA: The mass of an object is independent of the acceleration due to gravity.
optionB: The weight of an object is independent of the acceleration due to gravity.
optionC: In the SI system the unit of measurement for weight is the kilogram.
optionD: Mass = weight × volume.
explanationTotal:
Mass is typically defined as the amount of matter within an object. The SI unit of mass is the kilogram (kg).
Mass is constant regardless of gravity, but weight is not. Weight it the force exerted on a body by gravity:

W = m x g [N] ⇔ m = W ÷ g

Where g is gravitational acceleration.

g ≈ 9.81 m/s2 on Earth
W ≈ m x 9.81

title: The low speed and high speed buffet margins increase by:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Increasing load factor.
optionB: Increasing altitude.
optionC: Increasing speed.
optionD: Reducing Mass.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The buffet onset boundary chart has both high speed and low speed buffet limits. Where the low speed buffet boundary marks the onset of the pre stall buffet and the high speed buffet boundary marks the onset of high speed buffeting. The speeds for high and low speed buffeting are dependent on weight, altitude, load factor and CG position. On the buffet onset boundary chart we will find the variables for altitude, weight and load factor.

For each mass and altitude, a low and high speed buffet will be identified, which will then limit the range of speeds for the specific mass and altitude. The range of speeds (margin) between high and low speed buffeting can be decreased by:

  • Higher aircraft weight - As the aircraft mass increases, the low speed buffet increases and the high speed buffet decreases.

  • Higher altitude - As the aircraft climbs higher, the low speed buffet increases and the high speed buffet decreases. At the max altitude, there will be one available speed only (coffin corner).

  • Higher load factor

  • More forward CG position

title:
Refer to figure.
Which statement is correct regarding the pitching moment coefficient CM versus angle of attack diagram?
optionA: Line 3 shows an aeroplane with increasing static longitudinal stability at high angles of attack.
optionB: Line 1 shows an aeroplane with reducing static longitudinal instability at very high angles of attack.
optionC: Line 4 shows an aeroplane with a greater static longitudinal stability at low angles of attack than that shown in line 3.
optionD: Line 4 shows an aeroplane with reducing static longitudinal stability at very high angles of attack.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

Static longitudinal stability depends upon the relationship of angle of attack and pitching moment (CM).

A variation of CG position can cause large changes in the static longitudinal stability. In the conventional airplane configuration, the large changes in stability with CG variation are primarily due to the large changes in the wing contribution. If the incidence of all surfaces remains fixed, the effect of CG position on static longitudinal stability is typified by the chart in figure 1:

As the CG is gradually moved aft, the airplane static stability decreases, then becomes neutral then unstable. The CG position which produces zero slope and neutral static stability is referred to as the “neutral point”. The neutral point defines the most aft CG position without static instability.

Positive static stability is indicated by the curve with negative slope. Moving the CG forward, will increase static longitudinal stability and this is represented by a (steeper) negative slope.

Neutral static stability would be the result if the curve had zero slope. If neutral stability existed, the airplane could be disturbed to some higher or lower lift coefficient without change in pitching moment coefficient.

An airplane which demonstrates a positive slope of the CM versus CL curve would be unstable.

title: Assuming ISA conditions and a climb below the tropopause at constant Mach number and aeroplane mass, the:
optionA: lift coefficient increases.
optionB: TAS remains constant.
optionC: IAS increases.
optionD: lift coefficient decreases.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The Mach number is defined as the ratio between the TAS and the LSS (Local speed of sound).
It is an indication of how fast an aircraft is travelling with relation to the sound waves that surround it.

The Mach number may be calculated as follows:

M=TAS/LSS=(TAS(kt))/(38.95∗√(T(K)))

The speed of propagation of small pressure waves depends upon the temperature of the air ONLY.

Lift is defined by:

L=1/2∗ρ∗TAS2∗S∗CL

Effect on IAS of Climbing at a constant Mach number:

  • Temperature decreases with increasing altitude, so the speed of sound will decrease as altitude is increased.
  • If altitude is increased at a constant Mach number, the TAS decreases and to maintain Lift constant, CL increases.

title: To counter adverse yaw, an aircraft has aileron/rudder coupling. In a right turn, the left aileron goes (1) _____, the right aileron goes (2) _____, and the rudder automatically moves to the (3) _____.
optionA: (1) down; (2) up; (3) right.
optionB: (1) up; (2) up; (3) right.
optionC: (1)down; (2) down; (3) left.
optionD: (1) up; (2) down; (3) left.
explanationTotal:
Adverse yaw is a yawing motion opposite to the turning/rolling motion of the aircraft. Adverse yaw is caused by the drag on the down-going aileron being greater than that on the up-going aileron. This imbalance in drag causes the yawing motion around the normal/vertical axis. Since this yaw is adverse (i.e., in a banked turn to the left, the yaw is to the right), it is opposing the turn, which is detrimental to the aircraft's performance.

  • To counter adverse yaw, some aircraft incorporate aileron/rudder coupling which is a system that automatically applies a rudder input in a turn to counter the adverse yawing moments generated by the ailerons.
  • In a right turn, the left wing lift is increased by lowering the aileron. As we have described above, increased lift, increases induced drag, which generates a yawing moment in the opposite direction. As a result, the aircraft will be in an unbalanced turn. To re-balance the turn, right rudder must be applied.

title: A shock wave on a lift generating wing will:
optionA: reach its highest strength when flying at the critical Mach number.
optionB: move forward as Mach number is decreased.
optionC: move slightly forward in front of a downward deflecting aileron.
optionD: be situated at the greatest wing thickness when the aeroplane reaches the speed of sound.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
An airplane does not have to be flying at the local speed of sound for the airflow over the wings to be supersonic. A normal shockwave can develop at any time the airplane is in the transonic speed range. The function of the wing is to accelerate the air passing over its upper surface. The airflow may be subsonic at the leading edge of the wing but can be accelerated to become supersonic by the trailing edge of the wing, despite the fact that the airplane is flying at a speed of less than Mach 1.0. This is transonic flight, which usually occurs between Mach 0.75 and Mach 1.2.

At speeds less than Mach 0.75 all the airflow over the wing is subsonic and as the airplane accelerates the first shockwave will form on the upper surface at the wing root.

When the air over the upper surface of the wing becomes sonic, a shockwave forms because the pressure waves over the rear of wing at the wing root are attempting to move forward and meet the air moving aft from the leading edge at exactly the same speed but in the opposite direction. The meeting point is usually just aft of the point of maximum camber because this is where the air over the upper surface of the wing is accelerating at the greatest rate.

The meeting point of the two air-pressure waves is the shockwave and is where the airflow changes from being sonic or supersonic to become subsonic. Air passing through the shockwave experiences an increase of pressure, temperature, and density. If the airplane speed continues to increase the area of supersonic air on top of the wing spreads backward towards the trailing edge, resulting in the shockwave moving aft.

title:
You are flying from town A to airport B with a single engine piston when you experience an engine failure. Calculate the minimum height at A to reach airport B, given:

Elevation: 300 m
Distance from A to B: 60 km
L/D ratio: 30
explanationTotal:
Lift over drag (L/D) ratio determines the gliding range. The Glide ratio of an aircraft is the distance of forward travel divided by the altitude lost in that distance.

If L/D = 30 => Aircraft will fly 30 units over the ground per every unit down (assuming no wind).
Ground distance = 60 km = 60 000 m

  • Therefore, with a ground distance of 60 000 m (60 km) and L/D of 1:30, we get the following equation:
    1 / 30 = x / 60 000
    x = 2 000 m
  • Since the question asks for minimum height (not altitude), the correct option is 2 000 m.
Note: Altitude - The vertical distance of an object measured from mean sea level.
Height -The vertical distance of a level, a point, or an object considered as a point, measured from a specified datum.

title: An aeroplane in straight and level flight at 100 kt is subjected to a sudden disturbance in speed. Assuming the angle of attack remains constant initially and the load factor reaches a value of 2.25:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: the speed will have decreased by 25 kt.
optionB: the speed will have increased by 50 kt.
optionC: the speed will have increased by 25 kt.
optionD: the speed will have decreased by 50 kt.
explanationTotal:
Load factor is defined as:

n = Lift / Weight

Expanding the Lift Formula:

L = ½ x ρ x V2 x S x CL

n = (½ x ρ x V2 x S x CL) / W

By removing all the constants, we can say that:

n ∝ V2

To find the change in load factor (nΔ), we have to divide nNEW by nOLD:

nΔ = nNEW / nOLD

nΔ = VNEW2 / VOLD2

Rearranging the above formula in order to find VNEW:

VNEW = √(nΔ x VOLD2)

VNEW = √(2.25 x 1002)

VNEW = 150 kt

Knowing now that the new speed is 150 kt and the old speed was 100 kt, we can conclude that the airspeed increased by 50 kt.

title: Load factor is increased by:
optionA: an increase in aeroplane mass.
optionB: forward CG movement.
optionC: a decrease in air density.
optionD: upward gusts.
explanationTotal:
The Load Factor is the ratio of lift compared to weight of the aircraft denoted by "n":

Load Factor (n) = Lift (L) / Weight (W)

The value of load factor in steady wings level horizontal flight is exactly 1(g). Load factors greater or less than one (or even negative) are the result of maneuvers or wind gusts. The value is less than one in a steady wings level climb, because a vertical component of thrust is balancing some of the weight. So the value of wing lift required is less.

  • Turning. In a horizontal coordinated turn, load factor is always higher than 1 (n = 1 / cos Ø).
  • Climb and Descent. In a climb or descent, n < 1 (L = W cos y)
Note: Upgusts result in sudden increase of angle of attack which increases lift and load factor.

title: On which type of drag does airframe ageing have the greatest influence?
optionA: Wave drag
optionB: Form drag
optionC: Induced drag
optionD: Skin-friction drag

title: Consider an aircraft climbing at a constant CAS of 308 kt below the tropopause and in ISA conditions. The ATC requests the pilots to increase their rate of climb, and as a consequence, they change to a constant Mach number of M 0.72, which was the Mach number at the time of the request. How can this be a solution to the request made by ATC?
optionA: The aeroplane must pitch up to maintain a constant CAS and Mach number, and since the TAS reduces, the angle and rate of climb will both increase.
optionB: The aeroplane must increase the AoA to maintain lift as both the CAS and TAS are gradually reducing, resulting in an increased average rate of climb.
optionC: In order to maintain a constant Mach number, the aeroplane must reduce AoA, resulting in lower induced drag, giving an increased angle and rate of climb.
optionD: In order to maintain a constant Mach number, the aeroplane must pitch up slightly, resulting in the CAS reducing and an increased average rate of climb.
explanationTotal:
When flying at higher altitudes and speeds close to the speed of sound, it's common for aircraft to transition from IAS to Mach number as a reference for speed. This is because as the aircraft climbs, the speed of sound varies with temperature.

In this question, the pilot is flying at a constant calibrated airspeed (CAS) of 308 knots and is then asked by ATC to increase the rate of climb. The pilot transitions to a constant Mach number (M 0.72) and, in order to do so, adjusts the aircraft's pitch attitude.

Initially, the aircraft pitches up to maintain the constant Mach number, its calibrated airspeed (CAS) reduces. This reduction in CAS leads to a decrease in kinetic energy (associated with forward speed). However, the potential energy (associated with altitude) increases due to the upward climb. This shift from kinetic to potential energy contributes to the increased rate of climb, all while adhering to the requested constant Mach number.

title: During an approach and coming to land, the pilots configure for full flaps landing. However, the left leading edge slats do not extend. Which statement is true?
optionA: The right wing stalls if speed increases/decreases.
optionB: The left wing may stall if speed decreases.
optionC: The left wing may stall if speed increases.
optionD: No noticeable change for landing.
explanationTotal:
Leading-edge slats increase the wing's chamber area and mean aerodynamic chord (MAC), thereby increasing its coefficient of lift (CL) maximum, which reduces the aircraft's stall speed. The mass flow over the upper surface is increased and so is its energy when air flows through the venturi-shaped slot.

These effects combine to delay the forward movement of the separation point as angle of attack increases. The stall is delayed until a higher angle of attack is reached.

The wing where the slats did not extend (left) will stall at a lower angle of attack and higher airspeed than the right wing. Therefore, if speed drops, the left wing may stall if it reaches its new stalling speed.

title:
Determine the lift, in a straight and steady glide, with a glide angle of 30 degrees. Consider the following values:

Mass: 10 455 kg
Drag: 87 500 N
Assume that g = 10 m/s2
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Steady Descent

Weight is split into 2 components:

  • W cos y acts perpendicular to the flight path and balances lift;
  • W sin y acts forward along the flight path, adding to Thrust to balance drag.
Lift is less than Weight: Lift only has to balance the component of weight which acts perpendicular to the flight path (L = W cos y).

Thrust is less than drag: Weight gives a forward component in the same direction as thrust.

For a power-on descent, we get the following formulas:

D = T + W sin y
T = D – W sin y
L = W cos y

With regards to this question,
  • L = W cos y
  • L = 104 550 N x cos 30 = 90 543 N

title: What happens to the airflow’s static temperature (T), Mach number (M), and total pressure (Pt) when passing through a normal shock wave?
optionA: T decreases, M increases, Pt increases.
optionB: T decreases, M increases, Pt decreases.
optionC: T increases, M decreases, Pt increases.
optionD: T increases, M decreases, Pt decreases.
explanationTotal:
An airplane flying at low, subsonic, speeds causes air-pressure changes because of its movement but they are relatively small. It is convenient, therefore, to treat the air as though it could not be compressed.

However, the air-pressure changes caused by the movement of an airplane at high speed, close to the speed of sound, are considerable and cannot be ignored. The air is compressible and its effect on the airplane must be accounted for when it is travelling at high speed.

An airplane moving through the air creates a pressure wave around it, which is propagated away from it in all directions simultaneously at the speed of sound. For an airplane flying at a relatively low speed, less than the speed of sound, the air-pressure wave ahead of the airplane can move away from the airplane. Consequently, air-pressure, air-density, air-temperature, and air-velocity changes take place ahead of the leading edge of the wings and are a gradual process.

If, however, the airplane is travelling at the speed of sound then the air-pressure wave ahead of the airplane is unable to move away from the airplane and a wave of compressed air builds up at the leading edge of the wing.

This compression wave will create a discontinuity plane, where the airstream experiences the following changes:

Air Temperature - Increases (due to compression)
Static Pressure - Increases (due to compression)
Total Pressure - Decreases (Normal shockwave suffers greater loss than an oblique shockwave)
Air Density - Increases (Oblique shockwave has less compression)
LSS - Increases (due to the temperature increase)
Speed of Airflow - Decreases to less than Mach 1 (normal shockwave). Decreases but still above Mach 1.0 (oblique shockwave).

Minimum energy loss through a normal shock wave will occur when the Mach number of the airflow in front of the shock wave is small but supersonic.

title:
Refer to figure.
When spoilers are deployed, in which direction will the graph shift?
optionA: A
optionB: B
optionC: The graph will not change
optionD: Depending on the speed, the graph can move both ways
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
Spoilers are aerodynamic surfaces that exist on the top surface of some wings, and are used for many reasons. They are primarily used to increase drag and "dump" lift. (If they are just for drag then they are called speedbrakes, but aircraft manufacturers do blur these distinctions).

They are called spoilers because they "spoil" the airflow, sticking up into the airflow, causing a lift reduction similar to an up-going aileron and a similar drag increase to that of a split flap.

Of course, the spoiled airflow is not as effective at producing lift, and the stall speed therefore increases. There is, however, a counter-intuitive rise in the critical angle of attack.

Because the top surface of the wing goes up again with a spoiler extended, it acts the same as an up-going aileron, and even though the air behind the spoiler is incredibly turbulent, the air flowing along the surface becomes re-energised and will resist the stall at higher angles of attack than usual, increasing the critical angle of attack. Remember, in flight, spoilers are only extended a small amount, not like the ground spoilers which come up at around 90º to the wing.

  • The increased drag, decreased CLMAX , and increased stall speed will cause the graph to move down and to the right.

title: A transport aircraft has to carry some heavy cargo aft of the CG location. The cargo would ideally be placed further forwards within the aircraft, but it is very difficult to move. The Captain verifies that the aircraft is within CG limits currently, and continues with the flight preparation. What is the effect on stick force stability and how does the leading edge of the variable-incidence horizontal stabiliser move due to this cargo?
optionA: Stick force stability is increased and the stabiliser leading edge moves down.
optionB: Stick force stability is increased and the stabiliser leading edge moves up.
optionC: Stick force stability is decreased and the stabiliser leading edge moves up.
optionD: Stick force stability is decreased and the stabiliser leading edge moves down.
explanationTotal:
Weight and CG location massively affect the handling characteristics of an aircraft. When the aircraft's CG (Centre of Gravity) is located far forwards within the aircraft, the aircraft's stability is high, and its manoeuvrability is low. When the CG is located further aft, the aircraft is less stable, but more manoeuvrable. Pitch manoeuvrability is measured by the "stick force per G" (stick force stability), meaning how much force the pilot needs to apply to the controls to gain an extra 1G of vertical acceleration.

The higher the stick force stability, the lower the manoeuvrability, so in this question, as the CG has been moved aft by the cargo, the manoeuvrability will be increased, so the stick force stability will decrease.

The second part of this question is about the aircraft's trim in relation to the CG location.

Most large jet aircraft calculate different pitch trim settings to use for take-off, depending on the position of the CG and the take-off mass of the aircraft. This is so the pilot can always feel roughly the same force when rotating the aircraft, and during the first phase of flight. The trim is often done (and in this question certainly done) by an all moving tailplane, known as a variable-incidence horizontal stabiliser, so the whole stabiliser moves to perform the act of trimming.

If the aircraft has a far forward CG location, the nose will feel heavy to the pilot, so during the setup, the pilots will set a much more nose-up trim setting, so that at rotation, the feeling will be roughly the same.

This is what the question is referring to. Adding extra cargo behind the CG will move the CG backwards, making the aircraft more tail heavy. This will require more nose-down stabiliser trim to feel the same on take-off. A nose-down stabiliser trim is caused by providing less downforce (or extra lift force) on the tail. That is created by setting the horizontal stabiliser at a higher angle, with its leading edge pointing more upwards. This will be the same during the cruise, where less nose down moment will be required, so the leading edge of the stabiliser will be pointing more upwards than if the cargo was not loaded.

title: In a power-assisted flight control system, most of the force is provided by the…
optionA: servo valve.
optionB: hydraulic system.
optionC: pilot.
optionD: servo tab.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
If the required assistance for the pilot to move the controls cannot be provided by the preceding types of aerodynamic balance, then power assisted, or fully powered controls must be used.
The aerodynamic force on the controls will depend on the area of the control surface, its angular displacement, and the IAS. For large and fast aircraft, the resulting aerodynamic force can give hinge moments / stick forces which are too high for easy operation of the controls.
The pilot will require assistance to move the controls in these conditions, and this can be done either by using (hydraulic) powered flying controls or by using some form of aerodynamic balance.

title: Assuming ISA conditions, climbing at a constant Mach number up to tropopause the TAS will:
optionA: decrease.
optionB: increase.
optionC: remain constant.
optionD: first increase, then decrease.
explanationTotal:
Mach Number (N) is the ratio between speed of the undisturbed airflow (TAS) and local speed of sound, denoted as a or sometimes LSS. In a mathematical way:
  • M = TAS ÷ LSS

Where "M" is Mach number, TAS is the speed of the airflow [m/s] and LSS or "a" is local speed of sound [m/s].

Local Speed of sound (LSS)
  • LSS = 38.94 x √ K

Where "K" is the temperature expressed in Kelvin degrees.

As you can see from the above equation, the speed of sound varies with the temperature. Under standard atmospheric conditions, the temperature decreases with an increasing altitude. Rewriting the Mach number formula, TAS will equal Mach no multiplied by LSS: Therefore, if Mach number remains constant and temperature decreases, the TAS will decrease.

title: In a fully powered flight control system, the pilot supplies the force to...
optionA: move the servo valve.
optionB: move the spring tab.
optionC: move the servo tab.
optionD: provide the "aerodynamic feel".
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
If the required assistance for the pilot to move the controls cannot be provided by the preceding types of aerodynamic balance, then power assisted, or fully powered controls must be used.
The aerodynamic force on the controls will depend on the area of the control surface, its angular displacement, and the IAS. For large and fast aircraft, the resulting aerodynamic force can give hinge moments / stick forces which are too high for easy operation of the controls.
The pilot will require assistance to move the controls in these conditions, and this can be done either by using (hydraulic) powered flying controls or by using some form of aerodynamic balance.
The pitot and static air pressure is fed either side of a diaphragm in a hermetically sealed container. The dynamic pressure in this system causes diaphragm to operate a hydraulic servo-valve that applies pressure, equal to an amplified value of dynamic pressure, to the piston controlling the resistance to the control column movement.

title: Static lateral stability should not be too large, because:
optionA: constant aileron deflection would be required during cruise in case of crosswind.
optionB: too much aileron deflection would be required in a crosswind landing.
optionC: too much rudder deflection would be required in a crosswind landing.
optionD: the roll trim sensitivity would increase sharply.
explanationTotal:
Lateral stability refers to stability about the longitudinal axis. An aircraft is considered to be laterally stable, if in case of unexpected bank angle, the aircraft wants to reduce it to 0. The value of lateral stability should not be too low, nor too high.
  • Lateral stability too low: If lateral stability is lower than adequate, the aircraft simply does not get back to 0º bank angle in time, thus deviation from the position and altitude is excessive.
  • Lateral stability too high: An excessive lateral stability can cause problems during crosswind landings/take-offs. A high static lateral stability reduces controllability in roll.

title: Determine the approximate value of lift for an aircraft climbing at an angle of 9º with a weight of 1 250 000 N, drag of 300 000 N and a thrust of 600 000 N:
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
L = W cos y
L = 1 250 000 cos 9º
L = 1 234 610 N

  • Closest option: 1 200 000 N

Further information:

CLIMB

There are four forces that act on an aircraft in a steady unaccelerated climb: Lift, Weight, Thrust and Drag. Lift, Drag and Thrust are aerodynamic forces which are defined relative to the flight path. Where Lift is perpendicular to the flight path, whereas Drag and Thrust act along it. The Weight of an aircraft is directed towards the centre of the Earth and is, therefore, along the vertical axis.
Weight will be resolved into two different components, as you can see on the attached figure: a force which is opposite to the lift (W cos y) and another force which acts in the same direction as drag (W sin y).

  • In order for the aircraft to be in equilibrium in a steady climb, Thrust will be equal to Drag + backwards component of weight; and Lift must be equal to the opposing component of weight. Lift will be less than Weight because Lift only has to oppose a portion of Weight.

title: Typically the CL/CD ratio is:
optionA: maximum at an angle of attack of 16°.
optionB: minimum at an angle of attack of 16°.
optionC: minimum at an angle of attack of 4°.
optionD: maximum at an angle of attack of 4°.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
A typical modern jet has a maximum lift/drag ratio of about 19. Where this ratio reaches its maximum, the value of the angle gamma will be at its minimum. The lift drag ratio reaches its maximum value at 4 degrees angle of attack and is always at the speed VMD.

  • VMD is also known as the speed for L/D Max. The angle of attack at VMD is fixed at 4 degrees.

title: An aft CG shift:
optionA: decreases static longitudinal stability.
optionB: has no influence on longitudinal manoeuvrability.
optionC: decreases longitudinal manoeuvrability.
optionD: increases static longitudinal stability.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
A variation of CG position can cause large changes in the static longitudinal stability. In the conventional airplane configuration, the large changes in stability with CG variation are primarily due to the large changes in the wing contribution.

As the CG is gradually moved aft, the airplane static stability decreases, then becomes neutral then unstable. The CG position which produces zero slope and neutral static stability is referred to as the “neutral point”.

For an airplane to always have positive longitudinal static stability the CG must be ahead of the neutral point, so that the wing-pitching moment always exceeds the tail plane pitching moment. The further aft the neutral point is from the CG the greater is the static longitudinal stability.

title: Regarding the trim position, which of the following statements is correct related to centre of gravity and adjustable stabiliser position?
optionA: Because characteristic speeds at take off do not vary with centre of gravity location, the need for stabiliser adjustment is dependent on flap position only.
optionB: At the forward limit for centre of gravity, stabiliser trim is adjusted maximum nose down to obtain maximum elevator authority at take off rotation.
optionC: A nose heavy aeroplane requires that the stabiliser leading edge is lower than compared with a tail heavy aeroplane.
optionD: A nose heavy aeroplane requires that the stabiliser leading edge is higher than compared with a tail heavy aeroplane.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
A tail-heavy airplane (trimmed for nose-down) would require the stabilizer to be deflected up. When the variable incidence tail plane is trimmed, it has no elevator deflection.

The opposite is also true for an airplane trimmed for nose up: it would require the stabilizer to be deflected down. When the variable incidence tail plane is trimmed, it has no elevator deflection. When trimmed for a forward CG position (nose heavy), the stabiliser leading edge is lower than the trailing edge.

title: An aircraft is maintaining straight and level flight with constant power and no flaps deployed. In this condition the C<sub>L </sub>= 0.28. What will happen to C<sub>L</sub>, if the pilot extends the flaps and decreases the speed to maintain straight and level flight?
optionA: C<sub>L</sub> higher than 0.28 because C<sub>L</sub> always increases with the deployment of flaps.
optionB: C<sub>L</sub> higher than 0.28 to keep the the same altitude.
optionC: C<sub>L </sub>lower than 0.28.
optionD: C<sub>L</sub> is still 0.28 because it is independent on the deployment of flaps.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
LIFT = ½ρV²SCL
DRAG = ½ρV²SCD

Where: LIFT = Lift force DRAG = Drag force ρ = Air density V = Airspeed S = Wing surface area CL = Coefficient of lift CD = Coefficient of drag

The coefficient of lift (CL) is a parameter that depends on the angle of attack of the airfoil and the shape of the airfoil. CL can be altered in flight, for example, by lowering the flaps.

When a flap is deflected downwards, the camber of the airfoil increases, the coefficient of lift (CL) increases, resulting in higher lift production. However, to maintain a constant altitude, the increased lift needs to be compensated by reducing the airspeed (V), as stated in the question.

In simple terms, when the flaps are deployed, CL increases (CL higher than 0.28), but to keep the lift balanced and the altitude constant, the aircraft slows down (V decreases). As a result, even with the increased CL from the flaps, the overall lift remains the same.

title:
You are flying at 230 kts with a CL of 0.3. ATC instructs you to reduce the speed to 200 kts. What
is the new CL?
explanationTotal:
To solve this exercise you can use the following formula:

New CL x (New Speed)2 = Old CL x (Old Speed)2
New CL x 2002 = 0.3 x 2302
New CL = (0.3 x 2302) / 2002
New CL = 0.4

title: An Aircraft in straight and level flight at high altitude and at high Mach number encounters turbulence. During an updraft, the angle of attack increases and, if airspeed remains constant, the:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Drag divergence Mach number increases.
optionB: High-speed buffet margin decreases.
optionC: Critical Mach number remains constant.
optionD: Low-speed buffet margin increases.
explanationTotal: The greater the lift force, the greater will be the angle of attack and flow speed over the upper wing surface. This causes the high-speed buffet to occur at a slower speed and the low-speed buffet to occur at a faster speed. The result is a reduced buffet margin.

title: The pilots prepare and trim the aircraft for take-off, setting the trim for a CG position at 12% of the MAC. But due to an error, the real position of the CG is at 24% of the MAC. What could this cause?
optionA: The length of the runway may not be sufficient to take-off.
optionB: Large stick forces are required to achieve rotation.
optionC: Risk of over rotation that can lead to a tail strike.
optionD: Reduced climb performance after take-off.
explanationTotal:
Tail strike – the rotation is started before it is possible to lift-off, consequently angle of attack might be increased up to tail strike.

In this case, a 12% CG position will tend to hold the nose down. To counter this, the pilots need to set a nose up trim in order to create a nose-up pitching moment at rotation.

The actual CG position is however more aft (CG) which will naturally help lifting the aircraft nose. This natural tendency, combined with a nose-up trim, will result in a tendency of the nose lifting of earlier than intended and faster, increasing the risk of a tail strike.

title:
Which of these statements about the gust load factor on an aeroplane are correct or incorrect?

I. When the mass decreases, the gust load factor increases.
