II. When the altitude decreases, the gust load factor increases.
optionA: I is correct, II is correct.
optionB: I is correct, II is incorrect.
optionC: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
optionD: I is incorrect, II is correct.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
A gust is a localized sudden and rapid change to the speed of the air in the atmosphere that can be either horizontal or vertical. The horizontal gust is of little importance because it causes a change to an airplane’s dynamic pressure that results in an insignificant change to the load factor. The vertical gusts are far more important because they change the effective angle of attack, total lift, and the load factor.
The gust load is the extra load imparted to the airplane by vertical gusts or turbulence. Its magnitude is unaffected by increased altitude but is increased with increased aspect ratio and/or decreased mass.
The load factor for any given angle of attack can be derived from the basic load factor for the normal cruise angle of attack because it is increased by the same percentage as the increase of angle of attack.
The load factor deriving from a gust is determined by the magnitude of the vertical velocity of the gust and the forward speed of the airplane.
High wing loading reduces the ‘g’ increment in a gust. This is because the lift increment produced is a smaller proportion of the original lift force for the more heavily loaded aircraft.
For a given TAS and gust speed, the increase of lift will be proportional to the wing area. Therefore, the increase in load factor is inversely proportional to the wing loading.

Wing Loading = Weight/(Wing Area)

Decreasing mass, decreases wing loading which increases load factor. Therefore, statement 1 is correct.
With increasing altitude, density decreases and any aerodynamic force resulting from a gust will be smaller.
Thus, when comparing two aircraft flying at different altitudes, the one flying in thicker air (lower altitude) will experience an increased increment in load factor following a gust. Therefore, statement 2 is correct.

title: Consider an aircraft equipped with a variable pitch propeller. During the acceleration phase of the takeoff roll, the blade angle:
optionA: is increasing until the aeroplane reaches V<sub>MC</sub> then it is decreasing.
optionB: is increasing.
optionC: stays the same.
optionD: is decreasing.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
A propeller is a fan, fitted with between two and six aerodynamic blades that is used to convert rotational motion into forward thrust for the propulsion of an aeroplane through the air.

The blades of the propeller are small aerodynamic aerofoils mounted vertically on a horizontal shaft that is rotated by either a piston engine or a turbine-driven engine.

BLADE ANGLE (PITCH)

The angle between the blade chord and the plane of rotation.

ANGLE OF ATTACK

The path of the propeller through the air determines the direction of the relative airflow. The angle between the blade chord and the relative airflow is the angle of attack (α). The angle of attack (α) is the result of propeller rotational velocity (RPM) and aircraft forward velocity (TAS).

Because the rotational velocity of the blade increases with distance from the propeller shaft and the fact that the aeroplane is moving forward, then the angle of attack of the blade varies at different distances from the shaft.

CONSTANT SPEED PROPELLER

The purpose of a variable-pitch propeller is to either manually or automatically maintain the optimum angle of attack to maximize the lift/drag ratio of the propeller as the aeroplane speed changes.

Constant-speed propellers enable the pilot to select the RPM for maximum power or maximum efficiency and a propeller governor varies the propeller pitch angle as required to maintain the selected RPM.

Figure shows the conditions during the early stages of the take-off roll. The RPM is set to maximum and the TAS is low. The angle of attack is optimum and maximum available efficiency is obtained. As the aircraft continues to accelerate, the TAS will increase, which decreases the angle of attack of the blades. Less thrust will be generated and less propeller torque. This gives less resistance for the engine to overcome and RPM would tend to increase. The propeller governor senses the RPM increase and increases pitch to maintain the blade angle of attack constant.

title: How does the location of the CG influence VMCL?
optionA: A forward CG reduces VMCL.
optionB: A forward CG increases VMCL.
optionC: The CG location does NOT influence VMCL if within the permissible CG limits.
optionD: The CG location does NOT influence V<sub>MCL</sub>.
explanationTotal:
VMCL, the minimum control speed during approach and landing with all engines operating, is the calibrated airspeed at which, when the critical engine is suddenly made inoperative, it is possible to maintain control of the airplane with that engine still inoperative and maintain straight flight with an angle of bank of not more than 5°.

VMCL must be established with:

  • the airplane in the most critical configuration for approach and landing with all engines operating.
  • the most unfavorable CG.
  • the airplane trimmed for approach with all engines operating.
  • the most unfavorable weight.
  • for propeller airplanes, the propeller of the inoperative engine in the position it achieves without pilot action and go-around power or thrust setting on the operating engines(s).
In demonstrating VMCL:
  • the rudder force may not exceed 150 lb.
  • the airplane may not exhibit hazardous flight characteristics or require exceptional piloting skill, alertness, or strength.
  • lateral control must be sufficient to roll the airplane, from an initial condition of steady flight, through an angle of 20° in the direction necessary to initiate a turn away from the inoperative engine(s), in not more than 5 seconds.
Because the aircraft rotates around the CG, the position of the CG directly affects the length of the rudder arm and, thus, the power of the rudder and fin to maintain directional stability and control. The ‘worst case’ is with the CG at the aft limit. If the requirements can be met in this configuration, the ability to maintain directional control will be enhanced at any other CG location. A more forward CG decreases VMCL.

title: Modern aircraft are usually equipped with fly-by-wire technology. Flight envelope and manoeuvring envelope protections in fly-by-wire are called control laws. Which of the following is automatically controlled?
optionA: Pitch control.
optionB: Rudder pedal motion.
optionC: Altitude control.
optionD: Engine thrust control.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

Note: This question was formulated with limited feedback. We suspect it pertains to the learning objectives listed below. If you encounter this question during your official exam, kindly inform us. We appreciate your assistance.

081.05.07.01.01: Explain which parameters may be controlled in level flight with the pitch control law.

Fly-by-wire is a sophisticated system that substitutes the traditional manual-mechanical flight controls of an aircraft with an electronic interface. Within this system, a computer interface is interposed between the pilots and the final control surfaces. Modern commercial fly-by-wire aircraft integrate a flight-envelope protection system into their flight control software, which is housed within the flight control computer. This protection system serves the crucial role of preventing pilots from issuing control commands that could push the aircraft beyond its structural and aerodynamic operational boundaries.

In the realm of fly-by-wire technology, the concept of flight envelope and maneuvering envelope protections is employed. These are governed by predefined control laws that serve as a set of rules, guiding the computers in transforming input signals. One of the most commonly used control laws involves managing the load factor in pitch control. Essentially, this means that the trimmable horizontal stabilizer (THS) adjusts its position to maintain a specific load factor. When the pilot manipulates the sidestick, the THS moves accordingly, altering the load factor proportionally to the sidestick's deflection (refer to the attached diagram). This means that as long as the sidestick remains untouched, the aircraft will maintain its flight-path-angle-corrected load factor. For example, if the aircraft is in straight and level flight and the pilot pulls the sidestick, the aircraft will follow a curved trajectory, increasing its pitch angle until the sidestick is released.

title: The Never Exceed Speed (VNE) is set…
optionA: never above V<sub>D</sub>.
optionB: below V<sub>D</sub>.
optionC: equal to V<sub>D</sub>.
optionD: at 0.9 of V<sub>D</sub>.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
Important Note: This is a very similar question to Q815878, and whilst they are slightly different, we are unsure of which is being asked in exams (it could be both, but is less likely), and they are so close to each other, we are treating them as one.

We have recently changed the answer to this due to feedback. We find this question very odd, because "0.9 x VD" can be a range of values (as VD can be a range of values), and there are other factors to the calculation of VNE that you can see in the CS23 specifications below (CS25 aircraft do not have a VNE).

Also, we think the examiner is very misleading to include "VD" as an option, as it is certainly correct (VNE is always less than VD), but is less specific than "0.9 x VD", making it tough to decide between "less specific but absolutely correct" and "more specific but more complex to justify" answers.

Please keep on sending any exam feedback you have, and we will keep these questions as up to date as we can for you, thanks!

Each type of aircraft has its own specific flight envelope, within which it can be safely operated in accordance with the EASA Certification Specifications. This is represented on a velocity against load factor, or V-n diagram.

The high-speed limit for many (but not all) CS-23 aircraft is the never exceed speed (VNE) and is a design reference point for the aircraft beyond which the aircraft must not be flown. It provides a safety margin with the point at which structural damage or failure may occur(VD). VNE is the red radial line at the high speed end of the airspeed indicator.

Never Exceed Speed VNE: VNE is set below VD to allow for speed upsets to be recovered before reaching any point of possible damage. VNE equals 0.9 x VD in most cases, but please see the regulation for this below, as there is some "wiggle room" in the regulation that makes things slightly more complex (hence our unhappiness with these options).

CS 23.1505 - Airspeed Limitations
(a) The never-exceed speed VNE must be established so that it is –

(1) Not less than 0.9 times the minimum value of VD allowed under CS 23.335; and
(2) Not more than the lesser of –

(i) 0.9 VD established under CS 23.335; or
(ii) 0.9 times the maximum speed shown under CS 23.251.

title:
Which statement is correct regarding the gyroscopic effect of a clockwise rotating propeller on a single engine aeroplane?

I. Pitch up produces right yaw.
II. Right yaw produces pitch down.
optionA: I is correct, II is incorrect.
optionB: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
optionC: I is correct, II is correct.
optionD: I is incorrect, II is correct.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
On take-off, rotation of a single-engine propeller causes an aircraft to swing to one side, particularly those fitted with a tail-dragger undercarriage. The main causes of this are:

  • Slipstream effect
  • Torque reaction
  • Gyroscopic effect
  • Asymmetric blade effect

Gyroscopic Effect

A rotating propeller has the properties of a gyroscope - rigidity in space and precession. The characteristic which produces “gyroscopic effect” is precession. Gyroscopic precession is the reaction that occurs when a force is applied to the rim of a rotating disc. When a force is applied to the rim of a propeller, the reaction occurs 90° ahead in the direction of rotation and in the same direction as the applied force. As the aircraft is pitched up or down or yawed left or right, a force is applied to the rim of the spinning propeller disc.

Note: Gyroscopic effect only occurs when the aircraft pitches and/or yaws.

For a clockwise rotating propeller:

Pitch down - forward force on the top, force emerges 90° clockwise, left yaw.
Left yaw - forward force on the right, force emerges 90° clockwise, pitch up.
Pitch up - forward force on the bottom, force emerges 90° clockwise, right yaw. Therefore, statement 1 is correct.
Right yaw - forward force on the left, force emerges 90° clockwise, pitch down. Therefore, statement 2 is correct.

title: The load factor is greater than 1 (one):
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: during recovery after a wings level stall.
optionB: in steady wings level horizontal flight.
optionC: when weight is greater than lift.
optionD: during a steady wings level climb.
explanationTotal:
Load Factor - The ratio of the weight of an aircraft to the load imposed by lift. The correct symbol for load factor is (n), but it is colloquially known as (g).

Load Factor = Lift / Weight

Certain maneuvers require the lift force to be greater than the aircraft weight. For example, lift is greater than weight during a steady turn or during a pull-up maneuver.

title:
Considering subsonic incompressible airflow through a Venturi, which statement is correct?

1. The static pressure in the throat is lower than in the undisturbed airflow.
2. The speed of the airflow in the throat is lower than in the undisturbed airflow.
optionA: 1 is correct, 2 is incorrect.
optionB: 1 is incorrect, 2 is correct.
optionC: 1 is correct, 2 is correct.
optionD: 1 is incorrect, 2 is incorrect.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
To understand the venturi effect, we must first introduce two conditions: The conservation of mass (Continuity Equation) and the Conservation of Energy (Bernoulli’s Theorem).

Conservation of Mass (Continuity Equation)

The mass of air entering the pipe, in each unit of time, equals the mass of air leaving the pipe, in the same unit of time. The mass flow through the pipe must remain constant.

The mass air flow 'm' is the product of the density, the area and the velocity:

m= ρ*A*V

Continuity equation:

m1= m2= m3= ρ1* A1* V1= ρ2* A2* V2= ρ3* A3* V3=constant

The continuity equation explains the relationship between velocity and cross-sectional area: The speed is inversely proportional to the cross-sectional area.

Conservation of Energy (Bernoulli’s Theorem)

The total energy of an airstream comes in two forms: potential energy (static pressure) and kinetic energy (dynamic pressure).
The total pressure of the airstream is the sum of the static pressure and the dynamic pressure and must remain constant, according to the law of conservation of energy.
Thus, an increase in one form of pressure, must result in a decrease in the other.

Dynamic pressure (q) is expressed by:

q= 1/2* ρ* V2

Assuming the total pressure to be constant, the static pressure and the dynamic pressure vary inversely: If one increases the other decreases and vice-versa.

In Conclusion:

With a decrease in section area (from station 1 to station 2), flow speed increases, increasing dynamic pressure. If dynamic pressure increases, static pressure decreases. Statement 1 is therefore correct.
With a decrease in section area (from station 1 to station 2), flow speed increases, increasing dynamic pressure. Statement 2 is therefore incorrect.

title: If an aircraft enters a fully developed spin, what should be the pilot's first action?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Wing levelled
optionB: Full opposite rudder
optionC: Elevator down
optionD: Power idle
explanationTotal:
SPIN RECOVERY

Although the POH is the primary reference for recovery from a spin, the following can be used as a general procedure:

P - Retard the throttle to idle. In most aircraft, power hampers the recovery.
A - Ailerons neutral. Many pilots will attempt to recover from the spin using the ailerons. This may actually make the problem worse.
R - Apply full opposite rudder. Apply rudder opposite the rotation of the spin. If you have trouble determining which way the airplane is spinning, look at your turn coordinator or turn needle. It will indicate the direction of rotation.
E - Apply forward elevator. Immediately after applying opposite rudder, apply a quick forward motion on the control yoke and hold anti-spin controls until the aircraft starts to recover.
D - Recover from the dive. Once you have completed the four previous steps, and the rotation stops, recover from the dive. The descent rate may be over 5000 feet per minute and the airspeed will rapidly exceed redline. Remember to neutralize the rudder after the rotation stops.

title: An aeroplane where its CG is located forward of its Centre of Pressure suffers a premature tailplane stall as a result of ice contamination. Provided the wings do NOT stall, the outcome will be a(n)...
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: nose up pitch upset, the magnitude of which will depend on the location of the aeroplane’s CG.
optionB: uncommanded nose down pitch that will be accompanied by the activation of the stall warning system.
optionC: uncommanded nose up pitch that will be accompanied by the activation of the stall warning system.
optionD: nose down pitch upset, the magnitude of which will depend on the location of the aeroplane’s CG.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
STABILIZER STALL DUE TO ICE

The tailplane is an aerofoil, and because it is thinner than the wing, it is likely to experience icing before the wing does. The effect will be the same as for the wing; the stall will occur at a lower angle of attack.

The tailplane is normally operating at a negative angle of attack, producing a down load, so if the tailplane stalls and the down load is lost, the nose of the aircraft will drop and longitudinal control will be lost.

Stalling of an ice contaminated tailplane could be precipitated by extension of the wing flaps. Lowering the flaps increases the downwash, and this increases the negative angle of attack of the tailplane. If the tailplane has ice contamination, this could be sufficient to cause it to stall. Recovery procedure in this situation would be to retract the flaps again, thus reducing the downwash.

Take care when increasing an aircraft's forward airspeed to compensate for ice on the wings, since every knot of airspeed added to prevent wing stall brings the aircraft a knot closer to tailplane stall. Consequently, it is vital that the tailplane, like the wing, is free from contamination. This type of stall does not usually occur, but if it does, recovery is normally impossible.

title: The angle of attack of a two dimensional wing section is the angle between:
optionA: the fuselage core line and the free stream direction.
optionB: the chord line of the aerofoil and the fuselage centreline.
optionC: the chord line of the aerofoil and the free stream direction.
optionD: the chord line and the camber line of the aerofoil.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
Terminology definition angle of attack: angle between the chord line and the relative (undisturbed) air flow. Local airflow = downwash at the trailing edge of the airfoil for example.

Angle of attack (AOA, α - Greek letter alpha) is a term used in aerodynamics to describe the angle between the chord line of an airfoil and the vector representing the relative motion between the airfoil and the air through which it is moving. For a two-dimensional airfoil, angle of attack is the angle between the chord line and the direction of arrival of the incoming air.

In aviation, angle of attack is used to describe the angle between the chord line of the (three dimensional) wing of a fixed-wing aircraft and the vector representing the relative motion between the aircraft and the atmosphere. Since a wing can have twist, a chord line of the whole wing may not be definable, so an alternate reference line is simply defined. Often, the chord line of the root of the wing is chosen as the reference line.

The angle of attack is often confused with the pitch angle of an aircraft and the angle of incidence. Pitch angle and angle of incidence are measured from the same reference line as angle of attack (conceptually the chord line), but pitch refers to the horizon and angle of incidence to the longitudinal axis of the aeroplane. Whereas, the angle of attack is measured from the (same) reference line to the direction of the arrival of the air to the wing (caused by the relative motion between the wing and the atmosphere).

Note: Some tricky questions ask about the angle of attack of the aeroplane (not the wing) => angle between speed vector and longitudinal axis.

title: Which of the following statement correctly describes wing fences?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Flat plates fixed to the upper surfaces parallel to the wing chord.
optionB: Flat plates fixed to the upper surfaces perpendicular to the wing chord.
optionC: Small vertical fin attached to the rear and bottom of a fuselage.
optionD: Flat plates fixed to the lower surface of a wing at a 45 degree angle to the wing chord.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
If the tips stall on a sweptback wing, the overall reduction in lift causes the centre of pressure to move rapidly forward, thus reducing the overall nose-down pitch moment.

At the same time, the downwash from the inner wing sections becomes concentrated on the tailplane, giving a more severe nose-up pitch effect. The shift in the centre of pressure combined with the increase in downwash acting on the tailplane produces an overall nose-up pitching moment.

DEVICES TO ALLEVIATE WING TIP STALLING

Pitch-up may be prevented on sweptback wings by incorporating design features that help to alleviate tip stalling.

WING TIP FENCES

These are chordwise fences on the upper surface of the wing to restrict the outward flow of the boundary layer. This is instrumental in delaying wing tip stall.

title: A straight, cambered wing aeroplane is used to demonstrate slow flight and stalls to a student pilot. The pilot maintains straight and level flight while the speed decreases until the aeroplane eventually stalls. During this demonstration, the centre of pressure...
optionA: moves forward until the stall, then moves aft.
optionB: remains in the same position even through the stall.
optionC: moves aft until the stall, then moves forward.
optionD: remains in the same position until moving aft at the stall.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The centre of pressure moves towards the leading edge if the angle of attack is increased up to the critical angle of attack. Beyond critical angle of attack, it depends on the wing platform:

  • Centre of pressure moves backwards on a straight wing because of the lift distribution (flow separation).

  • On a swept-back wing, it further moves towards the leading edge. This is caused by the fact that wing tip stalls first, therefore creating much lower lift than the wing root section. Since the wing root section is more forward than the wing tip section, lift concentrates on the root section, causing forward centre of pressure movement.

title: The load factor is greater than 1 (one):
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: during a wings level stall before recovery.
optionB: in steady wings level horizontal flight.
optionC: when lift is greater than weight.
optionD: during a steady climb.
explanationTotal:
Load factor = Lift / Weight, and it will be greater than 1 when lift exceeds weight

The value of load factor in steady wings level horizontal flight is exactly 1(g).The value is less than one in a steady wings level climb, because a vertical component of thrust is balancing some of the weight. So the value of wing lift required is less.In a stall, lift has decreased and the aircraft will start to descend because lift is now less than weight.

title: What is the effect of exceeding M<sub>CRIT</sub> on the stick force stability of an aeroplane with swept-back wings without any form of stability augmentation?
optionA: A decrease, due to loss of lift in the wing root area.
optionB: No effect, because M<sub>CRIT</sub> is not relevant when considering stick force stability.
optionC: No effect, because stick force stability is independent of Mach number.
optionD: An increase, due to shock wave formation in the wing root area.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
In the subsonic range, maintaining altitude during an increase in airspeed requires a forward stick motion, which becomes more pronounced as the aircraft accelerates. This phenomenon is known as stick stability. However, beyond the critical Mach number (MCRIT), the center of pressure (CP) moves rearward due to mach tuck, resulting in a need to pull the stick aft to maintain altitude. This reversal causes a decrease in stick stability.

The loss of lift occurs in the wing root area due to the formation of shockwaves. These shockwaves typically form where the wing camber is at its thickest, resulting in a loss of lift at the root. In subsonic flight, swept wing aircraft will stall at the tip first, rather than at the root.

For a glide descent, we get the following formulas:

D = W sin y

With regards to this question:

title: The least ability to oppose the yawing moment from a failed engine occurs when the CG...
optionA: coincides with the centre of pressure.
optionB: is located at the aft limit of the CG range.
optionC: is located at the mid-point, halfway between the forward and aft CG limits.
optionD: is located at the forward limit of the CG range.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
When an engine fails on a multi-engine aircraft there will be a decrease in thrust and an increase in drag on the side with the failed engine:

  • airspeed will decay.
  • the nose will drop and.
  • most significantly, there will be an immediate yawing moment towards the failed engine.
The forces and moments acting on an aircraft following failure of the left engine are shown in figure 1. The aircraft has a yawing moment towards the dead engine. The pilot has applied rudder to stop the yaw. The vital action when an engine fails is to stop the yaw.
The rolling and yawing moments and the power of the flight controls to balance them will determine the controllability of an aircraft with asymmetric thrust. Rolling and yawing moments with asymmetric thrust are affected by:
  • Thrust on the live engine
  • Altitude
  • Drag from the dead engine and propeller
  • Asymmetric blade effect (also known as ‘P’ Factor)
  • CG position
The fore and aft CG location has no effect on the yawing moment from a failed engine, but will influence the rudder arm, hence the rudder moment. CG on the aft limit will give the smallest rudder arm and the least ability to oppose the yawing moment from a failed engine.
  • Torque reaction
  • Difference in lift due to slipstream
  • Rolling moment due to sideslip
  • Weight
  • Airspeed

title: A crew calculate landing speeds for a full flap landing (30⁰) but, due to distraction, omit to extend flaps further than the approach setting (15⁰). Which of the following statements is correct assuming the correct glidepath was flown to touchdown?
optionA: Landing Distance available may be insufficient and a tail strike is more likely.
optionB: Aircraft attitude on the glideslope will be lower than expected.
optionC: Thrust setting on the approach will be higher than expected.
optionD: There is less risk of a runway overrun.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
EFFECT OF FLAPS ON LANDING/TAKE-OFF RUN AND CLIMB GRADIENT

The use of high life devices (Flaps) will have an impact on the take-off and Landing roll and climb gradient.
For a given runway length and airplane weight, selecting a greater flap setting will increase the wing’s effective camber and the lift coefficient, which reduces the stalling speed.
  • As a consequence, the take-off speeds are reduced (the same lift will be created at smaller air speed due to greater lift coefficient). This will reduce the take-off run.
  • Flap extension during landings provides several advantages by:
producing greater lift and permitting lower landing speed;
producing greater drag, permitting a steep descent angle without airspeed increase.
=> Reducing the length of the landing roll.

title: An aircraft is flying on coastal line. After an engine failure at 10 000 ft. What will be the expected gliding distance of the aircraft if the L/D ratio is 9:1?
optionA: 45 NM
optionB: 18 NM
optionC: 10 NM
optionD: 15 NM
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
L/D ratio is 9:1 which means 1 000 ft lost during descending equals 9 000 ft gliding distance.
10 000 ft equals 90 000 ft gliding distance
Knowing that the 6 076 ft = 1NM.
90 000 / 6 076 = 14.81 NM ≈ 15 NM

title: Extending flap will (1)_____ CL, (2)_____ speed and (3)_____ stall speed?
optionA: (1) Increase, (2) decrease, (3) decrease
optionB: (1) Decrease, (2) decrease, (3) decrease
optionC: (1) Increase, (2) increase, (3) decrease
optionD: (1) Decrease, (2) decrease, (3) increase
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

The high lift devices of the trailing edge, called flaps, produce the required increase in lift at a lower geometrical angle of attack of the main aerofoil than with a clean wing (clean wing = without any flap deflection). However, the effective chord line and the effective camber changes with flaps selection. Flap deflection results in increased lift and drag at a given angle of attack and increases the maximum CL.

Wings with deflected flaps usually stall at a lower AoA than wings without flaps. This is due to the fact that the pressure gradients at the CL max for both cases are roughly equal.

When you extend the flaps on your plane, you lower your aircraft's stall speed, and at the same time, increase drag.

title: To pitch a conventional aeroplane nose up, the pilot applies backpressure on the control column. This moves the elevator relatively..
optionA: downwards, increasing the positive camber of the tailplane and elevator.
optionB: upwards, increasing the positive camber of the tailplane and elevator.
optionC: upwards, increasing the negative camber of the tailplane and elevator.
optionD: downwards, increasing the negative camber of tailplane and elevator.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The pilot applies backpressure on the control column, this causes the nose to rise and, if enough thrust is present, the aircraft to climb.
The control surface to cause the nose up movement is the elevator.

The elevator is positioned behind the Center of Gravity, while the nose is positioned in front of it.
Therefore, if the nose rises, the opposite action should happen at the tail.

This is done by the elevator generating negative lift (also called downforce).
The elevator does this by moving upwards, changing the aerodynamic camber of the tailplane to a negative camber.

Whereas positive camber generates positive lift, negative camber generates negative lift.
This effect pushes the tail (which is positioned behind the CG) downwards, which has an opposite reaction on the nose (in front of the CG), which comes up.

title: If the airspeed is doubled, whilst maintaining the same control surface deflection the aerodynamic force on this control surface will:
optionA: double.
optionB: become four times smaller.
optionC: increase by the square root of the airspeed.
optionD: become four times greater.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The formula for lift is described as follows;

Lift = ½ * ρ * S * V^2 * CL
If TAS (V) is multiplied by 2, the total lift will increase with 2^2= 4.

title: Total drag is the sum of:
optionA: friction drag and pressure drag.
optionB: induced drag and friction drag.
optionC: parasite drag, interference drag and pressure drag.
optionD: parasite drag and induced drag.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The total drag is the resulting factor if you add induced drag and parasite drag together. It acts in the direction of the relative wind. Lift is perpendicular to the relative wind.

Parasite drag is caused if an airfoil is moving through the air. It is the result of form drag and skin friction drag. Form drag arises from the shape of the object. The more streamlined the object, the less form drag is present. Shape and size are most important in the amount of form drag resulting. Form drag increases with increasing velocity, making it very important for high speed aircraft. Skin friction drag is caused by the friction of the fluid (in case of aircraft this fluid is the atmosphere) against the skin of the object moving through it. It is directly related to the surface area in contact with the fluid. Skin friction increases with the square of the velocity. Parasite drag is made up out of pressure drag, friction drag and interference drag.

Induced drag is caused when an object redirects the airflow. A wing produces lift by creating a pressure difference. This pressure difference is caused by the shape of the airfoil, causing the airflow on top to accelerate, creating a low pressure on top of the wing and high pressure below the wing. This pressure difference naturally wants to restore towards a uniform pressure, which creates vortices around the wingtip. These vortices are deflected downwards, this phenomenon is also called downwash. The induced drag decreases with airspeed (with a rate of 1/V²) and increases with angle of attack and increasing weight.

In the image we can see that the two vectors (induced and parasite drag) create a resulting vector, the total drag. Where the induced and parasite drag vectors collide, we have the minimum drag speed (VMD); the speed where the total drag is the lowest.

This leads us to understand that during an acceleration from a total stand still, the total drag first decreases up until the minimum drag speed and then starts increasing again.

title: The difference between a propeller’s blade angle and its angle of attack is called:
optionA: propeller slip.
optionB: the helix angle.
optionC: the effective pitch.
optionD: the propeller angle.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The Blade Angle

Sometimes called the pitch angle, is the angle subtended between the plane of rotation and the chord line of the propeller blade, which may be fixed or variable. When the airplane is moving it comprises two parts, the angle of attack and the helix angle, but when it is stationary the blade angle is equal to the angle of attack.

The Helix Angle

The angle that the actual path of the propeller makes to the plane of rotation.

Angle of Attack

The path of the propeller through the air determines the direction of the relative airflow. The angle between the blade chord and the relative airflow is the angle of attack (α).
The angle of attack (α) is the result of propeller rotational velocity (RPM) and aircraft forward velocity (TAS).

title: In a straight and steady power-on descent, thrust is...
optionA: less than drag only when the throttle is closed, because then the force of thrust is removed.
optionB: greater than drag, because lift is giving a rearward component in the same direction as drag.
optionC: less than drag, because weight is giving a forward component in the same direction as thrust.
optionD: equal to drag when the descent is steady, unaccelerated, and without any power changes.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The figure illustrates the forces in a steady power-on descent.
The force of Weight is split into two components. One component (W cos γ) acts perpendicular to the flight path and is balanced by Lift, while the other component (W sin γ) acts forward along the flight path and ‘adds’ to the Thrust to balance Drag. If the nose of the aircraft is lowered with a constant thrust setting, the increased component of Weight acting forward along the flight path will cause an increase in IAS. The increased IAS will result in an increase in Drag which will eventually balance the increased forward force of Weight and equilibrium will be re-established.
If the throttle is closed, the force of Thrust is reduced/removed, and a larger forward component of Weight must be provided to balance Drag and maintain a constant IAS. This is accomplished by lowering the nose of the airplane to increase the descent angle (γ).

In a descent, Lift is less than Weight. This is because Lift only has to balance the component of Weight perpendicular to the flight path (W cos γ).
L = W cosγ

In a descent, Thrust is less than Drag. This is because Weight is giving a forward component in the same direction as Thrust (W sin γ).
D = T + W sinγ

title:
Which of these statements about the strength of wing tip vortices are correct or incorrect?

1) Assuming no flow separation, the strength of wing tip vortices decreases as the angle of attack decreases.
2) The strength of wing tip vortices increases as the aspect ratio increases.
optionA: 1) is correct, 2) is incorrect.
optionB: 1) is incorrect, 2) is incorrect.
optionC: 1) is correct, 2) is correct.
optionD: 1) is incorrect, 2) is correct.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Whenever a wing produces lift, concentrated vortices form at the wing tips. The vortices are strongest at the wing tips and become progressively weaker toward the centerline of the aircraft.
The vortices induce downwash to the airflow behind the wing, causing the lift vector to tilt rearward. The horizontal component of lift opposes the forward flight of the aircraft and is known as induced drag.
The larger the vortex, the greater the induced downwash, and the greater the induced drag.

The induced drag can be defined by:

CDI= CL2 / π*AR
Where,
CDI – Induced Drag Coefficient
CL2 – Lift Coefficient squared
AR – Aspect Ratio

Increasing the angle of attack increases CL. From the formula we can deduct that Induced drag is directly proportional to CL squared. So, decreasing the angle of attack decreases CL, which decreases Induced drag. Therefore, statement 1 is correct.
From the formula we can deduct that Induced drag is inversely proportional to Aspect Ratio. So, as the Aspect Ration increases, the Induced Drag decreases. Therefore, statement 2 is incorrect.

title: Coefficient of lift is:
optionA: A variable depending on thrust and empange
optionB: A variable depending on dynamic pressure and the wing area
optionC: A variable depending on wing camber and static pressure
optionD: A variable depending on static pressure and the wing area
explanationTotal:
The lift coefficient is defined as: CL = L/QS

  • Where "L" is the lift force, "S" the area of the wing and "Q" is the dynamic pressure (1⁄2ρ V2).
CL = the Coefficient of Lift, or the product of aerofoil design (shape) and angle of attack, or relative pressure distribution. In other words, its ability to deflect air, so this can vary between aerofoils. The coefficient will be maximum at, or just before, the stall, which you can see from the formula - if CL increases on one side, the other side (L) will also increase, until lift can no longer be produced. Similarly, reducing speed (V) decreases lift. Thus, to keep the same lift, you must change the angle of attack (CL) if you change speed, and vice versa.

title:
Which of these statements about the effect of wing sweep on centre of pressure location are correct or incorrect?

1. The centre of pressure on an unswept wing moves forward as the angle of attack approaches and exceeds the critical angle of attack.
2. When sweep back increases the centre of pressure has an increased tendency to move aft as the angle of attack approaches and exceeds the critical angle of attack.
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: 1 is correct, 2 is incorrect.
optionB: 1 is correct, 2 is correct.
optionC: 1 is incorrect, 2 is correct.
optionD: 1 is incorrect, 2 is incorrect.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The lift from a wing is generated by airflow over it from front to back. If the span-wise flow increases, the boundary layer on the wing surface travels for longer.
This causes them to be thicker and more susceptible to transition to turbulence or flow separation.
The normal tip vortice on a swept wing joins up with a leading edge separation bubble, creating a larger vortex called the Ram’s horn vortex.
This vortex goes inboard along the wing’s leading edge.
The downward flow from the vortex induces pressure on the boundary layer at the wingtip, whereas on straight wings the exact opposite occurs.
With a swept wing, this creates a slow-moving layer of air at the wing tip.
This slow-moving air will separate into disturbed flow and will then stall the tip.

As the wingtips for a swept wing are positioned aft of the center of pressure (CP), the center of pressure upon a wing tip stall will move forward, creating a nose up moment.
This nose up moment will further increase the Angle of Attack if not corrected in time, increasing the layer of slow-moving air, worsening the situation.
Unswept wings do not have this problem.

The pitch up phenomenon is a dangerous characteristic of swept wing aircraft that move at high speed.
It could result in a quickly worsening stalling situation, making it very hard to recover.

title: A Cessna Skyhawk has a V<sub>A</sub> of 123 kts when its mass is 2 300 lbs. Determine its V<sub>A</sub> at a mass of 1 900 lbs:
optionA: 102 kt
optionB: 112 kt
optionC: 135 kt
optionD: 149 kt
explanationTotal:
Maneuvering Speed (VA) is the speed at which an airplane will stall before exceeding its maximum load limit. To calculate the VA we multiply the stall speed (VS1) by the square root of the load factor (n).

  • VA = VS1 x √n

VA is just a stalling speed. Thus, it varies with mass:

  • New VS = Old VS x √Change in mass factor

New VS = 123 x √ (1900 / 2300)

New VS = 111.8 kt

title:
Choose the correct statements with regard to the forces acting parallel and perpendicular to the flight path, for an aeroplane in a straight and steady glide. L = Lift, D = Drag, W = Weight, y = descent angle, x = multiplied by.

1. L and W act perpendicular to the flight path.
2. L and (W x cos y) act perpendicular to the flight path.
3. D and (L x cos y) act parallel to the flight path.
4. D and (W x sin y) act parallel to the flight path.
optionA: 1 and 4
optionB: 1 and 3
optionC: 2 and 4
optionD: 2 and 3
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
A descent may be with or without power. If it is with power, it will be at a very low setting to maintain a particular descent angle at a constant speed. A descent without power is a glide descent and has no thrust vector. The remaining force vectors, lift, mass and drag, however, must remain balanced.
The potential energy derived from the mass of the airplane, at altitude and descending at an angle enables the mass vector, which acts vertically downward, to be resolved into two component vectors.

The component that acts in the direction of flight, parallel to the longitudinal axis, directly opposes and balances the drag vector.
D = W sinγ

The component vector of the mass that acts downward at 90° to the longitudinal axis opposes and balances lift.
L = W cosγ

Only the airplane configuration and angle of attack affect the descent path angle and gradient.

title: Flying a jet transport aircraft, your fuel consumption is higher than expected. You calculate that you have enough to arrive safely, so decide to keep flying to your destination. ATC clears you to descend at your discretion. Whilst calculating your top of descent, what speed would you choose to descend at and why?
optionA: V<sub>MD</sub>: To increase range.
optionB: V<sub>MD</sub>: For minimum descent angle.
optionC: V<sub>MP</sub>: For minimum descent rate.
optionD: V<sub>MP</sub>: For more time in the air.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Note: We have received feedback confirming the correct answer, but find the examiner's choice difficult to justify absolutely. We are still receiving different pieces of information about this question and it may appear differently in the exam. Please put any further exam feedback in the comments or email it to info@atplquestions.com so we can verify the wording and answer, thank you!

As mentioned above, it is difficult to see what the examiner want from us, with 4 options that are quite close really.

Of course, if we have burnt more fuel than expected, we would like to fly for best range. This means flying at 1.32VMD (jet) in the cruise, and at VMD in the descent, which gives best "glide" range. we are not gliding in this scenario, we have idle thrust set (we would assume), but the result is quite similar.

Flying at VMP (minimum power) is sometimes desirable in a glide descent, as it provides the lowest descent rate, as even though the aircraft has slightly more drag, the speed is much lower, so the aircraft descends at a steeper angle, but more slowly (see annex above). If we wanted to spend a longer time at altitude, then VMP would be the speed to choose, but beware, it would mean that we have to fly further in the cruise before beginning descent.

We can therefore see what the examiner is thinking about with their answer of "VMP; for minimum descent rate", but we think it is still tenuous at best. We believe this must be something to do with staying at a higher altitude for longer, but without an in-depth analysis of the fuel savings of both, we cannot say with absolute certainty which is correct.

title: An aeroplane in straight and level flight at 300 kt is subjected to a sudden disturbance in speed. Assuming the angle of attack remains constant initially and the load factor reaches a value of 1.69:
optionA: the speed will have decreased by 30 kt.
optionB: the speed will have decreased by 90 kt.
optionC: the speed will have increased by 30 kt.
optionD: the speed will have increased by 90 kt.
explanationTotal:
In straight and level flight, the load factor is equal to 1, so the initial load factor is 1.

Old speed * √(new N / old N)
300 * √(1.69 / 1) = 390 kts
390 – 300 = 90 kts

title: Considering a fly-by-wire (FBW) system, what can be an advantage of using the CG position?
optionA: Elevator deflection can be optimised throughout the flight.
optionB: It prevents pitch control becoming too sensitive as CG moves forward.
optionC: It prevents roll control becoming too sensitive as CG moves forward.
optionD: It can gradually decrease elevator deflection throughout the flight.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
An aeroplane is trimmed when it will maintain its attitude and speed without the pilot having to apply any load to the cockpit controls.

If it is necessary for a control surface to be deflected to maintain balance of the aircraft, the pilot will need to apply a force to the cockpit control to hold the surface in its deflected position. This force may be reduced to zero by operation of the trim controls.

The aircraft may need to be trimmed in pitch as a result of:
- changes of speed.
- changes of power.
- varying CG positions.
- changes of configuration.

CG ADJUSTMENT

If the flying controls are used for trimming, this results in an increase of drag due to the deflected surfaces.

The out of balance pitching moment can be reduced by moving the CG, thus reducing the balancing load required and therefore the drag associated with it, increasing the aircraft's overall efficiency.

CG movement is usually achieved by transferring fuel between tanks at the nose and tail of the aircraft.

TRIM TANKS

The trim tank transfer system controls the center of gravity (CG) of the aircraft. When the aircraft is in cruise the system optimizes the CG position to increase the fuel economy by reducing the drag of the aircraft.

The system transfers fuel to the trim tank (aft transfer) or from the trim tank (forward transfer).

This movement of fuel changes the CG of the aircraft. Normal operation is automatic but the crew can manually select forward fuel transfer.

title: What are the possible consequences for an aircraft encountering wind shear on final approach?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: The aeroplane stalls when tailwind increases.
optionB: The aeroplane stalls when headwind increases.
optionC: The aeroplane tends to dive when crosswind increases.
optionD: Turbulence will be felt but there are no other hazards.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
MICROBURSTS
These are the most lethal forms of windshear. They normally occur in the vicinity of thunderstorms and are mainly associated with cumulonimbus clouds

THE EFFECT OF A MICROBURST ENCOUNTER DURING THE APPROACH

The attached depicts how an aircraft typically reacts when subject to a microburst during the approach:

- Increasing headwinds, causing the IAS to rise (temporary energy gain) and the aircraft to climb above the glidepath.

- A downdraught that increases the rate of descent and decreases the IAS, thereby causing the aircraft to drop further below the glidepath. The situation worsens if the nose is still high and the thrust setting low.

- On leaving the downdraught, increasing tail winds cause a further reduction in IAS (Temporary Energy Loss). The rate of descent may lessen due to increased thrust availability. This may lead to a reduction in airspeed below the stalling speed and if operating at high angles of attack, which are normally associated with the approach and landing phases of flight, the wing may stall.

A successful recovery from a microburst encounter depends on the altitude, thrust, and speed reserves available. In addition to these effects, severe wind, turbulence, heavy rain, and blinding flashes of lightning often accompany microbursts.

title: In a sideslip, how is the directional stability affected by sweepback?
optionA: Decreases because it increases the AoA.
optionB: Increases because it increases the AoA.
optionC: Increases because it decreases the AoA.
optionD: Decreases because it decreases the AoA.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
DIRECTIONAL STATIC STABILITY
The directional static stability of an aircraft is its natural tendency to recover from a disturbance in yaw, is mainly provided by the fin and involves moments about the normal axis and their relationship with yaw or sideslip angle.

The sideslip angle (β) is the displacement aircraft centre-line from the relative airflow. By convention it is positive when the relative airflow is displaced to the right of the aircraft centre-line.

The sideslip gives the symmetrical fin an angle of attack equal to the sideslip angle. This produces a small aerodynamic force, which, when multiplied by the distance from the centre of gravity, produces a strong restoring moment, and yaws the aircraft back to its original equilibrium position.

A swept wing provides a stable contribution depending on the amount of sweepback, which increases with increase in CL (i.e. at lower IAS). This contribution is relatively weak when compared with other components.

The inclination of the forward, right, wing to the relative airflow is greater than that of the rearward wing, so there is more lift and, hence, more induced drag, on the right side. The result of this discrepancy in drag on the two sides of the wing is a yawing moment to the right, which tends to eliminate the sideslip. This is a stabilizing effect, and may be important if the sweepback angle is quite large.

title:
Calculate the lift (N) when in a 30º gliding descent, given:

Drag: 103 500 N
Mass: 12 500 kg
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Start by converting kg into N: 12 500 kg x 9.81 m/s2 = 122 625 N

L = W cos y
L = 122 625 cos 30º
L = 106 196 N

GLIDE

A glide is a basic maneuver in which the airplane loses altitude in a controlled descent with little or no engine power; forward motion is maintained by the weight component along the flight path which balances drag.
There are only three forces that act on an aircraft in a steady glide: Lift, Weight, and Drag.

title: While performing a go-around, an aircraft with a right-hand propeller will initially tend to…
optionA: yaw to the right and roll to the left.
optionB: yaw to the right and roll to the right.
optionC: yaw to the left and roll to the right.
optionD: yaw to the left and roll to the left.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
At high propeller speeds and low forward speed (as in the take-offs, approaches to power-on stalls or go-around), the aircraft will have the tendecy to swing to one side, particularly those fitted with a tail-dragger undercarriage. The main causes of this are:

  • Slipstream effect
  • Torque reaction
  • Gyroscopic effect
  • Asymmetric blade effect

SLIPSTREAM EFFECT (figure 1)

As the propeller rotates clockwise, it imparts a rotational flow to the air and produces a slipstream, which passes around the fuselage and strikes the left side of the fin.

This causes the aircraft to yaw to the left. The actual amount of rotation imparted to the air is dependent on the power setting.

ASYMMETRIC BLADE EFFECT (figure 2)

This effect occurs when the axis of rotation of the propeller is inclined to the direction of flight. For example, when the tail wheel on a tail-dragger type aircraft is in contact with the ground, its longitudinal axis inclines above the horizontal.

This causes the down-going blade to have a greater effective angle of attack than the up-going blade, thus developing greater thrust .

The thrust asymmetry between the two blades causes the aircraft to yaw to the left.

TORQUE REACTION (figure 3)

This occurs because the air resists the motion of the propeller. In so doing, it tends to twist the engine and airframe in the opposite direction to the propeller (i.e. counter- clockwise).

This causes the aircraft to roll to the left and, whilst on the ground, places more weight on the left wheel than the right wheel. This effectively increases the rolling resistance (i.e. drag) of the left wheel, thus slowing the aircraft down and causing it to yaw to the left.

title: The critical Mach number of a conventional aerofoil section decreases if:
optionA: its camber is decreased.
optionB: it is flown at higher angles of attack.
optionC: its leading edge radius is decreased.
optionD: its thickness to chord ratio is reduced.
explanationTotal:
Critical Mach number (MCRIT) is the free stream Mach number at which local speed of the airflow somewhere around the aircraft reaches local sonic speed (M = 1).

MCRIT of the wing depends on (for a given configuration), amongst other, profile shape:

MCRIT ≈ 1 – 0.7 √t – 3.2 t √(3/CL)
Where “t” is the relative thickness.

From the formula, we can conclude that:

  • If relative thickness is higher, MCRIT is lower.
  • If CL is higher, MCRIT is lower. Since CL is a direct function of angle of attack, if angle of attack is increased, MCRIT reduces.
Consequently, if mass and/or load factors (i.e. turn) increases, CL has to increase, thus MCRIT reduces.

title: In asymmetric flight, yawing towards the live engine causes a sideslip and a side force on the fuselage...
optionA: behind the CG and similar to the rudder force.
optionB: behind the CG and opposite to the rudder force.
optionC: forward of the CG and similar to the rudder force.
optionD: forward of the CG and opposite to the rudder force.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
When we fly in stable (heading not changing) asymmetric flight, there is a complex combination of forces on the aircraft. If a force does not act directly through the aircraft's centre of gravity, then it also creates a moment (turning force). To be in equilibrium (heading and speed not changing), the aircraft's forces and moments must all match up and be equal.

As the question has mentioned sideslipping, then we can assume that we are in the wings level scenario, and are sideslipping towards the dead engine.

See the annex above, the top half shows us what we need to see for this question, the wings level scenario.

Assuming the right engine fails, the left engine is producing a clockwise moment (viewed from above). The rudder has to be deflected to the left to produce a right-wards side force on the aircraft tail, this anticlockwise moment evens out the thrust asymmetry moment, except now we are not longer flying straight, we are sideslipping to the right. The combination of forwards thrust and rightwards force mean we have the relative airflow hitting us from the right-hand side. This causes another force.

The extra force can have different names, but EASA are calling it the fuselage side force. It imagines the fuselage is a wing, and the air coming from the side is creating an angle of attack, creating a sidewards lifting effect, off to the left side, opposite to the rudder force direction. This is fine, but we have to consider what moment it might produce.

If it were just the fuselage to consider, then the lifting force would happen in front of the CG, but due to other features (mainly the large tail fin), the total force acts from behind the CG. In this way, it is an opposing moment to the rudder (it is acting with the thrust asymmetry), and means the required rudder force is higher. The diagram calls it the "weathercocking yawing moment".

Looking at the bottom half of the annex, you can see that the small bank angle to the live engine makes the sideslip go away and can reduce the complexity of the scenario greatly, and reduce drag.

title: You notice ice on the tailplane and, as a result, the tailplane stalls in the landing flare. How can you expect the aeroplane to behave?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Nose goes down and nose wheel touches ground first.
optionB: Nose goes down and may tailstrike.
optionC: Nose goes up and the aeroplane may enter a full stall.
optionD: The aeroplane will behave normally due to ground effect.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
Accumulation of ice on the tailplane will result in disruption of the normal airflow around that surface and will reduce the critical (or stalling) negative AOA of the horizontal stabiliser.

  • The landing flare is initiated by the tailplane producing a nose up pitching moment. If the tailplane stall, there will be a large decrease in nose up pitching moments, causing the nose to drop => As a result, the nose wheel may touch the ground first leading to structural damage.

title: What happens when a pilot moves the flight controls backwards?
optionA: The elevator deflects downwards and increases the tailplane's negative angle of attack.
optionB: The elevator deflects downwards and increases the tailplane's positive angle of attack.
optionC: The elevator deflects upwards and increases the tailplane's negative angle of attack.
optionD: The elevator deflects upwards and increases the tailplane's positive angle of attack.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The elevators respond to a forward or aft movement of the control column or control stick.

When the pilot moves the controls forward, the elevator surface is deflected downwards. This increases the camber of the horizontal stabilizer resulting in an increase in lift. When the pilot moves the controls backward, the elevator surface is deflected upwards. The upwards movement of the trailing edge of the aerofoil will increase an existing negative angle of attack.

title: When flying in icing conditions, ice build-up on an aerofoil will usually occur:
optionA: In the area of the stagnation point.
optionB: Close to the centre of pressure.
optionC: Close to the trailing edge.
optionD: On upper surface from leading to trailing edge.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
First of all, we can logically say that when an object is travelling through the air, water will strike the object on the front side. In our case this means that water or humidity will strike the leading edge of the wing and form into ice is conditions allow for the formation.
Therefore when flying ice usually forms at the leading edge, however when on the ground ice usually forms on the top of the wings.

Next, where does ice form on the leading edge specifically. The point where the airflow hits exactly 90 degrees on the surface is called the stagnation point. This is where water is most likely to stick to the wing and create ice. Water at the stagnation point will not be blown over the wing or under the wing because the air pushes on it at a 90 degree angle.That’s why ice always forms first at the stagnation point, then it usually spreads over the leading edge.

title: The critical Mach number of an aeroplane is the free stream Mach number at which for the first time, somewhere on the aeroplane, the following occurs:
optionA: supersonic flow.
optionB: buffet.
optionC: a shock wave.
optionD: local sonic flow.
explanationTotal:
Critical Mach number (MCRIT) is the free stream Mach number at which local speed of the airflow somewhere around the aircraft reaches local sonic speed (M = 1).

For all aircraft in flight, the speed of the airflow around the aircraft is not exactly the same as the airspeed of the aircraft due to the airflow speeding up and slowing down to travel around the aircraft structure. At the Critical Mach number, local airflow near some areas of the airframe reaches the speed of sound, even though the aircraft itself has an airspeed lower than Mach 1.0.

We can also say that MCRIT is the highest flight speed where there is no supersonic flow (M>1) over any portion of the airfoil.

title:
Which of these statements about drag divergence Mach number are correct or incorrect?

1. MCRIT is higher than the drag divergence Mach number.
2. Assuming a given angle of attack and for M < 1 the drag coefficient CD increases above the drag divergence Mach number.
optionA: 1 is incorrect, 2 is incorrect.
optionB: 1 is incorrect, 2 is correct.
optionC: 1 is correct, 2 is incorrect.
optionD: 1 is correct, 2 is correct.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The Mach number at which the aerodynamic drag begins to increase rapidly is called the drag divergence Mach number. The Drag Divergence Mach Number is usually close to, and always greater than, the Critical Mach Number. Therefore, statement 1 is incorrect.

As speed increases above MCRIT shock waves begin to form and drag increases more rapidly than it would have done without the shock waves. The additional drag is called wave drag and is due to energy drag and boundary layer separation.

The change in drag characteristics is shown by the CD curve for a basic section at a constant angle of attack in figure 1. The ‘hump’ in the curve from M 0.89 to M 1.2 is caused by:

  • The drag directly associated with the trailing edge shock waves (energy loss).
  • Separation of the boundary layer.
  • The formation of the bow shock wave above M 1.0.
The drag divergence Mach number is the Mach number at which the aerodynamic drag begins to increase rapidly. This increase in drag can be seen in figure 1. Therefore, statement 2 is correct.

title: A jet transport aeroplane exhibits pitch up when thrust is suddenly increased from an equilibrium condition, because the thrust line is below the:
optionA: drag line of action.
optionB: neutral point.
optionC: centre of pressure.
optionD: CG.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
POWER EFFECTS

Its effects may cause significant changes in trim left coefficient and static longitudinal stability.
The vertical location of the thrust line defines one of the direct contributions to stability.

  • If the thrust line is below the CG (the case of most airliners with underwing engines), a thrust increase will produce an added pitch-up moment => this will cause the airplane to slow down more than necessary (despite the added thrust). Creating an unstable situation. Therefore, the effect is destabilizing.
  • If the thrust line is above the CG, this is the opposite of the above and a thrust increase will produce a nose down moment (negative moment), and, in moderate amounts, can have a stabilising effect. The airplane will settle at a higher speed, which is presumably what the pilot wants (despite the "power controls altitude" mantra). When the line is too high, the airplane may even descend and accelerate more than necessary, until the aerodynamic moment balances out the thrust moment, but overall the condition is stable.
  • Thrust is in line with CG. The airplane will start to climb (or reduce descent) and will settle on the same AoA and roughly the same speed.

title: Considering bank angle and engine thrust, what limits are to be taken into account when defining VMC (minimum control speed with critical engine inoperative)?
optionA: Not more than 5° of bank, idle thrust.
optionB: Not more than 15° of bank, maximum available take-off thrust.
optionC: Not more than 5° of bank, maximum available take-off thrust.
optionD: Not more than 15° of bank, idle thrust.
explanationTotal:
VMCA is the calibrated airspeed at which, when the critical engine is suddenly made inoperative, it is possible to maintain control of the airplane with that engine still inoperative and maintain straight flight with an angle of bank of not more than 5°.

VMCA may not exceed 1.13VSR with:

  • maximum available take-off power or thrust on the engines.
  • the airplane trimmed for take-off.
  • the most unfavorable CG position.
  • maximum sea level take-off weight.
  • the airplane in its most critical take-off configuration (but with gear up); and
  • the airplane airborne and the ground effect negligible; and
  • if applicable, the propeller of the inoperative engine:
    • wind milling
    • feathered, if the airplane has an autmatic feathering device.
  • The rudder forces required to maintain control at VMCA may not exceed 150 lb. nor may it be necessary to reduce power or thrust on the operative engines.

Note: There is no performance requirement, just directional control.

Banking towards the live engine reduces the rudder deflection required and so allows a lower VMCA. The magnitude of VMCA increases with increased bank angle from 0° to 5°. The maximum limit is set at 5° because there is an increasing risk of fin stall above this limit.

title: Thunderstorms may cause an aircraft to encounter buffet or even enter a stall when flying at low level. Choose the correct option:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Severe horizontal wind shear may cause a reduction in airspeed to below stalling speed.
optionB: Microbursts are only a hazard to aircraft below 1 000 ft AGL.
optionC: Vertical wind shear is only a problem at high level.
optionD: Wing icing will not affect an aircraft at low level.
explanationTotal:
Gusts, or in other word abrupt wind changes (or windshear), are known to occur close to or in thunderstorm cells, thus particularly in ITCZ, in clear air turbulence (jet streams) and in wake turbulence.

If an aerofoil encounters an upgust, it will experience an increase in angle of attack. For a given gust velocity, the increment in angle increases as the aircraft TAS decreases. If the angle of attack is already large (low speed), the increment due to the gust could cause the wing to stall.

On the other hand, windshear may cause a sudden headwind drop. This may lead to a reduction in airspeed below the stalling speed.

title:
During a straight steady climb:

1 – lift is less than weight.
2 – lift is greater than weight.
3 – load factor is less than 1.
4 – load factor is greater than 1.
5 – lift is equal to weight.
6 – load factor is equal to 1.

Which of the following lists all the correct statements?
optionA: 1 and 3.
optionB: 1 and 6.
optionC: 5 and 6.
optionD: 2 and 4.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The balance of forces in steady climb show thrust is partly acting upwards and weight is partly adding to the drag.
Because the thrust is now assisting lift, there is less lift required than in level flight.
For steady speed, the thrust and two effects of aerodynamic drag and weight must be equal.

T= Thrust
W= Weight
D= Drag
T= D + W sin(alfa)

This means that the climb angle (sin alfa) depends on excess thrust and weight.

In descent the formula will become T= D – W sin(alfa)

The load factor is the relationship between lift and weight.
As the lift is now decreased and the load factor in straight and level flight is 1, the load factor will now be less than 1.

title:
Which of these statements about the equilibrium of forces and moments at VMCA are correct or incorrect?

I. Equilibrium of moments about the normal axis. is provided by rudder deflection.
II. Equilibrium of forces along the lateral axis does not require any side slip during a wings level condition.
optionA: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
optionB: I is correct, II is correct.
optionC: I is incorrect, II is correct.
optionD: I is correct, II is incorrect.
explanationTotal:
If an engine fails during the take-off of a multi-engine aircraft a significant yawing moment will be experienced due to asymmetric thrust. In order to maintain directional control and keeping the aircraft in equilibrium around the yaw axis, the pilot must apply corrective action. Above a certain speed this will be possible using aerodynamic controls only. If the aircraft is still on the ground this means the use of the rudder, if the aircraft is airborne, the pilot can also apply bank by using the ailerons. The greater the thrust of this operating engine(s), the greater the yawing moment will be and the greater the aerodynamic forces to counteract this yawing moment would be required.

VMCA = Minimum control speed in the take-off configuration with gear up – the minimum calibrated airspeed at which, when the critical engine is suddenly made inoperative, it is possible to maintain control and maintain straight flight using no more than 5° of bank without required exceptional piloting skill or the aeroplane adopting a dangerous attitude or changing heading by more than 20°. An increased bank angle beyond 5°, while keeping the rudder centered, may lead to a fin stall, due to an extreme sideslip angle, but when decreasing the bank angle below 5° to 0°, rudder deflection has to be increased and therefore VMCA will increase, too.

  • Equilibrium of moments about the normal axis (also called yaw or vertical axis) is provided by rudder deflection (yaw)
  • Equilibrium of moments about the lateral axis is provided by elevator deflection (pitch)
  • Equilibrium of moments about the longitudinal axis is provided by aileron deflection (roll)

Note: Forces along the lateral axis is not the same like moments around the lateral axis. Forces along the lateral axis act around the longitudinal axis. Therefore an equilibrium along the lateral axis always requires bank or sideslip.

title: What will happen in ground effect?
optionA: The induced angle of attack and induced drag decrease.
optionB: The wing tip vortices increase in strength.
optionC: The thrust required will increase significantly.
optionD: The wing downwash on the tail surfaces increases.
explanationTotal:
For a fixed wing aircraft, ground effect is the increased lift and decreased drag that the wings generate when they are close to the ground. Upon landing, ground effect can give the effect of floating. The stall speed may be temporarily reduced due to ground effect.

Ground effect is effective from the ground to approximately half the aircraft’s wingspan above ground. The effect is caused by the ground interrupting the wingtip vortices, decreasing the downwash angle. Below the airfoil, a higher pressure than if an airfoil travels at higher altitude is created, as the air below the airfoil is trapped in between the wing and the ground. This means that the aircraft needs a lower angle of attack for a certain amount of lift. This results in lower induced drag (decreasing induced angle of attack).

title:
A crop duster utility aircraft has a VSO (landing config) of 55 kt and a VS1 (clean) of 70 kt.
What is the VA for this aircraft?
optionA: 107 kt
optionB: 115 kt
optionC: 136 kt
optionD: 147 kt
explanationTotal:
Maneuvering Speed (VA) is the speed at which an airplane will stall before exceeding its maximum load limit. To calculate the VA we multiply the stall speed (VS1) by the square root of the load factor (n).
  • VA = VS1 x √n

CS 23.337 Limit manoeuvring load factors ED Decision 2003/14/RM

(a) The positive limit manoeuvring load factor n may not be less than –

  1. 2 ∙ 1 + 24000 𝑊+10000 for normal and commuter category aeroplanes (where W = design maximum take-off weight lb), except that n need not be more than 3•8;
  2. 4•4 for utility category aeroplanes; or
  3. 6•0 for aerobatic category aeroplanes.
VA = VS1 x √n
VA = 70 x √4.4
VA = 146.8 kt

title:
Maintaining a constant Flight Level and IAS, an aircraft flies into a colder airmass.
Choose the correct statement:
optionA: Mach number stays the same, but there is an increased risk of high speed buffet and a shock stall.
optionB: Mach number increases. There is a risk of a high speed warning.
optionC: Mach number decreases, There is a risk of a low speed warning.
optionD: Mach number stays constant.
explanationTotal:
Mach number = True Air Speed (TAS) / Local Speed of Sound (LSS)
LSS = 38.96 √ Absolute Temperature (K)

  1. IAS = 1/2 p V2 (Where V = TAS)
    When flying into a colder airmass, density "p" increases. In order to maintain IAS constant, TAS (V) must decrease.

  2. LSS will decrease in colder air.

As both TAS and LSS decreases, Mach number will not change.

title: Based on the two-dimensional drag formula, if the altitude increases while all other parameters remain constant, the drag will (1)_____ because the air density will (2)_____.
optionA: (1) increase; (2) decrease.
optionB: (1) increase; (2) increase.
optionC: (1) decrease; (2) increase.
optionD: (1) decrease; (2) decrease.
explanationTotal:
Drag increases with the density of the fluid (ρ). More density means more mass, which means more inertia, which means more resistance to getting out of the way. The two quantities are directly proportional. D ∝ ρ

  • As altitude increases, air density decreases. If all other parameters remain constant, drag will decrease.

title:
Refer to figure.
The dotted line represents how a lift curve changes when a high-lift device is deployed. To which of these devices could the curve apply to?

I. Krueger Flap
II. Fowler flap
III. Slats and slots
optionA: I and II
optionB: I and III
optionC: II and III
optionD: III
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Aircraft are fitted with high lift devices to reduce the take-off and landing distances and improve slow flying characteristics.

The three leading edge devices shown in the annex are:

  • Leading Edge Flaps - similar to trailing edge flaps, they increase the camber of the wing to increase CL and CLMAX
  • Krueger Flaps - part of the lower surface of the leading edge, which can be rotated about its forward edge to force more airflow over the top of the wing at high angles of attack. The graph for krueger flaps is not quite a simple as shown in the figure above, but for this question it is fine to use.
  • Slats - These are small "extra leading edges" that move forward in front of the leading edge of the wing, creating a small slot behind, where airflow is sped up and re-energised, delaying the stalling angle of attack without increasing the CL at normal angles of attack.

Kreuger Flaps and Slats are often used in conjunction, with Kreuger Flaps being used on the inboard section of an wing and slats being used outboard of the engine pylons, to promote root stall tendency due to the Kreuger Flaps being less effective.

For this question, the slats are the only leading edge device that fit the graph perfectly, and this is a very common high-lift device to use in questions, due to the distinctive CL vs AoA graph, so be familiar with it.

"Fowler Flap" Incorrect.
  • These are Trailing Edge devices. They change the graph in a different way to leading edge devices, and fowler flaps even moreso.

title:
Which of the following have an effect on rudder force in asymmetric flight?

1. Rudder deflection
2. Thrust setting
3. CG
4. Mass
5. TAS
6. IAS
explanationTotal:
A moment is defined by a force multiplied by an arm (distance).

The yawing moment generated by an engine failure has to be compensated for with rudder input. The moment generated by the rudder depends on the force the rudder is capable of producing multiplied by the arm.

The force exerted by the rudder depends on:
- Rudder deflection
- Dynamic pressure (IAS)

The rudder arm depends on:
- Position of CG

title:
Which drag components make up parasite drag?

1. pressure drag.
2. friction drag.
3. induced drag.
4. interference drag.

The combination that regroups all of the correct statements is:
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The total drag is the resulting factor if you add induced drag and parasite drag together. It acts in the direction of the relative wind. Lift is perpendicular to the relative wind.

Parasite drag is caused if an airfoil is moving through the air. It is the result of form drag and skin friction drag. Form drag arises from the shape of the object. The more streamlined the object, the less form drag is present. Shape and size are most important in the amount of form drag resulting. Form drag increases with increasing velocity, making it very important for high speed aircraft. Skin friction drag is caused by the friction of the fluid (in case of aircraft this fluid is the atmosphere) against the skin of the object moving through it. It is directly related to the surface area in contact with the fluid. Skin friction increases with the square of the velocity. Parasite drag is made up out of pressure drag, friction drag and interference drag.

Induced drag is caused when an object redirects the airflow. A wing produces lift by creating a pressure difference. This pressure difference is caused by the shape of the airfoil, causing the airflow on top to accelerate, creating a low pressure on top of the wing and high pressure below the wing. This pressure difference naturally wants to restore towards a uniform pressure, which creates vortices around the wingtip. These vortices are deflected downwards, this phenomenon is also called downwash. The induced drag decreases with airspeed (with a rate of 1/V²) and increases with angle of attack and increasing weight.

In the image we can see that the two vectors (induced and parasite drag) create a resulting vector, the total drag. Where the induced and parasite drag vectors collide, we have the minimum drag speed (VMD); the speed where the total drag is the lowest.

This leads us to understand that during an acceleration from a total stand still, the total drag first decreases up until the minimum drag speed and then starts increasing again.

title: A slotted flap will increase the CL<sub>MAX</sub> by:
optionA: increasing the critical angle of attack.
optionB: increasing only the camber of the aerofoil.
optionC: increasing the camber of the aerofoil and re-energising the airflow.
optionD: decreasing the skin friction.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

The slotted flap is a flap that moves downwards. Whenever it is extended, it leaves a small gap between the flap and the wing itself, re-energizing the airflow by creating a venturi effect. The flap moves downwards, thus increasing camber. Both these traits increase CLMAX. The slotted flap increases CL and CD when extended. Some flaps use multiple slots, to maximize the effect.

title: The two deformation modes that cause wing flutter are:
optionA: bending and elongation.
