optionB: torsion and shearing.
optionC: shearing and elongation.
optionD: torsion and bending.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Wing flutter is a dynamic instability of an aircraft associated with the interaction of aerodynamic (bending and torsion), elastic, and inertial forces. It is an uncontrolled oscillation that can occur on fixed surfaces which can lead to the catastrophic failure of the structure.

In flight, an aircraft is supported by its wings and they are bent upwards. When encountering a gust, it will shake the wings up and down. As a result, they will be flapping at a specific frequency. When this vibration is similar to that of the structure of the wing, it will begin to resonate. This resonance will amplify the flutter.

title: What could happen if the pilot of a large transport aircraft applied full rudder to turn right during the final approach to land?
optionA: The aircraft's fin could stall due to sideslip.
optionB: The right wing could stall due to increased drag.
optionC: The right wing could stall due to a skid.
optionD: The aircraft will make a smooth turn without any issues.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Imagine this scenario: You're making a right turn from base to final, but you're at risk of overshooting the runway. Here's a crucial mistake to avoid: Adding right rudder to tighten the turn without coordinating the bank and rudder, leading to a skid. This can result in a disastrous chain of events. The skid induces an over-banking tendency, prompting a subconscious response of adding opposite aileron, pulling the nose down. Suddenly, the aircraft stalls. If the airplane is skidding toward the outside of the turn, it will have a tendency to roll to the inside of the turn because the inside wing stalls first.

Why does the inside wing drop first in a skid? Aerodynamic factors come into play, but the fundamental principles are straightforward. In a skid, the aircraft turns too fast for the bank angle, yawing into the turn, often caused by excessive rudder input. This accelerates the outside wing, increasing its lift and causing the aircraft to roll into the turn. To counter this, opposite aileron is added, increasing the angle of attack on the inside, low wing.

As the inside wing surpasses the critical angle of attack, it stalls and drops.

title:
Refer to figure.
When compared to a clean configuration, the wing in the attached figure has a:
optionA: higher CL-CD ratio
optionB: lower CD and a lower CL-CD ratio
optionC: lower CL-CD ratio
optionD: higher C<sub>L</sub> and a lower C<sub>L</sub>-C<sub>D</sub> ratio
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The figure depicts speedbrakes (flight spoilers). Their operating principle is simple. Cross-sectional area increases, boundary layer becomes turbulent, which increases parasite drag and reduces lift. Since drag increases and lift reduces, lift to drag ratio reduces significantly. It is apparent that the CL/CD curve is shifted down and to the right (CL reduces and CD increases at the same angle of attack).

title:
Which of these statements about the buffet free range in a buffet onset boundary graph are correct or incorrect?

1. When speed increases the buffet free range decreases.
2. When altitude decreases the buffet free range decreases.
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: 1 is correct, 2 is incorrect.
optionB: 1 is incorrect, 2 is correct.
optionC: 1 is correct, 2 is correct.
optionD: 1 is incorrect, 2 is incorrect.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Stall boundaries set a lower limit to the operating speed, according to the load factor. In the case of a high-speed aircraft, there is also an upper limit which is due to the approach of shock stall and the associated buffet which occurs if the aircraft enters the transonic speed range. The limits associated with these effects give the buffet boundaries.

For a given aircraft there is a Mach number which, even at low angle of attack, cannot be exceeded because of the onset of shock stall. The EAS corresponding to this Mach number falls as altitude increases, so the range of operating speeds is reduced at both ends.

Flying at a different speed will not influence the buffet boundaries, therefore statement 1 is incorrect.

At altitude, the equivalent stalling speed increases with ‘g’ rather more rapidly than at sea level, because of the Mach number effect on CLMAX. Also, the buffet boundary becomes much more severe. Above a certain altitude the buffet boundary may intersect the stall boundary at a value of ‘g’ lower than the structural limit. This ‘point’ is another representation of “coffin corner”.

We can then conclude that decreasing altitude, increases the buffet margin, therefore statement 2 is incorrect.

title:
Consider two elevator control systems:

1. is fitted with a trim tab
2. is fitted with fully powered hydraulic controls and an adjustable horizontal stabiliser.

For both cases and starting from a trimmed condition, how will the neutral position of the control column change, after trimming for a speed increase?
optionA: 1 moves forward, 2 moves forward.
optionB: 1 moves forward, 2 does not change.
optionC: 1 does not change, 2 does not change.
optionD: 1 does not change, 2 moves forward.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
When speed is increased, angle of attack must be decreased, therefore the aircraft must be trimmed nose down otherwise the pilot will have to keep pushing the control column forward in order to keep level flight. When a trim tab is installed, in this case, it will move up in order to maintain the new elevator deflection. The control column is then held in a more forward position. Remember that the trim tab is deflected in the opposite direction than the elevator.

For a trimmable horizontal stabiliser, the whole stabiliser's incidence angle can be changes as trimming. The pilot can control the stabiliser by using the trim wheel. If the linkage is mechanic or power-assisted, the neutral point of the control column changes with trim setting. However, in a fully powered flight control system, neutral point will not change since there is no actual trim, only a feel unit (if you are trimmed, the elevator deflection is 0).

title: What kind of drag will you find on a wing with no lift?
optionA: No drag.
optionB: Only the drag you'd find in a two dimensional flow.
optionC: Same drag as in straight and level flight.
optionD: Parasite drag only.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The total drag is the resulting factor if you add induced drag and parasite drag together. It acts in the direction of the relative wind. Lift is perpendicular to the relative wind.

Parasite drag is caused if an airfoil is moving through the air. It is the result of form drag and skin friction drag. Form drag arises from the shape of the object. The more streamlined the object, the less form drag is present. Shape and size are most important in the amount of form drag resulting. Form drag increases with increasing velocity, making it very important for high speed aircraft. Skin friction drag is caused by the friction of the fluid (in case of aircraft this fluid is the atmosphere) against the skin of the object moving through it. It is directly related to the surface area in contact with the fluid. Skin friction increases with the square of the velocity. Parasite drag is made up out of pressure drag, friction drag and interference drag.

Parasite drag drag exists even if lift is not being created, (just from the airframe moving through the air). Induced drag, as the name suggests, is a drag produced due to lift.

title: During asymmetric flight, if the wings are kept level using ailerons, a side force on the fuselage is the result of:
optionA: Sideslip due to the rudder force away from the live engine.
optionB: Ballistic skid due to the rudder force towards the live engine.
optionC: Sideslip due to the rudder force away from the live engine. This force acts in the same direction of the fuselage side force.
optionD: Ballistic skid due to yaw from the live engine. This force acts in the same direction as the rudder force.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
This question is asking about stable asymmetric flight with wings level. This is one of the standard methods for flying with a failed engine, and the other method is to fly with a small bank angle towards the live engine (five to the live).

When we fly in stable (heading not changing) asymmetric flight, there is a complex combination of forces on the aircraft. If a force does not act directly through the aircraft's centre of gravity, then it also creates a moment (turning force). To be in equilibrium (heading and speed not changing), the aircraft's forces and moments must all match up and be equal.

See the annex above, the top half shows us what we need to see for this question, the wings level scenario.

Assuming the right engine fails, the left engine is producing a clockwise moment (viewed from above). The rudder has to be deflected to the left to produce a right-wards side force on the aircraft tail (a force away from the live engine), this anticlockwise moment evens out the thrust asymmetry moment, except now we are not longer flying straight, we are sideslipping to the right. The combination of forwards thrust and rightwards force mean we have the relative airflow hitting us from the right-hand side. This causes another force.

The extra force can have different names, but this question calls it the fuselage side force. It imagines the fuselage is a wing, and the air coming from the side is creating an angle of attack, creating a sidewards lifting effect, off to the left side, opposite to the rudder force direction. This is fine, but we have to consider what moment it might produce.

If it were just the fuselage to consider, then the lifting force would happen in front of the CG, but due to other features (mainly the large tail fin), the total force acts from behind the CG. In this way, it is an opposing moment to the rudder (it is acting with the thrust asymmetry), and means the required rudder force is higher. The diagram calls it the "weathercocking yawing moment".

It happens because of sideslip; ballistic skid appears to be a made-up phrase.

Looking at the bottom half of the annex, you can see that the small bank angle to the live engine makes the sideslip go away and can reduce the complexity of the scenario greatly, and reduce drag.

title: Whilst maintaining straight and level flight, extending trailing edge flaps enables an aircraft to fly at (1) _____ indicated air speeds due to a higher (2) _____.
optionA: (1) lower; (2) C<sub>D</sub>
optionB: (1) lower; (2) C<sub>L</sub>
optionC: (1) higher; (2) C<sub>D</sub>
optionD: (1) higher; (2) C<sub>L</sub>
explanationTotal:
Flaps are high-lift devices, primarily used to allow flight at slower airspeeds for take-off and landing. Flaps also increase aircraft drag, which can be useful for energy management, particularly on large jets.

Flaps increase the camber of the wing, and sometimes extend backwards to increase the wing are too. Increasing the camber leads to an increased coefficient of lift (CL), which allows a higher lift force to be produced from the same airflow. This means that an aircraft can fly slower without stalling, as the same amount of lift required to balance out the aircraft weight will be created at lower indicated air speeds.

We do not use flaps all the time because they also greatly increase the coefficient of drag (CD), but this is not the answer to the question as increased drag is just a side effect, and does not allow us to fly slower without stalling.

title: Select the correct statement with regard to positively cambered aerofoils.
optionA: The angle of attack will have a positive value when the lift coefficient equals zero.
optionB: They will always have a negative lift coefficient at all angles of attack.
optionC: The angle of attack will have a negative value when the lift coefficient equals zero.
optionD: They will always have a positive lift coefficient at all angles of attack.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The curvature or camber of the upper surface of a cambered airfoil is greater than that of the lower surface. As a result, the negative pressure generated by the acceleration of the airstream over the upper surface is greater than that beneath the lower surface.
Because of the different curvatures of the upper and lower surfaces of the airfoil even when the angle of attack is zero the airfoil will still generate a small amount of total lift.
From figure 1, we can conclude that for a positively cambered airfoil at zero lift coefficient, the angle of attack will be negative.

title:
Refer to figure.
The point on the polar curve corresponding to flight with minimum drag is:
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
POLAR CURVE

The polar curve of an airfoil is the graphical relationship of the coefficients of lift and drag plotted against each other, the resulting graph is as shown in the attached figure. It reveals that the total lift and total drag increase from point A to a maximum at point D, thus the angle of attack of the wings increases in the same manner. Therefore, the speed decreases from a maximum at point A to a minimum at point D.

  • Point B (point 2 - question annex) is the point at which a tangent from the origin touches the polar curve, which is at the point at which the total drag is minimum, the lift/drag ratio is maximum and the IAS in level flight is VMD. This is also the speed at which the longest glide distance will be achieved.

title:
Which statement is correct?

I. Stall speeds are determined with the CG at the forward limit.
II. Minimum control speeds are determined with the CG at the aft limit.
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
optionB: I is correct, II is correct.
optionC: I is correct, II is incorrect.
optionD: I is incorrect, II is correct.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

  1. Stall speeds are determined with the least favourible CG position. For an aircraft, this is the most forward point because then the main wing will be producing the most lift. With the CG furthest ahead of the centre of pressure, the horizontal stabilizer will be producing a downwards force, which the main wings will have to compensate for by producing more lift. The main wings will therefore have to be at a higher angle of attack and therefore be closer to the stall.

Hence the stall will occur at higher speeds with a forward CG then with a rearward CG.

  1. Minimum control speeds are also determined with the least favourible conditions. When considering an engine failure, we know that the aircraft will rotate around its CG, but the distance of the moment doesn’t change when it moves fore or aft, the engines moment would only change when we move it along the lateral axis of the aircraft. However, the position of the CG will influence the rudder arm, and hence the rudder moment. A CG on the af limit will provide a small arm and therefore the least ability to oppose the yawing moment of the engine failure.

title: Assuming ISA conditions and a descent above the tropopause at constant Mach number and aeroplane mass, the:
optionA: IAS decreases.
optionB: lift coefficient decreases.
optionC: TAS increases.
optionD: lift coefficient increases.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The Mach number is defined as the ratio between the TAS and the LSS (Local speed of sound). It is an indication of how fast an aircraft is travelling with relation to the sound waves that surround it.

The Mach number may be calculated as follows:

  • M = TAS/LSS
  • Where, LSS = 38.95x √T(K)

The speed of propagation of small pressure waves depends upon the temperature of the air only. Therefore, the mach number, local speed of sound and TAS will remain constant.

However, the pressure decreases with increasing altitude, even above the tropopause. Consequently, the pressure is increasing when the aircraft is descending. Increasing air pressure translates into higher lift. To maintain a constant mach number, the angle of attacke must reduce. Since the lift coefficient represents the angle of attack, it will decrease.

title: During a deep stall of aeroplanes equipped with a swept-back and T-tail stabiliser, what happens to the elevator?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Remains clear of the wing's increased downwash, making it difficult or impossible to decrease the angle of attack without a stick pusher system.
optionB: Lies completely in the wing's increased downwash, making it a more effective surface to decrease the angle of attack.
optionC: Remains clear of the separated airflow behind the stalled wing and thus can be used to decrease the angle of attack.
optionD: Lies completely in the airflow behind the stalled wing and reduces the effectiveness of the elevators to decrease the angle of attack.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
A deep stall is a dangerous phenomenon that occurs when the turbulence created by the main wing encompasses the horizontal stabilizer of the aircraft, preventing the aircraft from recovering from the stall.

The worst scenario is swept-wing and T-tail. Due to swept-back wing a deep stall occurs because of wing tip stall. Furthermore, stabilizer becomes ineffective because it is situated in the separated turbulent flow of the wing and fuselage.

Aircraft with swept-back wings are prone to deep stall, regardless of horizontal stabilizer position (T-tail or low tail). T-tail will worsen recovery characteristics.

title: The coefficient of drag can be defined as the...
optionA: sum of induced drag and parasite drag.
optionB: ratio of lift forces to drag forces.
optionC: measure of the efficiency of the aeroplane.
optionD: ratio of drag pressure to dynamic pressure.
explanationTotal:
Dynamic pressure takes into account the air density and velocity, but when combined with the wing planform surface area (S) it produces a force known as drag.
Like lift, drag is not exactly equal to the dynamic pressure times the area, but varies with shape and angle of attack. The Coefficient of Drag (CD ) represents these factors.

The general drag formula is thus:

D= CD * 1 / 2 * ρ * V2 * S
Where,
D – Drag
CD – Drag Coefficient
V2 – Airflow Speed squared
S – Surface Area
ρ – Air density
1 / 2 * ρ * V2 – Dynamic pressure

Re-arranging the formula in function of Drag Coefficient:
CD = D / (1 /2* ρ* V2*S)

title: The function of the slot between an extended slat and the leading edge of the wing is to:
optionA: cause a venturi effect, which energises the boundary layer.
optionB: slow the airflow in the slot so that more pressure is created under the wing.
optionC: reduce the wing loading.
optionD: allow space for vibration of the slat.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Whenever the slat is extended, it leaves a small gap between the slat and the wing itself, re-energizing the airflow by creating a venturi effect. This increase CLMAX and delay separation. They allow flight at higher angles of attack and reduce the stall speed. The slotted flap increases CL and CD when extended. Some slats use multiple slots, to maximize the effect.

title: You are flying an approach and encounter windshear. What might happen?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: A sudden extreme headwind can make you stall.
optionB: A feel bump and nothing more.
optionC: You will feel a drift from left which make the plane go into a dive.
optionD: A sudden extreme tailwind may make you stall.
explanationTotal:
Wind shear refers to the variation of wind over either horizontal or vertical distances. Wind shear has significant effects on the control of an aircraft, and it has been the sole or a contributing cause of many aircraft accidents.

Due to changes in wind speed turbulence will occur. Extreme tailwind can be especially dangerous as it is opposing the relative airflow around the aerofoil and slows it, separation may occur which can be followed by stall.

title: When deploying speedbrakes, you can expect the minimum drag to (1) _____ and the minimum drag speed to (2)_____.
optionA: (1) increase; (2) increase.
optionB: (1) increase; (2) decrease.
optionC: (1) decrease; (2) decrease.
optionD: (1) decrease; (2) increase.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Drag is the force which resists the forward motion of the aircraft. Drag acts parallel to and in the same direction as the relative airflow (in the opposite direction to the flight path).

Total Drag is sub-divided into two main types:

INDUCED DRAG - the result of lift generation.
PARASITE DRAG - independent of lift generation.

Parasite drag is further sub-divided into:

- Skin Friction Drag
- Form (Pressure) Drag
- Interference Drag

The sum of Parasite Drag and Induced Drag is the Total Drag.

The Total Drag will be minimum at the IAS where Parasite Drag = Induced Drag. This speed is called Minimum DragSpeed (VMD). Flying at a slower or faster speed than VMD will generate more drag.

PARASITE DRAG

If an aircraft were flying at zero lift angle of attack, the only drag present would be parasite drag.

FORM DRAG

Form drag is produced whenever the streamline airflow passing over an aircraft separates from the surface and becomes turbulent. An example of extreme form drag is the effect of a flat plate placed at right angles to the airflow.

EFFECT OF CONFIGURATION ON TOTAL DRAG

Extension of the landing gear, air brakes, or flaps will increase parasite drag but will not substantially affect induced drag. The effect of increasing parasite drag is to increase total drag at any IAS but to decrease the speed VMD compared to the clean aircraft.

title: One disadvantage of wing sweepback is:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: the tendency of the wing root section to stall prior to the wingtip section.
optionB: the tendency of the wingtip section to stall prior to the wing root section.
optionC: a severe pitch down moment when the centre of pressure shifts forward.
optionD: that the critical Mach number is significantly lower.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Assuming not wing twist, therefore changing the angle of incidence of the chord of the wing from the root to the tip of the wing, swept wings have the tendency to stall at the tips of the wings which can cause a dangerous pitch up at low speeds.

About the critical mach number, swept wings have higher critical mach number than the equivilant rectangular wing. Therefore that answer is incorrect.

title: Blade angle decreases from the root to the tip. How does the thrust of a basic propeller vary from root to tip?
optionA: Thrust increases away from the root, where it is low, but reduces back to zero at the tip.
optionB: Thrust is low at the blade root and high at the blade tip.
optionC: Thrust decreases away from the root, where it is high, to the tip, where it is lowest.
optionD: Thrust is highest at the blade root and tip.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
When the propeller is rotating, aerodynamic losses occur near the hub and at the blade tips. Near the hub, the airflow is disrupted where the propeller blade sections are thicker and near the engine.
Vortices form at the propeller blade tips in a similar manner as at the wing tips. This results in induced drag and a reduction in the actual amount of thrust developed in this region. In practice, only a small part of the propeller blade is effective in producing thrust at normal operating angles of attack. This is generally between 60% and 90% of the distance from the blade hub to the tip.
At positive angles of attack, the greatest useful thrust is produced at 75% of the tip radius. By convention, the blade angle at this radius is the reference pitch for the whole propeller blade.

title: What flying characteristics must an aeroplane have in order to meet the design certification standards if its leading edge slats are not mechanically connected?
optionA: Both slats and flaps must be interlinked to prevent asymmetry.
optionB: Only flaps need to have asymmetric protection.
optionC: The aircraft must not roll by more than 10 degrees.
optionD: Handling must remain acceptable at all stages of flight.
explanationTotal:
Deployment of high lift devices can produce large changes of lift, drag, and pitching moments. If the movement of the devices is not symmetrical on the two wings, the unbalanced forces could cause significant roll control problems.

On many flap control systems, the deflection on the two sides is compared while the flaps are moving, and if one side should fail, movement on the other side is automatically stopped.

On less sophisticated systems, a failure of the operating mechanism could lead to an asymmetric situation, known as flap asymmetry. The difference in lift will cause a rolling moment, which must be opposed by the ailerons, and the difference in drag will cause a yawing moment, which must be opposed by the rudder.

CS 25.701 requires in subparagraphs (a) and (d) that:

“(a) Unless the aeroplane has safe flight characteristics with the flaps or slats retracted on one side and extended on the other, the motion of flaps or slats on opposite sides of the plane of symmetry must be synchronised by a mechanical interconnection or approved equivalent means.“

title: An aircraft with a conventional, cambered aerofoil accelerates through the transonic speed range. Shock waves form on the upper and lower surfaces of the wing. While the aircraft continues to accelerate, the shock wave on the lower surface initially moves aft…
optionA: more quickly than the upper shock wave.
optionB: but remains ahead of the upper shock wave.
optionC: directly beneath the upper shock wave and at the same rate.
optionD: to the location of the upper shock wave, then remains static.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The curvature of the underside of a wing is usually less than that of the upper surface, therefore the acceleration of the airflow is less, consequently the airflow does not become sonic until the aeroplane is travelling at a higher airspeed.

At lower airspeeds the only shockwave occurs on the upper surface and first appears at the wing root. At speeds above this, a shockwave forms beneath the lower surface of the wing ahead of the upper surface shockwave.
The shock wave on the lower surface usually forms at a higher free stream Mach number than the upper surface shock, but it reaches the trailing edge first.

The meeting point of the two pressure waves occurs nearer the trailing edge.

title: What causes the deterrent buffet?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: High speed.
optionB: High angle of attack.
optionC: Buffet magnified by compressibility.
optionD: Too low mach number.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

  • At buffet initiation, the pilot starts to feel airfl ow separation on wings upper surface.
  • The buffet onset corresponds by defi nition to 1.3g (corresponding to 40° of bank angle in level fl ight).
  • The “deterrent buffet” is so strong that any pilot will feel he/she needs to leave these buffet conditions. It corresponds to one of the definitions of stall and is considered to be the stall limit on a jet transport aircraft.

Deterrent Buffet - the airplane exhibits sufficient buffet that the flight crew will be deterred from commanding even higher AOA.

title: If the yaw damper is inoperative the pilot must?
optionA: Pitch Down
optionB: Reduce mach Speed
optionC: Pitch Up
optionD: Increase Mach Speed
explanationTotal:
Aircraft with a tendency to Dutch roll are fitted with a Yaw Damper. This automatically displaces the rudder proportional to the rate of yaw to damp-out the oscillations.

If the Yaw Damper fails in flight, it is recommended that the ailerons be used by the pilot to damp-out Dutch roll or the speed to be reduced. Because of the response lag, if the pilot uses the rudder at a high speed, pilot induced oscillation (PIO) will result and the Dutch roll may very quickly become divergent, leading to loss of control.

title: The Lift Coefficient versus Angle Of Attack curve of a symmetrical aerofoil section intersects the horizontal axis of the graph...
optionA: at no point.
optionB: to the left of the origin.
optionC: at the origin.
optionD: to the right of the origin.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
If a symmetrical airfoil section is in a steady airstream at zero degrees Angle of Attack, a stagnation point forms on the leading edge.
The airflow velocity above and below the airfoil increases by an equal amount and the static pressures reduce by an equal amount. Consequently, no pressure differential exists, and no net lift is created.

title: For a given CG position, the aeroplane has an MCRIT of Mach 0.82. With an aft movement of the CG, the MCRIT would (1) _____, as the local air velocity on the top surface of the wing would (2) _____, due to the (3) _____ angle of attack required to maintain level flight.
optionA: (1) decrease; (2) decrease; (3) increased.
optionB: (1) decrease; (2) increase; (3) increased.
optionC: (1) increase; (2) increase; (3) increased.
optionD: (1) increase; (2) decrease; (3) decreased.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
081.02.03.01.02: Explain how a change in alpha, aeroplane weight, manoeuvres, and centre-of-gravity (CG) position influences MCRIT.

When air travels over an aerofoil in normal operation, the air above the aerofoil, near the leading edge, increases in velocity, due to the "squashing" of the streamlines together, causing a venturi effect, creating the low pressure zone that is required. This means that air is usually going faster over the top of the wing than anywhere else on the airframe.

As the aircraft approaches the speed of sound, Mach 1, the air above the wing will get there first, as it is faster than the freestream airflow (TAS). In particular, it is usually the air just above the wing root, where the wing is thickest, and the streamlines get "squashed" the most, that is the first bit of air to reach the sound barrier. The TAS at which the first particle of air becomes sonic (exactly Mach 1) is called MCRIT, and is the beginning of the transonic speed regime. Above this speed, shockwaves will begin to form on various parts of the airframe.

MCRIT is variable, and in particular depends on the airspeed increase over the wing. If the speed increase equates to M0.2, then the aircraft will have an MCRIT of M0.8, a higher MCRIT than if the speed increase due to the wing was M0.25, giving an MCRIT of M0.75. A higher MCRIT is better, as the drag increases rapidly just above the MCRIT, at MDD, the drag divergence speed, and we would like to fly as fast as possible with the lowest drag.

The higher the angle of attack of the wing, the higher the speed increase, and therefore the lower the MCRIT. This would come from anything that increases the angle of attack, such as higher weight, or a more forward CG, which acts like increased weight due to the increased downforce from the tailplane. Effectively, bad things for performance such as increased weight or forward CG, cause a bad effect, lower MCRIT, due to increased AoA.

Therefore, in this question, the more aft CG will cause a reduction in lift required by the main wing, which will require a lower angle of attack (lower lift coefficient for level flight), and the speed increase over the wing would be lower, so the aircraft can fly faster before getting shockwaves forming, thus a higher MCRIT, which is good.

title: What is the effect of increasing the number of blades on a propeller?
optionA: It decreases the drag of the propeller in power-off descent.
optionB: It decreases the power absorption of the propeller.
optionC: It decreases the propeller torque for a given RPM.
optionD: It increases the overall solidity of the propeller.
explanationTotal:
The ability of a propeller to convert engine power into forward thrust is its power-absorption capability.

It is affected by:

  • the propeller-blade shape.
  • the number of propeller blades.
  • the propeller solidity.
The number of propeller blades is usually limited to six because of the complexity of the pitch control contained in the propeller hub and aerodynamic interference between propeller blades. Having a large number of blades has the advantage that it decreases propeller noise, but its primary purpose is to improve the power absorption properties and efficiency of the propeller.

title: What is “Deterrent Buffet”?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: It is an indication to jet transport crews that higher alpha should be used with caution.
optionB: It is considered to be the stall limit on jet transport aircraft.
optionC: It is confirmation that the aircraft is in a full stall.
optionD: It is normal on take-off when fully loaded.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

  • At buffet initiation, the pilot starts to feel airfl ow separation on wings upper surface.
  • The buffet onset corresponds by defi nition to 1.3g (corresponding to 40° of bank angle in level fl ight).
  • The “deterrent buffet” is so strong that any pilot will feel he/she needs to leave these buffet conditions. It corresponds to one of the definitions of stall and is considered to be the stall limit on a jet transport aircraft.

Deterrent Buffet - the airplane exhibits sufficient buffet that the flight crew will be deterred from commanding even higher AOA.

title: A boundary layer fence on a swept wing will improve the:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: lift coefficient of the trailing edge flap.
optionB: Mach buffet characteristics.
optionC: Dutch roll characteristics.
optionD: low-speed stall characteristics.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
A boundary layer fence is an aerodynamic surface that is commonly fixed to the wing, inline with the free stream airflow.
The main goal of the boundary layer fence is to restrict the spanwise flow of air.

A swept wing at low speed has a large amount of spanwise airflow, this is because airflow hitting the leading edge will because of the angle be forced to move towards the tip of the wing. This leads to an almost completely diagonal airflow at the tip of the wing which causes it to stall first.

To prevent the tip stall, the boundary layer fences are installed, which decrease the spanwise flow, and therefore improve low-speed stall characteristics.

title: Fly-by-wire flight control systems convert pilot control inputs into electrical signals, which are processed and sent to electrically controlled hydraulic actuators, operating the control surfaces. Which control surface is operated when the pilot inputs a pitch command?
optionA: Ailerons
optionB: Rudder
optionC: Elevators
optionD: CG
explanationTotal:
The vast majority of this question is not required as fly-by-wire systems operate the same control surfaces as conventional manual, power assisted, or fully powered controls.

On a standard civilian aircraft, the ailerons control roll, the rudder controls yaw, and the elevators control pitch. Some fighter aircraft like the Eurofighter Typhoon as well as Concorde have different designs, with some jets using front mounted canards for pitch, and Concorde using elevons on its huge delta wing (both aileron and elevator function in the same control surfaces).

title: During takeoff, a pilot unintentionally selects full flaps. Takeoff distance will be...
optionA: Decreased
optionB: Increased
optionC: Increased then decreased
optionD: Decreased then increased
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
CLMAX AUGMENTATION

One of the main factors which determine the CLMAX of an aerofoil section is the camber. Increasing the camber of an aerofoil section increases the CL at a given angle of attack and increases CLMAX.

TRAILING EDGE FLAPS

Aircraft are fitted with high lift devices to reduce the take-off and landing distances and when low airspeeds are beneficial. This permits operation at greater weights from given runway lengths and enables greater payloads to be carried.

The increase in lift comes mainly from the variation in effective camber that occurs when the flaps are deflected. This alters the lift curve and also produces a higher maximum coefficient of lift.

In some instances, the trailing edge flaps may also increase the wing's surface area. Extending the trailing edge flaps alters the pressure distribution around the wing.

USE OF TRAILING EDGE FLAPS FOR TAKE-OFF

For take-off purposes, the flaps are normally lowered to a position that provides the best lift-drag ratio that can be obtained with the flaps in any position other than fully up. Since the required lift is obtained at a lower airspeed, the take-off run is also reduced.

Larger amounts of flap cause a significant increase in drag, which greatly reduces the acceleration and increases the take-off run. The reduced stalling angle of attack and increased drag associated with flaps also reduces the rate and angle of climb.

title: Flap extension at constant IAS whilst maintaining straight and level flight will increase the:
optionA: maximum lift coefficient (CL<sub>MAX</sub>) and the drag.
optionB: stall speed.
optionC: lift and the drag.
optionD: lift coefficient and the drag.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Slats and flaps increase lift. This can help the aircraft take off with a shortened ground roll, as the aircraft generates more lift at a lower speed with flaps and slats extended. However, flaps and slats shorten the ground roll, but also decrease climb performance as they generate drag. Therefore, after takeoff these two devices are retracted. Flaps and slats both decrease stall speed, but flaps generate much more drag. The flaps are therefore retracted first and slats afterwards.

Flaps increase CL for a specific angle of attack, giving a wing with flaps extended a higher CL and therefore higher lift than a wing without. Flaps also increase CLMAX and the CD for a wing, they decrease critical AoA. Slats do not necessarily increase CL for a specific AoA, but they increase the value for CLMAX, meaning that the aircraft stalls at a much higher AoA than normal. They also increase the drag a little on the wing where they are extended.

Flaps increase lift, but this question states straight and level flight. If we want to remain in level flight, lift should not be increased because otherwise the aircraft will climb. Therefore the AoA will have to be decreased and the CL will remain the same, drag will increase and CLMAX will be increased.

Note: Drag and Lift stay constant. At straight and level flight which means Lift=Weight (constant). IAS is said to have remained constant as well. Remember the lift and drag formula.

title:
Which statement is correct?

I. Stall speeds are determined with the CG at the aft limit.
II. Minimum control speeds are determined with the CG at the forward limit.
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: I is incorrect, II is correct.
optionB: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
optionC: I is correct, II is correct.
optionD: I is correct, II is incorrect.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

  1. Stall speeds are determined with the least favourible cg position. For an aircraft, this is the most forward point because then the main wing will be producing the most lift. With the cg furthest ahead of the centre of pressure, the horizontal stabilizer will be producing a downwards force, which the main wings will have to compensate for by producing more lift. The main wings will therefore have to be at a higher angle of attack and therefore be closer to the stall.

Hence the stall will occur at higher speeds with a forward cg then with a rearward cg.

  1. Minimum control speeds are also determined with the least favourible conditions. When considering an engine failure, we know that the aircraft will rotate around its cg, but the distance of the moment doesn’t change when it moves fore or aft, the engines moment would only change when we move it along the lateral axis of the aircraft. However, the position of the cg will influence the rudder arm, and hence the rudder moment. A cg on the af limit will provide a small arm and therefore the least ability to oppose the yawing moment of the engine failure.

title: A given aileron deflection affects...
optionA: bank angle and is dependent on TAS
optionB: bank angle and is dependent on IAS
optionC: roll rate and is dependent on TAS
optionD: roll rate and is dependent on IAS
explanationTotal:
Control effectiveness is dependent on airflow. Flying slower or through thinner air makes the controls less effective. Therefore, we can say that aileron deflection is dependent on IAS.

Furthermore, it is logical that the faster the aileron is deflected, the faster the aircraft will roll.

title: Skin friction drag is caused by the...
optionA: air’s viscosity producing shear forces within the boundary layer.
optionB: difference in pressure acting on the aerofoil’s surface in the direction of flight.
optionC: loss of momentum within an airflow caused by the aerofoil changing the flow direction.
optionD: friction between the surface and the air molecules in direct contact with the surface.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
Total Drag is sub-divided into two main types:
Parasite Drag - independent of lift generation, and
Induced Drag - the result of lift generation.

Parasite drag is further sub-divided into:

  • Skin Friction Drag
  • Form (Pressure) Drag, and
  • Interference Drag

NOTE: Skin Friction and Form Drag are together known as PROFILE DRAG.

Boundary Layer

Skin friction drag is a function of the layer of air closest to the surface. As air flows over a wing, the roughness of the surface and the viscous property of the air itself slow it down. Much like fluids, the more viscous the air, the greater its retardation. At the surface, the air particles adhere to it and their relative velocity is reduced to zero (figure 1).
Just above the surface, the air particles slow down due to the friction effects between the particles, but except for the layer in contact with the surface, the particles do not completely come to rest. The relative velocity of the air particles increases steadily with distance from the surface, until reaching a point where the particles do not slow up at all and instead travel at the free stream velocity.
The boundary layer is the layer of air between the surface and the free stream velocity in which local retardation takes place. Like the main airflow, the boundary layer flow can be either laminar or turbulent in nature (figure 2).

Skin Friction Drag

Skin friction is the reaction to the retardation of the airflow within the boundary layer.
The retarded air tries to drag the surface along with the flow, in much the same way as two solid surfaces sliding over each other do.
Known as shear stress, this is directly proportional to the speed of flow.
Figure 3 represents the shear stress patterns that exist between layers.
The gradual velocity change associated with the laminar boundary layer shows that low shear stresses exist near the surface, resulting in low skin friction drag. Conversely, the rapid velocity change associated with the turbulent boundary layer is evidence of high skin friction drag.

title: During approach, ATC asks an aircraft to keep its speed high, and this speed is near the maximum speed for the current configuration. Which of the following speed limits may be broken if the pilots extend the trailing edge flaps at this time?
optionA: V<sub>LO</sub>
optionB: V<sub>MO</sub>
optionC: V<sub>S</sub>
optionD: V<sub>FE</sub>
explanationTotal:
Learning Objective 081.06.01.03.03: Define ‘VFE’ and describe flap limiting speeds.

VFE is the maximum speed to be flown with flaps extended. Flaps are incredibly useful for aircraft to allow for slower take-off and landing, as well as increasing drag for increased control during descent and approach phases of flight, and changing the landing pitch attitude of some aircraft. They do have to sustain some very high aerodynamic loads though, as they stick out into the airstream below the wing, and produce very high forces of lift and drag. The maximum speed for flaps extended (VFE) therefore exists to make sure the pilots do not fly too fast with flaps extended, and cause damage to the flaps or their mechanisms. Some large aircraft actually have systems to reduce the flap extension when these speed limits are broken.

In this question then, during the approach phase of flight, the pilots will be wanting to extend flaps in preparation for landing, but if the speed is too high and the pilots extend flaps anyway, they may exceed the new (lower) VFE for the increased flap setting.

As for the other options:

  • VLO is the maximum speed for landing gear operation (it is often specified whether that is for extension or retraction)
  • VMO is the maximum operating IAS for the aircraft.
  • VS is the stall speed (not specified which).

title: The stabiliser of an aircraft, whose CG is within the normal range, is mistakenly set with its leading edge at a more positive angle of incidence than required. As a result the pilot will encounter...
optionA: lighter-than-normal control forces requiring a longer take-off run.
optionB: higher-than-normal control forces but would require a shorter take-off run.
optionC: lighter-than-normal control forces, which may lead to over-rotation.
optionD: higher-than-normal control forces, which may lead to a later-than-normal lift-off.
explanationTotal:
The position of the CG directly affects the amount of trim necessary for the angle of attack required. A forward CG adds to the inherent longitudinal stability of the airplane; the pilot may run out of elevator up movement and be unable to maintain the required attitude. An aft CG decreases the longitudinal stability and makes the airplane more difficult or impossible to control in pitch.

The CG must always remain within the CG safe envelope to ensure that the airplane remains controllable in all phases of flight. The elevator trim or stabilizer trim setting must be preset to a value for take-off and initial climb that will ensure a minimum stick force during this critical stage of flight.
Usually, there is a graph in the airplane performance manual from which the setting appropriate to the total mass and CG position for take-off can be determined.

Factors that affect the stabilizer trim position for take-off are:

  • CG position
  • Take-off mass
  • Flap setting
In comparison with a correctly balanced airplane during take-off, the position of the stabilizer for a nose-heavy airplane requires nose-up trim from a decreased stabilizer angle of incidence.

title: What are the components of Wave Drag?
optionA: Energy drag and boundary layer separation
optionB: Shock drag
optionC: MCRIT drag
optionD: Induced and Parasite drag
explanationTotal:
WAVE DRAG is a force, or drag, that retards the forward movement of an airplane, in both supersonic and Transonic Flight, as a consequence of the formation of shock waves
  • Heat is created at a shock wave, Shock waves radiate a considerable amount of energy, resulting in drag on the aircraft (energy drag).
  • The high Pressure found at the shock wave creates a strong adverse pressure gradient on the aircraft surface => causing immediate separation of the airflow. This flow separation causes high levels of drag (separation drag)

title:
Comparing the differences between a horizontal trimmable stabiliser and an elevator trim tab, which statement is correct?

I. A stabiliser trim is less suitable for jet transport aeroplanes because of their large speed range.
II. A trim tab is a more powerful means of trimming.
optionA: I is correct, II is incorrect.
optionB: I is correct, II is correct.
optionC: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
optionD: I is incorrect, II is correct.
explanationTotal:
The forces on a jet transport aeroplane are very high in flight.
The wing surfaces are large and travel at high speeds, generating lots of lift.

A trim tab is an easy solution in general aviation aircraft, as the forces are much smaller and it’s a lot cheaper than a stabilizer.
However, the trim tab is not able to withstand the forces at very high speeds and is not powerful enough to generate the loads required for a change in configuration.
A stabilizer is powerful enough and is therefore the best suitable option for transport jet aeroplanes.

title: Which factor should be taken into account when determining V<sub>A</sub>?
optionA: The ultimate load factor.
optionB: The safety factor.
optionC: The calculation factor.
optionD: The limit load factor.
explanationTotal:
VA = Maximum Design Manoeuvring Speed

VA is the maximum speed where an aircraft stalls at a sudden full elevator deflection (nose-up) but does not exceed the design limit load factor.

As any other speeds, VA depends on airplane mass. According to EASA regulations, designed VA speed is based on maximum mass of the airplane (MTOM). You can easily calculate VA for any other masses with the help of the following equation: VA = VA (MTOM) √(WACTUAL / WMTOM)

VA is linearly proportional with the root of weight.

title: The lift coefficient (C<sub>L</sub>) of an aeroplane in steady horizontal flight is 0.4. An increase in angle of attack of 1 degree will increase C<sub>L</sub> by 0.09. A vertical up gust instantly changes the angle of attack by 5 degrees. The load factor will be:
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
A gust is a localized sudden and rapid change to the speed of the air in the atmosphere that can be either horizontal or vertical. The horizontal gust is of little importance because it causes a change to an airplane’s dynamic pressure that results in an insignificant change to the load factor. The vertical gusts are far more important because they change the effective angle of attack, total lift, and the load factor.
The gust load is the extra load imparted to the airplane by vertical gusts or turbulence. Its magnitude is unaffected by increased altitude but is increased with increased aspect ratio and/or decreased mass.
The load factor for any given angle of attack can be derived from the basic load factor for the normal cruise angle of attack because it is increased by the same percentage as the increase of angle of attack.

It can be defined by:

load factor(n) = (Lift(L))/(Weight(W))

In straight and level flight, Lift = Weight, thus n = 1.
In this exercise, the increment in CL from a gust will be of 0.09 for every degree of angle of attack impacted by the gust. We also know that the aircraft encounters a gust which increases its angle of attack by 5°.

In straight and level flight n = 1 or:

n = (0.4)/(0.4)

A 5° increase in angle of attack,

5*0.09 = 0.45

Will give an increment of 0.45 in the CL:

0.4+0.45 = 0.85

A gust which increases the angle of attack by 5° will increase the load factor to:

n = 0.85/0.4 ≈ 2.13g

title: Both CS-23 and CS-25 specifications state that an aeroplane must have sufficient controllability at and just above the critical angle of attack to aid in stall recovery. Which of the following statements identifies a consideration which could influence the stall handling characteristics, unless particular design measures are taken to avoid this?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: High-wing aeroplane tend to have a greater pitch-up tendency, as an aeroplane progressively pitches up.
optionB: Supercritical aerofoils may increase the pitch-up tendency when compared to traditional cambered aerofoils.
optionC: Aft-fuselage mounted engines have a large pitching moment when thrust is increased during the recovery.
optionD: The vertical position of the horizontal stabiliser may affect the ability to recover, in particular a T-tail design.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
This question is asking about handling characteristics at the stall, and the correct answer is in reference to deep stalls.

A deep stall happens when an aircraft main wing stalls, but the angle of airflow means that the stalled air flows directly over the horizontal tailplane. This usually happens on T-tail aircraft, as the tail often becomes about level with the wing at critical angle of attack. This turbulent flow will mean that there is little or no elevator control, and the horizontal stabiliser is not producing any controllable lift. This can leave the aircraft without any pitch control, causing a potentially unrecoverable deep stall (a.k.a. a super stall). Aircraft with deep stall characteristics are often fitted with a stick-pusher to avoid reaching that point.

The other design feature they could ask about is underslung engines. Underslung engines are mounted under the main wings, as is most common on modern jets. When thrust is increased on these engines, a very large pitch-up moment is induced, due to their thrust line being far below the centre of gravity. As thrust is often added to recover from a stall, this could cause an upwards pitch which could overpower even full nose-down pitch control at low speeds. We call this thrust line "destabilising". The high mounted tail engines seen on many smaller jets are not susceptible to this effect, as they have a high thrust line and a "stabilising" thrust moment.

title: What is the approximate radius of a steady horizontal coordinated turn at a bank angle of 45° and a TAS of 200 kt?
optionA: 1 km.
optionB: 2 km.
optionC: 1.5 km.
optionD: 10 km.
explanationTotal:
To get the TAS to m/s we will multiply it with 0.5144

TAS = 200*0.5144 = 102.88 m/s

Radius = (TAS)2 / g * tan(bank angle)

102.882 / 10 tan(45) = 1058 metres = +/- 1 km

title: How is stall warning presented to the pilots of a large transport aeroplane?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Stick shaker and/or aerodynamic buffet.
optionB: Stall warning light only.
optionC: Aural warning only.
optionD: Stick pusher.
explanationTotal:
STALL WARNING SYSTEM
The purpose of the stall warning system is to warn the pilot of an impending stall. It does so when the aircraft approaches the stalling angle of attack for the current speed and configuration of the aircraft. The warning provided can be in the form of tactile, aural or visual or a combination of these signals. Most aircraft have warning provided by stick-shakers which vibrate the control column as well as produce a rattling noise. The stall warning must continue until the angle of attack is reduced to approximately that at which the stall warning is initiated.

  • Indications of an impending stall can include buffeting, stick shaker, or aural warning.
Note: Stall Protection System - a stall protection system may be fitted to large commercial aircraft, to prevent them from entering the stall (stick pusher).

title: An aircraft has a stalling speed of 100 kts, at 5.4 tonnes. Calculate the new stalling speed at a mass of 4.7 tonnes...
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: 107 kts
optionB: 93 kts
optionC: 232 kts
optionD: 217 kts
explanationTotal:
The stall speed is defined by:
VS = √((2∗W) / (ρ∗S∗CLMAX))

We can compare two stall speeds by applying the ration between the new stall speed and the old. In this exercise there is a decrease in mass, therefore (∝ means proportional):
VSNEW / VSOLD ∝ √(mNEW / mOLD) ⇔ VSNEW / 100 ∝ √(4.7/5.4)
VSNEW ∝ √(4.7/5.4) ∗ 100

VSNEW ≈ 93 knots
Reducing the mass from 5.4 tons to 4.7 tons, will reduce the stall speed from 100 knots to 93 knots.

title:
Refer to figure.
Where on the curve in the diagram does the aeroplane exhibit neutral static longitudinal stability?
optionA: Part 3.
optionB: Point 2.
optionC: Part 1.
optionD: The whole curve.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
Static longitudinal stability depends upon the relationship of angle of attack and pitching moment (CM).

A variation of CG position can cause large changes in the static longitudinal stability. In the conventional airplane configuration, the large changes in stability with CG variation are primarily due to the large changes in the wing contribution. If the incidence of all surfaces remains fixed, the effect of CG position on static longitudinal stability is typified by the chart in figure 1:

As the CG is gradually moved aft, the airplane static stability decreases, then becomes neutral then unstable. The CG position which produces zero slope and neutral static stability is referred to as the “neutral point”. The neutral point defines the most aft CG position without static instability.

Moving the CG forward, will increase static longitudinal stability and this is represented by a (steeper) negative slope.

Noticeable changes in static stability can occur at high lift coefficients (low speed). This condition is illustrated in figure 2.

The curve of CM versus CL of this illustration shows a good stable slope at low values of CL (high speed). Increasing CL gives a slight decrease in the negative slope hence a decrease in stability occurs. With continued increase in CL, the slope becomes zero and neutral stability exists. Eventually, the slope becomes positive and the airplane becomes unstable.

title:
Refer to figure.
Which force do lines 1 and 3 represent?
optionA: (1) Thrust, (3) torque.
optionB: (1) Lift, (3) drag.
optionC: (1) Torque, (3) Thrust.
optionD: (1) Drag, (3) lift.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The purpose of the propeller is to convert the power output from the engine into thrust. The power developed is transmitted to the propeller shaft as engine torque and rotates the propeller.

The rotation of a propeller creates a total reactive force at right angles to the chordline of the propeller blade. This can be divided into two components, that which is perpendicular to the relative airflow, the lift, and that which is parallel to the relative airflow, the drag.

Thrust acts parallel to the direction of flight, whilst propeller torque (the resistance to the motion in the plane of rotation) acts perpendicular to the direction of flight.

The propeller torque must thus be overcome or balanced by engine torque for a propeller section to provide thrust.

title:
Refer to figure.
Given the wing planform represented in the diagram with the following dimensions, calculate the aspect ratio:

Wingspan: 12.5 m
Tip chord: 1 m
Root chord: 1.5 m
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Aspect ratio

The aspect ratio of the wing closely affects the aerodynamic characteristics and structural strength/weight of a wing. Typical aspect ratios vary from 35 for a high-performance sailplane to as low as 3 for a jet fighter. The aspect ratio of a modern high-speed jet transport is about 12. Aspect Ratio is the measure of Span divided by Chord. As many wing planforms have variable chord lengths, there is a second formula which uses wing area instead, which effectively just makes use of the "average chord".

AR = b/c
or,
AR = b2 /S

Where:

  • AR - Aspect Ratio
  • b - Span
  • c - Average Chord
  • S - Wing Area

Therefore, for this wing, the aspect ratio can be calculated in a few different ways. The easiest is to just to say that the average chord is 1.25 m, and span / chord = 12.5 / 1.25 = 10.

Alternatively, you can calculate the wing area as two trapeziums (or any other way) as 2 x 6.25 x ((1 + 1.5) / 2) which gets you to 15.625 m2, and then do span2 / wing area, which is 12.52 / 15.625 = 10.

title: An aeroplane certified under the CS-25 flying WITHOUT failures, malfunctions, or adverse conditions remains within the flutter-free flight envelope if flown below an established speed limit. This speed is expressed as a(n)…
optionA: EAS
optionB: Mach number
optionC: IAS
optionD: TAS
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
FLUTTER

The rapid and uncontrolled oscillation of a surface resulting from imbalance. Flutter normally leads to a catastrophic failure of the structure.

An aircraft is subject to many aerodynamic excitations (gusts, control inputs, etc.) and the aerodynamic forces at various speeds have characteristic properties for rate of change of force and moment. The aerodynamic forces may interact with the structure and may excite (or negatively damp) the natural modes of the structure and allow flutter.

Flutter must not occur within the normal flight operating envelope and the natural modes must be damped if possible or designed to occur beyond VD / MD.

DESIGN DIVE SPEED (VD)

Point ‘D’ in the V-n Diagram (figure 1) is the design dive speed VD. This is the maximum speed which has to be considered when assessing the strength of the aircraft. It is based on the principle of an upset occurring when the aircraft is flying at VC, resulting in a shallow dive, during which the speed increases, until recovery is effected.

All design speeds, and design gust values, are EAS.

title: An aircraft is taking off, its V<sub>A</sub> is 260 kt. If weight decreases by 20%, the new V<sub>A</sub> will be…
optionA: 234 kt
optionB: 286 kt
optionC: 208 kt
optionD: 312 kt
explanationTotal:
VS1g NEW = VS1g OLD √(new weight / old weight)
VA = VS1g √n

The load factor “n” is the same for both weights. New VA:
VA NEW = VA OLD √(new weight / old weight)
VA NEW = VA OLD √(0.8 / 1)
VA NEW = VA OLD 0.9 (10% lower)
VA NEW = 260 x 0.9
VA NEW = 234 kt

or

260 kt x 10% = 26 kt
260 kt – 26 kt = 234 kt

title: What happens to the blade pitch of a fixed pitch propeller on ground roll during takeoff?
optionA: Increases.
optionB: Decreases.
optionC: Remains constant.
optionD: Initially increases and then decreases.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
A propeller is a fan, fitted with between two and six aerodynamic blades that is used to convert rotational motion into forward thrust for the propulsion of an aeroplane through the air.

The blades of the propeller are small aerodynamic aerofoils mounted vertically on a horizontal shaft that is rotated by either a piston engine or a turbine-driven engine.

BLADE ANGLE (PITCH)

The angle between the blade chord and the plane of rotation.

ANGLE OF ATTACK

The path of the propeller through the air determines the direction of the relative airflow. The angle between the blade chord and the relative airflow is the angle of attack (α). The angle of attack (α) is the result of propeller rotational velocity (RPM) and aircraft forward velocity (TAS).

Because the rotational velocity of the blade increases with distance from the propeller shaft and the fact that the aeroplane is moving forward, then the angle of attack of the blade varies at different distances from the shaft.

FIXED PITCH PROPELLER

The blade angle of a fixed-pitch propeller is constant but the helix angle and the angle of attack will vary according to its forward speed. To ensure its efficient operation the blade angle of attack of a fixed-pitch propeller must be close to the optimum and is that which produces the greatest excess of horizontal lift (thrust) over drag.

To operate the propeller in this manner will restrict the range of speeds within which the aeroplane can function. Thus, the blade angle selected during the design of the aeroplane is dependent on the operational requirements for that aeroplane.

Figure shows a “fixed pitch” propeller at constant RPM. Increasing TAS decreases the angle of attack of the propeller.

title: Which of the following aerodynamic balancing device enables big control surface change/movement with relatively small force needed to apply?
optionA: Anti-balance Tab.
optionB: Balance Tab.
optionC: Horn Balance.
optionD: Servo Tab.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The force required to operate the primary control surfaces, even using balance tabs, is often too great to be acceptable. To relieve the pilot of the need to apply so much force to operate the controls servo-tabs are fitted to carry out this function.
The servo-tab is a small tab hinged on the trailing edge of the primary control surface and linked directly to the control column. There is no direct link between the control column and the primary control surface.
The function and operation of the servo-tab is the same as the balance tab and moves the trim tab in the opposite direction to the movement of the primary control surface. However, at low IAS the servo-tab makes the main control surface less effective. The position of a servo-controlled primary control surface cannot be determined until a positive pressure is applied to the servo-tab by the airflow.

Note:
Anti-balance Tab: used to increase stick force when they're too light.
Balance Tab: moves when the control surface is moved.

title: Describe the airflow with regards to the induced drag...
optionA: From the top to the bottom via the tip.
optionB: From the bottom to the top via the trailing edge.
optionC: From the top to the bottom via the leading edge.
optionD: From the bottom to the top via the tip.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
INDUCED DRAG is an inevitable consequence of lift and is produced by the passage of an aerofoil through the air. The high pressure underneath the wing causes the airflow at the tips of the wings to curl around from bottom to top in a circular motion. This results in a trailing vortex.

title: What is VD?
optionA: The highest speed at which sudden, full elevator deflection (nose-up) can be made WITHOUT exceeding the design limit load factor.
optionB: The maximum tested airspeed where the aircraft is free from any signs of dynamic pressure overload, flutter, and/or control reversal.
optionC: A speed selected by the designer and used to assess the strength requirements in cruise.
optionD: A specially recommended penetration speed for severe turbulence.
explanationTotal:
Design Dive Speed (VD) is the maximum speed which was considered when the airframe structure was constructed. During test flights, VD are reached by test pilots with the objective to demonstrate that the aircraft structural integrity is not put at stake at these speeds, and that the aircraft remains safely recoverable at all times.

The aircraft is designed to be capable of diving to this speed (in very smooth air) and be free of flutter, control reversal or buffeting. Control surfaces have a natural vibration frequency where they begin to “flutter” like a flag in a stiff breeze

title: An aeroplane is equipped with 2 basic yaw dampers that operate independently of the flight controls. Due to a hydraulic leak, one of the yaw dampers becomes unserviceable. The aeroplane is allowed to fly as long as one yaw damper is operational, however the pilots must not commence flight if both yaw dampers are unserviceable. Why must the aeroplane have at least one serviceable yaw damper?
optionA: The yaw damper reduces the pilots workload by coordinating turns and improving the static lateral stability of the aeroplane.
optionB: The yaw damper enables the aeroplane to perform an Autoland since it uses rudder in order to maintain direction during landing.
optionC: The aeroplane becomes uncontrollable if there is NO yaw damper to improve slightly weak static directional stability.
optionD: The aeroplane suffers from Dutch roll but remains controllable if the remaining yaw damper fails during flight.
explanationTotal:
Aeroplanes with a tendency to Dutch roll are fitted with a Yaw Damper. This automatically displaces the rudder proportional to the rate of yaw to damp-out the oscillations. If the Yaw Damper fails in flight, there may be speed and altitude restrictions.

Note that an aircraft would only be allowed to take off with only one yaw damper serviceable if the aircraft remains controllable.

title: Comparing the lift coefficient and drag coefficient for conventional aeroplanes:
optionA: C<sub>L </sub>is lower than C<sub>D</sub>.
optionB: C<sub>L</sub> is much greater than C<sub>D</sub>.
optionC: C<sub>L</sub> is much lower than C<sub>D</sub>.
optionD: C<sub>L </sub>has approximately the same value as C<sub>D</sub>.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
The distribution of pressure is important in aerodynamics, since it determines:
- The amount of lift generated
- Any pitching moments
- The form drag of an aerofoil section

The lift and drag forces of a wing cross-section are dependent on the pressure distribution around the wing. The pressure distribution around an aerofoil is the resultant of the angle of the aerofoil chordline to the oncoming airflow, the angle of attack.

The pressure distribution varies with the angle of attack - at a normal angle of attack CL is greater than CD.

title: One method to compensate adverse yaw is:
optionA: a differential aileron.
optionB: an anti-balance tab.
optionC: a balance tab.
optionD: a balance panel.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
During a bank, the upgoing wing effectively experiences a decreased angle of attack whilst the effective angle of attack of the down going wing increases. Consequently, the slope of the total lift vector generates a rearward component on the upgoing wing and a forward component on the down going wing. These are yaw moments but in the opposite direction to that of the roll caused by the difference of the induced drag of each wing. This is adverse yaw, which is particularly significant at low airspeeds because of the large aileron deflection necessary to achieve the same rate of roll as at higher speeds with less deflection.

Adverse yaw may be counteracted by any one of the following devices:

  • rudder/aileron coupling.
  • slot/aileron coupling.
  • spoiler/aileron coupling.
  • frise ailerons.
  • differential aileron deflection.
The differential aileron deflection system ensures that the drag generated by both ailerons when rolling into or out of a turn is equal, thus eliminating adverse yaw. This is achieved by constructing the aileron system such that the angular deflection of the upgoing aileron is always proportionately greater than the deflection of the down going aileron.

title: An aircraft is taking off from a sea-level aerodrome with an outside air temperature below 15 degrees. What should a pilot be aware of regarding the controllability with one-engine inoperative?
optionA: A high VMC due to excessive rudder efficiency.
optionB: A low VMC due to the engine’s high performance.
optionC: A high VMC due to the engine's high performance.
optionD: A low V<sub>MC</sub> due to excessive rudder efficiency.
explanationTotal:
Minimum Control Speed - VMC

When an engine fails or is inoperative in-flight, the rudder is used to counteract the asymmetrical thrust yawing moment. Roll effects are counteracted by the ailerons. The counteracting forces generated by the aerodynamic control surfaces are proportional to the square of the airspeed (V2), to the area of the control surfaces (S) and to the air density. For a given size of the vertical tail with rudder, there is a speed below which the generated rudder side force is not large enough to counteract the asymmetrical thrust, or below which the ailerons are not effective anymore: the heading and/or bank angle cannot be maintained below this speed. This speed is called Minimum Control speed VMC.

  • With regards to this question,
    Cold air is more dense. Engines are able to produce more power in colder weather due to being able to achieve higher mass flow with the higher density air. As power increases, the operative engine requires more rudder authority to maintain directional stability due to the increase in thrust. As a result, the airplane requires higher indicated airspeeds to maintain directional stability. Therefore, VMCA increases.
    Low altitudes have the same effect on VMC as cold air.

title: In straight and level flight at a speed of 1.2 V<sub>S</sub>, the lift coefficient, expressed as a percentage of its maximum C<sub>LMAX</sub>, would be:
explanationTotal: Percentage of maximum C<sub>LMAX</sub> = 1 / V<sub>S</sub>^2 = 1 / 1.2^2 = 0.694 = 69%

title: A negatively cambered aerofoil will generate:
optionA: zero lift at zero angle of attack.
optionB: zero lift at a positive angle of attack.
optionC: lift at all angles of attack.
optionD: zero lift at a negative angle of attack.
explanationTotal:
Refer to the figure.
A negatively cambered aerofoil will produce drag and negative lift at an angle of attack of zero. As the angle of attack increases, the negative lift will decrease until there is no lift produced by the wing at all. This point is somewhere within the positive angle of attack region. Therefore the correct answer is: “zero lift at a positive angle of attack”.

The other answers are incorrect, because:

  • “Zero lift at a negative angle of attack” – This is the case for a positively cambered aerofoil, which is the opposite of a negatively cambered aerofoil.
  • “Lift at all angle of attack” – This is impossible, all wing profiles will produce no lift at a certain angle of attack.
  • “Zero lift at zero angle of attack” – This is the case for a symmetrical aerofoil.

title: An aircraft with a mass of 1500 kg has a 1 g stall speed of 73 kt. What is the stall speed when flying in a 45º bank turn at a mass of 1192 kg?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: 77 kt
optionB: 87 kt
optionC: 67 kt
optionD: 91 kt
explanationTotal:
The stall speed is defined by:

VS = √((2∗W) / (ρ∗S∗CLMAX))

In this exercise there is a decrease in mass and an increase in load factor due to the turn, therefore:

mNEW = 1192 kg
mOLD = 1500 kg
VS OLD = 73 kt
nNEW = 1/cos(45°)

Lets first calculate the new VS in straight and level flight (VS NEW 1G):

VS NEW 1G = √(mNEW /mOLD ) * VS OLD = √(1192/1500) * 73 = 65 kt

Finaly, the new VS with an angle of bank of 45°:

VS NEW = √(nNEW) * VS NEW 1G = √(1/cos(45°)) * 65 = 77 kt

VS NEW ≈ 77 kt

The new stall speed with decreased weight and increased load factor is 77 knots.

title: The highest value of the C<sub>L</sub>/C<sub>D</sub> ratio of an aeroplane is obtained:
optionA: in the configuration where both the leading and trailing edge flaps are fully extended.
optionB: in the configuration where only the trailing edge flaps are fully extended.
optionC: in the clean configuration.
optionD: in the configuration where only the leading edge slats are fully extended.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The total drag is the resulting factor if you add induced drag and parasite drag together.
Parasite drag is caused if an airfoil is moving through the air. It is the result of form drag and skin friction drag.
Form drag arises from the shape of the object. The more streamlined the object, the less form drag is present.
Shape and size are most important in the amount of form drag resulting.
Form drag increases with increasing velocity, making it very important for high speed aircraft.
Skin friction drag is caused by the friction of the fluid (in case of aircraft this fluid is the atmosphere) against the skin of the object moving through it.
It is directly related to the surface area in contact with the fluid. Skin friction increases with the square of the velocity.

Induced drag is caused when an object redirects the airflow. A wing produces lift by creating a pressure difference.
This pressure difference is caused by the shape of the airfoil, causing the airflow on top to accelerate, creating a low pressure on top of the wing and high pressure below the wing.
This pressure difference naturally wants to restore towards a uniform pressure, which creates vortices around the wingtip.
These vortices are deflected downwards, this phenomenon is also called downwash.
The induced drag decreases with airspeed and increases with angle of attack and increasing weight.

In the image we can see that the two vectors (induced and parasite drag) create a resulting vector, the total drag.
Where the induced and parasite drag vectors collide, we have the minimum drag speed (VMD); the speed where the total drag is the lowest.
This leads us to understand that during an acceleration from a total stand still, the total drag first decreases up until the minimum drag speed and then starts increasing again.
The CL/CD ratio is therefore biggest at VMD. Adding flaps or slats to this configuration will generate a large amount of drag, worsening the ratio.
Therefore the highest value of the CL/CD ratio is obtained in clean configuration at VMD.

title: An aeroplane accelerates from 80 kt to 160 kt at a load factor equal to 1. By what factors will the induced drag coefficient (i) and the induced drag (ii) change?
explanationTotal:
• Lift formula: L = CL x ½ rho V2 x S
Rho – does not change in level flight
If V doubles => CL must decrease by a factor of 4 (V is squared), in order to keep lift constant.
  1. CDI varies with CL2. Therefore, CDI must decrease by a factor of 16 => 42 when speed doubles.
  • Induced drag formula: Induced drag = CDI x ½ rho V2 x S
  1. Unlike lift, it varies with speed in level flight. If V is doubled => induced drag decreases by a factor of 4.
However, as we have seen previously Cdi has decreased by a factor of 16.
Overall, induced drag decreases by a factor of 4/16 = 1/4
Note:
Parasite drag changes by a factor of V2
Induced drag changes by a factor of 1/V2
Induced drag coefficient changes by a factor of 1/V4

title:
Refer to figure.
The diagram shows the parameter Y against TAS. What does the axis Y represent if horizontal flight is considered?
optionA: Lift coefficient.
optionB: Total lift force.
optionC: Parasite drag.
optionD: Total drag.
explanationTotal:
In horizontal flight, to maintain the same lift, coefficient of lift (CL) must be decreased if speed increases.

Induced drag is inversely proportional to speed and reducing CL will decrease the induced drag (due to the lower angle of attack).

  • We can, therefore, say that the Y axis can represent lift coefficient (CL) or induced drag.

Note: Parasite drag increases with increasing speed. Total lift force remains constant in “horizontal flight”.

title: Consider an aircraft flying in unaccelerated level flight in the non-stable region. What would be the result on Indicated Airspeed (IAS) and drag following a sudden decrease in aircraft speed with no change in thrust available?
optionA: IAS would further decrease due to the increased drag.
optionB: IAS would increase due to the increased drag.
optionC: IAS would increase due to the decreased drag.
optionD: IAS would further decrease due to the decreased drag.
explanationTotal:
See figure 1 for better visualization of situation described in the question.

Following a sudden decrease in speed; from the point in the speed unstable region where no change in thrust is available (intersection between thrust available and drag); the drag will increase, whilst the thrust available will remain the same. A thrust deficit will be created.

This thrust deficit, assuming no change in pitch is made to the aircraft, will result in a further decrease in airspeed until the aircraft cannot maintain altitude and stalls.

title: A powerful wartime piston single-engine aircraft equipped with a clockwise rotating propeller performs a go-around. If the throttle is increased to full power, what would be the most noticeable effect?
optionA: Roll to the right due to gyroscopic effect.
optionB: Yaw to the right due to gyroscopic effect.
optionC: Roll to the left due to gyroscopic effect.
optionD: Roll to the left due to torque effect which the pilot counters by using the ailerons.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
At high propeller speeds and low forward speed (as in the take-offs, approaches to power-on stalls or go-around), the aircraft will have the tendecy to swing to one side, particularly those fitted with a tail-dragger undercarriage. The main causes of this are:

  • Slipstream effect
  • Torque reaction
