Sections near the tip of the propeller are at a greater distance from the propeller shaft and travel through a greater distance. Tip speed is therefore greater. The blade angle must be decreased towards the tip to give a constant geometric pitch along the length of the blade.

title:
Refer to figure.
The point in the annex corresponding to CL for minimum horizontal flight speed is:
optionA: point C.
optionB: point B.
optionC: point A.
optionD: point D.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Figure 1 shows the lift curve of an airfoil section, with lift coefficient (CL) plotted against angle of attack. The lift curve is a convenient way to illustrate the properties of various configurations.
Lift coefficient increases with angle of attack up to a maximum (CLMAX), which corresponds to the “Critical” angle of attack. Continuing to increase the angle of attack beyond this point makes it impossible for the airflow to maintain its previous smooth flow over the contour of the upper surface, and lift will reduce.
Minimum airspeed is determined by the maximum lift coefficient (CLMAX), which occurs at a specific angle of attack (approximately 16°).

title: Where spoilers are used to assist ailerons with lateral control, when rolling to the right, the left aileron moves down and the right aileron moves up. How do the spoilers move?
optionA: The left spoilers remain flush and the right spoilers move up.
optionB: The left spoilers move up and the right spoilers remain flush.
optionC: The right spoilers and the left spoilers remain flush.
optionD: The right spoilers and the left spoilers move up.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Roll Spoilers operate asymmetrically in flight whenever the control wheel rotates, assisting the ailerons in providing roll control, particularly at high airspeeds. When this occurs, the appropriate spoiler servo valves are signaled by way of the aileron operating system and the requisite surfaces are deflected upward in proportion to the roll input.

During a roll, the spoilers on the lowering wing deflect upward, decreasing the wing’s overall lifting capability and increasing the aircraft’s roll rate, whilst the spoilers on the opposite wing remain retracted.

The innermost spoiler on the lowering wing also remains retracted to prevent tail buffet and degraded pitch control.

title: What locations are the most susceptible to ice build-up during flight?
optionA: Parts of the aircraft that have a small radius, bend sharply, and hence have a higher curvature, such as narrow leading edges of the wings and tail, probes and antennas.
optionB: The windscreens and other cockpit windows.
optionC: Parts of the aircraft that have a large radius, and hence are gently curving, with a lower curvature, such as leading edge of a thick wing, the radome, and the fuselage.
optionD: The radome, all the leading edges, upper wing surfaces, and the fuselage.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The formation of ice and frost on the airframe will:
- modify the profile of the aerofoil.
- increase the roughness of the aircraft surface.
- increase the weight of the aircraft.

Ice will normally form on and around the leading edges of wings and tailplane and can result in severe distortion of the leading edge profile. This will give a large increase in drag and a substantial decrease in CLMAX. The skin friction drag will increase and the boundary layer will have an earlier separation, giving a reduced critical angle of attack, thereby a higher stall speed.

Ice builds up on an aircraft when the super-cooled water droplets (SCWDs) hit the cold airframe and freeze onto the surface. This will happen most in particular sections of the aircraft, such as the leading edges of the wings, the nose, propeller spinners, the tail leading edges, and any protrusions such as the windshield, pitot tubes, AoA vanes, etc. These are obviously where the air is hitting the aircraft, and therefore some of the SCWDs will hit the airframe.

This effect is much more pronounced when the items are sharp, instead of curved. Take a wing for example. When it is a very curved wing, useful for low speed flight, it will have a leading edge with a large radius, and the pressure waves that propagate from the front of the wing during flight are effectively giving the air advanced warning that the wing is coming, so it can move out of the way. This means that the SCWDs also move out of the way, so do not hit the wing as much.

This means that sharp wings (with a smaller radius - used for higher speed flight) give less of a "warning" to the air, and the SCWDs will not move out of the way as much, thereby causing more ice accretion. This is the same for sharp protrusions such as the AoA vanes and pitot tubes.

title:
Which of these statements about the buffet free range in a buffet onset boundary graph are correct or incorrect?

1. During a push-over manoeuvre the buffet free range decreases.
2. When the mass increases the buffet free range decreases.
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: 1 is incorrect, 2 is incorrect.
optionB: 1 is correct, 2 is correct.
optionC: 1 is incorrect, 2 is correct.
optionD: 1 is correct, 2 is incorrect.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Stall boundaries set a lower limit to the operating speed, according to the load factor. In the case of a high-speed aircraft, there is also an upper limit which is due to the approach of shock stall and the associated buffet which occurs if the aircraft enters the transonic speed range. The limits associated with these effects give the buffet boundaries.

For a given aircraft there is a Mach number which, even at low angle of attack, cannot be exceeded because of the onset of shock stall. The EAS corresponding to this Mach number falls as altitude increases, so the range of operating speeds is reduced at both ends.

Also, an increase in load factor (bank angle) requires an increase in lift at a given EAS, hence an increase in angle of attack and a further reduction in limiting Mach number.
Thus, the greater the load factor (bank angle or gust), the more severe the limitation due to buffeting.

We can then conclude that decreasing load factor (push-over maneuver) increases the buffet margin, therefore statement 1 is incorrect.

The weight of the aircraft also affects the envelope. An increase in weight results in an increase in stall speed, and the stall boundary is moved to the right. It also results in an increase in angle of attack at any given speed, so that the Mach number at which buffeting occurs is reduced, and the buffet boundary is moved to the left. Finally, increase in weight implies a reduction in the maximum permissible ‘g’. Thus, all the boundaries are made more restrictive by an increase in weight.

We can then conclude that increasing weight (mass) decreases the buffet margin, therefore statement 2 is correct.

title: In the context of CS-23 certification for aircraft, what is the design manoeuvring speed (V<sub>A</sub>)?
optionA: VA represents the maximum landing speed for the aircraft.
optionB: V<sub>A</sub> is the maximum speed for normal cruise flight.
optionC: VA represents the stall speed with full flaps.
optionD: V<sub>A</sub> is the maximum speed at which the aircraft can safely manoeuvre in response to gusts without exceeding its structural limits.
explanationTotal:
Design Manoeuvring Speed (VA): Is the design manoeuvring speed and is the maximum speed at which it is possible to safely use maximum up elevator; if this speed is exceeded with the elevator deflected fully upward then the aeroplane may suffer permanent distortion.

VA is the highest speed at which the aeroplane will stall before exceeding the manoeuvre maximum load factor and does not need to exceed VC.

title: Frise ailerons are used to reduce adverse aileron yaw. To achieve this the...
optionA: up-going aileron moves through a larger angle than the down-going aileron.
optionB: down-going aileron moves through a larger angle than the up-going aileron.
optionC: leading edge of the up-going aileron protrudes below the lower surface of the wing, causing more drag.
optionD: leading edge of the down-going aileron protrudes above the upper surface of the wing, causing more drag.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
During a bank, the upgoing wing effectively experiences a decreased angle of attack whilst the effective angle of attack of the down going wing increases. Consequently, the slope of the total lift vector generates a rearward component on the upgoing wing and a forward component on the down going wing. These are yaw moments but in the opposite direction to that of the roll caused by the difference of the induced drag of each wing. This is adverse yaw, which is particularly significant at low airspeeds because of the large aileron deflection necessary to achieve the same rate of roll as at higher speeds with less deflection.

Adverse yaw may be counteracted by any one of the following devices:

  • slot/aileron coupling.
  • spoiler/aileron coupling.
  • differential aileron deflection.
  • rudder/aileron coupling.
  • frise ailerons.
To counteract adverse yaw the Frise ailerons are designed so that their leading edge produces sufficient profile drag on the upgoing aileron to equal the induced drag of the down going aileron and thus eliminate adverse yaw.

title:
An aircraft is flying a 3º approach path with engines at idle. Given the following information, calculate the drag.

Weight: 650 000 N.
Thrust: 30 000 N.
explanationTotal:
An aircraft's angle of descent is calculated by the formula:

(Drag - Thrust) / Weight = sin(Descent angle)

We have all the required information to find the drag. Remember, the engines do provide some thrust at idle, so you have to include it, which is different from some other questions you may see that are about gliding. First, we just have to rearrange the equation.

Drag - Thrust = Weight x sin(Descent angle)
Drag = Thrust + [Weight x sin(Descent angle)]
Drag = 30 000 + [650 000 x sin(3º)]

Drag = 64 018 N, closest answer 64 000 N

title: What is the approximate value of the lift of an aeroplane at a gross weight of 50000 N, in a horizontal co-ordinated 45 degrees banked turn?
explanationTotal:
In a steady horizontal turn, the total lift is greater than the weight. The conditions of equilibrium can be expressed in the form:

L cos φ = W
L = W / cos φ
Where (L) is the wing lift in newtons, (W) is the weight of the aircraft in newtons and φ the angle of bank.

  • Therefore, we have:
    L = 50 000 / cos 45
    L = 70 711 N
Note: Tip - remember that in a turn, lift will be greater than the weight to remain at the same altitude. Now, the cosine of any angle other than 0º is less than 1 => for L to be greater than W, the equation must be L cos φ = W (any bank angle requires a larger lift to balance the same weight).

title:
An aircraft with a mass of 60 tons is performing a co-ordinated level turn with 30 degrees of bank. In these conditions what is the magnitude of the Centripetal Force?
Assume g = 10 m/s2
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure
During a steady, co-ordinated turn, at a constant altitude, a force must continually act toward the centre of the turn (centripetal force). If it is not present, the aircraft will be unable to maintain a curved path, but instead will fly off at a tangent.

When the aircraft banks, the total lift force tilts; the horizontal component of lift provides the centripetal force and the vertical component of lift supports the weight of the aircraft.

The centripetal force acting on an aircraft gives it acceleration toward the centre of the turn (radial acceleration). In a steady, co-ordinated turn, an aircraft of weight (W - Newtons), travelling at a velocity (TAS) of (V - metres per second) around the circumference of a circle of radius (r - metres), has an acceleration toward the centre of the circle of (V2/r - metres per second per second), so that:

FC = (mass x V2) / r = (W / g) x (V2 / r)

Where:
W = Aircraft Weight (kg)
g = Acceleration due to Gravity (10 m/s2)

The resulting horizontal and vertical forces that exist during a steady, level turn are:

L x sin(ø)= (W / g) x (V2 / r) and L x cos (ø) = W

So that

Tan (ø) = V2 / (g x r), where ø = angle of bank

Replacing the above in the Centripetal Force formula:

FC = W x tan ø

In this exercise:

W = mass x g = 60 000 x 10 = 600 000 N and bank angle (ø) = 30º

FC = 600 000 x tan 30º = 346 410 N

title: Which part of an aeroplane provides the greatest positive contribution to static longitudinal stability?
optionA: The horizontal tailplane.
optionB: The wing.
optionC: The fuselage.
optionD: The engine.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The longitudinal static stability of an airplane is its ability to return to its original pitch attitude with no outside assistance, after the disturbance that caused a nose-up or a nose-down movement has ceased.

The main factors that affect the longitudinal static stability are the design of the tail plane and the position of the CG relative to the position of the CP because they determine the direction of the additional wing-pitching moment.

The tail plane and elevators act as a horizontal stabilizer and the degree of positive longitudinal static stability that they provide is dependent on the size of the restoring moment they can attain; nevertheless, they make the largest contribution to the longitudinal static stability. The tail plane design and the length of the moment arm from the tail plane CP to the CG condition the magnitude of the restoring moment.

title:
Refer to figure.
The trailing edge flaps are stuck in the position shown in the picture. Which high-lift device is causing the asymmetry, and what could be a possible consequence of this?
optionA: Flap asymmetry and right-wing stalls
optionB: Flap asymmetry and left-wing stalls
optionC: Slat asymmetry and left-wing stalls
optionD: Slat asymmetry and right-wing stalls
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Flap asymmetry will give different lift on the wings which causes a large rolling moment. This will happen at any speed since flap extension changes the camber of the wing. The value of lift will be increased on the right side due to the flap extension. As a result the aircraft will roll to the left. Due to the rolling movement, the angle of attack will be decreased on the right side (upgoing side) and increased on the left side (downgoing wing), possibly beyond its critical angle of attack and leading to a spin (left wing stalled).

title:
Which of the following statements are true regarding feathering a propeller after an engine failure?

1. Drag and yaw are increased for multi-engine aircraft.
2. The gliding distance is increased for single-engine aircraft.
3. Yaw is reduced for single-engine aircraft.
4. The engine-out flight performance is improved for multi-engine aircraft.
optionA: 1 and 4
optionB: 3
optionC: 2 and 4
optionD: 3 and 4
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
To prevent the propeller from ‘wind milling’ the propeller blade is rotated from the fine-pitch stop through the coarse-pitch stop to reach the angle of attack to the relative airflow that produces zero lift; and referred to as ‘feathering’ the propeller. It’s usually approximately 85°/90° because it is the best compromise for the whole blade length and accounts for the blade twist.
This blade position stops the propeller from rotating because there is no lift force to produce a torque reaction; it reduces the drag to a minimum level and prevents damage being caused to the engine.
For a single-engine airplane feathering the propeller blades improves the glide performance because it does not require such a steep glide angle to maintain the required airspeed. As such, feathering the propeller increases the gliding range and endurance. For a multi-engine airplane, the decreased drag reduces the amount of thrust required to counteract the asymmetric force of the propeller of the failed engine and there is sufficient rudder authority remaining to enable the pilot to safely control the airplane.

title:
Refer to figure.
The line representing the effect of wing contribution on the static stability of an aeroplane is line (1) _____. The slope will increase as the CG moves (2) _____.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Evidence of static stability is shown by a tendency to return to equilibrium, or “trim”, upon displacement.
Positive static longitudinal stability is indicated by a negative slope of CM versus CL. The degree of static longitudinal stability is indicated by the slope of the curve.

  • Line "Y" represents the wing effect. The wing effect is destabilizing and the slope will increase as the CG moves AFT.
  • Line "Z" represents the tail effect. The tail has a stabilising contribution for stability which is represented by a negative slope.

title: In order to reduce friction drag, some wings are designed so that, compared to a conventional aerofoil...
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: the transition point is further aft to have more area with laminar flow.
optionB: the transition point is further forward to have more area with turbulent flow.
optionC: the separation point is further forward, to keep the boundary layer off the wing.
optionD: the separation point is further aft to keep the boundary layer attached to the wing.
explanationTotal:
Friction drag is the drag caused by the friction between the air molecules and the boundary layer of the airfoil's surface.

It is also the energy lost due to friction within the boundary layer. Very close to the surface, the air molecules are slowed down and brought to a standstill relative to the aircraft's surface. All this is happening just a few millimetres of the surface.

The boundary layer exists in two forms:

  • Laminar flow is the thinnest layer, smooth and produces the least friction.
  • Turbulent flow is unsteady, thicker, the layers become mixed and as a result produces more friction drag.

The laminar layer transitions to the turbulent layer at the transition point. The airflow starts off as laminar flow, the speed increases steadily from the surface to the free stream and at some point along the airfoil's surface the airflow transits into turbulent flow.

The difference in drag caused by the two states of the boundary layer is very marked about the same order of magnitude as the effect of streamlining, so it's understandable that much design effort is focussed on keeping the flow laminar for as long as possible. Thus, some aerofoils are designed to delay the transition by making it occur further aft so there is a greater area of laminar flow.

But such aerofoils have their disadvantges:

  • They produce less lift, so they tend to be used on aircraft that fly at higher speeds.
  • The separtion point tends to move forward very quickly leading to a narrow stall region.

title: After an aircraft initiates a go-around, the climb performance is less than expected. Which of the following states may have caused this?
optionA: Early landing gear retraction.
optionB: The air density has increased.
optionC: The air temperature has decreased.
optionD: Late flap retraction.
explanationTotal:
This is a very simple question about go-around performance. As a go-around is effectively just a climb, from a descent, performance is greatest when thrust is highest, drag is lowest, and weight is low.

The way to manage this is by having high density (low density altitude), meaning high pressure and low temperature, for the best thrust output. For lowest drag, gear needs to be retracted as soon as possible, and flaps should be retracted as early as possible (as per the speed schedule of course) to get the highest climb gradient.

After covering all those points, the only option which is BAD for climb performance is the late flap retraction, as the aircraft will spend more time in a high drag state.

title: What kind of drag will a fairing smoothening the angles where the wing meets the fuselage at the wing root reduce?
optionA: Interference drag
optionB: Pressure drag
optionC: Friction drag
optionD: Induced drag
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Interference drag is part of the profile drag and occurs when two (or more) bodies are connected (interact). Interference drag is caused mainly by the wing and fuselage connection and the most drag is observed when two surfaces meet at perpendicular angles.

Interference drag can be minimized by the appropriate use of fairings and fillets to ease the transition between components. Fairings and fillets use curved surfaces to soften the transition at the junction of two aircraft components.

title: Yaw is followed by roll because the:
optionA: rudder is located above the longitudinal axis and when it is deflected, it causes a rolling moment in the same direction as the yaw.
optionB: rolling motion generated by rudder deflection causes a speed increase of the outer wing which increases the lift on that wing so the aeroplane starts to roll in the direction of the turn.
optionC: yawing motion generated by rudder deflection causes a speed increase of the inner wing, which increase the lift on that wing so that the aeroplane starts to roll in the same direction as the yaw.
optionD: yawing motion generated by rudder deflection causes a speed increase of the outer wing, which increases the lift on that wing so that the aeroplane starts to roll in the same direction as the yaw.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Moving the left rudder pedal forward moves the rudder to the left. In flight, this produces an aerodynamic force on the fin and the aircraft yaws to the left. Moving the right rudder pedal forward reverses the action, and the aircraft yaws to the right. The secondary effect of rudder is roll in the same direction as yaw.
This occurs because the outer wing travels faster than the inner wing, thereby generating more lift.

title: An aeroplane's sideslip angle is defined as the angle between the:
optionA: lateral axis and the horizontal plane.
optionB: speed vector and the horizontal plane.
optionC: speed vector and the plane of symmetry.
optionD: speed vector and normal axis.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The rotation of an aircraft about its normal, or vertical, axis is a yaw. If this movement is the result of an undesirable disturbance, then the ability of the airplane to return to its original heading without the assistance of any control-surface movement is a measure of its directional static stability. It is a measure of the aircraft’s ability to realign itself with the relative airflow.

Sideslip is the displacement angle of the airplane’s longitudinal axis (plane of symmetry) in azimuth from the relative airflow (speed vector).
It is positive when the relative airflow is to the right of the longitudinal axis and negative when the relative airflow is left of the longitudinal axis.

An airplane has directional static stability if, when in a sideslip with the airflow coming from the left initially the nose tends to yaw left. An airplane that has excessive directional static stability compared to its lateral static stability is more prone to spiral dive.

title: Two identical aeroplanes A and B, with the same mass, are flying steady level co-ordinated 20 degree bank turns. If the TAS of A is 130 kt and the TAS of B is 200 kt:
optionA: the load factor of A is greater than that of B.
optionB: the turn radius of A is greater than that of B.
optionC: the rate of turn of A is greater than that of B.
optionD: the lift coefficient of A is less than that of B.
explanationTotal:
We have two aircraft at different speeds, same mass and bank angle.

⇒ Radius of Turn is greater with faster speed [Radius = TAS2 ÷ (g x tan ɸ)]
⇒ Rate of Turn is greater with slower speed [Rate of Turn = 1/TAS]

As the TAS of aircraft A is lower than B, Rate of Turn of A is greater than B.

title: In order to improve the stalling characteristics of an airplane, the wing's angle of incidence was changed but within limits. What is likely to happen?
optionA: The wing will stall at a different angle of incidence.
optionB: The wing section with a bigger angle of incidence will stall.
optionC: There is an increased tendency to spiral dive.
optionD: No major consequeces should be expected.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
In some wing designs, separation tends to occur first in the region of the tip, reducing lift in those areas. If an actual wing were allowed to stall in this way, stalling would give aileron buffet and perhaps violent wing drop.

To give favourable stall characteristics, a tapered wing must be modified using one or more of the following:

Geometric twist (washout), a decrease in incidence from root to tip. This decreases the angle of attack at the tip, and the root will tend to stall first.

The aerofoil section may be varied throughout the span such that sections with greater thickness and camber are located near the tip. The higher CLMAX of such sections delays stall so that the root will tend to stall first.

title: Control surface flutter can be eliminated by:
optionA: reducing structural stiffness of the control surface attachment structure.
optionB: mass balancing of the control surface.
optionC: increasing airspeed.
optionD: aerodynamic balancing of the control surface.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Flutter is an oscillation of the control surface which can occur due to the bending and twisting of the structure under load.

If the control surface CG is behind the hinge line, inertia will cause the surface to oscillate about its hinge line. The oscillations can be divergent and cause structural failure.

Flutter involves:
- aerodynamic forces.
- inertia forces.
- the elastic properties of a surface.

An aircraft is subject to many aerodynamic excitations (gusts, control inputs, etc.) and the aerodynamic forces at various speeds have characteristic properties for rate of change of force and moment.

The interaction of the aerofoil mass and the aerodynamic load imposed on the aerofoil causes distortion by bending and torsion of the structure that can result in a violent vibration in the resonance frequency, which if excessive can cause structural failure. This is ‘flutter’ and the aeroelastic coupling will affect its characteristics. The risk of experiencing flutter increases with IAS.

CONTROL SURFACE FLUTTER
Control surface flutter can develop as a result of an oscillation of the control surface coupled with an oscillation in bending or twisting of the wing, tailplane or fin.

A control surface oscillation can result from backlash (free play) in the control system or from a disturbance (gust).

MASS BALANCE
Flutter may be prevented by adding weight to the control surface in front of the hinge line.

This brings the centre of gravity of the control forward to a position on, or slightly in front of the hinge, but always to the point required by the designers. This reduces the inertia moments about the hinge and prevents flutter developing.

title: A twin-engine propeller aircraft suffers an engine failure. Under which of the following circumstances is retention of control likely to be most difficult?
optionA: Aerodrome at low density altitude, critical engine failure at the point of go-around.
optionB: Aerodrome at low density altitude, critical engine failure after take-off.
optionC: Aerodrome at high density altitude, critical engine failure at the point of go-around.
optionD: Aerodrome at high density altitude, critical engine failure after take-off.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
ENGINE FAILURE

If one engine on a conventional twin-engine aircraft fails in flight, it adversely affects its performance and controllability.

With both engines operating at the same power setting on a twin-engine aircraft, the amount of thrust produced by each engine is identical and their lines of action are symmetrically displaced about the aircraft's normal axis.

If one engine fails in flight, the remaining thrust forces are asymmetrically displaced and the aircraft yaws in the direction of the failed engine.

YAWING MOMENT

The yawing moment is the product of thrust from the operating engine multiplied by the distance between the thrust line and the CG (thrust arm), plus the drag from the failed engine multiplied by the distance between the engine centre line and the CG.

The strength of the yawing moment will depend on:
- how much thrust the operating engine is developing (throttle setting and density altitude).
- the distance between the thrust line and the CG (thrust arm).
- how much drag is being produced by the failed engine.

The rudder moment, which balances the yawing moment, is the result of the rudder force multiplied by the distance between the fin CP and the CG (rudder arm)

The ability of the pilot to counteract the yawing moment due to asymmetric thrust will depend on:
- rudder displacement (affecting rudder force).
- CG position (affecting rudder arm).
- the IAS (affecting rudder force).

title: While performing an obstacle limited take-off, you inadvertently set a lower take-off flap setting (less flap) than the calculated and required. Compared to a take-off at the correct flap setting , the aircraft will pass the departure end of the runway at…
optionA: greater height, as the lower flap setting means that more lift is generated.
optionB: greater height, as the lower flap setting means that a shorter take-off distance is required.
optionC: lower height, as the lower flap setting means that a greater take-off distance is required.
optionD: lower height, as the lower flap setting means that more drag is generated.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
TRAILING EDGE FLAPS

Aircraft are fitted with high lift devices to reduce the take-off and landing distances and when low airspeeds are beneficial. This permits operation at greater weights from given runway lengths and enables greater payloads to be carried.

Returning the flaps to their neutral position when no longer required, returns the wing to its former aerodynamic characteristics. The increase in lift comes mainly from the variation in effective camber that occurs when the flaps are deflected. This alters the lift curve and also produces a higher maximum coefficient of lift.

In some instances, the trailing edge flaps may also increase the wing's surface area. Extending the trailing edge flaps alters the pressure distribution around the wing.

USE OF TRAILING EDGE FLAPS FOR TAKE-OFF

For take-off purposes, the flaps are normally lowered to a position that provides the best lift-drag ratio that can be obtained with the flaps in any position other than fully up. Since the required lift is obtained at a lower airspeed, the take-off run is also reduced.

Larger amounts of flap cause a significant increase in drag, which greatly reduces the acceleration and increases the take-off run. The reduced stalling angle of attack and increased drag associated with flaps also reduces the rate and angle of climb.

After take-off, a minimum climb gradient is required in the take-off configuration. Climb gradient is reduced by flap, so if climb gradient is limiting, a lesser flap angle may be selected even though it gives a longer take-off distance.

title: The wings which will have the most effective high lift devices are:
optionA: Sweep angle does not change the effectiveness of high lift devices.
optionB: Wings with 15 degrees sweep angle.
optionC: Wings with 25 degrees sweep angle.
optionD: Wings with zero sweep angle.
explanationTotal: The wing sweep decreases the amount of lift generated for a given angle of attack relative to the straight wing. Since high lift devices are part of the wing, increasing the sweep angle will result in a reduction of the extra lift they would otherwise generate when deployed. High lift devices are the most effective on straight wings.

title: You are the pilot flying of a medium jet aeroplane and you are using the autopilot to maintain a constant vertical speed and the autothrust is maintaining a constant airspeed (CAS) while flying a Continuous Descent Approach (CDA). As the aeroplane is gradually slowing down from minimum clean speed of 213 kt to 180 kt, you selected approach flaps. Disregarding any other factors, the...
optionA: trajectory will initially become steeper as the flaps are extended but this reduction is offset by the slower airspeed, provided the vertical speed is maintained constant.
optionB: vertical speed must be reduced to maintain the trajectory, and when the approach speed stabilises, the autothrust will demand more thrust to maintain the speed.
optionC: vertical speed must be increased to offset the greater lift produced when the flaps are extended, and the autothrust will demand less thrust due to lower airpeed.
optionD: trajectory will become more shallow as the flaps are extended and the speed reduces, which require a higher vertical speed to be selected.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
RATE OF DESCENT

The rate of descent is the vertical speed of an aeroplane, which is usually specified in feet per minute (fpm) and is the vertical component of the forward speed of the aeroplane along the climb path.

Rate of descent depends on both the angle of descent and the speed down the flight path. The attached graph shows that there is greater excess drag at high speed than at low speeds. The shallowest angle of descent is achieved by staying slow.

This means, that the slower speed requires a lower rate of descent to maintain the same descent path.

V/S AUTOPILOT MODE

Vertical Speed is an autopilot flight guidance vertical mode. In this mode, the Flight Management and Guidance Computer (FMCG) pitch mode guides the aircraft to the target V/S. The corresponding thrust mode is SPEED or MACH.

The increase in drag associated with flap deflection requires an increased power setting in order to maintain a given airspeed and attitude, or a steady rate of descent.

In conclusion: Using the V/S autopilot mode means that the autopilot is keeping a constant rate of descent. By slowing down, the vertical speed becomes excessive and the pilot must reduce the vertical speed to maintain a constant descent path. After slowing down to the approach speed, the added drag from the configuration will demand more power/thrust from the engines to keep the airspeed constant.

title: An example of a combined lateral and directional aperiodic motion is a:
optionA: short period oscillation.
optionB: Dutch roll.
optionC: phugoid.
optionD: spiral dive.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
An airplane may display spiral instability in case it has strong directional stability relative to its lateral stability. It looks similar to a spin, however, the wings are not stalled here.

When a wind gust makes an airplane with spiral instability to side-slip, powerful directional stability tends to yaw the airplane back into alignment with the relative wind. In this case the outside wing will generate more lift as it travels faster. This tends to roll the airplane in the direction of the yaw. The rolling force overcomes the weak dihedral effect, allowing further roll. As the vertical component of lift decreases, the relative wind has an upward component with the airplane swinging in alignment with the air stream, the nose begins to drop. This results in a gradually increasing spiral dive.

title: Assuming ISA conditions and a climb above the tropopause at constant Mach number and aeroplane mass, the:
optionA: TAS increases.
optionB: IAS decreases.
optionC: lift coefficient remains constant.
optionD: lift coefficient decreases.
explanationTotal:
Mach number = True Air Speed (TAS) / Local Speed of Sound (LSS)
LSS = 38.96 √Absolute Temperature (K)
  1. Above the tropopause, temperature remains constant. Local Speed of sound being only dependant on temperature, will not change.
    Since Mach number and LSS are constant => TAS must also remain the same.​​​​​​​
  2. Density and pressure continue to decrease with increasing altitude (also above the tropopause).
    IAS = 1/2 p V2 (Where V = TAS)
    When density "p" decreases in a climb and TAS remains contant => IAS decreases.

title:
Choose the correct/incorrect statements regarding the Mach number for critical drag rise (MCDR):

1. MCDR is less than MCRIT.
2. At a fixed angle of attack, at speeds below MCRIT the formation of shock waves causes an increase in CD.
optionA: 1. correct, 2. correct.
optionB: 1. incorrect, 2. incorrect.
optionC: 1. correct, 2. incorrect.
optionD: 1. incorrect, 2. correct.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
“MCDR is less than MCRIT” Incorrect.
The Mach number at which the aerodynamic drag begins to increase rapidly is called tha Drag Divergence Mach number, also know as Mach Number for Critical Drag Rise (not to be confused with critical Mach Number). The Drag Divergence Mach Number is usually close to, and always greater than, the Critical Mach Number.

“At a fixed angle of attack, at speeds below MCDR and MCRIT the formation of shock waves causes an increase in CD” Incorrect.
The Critical Mach Number (MCRIT) is the free stream Mach number at which the peak velocity on the surface of a body first becomes equal to the local speed of sound. As speed increases above MCRIT shock waves begin to form and drag increases more rapidly than it would have done without the shock waves. It is a fact that the formation of shock waves increases drag, however MCRIT is the speed when shock waves appear, there are no shock waves below MCRIT.

title: The aerodynamic centre of the wing is the point, where:
optionA: the aeroplane’s lateral axis intersects with the centre of gravity.
optionB: the pitching moment coefficient does not vary with angle of attack.
optionC: changes of lift due to variations in angle of attack are constant.
optionD: aerodynamic forces are constant.
explanationTotal: The <u>Aerodynamic Centre (AC)</u> is the point to which moments of the resultant forces are the same for the same dynamic pressure. In other words, moment coefficient does not change with changing angle of attack (moment is independent of the AOA), assuming no flow separation. Another way to define AC is "the point where all changes in the magnitude of the lift force effectively takes place".

title: The pilot of an aircraft changes its heading to the right, from 214º to 334º and makes a rate-1 turn. The duration of this manoeuvre is...
optionA: impossible to calculate, because we need the aircraft's TAS.
optionB: 40 seconds.
optionC: 30 seconds.
optionD: impossible to calculate, because we need the aircraft's angle of bank.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
If the turn is unbalanced, an aircraft either slips into, or skids out of the turn, thereby reducing the aerodynamic efficiency of the aircraft. To help correct for these unwanted conditions, the aircraft is flown using the balance part of the turn and balance indicator

During a balanced turn the ball remains in the centre of the balance indicator and the pilot remains upright in the seat relative to the aircraft, with no tendency to lean.

Rate of turn is the measurement of how long it takes for an aircraft to turn, measured in degrees per second. This is particularly important during instrument flying where rate-1 turns are usually carried out at a rate of 3° per second. This means that the aircraft turns through 180° in 1 minute, or 360° in 2 minutes. A steeper angle of bank is required to carry out a rate-1 turn at higher airspeeds.

To solve this exercise, first we need to calculate how many degrees was the turn performed and then apply the rate of turn:

334º - 214º = 120º at 3º/second (rate-1 turn)
120/3º = 40 seconds

title:
Comparing the differences between a horizontal trimmable stabiliser and an elevator trim tab, which of these statements are correct or incorrect?

I. When trimmed for zero elevator stick force a horizontal trimmable stabiliser causes more drag.
II. A horizontal trimmable stabiliser enables a larger CG range.
optionA: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
optionB: I is incorrect, II is correct.
optionC: I is correct, II is correct.
optionD: I is correct, II is incorrect.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
When trimmed for zero elevator stick force, a conventional tailplane causes more drag than a horizontal trimmable stabiliser, because the tailplane (stabiliser + elevator + trim tab) is forming a camber.

A horizontal trimmable stabiliser enables a larger CG and speed range than a conventional tailplane, because the whole stabiliser may be moved for trimming the aeroplane, instead of a relatively “small” elevator and trim tab only (a larger surface is much more effective). This also leads to more control difficulty due to a trim runaway, respectively less control difficulty with a trim tab runaway.

title: An aeroplane performs a steady horizontal, co-ordinated turn with 45 degrees of bank at 230 kt TAS. The same aeroplane with the same bank angle and speed, but at a lower mass will turn with:
optionA: the same turn radius.
optionB: a larger turn radius.
optionC: a higher rate of turn.
optionD: a smaller turn radius.
explanationTotal:
The Turn radius of turn varies with changes in either speed or bank:
  • Turn Radius = TAS2 ÷ (g x tan ɸ)
Therefore, if both aircraft have the same speed and bank angle, they will have the same turn radius.

title: After an engine failure on a twin-engine aircraft, banking towards the live engine is limited to 5 degrees. What is correct if greater angles of bank are used?
optionA: The lateral component of Weight decreases.
optionB: The risk of fin stall decreases.
optionC: The risk of fin stall increases.
optionD: The Lift required decreases.
explanationTotal:
COUNTERACTING ASYMMETRIC THRUST

Rudder to Stop Yaw - Bank Towards Live Engine. This method produces minimum drag and gives the best ability to climb and is the preferred method of putting the aircraft in equilibrium following engine failure.

  • The typical action is to apply rudder in the direction of the live engine to counteract this forward slip. However, while the nose will be aligned with the desired flight path doing this, the actual flight path is a side slip towards the dead engine side, which creates excess drag.
  • The only available counter to this is to bank the airplane into the direction of the live engine to counteract the rudder force using the horizontal component of lift. The application of 5 degrees of bank towards the live engine will help controlling the yaw. The angle of bank must not exceed 5°. Using more than 5º of bank may create enough sideslip towards the lower wing to give a risk of fin stall.

title: Consider a multi-engine aeroplane. In order to achieve the best possible climb performance, which of the following methods is used to maintain control after an engine failure?
optionA: Rudder to stop yaw, aileron to maintain wings level.
optionB: Rudder to stop yaw, aileron to bank towards the live engine.
optionC: Rudder to stop yaw, aileron to bank towards the failed engine.
optionD: Aileron to stop yaw, rudder to keep the slip indicator centred.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
When an engine fails on a multi-engine aircraft there will be a decrease in thrust and an increase in drag on the side with the failed engine:

  • airspeed will decay.
  • the nose will drop and.
  • most significantly, there will be an immediate yawing moment towards the failed engine.
The forces and moments acting on an aircraft following failure of the left engine are shown in figure 1. The aircraft has a yawing moment towards the dead engine. The pilot has applied rudder to stop the yaw. The vital action when an engine fails is to stop the yaw.
It is more aerodynamically efficient to balance the rudder side force by banking towards the live engine, so that lift gives a sideways component opposite to the rudder force. The angle of bank must not exceed 5°, to prevent excessive loss of vertical lift component.
Banking towards the live engine also reduces the side force on the fin from sideslip, which minimizes VMC, effectively reduces the yawing moment and gives more rudder authority to stop the yaw.
This method produces minimum drag and gives the best ability to climb and is therefore the preferred method of putting the aircraft in equilibrium following engine failure.

title:
Refer to figure.
When extending spoilers, what will happen to the stall speed and critical AOA?
optionA: Lower critical AOA and higher stall speed
optionB: Lower critical AOA and lower stall speed
optionC: Higher critical AOA and lower stall speed
optionD: Higher critical AOA and higher stall speed
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
Note: this question has had to be slightly modified from the original feedback for clarity and correctness. Please send any further exam feedback to us in the comments or by email to info@atplquestions.com, thank you.
Learning Objective 081.01.10.01.02: Describe the effect of spoilers on the CL-alpha graph and stall speed.

Spoilers are aerodynamic surfaces that exist on the top surface of some wings, and are used for many reasons. They are primarily used to increase drag and "dump" lift. (If they are just for drag then they are called speedbrakes, but aircraft manufacturers do blur these distinctions).

They are called spoilers because they "spoil" the airflow, sticking up into the airflow, causing a lift reduction similar to an up-going aileron and a similar drag increase to that of a split flap.

Of course, the spoiled airflow is not as effective at producing lift, and the stall speed therefore increases. There is, however, a counter-intuitive rise in the critical angle of attack.

Because the top surface of the wing goes up again with a spoiler extended, it acts the same as an up-going aileron, and even though the air behind the spoiler is incredibly turbulent, the air flowing along the surface becomes re-energised and will resist the stall at higher angles of attack than usual, increasing the critical angle of attack. Remember, in flight, spoilers are only extended a small amount, not like the ground spoilers which come up at around 90º to the wing.

title: When flutter damping of control surfaces is obtained by mass balancing, these weights will be located with respect to the hinge of the control surface:
optionA: in front of the hinge.
optionB: behind the hinge.
optionC: above the hinge.
optionD: below the hinge.
explanationTotal: Refer to figure.

title: In the transonic speed region the L/D ratio is...
optionA: always at its maximum.
optionB: reduced.
optionC: constant.
optionD: increased.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Although the curve of CL / CD is unique at low speeds, at transonic speeds when compressibility becomes significant, the curve will change.
Figure 1 shows the variation of CL / CD with Mach number. The point at which the tangent from the origin touches the curve corresponds to the maximum CL / CD.
In the transonic region, the CL / CD ratio is reduced.

title: While going around in an airport with temperature at negative 10 degrees, a light twin-engine aircraft with normally-aspirated piston engines experiences an engine failure. How will the environment described affect V<sub>MCA</sub>?
optionA: Decreased effectiveness of controls due to low air temperature will increase V<sub>MCA</sub>.
optionB: Increased effectiveness of controls due to high air density will decrease V<sub>MCA</sub>.
optionC: High engine performance on the operating engine due to high air density will decrease V<sub>MCA</sub>.
optionD: High engine performance on the operating engine due to high air density will increase V<sub>MCA</sub>.
explanationTotal:
The approach speed of a light twin engine aircraft is usually 1.3 times the stall speed, which is an indicated airspeed. Temperature (and the resulting density) is usually not a factor (when the temperature is within the operational limits) in determining the approach speed. With the same approach speed (in IAS) the effectiveness of control will be the same before and upon the initiation of go around.

The difference is that in a low temperature (higher density) environment a normally aspirated piston engine will produce a higher power output (with a higher manifold pressure) when compared with a high temperature (lower density) situation during go around in full throttle.

Therefore, with more power output at the engines during go around it becomes harder to counteract in an engine failure situation – which leads to an increased demand in the effectiveness of control during engine failure. That demand in higher control effectiveness will be achieved by flying faster – hence an increase in VMCA.

title: An aircraft is flying straight and level. Assuming there are no mechanical malfunctions or environmental errors affecting the indicator, what can be said to remain constant if the speed indicated in the Airspeed Indicator does not change?
optionA: The dynamic pressure.
optionB: The temperature.
optionC: The true airspeed.
optionD: The air density.
explanationTotal:
The Airspeed Indicator (ASI) measures dynamic pressure as the difference between the total pitot pressure measured in the instrument's capsule/diaphragm and the static pressure measured in the case. The dynamic pressure represents the indicated airspeed (lAS) as knots per hour.

When flying straight and level (static pressure remains the same), if the speed indicated in the ASI remains unchanged, the dynamic pressure is most likely constant.

title:
You are flying close to thunderstorms and you don’t want to stall the aircraft or mach buffet. Which statement is correct

1. Descend to a lower altitude.
2. Increase the mach number.
3. Climb above the thunderstorms.
4. Avoid cells by using weather radar.
explanationTotal:
Never regard any thunderstorm lightly, even when radar observers report the echoes are of light intensity. Avoiding thunderstorms is the best policy. Avoid thunderstorms by at least 20 NM => this general guideline applies even to jet fighters and large airliners. Hail and severe turbulence can exist well outside of the storm cloud.

• If you plan to deviate around a thunderstorm => fly on the upwind side so that your path does not converge with the path of the storm.

• Do not be tempted to try to fly under a thunderstorm, even if you can see through the rain on the other side => besides rain, hail and lighting, the area under a thunderstorm typically contains severe turbulence (including microbursts, windshear and downdrafts

• Trying to fly over a developing storm is also dangerous => the rising clouds can usually outclimb your aircraft.

“1. Descend to a lower altitude” CORRECT.
The AOA of the wing has the greatest effect on inducing the Mach buffet, or pre-stall buffet, at either the high or low speed boundaries for the airplane. The higher the plane flies, the thinner the air and the greater the AOA required to produce the lift needed to maintain level flight. Increasing the AOA increases the speed of the airflow over the wing and the chances of Mach buffet.

“4. Avoid cells by using weather radar” CORRECT.
If your aircraft is equipped with a weather avoidance system, such as a weather radar, you can use it to avoid thunderstorms. You should avoid intense thunderstorms echoes by at least 20 NM.
Airborne weather radar is designed for avoiding severe weather, not for penetrating it. It detects drops of precipitation. Therefore, do not try to use it to avoid instrument weather associated with clouds and fog – it does not provide any assurance of avoiding IFR weather conditions.

title: On a normally cambered airfoil which increases its speed through the transonic region, the lower shock wave…
optionA: moves aft until reaching the upper shock wave.
optionB: moves aft and reaches the trailing edge first.
optionC: moves aft slower than upper shock wave.
optionD: does not move.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The curvature of the underside of a wing is usually less than that of the upper surface, therefore the acceleration of the airflow is less, consequently the airflow does not become sonic until the aeroplane is travelling at a higher airspeed.

At lower airspeeds the only shockwave occurs on the upper surface and first appears at the wing root. At speeds above this, a shockwave forms beneath the lower surface of the wing ahead of the upper surface shockwave.

The shock wave on the lower surface usually forms at a higher free stream Mach number than the upper surface shock, but it reaches the trailing edge first.

The meeting point of the two pressure waves occurs nearer the trailing edge.

title: In a skidding turn (the nose pointing inwards), compared with a co-ordinated turn, the bank angle (i) and the "ball" or slip indicator (ii) are respectively:
optionA: (i) too large, (ii) displaced towards the low wing.
optionB: (i) too small, (ii) displaced towards the low wing.
optionC: (i) too small, (ii) displaced towards the high wing.
optionD: (i) too large, (ii) displaced towards the high wing.
explanationTotal:
A coordinated turn is a turn where there is no sideslip or skid, this is the most effective and therefore preferable way to turn.
In a coordinated turn, the turn and bank indicator in the plane shows the ball in the center.
If the turn is not coordinated, you’re either in a slip or a skid.
These two things are different and shall therefore be eliminated differently.

A slipping turn is a turn where the aircraft’s nose is outside of the turning radius and the tail is in the turn radius.
A slip is caused by using too much bank and too little rudder.
A skidding turn is a turn where the aircraft’s nose is inside of the turning radius and the tail is outside of the turn radius.
A skid is caused by using too much rudder and not enough bank.

The indicator works via the “step on the ball” principle. If the ball is right of center, you should give (more) right rudder and vice versa.

title: To which category is MMO applicable?
optionA: CS25
optionB: Neither category
optionC: CS23 & CS25
optionD: CS23
explanationTotal:
CS 25.1505 Maximum operating limit speed
'The maximum operating limit speed (VMO/MMO, airspeed or Mach number, whichever is critical at a particular altitude) is a speed that may not be deliberately exceeded in any regime of flight (climb, cruise, or descent), unless a higher speed is authorised for flight test or pilot training operations.(...)'

CS 23.1505 AIRSPEED LIMITATIONS
'This paragraph establishes the operational speed limitations which establish safe margins below design speeds. For reciprocating engine­ powered aeroplanes there is an option. They may either establish a never­ exceed speed (VNE) and a maximum structural cruising speed (VNO) or they may be tested in accordance with 23.335(b)(4) in which case the aeroplane is operated under a maximum operating speed concept (VMO/MMO). For turbine­ powered aeroplanes, a VMO/MMO should be established.(...)'

title: An aerofoil with positive camber at a positive angle of attack will have the highest flow velocity:
optionA: on the lower side.
optionB: on the upper side.
optionC: at the trailing edge.
optionD: In front of the stagnation point.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Camber is the asymmetry between two acting surfaces on an airfoil. For an aircraft, this is the top and the bottom of the wing. Positive camber means that a wing is thicker on the top end of the wing, than on the bottom if looked at from the chord. In case of positive camber, a wing will generate lift with airspeed, as the air on top of the airfoil will get accelerated more than on the bottom, creating a low pressure on the top and high pressure at the bottom. This is “pushing” the wing up into the air as the pressure difference wants to restore itself to 0 difference. In case of negative camber, the exact opposite happens and the lift coefficient for a certain speed is lower than for a positively cambered wing.

A completely symmetrical airfoil will intersect the vertical axis of the graph at the origin (0). A positively cambered airfoil will generate more lift at the same speed (and therefore has a higher CL) than a symmetrical airfoil and therefore intersects the vertical axis above the origin. A negatively cambered airfoil will generate less lift at the same speed (which translates into a lower CL at a certain speed) and therefore intersects the vertical axis below the origin.

The camber of an airfoil can be increased with the use of flaps. The end of the wing reaches out and/or downwards, changing the side profile of the wing and moving the CP aft, resulting in a nose down pitching moment. This generates a higher value of CL at the same Angle of Attack. Therefore if flaps are being retracted, the Angle of Attack should be increased.

title: Long-period oscillation about the aeroplane’s lateral axis with variations in pitch attitude, altitude and airspeed, with an aircraft constant angle of attack, is known as:
optionA: Dutch Roll
optionB: Phugoid
optionC: Buffet
optionD: Flutter
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Phugoid oscillations typically have long periods of 20 to 100 seconds. These are pitch oscillations at almost constant angle of attack with the exchange of an airplane’s kinetic (airspeed) and potential (altitude) energies. Phugoid oscillations often are lightly damped, with the damping factor inversely proportional to the aerodynamic efficiency: The higher the glide ratio, the less damping.

title: Regarding high-speed flight, if the angle of attack of an aeroplane is increased, it's critical Mach number will…
optionA: decrease, because of the reduced margin to the critical angle of attack.
optionB: decrease, because of greater acceleration on the top surface of the wing.
optionC: increase, because of reduced downwash at the tailplane.
optionD: increase, because of increased induced drag.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
CRITICAL MACH NUMBER

Critical Mach Number (MCRIT): The critical Mach number is the Mach number of the aircraft when the speed of the airflow over some part of the aircraft (usually the point of maximum thickness on the aerofoil) first reaches the speed of sound.

An aerofoil generates lift by accelerating air over the top surface. At small angles of attack the highest local velocity on an aircraft will usually be located at the point of maximum thickness on the wing.

At increased angles of attack the local velocity will be greater and further forward. Also, if the thickness/chord ratio were greater, the local speed will be higher.

Increased thickness/chord ratio and increased angle of attack cause greater accelerations over the top surface of the wing, so the Critical Mach number will decrease with increasing thickness/chord ratio or angle of attack.

title:
Refer to figure.
The maximum achievable load factor without buffet onset at FL380 at a mass of 90 tons is approximately:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: 2 g at M = 0.80.
optionB: 1.5 g at M = 0.80.
optionC: 1 g at M = 0.80.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
In the same way that separated airflow prior to a low speed stall can cause airframe buffet, shock induced separation (shock stall) at high speed can also cause buffeting.

Aerodynamic buffet is a valuable stall warning, but it can damage the aircraft structure. Because of the higher dynamic pressure when an aircraft is operating in the transonic speed region, any shock induced buffet will have a greater potential for severe airframe damage.

High speed buffet must be completely avoided. The aircraft must therefore be operated in such a manner that a (safety) margin exists before aerodynamic buffet will occur.

If the variables which affect both high speed and low speed stall are considered it will be possible to identify the conditions under which buffeting will occur and a chart can be drawn to show all the factors involved.

This is called a ‘Buffet Onset’ chart which is used by flight crews to ensure their aircraft is always operated with a specified minimum buffet margin.

In this exercise:

  • Start by drawing a vertical line from M0.80 to the FL380 curve.
  • From here, draw a straight line from left to right that intersects the 90-ton curve.
  • Finally, draw a vertical down to asset the load factor. In this case, the load factor is approximately 1.75 g.

title: On final approach to land you encounter a microburst and you have to go around. What is the risk of flying in these conditions?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Tailwind can make you stall.
optionB: Only light turbulence may be encountered.
optionC: Energy will increase.
optionD: Increases speed.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
MICROBURSTS
These are the most lethal forms of windshear. They normally occur in the vicinity of thunderstorms and are mainly associated with cumulonimbus clouds

THE EFFECT OF A MICROBURST ENCOUNTER DURING THE APPROACH

The attached depicts how an aircraft typically reacts when subject to a microburst during the approach:

- Increasing headwinds, causing the IAS to rise (temporary energy gain) and the aircraft to climb above the glidepath.

- A downdraught that increases the rate of descent and decreases the IAS, thereby causing the aircraft to drop further below the glidepath. The situation worsens if the nose is still high and the thrust setting low.

- On leaving the downdraught, increasing tail winds cause a further reduction in IAS (Temporary Energy Loss). The rate of descent may lessen due to increased thrust availability. This may lead to a reduction in airspeed below the stalling speed and if operating at high angles of attack, which are normally associated with the approach and landing phases of flight, the wing may stall.

A successful recovery from a microburst encounter depends on the altitude, thrust, and speed reserves available. In addition to these effects, severe wind, turbulence, heavy rain, and blinding flashes of lightning often accompany microbursts.

title: When the trailing-edge flaps are extended, the centre of pressure will move (1) _____, producing a pitch (2) _____ moment.
optionA: (1) forward; (2) up
optionB: (1) forward; (2) down
optionC: (1) aft; (2) down
optionD: (1) aft; (2) up
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

Trailing edge devices, also known as flaps, are designed to increase the wing camber which will increase the downwash and the circulation relative the aerofoil. It will also move the CP rearwards creating a nose-down moment.

The lift/drag ratio can be changed very effectively by means of the flaps. Small flap deflections increases the margin to stall with only a moderate increase in drag, whiles greater flap setting is set to increase the drag

title: While flying straight and level flight, maintaining constant IAS, one engine of a twin-engine propeller aircraft suddenly  becomes INOP. If density decreases, thrust will (1) _____ and the yawing moment (2) _____.
optionA: (1) increase; (2) increase
optionB: (1) increase; (2) decrease
optionC: (1) decrease; (2) decrease
optionD: (1) decrease; (2) increase
explanationTotal:
When a multi-engine aircraft suffers an engine failure several variables affect both the yawing moment and the rudder moment which is used to oppose it.

There is a minimum IAS (VMC), below which it is impossible for the pilot to maintain directional control with asymmetric thrust.

Airworthiness Authorities, in this case the EASA, have laid down conditions which must be satisfied when establishing the minimum airspeeds for inclusion in the Flight Manual of a new aircraft type. As in most other cases, the conditions under which the minimum control airspeeds are established are ‘worst case’.

VMCA is affected by the amount of thrust being developed by the operating engine. As altitude and/or temperature increases, the thrust from an unsupercharged engine will decrease.

In conditions of low air density, the engines produce a lower thrust output and the loss of the output from one engine during take-off is proportionate to the loss of a lower output. This will require a less amount of force to counteract the tendency to yaw, when compared to conditions of higher air density.

Air density will be lowest when the aerodrome pressure altitude is highest (low atmospheric pressure), the air temperature is highest and the water-vapour content of the air is highest.

title: Above M<sub>CRIT</sub> in the transonic speed regime, at a constant angle of attack, the CD will...
optionA: increase as Mach number increases.
optionB: decrease as Mach number increases.
optionC: remain constant in the entire regime.
optionD: vary depending on Mach number.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
As speed increases above MCRIT shock waves begin to form and drag increases more rapidly than it would have done without the shock waves. The additional drag is called wave drag and is due to energy drag and boundary layer separation.

The Mach number at which the aerodynamic drag begins to increase rapidly is called the drag divergence Mach number. The Drag Divergence Mach Number is usually close to, and always greater than, the Critical Mach Number, as seen in figure 1.

title: How does stall speed (IAS) vary with altitude?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: It remains constant.
optionB: It increases with increasing altitude, because the density decreases.
optionC: It remains constant at lower altitudes but increases at higher altitudes due to compressibility effects.
optionD: It remains constant at lower altitudes but decreases at higher altitudes due to compressibility effects.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The stall speed is defined by:

VS=√((2∗W)/(ρ∗S∗CLMAX))

At the stalling angle CLMAX and S are constant, and the indicated airspeed is given by the dynamic pressure 1 / 2 ρV2. Therefore, for the same airplane mass and configuration in straight and level flight, if the slight difference between EAS and IAS caused by compressibility is ignored, an airplane will stall at the same IAS at all altitudes.
If, however, compressibility is not ignored then the stalling IAS value slowly increases with increased altitude, but the change only becomes significant at very high altitudes.At a constant EAS, Mach number will increase as altitude increases.

Figure 1 shows the variation of stalling speed with altitude at constant load factor (n). Such a curve is called the stalling boundary for the given load factor, in which altitude is plotted against equivalent airspeed.At this load factor (1g), the aircraft cannot fly at speeds to the left of this boundary. Over the lower range of altitude, stall speed does not vary with altitude. This is because at these low altitudes, the Mach number at VS is too low for compressibility effects to be present. Eventually (approximately 30000 ft), Mach number at VS has increased with altitude to such an extent that these effects are important, and the rise in stalling speed with altitude is apparent.
As altitude increases, stall speed is initially constant then increases, due to compressibility.

title:
Refer to figure.
Which line in the diagram illustrates an aeroplane with neutral static longitudinal stability at all angles of attack?
optionA: Line 1.
optionB: Line 2.
optionC: Line 4.
optionD: Line 3.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Static longitudinal stability depends upon the relationship of angle of attack and pitching moment (CM).

A variation of CG position can cause large changes in the static longitudinal stability. In the conventional airplane configuration, the large changes in stability with CG variation are primarily due to the large changes in the wing contribution. If the incidence of all surfaces remains fixed, the effect of CG position on static longitudinal stability is typified by the chart in figure 1:

As the CG is gradually moved aft, the airplane static stability decreases, then becomes neutral then unstable. The CG position which produces zero slope and neutral static stability is referred to as the “neutral point”. The neutral point defines the most aft CG position without static instability.

Positive static stability is indicated by the curve with negative slope. Moving the CG forward, will increase static longitudinal stability and this is represented by a (steeper) negative slope.

Neutral static stability would be the result if the curve had zero slope. If neutral stability existed, the airplane could be disturbed to some higher or lower lift coefficient without change in pitching moment coefficient.

An airplane which demonstrates a positive slope of the CM versus CL curve would be unstable.

title: Assuming ISA conditions and a descent above the tropopause at constant Mach number and aeroplane mass, the...
optionA: lift coefficient remains constant.
optionB: IAS increases.
optionC: IAS decreases.
optionD: TAS decreases.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The Mach number is defined as the ratio between the TAS and the LSS (Local speed of sound).
It is an indication of how fast an aircraft is travelling with relation to the sound waves that surround it.

The Mach number may be calculated as follows:

M=TAS/LSS=(TAS(kt))/(38.95∗√(T(K)))

The speed of propagation of small pressure waves depends upon the temperature of the air ONLY.

The Indicated Airspeed is defined by dynamic pressure:

IAS=1/2∗ρ∗TAS2

Effect on TAS of descending at a constant Mach Number (above tropopause):

  • Above the tropopause the temperature is constant, so the speed of sound will remain the same.
  • If altitude is decreased at a constant Mach Number, the TAS is also constant. This is because, above the tropopause, LSS is constant.
  • Descending through the tropopause, density (ρ) will increase. Looking at the IAS formula, with a constant TAS, increasing density will increase IAS.

title: Assuming ISA conditions and a climb above the tropopause at constant Mach number and aeroplane mass, the:
optionA: TAS remains constant
optionB: TAS decrease
optionC: Lift coefficient remains constant
optionD: A lower AoA
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Mach number = True Air Speed (TAS) / Local Speed of Sound (LSS)
LSS = 38.96 √Absolute Temperature (K)

  1. Above the tropopause, temperature remains constant. Local Speed of sound being only dependant on temperature, will not change.
    Since Mach number and LSS are constant => TAS must also remain the same.

title: In aircraft with supercritical wings, what are the advantages of cruising at speeds slightly above M<sub>CRIT</sub>?
optionA: The speed versus drag ratio decreases.
optionB: Optimum altitude decreases.
optionC: Specific range decreases.
optionD: Specific range increases.
explanationTotal:
Even slightly beyond critical Mach number (but below the drag divergence Mach number) CL/CD ratio is still higher than in low-speed range. Should the aeroplane be fitted with supercritical aerofoils, the gap between MCRIT and MDIV is greater. Consequently, modern airliners can cruise slightly above MCRIT and it is beneficial to do so. Since CL/CD ratio is still high, their speed versus drag ratio is close to maximum here, which in turn means that specific range is also close to maximum at this velocity. Remember that Specific range (SR) is the distance an aircraft travels per unit of fuel consumed.

Thrust required can be calculated: TR = W x CD/CL
Thus, for a given velocity thrust required reduces with increasing CL/CD, as a consequence of which fuel consumption reduces.

title: Stall speed (IAS) varies with:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: density
optionB: altitude (below approximately 10000 ft)
optionC: weight
optionD: temperature
explanationTotal:
Any airplane, within the limits of its structure and the strength of the pilot, can be stalled at any airspeed.

VS = √(2W ÷ p S CLMAX)

The equation above well defines the factors affecting the stall speed, in summary; aircraft weight, air density, maximum lift coefficient, and the load factor.

AIRCRAFT WEIGHT.

Stall speed is proportional with the aircraft weight. Stall speed increases, as the weight increases; and decreases as the weight decreases.

AIR DENSITY.

Aircraft stall speeds are usually given in terms of CAS or IAS as an aircraft limitations. However, as seen in the equation above, it is actually a true airspeed which is inversely proportional with the density. Therefore, although it is constant in terms of CAS/IAS, it increases with the altitude because of the density variation.

MAXIMUM LIFT COEFFICIENT.

Maximum lift coefficient may be varied by high lift devices such as flaps and slats. Higher maximum lift coefficients will result in slower stall speeds. Lowest maximum lift coefficient is obtained when flaps are retracted (airplane in clean configuration), thus highest stall speed occurs in clean configuration.

LOAD FACTOR.

Stall speed is proportional with the load factor. It increases as the load factor increases. If VSS is the stall speed of an aircraft in steady level flight, then stall speed during maneuvers will be:
VSN =√n VSS

Or during a turn maneuver:
VSN = VSS ÷ √ cos a

title: The combination of factors that cause a spin to develop are:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Both wings stalled in coordinated flight.
optionB: One wing stalled in coordinated flight.
optionC: Both wings stalled, one more than the other, in uncoordinated flight.
optionD: Approaching the stall speed with the ball centered.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
SPIN. A stall must occur before a spin can take place. A spin occurs when one wing stalls more than the other - During the spin, the wings remain unequally stalled.

  • A spin is a yaw aggravated stall which results in rotation about the spin axis. The aircraft follows a steep, "corkscrew" like, downward path.

title: For a conventional aeroplane with the aerodynamic centre behind the aeroplane’s centre of gravity, the presence of significant ice on the leading edge of the tailplane can cause the tailplane to stall. This could cause an uncontrollable pitch...
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: up, and is more likely when the elevator is moved relatively down or the wing flaps are retracted.
optionB: down, and is more likely when the elevator is moved relatively up or when the wing flaps are extended.
optionC: down, and is more likely when the elevator is moved relatively up or the wing flaps are retracted.
optionD: up, and is more likely when the elevator is moved relatively down or when the wing flaps are extended.
explanationTotal:
The tail plane is an aero foil, and because it is thinner than the wing, it is likely to experience icing before the wing does. The effect will be the same as for the wing; the stall will occur at a lower angle of attack. The tail plane is normally operating at a negative angle of attack, producing a download, so if the tail plane stalls and the download is lost, the nose of the aircraft will drop, and longitudinal control will be lost.

Stalling of an ice contaminated tail plane could be precipitated by extension of the wing flaps. Lowering the flaps increases the downwash, and this increases the negative angle of attack of the tail plane. If the tail plane has ice contamination, this could be sufficient to cause it to stall. Recovery procedure in this situation would be to retract the flaps again, thus reducing the downwash.

title: What needs to be considered when descending at M<sub>MO</sub>/V<sub>MO</sub>?
optionA: Aerodynamic limitations at high altitude and aerodynamic limitations at low altitude.
optionB: Structural limitations at high altitude and aerodynamic limitations at low altitude.
optionC: Aerodynamic limitations at high altitude and structural limitations at low altitude.
optionD: Structural limitations at high altitude and structural limitations at low altitude.
explanationTotal:
The Buffet Onset Boundary Chart is limited by low speed and high speed buffet margins. These margins get tighter as altitude is increased.

Flying high and fast (close to MMO/VMO) means that we will be very close to the buffet boundary and buffet or even stall might occur. This is an aerodynamic limitation.

As we start to descend, the buffet margins become wider and less limiting. This means that if we fly at the MMO/VMO there's a possibility to overstress the aircraft due to excessive speed. At lower altitudes, the MMO/VMO becomes a structural limitation.

title: A multi-engined piston aeroplane is in the cruise at FL210 flying over the Alps when one propeller suffers a problem with the anti-icing system and icing starts to build up on one of the propellers. Which of the following is a possible hazard of propeller icing?
optionA: Reduced propeller efficiency means that the aircraft can NOT maintain cruising altitude.
optionB: The propeller mass becomes severely imbalanced and results in damages to the propeller.
optionC: Reduced thrust available means that the aircraft can NOT remain safely airborne.
optionD: Ice breaking off the propeller and damaging the landing gear wheels.
explanationTotal:
Ice contamination on the propeller has the same effect as ice on the wings, in that both reduce the efficiency of the aerofoils. Leading edge ice on the propeller reduces the generated thrust in the same way the lift of the wing is reduced.

Ice on a propeller blade reduces the efficiency of the propeller and reduces thrust. In addition, the weight of the ice increases the aircraft weight and therefore the lift required. If ice builds on an unprotected propeller, thrust reduces and you might not be able to climb out of the icing conditions or maintain the altitude.

The greatest quantity of ice normally collects on the spinner and inner radius of the propeller.
The estimated propeller efficiency loss is on the order of 15%-20%.

title: What will help against shock-induced separation of the boundary layer?
optionA: Using vortex generators.
optionB: Increasing the Mach number.
optionC: Increasing the Angle of Attack.
optionD: Deploying the high lift devices.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The unfavorable characteristics associated with compressibility are due to boundary layer separation behind the shock wave (shock stall).

Flow separation occurs because the boundary layer loses kinetic energy as it flows against the adverse pressure gradient. Shock wave formation increases the adverse pressure gradient so the loss of kinetic energy in the boundary layer will be greater.

Increasing the kinetic energy of the boundary layer will reduce flow separation. Simple devices called vortex generators are used to re-energize the boundary layer.
Vortex generators are small plates, vanes, blades, or wedges mounted in spanwise rows along the wing surface.

Each vortex generator produces a vortex at its tip which will induce high energy air from the free stream flow to mix with the boundary layer, thus increasing its kinetic energy and helping it flow through the shock wave with much less separation.

Vortex generators are usually located on the upper wing surface, particularly ahead of control surfaces, but may be used anywhere where separation is causing high drag or reduced control effectiveness.

It should be noted that vortex generators may also be used on subsonic aircraft to prevent separation caused by high adverse pressure gradients due to the contours of the surface.

title: Select the correct statement in regard to a steady subsonic airflow.
optionA: Velocity increases as streamlines converge.
optionB: Static pressure increases as streamlines converge.
optionC: Static pressure does not change as streamlines converge.
optionD: Velocity does not change as streamlines converge.
