explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
As an airfoil (wing) moves through the air, varying changes in velocity occur on its surfaces. Air particles move around it in specific trajectories. These trajectories are called streamlines.
The continuity equation is valid for steady-state flow, both in subsonic and supersonic flow.

For subsonic flow, the air is incompressible (its density remains constant) thus, for subsonic flow:

A1* V1 = A2* V2 = A3* V3 = constant.

From figure 1, we can then conclude that sections with smaller area have an increase in speed. These areas are also where streamlines appear closer together. This can be used to make an analogy with an airfoil where streamlines are enclosed into a streamtube (figure 2).

Therefore, we can conclude that:

- Diverging streamlines mean a decrease in airspeed.
- Converging streamlines imply an increase in airspeed.

title: Whilst maintaining straight and level flight with a lift coefficient C<sub>L</sub> = 1, what will be the new approximate value of C<sub>L</sub> after the speed is increased by 41%?
explanationTotal:
Lift can be calculated as follows:
L= CL × ½ rho × V2 × S

Where:

  • CL is lift coefficient (without dimension)
  • p is density
  • V is velocity [m/s] (velocity is TAS)
  • S is surface area [m2]
  • L is lift [N]
⇒ If the velocity increases by 41%, lift increases by 1.412 = 1.9881 (98.8%), which is almost double. To maintain lift constant (straight and level flight), lift coefficient (CL) must be 0.50 of the old CL (x 0.50): 1 ÷ 1.9881

title: Large jet aeroplanes are often made with supercritical aerofoils, rather than conventional aerofoils. Which of the following is one of the benefits of this, with regards to flying at speeds greater than MCRIT?
optionA: The aeroplane may fly at a greater Mach number and, initially, only experience a slight increase in drag.
optionB: Flying faster than M<sub>CRIT</sub> will NOT cause any shock waves around the profile until the aeroplane reaches Mach 1.0.
optionC: The aeroplane will have stronger, opposing shock waves that will cancel each other out and reduce drag.
optionD: Flying faster than MCRIT reduces the amount of wave drag as the shock waves are weaker than when flying below MCRIT.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
When air travels over an aerofoil in normal operation, the air above the aerofoil, near the leading edge, increases in velocity, due to the "squashing" of the streamlines together, causing a venturi effect, creating the low pressure zone that is required. This means that air is usually going faster over the top of the wing than anywhere else on the airframe.

As the aircraft approaches the speed of sound, Mach 1, the air above the wing will get there first, as it is faster than the freestream airflow (TAS). In particular, it is usually the air just above the wing root, where the wing is thickest, and the streamlines get "squashed" the most, that is the first bit of air to reach the sound barrier. The TAS at which the first particle of air becomes sonic (exactly Mach 1) is called MCRIT, and is the beginning of the transonic speed regime. Above this speed, shockwaves will begin to form on various parts of the airframe.

Above MCRIT, the air flowing over the top of the wing becomes supersonic, and at the point at which the air wants to decelerate back below Mach 1.0, a shockwave is formed. This shockwaves is a very thin surface where the characteristics of the air change dramatically, and can cause some airflow separation, leading to an effect called the shock stall.

There are many ways to delay MCRIT and the shock stall, one of which is to fly with a supercritical wing. A supercritical aerofoil has a much flatter top surface, which not only increases MCRIT​​​​​​​ and MDD (drag divergence)* but also creates a weaker shockwave when one is formed, just above MCRIT​​​​​​​. The shockwaves on a supercritical aerofoil quickly move to the trailing edge, making the shock stall a much smaller effect. For civilian applications, the main benefit is the faster speed that can be flown, before drag increases due to wave drag.

The higher MCRIT​​​​​​​/MDD and ability to fly just above MCRIT​​​​​​​ with little extra drag is very useful for long range jet aeroplanes, for extra range, speed and ability to fly at higher altitudes.

*MDD (drag divergence Mach number) is a speed which comes just above MCRIT​​​​​​​, where the drag begins to increase rapidly with increase in speed. This is what we really want to make higher, and using a supercritical aerofoil does exactly that.

title: What is the relation of V<sub>MO</sub> and V<sub>C</sub>?
optionA: V<sub>MO</sub> > V<sub>C</sub>
optionB: V<sub>MO</sub> ≤ V<sub>C</sub>
optionC: V<sub>MO</sub> = V<sub>C</sub>
optionD: V<sub>MO</sub> < V<sub>C</sub>
explanationTotal:
VC is the "Design Maximum Cruising Speed" which is a speed used during testing and certification to assess the structural strength of the aeroplane.

VMO is the “Maximum Operating Speed” and it is a speed that may not be deliberately exceeded in any regime of flight (climb, cruise or descent).

VMO vs VC

VMO is the speed that may not be deliberately exceeded in any regime of flight (climb, cruise or descent) and VMO must be less than VC.

  • VC is the design speed which then has a safety factor applied to give VMO.

title: Consider a twin propeller aeroplane with wing-mounted engines that has suffered an engine failure. Which of the following situations and engine configurations would result in the least asymmetric yaw and roll being developed?
optionA: The failure of the right engine on a twin with counter-rotating propellers that rotate inwards.
optionB: The failure of the right engine on a twin with counter-rotating propellers that rotate outwards.
optionC: The failure of the left engine on a twin with two right-hand propellers.
optionD: The failure of the left engine on a twin with counter-rotating propellers that rotate outwards.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
ENGINE FAILURE

If one engine on a conventional twin-engine aircraft fails in flight, it adversely affects its performance and controllability.

If one engine fails in flight, the remaining thrust forces are asymmetrically displaced and the aircraft yaws in the direction of the failed engine.

YAWING MOMENT

The yawing moment is the product of thrust from the operating engine multiplied by the distance between the thrust line and the CG (thrust arm), plus the drag from the failed engine multiplied by the distance between the engine centre line and the CG.

The strength of the yawing moment will depend on:
- how much thrust the operating engine is developing (throttle setting and density altitude).
- the distance between the thrust line and the CG (thrust arm).
- how much drag is being produced by the failed engine.

ASYMMETRIC BLADE EFFECT

If both engines rotate clockwise, the right engine has a longer thrust arm. Failure of the left engine will give a larger yawing moment.

This effect will be absent on an aircraft with counter-rotating propellers, contra-rotating propellers or jet engines.

COUNTER-ROTATING PROPELLERS

Some aircraft are made so the engines rotate the opposite of each other - called counter-rotating. The most effective method is have them both rotate inwards (right engine anticlockwise, left engine clockwise), as the down-going blades are close to the centre of the aircraft (smaller thrust arm), and there is less asymmetry after any engine failure.

title: Which moments or motions interact in a Dutch roll?
optionA: Pitching and rolling.
optionB: Rolling and yawing.
optionC: Pitching and adverse yaw.
optionD: Pitching and yawing.
explanationTotal:
DUTCH ROLL

Basically speaking, Dutch roll is a series of out-of-phase turns, when the aircraft rolls in one direction and yaws in the other. When the yaw is introduced, the strong “dihedral effect” will roll the aircraft due to the lift increase on the wing into wind. The increased induced drag on the rising wing will yaw the aircraft in the opposite direction, reversing the coupled oscillations.

  • This occurs when a strong lateral stability is coupled with weak directional stability.

title: Whilst climbing in a jet aircraft, all the pitot tubes become frozen over. The IAS is gradually increasing and eventually reaches the maximum operating airspeed. Which of the following is correct?
optionA: If the pilots do not recognise the unreliable airspeed condition, reducing thrust to control the IAS may cause the aircraft to stall.
optionB: The air data computers should notice this fault and apply a suitable correction to get the correct IAS indication.
optionC: The auto-throttle system will prevent you from exceeding limitations.
optionD: If the autopilot is engaged, it will detect the malfunction and fly the actual airspeed, no matter the pitot blockages.
explanationTotal:
This is quite close to being an instrumentation question, but has been seen in PoF exams recently.

If the pitot tubes get blocked in the climb, but the static ports remain free, then the indicated airspeed will initially stop changing with airspeed, and will now gradually increase with altitude as the static pressure reduces (acts like an altimeter). They tell us this in the question, perhaps because we are not expected to know that in the PoF exam.

In the climb, this may not be noticeable for a while, and might not be noticed at all if the autopilot was in certain modes, such as those which maintain a constant rate of climb (assuming constant thrust). Whatever happens, as the aircraft continues to climb, the actual airspeed is unknown whilst the indicated airspeed (IAS) is showing a continuous increase. If the aircraft does not stall beforehand, then when maximum airspeed is reached, the pilots or autopilot/autothrottle will either reduce thrust or pitch up to avoid further airspeed increase, which will very quickly lead to a stall.

As for the other options, the air data computer, autopilot and autothrottle systems have the same pitot inputs as the pilots do, so will not be able to protect the aircraft from this condition, that is one of the reasons that probe icing and blockages are so dangerous.

title:
A light aeroplane has flown in icing conditions and accumulated ice on the horizontal stabiliser.
If the pilot does nothing to account for the ice, then during the landing flare, the aircraft might suffer a tail stall and:
optionA: A nose-down pitch that may cause an undershoot of the runway.
optionB: A nose-down pitch causing the nose wheel to contact the runway first.
optionC: A nose-up pitch leading to a premature wing stall and a hard landing on the main wheels.
optionD: A gentle nose-down pitch that is easily controllable with the elevator.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Accumulation of ice on the tailplane will result in disruption of the normal airflow around that surface and will reduce the critical (or stalling) negative AOA of the horizontal stabiliser.

  • The landing flare is initiated by the tailplane producing a nose up pitching moment. If the tailplane stall, there will be a large decrease in nose up pitching moments, causing the nose to drop => As a result, the nose wheel may touch the ground first leading to structural damage.

title: For a given RPM of a fixed pitch propeller, the blade angle of attack will:
optionA: decrease when the TAS increases.
optionB: increase when the TAS increases.
optionC: remain constant when the TAS increases.
optionD: remain constant when the TAS decreases.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
The blade angle of a fixed-pitch propeller is constant, but the helix angle and the angle of attack will vary according to its forward speed. To ensure its efficient operation the blade angle of attack of a fixed-pitch propeller must be close to the optimum and is that which produces the greatest excess of horizontal lift (thrust) over drag.
Figure 1 shows a “fixed pitch” propeller at constant RPM. Increasing TAS (during take-off, for example) decreases the angle of attack of the propeller. Figure 2 shows a “fixed pitch” propeller at a constant TAS. Increasing RPM increases the angle of attack of the propeller.

title: During the initial climb out, the pilot is required to do a 15° turn to the left to avoid an obstacle. The total drag will:
optionA: Decrease and the climb gradient will increase.
optionB: Increase and the climb gradient will increase.
optionC: Increase and the climb gradient will decrease.
optionD: Decrease and the climb gradient will decrease.
explanationTotal:
Any manoeuvre such as a turn calls for more lift. Due to the bank angle of the aircraft, the lift vector is tilted, therefore only a component of lift counteracts weight. But since level flight must be maintained, the component of lift has to be equal to weight. Consequently, lift must be increased. By increasing the bank angle, load factor increases. Due to increased lift, induced drag also increases producing greater drag, this in turn increases total drag.

For a given aircraft mass the maximum climb gradient will occur when the excess thrust over drag is greatest. As seen above, the drag increases in a turn, provided that thrust remains the same, the climb gradient will decrease.

title:
Given a constant load factor, which of these statements about the variation of induced drag with changes of speed and mass are correct or incorrect?

1. When speed decreases, induced drag decreases.
2. When mass decreases, induced drag increases.
optionA: 1 is correct, 2 is incorrect.
optionB: 1 is incorrect, 2 is correct.
optionC: 1 is correct, 2 is correct.
optionD: 1 is incorrect, 2 is incorrect.
explanationTotal:
Induced drag is created as a byproduct of lift. The pressure differential between the top and bottom of the wing creates a upwash around the tip of the wing that turns into a downwash behind the wing. This is known as a vortex, which creates a rearward force known as induced drag.

This question is asking for the effect of:

  • Speed: The induced drag is inversely proportional to the speed. Therefore, induced drag increases as the speed decreases, and, induced drag decreases and the speed increases.
This is because, to maintain lift constant, as the velocity decreases, the coefficient of lift will have to be increased. At higher coefficients of lift, the pressure differential between the top and bottom of the wing will be greater and therefore produce stronger vortices = stronger induced drag. (and vice versa)
  • Changing mass: Induced drag is proportional to the mass. Therefore, induced drag increases with increasing aeroplane mass, and, induced drag decreases with decreasing aeroplane mass.

This is because, as the aircraft get heavier, the lift that the wings will have to produce increases. To achieve that, the coefficient of lift will have to increase, meaning a higher AoA, which creates stronger vortices. (and vice versa)

Summary:

  • Higher AR = Lower induced drag
  • Higher AoA = higher induced drag
  • Higher weight = higher AoA = higher induced drag
  • Higher speed = lower AoA = lower induced drag
  • Winglets = lower induced drag.

title: During the take-off roll, when the pilot raises the tail in a tail wheeled propeller driven aeroplane, the additional aeroplane yawing tendency is due to the effect of:
optionA: torque reaction.
optionB: slipstream.
optionC: asymmetric blade effect.
optionD: gyroscopic precession.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

GYROSCOPIC EFFECT
A rotating propeller has the properties of a gyroscope - rigidity in space and precession. The characteristic which produces “gyroscopic effect” is precession.

Gyroscopic precession is the reaction that occurs when a force is applied to the rim of a rotating disc. When a force is applied to the rim of a propeller, the reaction occurs 90° ahead in the direction of rotation and in the same direction as the applied force.

As the aircraft is pitched up or down or yawed left or right, a force is applied to the rim of the spinning propeller disc.

Note: Gyroscopic effect only occurs when the aircraft pitches and/or yaws.

For a clockwise rotating propeller:

  • Pitch down - forward force on the top, force emerges 90° clockwise, left yaw.
  • Left yaw - forward force on the right, force emerges 90° clockwise, pitch up.
  • Pitch up - forward force on the bottom, force emerges 90° clockwise, right yaw.
  • Right yaw - forward force on the left, force emerges 90° clockwise, pitch down.

title: Which statement about CG limits is correct?
optionA: The forward CG limit is mainly determined by the amount of pitch control available from the elevator.
optionB: If the aft CG limit is correctly chosen, the forward CG limit is automatically determined as well.
optionC: The forward CG limit is determined by stability considerations only.
optionD: The aft CG limit is determined by the maximum elevator deflection available.
explanationTotal:
The range within which the CG must always be located for safe operations is the CG envelope that, for transport aeroplanes, is defined as the area between the safe forward limit approximately 10% MAC and the safe aft limit approximately 30% MAC.

  • The forward limit: The forward limit of the envelope is determined by the amount of pitch control available from the elevators; that is the degree of manoeuvrability that an aeroplane of that type commands. With the CG in this position, the aeroplane has the greatest longitudinal stability. In the landing configuration, maximum elevator-up deflection is required when the CG is at the forward limit and full flap is selected.

  • The aft limit: The aft limit, which for safety reasons on a transport aeroplane is always forward of the neutral point, is confined by insufficient stick-force stability and/or excessive in-flight manoeuvrability. A CG position aft of this point would produce an unacceptably low value of manoeuvre stability and would make the aeroplane difficult to fly.

title:
An historical single-engine aeroplane which has a left-hand rotating propeller (ANTI-CLOCKWISE from the pilot's perspective) is on final approach, when the pilot decides to perform a go-around, applying full THRUST and a large PITCH-UP. Which of the following would occur:

1. Spiralling slipstream generates a yaw to the left.
2. Torque reaction makes the aircraft roll to the right.
3. Gyroscopic precession generates a yaw to the right
4. Asymmetric blade makes the aircraft yaw to the right.
optionB: 2 and 4.
optionC: 1 and 2.
optionD: 3 and 4.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
Note: This question was generated based on feedback which was posted on question 813311.

Propellers generate 4 main secondary effects on an aircraft:

  • Torque effect
  • Gyroscopic precession
  • Slipstream
  • Asymmetric blade effect
For this question, we can go through each statement and check whether the effect is correct or not for the scenario.

1. SLIPSTREAM
The spinning of the propeller affects the air that it pushes backwards, and imparts a spiral onto that air, in this case spiralling anti-clockwise around the aircraft, hitting the tail fin on the right hand side, causing a tail-left, nose-right moment. The slipstream increases with an increase in thrust, causing a yaw to the right. Statement 1 is incorrect.

2. TORQUE EFFECT
The anti-clockwise rotating propeller gains more anti-clockwise rotational momentum when the pilot adds thrust (higher RPM), so the aircraft experiences the opposite (clockwise) rotation, and is rolled to the right (this can be corrected using left aileron). Statement 1 is correct.

3. GYROSCOPIC PRECESSION
The propeller is a mass, spinning at high speed, and therefore acts as a gyroscope. That means that any rotation of the aircraft in pitch or yaw will gain a different force from the propeller due to gyroscopic precession. The force from the propeller will be rotated by 90º in the direction of rotation. In this case, the pitch-up will cause an forward force on the bottom of the propeller disc, which is rotated by precession to a forwards force on the right of the propeller disc. This creates a yaw to the left. Statement 2 is therefore incorrect.

4. ASYMMETRIC BLADE EFFECT
The asymmetric blade effect comes from the aircraft being at an angle of attack to the air, so the air does not flow perpendicular to the propeller disc. The down-going propeller blades always produce more thrust than the up-going blades, so the thrust line of this anti-clockwise propeller is to the left of centre. An increase in thrust will therefore cause a larger force through this location (left of centre), which yaws the aircraft to the right. Statement 4 is correct.

title:
Given the following information, what is the all-engine climb gradient for a two-engine aeroplane?

Thrust per engine: 118000 N
Mass: 67000 kg
Lift-to-drag ratio: 9:1
Assume g = 10 m/s2
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Consider an aircraft in a straight steady climb along a straight flight path inclined at an angle (γ) to the horizontal. γ (gamma) is the symbol used for climb angle. The forces on the aircraft consist of Lift, normal to the flight path; Thrust and Drag, parallel to it; and Weight, parallel to the force of gravity.
Weight is resolved into two components: one opposite Lift (W cos γ) and the other acting in the same direction as Drag (W sin γ), backwards along the flight path. The requirements for equilibrium are: Thrust must equal the sum of Drag plus the backwards component of Weight; and Lift must equal its opposing component of Weight. For equilibrium at a greater angle of climb, the Lift required will be less, and the backwards component of Weight will be greater.

L = W cosγ
T = D + W sinγ

In a straight steady climb, Lift is less than Weight because Lift only has to support a proportion of the weight, this proportion decreasing as the climb angle increases. The remaining proportion of Weight is supported by engine Thrust.
It can be seen that for a straight steady climb the Thrust required is greater than Drag. This is to balance the backward component of Weight acting along the flight path.

The climb gradient can be described as:

sin γ = (T−D)/W

For very shallow flight path angles (γ), we can assume that lift is approximately equal to Weight, therefore the climb gradient can be described as:

sin γ = T/W−D/L

In this exercise, Weight is equal to 670000 N, D/L ratio is equal to 1/9 and Thrust equal to 118000 N per engine.

For the all engines (two) climb gradient and applying the formula defined above:

sin γ = 236000/670000−1/9
sinγ = 0.241 ⇒ sinγ = 24.1%

The climb gradient is 24.1%.

title: An aircraft with a forward CG has the stabiliser trim set incorrectly for take-off with insufficient nose-up trim. At the correctly determined rotate speed, the normal rotation technique is followed. However, in this situation it is likely that...
optionA: higher-than-usual stick forces will be felt by the pilot and the rate of rotation may be reduced.
optionB: lighter-than-usual stick forces will be felt by the pilot and there maybe an increased possibility of a tail-strike.
optionC: a shorter taketoff distance will be required.
optionD: the aircraft will have an excessive rate of pitch change when rotated.
explanationTotal:
The position of the CG directly affects the amount of trim necessary for the angle of attack required. A forward CG adds to the inherent longitudinal stability of the airplane; the pilot may run out of elevator up movement and be unable to maintain the required attitude. An aft CG decreases the longitudinal stability and makes the airplane more difficult or impossible to control in pitch.

The CG must always remain within the CG safe envelope to ensure that the airplane remains controllable in all phases of flight. The elevator trim or stabilizer trim setting must be preset to a value for take-off and initial climb that will ensure a minimum stick force during this critical stage of flight.
Usually, there is a graph in the airplane performance manual from which the setting appropriate to the total mass and CG position for take-off can be determined.

Factors that affect the stabilizer trim position for take-off are:

  • CG position
  • Take-off mass
  • Flap setting
In comparison with a correctly balanced airplane during take-off, the position of the stabilizer for a nose-heavy airplane requires nose-up trim from a decreased stabilizer angle of incidence.

title:
A pilot is flying an aeroplane whose clean configuration stall speed is 60 kt. While cruising at 95 kt the pilot has to take avoiding action against another aeroplane.
The pilot banks the aeroplane sharply and during this manoeuvre, the aeroplane stalls.
Why did the aeroplane stall at 95 kt?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: A large movement of the ailerons causes both wings to stall at the tips.
optionB: In a turn, the aeroplane weight increases, which increases the stall speed.
optionC: A wing stalls when its critical angle of attack is exceeded, regardless of speed.
optionD: The change in airflow due to rapid rolling causes the up-moving wing to stall.
explanationTotal:
The low-speed stall occurs because boundary layer becomes detached from the upper surface of the wing.
The low-speed stall occurs at a particular angle of attack of the wing to the relative airflow, not at a specific airspeed.

title: An aeroplane flying at 200 kt in straight and level flight is subjected to a disturbance that suddenly decreases the speed by 100 kt. Assuming the angle of attack remains constant, the load factor will initially:
optionA: decrease to 0.50.
optionB: decrease to 0.75.
optionC: decrease to 0.25.
optionD: remain unchanged, since the angle of attack does not change.
explanationTotal:
Let’s start by identifying the equations used to answer the question.

Load factor is defined as:

n = L/W

Now we replace the lift with the full equation:

L = CL ½ rho V2 S

n = (CL ½ rho V2 S) / W

By removing all the constants, we can say that:

n = (CL ½ rho V2 S) / W

n ∝ V2

To find the change in load factor (nΔ), we have to divide nNEW by nOLD:

nΔ = nNEW / nOLD

nΔ = VNEW2 / VOLD2

For those who prefer remembering equations, remember the above

nΔ = 1002 / 2002

nΔ = 0.25

This means that the initial change in load factor due to the decrease in airspeed of 100 kt is 0.25

title: An aircraft has been parked outside overnight, in freezing conditions. The crew decides to depart WITHOUT having the airframe de-iced/anti-iced. What could be the principal danger during take-off?
optionA: Loss of control due to frozen deposits on the wings, which reduce C<sub>LMAX</sub>.
optionB: A higher stall speed due to wing contamination and reduced drag.
optionC: Uncommanded roll due to frozen deposits on the wings, which increase C<sub>LMAX</sub>.
optionD: A lower stall speed due to wing contamination and increased drag.
explanationTotal:
Stalling angle of attack: as ice builds up, the aerodynamic efficiency of the wing and its ability to prevent separation of the airflow and therefore stall is highly reduced. Ice will lead to sooner separation, smaller stalling angle of attack, therefore causing a lower CLMAX.

Stall speed: referring to the lift equation, and assuming all other factors stay the same, ice buildup decreases the CLMAX and increases the mass of the aircraft in flight. Firstly just by itself an increase in mass causes an increase in stall speed. Secondly, a smaller CLMAX means that a higher speed will have to be maintained in order to maintain the same lift. Therefore our stall speed will have increase due to ice accretion.

Controllability: on top of the fact that an increase in weight will mean that any input in the control surfaces will lead to a slower reaction by the aircraft, icing can also get stuck between the control surfaces and or completely nullify their effect. For example, icing on the horizontal stabilizer will occur before the main wing, and seeing as the tail is normally producing a downwards force, a stall of the tail plane will lead to a drop of the nose of the aircraft and controllability over the longitudinal axis will have been completely lost. Therefore controllability will decrease in icing conditions.

  • The ice changes the airfoil cross section and destroys lift, increases drag and raises the stalling speed.

title: The most important factor determining the required position of the Trimmable Horizontal Stabiliser (THS) for take off is the:
optionA: stall speed.
optionB: centre of gravity position of the fuel.
optionC: total mass of the aeroplane.
optionD: position of the aeroplane’s centre of gravity.
explanationTotal:
The forces on a jet transport aeroplane are very high in flight.
The wing surfaces are large and travel at high speeds, generating lots of lift.
A trim tab is an easy solution in general aviation aircraft, as the forces are much smaller and it’s a lot cheaper and lighter than a stabilizer.

However, the trim tab is not able to withstand the forces at very high speeds and is not powerful enough to generate the loads required for a change in configuration.
A stabilizer is powerful enough and is able to cope with larger CG ranges, because the forces required with a CG change will change drastically.
Therefore the stabilizer is the best suitable option for transport jet aeroplanes.

title: A light aircraft is following a medium range jet transport aircraft. What is the first action the light aircraft should perform in case he flies into the vortices produced by the wing tips of the jet aircraft?
optionA: Bank to the right
optionB: Start a descent
optionC: Bank to the left
optionD: Start a climb
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Typically the two trailing vortices remain separated by about three quarters of the aircraft’s wingspan, and in still air they tend to drift slowly downwards and level off, usually between 500 and 1000 ft below the flight path of the aircraft. Behind a large aircraft the trailing vortices can extend as much as nine nautical miles.
To avoid this vortices, the best course of action is to start a climb.

title: What can result if excessive rudder is used to tighten a low speed turn?
optionA: A slip which could lead to a stall.
optionB: A skid which could lead to spin.
optionC: Excessive pitch up which could lead to a stall.
optionD: Excessive pitch down,which could lead to a high rate dive.
explanationTotal:
SPINNING

When an aircraft is accidentally or deliberately stalled, the motion of the aircraft may in some cases develop into a spin.

A spin may be defined as an aggravated stall resulting in autorotation, which means the rotation is stable and will continue due to aerodynamic forces if nothing intervenes. During the spin, the wings remain unequally stalled.

PRIMARY CAUSES OF A SPIN

A stall must occur before a spin can take place. A spin occurs when one wing stalls more than the other. The wing that is more stalled will drop and the nose of the aircraft will yaw in the direction of the lower wing.

The cause of an accidental spin is exceeding the critical angle of attack while performing a manoeuvre with either too much or not enough rudder input for the amount of aileron being used (crossed-controls). If the correct stall recovery is not initiated promptly, the stall could develop into a spin.

Co-ordinated use of the flight controls is important, especially during flight at low airspeed and high angle of attack.

SKIDDING TURN

A skidding turn is a turn where the aircraft’s nose is inside of the turning radius and the tail is outside of the turnradius.

A skid is caused by using too much rudder and not enough bank.

title: Constant IAS in a climb, what will happen?
optionA: Maximum coefficient of lift increases with increasing Mach number
optionB: Coefficient of lift increases with increasing Mach number
optionC: Maximum coefficient of lift decrease with increasing Mach number
optionD: Coefficient of lift decrease with increasing Mach number
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
If altitude is increased at a constant IAS, Mach number will increase. At low speed CLMAX is fairly constant, but above M0.4 CLMAX decreases as shown in the figure.

title: As an aircraft accelerates through the transonic speed range, it exceeds its Critical Mach number. A normal shock wave forms on the upper surface of the wing, which induces flow separation. This causes...
optionA: up wash over the tail, causing a nose down pitching moment.
optionB: turbulent air to hit the tail, producing a severe airframe buffet.
optionC: turbulent air to hit the elevator causing only a light buffet.
optionD: downwash over the tail causing a nose up pitching moment.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Note: Recent feedback from Polish ULC indicates that the option containing "light buffet" is wrong, so we have changed the correct answer to that containing "severe buffet". We think that the "light buffet" is most correct, but this seems like the next best option for us, however we cannot be sure yet. Please let us know if you see this question in the exam, what the correct answer could have been (if you can find out) and which authority you sat the exam with, thank you!

When an aircraft accelerates through the transonic speed range and exceeds its Critical Mach number, a normal shock wave can form on the upper surface of the wing. This shock wave induces flow separation, causing turbulent airflow over the wing and along the fuselage. This turbulent airflow can create airframe buffet, which is felt throughout the aircraft. If the tailplane is aligned with the separated airflow, the turbulent airflow caused by the flow separation can also hit the tail of the aircraft, which may result in a change in the aerodynamic forces acting on the tail and buffet.

Option a) "up wash over the tail, causing a nose down pitching moment." is not correct because the flow separation on the wing does not cause upwash over the tail, but rather turbulent airflow and a slight reduction in downwash (naturally, due to the higher airspeed). There will be a nose-down pitching moment around this time, but it is due to the AC moving on the wing and the reduction in downwash, not upwash from the shockwave.

title: Trailing edge flap extension will:
optionA: decrease the critical angle of attack and increase the value of C<sub>LMAX</sub>.
optionB: decrease the critical angle of attack and decrease the value of C<sub>LMAX</sub>.
optionC: increase the critical angle of attack and increase the value of C<sub>LMAX</sub>.
optionD: increase the critical angle of attack and decrease the value of C<sub>LMAX</sub>.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Slats and flaps increase lift. This can help the aircraft take off with a shortened ground roll, as the aircraft generates more lift at a lower speed with flaps and slats extended. However, flaps and slats shorten the ground roll, but also decrease climb performance as they generate drag. Therefore, after takeoff these two devices are retracted. Flaps and slats both decrease stall speed, but flaps generate much more drag. The flaps are therefore retracted first and slats afterwards.

Flaps increase CL for a specific angle of attack, giving a wing with flaps extended a higher CL and therefore higher lift than a wing without. Flaps also increase CLMAX and the CD for a wing, they decrease critical AoA. Slats do not necessarily increase CL for a specific AoA, but they increase the value for CLMAX, meaning that the aircraft stalls at a much higher AoA than normal. They also increase the drag a little on the wing where they are extended.

title: What is correct about a Slat? A deployed slat will:
optionA: Increase the boundary layer energy, move the suction peak from the fixed part of the wing to the slat, so that the stall is postponed to higher angles of attack.
optionB: Increase the boundary layer energy and increase the suction peak on the fixed part of the wing, so that the stall is postponed to higher angles of attack.
optionC: Increase the camber of the aerofoil and increase the effective angle of attack, so that CLMAX is reached at higher angles of attack.
optionD: Decrease the boundary layer energy and decrease the suction peak on the slat, so that CLMAX is reached at lower angles of attack.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
Slats are aerodynamic surfaces on the leading edge of the wings. When deployed, the slat forms a slot which allows passage of air from the high pressure region below the wing to the low pressure region above it. Additional Kinetic Energy is added to the airflow through the slot by the slat forming a convergent duct.

When slats are deployed the boundary layer is re-energised. If Kinetic Energy is added to the boundary layer, boundary layer separation will be delayed to a much higher angle of attack.

In terms of the pressure distribution of the aerofoil with a slat extended, the slat provides a fair amount of lift itself due to its shape, and when extended, it flattens the peak of the low pressure zone somewhat, allowing the low pressure zone to be more evenly distributed over the top of the aerofoil. It increases the suction overall as it allows a much higher critical AoA and higher CLMAX, as the adverse pressure gradient occurs more gradually, delaying the stall.

Furthermore, the suction peak flattens, it does not move. This is why the CL location does not change very much when extending flaps.

Note: We are aware that the wording of the correct option here is a little off regarding the suction peak, as the peak should reduce, but the overall suction increases. We think this could be what the examiner is trying to say. We still think it is the most correct option by far out of the available options, but please send us any further feedback if you see this question in the exam, thank you!

title:
Refer to figure.
Assuming no pilot input the motion of the aeroplane in the diagram shows:
optionA: dynamic longitudinal stability.
optionB: neutral dynamic longitudinal stability.
optionC: static longitudinal instability.
optionD: dynamic longitudinal instability.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Dynamic Stability is the subsequent long-term response of an airplane to a disturbance to its equilibrium. It is the change to the stability of an airplane with the passage of time. Any disturbance causes changes to the aerodynamic forces and moments acting on the airplane that are complex, particularly if the displacement is to its directional stability because it affects the airplane in both the yawing and rolling planes.

An airplane that is statically stable is not necessarily dynamically stable. However, for an airplane to be dynamically stable it must be statically stable. In other words, it cannot have long-term stability without first having short-term stability. An airplane that has positive static stability may be dynamically neutral, stable, or unstable; but an airplane that is statically unstable can never attain dynamic stability. The dynamic stability of an airplane is dependent on the airplane design, its speed, and the altitude at which it is flying.

There are five states of dynamic stability and for each of them the airplane must have positive static stability.

Negative dynamic stability – the amplitude of the oscillation increases with the passage of time.

Neutral dynamic stability – the amplitude of the oscillation remains constant with the passage of time.

Positive dynamic stability – the amplitude of the oscillation decreases with the passage of time.

‘Dead beat’ positive dynamic stability – the oscillations cease immediately because they are heavily damped.

‘Divergent’ negative dynamic stability – the oscillations cease because the motion completely diverges from the original motion.

title: A body is placed in a certain airstream. If the density of the airstream decreases to half its original value, the parasite drag will decrease by a factor of:
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The force directly opposing the forward movement of the aeroplane through the air is referred to as drag. It is the resistance to forward motion and is assumed to act along a line parallel to the longitudinal axis.

Total Drag is sub-divided into two main types:

INDUCED DRAG - the result of lift generation.
PARASITE DRAG - independent of lift generation.

The parasite drag can be calculated from the formula:

Parasite Drag (DP) = CDP x 1/2 x ρ x V2 x S

Where,
CDP = Parasite Drag Coefficient
ρ = Air Density
V = True Airspeed (TAS)
S = Parasite Area

From the formula we can see that the Parasite Drag (DP) is directly proportional to the Air Density (ρ), therefore, if Air Density is halfed, the Parasite Drag will be halfed as well (reduced by a factor of 2).

title: When the lift coefficient of a positively cambered aerofoil section is zero, the pitching moment is...
optionA: negative.
optionB: positive.
optionC: maximum.
optionD: zero.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
Positively cambered aerofoils are profiles where the line connecting the center of the inscribed circles is curved downwards. This means that the line connecting the center of the circles will be above the chord line. (shown in the figure)
Positively cambered aerofoils, will because of the shape, produce a negative pitching moment, even at an angle of attack of zero. The angle at which the pitching moment created by a positively cambered aerofoil is zero will be at a negative angle of attack.

A negatively cambered aerofoil is one where the line connecting the center of the inscribed circles is curved upwards. This means that the line will be below the chord line of the profile.
Just like positively cambered aerofoils, negatively cambered aerofoils will produce a positive pitching moment at an angle of attack of zero. The angle for zero pitching moment of a negatively cambered aerofoil is at a positive angle of attack.

title: The speeds V<sub>NE</sub> and V<sub>MO</sub> refer to, respectively:
optionA: They can both refer to piston and jet aircraft.
optionB: V<sub>NE</sub> refers to pistons and V<sub>MO </sub>refers to jets.
optionC: V<sub>NE</sub> refers to jets and V<sub>MO</sub> refers to pistons.
optionD: They both apply to piston jet aircraft only.
explanationTotal:
VNE (IAS velocity) is the never-exceed velocity. It is associated with propeller-driven aircraft and is marked by a red line on the ASI.

VMO/MMO (lAS velocity/Mach) is the maximum operating speed permitted for all operations. It is normally associated with jet aircraft.

title: In a large jet aeroplane with swept back wings, when applying more rudder to the inside of the turn, skidding the aeroplane, one of the hazards to consider is (1) _____ in angle of attack on the (2) _____ wing due to (3) _____ roll.
optionA: (1) a decrease; (2) outer; (3) adverse
optionB: (1) an increase; (2) inner; (3) adverse
optionC: (1) an increase; (2) inner; (3) increased
optionD: (1) a decrease; (2) outer; (3) increased
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
A skid turn is characterized by an uncoordinated aircraft movement where the body slides sideways, diverging from the center of the turn. Skids result from centrifugal force surpassing the horizontal lift component. In a skid turn, the turn coordinator's ball shifts to the outer side of the turn, and the plane's nose points inward toward the turn.

The diagram depicts an uncoordinated skidding turn to the left, where the aircraft slips toward the outer side of the turn. This occurs due to excessive rudder input or insufficient aileron (bank) usage. To achieve coordination, applying right rudder pressure is necessary.

As you can see in the diagram, the down aileron (inner wing) has a higher angle of attack.

title: During a descent at a constant Mach number, which of these limiting speeds is the first to be reached without any pilot intervention?
optionA: Max operating airspeed (VMO).
optionB: Max operating Mach number (MMO).
optionC: Never exceed speed (VNE).
optionD: Shock stall speed (VSX).
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Learning Objective 032.04.05.01.05: Describe the following limiting speeds for descent: maximum operating speed (VMO); maximum Mach number (MMO).

Aircraft certified under CS-25 (and some aircraft under CS-23) are given maximum flight speeds as a VMO and MMO (maximum operating airspeed/Mach No.). Depending on the altitude and air temperature, one of these will correspond to a lower airspeed than the other. That one will be the most limiting.

The MMO is most limiting at high altitudes, which is when it is most useful for us to refer to our speed in Mach No., whereas at lower altitudes, the VMO is most limiting, and we should use IAS/CAS instead. The point where this crossover happens is called the crossover altitude. A common altitude for this is around 28000 ft, but it depends on the aircraft and conditions.

If descending at a constant mach number, the Mach number will not exceed the MMO (as it is constant), but using the ECTM graph above, we can see that the IAS will be increasing, and therefore the IAS may well reach and exceed VMO if the crossover is delayed to a lower altitude.

The other two options "shock stall speed" and "never exceed speed" can be discounted here, as aircraft with VMO/MMO do not have a VNE and the shock stall speed occurs based on the Mach No. and MMO, both of which we know remain constant (and it is not a limiting speed as such).

title: Choose the correct statement about the stall of a straight wing aeroplane:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: The nose down effect is the result of increasing downwash, due to flow separation.
optionB: Just before the stall the aeroplane will have a nose-down tendency.
optionC: The horizontal tail will stall at a higher speed than the wing.
optionD: Buffeting is the result of flow separation on the tail plane.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
For a straight wing, just before the stall the CP will move aft away from CG. Thus creating a nose pitch down moment.
For a swept wing, just before the stall, the CP will move forward in front of the CG. Generating a nose pitch up moment

title:
An aircraft is flying with NO POWER after losing all engines at a height of 10 000 ft. Considering the data below, what will the maximum glide range be?

L/D: 15
Average TAS: 200 kt
Wind component: 20 kt headwind
(Use 1NM = 6 080ft)
explanationTotal:
With a L/D ratio of 15, the aircraft will glide a distance of 15 miles for each mile of altitude lost in still air.

(1) Determine the aircraft’s height in NM: 1 NM = 6 080 ft
The aircraft is flying at an altitude of 10 000 / 6 080 = 1.645 NM

(2) Calculate the gliding range in still air (NAM):
Gliding range in still air (NAM) = 15 x 1.645 = 24.675 NAM

(3) Determine the gliding range taking the wind into consideration (NGM):
Knowing the TAS (200 kt) and the wind (20 kt head) we can obtain the GS => 180 kt. Now, simply apply the formula below:

NGM (Nautical Ground Miles) = NAM × GS ÷ TAS
NGM (Nautical Ground Miles) = 24.675 x 180 ÷ 200
NGM (Nautical Ground Miles) = 22.21 NM

title: A pilot maintains a constant bank angle while turning towards a given heading. If TAS increases the aeroplane’s rate of turn will (1) _____ and the turn radius will (2) _____.
optionA: (1) increase; (2) increase.
optionB: (1) decrease; (2) increase.
optionC: (1) decrease; (2) decrease.
optionD: (1) increase; (2) decrease.
explanationTotal:
Radius of turn is dependent on both airspeed and bank angle.

  • Turn Radius = V2 / g tan Ø
    Where V = True Airspeed, g = acceleration of gravity constant of 9.81 m/s2, Ø = angle of bank

The radius of turn at any given bank angle is directly proportional to the square of the airspeed. Which means that doubling the airspeed results in a radius of turn that is four times greater.

Rate of turn is the rate of change of heading or angular velocity of the turn.

  • Rate of turn = g tan Ø / V
Increasing the speed results in a decrease of rate of turn. Whereas increasing bank angle also increases the rate of turn.

title: Which of the following options best defines the oscillatory nature of a spiral dive and the direction of both yaw and roll?
optionA: The spiral dive is oscillatory, and yaw and roll act in the same direction.
optionB: The spiral dive is oscillatory, and yaw and roll act in opposite directions.
optionC: The spiral dive is non-oscillatory, and yaw and roll act in the same direction.
optionD: The spiral dive is non-oscillatory, and yaw and roll act in opposite directions.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Spiral divergence will exist when static directional stability is very large when compared to the dihedral effect. The character of spiral divergence is not violent. The aeroplane, when disturbed from the equilibrium of level flight, begins a slow spiral which gradually increases to a spiral dive.

When a small sideslip is introduced, the strong directional stability tends to restore the nose into the wind while the relatively weak dihedral effect lags in restoring the aeroplane laterally. The rate of divergence in the spiral motion is usually so gradual that the pilot can control the tendency without difficulty.

It is therefore considered non-oscillatory and both yaw and roll moments will occur to the same side.

title: The airframe structure must remain substantially intact after experiencing:
optionA: The design ultimate load times a 1.5 safety factor.
optionB: The design limit load plus the design ultimate load.
optionC: Three times the safety factor.
optionD: The design limit load times 150%.
explanationTotal:
081.06.02.01.02: Define limit and ultimate load factor, and explain what can happen if these values are exceeded.

Limit and Ultimate Load Factor

Limit load (factor) is the maximum load (factor) to be expected in service.
Ultimate load (factor) is the failing load of the structure.
  • Safety factor = Ultimate load/Limit load = 1.5 for aviation
Certain manoeuvres have the potential risk to cause deformation or structural failure if the ultimate load is exceeded. The safety factor on the airframe is 1.5. Failure of the structure will not occur at the load factor of 2.5, but at 2.5 × 1.5 = 3.75 g.

title: An aircraft is climbing at a constant IAS, just before the high speed buffet. What should the pilot expect during the climb?
optionA: C<sub>L</sub> increases and then decreases.
optionB: C<sub>L</sub> remains the same.
optionC: C<sub>L</sub> decrease.
optionD: C<sub>L</sub> increase.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
This graph demonstrates how Mach Number, TAS, EAS varies with altitude with constant IAS.

L = 1/2 rho V2 S CL

Where “1/2 rho V2” stands for dynamic pressure.

The climb is carried out in two phases: the first at a constant IAS and the second at a constant M, after the crossover altitude.

What happens to the dynamic pressure in each phase will tell us what needs to happen to CL to maintain lift.

Use ERTM to to find the relationship between the speeds.

  • In the constant IAS phase of the climb, density (rho) is decreasing and V is increasing which maintains dynamic pressure at a constant. Therefore, there is no change in CL.
  • In the constant Mach phase of the climb, density (rho) continues to decrease but now TAS is decreasing and therefore dynamic pressure decreases. To maintain lift we must increase alpha which means CL increases.

title:
Which statement is correct regarding the gyroscopic effect of a anti-clockwise rotating propeller on a single engine aeroplane?

I. Pitch down produces right yaw.
II. Left yaw produces pitch up.
optionA: I is correct, II is incorrect.
optionB: I is correct, II is correct.
optionC: I is incorrect, II is correct.
optionD: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
On take-off, rotation of a single-engine propeller causes an aircraft to swing to one side, particularly those fitted with a tail-dragger undercarriage. The main causes of this are:

  • Slipstream effect
  • Torque reaction
  • Gyroscopic effect
  • Asymmetric blade effect

Gyroscopic Effect

A rotating propeller has the properties of a gyroscope - rigidity in space and precession. The characteristic which produces “gyroscopic effect” is precession.

Gyroscopic precession is the reaction that occurs when a force is applied to the rim of a rotating disc. When a force is applied to the rim of a propeller, the reaction occurs 90° ahead in the direction of rotation and in the same direction as the applied force. As the aircraft is pitched up or down or yawed left or right, a force is applied to the rim of the spinning propeller disc.

Note: Gyroscopic effect only occurs when the aircraft pitches and/or yaws.

For a anti-clockwise rotating propeller:

Pitch up - forward force on the bottom, force emerges 90° clockwise, left yaw.
Right yaw - forward force on the left, force emerges 90° clockwise, pitch up.
Pitch down - forward force on the top, force emerges 90° clockwise, right yaw. Therefore, statement 1 is correct.
Left yaw - forward force on the right, force emerges 90° clockwise, pitch down. Therefore, statement 2 is incorrect.

title: During a climb at a constant IAS, the Mach number will:
optionA: increase initially and remain constant subsequently.
optionB: remain constant.
optionC: increase.
optionD: decrease initially and increase subsequently.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

The Mach number is defined as the ratio between the TAS and the LSS (Local speed of sound).
It is an indication of how fast an aircraft is travelling with relation to the sound waves that surround it.

The Mach number may be calculated as follows:
M=TAS/LSS=(TAS(kt))/(38.95∗√(T(K)))

The speed of propagation of small pressure waves depends upon the temperature of the air ONLY.

Effect on Mach Number of Climbing at a Constant IAS:

- Temperature decreases with increasing altitude, so the speed of sound will decrease as altitude is increased.
- If altitude is increased at a constant IAS, the TAS increases.
- Therefore, the Mach number will increase if altitude is increased at a constant IAS. This is because TAS gets bigger and LSS gets smaller.

title: Compaired to a wing with less camber, a wing with greater camber will:
optionA: MCRIT is not affected
optionB: Increase MCRIT
optionC: Camber percentage have no effect on MCRIT values
optionD: Decrease M<sub>CRIT</sub>
explanationTotal:
Wings not designed for high speeds may have a severe loss of lift at speeds above MCRIT, but wings designed specifically for high speed flight, with sweepback, thinner sections and less camber will have much less variation of lift through the transonic region.
A conventional trailing edge control surface works by changing the camber of the airfoil to increase or decrease its lift. Increasing camber by deflecting a control surface down will reduce MCRIT.

title: 470 ft/min corresponds to _____ m/s:
explanationTotal:
1 m = 3,27 ft
470 ft/min ÷ 3.27 = 144 m/min
144 m/min ÷ 60 sec. = 2.4 m/s

title:
Refer to figure.
From the following, select the graph or graphs that represent an aerofoil with negative camber.
optionA: 3 only
optionB: 1 and 3
optionC: 2 only
optionD: 1 only
explanationTotal:
Refer to the figure.
CAMBER LINE

A line joining the leading and trailing edges of an aerofoil, equidistant from the upper and lower surfaces.

When the camber line lies above the chord line the aerofoil is said to have positive camber, and if the camber line is below the chord line, it is said to have negative camber.

A symmetrical aerofoil has no camber because the chord line and camber line are coincidental.

A negatively cambered aerofoil will produce drag and negative lift at an angle of attack of zero. As the angle of attack increases, the negative lift will decrease until there is no lift produced by the wing at all. This point is somewhere within the positive angle of attack region.

title: If the nose of an aeroplane yaws left, this causes:
optionA: a roll to the right.
optionB: a decrease in relative airspeed on the right wing.
optionC: a roll to the left.
optionD: an increase in lift on the left wing.
explanationTotal:
Roll and yaw motions cannot really be separated from each other, since one triggers the other. Rudder deflection primarily triggers yaw motion and roll is a secondary effect.

Yaw causes a slight increase in airspeed over the outer wing of the turn and a decrease in airspeed over the inner wing. As a result, the outer wing will generate more lift than the other, introducing a rolling motion.

  • In this case, if an aircraft yaws left, the right wing will travel faster, generating more lift. This will cause a roll to the left.

title: The use of ailerons induces adverse (aileron) yaw. This occurs as a result of the...
optionA: up-going wing producing more drag than the down-going wing.
optionB: up-going wing having a higher rate of roll when compared to the down-going wing.
optionC: down-going wing producing more drag than the up-going wing.
optionD: up-going wing being subjected to more aerodynamic damping than the down-going wing.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

During a bank, the upgoing wing effectively experiences a decreased angle of attack whilst the effective angle of attack of the down going wing increases. Consequently, the slope of the total lift vector generates a rearward component on the upgoing wing and a forward component on the down going wing. These are yaw moments but in the opposite direction to that of the roll caused by the difference of the induced drag of each wing. This is adverse yaw, which is particularly significant at low airspeeds because of the large aileron deflection necessary to achieve the same rate of roll as at higher speeds with less deflection.

Adverse yaw may be counteracted by any one of the following devices:

  • rudder/aileron coupling.
  • slot/aileron coupling.
  • spoiler/aileron coupling.
  • frise ailerons.
  • differential aileron deflection.

title: Taper ratio is...
optionA: Negative (less than 0).
optionB: More than 1.
optionC: Equal to 1.
optionD: Less than 1.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Taper ratio is the ratio of tip chord to root chord (tip/root). As the tip chord is consistently shorter than the root chord, this ratio will always be less than 1.

title: From a polar curve of the entire aeroplane one can read:
optionA: the minimum drag coefficient and the maximum lift.
optionB: the minimum drag and the maximum lift.
optionC: the maximum C<sub>L</sub>/C<sub>D </sub>ratio and maximum lift coefficient.
optionD: the minimum C<sub>L</sub>/C<sub>D</sub> ratio and the minimum drag.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
A polar curve describes the relation the lift coefficient and drag coefficient.

From the curve you can derive the:

  • Parasite drag coefficient; Find this where CL is 0
  • Minimum drag speed (VMD); this is the best glide Angle providing maximum range. Here the ratio of Lift over drag is the highest
  • VMP; Minimum power speed, here you find the minimum sink rate

title: Which of the following describes the standard spin recovery?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Power to idle, ailerons neutral, opposite rudder, push controls forward.
optionB: Power to idle, ailerons opposite, rudder neutral, push controls forward.
optionC: Full Power, ailerons neutral, opposite rudder, pull controls backwards.
optionD: Full Power, ailerons opposite, rudder neutral, pull controls backwards.
explanationTotal:
SPIN RECOVERY

Although the POH is the primary reference for recovery from a spin, the following can be used as a general procedure:

P - Retard the throttle to idle. In most aircraft, power hampers the recovery.

A - Ailerons neutral. Many pilots will attempt to recover from the spin using the ailerons. This may actually make the problem worse.

R - Apply full opposite rudder. Apply rudder opposite the rotation of the spin. If you have trouble determining which way the airplane is spinning, look at your turn coordinator or turn needle. It will indicate the direction of rotation.

E - Apply forward elevator. Immediately after applying opposite rudder, apply a quick forward motion on the control yoke and hold anti-spin controls until the aircraft starts to recover.

D - Recover from the dive. Once you have completed the four previous steps, and the rotation stops, recover from the dive. The descent rate may be over 5000 feet per minute and the airspeed will rapidly exceed redline. Remember to neutralize the rudder after the rotation stops.

title: An increase in aircraft mass causes the VA to (1)_____ and the design limit load factor to (2)_____.
optionA: (1) decrease; (2) increase
optionB: (1) increase; (2) decrease
optionC: (1) increase; (2) remain the same.
optionD: (1) remain the same; (2) remain the same.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
VA is the design manoeuvring speed of an aircraft. It is better depicted on a diagram of speed vs load factor (V - n diagram).

The aircraft has a limiting load factor, an amount of acceleration that it can take without permanently damaging the airframe. Every aircraft also has a stalling curve, which dictates at what speed the aircraft will stall, when pulling a certain load factor. Put these two together on a diagram and you can see the V - n envelope of the aircraft, how fast we can fly and how many Gs we can pull at a particular speed, either limited by aerodynamic stall or by the structural limit load factor.

VA sits around where the positive stall curve touches the limit load factor. It dictates the point where you can pull the controls as hard as you want, and just as you reach the limit load factor (structural damage point), the aircraft will then stall, removing the chance of structural damage. Any slower and you will stall first, and any faster, and you could permanently damage the airframe. It is not always perfectly on that corner of the diagram, but that is past the scope of this question.

If the mass of an aircraft increases, it means that the aircraft requires more lift, and therefore the stall speed increases. When the stall speed increases, so does the manoeuvring speed (VA) by the same proportion. The design limit load factor, however, is fixed for an aircraft by the manufacturer, at a certain G-loading.

title:
Refer to figure.
The point on the diagram corresponding to the minimum value of drag is:
optionA: point 4.
optionB: point 1.
optionC: point 3.
optionD: point 2.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
A polar curve describes the relation the lift coefficient and drag coefficient. From the curve you can derive the:

  • Parasite drag coefficient; Find this where CL is 0
  • Minimum drag speed (VMD); this is the best glide Angle providing maximum range. Here the ratio of Lift over drag is the highest, find this at the point of tangency
  • VMP; Minimum power speed, here you find the minimum sink rate
  • CLMAX; faster than this might damage the aircraft, it is the maximum value of CL in the chart

title:
Refer to figure.
If an Aeroplane is flying such that the speed stability is negative, the CAS is in the region of the curve where...
optionA: induced drag is equal to parasite drag
optionB: parasite drag is at its greatest
optionC: induced drag is less than parasite drag
optionD: parasite drag is less than induced drag
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The figure represents the Total Drag curve. The area to the left of the minimum drag is known as the speed instability area, where a decrease in speed results in an increase in drag. This is due to the fact that the induced drag is higher than the parasite drag.

title: A student pilot is flying a spinning exercise. Included in the recovery actions from an incipient spin is:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Rudder deflection in the opposite direction to the yaw, with reference to the turn needle.
optionB: Aileron deflection in the opposite direction to the yaw, with reference to the turn needle.
optionC: Rudder deflection in the opposite direction to the yaw, with reference to the slip ball.
optionD: Aileron deflection in the opposite direction to the yaw, with reference to the slip ball.
explanationTotal:
SPIN RECOVERY

Although the POH is the primary reference for recovery from a spin, the following can be used as a general procedure:

P - Retard the throttle to idle. In most aircraft, power hampers the recovery.

A - Ailerons neutral. Many pilots will attempt to recover from the spin using the ailerons. This may actually make the problem worse.

R - Apply full opposite rudder. Apply rudder opposite the rotation of the spin. If you have trouble determining which way the airplane is spinning, look at your turn coordinator or turn needle. It will indicate the direction of rotation.

E - Apply forward elevator. Immediately after applying opposite rudder, apply a quick forward motion on the control yoke and hold anti-spin controls until the aircraft starts to recover.

D - Recover from the dive. Once you have completed the four previous steps, and the rotation stops, recover from the dive. The descent rate may be over 5000 feet per minute and the airspeed will rapidly exceed redline. Remember to neutralize the rudder after the rotation stops.

title: The boundary layer of a wing is:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: a turbulent flow around the wing.
optionB: created by the normal shock wave at transonic speeds.
optionC: caused by suction on the upper wing surface.
optionD: a layer on the wing in which the stream velocity is lower than the free stream velocity.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
BOUNDARY LAYER

When a solid is placed into a flow, there will be a layer, where the velocity is smaller than in the undisturbed stream, reducing to 0 at the surface of the body.

Boundary Layer is defined as a region where the velocity of the flow reaches a certain percentage (i.e. 90% or 99%) of the undisturbed stream velocity from zero. Inside the boundary layer, the viscosity of the fluid alters the flow, while outside of this layer viscosity can be neglected.

The boundary layer will exist in two forms, either laminar or turbulent. In general, the flow at the front will be laminar and become turbulent some distance back, known as the transition point.

title: Induced drag will decrease if ahead of the wing the upwash...
optionA: increases because effective angle of attack increases
optionB: increases because induced angle of attack increases
optionC: decreases because effective angle of attack decreases
optionD: decreases because induced angle of attack decreases
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
INDUCED DRAG

Whenever a wing produces lift, concentrated vortices form at the wing tips. The vortices are strongest at the wing tips and become progressively weaker toward the centre-line of the aircraft.

It is the production of the lift itself which reduces the magnitude of the lift force being generated. To replace the lift lost by the increased downwash, the aircraft must be flown at a higher angle of attack. This increases drag. This extra drag is called induced drag.

The stronger the vortices, the greater the induced drag.

When upwash and downwash are reduced, causes the effective angle of attack of the wing to increase:

- Downwash angle: Decreasing the effect of the vortices will decrease the downwash angle.

- Induced angle of attack: The decrease in upwash/downwash will cause the induced angle of attack to decrease leading to a decrease in induced drag.

Note: An increase/decrease in downwash is preceded by a respective increase/decrease in upwash.

title: Which of the following tab devices contributes positively to the effectiveness of a control surface?
optionA: A trim tab.
optionB: An anti-balance tab.
optionC: A servo tab.
optionD: A balance tab.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Because the hinge moment on some airplanes is too small, often as the result of the CP being too close to the hinge-line of the control surface, it is too easy to deflect the control surface against the aerodynamic load. Consequently, there is little control column load and there is a lack of feel to the controls. This could lead to excessive deflection of the control surface and result in serious overstressing of the airframe.

To counteract these characteristics and assist the pilot to use the control surfaces correctly it is necessary to have anti-balance tabs fitted. These operate in the opposite sense to the balance tab by deflecting the anti-balance tab in the same direction as that of the primary control surface and increase the aerodynamic loading.

title:
Which statement about an aeroplane entering ground effect is correct?

I. The downwash angle increases.
II. The induced angle of attack decreases.
optionA: I is correct, II is correct.
optionB: I is correct, II is incorrect.
optionC: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
optionD: I is incorrect, II is correct.
explanationTotal:
Refer to the figure.
When taking-off or landing, the proximity to the ground prevents full development of the trailing vortices, making them much weaker than in normal flight. This leads to a decrease in downwash, therefore a higher effect angle of attack which also means a smaller induced angle of attack.

This question is asking what will happen when entering ground effect:

  • Downwash angle: When entering ground effect, the effect of the vortices is decreased therefore our downwash angle will decrease. Therefore statement 1 is incorrect!
  • Induced angle of attack: When entering ground effect, because of the decrease in downwash, the induced angle of attack will decrease leading to a decrease in induced drag. Therefore statement 2 is correct!

title: On a wing flying in supersonic flow, the normal shock wave forms at an angle of…
optionA: less than 70° to the wing surface, that further reduces towards the edge of the shockwave.
optionB: 90° to the wing surface.
optionC: less than 70° to the wing surface.
optionD: more than 90° to the wing surface.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

During high-speed flight, significant changes occur in the flow and pressure distributions around the aircraft, which result in a loss of lift and an increase in drag. This is caused by the formation of shock waves, which adversely affect the stability and control characteristics of the aircraft.

The speed of sound is defined as the rate at which small pressure disturbances are propagated through the air, which is solely a function of air temperature.

THE DEVELOPMENT OF SHOCK WAVES
When aircraft fly through the air, every part of them sets up tiny pressure disturbances, which radiate outward at the speed of sound in all directions.

As Mach number increases, the flow over the wing continues to accelerate and eventually reaches a sonic value at a particular point on the wing, normally the point of maximum thickness.

With increasing Mach number, this point grows into an area of supersonic flow, so the air moving over the upper surface will be moving rearward faster than the pressure disturbances can move forward. These disturbances consequently pile up on each other and form a shock wave.

The shock wave acts perpendicular (90 degrees), or normal, to the surface, and is more commonly referred to as a normal shock wave. Notably, this occurs where the flow changes from supersonic back to subsonic.

The overall direction of the airflow remains the same, but as it passes through the shock wave, the following changes take place:
- The flow is rapidly decelerated to a subsonic Mach number.
- Static pressure increases.
- Temperature increases.
- Density increases.
- The energy of the airstream (total pressure) is greatly reduced.

title: The fundamental difference between the aerodynamic characteristics of two and three-dimensional flow is that, in a three-dimensional flow about a wing:
optionA: a spanwise component exists in addition to the chordwise speed component.
optionB: a downward component is added to the chordwise speed component of the flow behind the wing.
optionC: an upward component is added to the chordwise speed component.
optionD: flow separation occurs at the stall.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The 2-dimensional streamline flow pattern takes into account the chord-wise flow around the wing = around the upper and lower surfaces from the leading edge towards the trailing edge. The 3-dimensional streamline flow pattern adds the spanwise flow from the wing root towards the wing tip.

title: What does a fully powered system require compared to a partially-powered system?
optionA: Hydraulic servos.
optionB: Servo valve.
optionC: Servo-tab.
optionD: Artificial feel system.
explanationTotal:
FULLY POWERED SYSTEM

A fully powered system means that no control force is felt, since the deflection is done solely by hydraulic pressure. For a fully powered control system, artificial feel unit is needed. Without this system it would be easy to aerodynamically over-stress the aeroplane.

POWERED-ASSISTED SYSTEM
A power-assisted system is designed so that a part of the control force is felt by the pilot (the rest is done by hydraulic power).

title: Which statement with respect to the speed of sound is correct?
optionA: Increases always if the density of the air decreases.
optionB: Is independent of altitude.
optionC: Varies with the square root of the absolute temperature.
optionD: Doubles if the temperature increases from 9° to 36°C.
explanationTotal:
LOCAL SPEED OF SOUND (LSS)

The speed at which pressure waves propagate is proportional to the square root of the absolute temperature of the air. The higher the temperature, the higher the speed of propagation.

  • LSS = 38.95 x √ (K)
    Where LSS = Local Speed of Sound (kt) and K = Absolute temperature (Kelvin)

title: A four-engine aeroplane has an engine failure just after take-off at the maximum take-off thrust setting. The resulting moment around the normal axis will be greatest when an...
optionA: inboard engine fails and the airport is at high altitude.
optionB: outboard engine fails and the airport is at high altitude.
optionC: outboard engine fails and the airport is at low altitude.
optionD: inboard engine fails and the airport is at low altitude.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
For a multi-engine airplane, the largest asymmetric thrust moment occurs when an outboard engine fails. That engine failure which most adversely affects the performance is deemed the critical power unit and is used to determine the limiting control speeds that will ensure adequate directional control in such an event.
During a crosswind take-off an airplane tends to weathercock into wind. Because of this the failure of the outboard engine on the windward side of the airplane is the most difficult to counteract and is, therefore, the critical engine for jet-propelled aircraft. For propeller-driven airplanes the direction of propeller rotation determines the critical engine. Viewed from behind, a clockwise rotation dictate that the outboard left engine is critical.

title:
Refer to figure.
Assuming all bodies have the same cross-sectional area and are in motion, which body will have the highest form drag?
optionA: Shape 2.
optionB: Shape 3.
optionC: Shape 1.
optionD: Shape 4.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Total Drag is sub-divided into two main types:
Parasite Drag - independent of lift generation, and
Induced Drag - the result of lift generation.

Parasite drag is further sub-divided into:

  • Skin Friction Drag
  • Form (Pressure) Drag, and
  • Interference Drag

NOTE: Skin Friction and Form Drag are together known as PROFILE DRAG.

Form drag is produced whenever the streamline airflow passing over an aircraft separates from the surface and becomes turbulent. An example of extreme form drag is the effect of a flat plate placed at right angles to the airflow.
The pressure immediately in front of the plate is above atmospheric, whilst the pressure behind the plate is below atmospheric. This results in a sucking effect behind the plate and the formation of vortices. The more rapidly the airflow changes direction, the greater the pressure gradient, the earlier the separation, and the higher the form drag.
Changing the shape, or streamline, of a given object reduces drag by delaying the point at which the airflow separates.

title: A jet transport aircraft is on short final approach when a vehicle enters the runway and they have to go-around. Upon going around, the crew notices that the stabiliser trim has jammed. How will this affect controllability?
optionA: The aircraft will NOT be able to go around, and the crew must land.
optionB: The aircraft will respond less to the elevator in the opposite sense.
optionC: The aircraft's nose will tend to rise as the aircraft accelerates.
optionD: The aircraft's nose will tend to lower as the aircraft accelerates.
explanationTotal:
Modern jet transport aircraft have such a large speed range (often from around 100-140 kts up to 300+ knots IAS), that they need a huge trim range, to be able to fly in all those different trim conditions. They often use a variable incidence horizontal stabiliser, which just means that the whole tailplane moves in order to trim the aircraft and the elevators are a control surface on the back of this (some aircraft have a "slab tail" design where the elevator and trim are both done by an all-moving tailplane).

If this stabiliser becomes jammed, then the aircraft will remain trimmed for a particular configuration/speed, and can cause serious problems when flying in other configurations/speeds.

In this case, the pilot is trimmed for a low speed (forget flap settings for now because they make things overly complicated but don't change the answer), which means being trimmed for a high angle of attack. In reality, the basis behind trimming is actually quite complicated, but in essence, we trim to balance the aircraft at a particular angle of attack, which equates to a speed (there are a lot of assumptions in that statement but it's fine for this question).

When we accelerate from that speed, the aircraft will provide too much lift and pitch up naturally, this is where we would usually begin to trim down to decrease the angle of attack, but without a working trimmer, we have to hold it on the elevator control whilst out of the trimmed condition. Without an elevator, the aircraft will continue to pitch up until it stops accelerating.

If there isn't a separate elevator, then the aircraft will have to be trimmed with speed using thrust, faster makes it pitch up, slower makes it pitch down. The aircraft will attempt to hold the same angle of attack, which loosely equates to a speed. It can be flown like this, but it would not be easy. This question seems like there is a separate trimmer to the elevator, so that should not be necessary.

title: In straight, horizontal steady flight, the function of the tailplane is to maintain equilibrium by supplying...
optionA: an up force when the Centre of Pressure is behind the CG.
optionB: an up force when the CG approaches its permissible values.
optionC: a down force when the Centre of Pressure coincides with the CG.
optionD: a down force when the Centre of Pressure is behind the CG.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
An aft movement of the CG (or a forward movement of the CP) decreases the positive longitudinal static stability of an airplane because the arm measured from the CG to the CP is shortened, consequently the required restorative pitching moment is diminished; however, such a movement has the advantage that it increases the longitudinal maneuverability of the airplane because it increases the elevator up effectiveness, thus decreasing the amount of deflection required to produce a particular reaction.
