Thus, its static stability is reduced. Both the required downforce on the tail plane and the stalling speed are decreased.

title: A large jet transport aircraft equipped with a variable-incidence horizontal stabiliser for pitch trim is ready for departure. The flight has to cancel its departure and taxi back to the stand due to an ATC restriction. A short time later, the aircraft is preparing for departure once again, but the weather at the destination has become worse, so the Commander decides to uplift some extra fuel. On this aircraft type, fuel is stored in a tank aft of the current CG. What effect will this extra fuel have on the horizontal stabiliser position for take-off. The leading edge of the stabiliser will move...
optionA: up.
optionB: down.
optionC: forward.
optionD: aft.
explanationTotal:
Learning Objective 081.05.08.03.03: Explain the relationship between CG position, take-off trim setting, and stabiliser trim position.

Weight and CG location massively affect the handling characteristics of an aircraft. This is why most large jet aircraft calculate different pitch trim settings to use for take-off, depending on the position of the CG and the take-off mass of the aircraft. This is so the pilot can always feel roughly the same force when rotating the aircraft, and during the first phase of flight.

If the aircraft has a far forward CG location, the nose will feel heavy to the pilot, so during the setup, the pilots will set a much more nose-up trim setting, so that at rotation, the feeling will be roughly the same.

This is what the question is referring to. Adding extra fuel behind the CG will move the CG backwards, making the aircraft more tail heavy. This will require more nose-down stabiliser trim to feel the same on take-off. A nose-down stabiliser trim is caused by providing less downforce (or extra lift force) on the tail. That is created by setting the horizontal stabiliser at a higher angle, with its leading edge pointing more upwards.

title: An aircraft is on final approach, fully configured and cleared to land when suddenly a vehicle enters the runway. The pilot decides to go-around, but realises that the stabiliser trim is jammed. What should the pilot do?
optionA: The pilot cannot go around.
optionB: Go around but apply nose down pitch.
optionC: Go around but apply nose up pitch.
optionD: No major change in attitude is required since the aircraft is already trimmed.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
An aeroplane is trimmed when it will maintain its attitude and speed without the pilot having to apply any load to the cockpit controls. If it is necessary for a control surface to be deflected to maintain balance of the aircraft, the pilot will need to apply a force to the cockpit control to hold the surface in its deflected position. This force may be reduced to zero by operation of the trim controls.

The aircraft may need to be trimmed in pitch as a result of:
- changes of speed.
- changes of power.
- varying CG positions.
- changes of configuration.

A Trimmable Horizontal Stabiliser (THS) enables a larger CG and speed range than a conventional tailplane with stabiliser, elevator and trim tab, because the whole stabiliser may be moved for trimming the aeroplane, instead of a relatively “small” elevator and trim tab only (a larger surface is much more effective). This also leads to more control difficulty due to a jammed stabiliser.

An aircraft on final apporach is configured and trimmed for low speed, i.e. nose up trim. This means that, in case of go-around, the pilot should be prepared to apply nose down or trim nose down to prevent excessive pitch up caused by the additional power.

title: A manufacturer shortens the fuselage of a 9 seat plane to a 6 seat plane. They make the vertical fin and horizontal stabiliser bigger. How is directional stability influenced?
optionA: There is no impact on stability.
optionB: Negative, since the bigger stabiliser produces more drag.
optionC: Positive, since the higher vertical fin.
optionD: The rudder effectiveness is highly reduced.
explanationTotal:
When a manufacturer shortens the fuselage of an aircraft from 9 seats to 6 seats, the aircraft's overall dimensions and weight change. In this case, the manufacturer has increased the size of the vertical fin and horizontal stabilizer to account for the reduced fuselage length. The larger vertical fin provides greater surface area for controlling yaw, while the larger horizontal stabilizer increases pitch stability.

The larger vertical fin increases the surface area available to resist the yawing moment caused by asymmetrical thrust, crosswinds, or other factors that could cause the aircraft to turn left or right. This results in improved directional stability of the aircraft, which means that it is less likely to deviate from its intended course. Therefore, option "Positive, since the higher vertical fin." is the correct answer.

The increased size of the vertical fin and horizontal stabilizer should not reduce the effectiveness of the rudder, as the rudder is the primary control surface for yaw control. In fact, the larger surface area of the vertical fin may even enhance the rudder's effectiveness, as it provides more area for the rudder to deflect and generate a yawing moment.

title: How long is the gliding distance for an airplane with a L/D of 9 at 5000 feet?
optionA: 12 NM
optionB: 7.4 NM
optionC: 9.3 NM
explanationTotal:
A L/D ratio of 9 means that an aircraft will glide a distance of 9 NM for each NM of altitude lost (in still air).

Knowing that 1 NM = 6076 ft, the aircraft is flying at an altitude of:

  • 5 000 / 6076 = 0.82 NM

The gliging range:

  • 9 x 0.82 = approx. 7.4 NM

title: An increase in geometric dihedral in a steady sideslip condition at constant speed would:
optionA: not affect the required lateral control force.
optionB: decrease the required lateral control force.
optionC: increase the required lateral control force.
optionD: decrease the stick force per g.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
The angle of inclination subtended between the front view of a wing 25% chordline (the wing plane) and the lateral horizontal axis is shown in figure 1 and referred to as: dihedral if the inclination is upward.

The lateral static stability is a measure of the aeroplane’s tendency to return to the wings-level attitude after a disturbance has caused the aeroplane to be disturbed in the rolling plane.

Its ability to recover is dependent on the effect of sideslip.

The aeroplane design features that increase the lateral static stability are:

a. dihedral;
b. sweepback;
c. high-wing mounting;
d. increased effective dihedral;
e. large, high vertical fin;
f. low CG.

As a result, of the sideslip, different parts of the aeroplane produce forces that together create a correcting rolling moment, which tends to restore the aeroplane to its original wings-level attitude. The lateral static stability reacts to the sideslip velocity ‘v’ or the displacement in yaw shown in figure 2.

An aeroplane in a sideslip at a constant speed and constant sideslip angle increases the geometric dihedral of the wing, which requires an increased lateral control force or increased stick force.

title: The angle between the aeroplane longitudinal axis and the wing root chord line is the:
optionA: flight path angle.
optionB: angle of attack.
optionC: angle of incidence.
optionD: glide angle.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
ANGLE OF INCIDENCE

The angle between the wing root chord line and the longitudinal axis of the aircraft. This angle is fixed for the wing.

title: Which of the following wing designs would have the least effective high lift devices (airspeed and all other factors being constant)?
optionA: Wing with a sweepback angle of 15 degrees.
optionB: Wing with no sweep angle.
optionC: Wing with a sweepback angle of 25 degrees.
optionD: Sweep angle has no influence on the effectiveness of high lift devices.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
When compared to a straight wing of the same section, a swept wing is less aerodynamically efficient:

  • t a given angle of attack CL is less.
  • CLMAX is less and occurs at a higher angle of attack.
  • The lift curve has a smaller gradient (change in CL per degree change in alpha is less).
Therefore, comparing fitting the same high lift devices in a straight wing with fitting them in a wing with sweepback, the latter will produce the least amount of lift.

title: In which direction does the torque act, and what is its effect if you consider an aircraft with wing-mounted counter-rotating propellers?
optionA: opposite/stabilizing
optionB: same/stabilizing
optionC: same/destabilizing
optionD: opposite/destabilizing
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The propellers on most conventional twin-engine aircraft rotate clockwise, seen from behind. Co-rotating propellers (both clockwise) on a small twin will not give much torque reaction around the aeroplane’s centre of gravity until one engine fails. A left turning tendency would then occur.

Counter-rotating propellers on a small twin will reduce the torque reaction following an engine failure. Counter-rotating propellers rotate clockwise on the left-hand engine (Engine nr.1) and counter-clockwise on the right hand engine (Engine nr.2). The main advantage is balancing the effects of torque and P-factor, resulting in no critical engine in the case of an engine failure. The critical engine of a multi-engine aeroplane is the engine that, in case of failure, would result in the most adverse performance and handling abilities.

title: The point between the aerodynamic centres of the wing and tail, where the…
optionA: distance between the two centres is equal, is called the Neutral Point.
optionB: distance between the two centres is equal, is called the Static Point.
optionC: wing and tail moments are equal, is called Static Point.
optionD: wing and tail moments are equal, is called Neutral Point.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Longitudinal stability is motion about the lateral axis.

Static Longitudinal stability is the aircraft's natural tendency when disturbed in pitch, to return to its former trimmed angle of attack without pilot input, and is desirable throughout the aircraft's complete speed range.

For the study of stability, we consider the changes in magnitude of lift force due to changes in angle of attack, acting through a stationary point, the aerodynamic centre (AC).

There are two moments to consider: the wing moment and the tail moment. The wing moment is a function of the change in wing lift multiplied by arm ‘x’. The tail moment is a function of the change in tailplane lift multiplied by arm ‘y’. The length of both arms is dependent upon CG position. If the CG is considered in a more forward position, the tail arm is larger and the wing arm is smaller. A more forward CG position increases static longitudinal stability.

If the nose-down (negative) tail moment is greater than the nose-up (positive) wing moment, the aircraft will have static longitudinal stability.

NEUTRAL POINT

If you consider the CG moving rearwards from a position of static longitudinal stability:
- the tail arm ‘y’ will decrease and the wing arm ‘x’ will increase;
- the (negative) tail moment will decrease and the (positive) wing moment will increase.

Eventually the CG will reach a position at which the tail moment is the same as the wing moment. If a vertical gust displaces the aircraft nose-up, the sum of the moments will be zero and there will be no angular acceleration about the CG to return the aircraft towards its original position of equilibrium.

Because there is no resultant moment, either nose-up or nose-down, the aircraft will remain in its new position of equilibrium; the aircraft will have neutral static longitudinal stability.

The position of the CG when the sum of the changes in the tail moment and wing moment caused by the gust is zero is known as the neutral point.

title:
Which statement about a propeller is correct?

I. Asymmetric blade effect increases when engine power is increased.
II. Asymmetric blade effect increases when the angle between the propeller axis and airflow through the propeller disc increases.
optionA: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
optionB: I is correct, II is incorrect.
optionC: I is correct, II is correct.
optionD: I is incorrect, II is correct.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
On take-off, rotation of a single-engine propeller causes an aircraft to swing to one side, particularly those fitted with a tail-dragger undercarriage. The main causes of this are:

  • Slipstream effect
  • Torque reaction
  • Gyroscopic effect
  • Asymmetric blade effect

Asymmetric blade effect

To analyze these effects, consider a right-handed propeller, which rotates clockwise as viewed from the cockpit.
The Asymmetric blade effect is more significant in situations of high power (RPM) and low forward speed, such as take-off or low speed climbs. Therefore, statement 1 is correct.
This effect occurs when the axis of rotation of the propeller is inclined to the direction of flight. For example, when the tail wheel on a tail-dragger type aircraft is in contact with the ground, its longitudinal axis inclines above the horizontal. Therefore, statement 2 is correct.
This causes the down-going blade to have a greater effective angle of attack than the up-going blade, thus developing greater thrust.
The thrust asymmetry between the two blades causes the aircraft to yaw to the left on take-off. Conversely, if an aircraft is flying yawed, then the asymmetry of the thrust causes a pitching moment.

title: What causes a powerful old wartime piston single-engine aircraft with a anticlockwise rotating propeller to veer to the right when the throttle is increased to maximum power?
optionA: Torque effect.
optionB: Gyro effect.
optionC: Asymmetric effect.
optionD: Slipstream effect.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
At high propeller speeds and low forward speed (as in the take-offs, approaches to power-on stalls or go-around), the aircraft will have the tendecy to swing to one side, particularly those fitted with a tail-dragger undercarriage. The main causes of this are:

  • Slipstream effect
  • Torque reaction
  • Gyroscopic effect
  • Asymmetric blade effect

TORQUE REACTION

This occurs because the air resists the motion of the propeller. In so doing, it tends to twist the engine and airframe in the opposite direction to the propeller.

On a anti colckwise rotating propeller, this causes the aircraft to roll to the right and, whilst on the ground, places more weight on the left wheel than the right wheel. This effectively increases the rolling resistance (i.e. drag) of the left wheel, thus slowing the aircraft down and causing it to yaw to the left.

title: Given the following information, calculate the Lift, in a straight and steady glide with a glide angle of 30 degrees. Weight: 12380 kg, Drag: 9550 kg
optionA: 2830 kg
optionB: 6190 kg
optionC: 10721 kg
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
In a power-off descent or glide there are only three forces acting on the aeroplane (i.e., lift, weight and drag).

For relatively small descent angles, up to about 20°, lift can be considered as equal to the weight. The cos γ is close to 1, so the sin γ can be interpreted as the vertical change if the horizontal 1 unit is changed. Expressed as a percentage, it is called the descent or glide gradient.

In a descent Lift is less than Weight. This is because Lift only has to balance the component of Weight perpendicular to the flight path (W cos γ).

L = W x cos γ

In this exercise:

Drag = 85550 N
Weight = 12380 kg

Therefore:

L = 12380 * cos30
L ≈ 10721 kg

title: An aeroplane with excessive static directional stability would encounter controllability problems:
optionA: When flying with drift.
optionB: When flying with sideslip.
optionC: Making it prone to the phugoid.
optionD: Making it prone to dutch roll.
explanationTotal:
Static directional stability is defined as the initial tendency of an aircraft to return to, or depart from, its equilibrium angle of sideslip (normally zero) when disturbed.

When an aircraft is placed in a sideslip, aerodynamic forces develop which create moments about all three axes. The moments created about the normal-axis tend to turn the nose of the aircraft into or away from the relative wind. The aircraft has positive directional stability if the moments created by a sideslip angle tend to align the nose of the aircraft with the relative wind.

If directional stability is excessive, high turn rate is provided by the moment. This can result in excessive back and forth (left – right) turning if the wind is coming from alternating left – right side. Thus, it will be difficult to control the aircraft in case of sideslip. The sideslip angle relates the displacement of the aeroplane centre line from the relative airflow

title:
Which of these statements about the strength of wing tip vortices are correct or incorrect?

I. Assuming no flow separation, the strength of wing tip vortices increases as the angle of attack increases.
II. The strength of wing tip vortices is not affected by aspect ratio.
optionA: I is incorrect, II is correct.
optionB: I is correct, II is correct.
optionC: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
optionD: I is correct, II is incorrect.
explanationTotal:
Wing tip vortices are a byproduct of lift. They are caused by the pressure differential between the top and bottom of the wing, which causes an updraft of high pressure air around the tip of the wing. This updraft turn into a downdraft behind the wing, creating a vortex. The higher the pressure difference between the top and bottom of the wing, the stronger the vortices.

This question is specifically asking for:

  • Angle of attack: The strength of the vortices (and therefore also induced drag) is proportional to the angle of attack. Therefore; the strength of the vortices increase as the angle of attack increases. And also; the strength of the vortices decrease as the angle of attack decreases. Therefore statement 1 is correct!
  • Aspect ratio: The strength of the vortices is inversely proportional with the aspect ratio. Meaning that the strength of the wing tip vortices increase as the aspect ratio decreases. And vice versa: the strength decreases as the aspect ratio increases. Therefore statement 2 is incorrect!

title:
Which statements are correct or incorrect considering subsonic incompressible airflow through a Venturi?

1. The static pressure in the undisturbed airflow is the same as in the throat.
2. The speed in the undisturbed airflow is the same as in the throat.
optionA: 1. correct, 2. correct
optionB: 1. incorrect, 2. incorrect.
optionC: 1. correct, 2. incorrect.
optionD: 1. incorrect, 2. correct.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

A venturi is a practical application of Bernoulli's theorem, sometimes called a convergent/divergent duct.

  • A venturi (throat) tube has an inlet that narrows to a throat, forming a converging duct and resulting in: velocity increasing, pressure (static) decreasing, and (3) temperature decreasing.
  • The outlet section (undisturbed airflow) is relatively longer with an increasing diameter, forming a diverging duct and resulting in (1) velocity decreasing, (2) pressure (static) increasing, and (3) temperature increasing.

For a flow of air to remain streamlined, the mass flow through a venturi must remain constant. To do this and still pass through the reduced cross section of the venturi throat, the speed of flow through the throat must be increased. In accordance with Bernoulli's theorem, this brings about an accompanying drop in pressure and temperature. As the venturi becomes a divergent duct, the speed reduces, and thus the pressure and temperature increase.

title: At a load factor of 1 and the aeroplane's minimum drag speed, what is the ratio between induced drag D<sub>I</sub> and parasite drag D<sub>P</sub>?
optionA: D<sub>I</sub> / D<sub>P</sub> = 2.
optionB: D<sub>I</sub> / D<sub>P</sub> = 1 / 2.
optionC: D<sub>I</sub> / D<sub>P</sub> = 1.
optionD: It varies between aeroplane types.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The total drag is the resulting factor if you add induced drag and parasite drag together.
Parasite drag is caused if an airfoil is moving through the air.
It is the result of form drag and skin friction drag.
Form drag arises from the shape of the object
The more streamlined the object, the less form drag is present.
Shape and size are most important in the amount of form drag resulting.
Form drag increases with increasing velocity, making it very important for high speed aircraft.
Skin friction drag is caused by the friction of the fluid (in case of aircraft this fluid is the atmosphere) against the skin of the object moving through it.
It is directly related to the surface area in contact with the fluid.
Skin friction increases with the square of the velocity.

Induced drag is caused when an object redirects the airflow.
A wing produces lift by creating a pressure difference.
This pressure difference is caused by the shape of the airfoil, causing the airflow on top to accelerate, creating a low pressure on top of the wing and high pressure below the wing.
This pressure difference naturally wants to restore towards a uniform pressure, which creates vortices around the wingtip.
These vortices are deflected downwards, this phenomenon is also called downwash.
The induced drag decreases with airspeed and increases with angle of attack and increasing weight.

In the image we can see that the two vectors (induced and parasite drag) create a resulting vector, the total drag.
Where the induced and parasite drag vectors collide, we have the minimum drag speed (VMD); the speed where the total drag is the lowest.

This leads us to understand that during an acceleration from a total stand still, the total drag first decreases up until the minimum drag speed and then starts increasing again.

title:
Refer to figure.
Which type of flap is shown in the picture 3?
optionA: Fowler flap.
optionB: Split flap.
optionC: Plain flap.
optionD: Single slotted flap.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The flap forms part of the lower surface of the wing trailing edge, the upper surface contour being unaffected when the flap is lowered.
The split flap gives about the same increase in lift as the plain flap at low angles of attack but gives slightly more at higher angles as the upper surface camber is not increased, and so separation is delayed. The drag, however, is higher than for the plain flap due to the increased depth of the wake.

title: The strength of the yawing moment caused by an engine failure on a twin-engine aeroplane...
optionA: will be greater when the CG is located at the aft CG limit.
optionB: will be greater when the CG is located at the forward CG limit.
optionC: will be greater when the CG is located halfway between the forward and aft CG limits.
optionD: is independent of the location (fore or aft) of the CG.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
When an engine fails on a multi-engine aircraft there will be a decrease in thrust and an increase in drag on the side with the failed engine:

  • airspeed will decay.
  • the nose will drop and.
  • most significantly, there will be an immediate yawing moment towards the failed engine.
The forces and moments acting on an aircraft following failure of the left engine are shown in figure 1. The aircraft has a yawing moment towards the dead engine. The pilot has applied rudder to stop the yaw. The vital action when an engine fails is to stop the yaw.
The rolling and yawing moments and the power of the flight controls to balance them will determine the controllability of an aircraft with asymmetric thrust. Rolling and yawing moments with asymmetric thrust are affected by:
  • Thrust on the live engine
  • Altitude
  • Drag from the dead engine and propeller
  • Asymmetric blade effect (also known as ‘P’ Factor)
  • CG position
The fore and aft CG location has no effect on the yawing moment from a failed engine, but will influence the rudder arm, hence the rudder moment. CG on the aft limit will give the smallest rudder arm and the least ability to oppose the yawing moment from a failed engine.
  • Torque reaction
  • Difference in lift due to slipstream
  • Rolling moment due to sideslip
  • Weight
  • Airspeed

title: On a climb, if you keep the thrust setting constant while maintaining a fixed vertical speed, what will happen to the aeroplane’s IAS?
optionA: It will increase, because the pilot will have to reduce pitch attitude to maintain vertical speed, which will tend to increase as TAS increases with altitude.
optionB: It will decrease, because the pilot will have to increase pitch attitude to maintain vertical speed as Excess Thrust decreases with altitude.
optionC: It will increase, because the rearward component of Lift decreases with altitude, and as the thrust setting remains constant, the aeroplane will accelerate.
optionD: It wil decrease, because Drag increases with altitude, and as the trust settings remains constant, the aeroplane will decelerate.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
RATE OF CLIMB
The rate of climb is defined as the height change over a given time period, usually expressed in feet per minute or metres per second. Wind component has no effect on the rate of climb. It can be expressed by:

Rate of climb = Angle of climb x TAS

The magnitude of the rate of climb is determined by the excess power available over that required. The value of the rate of climb is diminished by high altitude, high temperature, high mass and high flap setting either individually or in any combination. Any acceleration or a turn made whilst climbing also reduces the rate of climb.

Because power is the rate of doing work then when dealing with a rate of climb the power curves must be used. To attain the maximum rate of climb the aircraft must be flown at the speed attained, at the point on the graph, at which the excess power available over that required is greatest.

Rate of Climb = (T x TAS) – (D x TAS) / W

So,

Rate of Climb = (Power Available – Power Required) / W

ALTITUDE vs. POWER REQUIRED

Power required is drag times TAS. Although the total drag curve as a CAS does not move as altitude increases, it moves to the right if drawn against TAS. This is because for the same CAS, the TAS increases as the air density reduces.

Figure 2 plots power available and power required against TAS and shows us that as altitude increases:

- The excess power and rate of climb reduce
- VY (TAS) increases to a slightly faster speed

VARIATION OF THRUST WITH ALTITUDE

As altitude increases, thrust available reduces because the air density and, therefore, mass flow reduce.

In an effort to keep rate of climb constant, while climbing with a fixed thrust setting, the aircraft will be forced to climb at a slower speed given that Thrust Available to overcome Drag reduces with altitude.

title:
Bernoulli's equation is:
(note: rho is density; PSTAT is static pressure; PDYN is dynamic pressure; PTOT is total pressure)
optionA: P<sub>STAT</sub> + ½rho × IAS2 = constant
optionB: P<sub>STAT</sub> + ½rho × TAS2 = constant
optionC: P<sub>DYN</sub> + ½rho × IAS2 = constant
optionD: P<sub>TOT</sub> + ½rho × TAS2 = constant
explanationTotal:
Bernoulli's theorem expresses the conservation of energy for a flow of a fluid (without friction, for irrotational flow). The following equation is used as Bernoulli's theorem;

Ps + p/2 V2 (dynamic pressure) = constant
or
Ps + q = constant

Or - in other words - if in a flow velocity is increase, dynamic pressure increases and static pressure reduces.

Since "V" in the dynamic pressure is TAS, the equation may be written as follows:
  • PSTAT + ½rho × TAS2 = constant

title: At speeds above the critical Mach number, vortex generators fitted to a wing’s upper surface will...
optionA: retard shock-induced separation.
optionB: reduce the kinetic energy within the boundary layer.
optionC: increase the stall speed.
optionD: promote shockinduced separation.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The unfavorable characteristics associated with compressibility are due to boundary layer separation behind the shock wave (shock stall).

Flow separation occurs because the boundary layer loses kinetic energy as it flows against the adverse pressure gradient. Shock wave formation increases the adverse pressure gradient so the loss of kinetic energy in the boundary layer will be greater.

Increasing the kinetic energy of the boundary layer will reduce flow separation. Simple devices called vortex generators are used to re-energize the boundary layer.

Vortex generators are small plates, vanes, blades, or wedges mounted in spanwise rows along the wing surface.

Each vortex generator produces a vortex at its tip which will induce high energy air from the free stream flow to mix with the boundary layer, thus increasing its kinetic energy and helping it flow through the shock wave with much less separation.

Vortex generators are usually located on the upper wing surface, particularly ahead of control surfaces, but may be used anywhere where separation is causing high drag or reduced control effectiveness.

It should be noted that vortex generators may also be used on subsonic aircraft to prevent separation caused by high adverse pressure gradients due to the contours of the surface.

title: A twin-engine commercial jet is flying straight and level when suddenly an engine fails. Which combination of environmental factors would require a larger rudder input to control the yaw moment after an engine failure?
optionA: High temperature and high atmospheric pressure.
optionB: Low temperature and high atmospheric pressure.
optionC: High temperature and low atmospheric pressure.
optionD: Low temperature and low atmospheric pressure.
explanationTotal:
When a multi-engine aircraft suffers an engine failure several variables affect both the yawing moment and the rudder moment which is used to oppose it.

There is a minimum IAS (VMC), below which it is impossible for the pilot to maintain directional control with asymmetric thrust.

Airworthiness Authorities, in this case the EASA, have laid down conditions which must be satisfied when establishing the minimum airspeeds for inclusion in the Flight Manual of a new aircraft type. As in most other cases, the conditions under which the minimum control airspeeds are established are ‘worst case’.

VMCA is affected by the amount of thrust being developed by the operating engine. As altitude and/or temperature increases, the thrust from an unsupercharged engine will decrease.

In conditions of high air density, the engines produce a high thrust output and the loss of the output from one engine during take-off is a proportionate loss of a high output. This will require a considerable amount of force to counteract the tendency to yaw.

Air density will be highest when the aerodrome pressure altitude is lowest (high atmospheric pressure), the air temperature is lowest and the water-vapour content of the air is lowest.

title: Located on the underside of a wing’s leading edge, Vortilons produce a vortex on the wing’s…
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: lower surface, at low angles of attack, to provide improved roll control.
optionB: upper surface, at cruise angles of attack, to keep the boundary layer attached to the wing.
optionC: lower surface, at high angles of attack, to keep the boundary layer attached to the wing.
optionD: upper surface, at high angles of attack, to reduce the spanwise flow of air.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
WING FENCE (figure 1)

Wing fences (boundary layer fences), are thin metal fences which generally extend from the leading edge to the trailing edge on the top surface and are intended to prevent outward drift of the boundary layer.

VORTILON (figure 2)

Vortilons, are also thin metal fences, but are smaller than a full chordwise fence. They are situated on the underside of the wing leading edge. The support pylons of pod mounted engines on the wing also act in the same way.

At high angles of attack a small but intense vortex is shed over the wing top surface which acts as an aerodynamic wing fence - minimizing spanwise flow of the boundary layer.

title: Fixed-pitch propellers are usually designed for maximum efficiency at:
optionA: cruising speed
optionB: full throttle
optionC: idling
optionD: take-off
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
A fixed-pitch propeller is designed to be efficient only when flying at a small range of speeds. Usually, this corresponds to the cruising speed as the airplane is spending more time during the cruise than any other flight phase. Therefore, your piston engine fitted with a fixed-pitch propeller will have increasingly better performance as airspeed is building up after take-off. On the other hand, variable pitch propellers are designed to operate at a constant RPM and be efficient over a wide range of speeds. You can see the speed vs. efficiency graph for different pitch settings in the attached figure.

title: What should the pilot do to prevent uncontrollable yaw in a twin-engine aircraft if one engine fails and the speed is below V<sub>MC</sub>?
optionA: Apply rudder and ailerons.
optionB: Apply rudder.
optionC: Set full throttle on the operating engine.
optionD: Close the throttle on the operating engine.
explanationTotal:
VMC or minimum control speed is the CAS below which directional or lateral control cannot be maintained after the failure of one or more engines. At a certain low speed, the rudder moment is not able anymore to balance the yawing moment from the life engine(s).

Assume the rudder is at full deflection with a CG is at the rear limit (shortest rudder arm) and the IAS (dynamic pressure) is just sufficient for the rudder force to give a rudder moment equal to the yawing moment (no yawing).

Any decrease in IAS will cause the aircraft to yaw uncontrollably towards the failed engine. The only way to regain control of the aeroplane is to close the throttle(s) on the operating engine(s). This reduces the yawing moment and the pilot regains control.

title:
Refer to figure.

The two aeroplanes from the annex have conventional flight controls but different design principles. On a manually flown approach, they are instructed by ATC to go-around, which requires a change in pitch attitude from +2° to approximately +12°, whilst maintaining speed. The pilots in both aeroplanes select full thrust, which makes aeroplane 1...
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: pitch up, requiring a push force to maintain the climb attitude, while aeroplane 2 requires a pull force to counteract the pitching motion caused by the engines.
optionB: and aeroplane 2 pitch up since they are statically speed-stable, requiring only small control inputs by the pilots in order to refine the appropriate attitude and speed.
optionC: accelerate, unless a slight pull force is applied to achieve the climb attitude, while aeroplane 2 requires a push force to prevent over-rotation and speed loss.
optionD: and aeroplane 2 require a pull force to achieve the appropriate attitude and speed since they are statically stable and resist moving from the trimmed position.
explanationTotal:
In this scenario, it is all about the engine location. Aeroplane 1 has a high tail-mounted engine design, whereas aeroplane 2 has underslung wing-mounted engines. This means that the two aircraft will be affected by thrust changes in different ways.

We call the high mounted engines on aeroplane 1 "thrust stabilising", as they produce thrust through or above the line of our CG, so cause a small pitch down moment when extra thrust is applied, which gains airspeed.

The underslung engines on aeroplane 2 have a much lower thrust line, so the aircraft will pitch up significantly when thrust is increased. This is a de-stabilising effect, as the airspeed may actually reduce with increased engine thrust, due to the pitch up moment.

In the go-around then, aircraft 1 will handle as expected, with full thrust causing an acceleration, and pitch up command required to achieve the +12º go-around attitude.

In aircraft 2, it is highly likely that applying full power will pitch the aeroplane so much nose up that the pilots will have to push on the controls to avoid over-rotating and losing valuable speed.

Note: there are a few other questions with this (or a very similar) graphic, so make sure to read the question and options carefully. We can pretty much guarantee that the examiner will mix and match some options to catch out people who mistake the question for a different one.

title: Vortex generators:
optionA: take kinetic energy out of the boundary layer to reduce separation.
optionB: transfer energy from the free airflow into the boundary layer.
optionC: reduce the spanwise flow on swept wing.
optionD: change the turbulent boundary layer into a laminar boundary layer.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Flow separation occurs because the boundary layer loses kinetic energy as it flows against the adverse pressure gradient.

Increasing the kinetic energy of the boundary layer will reduce flow separation. Simple devices called vortex generators are used to re-energize the boundary layer.

Vortex generators are small plates, vanes, blades or wedges mounted in spanwise rows along the wing surface.

Each vortex generator produces a vortex at its tip which will induce high energy air from the free stream flow to mix with the boundary layer, thus increasing its kinetic energy and with retarding separation.

title: The never exceed speed (V<sub>NE</sub>) is set so it never exceeds…
optionA: V<sub>D</sub>
optionB: V<sub>C</sub>
optionC: (0.9) x V<sub>C</sub>
optionD: (0.9) x V<sub>D</sub>
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
Important Note: This is a very similar question to Q817027, and whilst they are slightly different, we are unsure of which is being asked in exams (it could be both, but is less likely), and they are so close to each other, we are treating them as one.

We have recently changed the answer to this due to feedback. We find this question very odd, because "0.9 x VD" can be a range of values (as VD can be a range of values), and there are other factors to the calculation of VNE that you can see in the CS23 specifications below (CS25 aircraft do not have a VNE).

Also, we think the examiner is very misleading to include "VD" as an option, as it is certainly correct (VNE is always less than VD), but is less specific than "0.9 x VD", making it tough to decide between "less specific but absolutely correct" and "more specific but more complex to justify" answers.

Please keep on sending any exam feedback you have, and we will keep these questions as up to date as we can for you, thanks!

Each type of aircraft has its own specific flight envelope, within which it can be safely operated in accordance with the EASA Certification Specifications. This is represented on a velocity against load factor, or V-n diagram.

The high-speed limit for many (but not all) CS-23 aircraft is the never exceed speed (VNE) and is a design reference point for the aircraft beyond which the aircraft must not be flown. It provides a safety margin with the point at which structural damage or failure may occur(VD). VNE is the red radial line at the high speed end of the airspeed indicator.

Never Exceed Speed VNE: VNE is set below VD to allow for speed upsets to be recovered before reaching any point of possible damage. VNE equals 0.9 x VD in most cases, but please see the regulation for this below, as there is some "wiggle room" in the regulation that makes things slightly more complex (hence our unhappiness with these options).

CS 23.1505 - Airspeed Limitations
(a) The never-exceed speed VNE must be established so that it is –

(1) Not less than 0.9 times the minimum value of VD allowed under CS 23.335; and
(2) Not more than the lesser of –

(i) 0.9 VD established under CS 23.335; or
(ii) 0.9 times the maximum speed shown under CS 23.251.

title: What will the extension of the leading-edge flaps result in?
optionA: A greater reduction of the stalling speed, compared to the reduction achieved by the extension of the trailing-edge flaps.
optionB: A reduction of the stalling speed, while extension of the trailing-edge flaps will increase the stalling speed.
optionC: An increase of the stalling speed, while extension of the trailing-edge flaps will reduce the stalling speed.
optionD: A lesser reduction of the stalling speed, compared to the reduction achieved by the extension of the trailing-edge flaps.
explanationTotal:
Leading-edge slats increase the wing's chamber area and mean aerodynamic chord (MAC), thereby increasing its coefficient of lift (CL) maximum, which reduces the aircraft's stall speed. The mass flow over the upper surface is increased and so is its energy when air flows through the venturi-shaped slot.

Slats give a relatively larger reduction in stall speed with little increased drag, in comparison to trailing-edge devices.

title: The lift coefficient CL versus angle of attack curve of a positive cambered aerofoil section intersects the vertical axis of the graph:
optionA: Below the origin.
optionB: Above the origin.
optionC: Nowhere.
optionD: At the point of origin.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The curvature or camber of the upper surface of a cambered airfoil is greater than that of the lower surface. As a result, the negative pressure generated by the acceleration of the airstream over the upper surface is greater than that beneath the lower surface.
Because of the different curvatures of the upper and lower surfaces of the airfoil even when the angle of attack is zero the airfoil will still generate a small amount of total lift.
To produce no lift at all a cambered airfoil must have a negative angle of attack.

title: A statically stable aeroplane:
optionA: can show positive, neutral or negative dynamic longitudinal stability.
optionB: will never show positive dynamic longitudinal stability, but always neutral dynamic longitudinal stability.
optionC: is always dynamically stable.
optionD: is never dynamically stable.
explanationTotal:
Dynamic Stability is the subsequent long-term response of an airplane to a disturbance to its equilibrium. It is the change to the stability of an airplane with the passage of time. Any disturbance causes changes to the aerodynamic forces and moments acting on the airplane that are complex, particularly if the displacement is to its directional stability because it affects the airplane in both the yawing and rolling planes.

An airplane that is statically stable is not necessarily dynamically stable. However, for an airplane to be dynamically stable it must be statically stable. In other words, it cannot have long-term stability without first having short-term stability. An airplane that has positive static stability may be dynamically neutral, stable, or unstable; but an airplane that is statically unstable can never attain dynamic stability. The dynamic stability of an airplane is dependent on the airplane design, its speed, and the altitude at which it is flying.

title: You fly a multi engine airplane and get an engine failure on the right engine with flaps down. How will the airplane roll and how do the flaps affect it?
optionA: Right roll, flaps reduce roll
optionB: Left roll, flaps reduce roll
optionC: Left roll, flaps increase roll
optionD: Right roll, flaps increase roll
explanationTotal:
If a multi-engine aircraft suffers an engine failure when airborne, there are two immediate aerodynamic effects:
  • The initial effect is the yawing that occurs due to the asymmetry of the thrust line.
  • The second effect is roll. This occurs when the aircraft continues to yaw towards the failed engine resulting in a decrease in lift from the retreating wing and a yaw-induced roll towards the failed engine.
In this case, when experiencing a right engine failure, the aircraft will bank towards the right. This roll will be more marked if the flaps are extended, the left wing will create significantly greater lift.

title: When altitude increases, the stall speed (IAS) will:
optionA: increase due to decreasing M<sub>CRIT</sub>.
optionB: increase due to increasing compressibility effects as a result of increasing Mach number.
optionC: decrease due to decreasing temperature and decreasing Mach number.
optionD: decrease due to increasing M<sub>CRIT</sub>.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The stall speed is defined by:
VS=√((2∗W)/(ρ∗S∗CLMAX))

At the stalling angle CLMAX and S are constant, and the indicated airspeed is given by the dynamic pressure 1 / 2 ρ V2. Therefore, for the same airplane mass and configuration in straight and level flight, if the slight difference between EAS and IAS caused by compressibility is ignored, an airplane will stall at the same IAS at all altitudes.

If, however, compressibility is not ignored then the stalling IAS value slowly increases with increased altitude, but the change only becomes significant at very high altitudes.
At a constant EAS, Mach number will increase as altitude increases.

Figure 1 shows the variation of stalling speed with altitude at constant load factor (n). Such a curve is called the stalling boundary for the given load factor, in which altitude is plotted against equivalent airspeed.

At this load factor (1g), the aircraft cannot fly at speeds to the left of this boundary. Over the lower range of altitude, stall speed does not vary with altitude. This is because at these low altitudes, the Mach number at VS is too low for compressibility effects to be present. Eventually (approximately 30000 ft), Mach number at VS has increased with altitude to such an extent that these effects are important, and the rise in stalling speed with altitude is apparent.

As altitude increases, stall speed is initially constant then increases, due to compressibility.

title: With regard to the Centre of Gravity limits of an aircraft, which one of the following statements is true?
optionA: The aircraft operator’s CG limitations can be more restrictive than the manufacturer’s CG limitations.
optionB: The manufacturer’s CG limitations can be more restrictive than the aircraft operator’s CG limitations.
optionC: It depends on the state of registry whether the manufacturer’s or the aircraft operator’s limitations on CG are more restrictive.
optionD: The CG limitations of the operator always have to be the same as the manufacturer’s limitations.
explanationTotal:
The aircraft must be always loaded so that, not only is the Centre of Gravity (CG) within limits, but also that no structural or performance limited masses are exceeded.

The controlling regulations for Mass and Balance are described in EU-OPS. These specify that the loading, mass and CG of the aeroplane must comply with limitations in the Aeroplane Flight Manual or the Operations Manual, whichever is more restrictive and set out the requirements to be included in the Operations Manual.

title:
Refer to figure.
The tab in the figure represents:
optionA: a balance tab.
optionB: an anti-balance tab.
optionC: a trim tab.
optionD: a servo tab.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The force required to operate the primary control surfaces, even using balance tabs, is often too great to be acceptable. To relieve the pilot of the need to apply so much force to operate the controls servo-tabs are fitted to carry out this function.
The servo-tab is a small tab hinged on the trailing edge of the primary control surface and linked directly to the control column. There is no direct link between the control column and the primary control surface.
The function and operation of the servo-tab is the same as the balance tab and moves the trim tab in the opposite direction to the movement of the primary control surface. However, at low IAS the servo-tab makes the main control surface less effective. The position of a servo-controlled primary control surface cannot be determined until a positive pressure is applied to the servo-tab by the airflow.

title: In a glide descent, how does the extension of flaps affect the glide distance and time?
optionA: Glide distance decreases and glide time decreases.
optionB: Glide distance increases and glide time decreases.
optionC: Glide distance remains the same and glide time increases.
optionD: Glide distance increases and glide time remains the same.
explanationTotal:
Flaps are very useful on aircraft for decreasing the stall speed, allowing aircraft to safely land and take-off at much lower speeds than they would with a clean wing. This has numerous benefits, including the shortening of runways.

Flaps have very limited uses in flight, though, and there is a good reason why pilots are so hasty to get rid of them after take-off. Flaps increase the drag of a wing, reducing climb rates and increasing fuel burn.

The use of flaps in a glide descent increases the drag for no real increase in lift (flaps can increase lift, but the aircraft has not got any heavier, so does not need it), and therefore drastically reduce the L/D ratio (Lift to Drag ratio). The L/D ratio is what decides the glide angle, and is highest in a clean configuration. Flaps cause a steeper glide angle, decreasing the possible glide distance. This extra drag also leads to a greater rate of descent, meaning that the aircraft will have less glide endurance, and the glide time is therefore decreased.

If the question mentioned that the pilot slowed down due to extending flaps, then it is possible that the glide time could remain the same or increase, as the lower airspeed means that, even at a steeper glide angle, the aircraft might have a similar or possibly lower rate of descent. As no mention was made of this in the question, and none of the options allow it anyway, we will discount it, but please be aware that it could be asked in such a way, and that may be the correct answer. No matter what the question though.

title: What happens to the stability of the fuselage and overall directional stability of the aircraft when the CG moves aft?
optionA: The fuselage stability increases and the directional stability decreases.
optionB: The fuselage stability decreases and the directional stability decreases.
optionC: The fuselage stability increases and the directional stability increases.
optionD: The fuselage stability decreases and the directional stability increases.
explanationTotal:
Stability of an aeroplane is its tendency to return to an original point after a disruption.

The movement (forward/aft) of the CG is incredibly important to longitudinal and directional stability (stability in pitch and yaw movements), as the aircraft rotates around the CG, and the effect of the aircraft's aerodynamics act differently, depending on how far forward/backwards the CG is.

We can think of stability like a dart, the further forward the mass, and the further backwards all the aerodynamic bits (the fins), the more stable an aircraft is. This is why a dart is very nose heavy. This shows us that the further forward the CG, the greater the stability.

Each component has its own effect on aircraft stability, in each axis. So the fuselage's effect actually depends on the fuselage and CG position, but it usually destabilising, due to the large nose that sticks out ahead of the CG, but the tail fin (vertical stabiliser) is massively stabilising, because it is a large aerodynamic surface at the rear of the aircraft.

Shifting the CG backwards makes the whole aircraft more tail heavy, which reduces the stability of every element of the aircraft, and reduces the overall stability in every axis except lateral (roll), therefore including directional (yaw) and longitudinal (pitch).

title:
Refer to figure.
Which figure correctly shows how the drag and thrust available curves change when an aircraft suffers an engine failure? The continuous line is with two operative engines and the dashed line is with one engine inoperative.
optionA: Figure 1
optionB: Figure 2
optionC: Figure 3
optionD: Figure 4
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Note: The figure here has been made based on feedback, but we think it should be slightly different. We believe that the engine failed drag curve should be tilted slightly to show how induced drag remains the same but parasite drag increases with an engine failure. Nonetheless, there is still only one answer that is correct here, so until we receive further feedback, we will keep the figure as it is.

In the climb, if one of the engines is lost, then the thrust available is now reduced by half and drag is increased due to a stopped or windmilling propeller/engine. This significantly reduces the excess performance of the aircraft, meaning that the rate of climb will be much lower, and the aircraft will not be able to climb to as high of an altitude. At high altitudes, this makes the aircraft unable to reach equilibrium forces, and the pilots have to descend in order to maintain airspeed., and in some light piston twins, requires very precise flying to climb at all.

On the graphs, when an engine failure occurs, the drag curve (the curve at the bottom) will get higher whilst the thrust available (the straight line for a jet aircraft) gets lower. As those lines get closer together, the aircraft has less excess performance and a much smaller operating speed range.

Not only do you have to identify which curve is which on the graphs, but you also have to know what changes will happen to each in the event of an engine failure.

title: When is the dutch roll tendency the highest?
optionA: At high Mach numbers.
optionB: Low lateral stability and high directional stability.
optionC: High longitudinal stability and low directional stability.
optionD: At low Mach numbers.
explanationTotal:
DUTCH ROLL. This is an oscillation involving roll, yaw and sideslip. Because of these characteristics of the Dutch roll oscillation, lateral dynamic stability has always been more of a problem than longitudinal dynamic stability.

With a dominant lateral stability this will, when a yaw is introduced, roll the aircraft due to the lift increase on the wing into the wind. The increased induced drag on the rising wing will yaw the aircraft in the opposite direction, reversing the coupled oscillations. This is called Dutch roll. Dutch roll might occur when the lateral stability is large compared to the directional stability. Therefore, the moments involved are roll and yaw. With increasing altitude (decreasing density) or increasing Mach number, the possibility of a Dutch roll increases. The CG position has little influence on the lateral stability, but an aft CG will reduce the directional stability because the Moment Arm of the stabilizing moment from the fin will decrease and thus increasing the likelihood of a Dutch roll.

  • To reduce the aircraft tendency to Dutch roll, either the lateral stability should be decreased or the directional stability increased => anhedral would decrease the lateral stability. Aircraft with a tendency to Dutch roll are also fitted with yaw damper. This automatically displaces the rudder proportional to the rate of yaw to damp out the oscillation.
Note: Dutch roll is a result of high Lateral stability with relatively low Directional stability. Furthermore, Longitudinal stability is not a factor.

title: Whilst performing a take-off in icing conditions, the aircraft nose feels heavy, and it takes a long time to rotate. What could have caused this?
optionA: Anti-icing fluid has built up between the elevator and horizontal stabiliser.
optionB: The control cables connecting the control column to the elevator have torn.
optionC: The ailerons have frozen in position.
optionD: The increased air density means insufficient thrust is being produced to reach V<sub>R</sub>.
explanationTotal:
This is an odd question as it is not mentioned in the current iteration of the learning objectives. For many candidates, this question is simply solved by removing the incorrect options and seeing what you have left:

  • "Anti-icing fluid has built up between the elevator and horizontal stabiliser."
    • This is actually possible, and in fact there have been quite a few reports over the years of rejected take-offs at rotation when the aircraft has failed to rotate correctly after de-icing. So much so that EASA commissioned a report to be made, testing de-icing fluid and its effects on a horizontal stabiliser section. The build-up of thickening fluids on the front of the elevator can make it very resistive to movements during take-off, especially with manual flight controls. Although it is not in the current learning objectives, it seems that an examiner wants you to know about it. Thankfully, it is the only possible correct option.
  • "The control cables connecting the control column to the elevator have torn."
    • This would not be a case that is specific to icing conditions, and the cables tearing could cause a few different feelings on the control column, but most likely very light resistance to movement, not heavy. The aircraft also would not respond at all.
  • "The ailerons have frozen in position."
    • The ailerons provide roll control, so whilst this is a bad situation, a pilot would not notice that the nose was heavy, as the pitch is controlled by the elevators.
  • "The increased air density means insufficient thrust is being produced to reach VR."
    • Quite the other way, high air density due to the cold air would cause higher thrust from the engine, and better performance.

title: During cruise Flight, an aircraft encounters severe turbulence. The pilot promptly reduces the airspeed to the recommended rough air speed (V<sub>RA</sub>). The expected speed variations due to turbulence will:
optionA: Cause deviation from flight path, but these will be within acceptable limits.
optionB: Maintain the load factor between the positive and ultimate load limits.
optionC: NOT cause frequent overspeed warnings.
optionD: NOT cause any stall warning.
explanationTotal:
CS 25.1517 Rough air speed, VRA

(a) A rough air speed VRA for use as the recommended turbulence penetration air speed, and a rough air Mach number MRA, for use as the recommended turbulence penetration Mach number, must be established to ensure that likely speed variation during rough air encounters will not cause the overspeed warning to operate too frequently.

title: When a jet transport aeroplane takes off with the CG at the forward limit and the trimmable horizontal stabiliser (THS) is positioned at the maximum allowable nose down position for take-off:
optionA: rotation will require a higher than normal stick force.
optionB: early nose wheel raising will take place.
optionC: rotation will be normal using the normal rotation technique.
optionD: there will be a tendency to over-rotate.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
A forward CG position (nose-heavy airplane) results in the greatest nose-down tendency and the aircraft rotates slowly on take-off. The position of the stabiliser for a nose-heavy aeroplane requires nose-up trim.

Therefore, the combination of a forward CG position and a nose-down trim will result in higher than normal stick forces being required.

title: Which boundary layer, when considering its velocity profile perpendicular to the flow, has the greatest change in velocity close to the surface?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Turbulent boundary layer.
optionB: No difference.
optionC: Laminar boundary layer.
optionD: The boundary layer in the transition between turbulent and laminar.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Although the wording could be clearer, they are asking us to compare the slope of the velocity profile in a laminar and a turbulent boundary layer at the surface. The boundary layer has a velocity of 0 at the wall, and velocity equal to the free flow at the top. The time-averaged turbulent flat plate (zero pressure gradient) boundary layer velocity profile is much fuller than the laminar flat plate boundary layer profile, and therefore has a larger slope at the wall, leading to greater skin friction drag along the wall.

The answer is mathematically demonstrable, however it's quite hard to do so and it's way beyond the syllabus. However, it is clear: The turbulent boundary layer has the highest increase of velocity close to the wall from the 2 boundary layers.

title: Your aircraft weight is reduced from 70 000 kg to 30 000 kg, how will this affect the gust load?
optionA: Initially increases and then decreases.
optionB: It remains the same.
optionC: It increases.
optionD: It decreases.
explanationTotal:
Gust load depends on various factors. Below we will discuss the effect of Wing Loading on Gust Load:
  • Aircraft with smaller Wing Loading will suffer higher loads (gust is inversely proportional to wing loading). Decreasing airplane mass will increase gust load as it decreases Wing Loading.

title: The manouveuring speed (V<sub>A</sub>) of a Cessna Skyhawk at 2550 lb is 102 kt. What is the V<sub>A</sub> at mass of 1900 lb?
explanationTotal:
The following formula may be used:

VNEW = VOLD x √ New weight ÷ Old weight
VNEW = 102 x √(1 900 ÷ 2 550)
VNEW = 88 kt

title:
In any given airflow, rho x A x V = constant, where:

rho = density
A = cross-sectional area of the flow
V = Velocity

What is this principle known as?
optionA: Equation of continuity.
optionB: Magnus effect.
optionC: Bernoulli's principle.
optionD: Venturi effect.
explanationTotal:
Equation of continuity

Energy and mass can neither be created nor destroyed. When a fluid is in motion, it must move in such a way that mass is conserved. Mass flow will remain a constant value at all points along the tube. The air mass flow through the tube will be the product of the cross-sectional area (A), the airflow velocity (V) and the air density (rho).

  • Equation of Continuity:
    A × V × rho = Constant

title: Which of these statements about boundary layers is correct?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: A turbulent boundary layer produces less friction drag than a laminar one.
optionB: A turbulent boundary layer turns into a laminar one at the transition point.
optionC: A laminar boundary layer is thinner than a turbulent one.
optionD: Compared with a turbulent boundary layer, a laminar boundary layer is better able to resist a positive pressure gradient before it separates.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Lets look at each answer and see why each is correct or incorrect:

  • “A turbulent boundary layer produces less friction drag than a laminar one.”
A turbulent boundary layer produces more friction than a laminar boundary layer. This is because the average velocity of the air close to the surface is higher than in a laminar boundary layer, this creates more skin friction and therefore increases drag. – Incorrect!
  • “A turbulent boundary layer turns into a laminar one at the transition point.”
As we can see from the figure, the laminar boundary layer can turn into a turbulent one. This process cannot be reversed, therefore once turbulent, a layer will never return to being laminar. – Incorrect!
  • “A laminar boundary layer is thinner than a turbulent one.”
A laminar boundary layer is indeed thinner than a turbulent boundary layer, as we can see from the figure. – Correct!
  • “Compared with a turbulent boundary layer, a laminar boundary layer is better able to resist a positive pressure gradient before it seperates.”
A laminar layer cannot exist when pressure is rising in the direction of the flow. On a curved surface like an airfoil where the pressure starts increasing from the point of maximum thickness, the transition from laminar to turbulent usually occurs at the point of maximum thickness. Therefore, turbulent boundary layer is actually better at resisting a positive pressure gradient. – Incorrect!

title: An aeroplane has a C<sub>L</sub> (lift coefficient) of 0.6 and a C<sub>DI</sub> (induced drag coefficient) value of 0.1 in level flight. The aeroplane slows down while maintaining level flight. The lift coefficient increased by a factor of 1.5 to maintain lift at the lower speed. If there is NO change in configuration, what is the new C<sub>DI</sub>?
explanationTotal:
The key factor in addressing this question is the assertion that the aircraft configuration remains constant. If this condition holds, then the aspect ratio remains the same before and after the increase in CL. Expressing this relationship in equation form (AROLD = ARNEW) enables us to determine the new CDI by manipulating the formula for aspect ratio.

The lift coefficient increased by a factor of 1.5 to maintain lift at the lower speed:

  • New CL = 0.6 x 1.5 = 0.9
Aspect Ratio = CL2 ÷ CDI
AROLD = ARNEW
0.62 ÷ 0.1 = 0.92 ÷ CDI NEW
3.6 = 0.81 ÷ CDI NEW
CDI NEW = 0.81 ÷ 3.6
CDI NEW = 0.225
Alternatively,
An important formula to calculate the indiced drag coefficient (CDI) is as follows:
  • CDI = CL2 ÷ (π AR)
  • CDI∝ CL2
From the above, we can see that CDI varies with the (change in CL)2.
New CDI = 0.1 x 1.52 = 0.225

title: The positive manoeuvring limit load factor for a light aeroplane in the utility category in the clean configuration may not be less than:
explanationTotal:
EASA regulations for flight manoeuvring envelope
The load factor and speed limits for a given aircraft are strictly regulated by EASA. The requirements are described in CS-25 (Certification Specification 25) for transport aircraft MTOW > 5 700 kg and in CS-23 for smaller aircraft MTOW < 5 700 kg.

Note: This is not the full description of classification of CS-23 and CS-25 aircraft but it is enough for us to know.

For the CS-25 category, the maximum positive and minimum negative limitation of load factor is:
nMAX = 2.5; nMIN = -1 in clean configuration (high lift devices not extended)

The CS-23 category includes three subparts:

Normal [N] nMAX = 3.8 nMIN = -1.52
Utility [U] nMAX = 4.4 nMIN = -1.76
Aerobatic [A] nMAX ≥ 6

nMIN ≤ 3

If flaps are deployed nMAX = 2; nMIN = 0 are the required limits for both categories.

title:
Refer to figure.
Which line in the diagram represents an aeroplane with static longitudinal instability at all angles of attack?
optionA: Line 2.
optionB: Line 3.
optionC: Line 1.
optionD: Line 4.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Static longitudinal stability depends upon the relationship of angle of attack and pitching moment (CM).

A variation of CG position can cause large changes in the static longitudinal stability. In the conventional airplane configuration, the large changes in stability with CG variation are primarily due to the large changes in the wing contribution. If the incidence of all surfaces remains fixed, the effect of CG position on static longitudinal stability is typified by the chart in figure 1:

As the CG is gradually moved aft, the airplane static stability decreases, then becomes neutral then unstable. The CG position which produces zero slope and neutral static stability is referred to as the “neutral point”. The neutral point defines the most aft CG position without static instability.

Positive static stability is indicated by the curve with negative slope. Moving the CG forward, will increase static longitudinal stability and this is represented by a (steeper) negative slope.

Neutral static stability would be the result if the curve had zero slope. If neutral stability existed, the airplane could be disturbed to some higher or lower lift coefficient without change in pitching moment coefficient.

An airplane which demonstrates a positive slope of the CM versus CL curve would be unstable.

title: What is correct about a fully developed spin?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Speed is low and constant, spinning rate increases.
optionB: Speed increases and spinning rate increases.
optionC: Speed is low and constant and spinning rate is constant.
optionD: Speed increases and spinning rate is constant.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.

(1) Incipient Stage

In the develped stage, a state of equilibrium is reached, characterised by a low and constant airspeed. Rates of descent will be as high as 5000 to 8000 feet per minute. At this stage the spin will be self-perpetuating. If the pilt does nothing about it, the spin is likely to continue until the aircraft hits the ground. Positive anti-spin control inputs will be required to recover from the fully developed spin.

  • Airspeed, vertical speed, and rate of rotation are established. Small training aircraft lose approximately 500 ft during each three-second turn.
