title:
Which statement is correct for a propeller of given diameter and at constant RPM?

I. Assuming blade shape does not change power absorption increases if the number of blades increases.
II. Power absorption increases if the mean chord of the blades increases.
optionA: I is correct, II is correct.
optionB: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
optionC: I is incorrect, II is correct.
optionD: I is correct, II is incorrect.
explanationTotal:
The ability of a propeller to convert engine power into forward thrust is its power-absorption capability.
It is affected by:
  • the propeller-blade shape.
  • the number of propeller blades.
  • the propeller solidity.
The number of propeller blades is usually limited to six because of the complexity of the pitch control contained in the propeller hub and aerodynamic interference between propeller blades. Having a large number of blades has the advantage that it decreases propeller noise, but its primary purpose is to improve the power absorption properties and efficiency of the propeller. Therefore, statement 1 is correct.
Increasing the blade chord has the advantages that blade interference is reduced; the blade area is increased to transmit the power available within a set diameter and the power absorption is improved. Therefore, statement 2 is correct.

title: Assuming constant IAS, when an aeroplane leaves ground effect:
optionA: downwash does not change.
optionB: induced drag increases.
optionC: the induced angle of attack decreases.
optionD: the effective angle of attack increases.
explanationTotal:
Refer to the figure.
When leaving ground effect, due to movement away from the ground, the downwash will be increase. As you can figure out from the diagram this will lead to the following:

  • A decrease in the effective angle of attack
  • An increase in the induced angle of attack, and therefore also;
  • An increase in induced drag
For those struggling to remember the changes, we recommend that you simply sketch out the diagram and move the effective airflow line according to the question. Therefore when leaving ground effect, the downwash will increase and “raise” the line, increasing the induced angle of attack and decreasing the effect angle of attack. The change in drag is proportional to the induced angle of attack therefore a higher induced angle of attack will increase the induced drag.

title:
Which statement regarding the manoeuvre and gust load diagram in the clean configuration is correct?

I. The gust load diagram has a symmetrical shape with respect to the n = 1 line for speeds above VB.
II. The manoeuvre load diagram does not extend beyond the speed VC.
optionA: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
optionB: I is incorrect, II is correct.
optionC: I is correct, II is incorrect.
optionD: I is correct, II is correct.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
Gust Loads

To avoid stalling and exceeding the limiting load factor an airplane must be operated within the limitations imposed by the gust envelope, which is graphically constructed by using the arbitrary values of gust speed against the EAS of the airplane originating from a load factor value of +1.0 and specified in CS 25.341(a)(5)(I), as shown in figure 2.
As seen in figure 2, the gust load diagram has a symmetrical shape for speeds above VB, considering the n = 1 line. Therefore, statement 1 is correct.

The Maneuver Envelope (V - n Diagram)

The maximum load factors which must be allowed for during maneuvers are shown in an envelope of load factor against speed (EAS). Figure 1 shows a typical maneuver envelope or V - n diagram. The limit load factors will depend on the design category of the aircraft.
Point ‘D’ in is the design dive speed VD. This is the maximum speed which has to be considered when assessing the strength of the aircraft. Therefore, statement 2 is incorrect.

title:
Refer to figure.
A typical curve representing propeller efficiency of a fixed pitch propeller versus TAS at constant RPM is:
optionA: diagram 4.
optionB: diagram 2.
optionC: diagram 3.
optionD: diagram 1.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
The efficiency of any system is determined by the ratio of the output power to the input power. The force developed by the engine and delivered to the propeller via the shaft is the rotational force of the propeller, the propeller torque.
The power delivered to the propeller is the product of the torque and the angular velocity of the propeller shaft (Torque × Rotational Speed).
The thrust developed by the propeller is the product of the mass of air moved and the acceleration given to it by the propeller. The power developed by the propeller is the product of the thrust and the TAS (Thrust × Axial Speed).
Propeller efficiency is the ratio of the propeller power developed to the engine power delivered. A well-designed propeller is typically 80% efficient when operating at its optimum blade angle of attack.

Propeller Efficiency = ((Thrust × Axial Speed))/((Torque × Rotational Speed))

title: A jet transport aircraft flying at its cruising level starts a climb from FL350 to FL370. The climb to the new level is performed at a constant Mach number. What is the effect of the change in level on the buffet margin?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: The buffet margin will be larger, and buffet will occur at a lower load factor.
optionB: There will be NO effect on the buffet margin, and buffet will occur at the same load factor.
optionC: The buffet margin will be smaller and the buffet will occur at a lower load factor.
optionD: The buffet margin will be larger and buffet will occur at a higher load factor.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

In the same way that separated airflow prior to a low speed stall can cause airframe buffet, shock induced separation (shock stall) at high speed can also cause buffeting.

Aerodynamic buffet is a valuable stall warning, but it can damage the aircraft structure. Because of the higher dynamic pressure when an aircraft is operating in the transonic speed region, any shock induced buffet will have a greater potential for severe airframe damage.

High speed buffet must be completely avoided. The aircraft must therefore be operated in such a manner that a (safety) margin exists before aerodynamic buffet will occur.

If the variables which affect both high speed and low speed stall are considered it will be possible to identify the conditions under which buffeting will occur and a chart can be drawn to show all the factors involved.

This is called a ‘Buffet Onset’ chart which is used by flight crews to ensure their aircraft is always operated with a specified minimum buffet margin.

For any given combination of mass, center of gravity position and airspeed, the maximum operating altitude is that altitude at which a normal positive acceleration increment of 0.3 g, without exceeding the buffet onset boundary, is possible.

Any of the following factors reduces the margins between cruising speed and the high-speed and the low-speed buffets:

- increased altitude
- increased mass
- increased load factor
- a forward CG position
- an increased bank angle

title: During straight and level flight, the pilot starts extending flaps to the landing configuration. Due to a malfunction, the trailing edge flaps on the right wing remain retracted. If the malfunction goes unnoticed, the possible consequence is:
optionA: The aircraft will roll to the right and the right wing could stall.
optionB: The aircraft will roll to the left and the right wing could stall.
optionC: The aircraft will roll to the right and the left wing could stall.
optionD: The aircraft will roll to the left and the left wing could stall.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

Flap asymmetry will give different lift on the wings which causes a large rolling moment. This will happen at any speed since flap extension changes the camber of the wing. The value of lift will be increased on the left side due to the flap extension. As a result the aircraft will roll to the right. The angle of attack will be increased on the right side (downgoing wing) and decreased on the left side (upgoing side) strong enough to reduce lift, possibly leads to a spin (right wing stalled)

title: You are descending and your altitude is decreasing. Which statement regarding your buffet margin is correct?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: M<sub>MIN</sub> and M<sub>MAX</sub> both decrease
optionB: The difference between M<sub>MIN</sub> and M<sub>MAX</sub> increases
optionC: The difference between M<sub>MIN</sub> and M<sub>MAX</sub> decreases
optionD: M<sub>MIN</sub> and M<sub>MAX</sub> both increase
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The ‘buffet boundary’ is the speed range between the high-speed buffet and the low-speed buffet, which decreases with increased altitude. The separation of the cruising speed from the buffet-onset speed is the ‘buffet margin.’ There is a low-speed margin and a high-speed margin.

title: In the event of a flap overspeed, a flap load relief system will...
optionA: partially extend the flight spoilers to reduce the load factor, to prevent flap damage.
optionB: retract the trailing-edge flaps to an intermediate position, to protect the flaps.
optionC: lock movement of the flap lever towards the extended direction, to avoid a flap overload.
optionD: block trailing-edge flap movement if an asymmetry or misalignment is detected, to limit the flap loads.
explanationTotal:
Flaps take quite a lot of force in normal operation due to the heavy aerodynamic load they have to withstand. This increases with the square of the velocity, and can become really very large. Flaps are therefore made to be very strong, but as they are only useful in the lower speed range, they are not built to be used at high airspeeds. Each flap setting has a VFE speed, which is the maximum flaps extended speed. Above this speed, the flaps will take too much load, and could be damaged.

Modern jet transport aircraft often have a flap load relief system, which detects flap overspeed, and can disengage the flap lock, allowing the airflow to push the flaps to a lower setting, or some intermediate value, so that the flaps do not get damaged. Some systems use hydraulic pressure and physically move the flaps using the standard system, whereas others use the "blowback" system mentioned above.

title: Which of the following statements best describes VA?
optionA: The speed for maximum gust velocity.
optionB: A specifically designated speed to use when penetrating turbulence.
optionC: A speed chosen by the manufacturer for evaluating performance criteria.
optionD: The design manoeuvring speed, at or near which rapid, full control reversal should be avoided due to risk of damage to aircraft.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
VA is the design manoeuvring speed of an aircraft. It is better depicted on a diagram of speed vs load factor (V - n diagram).

The aircraft has a limiting load factor, an amount of acceleration that it can take without permanently damaging the airframe. Every aircraft also has a stalling curve, which dictates at what speed the aircraft will stall, when pulling a certain load factor. Put these two together on a diagram and you can see the V - n envelope of the aircraft, how fast we can fly and how many Gs we can pull at a particular speed.

VA sits around where the positive stall curve touches the limit load factor. It dictates the point where you can pull the controls as hard as you want, and just as you reach the limit load factor (structural damage point), the aircraft will then stall, removing the chance of structural damage. Any slower and you will stall first, and any faster, and you could permanently damage the airframe. It is not always perfectly on that corner of the diagram, but that is past the scope of this question

To look at all the options

  • "The speed for maximum gust velocity."
    • No. The speed for maximum gust velocity is VB, and occurs just above the VA. It is the speed that the aircraft is certified to handle the highest level of gusts (66 fps).
  • "A specifically designated speed to use when penetrating turbulence."
    • The turbulence penetration speed is actually VB also, where the strongest gusts can be handled by the aircraft without stalling or damage occurring.
  • "A speed chosen by the manufacturer for evaluating performance criteria."
    • There are many different speed to evaluate performance criteria with, but they would never use VA, as it is not usually anywhere near speeds such as best range, minimum drag, etc.
  • "The design manoeuvring speed, at or near which rapid, full control reversal should be avoided due to risk of damage to aircraft."
    • Whilst the wording is (intentionally) poor for this option, it is the only one left. We believe that the "control reversal" would just mean going from one full deflection to the other side full deflection. That is really not advisable at any speed, but at and above VA would cause damage to the aircraft. Even just below VA, full control deflection from no deflection is fine (though you may stall), but reversal is not accounted for in the regulations, so in reality the examiner can say what they like to try and confuse you. This is the only remaining option, and correctly stated that it is the design manoeuvring speed, so we are happy to agree that it is most correct.

title: An aeroplane climbs to cruising level with a constant pitch attitude and maximum climb thrust (assume no supercharger). How do the following variables change during the climb? (gamma = flight path angle)
optionA: Gamma decreases, angle of attack increases, IAS decreases.
optionB: Gamma remains constant, angle of attack remains constant, IAS decreases.
optionC: Gamma decreases, angle of attack increases, IAS remains constant.
optionD: Gamma decreases, angle of attack remains constant, IAS decreases.
explanationTotal:
Pitch attitude = nose-up angle of the aircraft. Such angle is made up of the flight path angle (gamma) and the angle of attack in a climb.

Formula: Sin gamma = (Thrust – Drag) / Weight

Unless the aircraft is equipped with a supercharger, thrust decreases in a climb. Consequently, gamma decreases.

If the pitch angle remains the same, the angle of attack must have to be increased (which increases CL). However, lift remains the same. According to the lift formula, with an increased CL, IAS must be decreased in order to maintain lift constant.

L = ½ p x V2 x CL x S

title:
Which of these statements about the buffet free range in a buffet onset boundary graph are correct or incorrect?

1. When speed increases the buffet free range does not change.
2. When altitude decreases the buffet free range decreases.
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: 1 is correct, 2 is correct.
optionB: 1 is incorrect, 2 is correct.
optionC: 1 is correct, 2 is incorrect.
optionD: 1 is incorrect, 2 is incorrect.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

Stall boundaries set a lower limit to the operating speed, according to the load factor. In the case of a high-speed aircraft, there is also an upper limit which is due to the approach of shock stall and the associated buffet which occurs if the aircraft enters the transonic speed range. The limits associated with these effects give the buffet boundaries.

For a given aircraft there is a Mach number which, even at low angle of attack, cannot be exceeded because of the onset of shock stall. The EAS corresponding to this Mach number falls as altitude increases, so the range of operating speeds is reduced at both ends.

Flying at a different speed will not influence the buffet boundaries, therefore statement 1 is correct.

At altitude, the equivalent stalling speed increases with ‘g’ rather more rapidly than at sea level, because of the Mach number effect on CLMAX. Also, the buffet boundary becomes much more severe. Above a certain altitude the buffet boundary may intersect the stall boundary at a value of ‘g’ lower than the structural limit. This ‘point’ is another representation of “coffin corner”.

We can then conclude that decreasing altitude, increases the buffet margin, therefore statement 2 is incorrect.

title: After suspecting a fuel leak, the aircrew flying a jet transport aircraft decides to divert to the nearest suitable airport. At what speed should they fly?
optionA: Maximum Range Speed
optionB: Maximum Endurance Speed
optionC: M<sub>MO</sub>
optionD: Long Range Speed
explanationTotal:
Note: This question does not have a lot of information, and in fact none of the answers are what we would consider to be fully correct. The most correct answer we believe is best range, but please let us know in the comments if you see this question in an exam, and any information you have about it, as our feedback may not be complete. Alternatively, feedback can be sent to info@atplquestions.com, thank you. We are also under the impression that this has been seen in Principles of Flight, but believe it to be more of a Performance question, so let us know which exam you see this in, thanks.

In the event of a fuel leak, our main problem as a flight crew is the chance of fuel exhaustion before a safe landing has been made. It is for that reason that we must make our way to the nearest suitable airfield as fast as possible, but by using the least amount of fuel; after all, we do not want to run out of fuel faster than we have to, by using it or by leaking it.

It is for this reason that we have to fly at the best range speed, the same as we would when we want to reach a destination whilst using as little fuel as possible. However, this is a different "best range" speed. When we are leaking out fuel, our total fuel "consumption" changes, and goes from the standard fuel consumption/speed curve (which closely follows the drag curve), to the same curve, just lifted up, as the fuel consumption has been increased across the board by whatever rate the fuel is leaking at. Of course, the leak could be variable with speed or pressure, etc. but this is the general idea of it, and we should not have to delve as far as those factors.

The best range of an aircraft is the point at which the fuel consumption is lowest for the highest speed, and this is shown on the graph by the point where a line from the origin first touches the curve. As you can see in the annex above, the best range speed is higher for the curve with the fuel leak.

This is because the fuel is also leaking from the tank, and the faster we go, the less we allow to leak from the tank overall, so the more we have available to burn. This finds an equilibrium with how much drag we are willing to accept by flying faster, and therefore burning fuel at a higher rate.

The faster the fuel leak, the higher this optimal speed becomes, starting at the normal "Best Range" speed for a very small/no leak, and increasing to VMO for incredibly fast fuel leaks.

Further note: We would prefer an answer that mentions something to do with the increased best range speed, or perhaps a speed between best range speed and VMO.

title: What is coefficient of lift, C<sub>L</sub>?
optionA: A dimensionless number that gives the relationship between lift force per unit wing area and dynamic pressure.
optionB: A dimensionless number that gives the relationship between lift force per unit area and true airspeed.
optionC: A number, measured in units of pressure, that gives the dynamic pressure produced at a given airspeed.
optionD: A number, measured in units of force, that gives the lift force at a given airspeed.
explanationTotal:
Coefficient of lift (CL) is a dimensionless coefficient and is the lifting ability of a particular wing. It depends on both the shape of the wing section (fixed design feature) and the angle of attack. This equation is simply a rearrangement of the lift equation where we solve for the lift coefficient in terms of the other variables. The lift coefficient CL is equal to the lift L divided by the quantity: density times half the velocity V squared times the wing area A.

CL = L / (1/2 x q x S x V2)

The quantity one half the density times the velocity squared is called the dynamic pressure (q).

title: During a glide with idle power and constant IAS, if the RPM lever of a constant speed propeller is pushed full forward from its normal cruise position, the propeller pitch will:
optionA: decrease and the rate of descent will increase.
optionB: increase and the rate of descent will decrease.
optionC: increase and the rate of descent will increase.
optionD: decrease and the rate of descent will decrease.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

A single engine airplane fitted with a constant speed propeller may not have a “feathering” capability, as such. However, following engine failure, drag can be reduced to a minimum by “pulling” the RPM (prop) control to the fully coarse position.
In a steady glide with no shaft power from the engine (throttle closed), if the propeller pitch is decreased by pushing forward the prop’ lever, the aircraft Lift/Drag ratio will decrease. This will increase the rate of descent.
The opposite will be true if the propeller pitch is increased.

title: What is a ventral fin and its purpose?
optionA: Fins added above the fuselage to increase directional stability.
optionB: Fins added under the fuselage to increase longitudinal stability.
optionC: Fins added under the fuselage to increase directional stability.
optionD: Fins added above the fuselage to increase longitudinal stability.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Dorsal and ventral fins are used to overcome the instability in the fuselage. A dorsal fin is mounted on top of the fuselage near the rear. Whereas a ventral fin is mounted below.

If the aircraft is yawed to the right, the dorsal and ventral fins will create a side force to the right. The line of action of this force is well aft of the aircraft CG, giving a yawing moment to the left (a stabilizing effect). Directional stability is, consequently, increased

title: On the rear part of the upper surface of an assymetrical aerofoil, when the angle of attack increases, the area covered by an adverse pressure gradient (1) _____ and the speed of the airflow in that area (2) _____.
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: (1) increases; (2) increases
optionB: (1) increases; (2) decreases
optionC: (1) decreases; (2) increases
optionD: (1) decreases; (2) decreases
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
Over an aerofoil, airflow creates a series of static pressure zones, some low pressure and some high, depending on whether the air is fast or slow there. The air all arrives at "freestream" velocity, which we call the TAS, True Airspeed, but the way the streamlines split between top and bottom of the wing causes some stretching or squashing of the streamlines, which increases or decreases the speed of the air. If you are familiar with the venturi tube, you know that air in the throat is faster than air at the mouth, due to lower cross-sectional area. Well this happens above a wing also; the streamlines some distance above the wing remain straight, but the wing squashes the other streamlines into them, therefore faster air, and lower static pressure. Also, the opposite for streamlines that get further apart, the air slows down, creating a high static pressure zone.

This creates a pressure pattern around the wing, which obviously changes with the angle of attack, how the wing presents to the airflow.

Notice the low pressure zone on the top of the wing; that will get stronger and further towards the leading edge up until the stall, as it is squeezing the air streamlines more, and the air is having to go much faster. Notice also how there is little to know pressure zone at the back, which can remain like that, or become a slight high pressure zone at high angles of attack. This is a further contributing factor to what we call an "adverse pressure gradient".

The top surface of the wing has air flowing along it, but due to the air interacting with other air (we call this viscosity), this airflow does not reach the surface of the wing. The particles of air on the surface of the wing are stationary, and there is an increasing amount of airflow in each subsequent particle, moving away from the wing. We call this the boundary layer.

The boundary layer obviously has some slow moving air, whereas the freestream air over the wing is quite fast. When an adverse pressure gradient builds up on the top surface of the wing, the particles in the boundary layer become more and more excited to flow from the high to low pressure, which means flowing backwards along the surface of the wing. This initially turns the laminar boundary layer into a turbulent one. The problem is, as soon as pressure gradient reaches a certain threshold, the particles will begin to flow backwards uncontrollably, creating vortices which separate from the wing and creates the stall (see annex above). This is compounded by the low energy of the boundary layer at high angles of attack, causing a lower speed airflow, to make stall happen at an even lower angle of attack.

In terms of this question, the area covered by an adverse pressure gradient on the top of the aerofoil gets larger with increasing angle of attack, and the pressure gradient gets stronger also. The air in that area will have lower energy, and therefore lower speed due to this, eventually causing the stall.

title:
Which of these statements about the strength of wing tip vortices are correct or incorrect?

I. Assuming no flow separation, the strength of wing tip vortices decreases as the angle of attack increases.
II. The strength of wing tip vortices decreases as the aspect ratio decreases.
optionA: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
optionB: I is incorrect, II is correct.
optionC: I is correct, II is correct.
optionD: I is correct, II is incorrect.
explanationTotal:
Wing tip vortices are a byproduct of lift. They are caused by the pressure differential between the top and bottom of the wing, which causes an updraft of high pressure air around the tip of the wing. This updraft turn into a downdraft behind the wing, creating a vortex. The higher the pressure difference between the top and bottom of the wing, the stronger the vortices.

This question is specifically asking for:

  • Angle of attack: The strength of the vortices (and therefore also induced drag) is proportional to the angle of attack. Therefore; the strength of the vortices increase as the angle of attack increases. And also; the strength of the vortices decrease as the angle of attack decreases. Therefore statement 1 is incorrect!
  • Aspect ratio: The strength of the vortices is inversely proportional with the aspect ratio. Meaning that the strength of the wing tip vortices increase as the aspect ratio decreases. And vice versa: the strength decreases as the aspect ratio increases. Therefore statement 2 is incorrect!

title: Design Manoeuvring Speed (VA) is:
optionA: the maximum speed at which maximum elevator deflection up is allowed.
optionB: the speed that should not be exceeded in the climb.
optionC: the maximum speed at which rolls are allowed.
optionD: the speed at which a heavy transport aeroplane should fly in turbulence.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Design Manoeuvring Speed (VA)

This is the highest speed at which sudden, full elevator deflection can be made without exceeding the design limit load factor.

When establishing VA, the aeroplane is assumed to be flying in straight and level flight and the flight control is suddenly moved to obtain the maximum positive pitch acceleration (nose-up).

VA is slower than the speed at the intersection of the CLMAX line and the positive limit load factor line (point A) to safeguard the tail structure, because of the higher load on the tailplane during the pitch manoeuvre.

title: A multi-engine aircraft with clockwise rotating propellers suffers an engine failure after takeoff. Considering the aircraft maintains a zero bank and no power changes, which situation would lead to the largest rudder deflection?
optionA: Left crosswind, left engine failure.
optionB: Left crosswind, right engine failure.
optionC: Right crosswind, left engine failure.
optionD: Right crosswind, right engine failure.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
For a propeller aircraft the length of the thrust arm is determined by the asymmetric effect of the propeller. At a positive angle of attack and when viewed from the rear, the thrust line of a clockwise rotating propeller is displaced to the right of the engine centre line because the down going blade generates more thrust than the up going blade. Therefore, if both engines rotate clockwise, the right engine will have a longer thrust arm than the left engine. Thus, if the left engine fails, the thrust of the right engine acts through a longer thrust arm and will give a bigger yawing moment. The critical engine is the engine, the failure of which would give the biggest yawing moment. Consequently, we can safely say that with clockwise rotating propellers, the critical engine is the left one.

The aircraft has the natural tendency to swing its nose into the wind in response to a sideslip (left wind results in left yaw).

  • This will add to the already existent tendency to yaw towards the left due to the left engine failure and will increase the difficulty to control and the need for a larger rudder deflection.

Note: This question was reported for AGK, however it should not appear in this subject. We would kindly ask that you inform us if you come across this question in your AGK/POF exam.

title:
Which of these statements about the gust load factor on an aeroplane are correct or incorrect?

I. When the mass decreases, the gust load factor increases.
II. When the altitude increases, the gust load factor increases.
optionA: I is correct, II is correct.
optionB: I is incorrect, II is correct.
optionC: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
optionD: I is correct, II is incorrect.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
A gust is a localized sudden and rapid change to the speed of the air in the atmosphere that can be either horizontal or vertical. The horizontal gust is of little importance because it causes a change to an airplane’s dynamic pressure that results in an insignificant change to the load factor. The vertical gusts are far more important because they change the effective angle of attack, total lift, and the load factor.
The gust load is the extra load imparted to the airplane by vertical gusts or turbulence. Its magnitude is unaffected by increased altitude but is increased with increased aspect ratio and/or decreased mass.
The load factor for any given angle of attack can be derived from the basic load factor for the normal cruise angle of attack because it is increased by the same percentage as the increase of angle of attack.
The load factor deriving from a gust is determined by the magnitude of the vertical velocity of the gust and the forward speed of the airplane.
High wing loading reduces the ‘g’ increment in a gust. This is because the lift increment produced is a smaller proportion of the original lift force for the more heavily loaded aircraft.
For a given TAS and gust speed, the increase of lift will be proportional to the wing area. Therefore, the increase in load factor is inversely proportional to the wing loading.

WingLoading = Weight/(WingArea)

Decreasing mass, decreases wing loading which increases load factor. Therefore, statement 1 is correct.
With increasing altitude, density decreases and any aerodynamic force resulting from a gust will be smaller.
Thus, when comparing two aircraft flying at different altitudes, the one flying in thinner air (higher altitude) will experience a decreased increment in load factor following a gust. Therefore, statement 2 is incorrect.

title:
Refer to figure.
Which line in the diagram represents decreasing positive static longitudinal stability at higher angles of attack?
optionA: Line 3.
optionB: Line 4.
optionC: Line 2.
optionD: Line 1.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Static longitudinal stability depends upon the relationship of angle of attack and pitching moment (CM).

A variation of CG position can cause large changes in the static longitudinal stability. In the conventional airplane configuration, the large changes in stability with CG variation are primarily due to the large changes in the wing contribution. If the incidence of all surfaces remains fixed, the effect of CG position on static longitudinal stability is typified by the chart in figure 1:

As the CG is gradually moved aft, the airplane static stability decreases, then becomes neutral then unstable. The CG position which produces zero slope and neutral static stability is referred to as the “neutral point”. The neutral point defines the most aft CG position without static instability.

Positive static stability is indicated by the curve with negative slope. Moving the CG forward, will increase static longitudinal stability and this is represented by a (steeper) negative slope.

Neutral static stability would be the result if the curve had zero slope. If neutral stability existed, the airplane could be disturbed to some higher or lower lift coefficient without change in pitching moment coefficient.

An airplane which demonstrates a positive slope of the CM versus CL curve would be unstable.

title: For any propeller:
optionA: thrust is the component of the total aerodynamic force on the propeller parallel to the rotational axis.
optionB: the force contributing to propeller torque is perpendicular to the propeller plane of rotation.
optionC: the total aerodynamic force on a blade element may be resolved into two components, torque and lift.

title: Which of the following is/are required in a fully-powered control system but not required for power-assisted controls?
optionA: Power flying control unit.
optionB: Hydraulic servos.
optionC: Artificial feel system.
optionD: Balance tabs and mass balance.
explanationTotal:
FULLY POWERED SYSTEM

A fully powered system means that no control force is felt, since the deflection is done solely by hydraulic pressure. For a fully powered control system, artificial feel unit is needed. Without this system it would be easy to aerodynamically over-stress the aeroplane.

title: Which of the following, in combination with an aural warning, indicates that a light aircraft has entered a fully developed stall?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: IAS significantly below the normal cruising speed.
optionB: Strong yawing tendency that is difficult to control.
optionC: Heavy buffeting felt through the flight controls.
optionD: The nose repeatedly pitching up and down.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
STALL. A stall is an aerodynamic condition which occurs when smooth airflow over the airplane’s wings is disrupted, resulting in loss of lift. Remember that it is possible to exceed the critical AOA at any airspeed, at any attitude, and at any power setting.

  • Impending Stall—an impending stall occurs when the AOA causes a stall warning, but has not yet reached the critical AOA. Indications of an impending stall can include buffeting, stick shaker, or aural warning.
  • Full Stall—a full stall occurs when the critical AOA is exceeded. Indications of a full stall are typically that an uncommanded nose-down pitch cannot be readily arrested, and this may be accompanied by an uncommanded rolling motion. For airplanes equipped with stick pushers, its activation is also a full stall indication.
The longer it takes for the pilot to recognize an impending stall, the more likely it is that a full stall will result.

A stalled wing may be accompanied by one or more of the following:

  • Buffet
  • Poor pitch authority poor roll control (unresponsive flight controls).
  • An inability to arrest descent.

title: A low wing aircraft entering the ground effect during the landing phase will experience...
optionA: a reduction in interference drag and tendency to float.
optionB: an increase in wing-tip vortices.
optionC: a nose-down pitching moment and tendency to float.
optionD: an increase in induced drag.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
When an airplane flies at a height equal to or less than the length of its wingspan the efficiency of its wings is considerably improved. A low wing airplane, just before touchdown, experiences a 50% reduction of its total drag. This phenomenon is ground effect.
Ground effect occurs because the surface alters the airflow pattern around the wings. Primarily, the surface restricts the formation of the wingtip vortices.
When an aircraft enters ground effect during the landing phase of flight, the sudden increase in lift and reduction in drag cause it to experience a floating tendency. The aircraft also tends to pitch nose-down due to the reduction in download on the tail plane.
The magnitude of the wing tip vortices, and thus downwash, also determine the amount of induced drag produced by the wing. The closer the aircraft is to the surface, the greater the reduction in induced drag at any given angle of attack.

Aircraft entering ground effect:

  • Downwash decreases.
  • The effective angle of attack increases.
  • Increased lift during landing if the angle of attack remains constant.
  • The induced angle of attack decreases.
  • Induced drag decreases.
Aircraft leaving ground effect:
  • Downwash increases.
  • The effective angle of attack decreases.
  • Decreased lift during take-off if the angle of attack remains constant.
  • The induced angle of attack increases.
  • Induced drag increases.
Another characteristic associated with ground effect is the change in aircraft trim and stability.
This occurs because the surface deflects the downwash acting behind the wing, thus altering the angle at which the airflow meets the tail plane
This places the tail plane at a less negative, or increased angle of attack, and reduces the download acting on the tail plane. In this condition, the aircraft experiences a nose-down pitching moment (figure 2).
A high T tailed aircraft do not respond in this manner since the tail plane is outside the influence of the downwash.

title: The following factors increase stall speed:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: increasing bank angle, increasing thrust, slat extension.
optionB: a higher weight, selecting a higher flap setting, a forward CG movement.
optionC: an increase in load factor, a forward CG movement, decrease in thrust.
optionD: a lower weight, decreasing bank angle, a smaller flap setting.
explanationTotal:
A forward CG shift will result in a larger downforce required by the tailplane which increases the need for lift. If thrust decreases, the support of weight decreases. Consequently, more lift is required which means that the angle of attack must be increased. This will increase the stall speed.

Any airplane, within the limits of its structure and the strength of the pilot, can be stalled at any airspeed.

VS = √(2W ÷ p S CLMAX)

The equation above well defines the factors affecting the stall speed, in summary; aircraft weight, air density, maximum lift coefficient, and the load factor.

AIRCRAFT WEIGHT.

Stall speed is proportional with the aircraft weight. Stall speed increases, as the weight increases; and decreases as the weight decreases.

AIR DENSITY.

Aircraft stall speeds are usually given in terms of CAS or IAS as an aircraft limitations. However, as seen in the equation above, it is actually a true airspeed which is inversely proportional with the density. Therefore, although it is constant in terms of CAS/IAS, it increases with the altitude because of the density variation.

MAXIMUM LIFT COEFFICIENT.

Maximum lift coefficient may be varied by high lift devices such as flaps and slats. Higher maximum lift coefficients will result in slower stall speeds. Lowest maximum lift coefficient is obtained when flaps are retracted (airplane in clean configuration), thus highest stall speed occurs in clean configuration.

LOAD FACTOR.

Stall speed is proportional with the load factor. It increases as the load factor increases. If VSS is the stall speed of an aircraft in steady level flight, then stall speed during maneuvers will be:
VSN =√n VSS

Or during a turn maneuver:
VSN = VSS ÷ √ cos a

title: A go-around is performed by the crew of a commercial jet aircraft with under-wing-mounted engines and conventional controls. Which of the following is correct?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Nose-down elevator deflection must be applied in order to counteract the large thrust pitch-up couple and to avoid a stall.
optionB: The size of the elevator is sufficient to give enough pitch control regardless of the trim position and applied thrust.
optionC: To counteract the thrust-pitch couple, application of nose-up trim will be required to regain elevator authority.
optionD: The engine's line-of-thrust offset, relative to the fuselage centreline, will produce a nose-down pitch couple.
explanationTotal:
When applying TOGA (takeoff go-around power or thrust) a significant increase in thrust occurs. With underwing mounted engines, as most jet transport category aeroplanes, the engines will create a pitch up moment around the CG. Combined with the commanded pitch-up by the pilot, the pitch attitude can increase too much. This can exceed the critical angle of attack, resulting in a stall.

The acceleration forces felt by the pilot can trigger a sensation of too much pitch-up, resulting in the pilot commanding a pitch-down.

Mitigation during a go-around consists of a good scanning of all the flight parameters by the pilot and giving priority on the instruments instead of sensations. The aeroplane manufacturer can improve this by integrating active flight envelope protection.

title: Consider a swept back wing, with a sideslip to the right. The right wing experiences (I)_____ sweep, (II)_____ lift, and that (III)_____ the lateral stability.
optionA: (I) less; (II) more; (III) increases.
optionB: (I) less; (II) less; (III) decrease.
optionC: (I) more; (II) more; (III) Increase.
optionD: (I) more; (II) less; (III) Decrease.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Wing sweep will help promote lateral stability. When a swept-wing airplane is sideslipping, the wing toward the sideslip will experience a higher velocity normal to the wing's leading edge than the wing away from the sideslip. More lift is generated on the wing toward the sideslip and a roll moment arises that tends to diminish the bank angle and return the airplane to equilibrium.

  • In this case, the airflow over the right wing becomes straighter (less swept). Straighter wings produce more lift, resulting in a larger rolling moment to the left returning the aircraft to a level condition.

title:
Which of these statements about propellers is correct or incorrect?

I. A cruise propeller has a greater geometric pitch compared with a climb propeller.
II. A coarse pitch propeller is more efficient during take-off and in the climb, but is less efficient in the cruise, when compared with a fine pitch propeller.
optionA: I is correct, II is incorrect.
optionB: I is incorrect, II is correct.
optionC: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
optionD: I is correct, II is correct.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The blade angle of a fixed-pitch propeller is constant, but the helix angle and the angle of attack will vary according to its forward speed. To ensure its efficient operation the blade angle of attack of a fixed-pitch propeller must be close to the optimum and is that which produces the greatest excess of horizontal lift (thrust) over drag.
A large blade angle or coarse pitch is suitable for high-speed flight (cruise). The geometric pitch is the distance the propeller would travel forward in one complete revolution if it were moving through the air at the blade angle. The higher the blade angle the higher the geometric pitch. Therefore, statement 1 is correct.
In low forward speed flight, the angle of attack is large. This produces a large amount of thrust but at the same time it creates a large amount of drag. To maintain a constant RPM, it is essential to overcome the drag and that requires a high propeller torque. The propeller efficiency in these circumstances is low.
By increasing the speed, the helix angle increases. Although the angle of attack of is smaller and less thrust is produced the amount of drag induced is significantly less, this makes the propeller efficiency proportionately greater. It is this speed that attains the greatest propeller efficiency. Therefore, statement 2 is incorrect.

title: What is the SI unit of measurement for pressure?
optionA: bar/dm<sup>2</sup>
optionB: kg/m<sup>3</sup>
optionC: lb/gal
optionD: N/m<sup>2</sup>
explanationTotal: Pressure is the amount of force applied perpendicular to the surface of an object per unit area. The SI unit for pressure is the pascal (Pa), equal to one newton per square metre (N/m<sup>2</sup>).

title:
Refer to figure.
Assuming zero thrust, the point on the diagram corresponding to the value for minimum sink rate is:
optionA: Point 1.
optionB: Point 3.
optionC: Point 4.
optionD: Point 2.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The polar curve of an airfoil is the graphical relationship of the coefficients of lift and drag plotted against each other, the resulting graph is as shown in figure 1. It reveals that the total lift and total drag increase from point A to a maximum at point D, thus the angle of attack of the wings increases in the same manner. Therefore, the speed decreases from a maximum at point A to a minimum at point D.
Long Range Cruise (LRC) speed is the speed above the maximum-range cruise (MRC) speed which provides 99 percent of the absolute maximum specific range. The advantage is that 1 percent of range is traded for 3 to 5 percent higher cruise velocity.
Point A: is between VMD and the maximum speed and has the minimum drag coefficient. It therefore approximates VY for a jet airplane.
Point B: is the point at which a tangent from the origin touches the polar curve, which is at the point at which the total drag is minimum, the lift/drag ratio is maximum and the IAS in level flight is VMD. This is also the speed at which the longest glide distance will be achieved.
Point C: falls between VMD and VS and is approximately VMP, which approximates to the speed of VY for a piston/propeller airplane and indicates the value at which the minimum sink rate will occur. It is the speed that will attain the maximum endurance during a descent.
Point D: is where CL and CD are both maximum and the point at which the minimum speed in level flight, the stalling speed, VS is attained.

title: Assuming constant IAS, when an aeroplane leaves ground effect it experiences...
optionA: Increased downwash, induced angle of attack increases and induced drag increases.
optionB: Decreased downwash, induced angle of attack increases and induced drag increases.
optionC: Decreased downwash, induced angle of attack decreases and induced drag decreases.
optionD: Increased downwash, induced angle of attack decreases and induced drag decreases.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Ground effect is the aerodynamic effect of more lift and less drag when the wings are relatively close to a fixed surface. Several aerodynamical parameters are changed by the presence of the ground or water surface.

Aircraft entering ground effect:

  • Downwash decreases.
  • The effective angle of attack increases.
  • Increased lift during landing if the angle of attack remains constant.
  • The induced angle of attack decreases.
  • Induced drag decreases.
Aircraft leaving ground effect:
  • Downwash increases.
  • The effective angle of attack decreases.
  • Decreased lift during take-off if the angle of attack remains constant.
  • The induced angle of attack increases.
  • pof.

title: What happens to the blade pitch of a constant speed propeller on ground roll during takeoff?
optionA: Increases.
optionB: Decreases.
optionC: Remains constant.
optionD: Same effect as the fixed pitch propeller.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
A propeller is a fan, fitted with between two and six aerodynamic blades that is used to convert rotational motion into forward thrust for the propulsion of an aeroplane through the air.

The blades of the propeller are small aerodynamic aerofoils mounted vertically on a horizontal shaft that is rotated by either a piston engine or a turbine-driven engine.

BLADE ANGLE (PITCH)

The angle between the blade chord and the plane of rotation.

ANGLE OF ATTACK

The path of the propeller through the air determines the direction of the relative airflow. The angle between the blade chord and the relative airflow is the angle of attack (α). The angle of attack (α) is the result of propeller rotational velocity (RPM) and aircraft forward velocity (TAS).

Because the rotational velocity of the blade increases with distance from the propeller shaft and the fact that the aeroplane is moving forward, then the angle of attack of the blade varies at different distances from the shaft.

CONSTANT SPEED PROPELLER

The purpose of a variable-pitch propeller is to either manually or automatically maintain the optimum angle of attack to maximize the lift/drag ratio of the propeller as the aeroplane speed changes.

Constant-speed propellers enable the pilot to select the RPM for maximum power or maximum efficiency and a propeller governor varies the propeller pitch angle as required to maintain the selected RPM.

Figure shows the conditions during the early stages of the take-off roll. The RPM is set to maximum and the TAS is low. The angle of attack is optimum and maximum available efficiency is obtained. As the aircraft continues to accelerate, the TAS will increase, which decreases the angle of attack of the blades. Less thrust will be generated and less propeller torque. This gives less resistance for the engine to overcome and RPM would tend to increase. The propeller governor senses the RPM increase and increases pitch to maintain the blade angle of attack constant.

title: Following de-icing on a foggy morning, a pilot has to apply more thrust than expected during the take-off roll. Which of the following could have caused this?
optionA: A higher angle of attack due to the higher speed in icing conditions.
optionB: Ice build-up remaining on the fuselage means that the aircraft is heavier than expected.
optionC: Increased fuel density due to low temperatures.
optionD: Reduced air density due to low temperatures.
explanationTotal:
Ice build-up on an airframe:
  • Increases drag - By significantly disturbing the shape of the airframe, parasite drag is increased.
  • Decreases lift - By disturbing the shape of the wings, ice can cause a large reduction in lift.
  • Increase Weight - Ice build-up can be quite significant, and water is a naturally heavy substance, so lots of weight can be added by the presence of ice.

During de-icing on the ground, the fuselage does not always need to be de-iced. Frost or thin layers of ice are usually acceptable to leave on the fuselage, as long as it is not deemed a critical area, such as the wings, control surfaces, engine inlets, propellers, etc. (aircraft with rear mounted engines often have to de-ice the whole fuselage to stop ice shedding off into the engines).

This build-up could allow extra weight to be carried in the form of ice or frost during the take-off roll. Whilst it is hoped that only a small amount of ice/frost would be carried, on a large fuselage, that could amount to quite a large weight that is unaccounted for and unknown in value. This could be felt by the pilot as a lack of thrust due to the lower acceleration, and they might have to apply more thrust to account for this.

To address the other options:

  • "A higher angle of attack due to the higher speed in icing conditions."
    • Higher speed would cause a lower angle of attack, so this is not correct.
  • "Ice build-up remaining on the fuselage means you are heavier than expected."
    • As discussed above, whilst this should be kept to a minimum, it is possible for this to be the case.
  • "Increased fuel density due to low temperatures."
    • Yes, low temperatures will cause higher fuel density, but large aircraft are fuelled up by mass, and not by volume, so this will just mean that the fuel uses up less of the tank volume than it would in warmer conditions.
  • "Reduced air density due to low temperatures."
    • Low temperatures cause high air density, which would feel like more power than usual.

title: If the lift generated by a given wing is 1000 kN, what will be the lift if the wing area is doubled?
explanationTotal:
Lift can be calculated as follows:
L= CL × ½ rho × V2 × S

Where:

  • CL is lift coefficient (without dimension)
  • p is density
  • V is velocity [m/s] (velocity is TAS)
  • S is surface area [m2]
  • L is lift [N]
From the lift equation, we can see that if wing area increases, lift will increase in the same proportion. Therefore, if wing area is doubled, lift will double: 1 000 kN x 2 = 2 000 kN

title: The following is a correct design gust value factor applied in certification under EASA CS-25:
optionA: 25 ft/sec at V<sub>D</sub>.
optionB: 50 ft/sec at V<sub>D</sub>.
optionC: 55 ft/sec at V<sub>B</sub>.
optionD: 66 ft/sec at V<sub>C</sub>.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
It is a design requiremnt of CS25 (old JAR25) that an airframe structure must be strong enough to withstand gusts both positive and negative that would cause a change of angle of attack so increasing load factor at three specified design speeds.

  • Speed VB (max gust intensity speed): +/- 66 ft/sec
  • Speed VC (design cruise speed): +/- 50 ft/sec
  • Speed VD (design dive speed): +/- 25 ft/sec.

VB is quite a low airspeed so the aircraft would be flying at high alpha and it would take some time for an aircraft to slow from VC (the design cruising speed) to VB if it flew into turbulence. Therefore, another design strength requirement is for the aircraft also to be strong enough to withstand a vertical gust of 50 ft/ sec at VC.

title: What would happen to an aircraft’s rate of descent and the angle of descent when deploying the speed brakes in flight?
optionA: The rate of descent will increase and the descent angle will decrease.
optionB: Both the rate of descent and the descent angle will decrease.
optionC: Both the rate of descent and the descent angle will increase.
optionD: The rate of descent will decrease and the descent angle will increase.
explanationTotal:
The overall rate of descent and angle of descent will be higher with more Drag.
In flight, it is sometimes necessary to decrease VMD by deliberately increasing the total drag. The use of speed brakes or spoilers causes an increase in profile drag.
Speed brakes are devices to increase the drag of an aircraft when it is required to decelerate quickly or to descend rapidly.

title: When entering ground effect, maintaining the same coefficient of lift, C<sub>L</sub>, requires...
optionA: flaps to be set to the landing configuration.
optionB: a greater angle of attack.
optionC: a lower angle of attack.
optionD: an increase in thrust.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
When an airplane flies at a height equal to or less than the length of its wingspan the efficiency of its wings is considerably improved. A low wing airplane, just before touchdown, experiences a 50% reduction of its total drag. This phenomenon is ground effect.
Ground effect occurs because the surface alters the airflow pattern around the wings. Primarily, the surface restricts the formation of the wingtip vortices.
When an aircraft enters ground effect during the landing phase of flight, the sudden increase in lift and reduction in drag cause it to experience a floating tendency. The aircraft also tends to pitch nose-down due to the reduction in download on the tail plane.
The magnitude of the wing tip vortices, and thus downwash, also determine the amount of induced drag produced by the wing. The closer the aircraft is to the surface, the greater the reduction in induced drag at any given angle of attack.

Aircraft entering ground effect:

  • Downwash decreases.
  • The effective angle of attack increases.
  • Increased lift during landing if the angle of attack remains constant.
  • The induced angle of attack decreases.
  • Induced drag decreases.
Aircraft leaving ground effect:
  • Downwash increases.
  • The effective angle of attack decreases.
  • Decreased lift during take-off if the angle of attack remains constant.
  • The induced angle of attack increases.
  • Induced drag increases.
As seen in figure 2, when entering ground effect, for the same angle of attack, lift is increased. Thus, to maintain the same CL as when before entering ground effect, the angle of attack should be decreased in order to decrease CL.

title: What happens following the deployment of leading edge devices, while the trailing edge flaps remain retracted?
optionA: C<sub>LMAX</sub> is increased, approach and landing speeds are decreased, and the nose down attitude gives the pilot a better view of the runway.
optionB: C<sub>LMAX</sub> is decreased, approach and landing speeds are increased, but the nose down attitude gives the pilot a better view of the runway.
optionC: C<sub>LMAX</sub> is increased, approach and landing speeds are decreased, but the nose-up attitude will give the pilot a poorer view of the runway.
optionD: C<sub>LMAX</sub> is decreased, approach and landing speeds are decreased, but the nose up attitude gives the pilot a poorer view of the runway.
explanationTotal:
Leading edge devices increase lift at the leading-edge part of the wing, consequently, pitch up moment is generated while lowering them, which may result in a poorer view of the runway.

The contribution to CL is approximately 0.8 – 1, which is very high and the greatest among leading and trailing edge devices. CLMAX is also increased, which allows lower approach and landing speeds. In practice, they increase critical angle of attack as well

title: Which of the following factors leads to the maximum flight time of a glide?
optionA: Headwind.
optionB: Low mass.
optionC: High mass.
optionD: Tailwind.
explanationTotal:
The best glide angle occurs at VMD, flying at this speed will give the best range in a glide. Glide angle (and glide range) itself is independent of aircraft mass - provided the aircraft glides at VMD, since it is the lift over drag (L/D) ratio that determines the gliding range and it is unchanged with mass. However, a Speed faster or slower than VMD will lead to steeper glide angles.

Glide angle = CD / CL

GLIDING DISTANCE

Wind speed is an important practical influence on gliding distance over the surface.

  • With a tailwind, the glide distance achieved will be increased as a result of the increased groundspeed.
    Whereas with a headwind, it will be reduced because of the consequently slower groundspeed.
GLIDING TIME
The aircraft's mass varies the time the aircraft will glide for.
  • The heavier the aircraft is, the higher the airspeed must be to obtain the same glide ratio (higher VMD) => Glide duration will be decreased.
    If two aircraft have the same L/D ratio but different weights and start a glide from the same altitude, the heavier aircraft gliding at a higher airspeed will arrive at the same touchdown point in a shorter time. However, both aircraft will cover the same distance but the lighter one will take a longer time to do so.
SUMMARY:

Glide Distance (Varies with wind)

=> Tailwind increases glide distance
=> Headwind decreases glide distance

Glide Duration (Varies with mass)

=> Low mass increases glide duration
=> High mass decreases glide duration

title: A manufacturer shortens the fuselage of a 9 seat plane to a 6 seat plane. They make the vertical fin and horizontal stabiliser bigger. What is the effect of increasing the surface of the vertical fin?
optionA: Pitch up, due to more drag of the higher fin creating a pitch up moment.
optionB: Lateral stability inceases because of the height of the fin increses.
optionC: Increasing stick force because of the bigger rudder.
optionD: Decreasing longitudinal stability because of the shorter fuselage.
explanationTotal:
IMPORTANT NOTE: Based on the feedback received, it's noted that the official question is longer. However, no additional comments on its wording have been received. Please let us know if you come across this question.

Factors that contribute positively to static lateral stability include dihedral, a high wing configuration, sweepback, and a large vertical stabilizer (fin).

The diagram illustrates that the fin can contribute a slight dihedral effect. When the fin is sizable, the side force generated during a sideslip can induce both a rolling moment and a significant yawing moment. However, it's essential to note that the fin's contribution to pure lateral static stability is typically minimal.

title: What combined lateral/directional phenomenon can be caused by a yaw disturbance in the transonic speed range?
optionA: Spiral divergence
optionB: Long period oscillation
optionC: Phugoid
optionD: Dutch roll
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
Learning Objective 081.04.06.03.03: Describe how the asymmetric nature of shock waves on both wings, at high Mach numbers, can lead to Dutch roll.

Dutch Roll

Dutch roll is a coupled lateral and directional oscillation which is undesirable because of the oscillatory nature. Dutch roll can occur when the static lateral stability (caused by dihedral, etc.) is high in comparison to the static directional stability (caused by the tail fin, etc.)

Asymmetric shockwaves

Modern transport jet aircraft tend to cruise at high altitudes with high Mach numbers, very close to - or just inside - the transonic regime. This is the range of speeds (At and above MCRIT) where some of the aircraft experiences supersonic airflow, but not all the aircraft does. This brings rise to shockwaves, first on the upper wing surfaces near the roots, then spreading to other areas of the aircraft. Shockwaves produce quite high drag forces, classed as "wave drag".

If the shockwaves form asymmetrically on the aircraft, whether due to different airflow patterns over the wings, small differences in the aircraft structure, control surfaces, etc., then the different drag forces can cause a yawing motion, which sets off the oscillation known as Dutch roll. This Dutch roll would be made worse by the shockwaves forming on the faster wing, reducing lift and increasing drag to drop it down and drag it back, exacerbating the Dutch roll.

title: You are on an approach when extending flaps, due to a malfunction the right flap does not extend. What will happen to the aircraft?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Plane will bank right and left wing may stall.
optionB: Plane will bank left and right wing may stall.
optionC: Plane will bank right and right wing may stall.
optionD: Plane will go into a spin.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Since flaps significantly change the aerodynamic characteristics of the wing both by increased lift and increased drag, abnormal asymmetric operation of the augmentation device could seriously jeopardise flight safety by asymmetrically loading the wings.

If the situation is allowed to progress unchecked, it will result in a pronounced roll towards the wing with the lessor amount of flap extended. In this case, it is possible that the induced roll could exceed the amount of aileron authority available and could result in a spin or other loss of control situation.

In all cases of asymmetric flap, the wing with the greater amount of flap extended is producing a substantially higher amount of lift. At the same time, increased drag on the flaps-down side creates a pronounced adverse yaw situation, with the nose swinging toward the wing with most flaps deflected.

title: Which of the following speeds would be used to calculate the climb gradient?
optionA: IAS
optionB: TAS
optionC: CAS
optionD: EAS
explanationTotal:
The climb gradient is a measure of how much altitude is gained per unit of distance travelled horizontally. It is usually measured as a percentage, so is how many feet are gained vertically for each 100 feet travelled horizontally.

To calculate it in still air (no wind), the following formula can be used:

Rate of Climb (ft/min) = Climb Gradient (%) x TAS (kt)

Therefore:

Climb Gradient = Rate of Climb / TAS

This formula is a slight approximation, but is still very accurate.

TAS (True Air Speed) is used in this formula, as that is the actual speed of the air flowing over the aircraft, not one of the other airspeeds, which are differen by either density, compressibility, or measurement inaccuracies.

To calculate the climb gradient including wind, use ground speed instead of TAS.

title: When a turn is initiated, adverse yaw is:
optionA: a momentary yawing motion opposite to the turn due to an incorrect differential aileron movement.
optionB: the tendency of an aeroplane to yaw in the same direction of turn due to the different wing speeds.
optionC: the tendency of an aeroplane to yaw in the opposite direction of turn mainly due to the difference in aileron form drag.
optionD: the tendency of an aeroplane to yaw in the opposite direction of turn mainly due to the difference in induced drag on each wing.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Adverse yaw is the tendency of an airplane to yaw in the opposite direction of the turn. For example, as you roll to the right, your aircraft may initially yaw to the left.

When you roll your aircraft to the right, your right aileron goes up, and your left aileron goes down. The aileron in the upward position (the right aileron in this example) creates less lift and less drag than the aileron that is lowered. The aileron angled downward (the left aileron in this example) produces more drag and more lift, initially yawing the airplane in the opposite direction of your roll.

title: To side slip an aircraft to the right, the pilot would apply:
optionA: Control column right, rudder right.
optionB: Control column left, rudder right.
optionC: Control column right, rudder left.
optionD: Control column left, rudder left.
explanationTotal:
Intentional slip, either forward slip or sideslip, is an intentional cross control manoeuver in which the pilot has made an aileron input in one direction with a simultaneous rudder input in the opposite direction.

To side slip and aircraft to the right, left rudder must be applied to yaw the aircraft to the left. The secondary effect of a left yaw will be a left roll. To prevent this secondary effect, right aileron must be applied simultaneously.

title:
Which of these statements about flutter are correct or incorrect?

I. If flutter occurs, IAS should be kept constant.
II. Resistance to flutter increases with reducing wing stiffness.
optionA: I is incorrect, II is correct.
optionB: I is correct, II is incorrect.
optionC: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
optionD: I is correct, II is correct.
explanationTotal:
Flutter is a phenomenon that can occur when an airfoil is subjected to aerodynamic forces.
Flutter is an oscillation caused by interaction of aerodynamic forces, structural elasticity and inertial effects.

Flutter happens when the eigenfrequencies of two oscillations move close together so their motions can reinforce themselves mutually.

When that happens, then the amplitude will increase with each oscillation, up to a point where the amplitude is big enough to break things.

Flutter is a very dangerous condition; if it is not stopped, it can cause structural failure and potentially lead to a fatal accident.

There are four ways to stop flutter.

  1. Limit the flight envelope; immediately leave the speed at which flutter is possible
  2. Increase damping; this can be done by for instance adding some friction
  3. Increase stiffness; this reduces eigenfrequencies which makes flutter less likely
  4. Reduce mass; If a wing is made lighter, the eigenfrequency will move up, increasing flutter speeds.

title: Above tropopause, an aircraft is descending from FL300 at a constant mach. Which of the following is correct?
optionA: TAS constant.
optionB: IAS decrease.
optionC: C<sub>L</sub> increase.
optionD: TAS increases.
explanationTotal:
Mach number = True Air Speed (TAS) / Local Speed of Sound (LSS)
LSS = 38.96 √Absolute Temperature (K)
  1. Above the tropopause, temperature remains constant. Local Speed of sound being only dependant on temperature, will not change.
    Since Mach number and LSS are constant => TAS must also remain the same.
  2. Density and pressure continue to decrease with increasing altitude (also above the tropopause). Therefore, in a descent, density is increasing.
    IAS = 1/2 p V2 (Where V = TAS)
    When density "p" increases in a descent and TAS remains contant => IAS increases.

title: Given an aeroplane with a propeller turning clockwise as seen from behind, the torque effect during the take off run will tend to:
optionA: roll the aeroplane to the left.
optionB: roll the aeroplane to the right.
optionC: pitch the aeroplane nose down.
optionD: pitch the aeroplane nose up.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
On take-off, rotation of a single-engine propeller causes an aircraft to swing to one side, particularly those fitted with a tail-dragger undercarriage. The main causes of this are:

  • Slipstream effect
  • Torque reaction
  • Gyroscopic effect
  • Asymmetric blade effect

Torque reaction

To analyze these effects, consider a right-handed propeller, which rotates clockwise as viewed from the cockpit.
This occurs because the air resists the motion of the propeller. In so doing, it tends to twist the engine and airframe in the opposite direction to the propeller (counterclockwise).
This causes the aircraft to roll to the left and, whilst on the ground, places more weight on the left wheel than the right wheel. This effectively increases the rolling resistance (drag) of the left wheel, thus slowing the aircraft down and causing it to yaw to the left.

title:
Refer to figure.
Assuming no pilot input the motion of the aeroplane in the diagram shows:
optionA: dynamic longitudinal stability.
optionB: dynamic longitudinal instability.
optionC: static longitudinal instability.
optionD: neutral dynamic longitudinal stability.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Dynamic Stability is the subsequent long-term response of an airplane to a disturbance to its equilibrium. It is the change to the stability of an airplane with the passage of time. Any disturbance causes changes to the aerodynamic forces and moments acting on the airplane that are complex, particularly if the displacement is to its directional stability because it affects the airplane in both the yawing and rolling planes.

An airplane that is statically stable is not necessarily dynamically stable. However, for an airplane to be dynamically stable it must be statically stable. In other words, it cannot have long-term stability without first having short-term stability. An airplane that has positive static stability may be dynamically neutral, stable, or unstable; but an airplane that is statically unstable can never attain dynamic stability. The dynamic stability of an airplane is dependent on the airplane design, its speed, and the altitude at which it is flying.

There are five states of dynamic stability and for each of them the airplane must have positive static stability.

Negative dynamic stability – the amplitude of the oscillation increases with the passage of time.

Neutral dynamic stability – the amplitude of the oscillation remains constant with the passage of time.

Positive dynamic stability – the amplitude of the oscillation decreases with the passage of time.

‘Dead beat’ positive dynamic stability – the oscillations cease immediately because they are heavily damped.

‘Divergent’ negative dynamic stability – the oscillations cease because the motion completely diverges from the original motion.

title:
(For this question use annex 081-025 issue date July 2006).
Which statement is correct regarding the pitching moment coefficient CM versus angle of attack diagram?
optionA: Line 3 shows an aeroplane with reducing static longitudinal stability at high angles of attack.
optionB: Line 4 shows an aeroplane with reducing static longitudinal stability at very high angles of attack.
optionC: Line 4 shows an aeroplane with greater static longitudinal stability at low angles of attack than that in shown line 3.
optionD: Line 1 shows an aeroplane with increasing static longitudinally instability at very high angles of attack.
explanationTotal:
The point where an aircraft’s total sum of a pressure field is acting upon the body is called the Center of Pressure (CP).
This is the point where the resultant vector of lift is said to be operating.
As the airfoil or Angle of attack changes (thus changing the lift coefficient), this pressure field will change and so will the center of pressure.

Aircraft longitudinal stability is directly related to Centre of Gravity (CG) position.
An aircraft with a more forward CG is more longitudinally stable than an aircraft with a more aft CG.
Placing the CG beyond the forward limit can cause an unacceptably high value of longitudinal stability, decreasing manoeuvrability by a significant amount.

If an aircraft is longitudinally stable, an increase in Angle of Attack (α) results in a negative pitching moment.
The nose will slightly fall down, decreasing the Angle of Attack.
If this aircraft has a decrease of Angle of Attack, the nose will come slightly upwards again, creating a positive pitching moment again by slightly raising the nose.

We see that line 3 starts off as having static longitudinal stability, as the line moves downward at first.
This means that for a higher Angle of attack, a pitch down moment is induced.
Towards the middle of this line, we see that the line flattens out, reducing static longitudinal stability at higher angles of attack.

title: An aeroplane is flying at its 1.3 g buffet margin maximum altitude for a given mass, CG position and speed. If parameters remain unchanged while maintaining level flight, the aeroplane will be able to:
optionA: Perform any manoeuvre with load factor of 2.0 g without experiencing low speed of high speed buffet.
optionB: Sustain a positive normal acceleration of 0.3 g Without experiencing either low or high speed buffet.
optionC: Sustain a positive normal acceleration increment of 1.0 g without experiencing high speed buffet.
optionD: Perform a level turn with 45 of bank without experiencing low speed buffet.
explanationTotal:
This is a poorly worded question.
In straight and level flight, the aircraft experiences a load factor of 1 (1 g). The aircraft would be able to withstand a positive normal acceleration of 0.3 g, which totals the buffet margin of 1.3 g.

“performs a level turn with 45 of bank without experiencing low speed buffet” Incorrect.
Load factor = 1 /cos (bank angle)
Load factor = 1 / cos (45º) = 1.41 g
  • 1.41 g exceeds the buffet margin (1.3 g).

title: An aircraft is climbing at a constant IAS close to V<sub>MO</sub> above FL230. What could the flight crew do to avoid accidentally exceeding M<sub>MO</sub>? The flight crew must...
optionA: decelerate past V<sub>S0</sub> to avoid exceeding M<sub>MO</sub>.
optionB: stop flying at a constant IAS and fly at a constant TAS.
optionC: stop flying at a constant IAS and fly at a constant Mach number.
optionD: accelerate past V<sub>MO</sub> to avoid exceeding M<sub>MO</sub>.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The Mach number is defined as the ratio between the TAS and the LSS (Local speed of sound).
It is an indication of how fast an aircraft is travelling with relation to the sound waves that surround it.

The Mach number may be calculated as follows:

M=TAS/LSS=(TAS(kt))/(38.95∗√(T(K)))

The speed of propagation of small pressure waves depends upon the temperature of the air ONLY.

Effect on Mach Number of Climbing at a Constant IAS:
- Temperature decreases with increasing altitude, so the speed of sound will decrease as altitude is increased.
- If altitude is increased at a constant IAS, the TAS increases.
- Therefore, the Mach number will increase if altitude is increased at a constant IAS. This is because TAS gets bigger and LSS gets smaller.

As the climb continues, an altitude will be reached at which the flight crew must stop flying at a constant IAS and fly at a constant Mach number, to avoid accidentally exceeding MMO.

title: As an aeroplane slows down during the approach, the wing tip vortices and downwash will vary in intensity. How does this affect the induced angle of attack? Induced angle of attack will...
optionA: decrease, especially near the wing tip.
optionB: increase, especially at the leading edge.
optionC: increase, especially near the wing tip.
optionD: decrease, especially at the leading edge.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The airflow around an aerofoil section sets up a pressure differential between the upper and lower surfaces.

The lower surface of a wing is normally at a pressure above atmospheric, whilst the upper surface is at a pressure below atmospheric. Beyond the wing tips the air is nominally at atmospheric pressure. This causes a spanwise flow of air outward away from the fuselage on the lower surface and an inward flow toward the fuselage on the upper surface. At the trailing edge of the wing, where the two flows meet, a twisting motion is imparted to the air and a series of vortices form. These are trailing edge vortices.

The effect of these vortices is to create more down wash behind the wing than up wash in front of the wing. This results in the effective air flow (EAF) being inclined to the relative air flow (RAF) by an angle called the induced angle of attack (αi).

Because of this local increase in induced angle of attack, the overall lift generated by a wing will be below the value that would be generated if there were no spanwise pressure differential.

It is the production of lift itself which reduces the magnitude of the lift force being generated. To replace the lift lost by the increased downwash, the aircraft must be flown at a higher angle of attack. This increases drag. This extra drag is called induced drag. The stronger the vortices, the greater the induced drag.

Induced drag increases with decreasing speed (for a constant lift force). This is because, as speed decreases, the downwash caused by the tip vortices becomes more significant, the rearward inclination of the lift is bigger, and therefore induced drag is higher.

title: The pitch up tendency of an aeroplane with swept back wings during a stall is caused by the:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: aft movement of the centre of gravity.
optionB: forward movement of the centre of pressure.
optionC: aft movement of the centre of pressure.
optionD: forward movement of the centre of gravity.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Firstly, to answer of question you don’t even know the tendency of a swept wings during a stall. A pitch tendency can only be cause by either a forward movement of the centre of pressure or a aft movement of the centre of gravity.
