optionC: The engines may overspeed as the autothrottle attempts to maintain airspeed.
optionD: The aeroplane may overspeed in an attempt to maintain the rate of climb.
explanationTotal:
The autopilot's vertical speed mode allows you to perform constant-rate climbs and descents. In this mode, the vertical speed is prioritised over airspeed. When you engage the vertical speed mode, the FD/autopilot will attempt to maintain the specified vertical speed until you choose a different setting in autopilot, the aircraft reaches an assigned altitude set into the assigned altitude selector/alerter, or the autopilot is disconnected.

As altitude increases and the air gets thinner, the power available and the IAS will reduce for a given pitch setting - the vertical speed will reduce for a certain pitch attitude. Consequently, the autopilot will gradually increase pitch to chase the selected vertical speed. This results in further decreased IAS. Ultimately, this could lead to a stall.

title: One of the main disadvantages of stabiliser trim system, compared to a conventional trim tab system, is that...
optionA: it reduces the effective range of pitch control.
optionB: it is more complex and heavy.
optionC: it is less powerful and gives a decreased ability to trim for larger CG ranges.
optionD: the drag is greater in the trimmed state.
explanationTotal:
The forces on a jet transport aeroplane are very high in flight.
The wing surfaces are large and travel at high speeds, generating lots of lift.

A trim tab is an easy solution in general aviation aircraft, as the forces are much smaller and it’s a lot cheaper and lighter than a stabilizer.
However, the trim tab is not able to withstand the forces at very high speeds and is not powerful enough to generate the loads required for a change in configuration.
A stabilizer is powerful enough and is therefore the best suitable option for transport jet aeroplanes.

title: When a jet transport aeroplane takes off with the CG at the aft limit and the trimmable horizontal stabiliser (THS) is positioned at the maximum allowable nose down position for take-off:
optionA: rotation will require higher than normal stick force.
optionB: early nose wheel raising will take place.
optionC: there will be a tendency to under-rotate.
optionD: rotation will be normal using the normal rotation technique.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
With CG in an aft position, within the CG envelope, the aeroplane is tail-heavy, which causes the stick force to be much less than it would be for a neutral CG position. This “very light nose” effect of too aft CG position gives the greatest tendency for the nose to lift which makes the rotation so easy that it could as easily lead to a tail strike.

However, if combined with the trimmable horizontal stabiliser (THS) positioned at the maximum allowable nose down position for take-off, rotation will be normal.

title: In order to keep straight and level, if the airspeed increases, the EAF is (1) _____, the effective AoA is (2) ______ and the induced drag is (3) ______.
optionA: (1) shallower, (2) greater, (3) smaller
optionB: (1) steeper, (2) greater, (3) greater
optionC: (1) shallower, (2) smaller, (3) smaller
optionD: (1) shallower, (2) greater, (3) greater
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
The purpose of this question is to combine two different items from the Learning Objectives.

The first is to use the lift formula:

LIFT = ½ x ρ x V2 x S x CL

and determine that in order to keep straight and level flight (L=W), an increase in speed must be balanced with a decrease in CL, which is achieved by decreasing the angle of attack.

The other part is to establish a relationship between induced drag and speed. From the graph attached to this explanation, we can conclude that an increase in speed leads to an decrease in induced drag. If you refer to the second attached figure, we can conclude how the Effective Airflow, Effective Angle of Attack, and Induced Drag behave:

Wing tip vortices create certain vertical velocity components in the airflow in the vicinity of the wing, both in front of and behind it. These vertical velocities strengthen upwash and downwash, which reduce the effective angle of attack. The stronger the vortices, the greater the reduction in effective angle of attack.

The effective angle of attack is the actual or effective angle of attack at the aerofoil.

In level flight at a given mass the lift generated is the same at all forward speeds above the stalling speed. Because the angle of attack must decrease with increasing speed the same downwash speed has less effect at a high speed than it does at a low forward speed because it has a smaller downwash vector.

Thus, the downwash angle is less at higher speeds than it is at lower forward speeds. Therefore, the induced drag is decreased at high speeds.

title:
Which statement about an aeroplane leaving ground effect is correct?

I. The downwash angle remains constant.
II. The induced angle of attack decreases.
optionA: I is correct, II is correct.
optionB: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
optionC: I is correct, II is incorrect.
optionD: I is incorrect, II is correct.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
When taking-off or landing, the proximity to the ground prevents full development of the trailing vortices, making them much weaker than in normal flight. This leads to a decrease in downwash, therefore a higher effect angle of attack which also means a smaller induced angle of attack.

This question is asking what will happen when leaving ground effect:

  • Downwash angle: When leaving ground effect, the effect of the vortices is increased therefore our downwash angle will increase. Therefore statement 1 is incorrect!

  • Induced angle of attack: When leaving ground effect, because of the increase in downwash, the induced angle of attack will increase leading to an increase in induced drag. Therefore statement 2 is incorrect!

title:
Refer to figure.
The 2 aircraft in the annex above encounter a degradation in their fly-by-wire control system. Which statement is correct?
optionA: Both aeroplanes will have significant changes in control.
optionB: Only aircraft 2 will have significant changes in control.
optionC: The control of both aircraft will be unaffected.
optionD: Only aircraft 1 will have significant changes in control.
explanationTotal:
Note: We have very minimal and broken feedback about this but a few reports of it coming up, so please read the exam question carefully and do report back if you had this in the exam, along with anything you can remember about it, thank you!

This question is incredibly vague, and as yet we really don't know what the examiner wants from us, and the answer is not confirmed (we are not very sure of it either). In particular, we don't know how degraded the FBW system is, and what the options are regarding the control differences.

FLY-BY-WIRE
In a fly-by-wire aircraft, the pilot inputs commands via a sidestick or yoke to a computer. The computer then processes these inputs and sends corresponding electrical signals to the servo valve which in turn controls the movement of a hydraulic actuator, which will hydraulically deflect a flight control surface. There are numerous advantages to fly by wire systems, including weight savings and safety features that can be incorporated into the computer software.

FBW also enables highly reliable flight envelope protection systems which, provided the FBW system functions at its normal level, significantly enhances safety. Feedback control of airspeed, Mach Number, attitude, and angle of attack can be used to ensure that the FBW aircraft stays within its certificated flight envelope.

FBW has multiple different modes of "control laws" which can be used.

  • Normal Law - All control augmentations and protections are in place.
  • Alternate Law - Some protections are lost, some features act differently to normal, and the autopilot may be lost (depending on the fault).
  • Direct Law - In direct law, the pilot's controls are NOT augmented at all by the internal computers (for flight envelope protection, etc.), and the exact control movement is sent exactly as it is to the hydraulic servo valves. Autopilot is always lost. Stall and over speed warnings are still available.
  • Mechanical back-up - Not really a control law at all, if FBW has failed, then all that is left is some form of mechanical back-up, for instance on the A320, it is some rudder control and manual trimming.

Therefore, a large degradation of the aircraft, down to direct law or mechanical back-up will cause large changes in control for the pilots. It will often be quite a different aircraft to fly in this case.

As for why the two aircraft might have different reactions to a degradation in FBW, we don't really know. We need more information to be able to dig into that.

title: When increasing speed in straight and level flight, induced drag (1)_____ and parasite drag (2)_____.
optionA: (1) increases; (2) decreases
optionB: (1) decreases; (2) increases
optionC: (1) decreases; (2) decreases
optionD: (1) increases; (2) increases
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The total drag is the resulting factor if you add induced drag and parasite drag together.
Parasite drag is caused if an airfoil is moving through the air. It is the result of form drag and skin friction drag.
Form drag arises from the shape of the object.

The more streamlined the object, the less form drag is present. Shape and size are most important in the amount of form drag resulting.
Form drag increases with increasing velocity, making it very important for high speed aircraft.

Skin friction drag is caused by the friction of the fluid (in case of aircraft this fluid is the atmosphere) against the skin of the object moving through it.
It is directly related to the surface area in contact with the fluid. Skin friction increases with the square of the velocity.

Induced drag is caused when an object redirects the airflow.
A wing produces lift by creating a pressure difference.

This pressure difference is caused by the shape of the airfoil, causing the airflow on top to accelerate, creating a low pressure on top of the wing and high pressure below the wing.
This pressure difference naturally wants to restore towards a uniform pressure, which creates vortices around the wingtip.

These vortices are deflected downwards, this phenomenon is also called downwash.
The induced drag decreases with airspeed.

In the image we can see that the two vectors (induced and parasite drag) create a resulting vector, the total drag.
Where the induced and parasite drag vectors collide, we have the minimum drag speed (VMD); the speed where the total drag is the lowest.

This leads us to understand that during an acceleration from a total stand still, the total drag first decreases up until the minimum drag speed and then starts increasing again.

title: CS23 and CS25 specify the requirements for an aircraft's design manoeuvring speed (VA). Given that VA is an equivalent airspeed (EAS), it remains relevant for aeroplanes with conventional flight controls, however its value may become unreliable at high altitudes as…
optionA: airspeed indication is based on a Mach number at high altitude, making V<sub>A</sub> as an EAS irrelevant.
optionB: higher stall speed and low control forces make it easier to produce a high load factor at high altitudes.
optionC: airspeed indication is invalid due to the compressibility effects at high subsonic Mach numbers.
optionD: the wings may enter a shock stall if flying at the low-altitude V<sub>A</sub> since the aeroplane will exceed M<sub>CRIT</sub>.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Learning Objective 081.06.02.02.03: Explain why VA loses significance at higher altitude.

Manoeuvring speed (VA) is defined as the calibrated airspeed (CAS) below which the aircraft will stall before the onset of structural damage or aerodynamic buffeting occurs. It is a function of the aircraft's weight, altitude, and the configuration of the aircraft (flap and landing gear positions). VA is calculated based on EAS, which is the airspeed corrected for instrument and position errors.

When jet transports cruise at high altitude, the significance of manoeuvring speed (VA) diminishes since it is not possible to achieve 2.5 g, or similar load factors, at high altitude. Consequently, when a single VA is published, it only applies to low-level flight. As altitude increases, the values of equivalent airspeed (EAS) that correspond to the same Mach numbers increase. The increase in Mach number results in a reduction in CLMAX, and the stall limit curves become shallower, causing both VS1 and VA to occur at higher EAS values.

The increased stall speed (VS) means that the low altitude VA is around the low-speed stall at high altitude. Therefore, option "B" is more likely correct, as flying the low altitude VA at high altitudes may result in a low-speed stall of a typical jet aircraft rather than a shock stall.

Note: This question was made from broken feedback, so the wording may be different from in the exam, please let us know if you see this question in the exam, thank you!

title:
Refer to figure.
The high lift device shown in the figure 1 is a:
optionA: Fowler flap.
optionB: Krueger flap.
optionC: slotted flap.
optionD: slot or slat.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Krueger flap

The plain Krueger flap is a small flap on the inboard, leading edge, and underside of a wing that is hinged at the leading edge of the wing and extends forward. With the variable camber Krueger flap the amount of downward extension can be selected and controlled. For small angular deflections it reduces the amount of lift produced but when fully extended it can increase the lift by approximately 50% and also increase the stalling angle up to 25◦. The pitching moment can vary considerably during extension but when fully extended it will cause a nose-up pitching moment requiring considerable changes of trim.

title: Consider an A320 in a 10-degree bank turn, flying at a speed of 220 kt. Assuming an acceleration of gravity of 10 m/s<sup>2</sup>, calculate the turn radius.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
In a turn, the turn radius is defined as:

Turn radius = TAS 2 ÷ (g x tan Ø)

Where Ø represents the bank angle.

Therefore, turn radius is directly proportional to TAS squared and inversely proportional to bank angle.

In this example, we should first convert 220 kt to m/s:

220 x 0.5144 = 113.168 m/s

And then, calculate the turn radius using the above formula:

Turn radius = (113.168) 2 ÷ (10 x tan 10º)
Turn radius ≈ 7264 m

title:
Refer to figure.
The annex illustrates an aeroplane suffering an engine failure, while flying at the normal cruising speed. After dealing appropriately with the failure, the pilot prepares the aeroplane for landing. The pilot maintains wings level as the aeroplane is slowing down; as the airspeed decreases, larger variations in rudder input are required to maintain direction, even if thrust remains constant. One reason for this is because the…
optionA: amount of sideslip decreases with speed, making the airflow arrive at the vertical stabiliser at a smaller angle, thereby reducing the rudder’s effectiveness.
optionB: amount of sideslip increases as speed decreases, making the airflow arrive at the vertical stabiliser at a greater angle, thereby reducing the rudder’s effectiveness.
optionC: left side of the vertical stabiliser is stalling since the rudder increases the effective camber to the point where the airflow separates, thereby reducing the rudder’s effectiveness.
optionD: right side of the vertical stabiliser is stalling, since the sideslip, combined with the rudder input, results in an airflow that is beyond the stabiliser’s critical angle of attack.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
In the event of an engine failure of a multi-engined aeroplane the strength of the asymmetric yawing moment caused by its failure is dependent on the distance of the failed engine from the CG, measured at right angles to the longitudinal axis. The further outboard the failed engine is located the greater is the induced yawing moment.

On suffering an engine failure the unbalanced thrust and drag produces a yawing moment that must be counteracted by the deflection of the rudder. The side force generated by the rudder deflection when multiplied by the moment arm (the distance that the centre of pressure of the rudder is from the CG) has to produce a counteracting moment equal to and opposite to the yawing moment.

The yawing moment from the live engine will increase with decreasing EAS. This increased yawing moment must be counteracted with larger rudder input. This, in turn, will increase the sideslip which progressively decreases rudder effectiveness.

title: Which of the following curves will have a greater load factor?
optionA: Steeper C<sub>L</sub>, low aspect ratio.
optionB: Steeper C<sub>L</sub>, high aspect ratio.
optionC: Shallow C<sub>L</sub>, low aspect ratio.
optionD: Shallow C<sub>L</sub>, high aspect ratio.
explanationTotal:
The increase in load factor (g) will depend on the increase in the coefficient of lift (CL) vs angle of attack.
  • The increase of CL per unit of angle of attack is greater for a steep curve. Consequently, the load factor will be larger.
Factors which affect the lift curve are aspect ratio and wing sweep.
Wings having a low aspect ratio, or sweep, will have a lower lift curve slope, and so will give a smaller increase in ‘g’ when meeting a given gust at a given TAS.

title:
What will happen to the rate of descent if an aircraft descending at VMD slows down?

VMD: speed for minimum drag.
VMP: speed for minimum power required.
optionA: It will increase.
optionB: it will increase until V<sub>MP</sub> is reached, and then decrease.
optionC: it will decrease.
optionD: It will decrease until V<sub>MP</sub> is reached, and then increase.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
An aircraft's angle of descent is calculated by the formula:

(Drag - Thrust) / Weight = sin(Descent angle)

Which, when gliding is just:

Drag / Weight = sin(Descent angle)

This means that minimum drag will always give us minimum angle of descent, so VMD is always going to provide the longest range in a descent, which is particularly important to know, as gliding in a powered aircraft is usually trying to get to a safe landing site. Similar to the way we improve our rate of climb by going much faster up a smaller climb angle, we can also descend slower, by having a steeper descent angle but a much lower speed.

Nicely, this speed where we get best glide endurance is VMP, the speed for minimum power required. It gives us a steeper descent angle, but at a much slower airspeed, so our actual rate of descent is lower, and we can remain in the air for longer. VMP is a slower speed than VMD.

Therefore, beginning at VMD and decreasing airspeed, the rate of descent will initially decrease, until reaching VMP, and then will begin to increase again, with the high induced drag at low speeds.

title: What may happen if the "ultimate load factor" is exceeded?
optionA: Elastic or temporary deformation only.
optionB: No structural failure, only plastic or permanent deformation.
optionC: Structural failure.
optionD: Flutter.
explanationTotal: Exceeding limit load factors can lead to structural failure. For safety reasons these are multiplied by a 1.5 safety factor. This value is also named as ultimate load factor. Aircraft structures are designed to withstand the ultimate load factor for 3 seconds, therefore it is very likely that a structural failure will occur if the ultimate load factor is exceeded.

title: The speed VD in gust diagram...
optionA: equals 50 ft /s.
optionB: equals 66 ft/s.
optionC: equals 55 ft/s.
optionD: equals 25 ft/s.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
It is a design requirement of CS25 (old JAR25) that an airframe structure must be strong enough to withstand gusts both positive and negative that would cause a change of angle of attack so increasing load factor at three specified design speeds.

  • Speed VB (max gust intensity speed): +/- 66 ft/sec
  • Speed VC (design cruise speed): +/- 50 ft/sec
  • Speed VD (design dive speed): +/- 25 ft/sec.

title: What is/are the force(s) acting on a symmetrical aerofoil element when the upstream airflow is parallel to the chord line?
optionA: Weight and drag.
optionB: Lift and drag.
optionC: Weight only.
optionD: Zero force because zero lift is generated.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Symmetrical Aerofoil

If a symmetrical airfoil section is in a steady airstream at zero degrees Angle of Attack (airflow is parallel to the chord line), a stagnation point forms on the leading edge.
The airflow velocity above and below the airfoil increases by an equal amount and the static pressures reduce by an equal amount. Consequently, no pressure differential exists, and no net lift is created.

  • Weight and Drag will be acting on the aerofoil. There will be a certain amount of Parasite drag and Weight is due to the the aircraft's mass.

title: After an engine failure on a twin-engine aircraft, banking towards the live engine is limited to 5 degrees. What is correct if greater angles of bank are used?
optionA: The lateral component of Lift decreases.
optionB: Lift required and Drag both decrease.
optionC: The risk of fin stall decreases.
optionD: Drag increases.
explanationTotal:
COUNTERACTING ASYMMETRIC THRUST

Up to 5 degrees bank into the live engine

During engine-out flight, keeping the ball centered and the wings level will actually cause a side-slip situation because of the one failed engine and the resulting drag and loss of lift. A sideslip would make stall characteristics worse, would decrease climb and acceleration capability, and would increase VMC. Turning up to 5 degrees towards the good (operating) engine will prevent the airplane from being in a sideslip condition, will improve climb capabilities, improve stall capabilities, improve performance and will decrease VMC.

  • The angle of bank must not exceed 5°. Using more than 5º of bank may create enough sideslip towards the lower wing to give a risk of fin stall. When using bank angles greater than 5 degrees, the lift required increases and so does the drag.

title: The local speed of sound in air is proportional to the…
optionA: Square root of the air temperature in degrees Celsius (ºC).
optionB: Air temperature in degrees Celsius (ºC).
optionC: Square root of the air temperature in Kelvin (K).
optionD: Air temperature in Kelvin (K).
explanationTotal:
LOCAL SPEED OF SOUND (LSS)

The speed at which pressure waves propagate is proportional to the square root of the absolute temperature of the air. The higher the temperature, the higher the speed of propagation.

  • LSS = 38.95 x √ (K)
    where LSS = Local Speed of Sound (kt) and K = Absolute temperature (Kelvin)

title: While briefing for an IFR approach, the pilot notices a maximum speed requirement on the reversal procedure. Exceeding the defined maximum speed might be hazardous, because he/she might NOT be able to comply with the required (1) _____, due to exceeding the expected (2) _____.
optionA: (1) bank angle; (2) rate of turn
optionB: (1) limits of the protected areas; (2) rate of turn
optionC: (1) limits of the protected areas; (2) radius of turn
optionD: (1) bank angle; (2) radius of turn
explanationTotal:
081.08.01.05.12: Explain situations in which turn radius is relevant for safety, such as maximum speed limits on departure or arrival plates, or outbound speed categories on approach plates, and the implications/hazards of exceeding given speeds.

Turn radius is dependent on airspeed and bank angle only. However, during normal airline operations, bank angle is limited (normally to 30º) to ensure a coordinated turn with the average piloting skills. As bank angle is maximized, turn radius is a function of speed only. Therefore, should any arrival or approach area be limited by, for example, airspace structure or terrain, speed must also be limited.

Alternative Explanation:

ICAO Doc 8168
1.3.8 The instrument approach chart (IAC) will specify the individual categories of aircraft for which the procedure is approved. Normally, procedures will be designed to provide protected airspace and obstacle clearance for aircraft up to and including Category D. However, where airspace requirements are critical, procedures may be restricted to lower speed categories.
1.3.9 Alternatively, the procedure may specify a maximum IAS for a particular segment without reference to aircraft category. In any case, it is essential that pilots comply with the procedures and information depicted on instrument flight charts and the appropriate flight parameters shown in Tables I-4-1-1 and I-4-1-2 if the aircraft is to remain in the areas developed for obstacle clearance purposes.

  • To stay within limits of the protected area, the radius of turn has to be restricted in order to control the physical flight path.

The rate of turn implies the rate of change of heading. A certain rate of change of heading can be achieved by either modifying the TAS or the radius of turn (Rate of turn = TAS/radius of turn). Therefore, specifying a certain rate of turn alone does not guarantee the physical flight path will stay in the protected area (e.g. To stay below a certain rate of turn, the radius of turn can be increased at a constant TAS).

title: How do roll spoilers assist the ailerons during turns?
optionA: By decreasing the lift on the downward-going wing; they also reduce the adverse aileron yaw.
optionB: By decreasing the lift on the downward-going wing; however, they have NO impact on adverse aileron yaw.
optionC: By increasing the lift on the upward-going wing; however, they have NO impact on adverse aileron yaw.
optionD: By increasing the lift on the upward-going wing; they also reduce the adverse aileron yaw.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
Ailerons are the primary roll control surface on an aircraft, however, ailerons do present a few issues that must be overcome. Ailerons produce adverse yaw, which is where the down-going aileron increases the camber of the wing, and acts similar to a flap, increasing lift, as it is supposed to, but also increasing drag. The up-going aileron reduces the wing camber, reducing drag. This causes an unwanted yaw towards the upward-going wing during a bank. Ailerons can also be affected by the twisting of a wing at high speeds, in an effect known as high speed aileron reversal.

Adverse yaw from ailerons can be counteracted in a fe different ways:

  • Roll spoilers.
  • Frise ailerons.
  • Differential ailerons.

Roll spoilers are the subject of this question. Spoilers are aerodynamic devices that stick out of the top of a wing, giving a loss of lift similar to an up-going aileron and an increased drag similar to a split flap. They are used on almost all modern commercial jets. When spoilers are used as "roll spoilers", they are a primary flight control. They assist or replace the ailerons on the down-going wing by increasing drag and reducing lift.

They use this increased drag to even out the drag of the down-going ailerons on the opposite wing, reducing or removing adverse aileron yaw.

title:
VMCA is the minimum speed at which directional control can be maintained when, amongst others:

1. maximum take-off thrust was set and is maintained on the remaining engines.
2. a sudden engine failure occurs on the most critical engine.
3. flaps are in any position.
4. the gear is either up or down.
5. the aeroplane is either in or out of ground effect.

The combination that regroups all of the correct statements is:
optionA: 1 and 2 are correct.
optionB: 1, 2 and 4 are correct.
optionC: 3, 4 and 5 are correct.
optionD: 2, 3 and 5 are correct.
explanationTotal:
VMCA is the calibrated airspeed at which, when the critical engine is suddenly made inoperative, it is possible to maintain control of the airplane with that engine still inoperative and maintain straight flight with an angle of bank of not more than 5°.

VMCA may not exceed 1.13VSR with:

  • maximum available take-off power or thrust on the engines.
  • the airplane trimmed for take-off.
  • the most unfavorable CG position.
  • maximum sea level take-off weight.
  • the airplane in its most critical take-off configuration (but with gear up); and
  • the airplane airborne and the ground effect negligible; and
  • if applicable, the propeller of the inoperative engine:
    • wind milling
    • feathered, if the airplane has an autmatic feathering device.
  • The rudder forces required to maintain control at VMCA may not exceed 150 lb. nor may it be necessary to reduce power or thrust on the operative engines.
Note: There is no performance requirement, just directional control.

title: Consider a conventional aircraft with normal manoeuvring stability characteristics which does NOT require any augmentation. During initial climb, the elevator trim system remains stuck in the low speed regime with the aircraft’s control surfaces trimmed in the neutral position. The aircraft continues to climb at the same speed with the throttles fixed on the trimmed thrust setting. How will the stick force be experienced by the pilot during climb if the load factor is kept constant? The pilot will…
optionA: experience a slight increase in stick force, as at higher altitude and speed, less force is required for a similar control surface deflection.
optionB: NOT notice any change in stick force as the aircraft was trimmed neutral when the failure occurred.
optionC: experience an increase in stick force for a similar control surface the deflection.
optionD: experience a decrease in stick force for a similar control surface deflection.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The most direct appreciation of the manoeuvring stability of an aeroplane is obtained from a plot of stick forceversus load factor. The aeroplane with positive manoeuvring stability should demonstrate a steady increase in stick force with increase in load factor or “g”.

The pitch damping of the aeroplane is related to air density. At high altitudes the pitch damping reduces. Thus, a decrease in stick force can be expected with increased altitude.

title: Where is the Centre of Pressure (CP) in relation to the Aerodynamic Centre (AC) on a positively cambered aerofoil?
optionA: The CP is above the AC.
optionB: The CP is ahead of the AC.
optionC: The CP is behind the AC.
optionD: The position of the AC is independent of the position of the CP.
explanationTotal:
NOTE: This answer is backed up by the most recent feedback from both Poland and Slovakia. Whilst we believe that it is not completely correct (it is only the case for normal ranges of flight, but not some possible scenarios), it is still mostly correct, and better than the other options. We think the wording of the "independent" option might also disqualify it from being the most correct answer, as it refers to the AC in relation to the CP, which is the opposite of what the question asks (CP in relation to the AC).

Please let us know if you see this in the exam so we can verify it, as well as which authority you sat your exam under, thank you!

Refer to figure.
The centre of pressure of a wing (aerofoil) is dictated by the pressure layout around the wing. This pressure layout changes dramatically depending on the shape, angle of attack, and speed of the relative airflow. The centre of pressure is kind of the "average" point of the pressure layout, where the sum of all the pressures acts through on the aerofoil. It is therefore the point through which the lift and drag act. It moves, depending on the angle of attack of a wing. For a positively cambered (normal) aerofoil in standard flight, the CP moves further towards the leading edge as the angle of attack increases, up until the stall.

The aerodynamic centre is slightly more complex. When you add up all the forces on an aerofoil, there will be a resultant force through the centre of pressure, and this is split into lift and drag. The centre of pressure will not have any turning force around it, only forces acting directly through it. However, every other point on the wing will have a force acting around it, imagine holding the leading edge of an aerofoil in a wind tunnel, not only would it try and pull away from you, but it would also try to twist due to these moments.

There is a point where the moments (turning forces around that point) stay the same, no matter the angle of attack (for the same IAS). This is called the aerodynamic centre, and it does not move (for a range of normal angles of attack and in the low subsonic speed regime).

As you can see from the figure, the CP is behind the AC, and for normal ranges of flight, this will be the case.

title: Regarding Dutch Roll, a shockwave tends to (1)_____ the aircraft at speeds (2)_____ MCRIT.
optionA: (1) roll; (2) above
optionB: (1) yaw; (2) below
optionC: (1) roll; (2) below
optionD: (1) yaw; (2) above
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.

Dutch Roll

Dutch roll is a coupled lateral and directional oscillation which is undesirable because of the oscillatory nature. Dutch roll can occur when the static lateral stability (caused by dihedral, etc.) is high in comparison to the static directional stability (caused by the tail fin, etc.)

Asymmetric shockwaves

Modern transport jet aircraft tend to cruise at high altitudes with high Mach numbers, very close to - or just inside - the transonic regime. This is the range of speeds (At and above MCRIT) where some of the aircraft experiences supersonic airflow, but not all the aircraft does. This brings rise to shockwaves, first on the upper wing surfaces near the roots, then spreading to other areas of the aircraft. Shockwaves produce quite high drag forces, classed as "wave drag".

If the shockwaves form asymmetrically on the aircraft, whether due to different airflow patterns over the wings, small differences in the aircraft structure, control surfaces, etc., then the different drag forces can cause a yawing motion, which sets off the oscillation known as Dutch roll. This Dutch roll would be made worse by the shockwaves forming on the faster wing, reducing lift and increasing drag to drop it down and drag it back, exacerbating the Dutch roll.

title: After take-off the slats (when installed) are always retracted later than the flaps. Why?
optionA: Because V<sub>MCA</sub> with SLATS EXTENDED is more favourable compared with the FLAPS EXTENDED situation.
optionB: Because SLATS EXTENDED gives a large decrease in stall speed with relatively less drag.
optionC: Because SLATS EXTENDED provides a better view from the cockpit than FLAPS EXTENDED.
optionD: Because FLAPS EXTENDED gives a large decrease in stall speed with relatively less drag.
explanationTotal: Slats and flaps increase lift.This can help the aircraft take off with a shortened ground roll, as the aircraft generates more lift at a lower speed with flaps and slats extended.However, flaps and slats shorten the ground roll, but also decrease climb performance as they generate drag.Therefore, after takeoff these two devices are retracted.Flaps and slats both decrease stall speed, but flaps generate much more drag.The flaps are therefore retracted first and slats afterwards.

title: What could be an indication of a tail stall due to icing?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Elevator buffet
optionB: Nose up deflection
optionC: Oscillations in pitch
optionD: Stall warning horn sounds
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
STABILIZER STALL DUE TO ICE

The tailplane is an aerofoil, and because it is thinner than the wing, it is likely to experience icing before the wing does. The effect will be the same as for the wing; the stall will occur at a lower angle of attack.

The tailplane is normally operating at a negative angle of attack, producing a down load, so if the tailplane stalls and the down load is lost, the nose of the aircraft will drop and longitudinal control will be lost.

Stalling of an ice contaminated tailplane could be precipitated by extension of the wing flaps.

Lowering the flaps increases the downwash, and this increases the negative angle of attack of the tailplane. If the tailplane has ice contamination, this could be sufficient to cause it to stall.

Recovery procedure in this situation would be to retract the flaps again, thus reducing the downwash.

Undetected stalling at speeds significantly above the normal stalling speed are generally accompanied by violent roll oscillations.

The stall warning system installed on the aeroplane may not alert the pilot to the insidious icing-induced wing-stall (angle of attack will be below that required to trigger the switch), so should not be relied upon to give a warning of this condition. Airframe buffet, however, may assist in identifying the onset of wing-stall;

title:
Refer to figure.
Which of the following statements is correct with regards to 1 and 2 in the annex above?
optionA: 2 has a lower C<sub>L</sub> but higher critical angle.
optionB: 2 has a higher C<sub>L</sub> but a lower C<sub>D</sub>.
optionC: 1 has a higher C<sub>L</sub>/C<sub>D </sub>than 2.
optionD: 2 has higher C<sub>L</sub> than 1, but a higher C<sub>D</sub>.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Note: this question has been created from incomplete feedback, and as such, the options may be different. Please send us any further exam feedback you have, either in the comments or by email to info@atplquestions.com, thank you!

The figure shows 4 types of flaps:

  • Plain flap -The standard for many light aircraft, increases available lift and increases drag. Easy to manufacture
  • Slotted flap - Increases maximum lift by more than plain flaps, due to the slots allowing high velocity air through to re-energise the boundary layers, preventing separation. Increases drag also over plain flaps. Used commonly on large jet aircraft for slow flight and landing (sometimes in conjunction with the fowler flaps below).
  • Split flap - Increases drag heavily due to the open trailing edge. Very easy to manufacture.
  • Fowler flap - Complex to design and fit, but increase lift by a large amount due to the increased wing area and camber. Increase in drag over plain flaps is smaller than the increased lift, so they provide a high L/D ratio, and are often used in conjunction with multiple levels of slotted flaps on larger aircraft.

So from those descriptions, we can definitely see that type 2 (slotted) flaps have a much larger available CL than type 1 (plain) flaps, which doesn't narrow down our answers much. We can also say that the slots increase the CD also, and this happens because the airflow has to get squeezed through the slots. Therefore, 2 has a higher CL and higher CD than type 1.

Whilst it is difficult to consider this vague question, given it has not specified an angle of attack or angle of extension, answers A and B are saying the exact same thing (in opposite phrasing), and cannot both be correct, and answer C (L/D ratio) would also be absolutely correct in that case, leaving us only with our correct answer "2 has a higher CL and a higher CD.".

title: If the thrust line is above the CG, how will this affect the airplane?
optionA: Pitch down, stabilising.
optionB: Pitch down, destabilising.
optionC: Pitch up, stabilizing.
optionD: Pitch up, destabilising.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
POWER EFFECTS

Its effects may cause significant changes in trim left coefficient and static longitudinal stability.
The vertical location of the thrust line defines one of the direct contributions to stability.

  • If the thrust line is below the CG (the case of most airliners with underwing engines), a thrust increase will produce an added pitch-up moment => this will cause the airplane to slow down more than necessary (despite the added thrust). Creating an unstable situation. Therefore, the effect is destabilizing.
  • If the thrust line is above the CG, this is the opposite of the above and a thrust increase will produce a nose down moment (negative moment), and, in moderate amounts, can have a stabilising effect. The airplane will settle at a higher speed, which is presumably what the pilot wants (despite the "power controls altitude" mantra). When the line is too high, the airplane may even descend and accelerate more than necessary, until the aerodynamic moment balances out the thrust moment, but overall the condition is stable.
  • Thrust is in line with CG. The airplane will start to climb (or reduce descent) and will settle on the same AoA and roughly the same speed.

title: How do you get out of a spin?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Full power, Ailerons opposite, Rudder neutral, Pull yoke
optionB: Full power, Ailerons neutral, Full Rudder opposite, Pull yoke
optionC: Power Idle, Ailerons opposite, Rudder neutral, Push yoke
optionD: Power Idle, Ailerons neutral, Rudder opposite, Push yoke
explanationTotal:
SPIN RECOVERY

Although the POH is the primary reference for recovery from a spin, the following can be used as a general procedure:

P - Retard the throttle to idle. In most aircraft, power hampers the recovery.
A - Ailerons neutral. Many pilots will attempt to recover from the spin using the ailerons. This may actually make the problem worse.
R - Apply full opposite rudder. Apply rudder opposite the rotation of the spin. If you have trouble determining which way the airplane is spinning, look at your turn coordinator or turn needle. It will indicate the direction of rotation.
E - Apply forward elevator. Immediately after applying opposite rudder, apply a quick forward motion on the control yoke and hold anti-spin controls until the aircraft starts to recover.
D - Recover from the dive. Once you have completed the four previous steps, and the rotation stops, recover from the dive. The descent rate may be over 5000 feet per minute and the airspeed will rapidly exceed redline. Remember to neutralize the rudder after the rotation stops.

title: Which of these statements concerning propellers is correct?
optionA: The blade angle of a feathered propeller is approximately 0 degrees.
optionB: The blade angle of a feathered propeller is approximately 180 degrees.
optionC: A windmilling propeller causes less drag than a feathered propeller.
optionD: When compared with a non-feathered propeller, a feathered propeller improves the handling of a multi-engine aeroplane with one engine inoperative.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
To prevent the propeller from ‘wind milling’ the propeller blade is rotated from the fine-pitch stop through the coarse-pitch stop to reach the angle of attack to the relative airflow that produces zero lift; and referred to as ‘feathering’ the propeller. It is usually approximately 85◦ because it is the best compromise for the whole blade length and accounts for the blade twist.
This blade position stops the propeller from rotating because there is no lift force to produce a torque reaction; it reduces the drag to a minimum level and prevents damage being caused to the engine.
For a single-engine airplane feathering the propeller blades improves the glide performance because it does not require such a steep glide angle to maintain the required airspeed. As such, feathering the propeller increases the gliding range and endurance. For a multi-engine airplane, the decreased drag reduces the amount of thrust required to counteract the asymmetric force of the propeller of the failed engine and there is sufficient rudder authority remaining to enable the pilot to safely control the airplane.

title: The reduction in downwash behind the shock-induced separation will contribute to...
optionA: increase in induced drag
optionB: a reduction in drag
optionC: tuck under
optionD: the lift coefficient increasing
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
In transonic flight it is the nature of the airflow behind a shock wave that determines the stability characteristics of the aircraft.

Longitudinal stability is the most commonly affected form of stability. It is determined by movement of the centre of pressure, coupled with changes in the coefficient of lift and the amount of downwash acting on the tailplane.

The nose-down pitching moment produced by the wing is counteracted by placing a small download on the tailplane. If the shock stall occurs, any lift aft of the shock wave is destroyed and the tailplane becomes covered in disturbed airflow.

The downwash acting on the tailplane is consequently eliminated causing a smooth and radical change in its angle of attack. The angle of attack becomes more positive and the download acting on the tailplane becomes an upload which, in conjunction with the wing pitching moment, causes a violent nose-down pitching moment, known as tuck-under.

The exact nature and strength of the changes in trim and stability depend on the design of the aircraft.

title:
Assuming no flow separation, which of these statements about the flow around an aerofoil as the angle of attack decreases are correct or incorrect?

I. The stagnation point moves down.
II. The point of lowest static pressure moves forward.
optionA: I is incorrect, II is correct.
optionB: I is correct, II is correct.
optionC: I is correct, II is incorrect.
optionD: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
explanationTotal:
Refer to the figure.
The stagnation point is the point on the leading edge of the wing where the speed is reduced to zero, where the air comes to a complete standstill.

The point of lowest static pressure is equal to the point of highest dynamic pressure. The point along the profile where the speed is highest is along the upper side of the wing, and moves forward as the angle of attack increases, and backwards when the angle of attack decreases.

Therefore as the angle of attack decreases:

  • The stagnation point will move up
  • The point of lowest static pressure moves aft
Therefore, statement 1 is incorrect, and statement 2 is also incorrect.

title: For a given gust speed and aircraft TAS, what is the impact of the lift curve’s slope on the gust load factor?
optionA: The steeper the lift curve’s slope, the greater the gust load factor.
optionB: The steeper the lift curve’s slope, the smaller the gust load factor.
optionC: The lift curve’s slope has no impact on the gust load factor.
optionD: The shallower the lift curve’s slope, the greater the gust load factor.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
Vertical gusts will affect the load factor (n) by changing the angle of attack of the wing.
For a given gust speed and aircraft TAS, the increment in the load factor depends on the increase in CL per change in angle of attack due to the gust (the slope of the lift curve). If the lift curve has a steep slope, the ‘g’ increment will be greater. Factors which affect the lift curve are aspect ratio and wing sweep.
Wings having a low aspect ratio, or sweep, will have a lower lift curve slope, and so will give a smaller increase in ‘g’ when meeting a given gust at a given TAS.

title: An airplane has a 60 kt stall speed. A pilot is flying at 90 kt and then banks sharply to avoid other traffic and stalls the aircraft. Which of the following statements is correct with regards to this situation?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: As the pilot is in a turn, the stall will lead to a spin and this is unrecoverable.
optionB: The aircraft will pitch down, build speed and recover by itself.
optionC: As long as the airspeed is above the stall speed for the given configuration, an aircraft cannot stall.
optionD: When the wing exceeds its critical angle of attack it will stall regardless of airspeed.
explanationTotal:
Stall is defined as a sudden reduction in the lift generated by an aerofoil when the critical angle of attack is reached or exceeded.

It is important for the pilot to understand that a stall is the result of exceeding the critical AOA, not of insufficient airspeed. Therefore, if the angle of attack is increased up to or beyond the critical angle, an aeroplane can be stalled at any airspeed or flight attitude.

title: When comparing an elevator trim system with a stabiliser trim system, which of these statements is correct?
optionA: An elevator trim system is able to compensate larger changes in pitching moments.
optionB: An elevator trim system is better adapted to larger flight speed ranges.
optionC: An elevator trim system is more suitable for aeroplanes with a large CG range.
optionD: An elevator trim system is more sensitive to flutter.
explanationTotal:
The design of the majority of airliners and transport aircraft incorporates a trimmable horizontal stabilizer which features a fully moving horizontal tail surface. The trimmable stabilizer's primary advantage is that it provides tremendous trimming power over the full speed range of the airplane since the entire stabiliser may be moved to trim the aircraft.

The trimmable horizontal stabiliser is also less sensitive to flutter, compared to an elevator trim tab, due to its larger mass and stability. Flutter is a divergent oscillatory motion of a control surface caused by the interaction of aerodynamic forces, inertia forces and the stiffness of the structure.

title: When air has passed through a shock wave the local speed of sound is:
optionA: increased.
optionB: not affected.
optionC: decreased and beyond a certain Mach number start increasing again.
optionD: decreased.
explanationTotal:
An airplane flying at low, subsonic, speeds causes air-pressure changes because of its movement but they are relatively small. It is convenient, therefore, to treat the air as though it could not be compressed.

However, the air-pressure changes caused by the movement of an airplane at high speed, close to the speed of sound, are considerable and cannot be ignored. The air is compressible and its effect on the airplane must be accounted for when it is travelling at high speed.

An airplane moving through the air creates a pressure wave around it, which is propagated away from it in all directions simultaneously at the speed of sound. For an airplane flying at a relatively low speed, less than the speed of sound, the air-pressure wave ahead of the airplane can move away from the airplane. Consequently, air-pressure, air-density, air-temperature, and air-velocity changes take place ahead of the leading edge of the wings and are a gradual process.

If, however, the airplane is travelling at the speed of sound then the air-pressure wave ahead of the airplane is unable to move away from the airplane and a wave of compressed air builds up at the leading edge of the wing.

This compression wave will create a discontinuity plane, where the airstream experiences the following changes:

Air Temperature - Increases (due to compression)
Static Pressure - Increases (due to compression)
Total Pressure - Decreases (Normal shockwave suffers greater loss than an oblique shockwave)
Air Density - Increases (Oblique shockwave has less compression)
LSS - Increases (due to the temperature increase)
Speed of Airflow - Decreases to less than Mach 1 (normal shockwave). Decreases but still above Mach 1.0 (oblique shockwave).

Minimum energy loss through a normal shock wave will occur when the Mach number of the airflow in front of the shock wave is small but supersonic.

The Local Speed of Sound is defined by:

LSS=38.95∗√(T(K))

The speed of propagation of small pressure waves depends upon the temperature of the air ONLY. Thus, if behind a shock wave temperature increases, the LSS also increases.

title:
Refer to figure.
How are the speeds (shown in the figure) at point 1 and point 2 related to the relative wind/airflow V?
optionA: V<sub>1</sub> < V<sub>2</sub> and V<sub>2</sub> < V
optionB: V<sub>1</sub> = 0 and V<sub>2</sub> > V
optionC: V<sub>1</sub> = 0 and V<sub>2</sub> = V
optionD: V<sub>1</sub> > V<sub>2</sub> and V<sub>2</sub> < V
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
TWO-DIMENSIONAL FLOW

As air flows around an aeroplane its speed and pressure changes. The spacing of the streamlines indicates the change of speed; streamlines close together indicate a high airspeed and those further apart a low airspeed.

The ‘equation of continuity’ states that mass can neither be created nor destroyed; air mass flow is constant.

From Bernoulli’s theorem it can be deduced that an increase of airspeed around an aerofoil results in a decrease of air pressure and vice versa.

THE STAGNATION POINT

The stagnation point is that point on an aerofoil at which the approaching airflow becomes stationary. It is located on the leading edge of the aerofoil just below the maximum point of curvature and moves downward and aft along the lower surface of the aerofoil profile as the angle of attack increases.

AEROFOIL UPPER-SURFACE AIRFLOW

The flow over the top of the section accelerates rapidly around the nose and over the leading portion of the surface - inducing a substantial decrease in static pressure in those areas. The rate of acceleration increases with increase in angle of attack, up to about 16°.

The pressure reduces continuously from the stagnation value through the free stream value to a position on the top surface where a peak negative value is reached. From there onwards the flow continuously slows down again and the pressure increases back to the free stream value in the region of the trailing edge.

title: Which instrument can a pilot use to determine the spin's direction when it occurs while they are flying in a cloud?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Turn coordinator
optionB: Attitude indicator
optionC: Ball slip indicator
optionD: Magnetic compass
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The spin is a complex flight manoeuvre. It may be defined as an aggravated stall resulting in a rotation. The rotation is stable and will continue due to remaining aerodynamic forces. During the spin, the wings remain unequally stalled.

Recovery from a normal stall is achieved by reducing the angle of attack which restores the airflow over the wing. Spin recovery additionally involves stopping the rotation. The more complex aerodynamics of a spin require different recovery procedures depending on the aeroplane design.

The recommended general recovery procedure is reducing the power to idle and releasing the pressure on the controls. The design of some aircraft is such that recovery from a developed spin requires definite control movements, precisely timed to coincide with certain points in the rotation, for several turns.

These four main items can be accomplished relative simultaneously:

- Moving the throttle to idle minimizes altitude loss and reduces the possibility of a flat spin developing. It also eliminates possible asymmetric thrust on multi-engine aeroplanes.

- Neutralize the ailerons. Aileron position is often a contributory factor to flat spins or to higher rotation rates in normal spins.

- Apply full rudder against the spin rotation. Spin direction is most reliably determined from the turn co-ordinator or by looking outside. Do not use the ball in the slip indicator as its indication is not reliable and may be affected by its location within the flight deck.

- Move the elevator control to the neutral position.

title: Your Mach number is 0.7, and you are flying at constant CAS. After considerable time passed, all other variables remained the same, but the temperature SAT of -35°C increased to -30°C.
optionA: Mach will increase because it is a function of temperature.
optionB: Mach decreases but, after some time, increases once again because of increasing TAT.
optionC: Mach remains constant because both LSS and TAS increase.
optionD: Mach will decrease because LSS will increase with increases in temperature.
explanationTotal:
The speed of sound (LSS) is the speed at which sound or pressure waves move through a gas, liquid, or solid. The speed of sound is proportional to the square root of the temperature; the speed of sound (LSS) will increase as the temperature increases.

A higher SAT leads to a higher TAS. As the SAT increases, the air molecules become less dense, resulting in a higher TAS for a given CAS. Therefore, in the given scenario, where the temperature SAT increases from -35°C to -30°C, the TAS will also increase.

The Mach number (M) is the ratio of the true airspeed (TAS) to the local speed of sound (LSS), and it’s a measure of compressibility.

M = TAS / LSS

  • In this scenario, both TAS and LSS increase, therefore Mach number remains constant, given that the CAS remains constant.

title: When roll spoilers are extended, the part of the wing on which they are mounted:
optionA: experiences a reduction in lift, which generates the desired rolling moment. In addition there is a local increase in drag, which suppresses adverse yaw.
optionB: experiences extra drag, which generates a yawing moment. The speed difference between both wings generates the desired rolling moment.
optionC: is forced downwards as a reaction to the increased drag.
optionD: stalls. This causes a difference in lift between both wings, which generates the desired rolling moment.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Roll control may be provided by ailerons and flight spoilers.

The ailerons provide roll control around the airplane’s longitudinal axis. The ailerons are positioned by the pilots' control wheels.

Roll spoilers are flat panels mounted in the upper surface of the wings that deploy asymmetrically to assist the downward wing aileron effect a turn by decreasing the lift and increase the drag on that wing. The increased drag reduces adverse yaw by generating a benign yaw moment. Thus, if a roll right is demanded then the right aileron will move up and the right spoiler will reduce the lift generated by the right wing. Usually, on transport aeroplanes, the roll spoilers are connected to one of the two control columns and the ailerons to the other control column.

title: A crew is operating a fly-by-wire aircraft which offers protections to ensure stability with regards to aeroplane mass and centre of gravity. If the crew enters the wrong CG location pre-flight, what may happen during take-off?
optionA: The aircraft might become unstable in certain configurations.
optionB: The aircraft will never become unstable due to regulations preventing this.
optionC: Fuel consumption will increase because the aircraft moves the stabiliser to correct for the incorrect CG position.
optionD: Drag increases because the aircraft will try to trim for the actual CG.
explanationTotal:
Fly-by-wire is the control system that connects the pilots inputs to the aircraft control surfaces by computers, giving no direct physical connection, but providing benefits such as flight envelope protection and reduced weight of control systems.

In particular for pilots, the flight envelope protections are very useful, and stop unusual attitudes such as excessive bank angle, too much pitch up/down, overspeed, stall, etc. This question is talking about stability, which is quite a broad subject, and refers to the aircraft behaving "as you would expect", in that it tries to fight against any changes in attitude from the trimmed position.

FBW systems allow for a lot of extra stability for the pilots. Take modern fighter jets, for example, like the Eurofighter Typhoon. It is designed to be statically unstable, but the FBW system installed makes sure that the aircraft is stable for the pilot to fly. Of course, civilian aircraft are still statically stable without the FBW system engaged, but not as much as they used to be before FBW was used. The designers can play with a lot finer margins of stability to gain other efficiencies, as the aircraft will always be able to even out any control/stability differences due to fly-by-wire.

Fly-by-wire also make sure that the pilot feels the same force to pull a manoeuvre, no matter the weight or CG position. Therefore, when inputting the weight and CG, it is incredibly important to input them correctly, as if you inputted one too far forward for example, the FBW system would initially think that it needs to make a larger control deflection, overcontrolling the whole aircraft. Due to the fine margins, this could put the aircraft in an unstable condition. There are a lot of conditions that could be considered as unstable from an aircraft perspective, as it can simply mean that controls do not affect an aircraft within certain margins of what is expected.

Fly-by-wire allows the aircraft to be constructed with a less stable nature, as it is never intended to be flown without the FBW system active, and this less stable nature allows for a further forward wing placement, the CG being closer to the CP, and therefore a lower downforce required from the tailplane, allowing reduced trim drag over a plane that was not built with FBW controls in mind.

To remove for two other options, the fuel consumption will remain the same in the cruise as if the crew entered the correct CG location, as the aircraft trims depending on a feedback loop of revised outputs, until the aircraft flies level, which has nothing to do with the inputted CG, only the actual CG. Also, this does not apply at take-off, as required by the question.

title: By lowering the trailing edge flaps...
optionA: wing tip vortex increase due to CP closer to wing root.
optionB: wing tip vortex increase due to CP closer to wing tip.
optionC: wing tip vortex decrease due to CP closer to wing root.
optionD: wing tip vortex decrease due to CP closer to wing tip.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
INDUCED DRAG

Whenever a wing produces lift, concentrated vortices form at the wing tips. The vortices are strongest at the wing tips and become progressively weaker toward the centre-line of the aircraft.

It is the production of lift itself which reduces the magnitude of the lift force being generated. To replace the lift lost by the increased downwash, the aircraft must be flown at a higher angle of attack. This increases drag. This extra drag is called induced drag.

The stronger the vortices, the greater the induced drag.

WING TIP VORTICES vs. FLAPS

A stronger pressure differential above and below the wing generates stronger wing tip vortices. This may be achieved by flying at a higher angle of attack (flying a heavier airplane or flying slower).

Vortex strength is greatest with aircraft in a “clean” configuration (for a given speed and weight). This is because, with flaps extended the outboard portion of extended flaps offer another opportunity for higher-pressure air below the wing to move up.

With flaps extended, the aircraft generates four main vortices, weakening their overall effect. With the flaps retracted, those four vortices become two stronger ones.

title: An airplane cruises with a Mach number slightly higher than M<sub>CRIT</sub>, what are the benefits?
optionA: A higher speed for a small increase in C<sub>D</sub>.
optionB: There are no benefits and it is highly dangerous to exceed M<sub>CRIT</sub>.
optionC: No shockwaves are present upon passing M<sub>CRIT</sub>, they don't develop until Mach 2.
optionD: The lowest safety speed in relation to shock stall.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
A wing accelerates air over its upper surface, which, at high subsonic speeds, has the effect of causing that air to become supersonic (above Mach 1). The speed at which this first happens is known as MCRIT, above which speed, a shockwave will form on the upper section of the wing, usually near the wing root.

In aircraft which are not designed for these high speeds, that can be dangerous, as the shockwave can cause airflow separation and loss of lift behind it.

However, modern high speed jet aircraft are designed with this in mind, with swept back, supercritical wings, etc. These allow the aircraft to operate just above MCRIT, with a small penalty of increased drag, in return for extra speed. This means that these aircraft often cruise with a very small shockwave on top of the wing. Whilst they stay below the Drag Divergence Number, the drag is not increasing too much and it is worth it for the extra speed.

title: An aircraft is very close to the stall due to increase in tailwind. What should the pilot's first action be?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: Increase power before changing the pitch.
optionB: Increase AOA and then increase power.
optionC: Use the weather radar to escape.
optionD: Retract the gear to reduce drag and then increase power.
explanationTotal:
If you are caught in a microburst during the approach or landing, the following recovery actions should be taken without delay:

  • Select the takeoff/go-around (Take-off/Go-around (TOGA) Mode) mode and set and maintain maximum go-around thrust.
  • Follow the Flight Director pitch command (if the FD provides wind shear recovery guidance) or set the pitch-attitude target recommended in the QRH.
  • If the AP is engaged and if the FD provides wind shear recovery guidance, keep the AP engaged; otherwise, disconnect the AP and set and maintain the recommended pitch attitude
  • Do not change the flap configuration or landing-gear configuration until out of the wind shear
  • Level the wings to maximize climb gradient, unless a turn is required for obstacle clearance
  • Allow airspeed to decrease to stick-shaker onset (intermittent stick-shaker activation) while monitoring airspeed trend
  • Closely monitor airspeed, airspeed trend and flight path angle (if flight-path vector is available and displayed for the PNF) and,
  • When out of the wind shear, retract the landing gear, flaps and slats, then increase the airspeed when a positive climb is confirmed and establish a normal climb profile.

title:
Refer to figure.
The trailing edge flaps are stuck in the position shown in the picture. What would the pilot have to do?
optionA: Trim ailerons to lower the left wing down and rudder to put the nose to the left.
optionB: Trim ailerons to lower the right wing down and rudder to put the nose to the left.
optionC: Trim ailerons to lower the left wing down and rudder to put the nose to the right.
optionD: Trim ailerons to lower the right wing down and rudder to put the nose to the right.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Flap asymmetry will give different lift on the wings which causes a large rolling moment. This will happen at any speed since flap extension changes the camber of the wing. The value of lift will be increased on the right side due to the flap extension. As a result the aircraft will roll to the left. The angle of attack will be decreased on the left side (upgoing wing) and increased on the right side (downgoing side).

You'll counter the roll from asymmetric flaps with right control input (aided by right aileron trim). The extra drag from the right wing creates a yawing moment to the right. You'll counter the yaw with substantial opposite rudder (left). This results in your airplane flying in a cross-controlled condition.

title:
Refer to figure.
Consider a subsonic airflow moving steadily through the Venturi Tube with no leaks, as represented in the image. "1, 2, 3, 4" identify areas of different speeds. Which of the following sequences correctly identifies the areas in order of increasing airspeed?
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The Venturi effect states that in a situation with constant mechanical energy, the velocity of a fluid passing through a constricted area (throat) will increase and its static pressure will decrease. The effect utilizes both the principle of continuity as well as the principle of conservation of mechanical energy.

In the tube depicted in the attached figure, a fluid flows from left to right at a constant volume flow rate. To maintain this flow, the fluid must be moved at the same rate, despite the constricted space (throat) in the middle of the tube. Therefore, the velocity of the fluid is increased, as the fluid needs to flow faster in the constricted area.

Continuity equation: Mass flow = A x p x V
A- cross section area; p- air density; V- velocity

With regards to this question, the airflow starts to accelerate when the diameter of the tube starts reducing (1) and the speed is the highest at the centre of the venturi (2). As we can see, at “4” the diameter has not expanded to its full width, therefore it is faster than at “1”. The speed at “2” is lower than at “3” because the reduction in diameter is not yet complete.

  • Sequence of increasing magnitude of airflow speed: 1, 4, 2, 3

title: A transport aircraft needs to be flown back to the maintenance facility empty following a cabin pressurisation issue. What should the crew be aware of regarding the one-engine inoperative controllability after takeoff?
optionA: An increased safety margin to VMC due to the low operating speeds associated with low mass
optionB: A decreased safety margin to V<sub>MC</sub> due to the low operating speeds associated with low mass
optionC: An increased safety margin to VMC due to the high rudder ineffectiveness at low altitudes
optionD: A decreased safety margin to V<sub>MC</sub> due to the high rudder ineffectiveness at low altitudes
explanationTotal:
VMC or minimum control speed is the CAS below which directional or lateral control cannot be maintained after the failure of one or more engines. At a certain low speed, the rudder moment is not able anymore to balance the yawing moment from the life engine(s).

The effectiveness of the flight controls depends on dynamic pressure and flight control displacement. A measure of dynamic pressure at low airspeeds is given by the calibrated airspeed (CAS). A higher CAS or IAS gives more flight control effectiveness, e.g., a larger available rudder moment to balance the yawing moment from a failed engine. A lower IAS will reduce the available rudder moment if the other parameters remain the same.

Many operational speeds are based on the 1g stall speed. Low weights will result in a low 1g stall speed and low operational speeds. If the rudder is deflected at relative low speeds, the generated aerodynamic resultant will be smaller.

At a certain low speed, the rudder may not be capable of generating the required force and moment, which results in a controllability problem. In this scope, it is not allowed to fly certain speeds below the VMC or minimum control speed.

title:
Which of these statements about the effect of wing sweep on centre of pressure location are correct or incorrect?

1. The centre of pressure on an unswept wing moves forward as the angle of attack approaches and exceeds the critical angle of attack.
2. When sweep back increases the centre of pressure has an increased tendency to move forward as the angle of attack approaches and exceeds the critical angle of attack.
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: 1 is incorrect, 2 is correct.
optionB: 1 is incorrect, 2 is incorrect.
optionC: 1 is correct, 2 is correct.
optionD: 1 is correct, 2 is incorrect.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The center of pressure is the theoretical point through which the lift is assumed to act.

  • Center of pressure of rectangular wing approaching stall: As you can see in the diagram, rectangular wings have the tendency to create a pitch down moment when approaching stalls. This is because of the aft movement of the center of pressure when approaching the stall. Therefore statement 1 is incorrect!
  • Center of pressure of swept wing approaching stall: As you can see in the diagram, swept wings have the dangerous tendency to stall at the tips first when approaching stalls, leading to a pitch up effect that could lead to a deep stall. This is because as the tip stalls, relative to before most of the lift will be created at the front of the wing, hence the center of pressure will move forward. Therefore statement 2 is correct!

title: You are planning to take off on runway XX. Field elevation is 52 ft. Wing span 20 m. At what height is the downwash least?
optionA: 30 ft
optionB: 60 ft
optionC: 80 ft
optionD: 120 ft
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Ground effect basically comes down to how big your wingtip vortices are, and how much downwash they're creating. Take a look at the Cirrus SR-22 examples in the attached figure. Notice the difference in wingtip vortex size at altitude, vs. near the ground?

When your wing is close to the ground, wingtip vortices can't get as big, because as they spin around your wingtip, they impact the ground and dissipate. The result? A reduction in downwash. Less downwash, less drag.

  • Summary: Flying low to the ground limits your vortices, making them smaller. This means that the air flowing off the back of your wing has less downwash.
Ground effect is definitely experienced within half a wingspan. In this question, the wingspan equals 20 m which equals approximately 60 ft (65 ft to be exact).

title: When "spoilers" are used as speed brakes:
optionA: at the same angle of attack, C<sub>D</sub> is increased and C<sub>L</sub> is decreased.
optionB: at the same angle of attack, C<sub>L</sub> remains unaffected.
optionC: the C<sub>LMAX</sub> is not affected.
optionD: for the same C<sub>L</sub>, the angle of attack must be reduced.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.

SPOILERS
Spoilers are flap type control surfaces, normally located on the upper surface of the wing, just in front of the trailing edge flaps.

These surfaces individually hinge at their leading edges and are actuated by hydraulic power supplied by dedicated power control units. The main purpose of the surfaces is to disturb the smooth airflow over the top of the wing, thereby reducing the wings lifting capability. When fully extended, they considerably increase aircraft drag.

The maximum deflection angles are greater in the ground mode than the flight mode. With the spoilers in their fully extended position, approximately 80% of the wing/flap lift is destroyed and the aerodynamic drag of the aircraft more than doubles.

title: The critical Mach number of a conventional aerofoil section increases if:
optionA: its leading edge radius is increased.
optionB: it is flown at higher angles of attack.
optionC: its camber is increased.
optionD: its thickness to chord ratio is reduced.
explanationTotal:
CRITICAL MACH

At the point where the first hint of supersonic air flow occurs above the wing, the aerofoil is said to be at its critical Mach number.

OBTAINING A HIGHER CRITICAL MACH NUMBER

  • In order to obtain a high critical Mach number from an airfoil at some low lift coefficient the section must have:
    1. Low thickness ratio. The point of maximum thickness should be aft to smooth the pressure distribution.
    2. Low camber. The mean camber line should be shaped to help minimize the local velocity peaks.
  • If supersonic flight is a possibility the thickness ratio and leading edge radius must be small to decrease wave drag.
SUMMARY:
In supersonic flight the streamline curvatures are small and the requirement is for slender, indeed sharp, leading edges for the inlet in order to reduce the pressure drag associated with bluntness-induced shock detachment.
MCRIT decreases when the airflow over the upper surface of the wing is given greater acceleration. Its speed will then reach M=1 at a lower speed. Increasing leading edge radius gives the aerofoil a thicker, more rounded leading edge, which gives greater airflow acceleration.

title: Which definition of propeller parameters is correct?
optionA: Blade angle is the angle between the blade chord line and the plane of rotation.
optionB: Helix angle is the angle between the actual path of the propeller and the propeller axis.
optionC: Angle of attack is the angle between the blade chord line and the propeller vertical plane.
optionD: Geometric pitch is the actual distance a propeller would advance in one revolution.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
The blade angle, sometimes called the pitch angle, is the angle subtended between the plane of rotation and the chord line of the propeller blade, which may be fixed or variable. When the airplane is moving it comprises two parts, the angle of attack and the helix angle, but when it is stationary the blade angle is equal to the angle of attack.
It is usually referenced at 75% of the blade radius measured from the center of the shaft.
A small blade angle is called “fine pitch”.
A large blade angle is called “coarse pitch”.

title:
Which statement about an aeroplane leaving ground effect is correct?

I. The downwash angle increases.
II. The induced angle of attack decreases.
optionA: I is incorrect, II is correct.
optionB: I is correct, II is correct.
optionC: I is correct, II is incorrect.
optionD: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
explanationTotal:
For a fixed wing aircraft, ground effect is the increased lift and decreased drag that the wings generate when they are close to the ground.Upon landing, ground effect can give the effect of floating.The stall speed may be temporarily reduced due to ground effect.

Ground effect is effective from the ground to approximately half the aircraft’s wingspan above ground.The effect is caused by the ground interrupting the wingtip vortices, decreasing the downwash angle.Below the airfoil, a higher pressure than if an airfoil travels at higher altitude is created, as the air below the airfoil is trapped in between the wing and the ground.This means that the aircraft needs a lower angle of attack for a certain amount of lift.This results in lower induced drag (decreasing induced angle of attack).

title: How is adverse yaw compensated for during entry into and roll out from a turn?
optionA: Horn balanced controls.
optionB: Differential aileron deflection.
optionC: Servo tabs.
optionD: Anti-balanced rudder control.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Adverse yaw is a yawing motion opposite to the turning/rolling motion of the aircraft. Adverse yaw is caused by the drag on the down-going aileron being greater than that on the up-going aileron. This imbalance in drag causes the yawing motion around the normal/vertical axis. Since this yaw is adverse (i.e., in a banked turn to the left, the yaw is to the right), it is opposing the turn, which is detrimental to the aircraft's performance. Adverse (aileron) yaw is corrected in the design by the use of either differential ailerons or Frise ailerons.

The differential aileron deflection system ensures that the drag generated by both ailerons when rolling into or out of a turn is equal, thus eliminating adverse yaw. This is achieved by constructing the aileron system such that the angular deflection of the upgoing aileron is always proportionately greater than the deflection of the down going aileron.

title: Increasing the aspect ratio of a wing:
optionA: decreases gust load.
optionB: increases stall speed.
optionC: increases induced drag.
optionD: decreases induced drag.
explanationTotal:
Wing tip vortices increase if we increase induced drag.This can be caused by for example increased speed, density or lift coefficient.If we increase Angle of Attack, lift will be increased, also increasing the strength of wing tip vortices.

Another factor increasing wing tip vortices is the aspect ratio (λ) of the wing.This is the ratio of the wing span to its mean chord.The aspect ratio of the wing is equal to the square of the wingspan divided by the wing surface area.
