Therefore a short but wide wing has a low aspect ratio but a long, narrow wing has a high aspect ratio.With a lower aspect ratio, the induced drag is higher, thus increasing wing tip vortices.With a high aspect ratio, the induced drag is lower, reducing wing tip vortices.We can therefore state that the relationship between wing tip vortices and aspect ratio is inversely proportional.

title: The limiting load factor of an aircraft is based on its...
optionA: maximum design mass.
optionB: minimum design mass.
optionC: minimum flight mass.
optionD: maximum landing mass.
explanationTotal:
The regulations require transport aircraft to be designed to meet specified acceleration and gust limits and require maximum design speeds (VNE, VNO, MMO, VMO, etc.) to be defined so that any upset that occurs does not lead to acceleration to a point where the aircraft's structure fails.

These speed limitations are normally set to prevent them from suffering structural damage due to high air loads and to avoid handling difficulties created by the trim changes they sometimes create at higher speeds.

A manoeuvre load diagram displays the load factor limitations and speed limitations together and indicates the combinations of these where we can fly.

The "g" limits laid down by the regulations in CS 25 are +2.5g and -1g at maximum design mass for transport aircraft flying with flaps up. Sometimes these are also referred to as the "Limit Load Factor".

Exceeding these limits might cause some permanent deformation of the airframe.

With the term "design" we mean the figures used during the design process and the aircraft has to meet those design requirements. Once the aircraft is released for operation, flight manuals use authorised figures, which may be equal to but do not exceed the "design" figures.

title: Compared with the low subsonic regime, in the high subsonic regime the streamlines ahead of the wing change direction...
optionA: further from the leading edge, resulting in a reduced Mach number for the high-speed stall.
optionB: at the same distance from the leading edge but are closer together above the wing due to compressibility.
optionC: closer to the leading edge, resulting in an increased indicated stall speed.
optionD: further from the leading edge, resulting in an increased Mach number for the low-speed stall.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
As an aircraft flies faster, the streamline pattern around the wing changes. Faster than about four tenths the speed of sound (M 0.4) these changes start to become significant. This phenomenon is known as compressibility.

Figure 1 shows that at low speed, the streamline pattern is affected far ahead of the wing and the air has a certain distance in which to upwash. As speed increases, the wing gets closer to its leading pressure wave, and the streamline pattern is affected a shorter distance ahead so must approach the wing at a steeper angle.

This change in the streamline pattern accentuates the adverse pressure gradient near the leading edge and flow separation occurs at a reduced angle of attack. Above M0.4 CLMAX decreases as seen in figure 2.

The stall speed is defined by:

VS=√((2∗W)/(ρ∗S∗CLMAX))

At the stalling angle CLMAX and S are constant, and the indicated airspeed is given by the dynamic pressure 1/2ρV2 . Therefore, for the same airplane mass and configuration in straight and level flight, if the slight difference between EAS and IAS caused by compressibility is ignored, an airplane will stall at the same IAS at all altitudes.

If, however, compressibility is not ignored then the stalling IAS value slowly increases with increased altitude, but the change only becomes significant at very high altitudes.

At a constant EAS, Mach number will increase as altitude increases.

Figure 3 shows the variation of stalling speed with altitude at constant load factor (n). Such a curve is called the stalling boundary for the given load factor, in which altitude is plotted against equivalent airspeed.

At this load factor (1g), the aircraft cannot fly at speeds to the left of this boundary. Over the lower range of altitude, stall speed does not vary with altitude. This is because at these low altitudes, the Mach number at VS is too low for compressibility effects to be present. Eventually (approximately 30000 ft), Mach number at VS has increased with altitude to such an extent that these effects are important, and the rise in stalling speed with altitude is apparent.

As altitude increases, stall speed is initially constant then increases, due to compressibility.

title:
Refer to figure.
At a mass of 140 tons:
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: the buffet free range in a level 30 degree bank turn at FL360 is from approximately M = 0.74 to M = 0.84.
optionB: buffet free flight at 1 g at FL410 is possible.
optionC: at FL410 buffet free flight is possible at M = 0.80 only.
optionD: the buffet free range in 1 g flight at FL400 is from approximately M = 0.76 to M = 0.835.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
In the same way that separated airflow prior to a low speed stall can cause airframe buffet, shock induced separation (shock stall) at high speed can also cause buffeting.

Aerodynamic buffet is a valuable stall warning, but it can damage the aircraft structure. Because of the higher dynamic pressure when an aircraft is operating in the transonic speed region, any shock induced buffet will have a greater potential for severe airframe damage.

High speed buffet must be completely avoided. The aircraft must therefore be operated in such a manner that a (safety) margin exists before aerodynamic buffet will occur.
If the variables which affect both high speed and low speed stall are considered it will be possible to identify the conditions under which buffeting will occur and a chart can be drawn to show all the factors involved.

This is called a ‘Buffet Onset’ chart which is used by flight crews to ensure their aircraft is always operated with a specified minimum buffet margin.

In this exercise:

  • Start by drawing a line from de 30° bank that intersects the 140-ton curve.
  • From here, draw a straight line from right to left that intersects the FL360 curve.
  • The goal is to have to intersection points, which correspond to the lowest and highest limits of the buffet boundaries. In this case, the low speed boundary is M0.74 and the high-speed boundary is M 0.84.

title:
Which of these statements about a steady subsonic flow are correct or incorrect?

1. The static pressure does not change as the streamlines diverge.
2. The velocity decreases as the streamlines diverge.
optionA: 1 is correct, 2 is incorrect.
optionB: 1 is incorrect, 2 is correct.
optionC: 1 is incorrect, 2 is incorrect.
optionD: 1 is correct, 2 is correct.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
To understand the venturi effect, we must first introduce two conditions: The conservation of mass (Continuity Equation) and the Conservation of Energy (Bernoulli’s Theorem).

Conservation of Mass (Continuity Equation)

The mass of air entering the pipe, in each unit of time, equals the mass of air leaving the pipe, in the same unit of time. The mass flow through the pipe must remain constant.

The mass air flow 'm' is the product of the density, the area and the velocity:

m = ρ * A * V

Continuity equation:

m1 = m2 = m3 = ρ1 * A1 * V1 = ρ2 * A2 * V2 = ρ3 * A3 * V3 = constant

The continuity equation explains the relationship between velocity and cross-sectional area: The speed is inversely proportional to the cross-sectional area.

Conservation of Energy (Bernoulli’s Theorem)

The total energy of an airstream comes in two forms: potential energy (static pressure) and kinetic energy (dynamic pressure).
The total pressure of the airstream is the sum of the static pressure and the dynamic pressure and must remain constant, according to the law of conservation of energy.
Thus, an increase in one form of pressure, must result in a decrease in the other.

Dynamic pressure (q) is expressed by:

q = 1 / 2 * ρ * V2

Assuming the total pressure to be constant, the static pressure and the dynamic pressure vary inversely: If one increases the other decreases and vice-versa.
As an airfoil (wing) moves through the air, varying changes in velocity occur on its surfaces. Air particles move around it in specific trajectories. These trajectories are called streamlines.
Diverging streamlines mean a decrease in airspeed.
Converging streamlines imply an increase in airspeed.

In Conclusion:

With an increase in section area (from station 2 to station 3), flow speed decreases, decreasing dynamic pressure (streamlines diverge). If dynamic pressure decreases, static pressure increases. Statement 1 is therefore incorrect.

With an increase in section area (from station 2 to station 3), flow speed decreases, decreasing dynamic pressure (streamlines diverge). Statement 2 is therefore correct.

title:
The following conditions have an adverse effect on control in asymmetric flight:

1. Low altitude
2. High air density
3. High temperature
4. Low temperature
explanationTotal:
FACTORS AFFECTING CONTROLLABILITY

One of the factors which affect controllability is the power output of live engine. As the force giving the yaw is proportional to the thrust on the live engine, more rudder is required to maintain directional control as the thrust is increased for a given IAS. Therefore, the higher the thrust from the live engine, the greater are the yawing moments in asymmetric flight.

We can then conclude that factors which increase thrust will have an adverse effect on control in asymmetric flight.

Thrust is dependent on the density of air. A greater density means a greater mass, and a greater mass means a greater force. Thus, the amount of thrust generated must increase when the fluid density increases. Low altitude and low temperatures increase air density, which increases engine thrust.

title: Whilst setting up for landing, the crew are distracted by an external event on the radio. In doing so, they forget to set the final stage of flaps. The aircraft system automatically adjusts the approach speed for the reduced flap setting, but does not notify the pilots, so they land with a lower flap setting (less flaps) than planned and computed. The landing distance will (1) _____ due to (2) _____ being generated by the lower flap setting, which requires a (3) _____ touchdown speed.
optionA: (1) increase; (2) less lift; (3) higher
optionB: (1) increase; (2) more drag; (3) higher
optionC: (1) decrease; (2) more lift; (3) lower
optionD: (1) decrease; (2) less drag; (3) lower
explanationTotal:
Learning Objective 081.01.09.01.09: Explain the effects of flap-setting errors, such as mis-selection and premature/late extension or retraction of flaps, on: take-off and landing distance and speeds; climb and descent performance; stall buffet margins.

This scenario is effectively asking what happens if we land with less flaps. Well of course, with less flaps, our stall speed will be higher, as flaps increase the camber (and sometimes area) of the wing, allowing an aircraft to fly slower with the same amount of lift.

With a higher stall speed, the approach speed VREF will be higher, the aircraft will touch down with more groundspeed, causing a longer landing distance than if a higher flap setting were to be used.

So that is (1) and (3) answered, and we must remember that with a lower flap setting we have less lift available for the same IAS, and lower drag. The component that influences our landing distance is the lift, though, as the lack of lift means we have to fly at a higher speed, and land at a higher speed. The extra drag from more flaps would not really reduce our landing distance, as all the braking action during landing comes from the brakes (and reverse thrust, if available), and the flaps actually reduce the weight of the aircraft on the wheels, so reduce braking ability slightly.

title:
Given:

Aeroplane mass: 50000 kg.
Lift/Drag ratio: 10.
Thrust per engine: 60000 N.
Assumed g: 10 m/s²

For a straight, steady, wings level climb of a twin engine aeroplane, the all-engines climb gradient is:
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Consider an aircraft in a straight steady climb along a straight flight path inclined at an angle (γ) to the horizontal. γ (gamma) is the symbol used for climb angle. The forces on the aircraft consist of Lift, normal to the flight path; Thrust and Drag, parallel to it; and Weight, parallel to the force of gravity.
Weight is resolved into two components: one opposite Lift (W cos γ) and the other acting in the same direction as Drag (W sin γ), backwards along the flight path. The requirements for equilibrium are: Thrust must equal the sum of Drag plus the backwards component of Weight; and Lift must equal its opposing component of Weight. For equilibrium at a greater angle of climb, the Lift required will be less, and the backwards component of Weight will be greater.

L = W cos γ
T = D + W sin γ

In a straight steady climb, Lift is less than Weight because Lift only has to support a proportion of the weight, this proportion decreasing as the climb angle increases. The remaining proportion of Weight is supported by engine Thrust.
It can be seen that for a straight steady climb the Thrust required is greater than Drag. This is to balance the backward component of Weight acting along the flight path.

The climb gradient can be described as:

sin γ = (T−D)/W

For very shallow flight path angles (γ), we can assume that lift is approximately equal to Weight, therefore the climb gradient can be described as:

sin γ = (T/W)−(D/L)

In this exercise, Weight is equal to 500000 N, D/L ratio is equal to 1/10 and Thrust equal to 60000 N per engine.

For the all engines (two) climb gradient and applying the formula defined above:

sin γ = (120000/500000) − (1/10)
sin γ = 0.14 ⇒ sinγ = 14%

The climb gradient is 14%.

title: Consider a modern large aeroplane fitted with a Fly-By-Wire (FBW) system. Following a failure, the Flight Control System Control Laws fall one level to the first level of degradation. What would be one of the most noticeable consequences?
optionA: The autopilot is NOT available, but all protections remain in place.
optionB: The autopilot may or may not be available, depending on the specific failure.
optionC: The autopilot is required to remain available according to airworthiness regulations but, depending on the specific failure, some protections may be lost.
optionD: A reversion to the mechanical back-up mode.
explanationTotal:
A Fly-By-Wire (FBW) system uses computers to process the pilot's/autopilot's flight control inputs and send corresponding electrical signals to the flight control surfaces' actuators.

Currently, it is generally accepted there are four levels of service employed within Fly-By-Wire systems; in descending order they are:

  • Under Normal Control Law, normal operation, the computers ensure that flight manoeuvre envelope limits are not exceeded.
  • Under Alternate Control Law, entered into after certain computer failures, the aircraft should handle almost exactly as in Normal control, but some protection features will be lost, including the possibility of losing autopilot function, dependent on the specific failures.
  • In Direct Control Law, all protections are lost and flying control input is translated directly into movement of the control surfaces without calculation or correction.
  • The final degradation is Mechanical back-up. The aircraft is flown in pitch through use of the pitch trim wheel and roll by a mechanical connection retained to the rudder pedals (through the secondary effect of yaw). It is designed to allow the pilots to maintain control of the aircraft, while restoring flight control computers, after a complete power interruption. In the event of computer failure on a FBW aircraft, some form of back-up mode is required in the event of total computer failure.
For this question, the statement "to the first level of degradation", means degradation to the "Alternate Law", where some protections may be lost.

title: What could happen as a consequence of climbing to a higher level using the autopilot "Vertical Speed" (V/S) mode?
optionA: Decreasing airspeed and the aeroplane may stall.
optionB: Increasing airspeed and the aeroplane may stall.
optionC: Increased risk of super stall.
optionD: Use of V<sub>S</sub> mode is not permitted in the climb.
explanationTotal:
Vertical Speed is an autopilot flight guidance vertical mode. In this mode, the Flight Management and Guidance Computer (FMCG) pitch mode guides the aircraft to the target V/S. The corresponding thrust mode is SPEED or MACH.

The V/S guidance has priority over the speed guidance. If the selected target V/S is too high (relative to the current thrust condition and speed), the FMGC will steer the aircraft to the target V/S, but the aircraft will also accelerate or decelerate.

As altitude increases and the air gets thinner, the IAS will reduce for a given pitch setting. Consequently, the angle of attack also reduces. As a result, the vertical speed will reduce for a certain pitch attitude. The autopilot will therefore chase the selected vertical speed by pitching up. This results in further decreased IAS. Ultimately, this could lead to a stall.

title: The total drag of an aerofoil in two dimensional flow comprises:
optionA: induced drag and form drag.
optionB: interference drag and skin friction drag.
optionC: skin friction drag and induced drag.
optionD: pressure drag and skin friction drag.
explanationTotal:
On a wing (aerofoil), the aircraft would experience form/pressure drag and skin friction drag only. The aircraft would have interference drag.

Skin Friction Drag is drag caused by the friction of a fluid against the surface of an object that is moving through it. It is directly proportional to the area of the surface in contact with the fluid and increases with the square of the velocity.

Form drag, pressure drag or profile drag arises from the form of the object and is caused by pressure difference , i.e. the pressure is higher in front of the body than behind it.

title: V<sub>LE</sub> is defined as the:
optionA: maximum flap extended speed.
optionB: maximum speed at which the landing gear may be extended or retracted.
optionC: maximum authorised speed.
optionD: maximum landing gear extended speed.
explanationTotal:
VLE = Landing Gear Extended speed.

VLE is the maximum speed you can fly with the landing gear extended under normal operation of the aircraft.

title: A medium range jet transport aeroplane is flying straight and level when an upgust increases the load factor to 1.5 g. If the straight and level stall speed (V<sub>S</sub>) is 172 kt, what will V<sub>S</sub> be during the gust encounter?
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: 258 kt
optionB: 211 kt
optionC: 272 kt
optionD: 140 kt
explanationTotal:
The load factor is the actual lift divided by the weight, and lift is proportional to airspeed². A load factor of 1.5 describes an increase in lift to a new value of 1.5 × lift.

Therefore we can calculate this question by the following formula:

(VNEW ÷ VOLD)² = n

Where VOLD = 172kt and n = 1.5g

√n = VNEW ÷ VOLD
VNEW = √n × VOLD
VNEW = √1.5 × 172 kt
VNEW = 211 kt

The gust encounter will cause an increase in the stall speed (VS) to 211kt.

title:
A twin-engine turboprop aeroplane has an engine failure in flight. Select the correct statements with regard to the asymmetric effects of the propeller slipstream.

1. Slipstream-induced lift will be lost on the side with the failed engine.
2. A rolling moment towards the live engine will be induced.
3. Total lift will be reduced, giving a tendency to descend.
4. Use of leading edge devices can counter the effects of lost slipstream.
optionA: 3 and 4
optionB: 1 and 2
optionC: 1 and 3
optionD: 2 and 4
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Following an in-flight engine failure on a twin-engine turboprop, there are two immediate effects:

  • The initial effect is the yawing towards the dead engine that occurs due to the asymmetry of the thrust line.
  • The second effect is roll, which occurs when the airplane continues to yaw towards the failed engine, resulting in a decrease in lift from the ‘retreating’ wing and a yaw-induced roll towards the failed engine. This roll is reinforced by the offset of the wings and the loss of the slipstream lift in airplanes with the propeller in front of the engine.
The use of leading edge devices is not recommended. LE devices will increase lift on both wings. The difference in lift between the two wings will increase which will result in an even larger rolling moment. Drga will also be increases which may result in a serious lack of performance,

title: V<sub>LO</sub> is the speed at which it is safe to fly with the...
optionA: landing gear extended.
optionB: leading edge devices in transit.
optionC: landing gear in transit.
optionD: leading edge devices extended.
explanationTotal:
LANDING GEAR SPEED LIMITATIONS

The landing gear will normally be retracted as soon as possible after take-off to reduce drag and increase the climb gradient. There is no normal requirement for the gear to be operated at high IAS so the retract and extend mechanism together with the attachment points to the structure are sized for the required task.

LANDING GEAR EXTENDED SPEED - VLE

There may be occasions when it is necessary to ferry the aircraft with the gear down, and to do this a higher permissible speed would be convenient. VLE is the speed at which it is safe to fly the aircraft with the landing gear secured in the fully extended position.

LANDING GEAR OPERATING SPEED - VLO

This is the speed at which it is safe both to extend and to retract the landing gear. If the extension speed is not the same as the retraction speed, the two speeds must be designated as VLO (EXT) and VLO (RET).

When the gear is retracted or extended the doors must open first. The doors merely streamline the undercarriage bay and are not designed to take the aerodynamic loads which would be placed on them at high IAS. Consequently VLO is usually lower than VLE.

title: On which part of the propeller is the most thrust generated?
optionA: Thrust generation is uniform.
optionB: 3/4 measured from root.
optionC: At the root.
optionD: At the tip.
explanationTotal: Propeller thrust is a component at right angles to the plane of rotation. The thrust force will vary along the length of each blade. Thrust reduces at the tip where the pressures equalize and towards the root where the rotational velocity is low.

title: The difference between the effects of slat and flap asymmetry is that: ("large" in the context of this question means not or hardly controllable by normal use of controls)
optionA: flap asymmetry causes a large yawing moment whereas slat asymmetry causes a large rolling moment at any speed.
optionB: flap asymmetry causes a large rolling moment whereas slat asymmetry causes a large yawing moment.
optionC: flap asymmetry causes a large difference in C<sub>LMAX</sub> whereas slat asymmetry causes a large rolling moment at any speed.
optionD: flap asymmetry causes a large rolling moment at any speed whereas slat asymmetry causes a large difference in C<sub>LMAX</sub>.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
Flap asymmetry will give different lift on the wings that causes a large rolling moment. This will happen at any speed since flap extension changes the camber of the wing. Slat asymmetry on the other hand will only be noticeable at very high angles of attack because slats extends the lift coefficient curve. The two wings would therefore have a difference in the max. value of CL. There would be a slight difference in drag, which is leading to a yawing moment, but not enough to be termed "large".

title:
You are flying from town A to airport B with a single engine piston when you experience an engine failure. Calculate the minimum altitude at A to reach to airport B, given:

Elevation: 300 m
Distance from A to B: 60 km
L/D ratio: 30
explanationTotal:
Lift over drag (L/D) ratio determines the gliding range. The Glide ratio of an aircraft is the distance of forward travel divided by the altitude lost in that distance.

If L/D = 30 => Aircraft will fly 30 units over the ground per every unit down (assuming no wind).
Ground distance = 60 km = 60 000 m

  • Therefore, with a ground distance of 60 000 m (60 km) and L/D of 30, we get the following equation:
    1 / 30 = x / 60 000
    x = 2 000 m
  • Now, we must add the elevation of 300 m.
    Minimum altitude = 2 000 m + 300 m = 2 300 m
Note:
Altitude - The vertical distance of an object measured from mean sea level.
Height -The vertical distance of a level, a point, or an object considered as a point, measured from a specified datum.

title: During the take-off roll, when the pilot raises the tail in a tail wheeled, clockwise (seen from pilot's perspective) rotating propeller driven aeroplane , a strong left yaw is generated, forcing the pilot to apply almost full right rudder to keep the aeroplane on the centreline. Before the tail is raised, the left yaw is caused by (I) and after the tail is raised the left yaw is caused by (II).
optionA: (I) spiralling slipstream; (II) gyroscopic precession
optionB: (I) gyroscopic precession; (II) asymmetric blade effect
optionC: (I) spiralling slipstream; (II) asymmetric blade effect
optionD: (I) torque reaction; (II) asymmetric blade effect
explanationTotal:
Refer to figures.
On take-off, rotation of a single-engine propeller causes an aircraft to swing to one side, particularly those fitted with a tail-dragger undercarriage. The main causes of this are:

  • Slipstream effect
  • Torque reaction
  • Gyroscopic effect
  • Asymmetric blade effect

SLIPSTREAM EFFECT (figure 1)
The high-speed rotation of an aircraft propeller gives a corkscrew or spiralling rotation to the slipstream. At high propeller speeds and low forward speed (as in the take-offs and approaches to power-on stalls), this spiralling rotation is very compact and exerts a strong sideward force on the aircraft’s vertical tail surface.

When this spiralling slipstream strikes the vertical fin, it causes a yawing moment about the aircraft’s vertical axis. The more compact the spiral, the more prominent this force is.

As the forward speed increases, however, the spiral elongates and becomes less effective. The corkscrew flow of the slipstream also causes a rolling moment around the longitudinal axis.

GYROSCOPIC EFFECT (figure 2)
A rotating propeller has the properties of a gyroscope - rigidity in space and precession. The characteristic which produces “gyroscopic effect” is precession.

Gyroscopic precession is the reaction that occurs when a force is applied to the rim of a rotating disc. When a force is applied to the rim of a propeller, the reaction occurs 90° ahead in the direction of rotation and in the same direction as the applied force.

As the aircraft is pitched up or down or yawed left or right, a force is applied to the rim of the spinning propeller disc.

Note: Gyroscopic effect only occurs when the aircraft pitches and/or yaws.

For a clockwise rotating propeller:

Pitch down - forward force on the top, force emerges 90° clockwise, left yaw.
Left yaw - forward force on the right, force emerges 90° clockwise, pitch up.
Pitch up - forward force on the bottom, force emerges 90° clockwise, right yaw.
Right yaw - forward force on the left, force emerges 90° clockwise, pitch down.

title: What are the propeller effects which may be experienced on take-off?
optionA: Slipstream, torque, and gyroscopic effect.
optionB: Slipstream and gyroscopic effect only.
optionC: Torque and gyroscopic effect only.
optionD: Slipstream and torque effect only.
explanationTotal:
SECONDARY EFFECTS OF THE PROPELLER

Due to its rotation a propeller generates yawing, rolling and pitching moments. These are due to several different causes: Torque reaction, Gyroscopic precession, Spiral (asymmetric) slipstream effect and Asymmetric blade effect.

  • Torque reaction. A counter-clockwise rotating propeller produces a clockwise moment that must be counteracted by ailerons. During take-off this will apply a greater down load to the left wheel, causing more rolling resistance on the left wheel making the aircraft want to yaw to the left.

  • Gyroscopic precession. Propeller can also be considered a gyroscope as it is a certain mass, which is rotating. Gyroscopes want to maintain their plane of rotation. When a force is applied to the rim of a propeller, the reaction occurs 90° ahead in the direction of rotation and in the same direction as the applied force. if an aircraft with a clockwise rotating propeller is pitched nose-up, imagine that a forward force has been applied to the bottom of the propeller disc. The force will “emerge” at 90° in the direction of rotation, i.e. a right yawing moment.

  • Spiral Slipstream. As the propeller rotates it produces a backward flow of air, or slipstream, which rotates around the aircraft. This spiral slipstream causes a change in airflow around the fin (vertical stabilizer). Due to the direction of propeller rotation (clockwise) the spiral slipstream meets the fin at an angle from the left, producing a sideways force on the fin to the right.

title: The lift formula can be written as: (rho = density)
optionA: L= C<sub>L</sub> × ½ rho × V<sup>2</sup> × S
optionB: L = C<sub>L</sub> × rho × V<sup>2 </sup>× S.
optionC: L = C<sub>L</sub> × ½ rho × V × S.
optionD: L = C<sub>L</sub> × 2 rho × V<sup>2</sup> × S.
explanationTotal:
The lift formula equals:

L = CL * ½ * ρ * V2 * S
L = Lift
CL = Lift coefficient
ρ = Rho, it stands for the density
V = velocity
S = wing area

title: You are the pilot flying of a commercial jet aircraft and just started your descent by using the autopilot, which controls the speed with pitch control. Passing FL340, the aeroplane passes through a jet stream and experiences a sudden positive wind shear. The speed increases momentarily to M0.85 causing the autopilot to demand a pitch up to arrest the speed increase. Since M0.85 is approximately 5 kt faster than M<sub>MO</sub>, you may...
tags: 081-03 - Stall, Mach Tuck and Upset Prevention and Recovery
optionA: feel a slight vibration as a result of the increased positive load factor creating some buffet, due to shock waves during the overspeed.
optionB: experience a slight “Mach tuck” effect as shock waves increase in strength, leading to further speed increase and loss of speed control.
optionC: experience momentary loss of control due to incipient shock stall until the aeroplane recovers and speed reduces below M<sub>MO</sub>.
optionD: feel significant buffeting from the shock waves, which from at speeds above M<sub>MO</sub>, further enhanced by the increased load factor.
explanationTotal:
Refer to figure.
In the same way that separated airflow prior to a low speed stall can cause airframe buffet, shock induced separation (shock stall) at high speed can also cause buffeting.

Aerodynamic buffet is a valuable stall warning, but it can damage the aircraft structure. Aircraft must therefore be operated with a (safety) margin to aerodynamic buffet.

Because of the higher dynamic pressure when an aircraft is operating in the transonic speed region, any shock induced buffet will have a greater potential for severe airframe damage. High speed buffet must be completely avoided.

If the variables which affect both high speed and low speed stall are considered it will be possible to identify the conditions under which buffeting will occur and a chart can be drawn to show all the factors involved:

- Load factor.
- Mach number.
- Angle of attack.
- Pressure altitude.
- Weight.
- CG position.

Stall boundaries set a lower limit to the operating speed, according to the load factor. In the case of a high-speed aircraft, there is also an upper limit which is due to the approach of shock stall and the associated buffet which occurs if the aircraft enters the transonic speed range. The limits associated with these effects give the buffet boundaries.
